Per-pupil spending is a district's total operating spending divided by its number of students. U.S. public school funding comes from local sources (mostly property taxes), state aid, and a smaller federal share. Nationally, per-pupil spending is roughly $15,000 a year.

To compare it with the cost of a tool, convert both to the same unit. For example, $15,000 spread over a 180-day school year is about $83 per student per school day, the figure Chapter 1 uses. A Level 2 program costing $5.80 per student per year is about three cents per school day, a tiny fraction of that budget. Alpha School's tuition of $40,000 to $65,000 is roughly three to four times typical public spending.

This baseline matters because every claim about an AI-native model, whether a vendor quote or a promise of savings, should be checked against it. Chapter 2 scales it up: thirteen years of K-12 education cost the public roughly $200,000 per student.

docs.title: How much does AI tutoring cost, and why is the price falling?
docs.text:
AI inference cost is the cost of running a trained model to produce an answer, usually priced per million tokens (a token is roughly part of a word). For a fixed capability level, that cost has fallen sharply. Chapter 4 cites the Stanford AI Index 2025: GPT-3.5-level performance cost about $20 per million tokens in November 2022 and about $0.07 in October 2024, a drop of more than 280-fold.

The chapter works the arithmetic for a student who uses 20,000 tokens a day for 180 days, 3.6 million tokens a year. At the 2022 price that is $72 per student per year; at the 2024 price, about $0.25. A 12,000-student district would pay about $3,000 instead of about $864,000. The caution is that this is a GPT-3.5-level model, and a stronger tutor costs more per token. Chapter 5 notes that falling AI costs compound over time, and Chapter 7 builds the full per-level cost table.

docs.title: How does learning analytics help a teacher?
docs.text:
Learning analytics is the use of student learning data across a class or school to understand and improve teaching. It starts from mastery data: the judgments, made with a stated rule, about which concepts each student has mastered. Laid out as a grid with students as rows and concepts as columns, the data shows patterns no single score reveals.

Chapter 8 gives a simple reading rule. A dark column, where most students have not mastered one concept, points at the teaching: the lesson or MicroSim for that concept may need to change. A dark row, where one student has not mastered several concepts, points at the student, who may have a root gap or a need outside the lesson. For example, a teacher who sees that 20 of 26 students missed "doubling time" should reteach it to the whole class tomorrow, while a student whose row is dark across a whole unit needs a conversation. Analytics should inform teachers, not rank students on a public board.

docs.title: What counts as personally identifiable student data?
docs.text:
Personally identifiable data is information that can identify a student, either directly or indirectly. Direct identifiers include a name, student ID, email address, or photograph. Indirect identifiers become identifying in combination or in a small group: a birth date plus a zip code, or "the only eighth-grade girl in the robotics club." Student data privacy covers both keeping such data secure and using it only in appropriate ways.

Chapter 10 has you test fields one at a time. A student's score on one quiz, reported only as a class average, is not identifying. The same score attached to a student ID is. A report on a group of three students can identify each of them even without names, which is why many districts suppress results for very small groups. In practice, the safest Level 3 design keeps identifiers in one governed store, uses pseudonymous IDs elsewhere, and makes a data map showing every field, where it lives, and who can see it.

docs.title: What does evidence-based practice mean for a school?
docs.text:
Evidence-based practice means making decisions by combining three things: the best available research, professional judgment, and local context. It is not the same as "doing whatever a study says." A strategy that worked in a large urban district may not fit a small rural school, and a teacher's knowledge of particular students still matters.

The levels of evidence rank the design of a study, not the size of its claim. A randomized controlled trial ranks higher than a comparison of volunteers, which ranks higher than testimonials. Chapter 2 opens with a vendor brochure claiming large gains for a math product. The questions it teaches are "compared with whom, chosen how, measured by whom?" For example, a brochure reporting that students who used the product scored higher than those who did not, with no word on how students were chosen, may only show that motivated students chose to use it. Chapter 3 adds that an independent evaluation carries more weight than self-reported results.

docs.title: Why do so many technology reforms in schools fail?
docs.text:
Chapter 23 finds four recurring reasons: technology came before pedagogy, the existing culture absorbed the change, trust was not built, and hype outran evidence. The failures mostly show planning, trust, culture, and procurement failing, not the technology itself, which repeats a century-long pattern in the history of educational technology.

The cases make each pattern concrete. The Los Angeles iPad rollout (2013) began a $1.3 billion plan to give every student an iPad with Pearson curriculum and was cancelled amid technical problems, weak curriculum, and a contract scandal: devices before a teaching plan. AltSchool raised more than $170 million and closed its schools without building a lasting culture. Summit Learning met student walkouts in Brooklyn and family protests in Kansas over long screen hours and too little teacher contact. inBloom lost family trust. Each failure points to a practice that would have caught it, such as a teaching plan before devices, a procurement check, or listening to students.

docs.title: What went wrong with the Los Angeles "Ed" chatbot?
docs.text:
In 2024 Los Angeles Unified committed about $6 million to the startup AllHere for an AI chatbot called "Ed" and spent about $3 million of it. The company collapsed within months of launch. In November 2024 its founder was charged with defrauding investors of nearly $10 million.

The lesson is about procurement, not chatbots. The district bought quickly, depended on a single unproven vendor, and sent student data to a company it had not checked well. Chapter 20 and Chapter 21 answer it with procurement criteria: a weighted vendor scorecard with knockout rules, contract due diligence on data use, breach notice, deletion, portability, price, and term, and a requirement that the product's level be verified with a product level assessment rather than taken from the vendor's own claim.

docs.title: Should schools use AI cheating detectors?
docs.text:
The book says no, or at least not as the main response. A 2023 Stanford study by Liang and colleagues found that popular AI-writing detectors often wrongly flagged essays by non-native English writers as AI-generated. Detectors produce false positives, and the false positives fall unevenly, which creates an equity problem.

Chapter 20 works the arithmetic. Even a detector that sounds accurate can produce many false accusations when most students are honest: in the chapter's illustration, about two in five flags are false. Each false flag is a student accused of something they did not do. The book's answer is redesign, not policing: assignments with drafts and in-class work, oral defenses, performance and portfolio assessment, and clear rules about when AI use is allowed. Writing, debate, and making things also move into the afternoon, where they happen in front of people.

docs.title: How do I know if an AI tutor is helping or hurting learning?
docs.text:
Check its design against the five guardrails in Chapter 12, starting with the essential one: does it give hints instead of answers? A quick test is to ask it directly for the answer to a homework problem. A helpful tutor responds with a question or a small hint; a harmful one gives the full solution.

Then watch for signs of over-reliance in students: asking for answers before trying, accepting output without checking it, and being unable to do the task without the tool. The Turkish study's pattern is the warning sign: practice scores rise while performance without the tool falls. The fairest evidence comes from comparing exam results taken without AI between students who used the tutor and students who did not. Also check the tutor for confidently wrong answers, especially in math, and for sycophancy, where it agrees with a student's mistaken reasoning to be pleasant.

docs.title: Isn't more screen time bad for students?
docs.text:
It can be, and the book takes the concern seriously. Summit Learning is its clearest cautionary case: students walked out in Brooklyn and families protested in Kansas over long hours on screens and too little teacher contact. That is one reason the model insists the AI morning stays short and the afternoon is with other people.

The book also argues that screen time depends on what students do, not only how long. An hour of adaptive practice with immediate feedback, which keeps student engagement high, differs from an hour of passive video. Chapter 12 recommends morning screen-time limits: cap the total, take a break every 25 to 30 minutes, and protect time for students' own questions. Chapter 20 gives the youngest students the least screen time. For a family, the useful question is how the whole day adds up, which in the morning-afternoon model can include less screen time than a traditional day plus homework on a laptop.

docs.title: Will AI replace teachers?
docs.text:
The book's answer is that the role changes and the need for adults does not shrink. In the 280-student school in Chapter 20, the redesigned day needed about 10 percent more adult-hours than before, because afternoon ensembles, teams, and projects need trained adults. What changes is what those adults do: less whole-class lecturing, more coaching, mentoring, and facilitating.

The book does not dismiss the fear. Chapter 19 treats fear of job loss as a legitimate concern that needs an honest answer, not a slogan. Roles such as afternoon specialist staff will be new, some teachers will need different skills, and unions should be engaged early. The positive example is Tutor CoPilot, in which AI gave human tutors live suggestions during sessions; student mastery improved and the weakest tutors improved most. AI that makes teachers better is the model the book recommends.

docs.title: What should I do when teachers resist the change?
docs.text:
Treat resistance as information. Chapter 19 identifies sources of resistance and separates legitimate concerns, which deserve a real response, from habit or fear that needs patience. A teacher who says "the software's reading passages are too hard for my English learners" may be right and has handed you a problem to fix.

Respond with empathy before information. A teacher at a personal stage of concern, worried about their job or competence, will not hear a data presentation until the worry is acknowledged. Then match the move to the person. Use CBAM to identify the stage of concern, and the adopter category to choose the messenger: a late-majority skeptic is more likely to be moved by a respected colleague's results in a pilot classroom than by an enthusiastic leader. Chapter 17 adds that early questions are self concerns, not resistance, and need direct answers.

docs.title: What is the implementation dip, and should it worry me?
docs.text:
The implementation dip is a temporary fall in performance as people learn a new practice. Teachers using a new morning model for the first time are slower and less skilled than they were with the old one, and early results often drop before they rise. Michael Fullan's research on educational change describes the dip as normal.

Chapter 16 gives two ways to read it. A normal dip bottoms early and recovers within a term or two. A dip that keeps falling is a sign something in the design is wrong. The absence of any dip can mean the change is shallow, that people are using the new tool the old way. The book recommends managing expectations by telling families and the board in advance what the dip will look like, which turns it from a surprise into part of the plan and protects trust.

docs.title: Why might a successful pilot not scale?
docs.text:
A pilot classroom usually has advantages the rest of the school does not: a volunteer teacher who is an early adopter, extra attention, and close support. When the program expands to the early and late majority, those advantages disappear, which is the chasm in Chapter 15.

Capacity is the other limit. Chapter 21 shows that coach capacity sets the speed of scale-up: at 12 teachers per coach, 40, 150, and 400 teachers need about 4, 13, and 34 coaches. A district that expands faster than it can coach will see results fall. A systems view adds a balancing loop: more teachers starting means less coaching per teacher. The practical answer is to scale in stages paced by coaching capacity, with a written decision rule for each stage.

docs.title: How can an AI-native model widen achievement gaps?
docs.text:
If every group improves but advantaged students improve faster, averages rise while the gap widens. Chapter 21 works an example of exactly this, and recommends checking whether a program is closing or widening gaps by measuring the gap itself, not only the average.

There are several ways the model can widen gaps. Students without reliable home devices or internet fall behind on any work assigned outside school. Self-paced software rewards students who already manage their own learning. Detectors and adaptive systems can carry algorithmic bias against English language learners. Paid afternoon programs exclude families who cannot pay. And the private version of the model, at $40,000 to $65,000 tuition, is out of reach for most families. Equity of access in Chapter 20 means devices, accessibility, language support, a free afternoon, and partnerships that serve every neighborhood.

docs.title: How do I evaluate a vendor's results claim?
docs.text:
Use the six questions from Chapter 23:

  1. Where did students start?
  2. Compared with whom?
  3. Who measured it?
  4. Has anyone independent checked it?
  5. How big was the effect, and how long did it last?
  6. What exactly was measured?

Unbound Academy shows why. It claims students learn 2.8 times faster on its own growth tests, while a board slideshow reportedly showed 10 percent proficiency in math and 28 percent in English Language Arts, below state averages. Without knowing where students started, neither number tells you how much they grew. A claim measured by the vendor on its own test, with no comparison group and no independent check, is a lead, not evidence. Chapter 3 adds that a preprint is a lead until peer review, and an independent evaluation carries more weight than self-reported results.

docs.title: Why are textbook publishers being disrupted, and what still has value?
docs.text:
A textbook publisher's costs are mostly up-front: authors, editors, artwork, reviews, and permissions. The publisher business model recovered those costs by selling many copies at a high textbook price and revising every few years so used copies lost value. AI-generated content breaks that model by driving falling production cost. In Chapter 7's illustration, a chapter that cost about $4,000 to produce costs about $1,120 with AI assistance, provided the human review stays.

When content becomes cheap to make and nearly free to copy, content commoditization pushes its price toward cost. That is publisher disruption. What remains valuable is everything around the content: trust, assessment, integration, training, support, and data protection. The chapter breaks down a $900,000 publisher proposal for a 12,000-student district: only $240,000 is the textbook license, while the rest pays for an adaptive platform, an assessment bank and dashboard, training, and support. A district comparing that proposal with free open content should ask which of those services it actually needs, and what each costs on its own.

docs.title: How do I classify an AI product's level?
docs.text:
Use the four-step product level assessment in Chapter 6: gather documentation and a demonstration, test what the product does for students rather than what the brochure says, identify the highest defining capability it delivers, and record what student data it needs at that level. The checklist asks, in order:

  1. Does it do anything but show fixed content? If not, Level 1.
  2. Does it respond to the learner's actions on the page? At least Level 2.
  3. Does it keep a record of each student and change what it shows from that record? At least Level 3.
  4. Can a student hold an open conversation with it about the material? At least Level 4.
  5. Does it generate the content itself, for each student, in real time? Level 5.

For example, a product sold as "AI-powered personalized learning" that turns out to be quizzes with feedback and no stored records is Level 2. A vendor's own level claim is a self-report to test, not reject.

docs.title: How should a school start with intelligent textbooks?
docs.text:
Start at Level 2. Interactive textbooks with MicroSims, self-check quizzes, and learning graphs deliver much of the benefit, cost very little, need no student records, and can run offline. Adopting open Level 2 content is one of the book's no-regret moves: it pays off whether or not the AI forecast holds.

Move to Level 3 only when the school is ready to govern student data. Chapter 10 gives a governance-readiness check: data minimization, informed consent, a retention policy, clear data ownership, vendor contracts, and a plan for breaches. Add Level 4 chatbot tutoring selectively, where it adds real value, with hint-first guardrails. For example, a middle school might begin with an open Level 2 math textbook in one grade, add a Learning Record Store the following year after the board adopts a retention policy, and pilot a guided chat tutor for one unit after that.

docs.title: How do I design a good pro-social afternoon activity?
docs.text:
Check it against two tests from Chapter 14. The four-feature test asks whether the activity needs other people, has a shared goal, has a real audience or stakes, and ends with reflection. The SAFE check asks whether it is sequenced, active, focused on a personal or social skill, and explicit about its goals.

For example, a ten-week ensemble passes both. Students depend on each other, share the goal of a concert, perform for families, and debrief after each rehearsal; the rehearsals build in sequence and name the listening skills being practiced. An open gym where students choose what to do with no adult goals fails both and is the drift the book warns about. Start small: the chapter's ten-week launch plan begins with three activities chosen from student and family surveys, trains adults in SAFE practices and a three-minute debrief, and pilots one block a week before expanding.

docs.title: What makes project-based learning work?
docs.text:
Chapter 14 describes seven essential elements of project-based learning and singles out two as the most important: a driving question and a public exhibition. A driving question is open, important to students, and cannot be answered by a quick search: "How can we cut the food our cafeteria throws away by half?" rather than "What is food waste?" A public exhibition gives the work a real audience and real stakes.

High Tech High in San Diego is the book's model: students work in teams on real projects and present them at public exhibitions. Finland's phenomenon-based learning applies a similar idea across subjects, with students studying a real-world topic such as climate or migration through science, math, and language together. Projects also need structure inside the team: shared goals, rotating roles, and individual accountability, so the work does not fall on one student. Chapter 13 gives worked examples of each.

docs.title: How should a school plan and run a pilot?
docs.text:
Write the rules before the pilot starts. Chapter 20 and Chapter 21 recommend:

  • A school readiness assessment before the pilot begins.
  • Written pilot goals and a balanced set of success measures, chosen in advance, covering academics, engagement, well-being, equity, and cost.
  • Pilot governance that names who decides and what would stop the pilot.
  • A decision rule that says what results mean expand, revise, or end.
  • A comparison group, ideally through delayed access, and independent evaluation where possible.

The pilot risk checklist in Chapter 22 adds one line per known risk, such as screen time, offloading, wrong answers, privacy, equity, job fears, and afternoon drift, with a response for each. For example, a pilot plan with strong academic measures but no measure of afternoon quality has a gap the checklist will catch.

docs.title: What should be in an AI vendor contract?
docs.text:
Chapter 21 lists the clauses that protect students under contract due diligence: how student data may be used (never for advertising, and never shared with unnamed third parties), breach notification within a set time, deletion at the end of the contract, data portability in a standard format, price and price increases, contract term, and what happens when the vendor changes the underlying AI model.

The chapter's rule is that two red flags end the conversation. A vendor that claims ownership of student data, refuses deletion, or will not say where data is stored is not one to negotiate with. To avoid vendor lock-in, require open standards and data export, keep terms short, and keep an open Level 2 fallback so the school can leave if it must. The Los Angeles "Ed" chatbot case shows what can happen without these checks.

docs.title: How should a school communicate with families about the change?
docs.text:
Communicate before rumors spread. Chapter 19 recommends a communication calendar that starts before any decision is announced, with family nights, plain-language handouts, and chances to try the tools. Families who first hear about a change through social media fill the gap with their own worst guesses.

Be specific and honest. Say what students will do in the morning and the afternoon, how much screen time is involved, what data is collected, where it is stored, and who can see it. Say in advance what the implementation dip may look like. Invite questions you cannot yet answer. inBloom's closure is the cautionary example: it failed because families were not part of the decision. Chapter 10 puts the principle simply: build trust by collecting little, saying what you hold, and acting consistently.

docs.title: How should assessment change in an AI-native school?
docs.text:
Redesign assessment rather than police it. Chapter 20 recommends combining three kinds:

  • Mastery-based assessment from the morning, where the Learning Record Store shows which concepts each student has mastered.
  • Performance assessment, where students show a skill by doing it, such as presenting, debating, or building.
  • Portfolio assessment, a collection of work over time showing growth.

Each needs checks for reliability. Chapter 21 gives a teamwork rubric scored by two raters, so afternoon work can be assessed fairly. This approach also answers the cheating problem better than detectors, because a student explaining a design to a panel or revising a draft in class is showing their own thinking. A student's record then shows both what they mastered in the morning and what they built and contributed in the afternoon.

docs.title: How should a district choose a change model?
docs.text:
Match the model to the question. Chapter 16 treats the models as tools for different jobs, not rivals:

  • Kotter for an ordered leadership plan.
  • Lewin for the three broad phases and force field analysis.
  • ADKAR to diagnose one person's missing element.
  • Bridges for the feelings of loss.
  • Schein to read the culture.
  • Senge to build a learning organization.
  • Fullan for the specifics of schools, including the implementation dip and coherence.
  • CBAM to track each teacher's concerns and use.

Chapter 18 adds that the choice depends on size, culture, history, and time. A small school with high trust might need only Lewin's phases and CBAM. A large district with a history of failed initiatives and change fatigue needs Fullan's coherence framework, fewer connected priorities, and serious capacity building.

docs.title: What can we learn from Estonia's AI Leap?
docs.text:
Estonia's AI Leap (TI-Hüpe), launched in 2025, is a national program giving secondary students and teachers access to AI learning tools along with teacher training. It builds on the country's earlier success bringing computers into schools. The book uses it as the example of a whole system adopting AI on purpose: with a plan, training, and public support.

The lesson for districts is coherence. Estonia paired access with training, and built on prior trust and capacity rather than starting cold. Chapter 18 contrasts it with a rapid national mandate in South Korea that, as reported, met resistance. A district can apply the same lessons at its own scale: connect the AI initiative to existing priorities rather than adding it on top, train teachers before students arrive, and build public understanding before rollout. See also Chapter 15.

docs.title: How do I write a school board recommendation for an AI-native pilot?
docs.text:
Chapter 23 gives a one-page outline. A strong recommendation states:

  1. The ask: exactly what the board is asked to approve, such as a one-year pilot in two grade-6 classes.
  2. The case: the problem the pilot addresses.
  3. The evidence, with its level: what is known from randomized trials, what is self-reported, and what is unknown.
  4. The risks and responses: one line per risk, from the pilot risk checklist.
  5. The equity analysis: who could be helped or left out, and how gaps will be measured.
  6. The cost: including devices, staffing, and training, not just software.
  7. The decision rule: what results will lead to expansion, revision, or ending.

A recommendation that names both sides is more persuasive to a careful board than one that only promises gains. Stating the decision rule in advance also protects the board from being asked to judge the pilot by mood rather than evidence.

docs.title: How do bright spots help lead change?
docs.text:
A bright spot is a person or group already succeeding at something within the system, despite the same constraints as everyone else. Positive deviance is the practice of finding those exceptions and spreading what they do. Both come from the Switch framework in Chapter 19, which describes change as directing the rider (the rational mind), motivating the elephant (emotion), and shaping the path (the environment).

Bright spots work because they are proof from inside. For example, if one fifth-grade teacher's students already make strong gains with self-paced practice, other teachers can watch that class, learn the specific moves the teacher makes, and see that it works with students like theirs. That is more persuasive than a vendor's case study from another state. It also respects teachers' expertise, since the solution comes from a colleague rather than from outside.

docs.title: How should formative assessment, spaced practice, and retrieval practice fit an adaptive morning?
docs.text:
These three practices from Chapter 1 are what turn a morning of screen time into lasting learning, so an adaptive textbook should build them in.

  • Formative assessment uses evidence during learning to change what happens next. In an adaptive textbook, every self-check question is formative: a wrong answer triggers a hint, a different explanation, or a prerequisite review.
  • Spaced practice spreads review over days and weeks instead of cramming it into one session.
  • Retrieval practice asks students to recall what they learned, rather than reread it, which strengthens memory.

For example, after a student masters a concept on Monday, a well-designed textbook brings back two or three short recall questions on it the following Monday and again a month later, mixed in with new work. If the student misses them, the concept is marked for review rather than left as "mastered." When choosing a product, ask whether its mastery rule ever looks back, or whether a concept passed once stays passed forever. Teachers can apply the same idea in the afternoon by having teams explain earlier concepts from memory as part of a project.

docs.title: How do I build social-emotional learning into afternoon projects?
docs.text:
Social-emotional learning (SEL) covers self-awareness, empathy, perspective taking, relationship skills, and belonging. Chapter 13 finds that these skills are best taught inside real projects rather than in separate lessons, because a real project creates real moments that need them: a disagreement, a teammate who falls behind, an audience to understand.

Build them in with structure. Assign team roles that rotate, so every student practices leading, recording, and checking. Teach communication skills such as active listening: paraphrase what a teammate said, ask a clarifying question, and reflect the feeling. Teach conflict resolution by looking at interests rather than positions. End each session with a short reflection naming one thing that went well and one to change. For example, a team building a community garden might hold a mid-project check-in where each member says what they need from the others. That is perspective taking and relationship skills in practice, tied to a goal everyone cares about. When a team stalls, ask the structure questions first: is the goal shared, are the roles clear, and is each member accountable?

docs.title: How would I design an AI-native day for elementary, middle, and high school?
docs.text:
The model changes by grade band. Chapter 21 describes an elementary school model, a middle school model, and a high school model, and Chapter 20 works a full middle school day.

The elementary school model keeps one home-room teacher with a class for most of the day, for a stable relationship. The morning is short, mostly teacher-led and hands-on, with a brief adaptive block for reading and number practice; the afternoon is play, movement, music, stories, and projects. The middle school model adds an advisory teacher who follows a student for several years, an adaptive morning of about 150 minutes with breaks every 25 to 30 minutes, and afternoon projects with public exhibitions. The high school model builds around credits: a morning that mixes adaptive work with seminars and labs, and an afternoon of capstone projects, internships, dual enrollment, ensembles, and service, often in block scheduling of 80 to 90 minutes. Every band must still meet legal instructional-time rules and do all the jobs a school does, including meals, supervision, and support services. A design exercise is to start from a blank bell schedule and place each block against those constraints.

docs.title: Does an AI-native model pay for itself?
docs.text:
Partly, but not fully, according to the book's example. Software and content costs can fall a great deal: open Level 2 content costs very little, and the affordable Alpha model in Chapter 23 adds only about $64 per student per year after print savings for the morning. The main cost is the afternoon, which needs trained adults.

Chapter 21 tests whether budget reallocation can cover it, for example by shifting spending from print textbooks and some direct-instruction time. In its example, reallocation does not fully pay for the afternoon. That means a district has to decide whether the gains in collaboration, engagement, and human skills are worth new money, or find partners such as arts organizations, community groups, and youth sports programs. A sound plan states the gap honestly rather than promising that technology savings cover everything.

docs.title: How do I plan for uncertainty in the AI forecast?
docs.text:
Chapter 5 recommends four tools. Use scenarios: write plans for a fast trend, the central trend, and a slow or stalled trend, since the doubling time drives most of the uncertainty. Prefer no-regret moves, which pay off in every scenario, such as open Level 2 content, better data governance, staff AI literacy, and a stronger afternoon program. Make decisions reversible where you can, with short contracts and data export. Set trip-wires, measurable signals that trigger a planned response, such as "if independent studies of AI tutors in our grade band show gains over two consecutive years, expand the pilot."

State the prediction assumptions behind the plan and test it against a prediction failure scenario: if AI capability stalled tomorrow, what in the plan would still be worth doing? A plan that only makes sense if the trend continues is a bet, not a plan.

docs.title: How can a school keep AI costs and energy use low at scale?
docs.text:
Use AI where its cost is paid once, and avoid it where its cost is paid per student per question. Generate once, serve many pays for content creation once and serves static pages for a fraction of a cent. Adaptation without live AI uses a Learning Record Store, a mastery threshold, and a learning-graph lookup to choose each student's next step, with no model call at all.

Where chat tutoring adds real value, use it selectively. In Chapter 12, limiting chatbot use to the moments a student is stuck, rather than chat for everything, cut inference cost and energy by 80 percent or more. Chapter 5 puts energy in perspective: a chatbot tutoring session uses roughly 12 watt-hours in its example, which is modest, while video generation and long agent tasks use far more. Inference cost for a fixed capability level fell more than 280-fold from November 2022 to October 2024, so selective use gets cheaper over time too.

docs.title: How would I evaluate a pilot so the result is trustworthy?
docs.text:
Build the evaluation into the pilot before it starts. Chapter 21 recommends a logic model that links resources and activities to the outcomes you expect, so you know what to measure at each stage. Choose a balanced set of success measures in advance, so no one can pick the favorable ones afterward.

Use a comparison. The fairest practical design is A/B testing with delayed access: randomly choose which classes start this term, and give the program to the rest next term. That answers the ethical objection that some students are denied a benefit, since everyone gets it. Measure outcomes without AI assistance, as the Turkish study did, so that practice gains are not mistaken for learning. Check the gap between groups, not only the average. Where possible, have an independent evaluator analyze the results. Then apply the decision rule written at the start, even if the result is disappointing.

docs.title: What would a two-sided story about an AI-native school look like?
docs.text:
A two-sided story shows a benefit, a risk, and how the school responds, which is the book's risk-and-response framework in miniature. Chapter 22 reads each case as benefit, risk, response, and lesson, and Chapter 23 shows how to write one.

For example: Maya, a sixth grader, moves through her math morning at her own pace and finishes a unit two weeks early (benefit). Her teacher notices that Maya has started asking the tutor for answers whenever she is stuck, and her quiz scores without the tutor are dropping (risk: cognitive offloading). The school switches the tutor to hint-first mode, adds a weekly no-AI check, and pairs Maya with a peer to explain her reasoning in the afternoon (response). The lesson is that design and adult attention, not the software alone, decide the outcome. Writing stories this way keeps a school from either hiding risks or giving up on benefits.

docs.title: How might Level 5 autonomous textbooks change schools, and what safeguards would they need?
docs.text:
A Level 5 autonomous AI textbook would generate each lesson in real time for each student, with full personalization of examples, pacing, and explanations. Chapter 6 places it as technically plausible around three years out on the central trend, but dependent on reliability and trust.

The risks are new in kind. A generated lesson may contain confident errors that no editor has seen. Two students may receive different explanations of the same concept, making it harder for teachers and families to know what was taught. Full personalization needs the richest student data of any level. The book's level-specific policy for Level 5 is human review of generated lessons, on top of every safeguard from Levels 1 to 4: accessibility, simulation accuracy, governed records with bias audits, and chat guardrails. A reasonable design question is what share of generated content must be reviewed, by whom, and how fast, before a Level 5 product could be trusted with a whole course.

docs.title: How can the afternoon be equitable when families have different resources?
docs.text:
Make the afternoon part of the free school day, not an add-on families pay for. Chapter 20 lists a free afternoon among the requirements for equity of access, alongside devices, accessibility, and language support. Private models charge tuition of $40,000 to $65,000, which is the cost barrier the public model is meant to remove.

Partnerships help but need care. Chapter 14 covers community partnerships with arts groups, youth sports, libraries, and local employers, with written agreements covering safety, schedules, and goals. Partnerships tend to cluster in better-resourced neighborhoods, so a district should map where they are and fill gaps deliberately. Activity-skill matching ensures every student gets a spread of skills across the week, not just the activities their friends or parents chose. Transportation, equipment, and instrument loans matter as much as the program design. El Sistema's youth orchestras, which use group music to build belonging in low-income communities, show the afternoon can serve the students with the least.

docs.title: 2 Hour Learning
docs.text:
The name of Alpha School's model and adaptive academic software, in which students spend about two hours a day on core academics.

The same software runs at Unbound Academy, where results without in-person afternoons have been weaker.

See also: Alpha School, Unbound Academy, Two-to-Three-Hour Learning

docs.title: 50 Percent Time Horizon
docs.text:
The task length, in human working time, at which an AI model succeeds on half of the attempted tasks, used by METR as its main capability measure.

Example: A model that succeeds on half of the 30-minute tasks, more often on shorter tasks and less often on longer ones, has a 50 percent time horizon of about 30 minutes.

See also: Task Horizon, Task Success Rate

docs.title: 5R Permissions
docs.text:
The five rights that define openness in educational resources: to retain, reuse, revise, remix, and redistribute the material.

Example: A teacher keeps a copy of an open chapter, revises it, combines it with another, and shares the result with her district.

See also: Open Educational Resource, Reusability Subscore

docs.title: A/B Testing
docs.text:
Comparing two versions of a design by randomly assigning users to each and measuring which produces better results.

Example: Half of students see hints after one wrong answer and half after two, and the system compares learning.

See also: Randomized Controlled Trial, Program Evaluation

docs.title: Abstraction
docs.text:
Focusing on the information that matters for a problem while setting aside details that do not.

See also: Computational Thinking, Decomposition

docs.title: Academic Integrity
docs.text:
Honesty and responsibility in academic work, including doing one's own work and giving credit for others' ideas.

See also: Redesign Not Policing, AI Cheating Detector

docs.title: Academic Morning
docs.text:
The first part of the AI-native school day, in which students work on core academic subjects through adaptive, mastery-based materials.

Example: From 8:30 to 11:00, students work through math and reading in their adaptive textbooks with teachers circulating.

See also: Compressed Academic Morning, Morning-Afternoon Model

docs.title: Achievement Gap
docs.text:
A persistent difference in average academic performance between groups of students, such as groups defined by income, race, language, or disability.

Example: A district finds that students from low-income families score on average well below their classmates on the state math test.

See also: Educational Equity, Closing or Widening Gaps

docs.title: Active Listening
docs.text:
Giving full attention to a speaker, checking understanding, and responding in ways that show the speaker's message was received.

Example: A student restates a teammate's idea, "So you think the bridge needs a wider base?", before adding his own.

See also: Communication Skills, Empathy

docs.title: Activity-Skill Matching
docs.text:
Choosing afternoon activities deliberately so that, across a student's week, they build the full range of human skills rather than whatever happens to be available.

Example: A school makes sure each student's week includes one team sport, one art, and one building project.

See also: Pro-Social Activity, Afternoon Program

docs.title: Actor Verb Object
docs.text:
The basic three-part structure of an xAPI statement: who did something, what they did, and what they did it to.

See also: xAPI Statement

docs.title: Adaptation Without Live AI
docs.text:
Personalizing learning with stored records, stated rules, and a learning graph, instead of running an AI model for each student interaction.

Example: A rule that unlocks the next concept when a student reaches the mastery threshold needs no AI at run time.

See also: Low-Cost Adaptive Design, Next-Concept Selection

docs.title: Adaptive Learning
docs.text:
Instruction in which the content, sequence, difficulty, or pace changes in response to each student's demonstrated performance.

Example: A student who answers three fraction questions correctly moves on, while one who misses them gets a review lesson.

See also: Level 3 Adaptive Textbook, Mastery Learning

docs.title: ADKAR Ability
docs.text:
The fourth element of the ADKAR model: being able to apply knowledge in actual daily work at the required level of performance.

Example: A teacher can run small-group coaching smoothly while the rest of the class works in the adaptive textbook.

See also: ADKAR Model, ADKAR Reinforcement

docs.title: ADKAR Awareness
docs.text:
The first element of the ADKAR model: understanding why a change is needed and what risks come from not changing.

Example: Teachers see data on how much class time is spent re-teaching material students already know.

See also: ADKAR Model, ADKAR Desire

docs.title: ADKAR Desire
docs.text:
The second element of the ADKAR model: a personal willingness to support and take part in a change.

Example: A teacher becomes keen once she sees the new schedule gives her afternoons coaching the debate team.

See also: ADKAR Model, ADKAR Knowledge

docs.title: ADKAR Knowledge
docs.text:
The third element of the ADKAR model: knowing how to change, including the skills, processes, and information required.

Example: Teachers attend workshops on reading mastery dashboards.

See also: ADKAR Model, ADKAR Ability

docs.title: ADKAR Model
docs.text:
Prosci's model of individual change, which holds that each person needs awareness, desire, knowledge, ability, and reinforcement, in that order, for a change to succeed.

Example: A coach finds a teacher who knows how to use the new tool but does not yet want to, and works on desire.

See also: ADKAR Awareness, ADKAR Reinforcement

docs.title: ADKAR Reinforcement
docs.text:
The fifth element of the ADKAR model: the recognition, rewards, and structures that keep a change in place and prevent a return to old habits.

Example: The principal highlights coaching successes at staff meetings and builds them into evaluations.

See also: ADKAR Model, Refreeze Stage

docs.title: Adoption Readiness
docs.text:
The degree to which a person, school, or system is prepared to take up an innovation, in terms of skills, resources, attitudes, and infrastructure.

Example: A school with reliable Wi-Fi, trained staff, and a privacy policy is more ready than one without.

See also: School Readiness Assessment, Governance Readiness

docs.title: Affordable Alpha Model
docs.text:
The book's design for offering a short adaptive morning and a people-centered afternoon to every student at a public school budget, using open textbooks, MicroSims, learning graphs, xAPI, and a Learning Record Store instead of costly live AI.

Example: A public district builds its morning on free Level 2 and Level 3 textbooks and spends its savings on afternoon staff.

See also: Low-Cost Adaptive Design, Cost Barrier to AI Schools, Alpha School

docs.title: Afternoon Program
docs.text:
The planned set of activities that fill the second part of the AI-native school day, after the academic morning.

Example: A program offering robotics, orchestra, soccer, and a community garden project on rotating days.

See also: Pro-Social Afternoon, Afternoon Program Quality

docs.title: Afternoon Program Quality
docs.text:
How well the afternoon's activities achieve their goals, judged by clear purposes, trained adults, participation, safety, and evidence of skill growth.

Example: A school reviews teamwork rubric scores and attendance each term to decide which activities to keep.

See also: Structured Afternoon, Teamwork Rubric

docs.title: Afternoon Specialist Staff
docs.text:
Adults other than classroom teachers, such as artists, musicians, coaches, makers, and community experts, who lead afternoon activities, often part time or under contract.

They need background checks, training, and clear lines of supervision.

See also: Staffing Model, Community Partnership

docs.title: Age-Appropriate AI Design
docs.text:
The practice of fitting an AI system's content, interactions, data collection, and defaults to the developmental stage of the children who use it.

Example: A tutor for eight-year-olds uses short sentences, avoids persuasive nudges, and sets privacy protections on by default.

See also: Responsible AI with Minors

docs.title: Age-Based Grade Levels
docs.text:
The practice of grouping students into classes by birth year, so that children of the same age study the same material at the same pace regardless of what each already knows.

Example: A ten-year-old who already reads at an eighth-grade level is still placed in fifth-grade reading because of her age.

Contrast with: Self-Paced Learning, Mastery Learning

docs.title: AI Agent
docs.text:
An AI system that plans and carries out a sequence of actions toward a goal, using tools such as web search, files, or software, with limited human direction at each step.

Example: An agent asked to build a quiz finds the chapter, writes the questions, formats them, and saves the file.

See also: Long-Running Task, Task Horizon

docs.title: AI Benchmark
docs.text:
A standardized set of tasks or questions used to measure and compare the performance of AI systems.

Example: A benchmark of thousands of math word problems on which each new model's accuracy is reported.

See also: Benchmark Task Suite, METR

docs.title: AI Capability
docs.text:
The range and difficulty of tasks an AI system can complete correctly, as measured by tests, benchmarks, or real-world use.

Example: METR measures AI capability by the length of tasks, in human working time, that a model can complete.

See also: AI Benchmark, Task Horizon

docs.title: AI Cheating Detector
docs.text:
Software that claims to estimate whether a piece of writing was produced by AI rather than by a student.

Example: A teacher runs essays through a detector that labels one as "likely AI-written."

See also: Detector False Positives, Stanford Detector Study

docs.title: AI Coaching Teachers
docs.text:
Using AI to help teachers improve their practice, for example by offering live suggestions during tutoring or feedback on lesson plans.

Example: In the Tutor CoPilot study, live AI suggestions to human tutors raised student mastery, most for the weakest tutors.

See also: Tutor CoPilot, Instructional Coaching

docs.title: AI Energy Use
docs.text:
The electricity consumed by training and running AI models.

It matters because energy is a possible limit on AI growth and because a school's choice of AI tool has an environmental footprint.

See also: Data Center Energy, Energy-Efficient Learning

docs.title: AI Guardrails
docs.text:
Design limits built into an AI system to keep its behavior safe and suited to its purpose, such as refusing to give final answers or blocking inappropriate topics.

Example: A math tutor that responds to "just tell me the answer" with a hint about the next step.

See also: Hints Instead of Answers, Guided AI vs Open AI

docs.title: AI Hallucination
docs.text:
Output from an AI system that is stated fluently and confidently but is false, invented, or unsupported by its sources.

Example: A chatbot cites a research paper with a plausible title and authors that does not exist.

See also: Confidently Wrong Answers, AI Tutor Failures

docs.title: AI in Education
docs.text:
The use of artificial intelligence to support teaching, learning, assessment, and school operations.

Example: AI tutors, automated feedback on writing, and adaptive practice systems are uses of AI in education.

See also: AI Tutor, Intelligent Textbook

docs.title: AI Inference Cost
docs.text:
The cost of running a trained AI model to produce an output, such as answering one question, usually charged per unit of text processed.

Example: A district estimates the yearly cost of letting 12,000 students chat with a tutor for an hour each day.

See also: Falling AI Costs, Selective Chatbot Use

docs.title: AI Literacy
docs.text:
The knowledge and skills needed to understand what AI systems are, how they work in broad terms, what they can and cannot do, and how to use them responsibly.

Example: Students learn to check a chatbot's answer against a reliable source before using it.

See also: Staff AI Literacy, AI Hallucination

docs.title: AI Prediction for Schools
docs.text:
The book's forecast that free, adaptive, interactive textbooks will soon be available to almost every student, freeing much of the school day now spent on direct instruction.

Example: A principal uses the prediction to ask what her school would do with three extra hours each afternoon.

See also: Three-to-Four-Year Forecast, Freed-Up School Time

docs.title: AI Tutor
docs.text:
A software system that uses AI to guide a student through learning by explaining, asking questions, giving feedback, and adjusting to the student's responses.

Example: The Harvard physics tutor guided students through problems step by step using proven teaching practices.

See also: AI Tutor Strengths, AI Tutor Failures, Khanmigo

docs.title: AI Tutor Failures
docs.text:
The ways an AI tutor can harm learning, such as giving wrong answers, doing the student's thinking for them, encouraging over-reliance, or being little used.

Example: In the Turkish study, an open chatbot raised practice scores but lowered later exam scores.

See also: Confidently Wrong Answers, Over-Reliance on AI

docs.title: AI Tutor Strengths
docs.text:
The advantages an AI tutor offers, such as unlimited patience, availability at any hour, instant feedback, and the ability to adjust explanations to each student.

Example: A student asks the same question five ways at 9 p.m. and gets a fresh explanation each time.

See also: AI Tutor, Skills AI Teaches Well

docs.title: AI-First School
docs.text:
A school that puts AI technology at the center of how it delivers instruction, often described by how much AI software students use.

Example: Alpha School, where students spend about two hours a day on adaptive academic software.

See also: AI-Native School, Benefits of AI-First Schools, Risks of AI-First Schools

docs.title: AI-Generated Content
docs.text:
Text, images, questions, simulations, or other material produced in whole or in part by an AI system.

In this book, such content is produced once and checked by people before students see it.

See also: Generative AI, Generate Once Serve Many

docs.title: AI-Native School
docs.text:
A school designed from the start around the expectation of capable, low-cost AI, using it to shorten academic instruction and reinvesting the freed time in human, social learning.

Example: A new public school that opens with a two-and-a-half-hour adaptive morning and a staffed afternoon program.

Contrast with: AI-First School

See also: Morning-Afternoon Model

docs.title: AI-Native School Day
docs.text:
The daily schedule that results from the morning-afternoon model, including the adaptive morning, screen limits, a curiosity block, and the afternoon program.

Example: 8:30 to 11:00 adaptive academics with breaks, 11:00 to 11:30 curiosity block, lunch, then two hours of projects and arts.

See also: Morning-Afternoon Model, Schedule Redesign

docs.title: AI-Powered Marketing Claims
docs.text:
Promotional statements that a product uses AI or is "AI-powered," often without saying what the AI does or what level of capability it delivers.

Example: A flashcard app labeled "AI-powered" that only shuffles cards in a fixed order.

See also: Vendor Level Claim, Hype Cycle

docs.title: Algorithmic Bias
docs.text:
Systematic and unfair differences in how a computer system treats or affects different groups of people, arising from its data, design, or use.

Example: AI writing detectors flag essays by English-language learners as AI-written far more often than essays by native speakers.

See also: Algorithmic Bias Auditing, Bias Against ELL Writers

docs.title: Algorithmic Bias Auditing
docs.text:
Systematic testing of an automated system to find whether its outcomes differ unfairly across groups of users.

Example: A district checks whether an adaptive system moves boys and girls, or English learners and native speakers, ahead at similar rates when their scores are similar.

See also: Algorithmic Bias, Algorithmic Transparency

docs.title: Algorithmic Thinking
docs.text:
Designing a clear, ordered series of steps that solves a problem or completes a task and can be followed the same way each time.

See also: Computational Thinking

docs.title: Algorithmic Transparency
docs.text:
The degree to which the rules, data, and reasoning behind an automated decision are disclosed and understandable to the people affected.

Example: A vendor publishes the mastery threshold and next-concept rules its adaptive system uses.

See also: Algorithmic Bias Auditing, Adaptation Without Live AI

docs.title: AllHere Collapse
docs.text:
The 2024 failure of AllHere, the startup building LA Unified's "Ed" chatbot, within months of launch, followed by fraud charges against its founder in November 2024.

It shows why schools need vendor evaluation and procurement rules before buying AI products.

See also: LAUSD Ed Chatbot, Vendor Risk

docs.title: Alpha Adult Guides
docs.text:
The adults at Alpha School who support students' motivation, effort, and progress in the morning and lead workshops and projects in the afternoon, instead of lecturing.

Their role raises the question of how much of Alpha's results come from the adults rather than the software.

See also: Learning Guide, Alpha School

docs.title: Alpha School
docs.text:
A private school network, begun in Austin, Texas, in 2014, whose students spend about two hours a day on adaptive academic software and the rest of the day on life-skills workshops and projects led by adult guides.

It shows the morning-afternoon structure can work, but at private-school prices.

See also: Alpha Tuition Range, Alpha Adult Guides, 2 Hour Learning

docs.title: Alpha Tuition Range
docs.text:
Alpha School's yearly tuition, about 40,000 dollars at the original Austin campus to about 65,000 dollars at newer campuses such as Boston, Miami, and New York.

The range shows why the book seeks a lower-cost version of the same structure.

See also: Alpha School, Cost Barrier to AI Schools, Affordable Alpha Model

docs.title: AltSchool
docs.text:
A network of "personalized learning" microschools launched in Silicon Valley in 2013 on its own software, which raised more than 170 million dollars, closed its schools within a few years, and shifted to selling software.

Its lesson is that technology-led personalization without a lasting school culture does not last.

See also: Software Is Not the Model, Microschool

docs.title: Anchoring in Culture
docs.text:
Making a change last by connecting new practices to the organization's values, stories, hiring, and leadership, the final Kotter step.

Example: The school hires new teachers specifically for coaching skill and celebrates the afternoon program in its traditions.

See also: Kotter's Eight Steps, Sustaining Change

docs.title: Applying Thinking on Teams
docs.text:
Using decomposition, pattern recognition, abstraction, algorithmic thinking, evidence evaluation, and argument analysis inside group work, so a team decides with reasons rather than by volume.

Example: A team settles a design dispute by testing both versions and comparing the data.

See also: Team Problem Solving, Computational Thinking

docs.title: Argument Analysis
docs.text:
Breaking an argument into its claim, reasons, and evidence, and checking whether the reasoning holds.

Example: A debate team identifies the hidden assumption in the other side's main point.

See also: Critical Thinking, Evidence Evaluation

docs.title: Artificial Intelligence
docs.text:
The field of computing concerned with building systems that perform tasks normally associated with human intelligence, such as understanding language, recognizing patterns, reasoning, and making decisions.

See also: Machine Learning, Generative AI

docs.title: Arts Education
docs.text:
Instruction in music, dance, theater, visual arts, and other art forms, covering both creating and appreciating them.

See also: Music Education, Visual Arts

docs.title: Assessment Redesign
docs.text:
Changing what, how, and when student learning is assessed to fit new goals and tools.

Example: A school replaces take-home essays with in-class writing, oral defenses, and portfolios.

See also: Redesign Not Policing, Combined Assessment Plan

docs.title: Basic Assumptions
docs.text:
In Schein's model, the deepest layer of culture: unspoken, taken-for-granted beliefs that guide behavior without being questioned.

Example: Staff assume that a quiet classroom is a well-managed one.

See also: Schein's Culture Model, Mental Models

docs.title: Beachhead Strategy
docs.text:
Focusing first on one narrow, well-defined group of adopters and serving it completely before expanding to others.

Example: A district starts with ninth-grade algebra in two schools and expands only after success there.

See also: Crossing the Chasm, Pilot Program

docs.title: Behavioral Data
docs.text:
Information about how a person acts while using a system, such as clicks, pauses, time on task, and patterns of activity.

See also: Detailed Learning History, Data Minimization

docs.title: Bell Schedule
docs.text:
The fixed timetable of periods, passing times, and breaks that structures a school day, usually signaled by bells or tones.

See also: Block Scheduling, Schedule Redesign

docs.title: Belonging
docs.text:
The feeling of being accepted, valued, and included as a member of a group or community.

Example: A student who joins the school orchestra says it is the first place she feels she fits in.

See also: Human Connection, El Sistema

docs.title: Benchmark Task Suite
docs.text:
The specific collection of tasks that a benchmark runs, ideally spanning many difficulties and lengths and each with a clear way to judge success.

Example: METR's suite ranges from tasks a person finishes in seconds to tasks that take many hours.

See also: AI Benchmark, METR

docs.title: Benefits of AI-First Schools
docs.text:
The positive results AI-centered schools can produce, such as faster mastery, personalized pacing, more time for projects and relationships, and support for teachers.

Example: The Harvard physics tutor helped students learn more in less time than an active-learning class.

See also: Risks of AI-First Schools, Strengthen the Positives

docs.title: Bias Against ELL Writers
docs.text:
The finding that AI-writing detectors are more likely to flag the writing of English-language learners as AI-generated than the writing of native speakers.

Example: In a 2023 Stanford study, more than half of non-native speakers' essays were wrongly labeled as AI-written on average.

See also: Stanford Detector Study, Algorithmic Bias

docs.title: Block Scheduling
docs.text:
A schedule in which the day is divided into fewer, longer class periods, often 80 to 120 minutes, instead of many short ones.

See also: Schedule Redesign, Bell Schedule

docs.title: Bloom's Taxonomy
docs.text:
A hierarchy of cognitive processes, revised in 2001, that orders learning goals from remembering and understanding through applying, analyzing, and evaluating to creating.

Example: A teacher writes one quiz question asking students to recall a definition and another asking them to evaluate two competing arguments.

See also: Higher-Order Thinking, Learning Outcome

docs.title: Bloom's Two-Sigma Problem
docs.text:
Benjamin Bloom's 1984 finding that students tutored one-on-one with mastery methods performed about two standard deviations better than students in conventional classes, and his challenge to find group methods that come close.

Example: AI tutors are often presented as a possible answer to this challenge.

See also: One-on-One Tutoring, Effect Size

docs.title: Board Presentation
docs.text:
A formal presentation to a school board explaining a proposal, its evidence, costs, and risks, usually to seek approval.

Example: A principal presents pilot results and a cost model to the board before requesting expansion.

See also: School Board Recommendation, School Board

docs.title: Bridges' Transition Model
docs.text:
William Bridges' model of the inner, psychological process people go through during change: endings, a neutral zone, and new beginnings.

Example: A principal holds a session to honor the old schedule before introducing the new one.

See also: Endings and Losses, Neutral Zone, Change Versus Transition

docs.title: Bright Spots
docs.text:
Examples of success already happening within a system, which can be studied and copied.

Example: A principal finds the one classroom where afternoon projects are working well and asks that teacher to share her methods.

See also: Positive Deviance, Direct the Rider

docs.title: Browser-Based Simulation
docs.text:
An interactive model that runs entirely inside a web browser, requiring no installation and often working offline once loaded.

Example: A circuit simulation that works the same on a Chromebook, a tablet, and a home laptop.

See also: MicroSim, Web Browser

docs.title: Budget Reallocation
docs.text:
Moving funds from existing expenses to new priorities without increasing the total budget.

Example: A district shifts textbook purchase money to pay afternoon specialist staff after adopting free open textbooks.

See also: Public School Funding, Cost Modeling

docs.title: Building on Change
docs.text:
Using the credibility gained from early wins to tackle bigger problems, instead of declaring victory too soon.

Example: After the pilot succeeds in one grade, the school uses its results to redesign the whole schedule.

See also: Short-Term Wins, Scaling a Pilot

docs.title: Capacity Building
docs.text:
Developing the knowledge, skills, resources, and relationships that people and organizations need to carry out a change.

Example: A district funds two years of coaching for every teacher moving to the new model.

See also: Professional Development, Instructional Coaching

docs.title: Carnegie Unit
docs.text:
A standard measure of high school credit, defined as about 120 hours of class contact time in one subject over a school year, that ties credit to time spent rather than mastery.

See also: Seat Time

docs.title: Case Study Method
docs.text:
An approach to research and teaching that examines one real situation in depth, describing what happened and drawing transferable lessons from it.

Example: Studying the inBloom shutdown to understand why student data projects need family trust.

See also: Real Case Study, Lesson From a Case

docs.title: Causal Loop Diagram
docs.text:
A diagram that shows how variables in a system influence one another, using arrows marked as increasing or decreasing, to reveal feedback loops.

Example: A diagram linking teacher workload, burnout, turnover, and new-teacher training needs.

See also: Feedback Loop, Systems Thinking

docs.title: Centralized Student Records
docs.text:
Student information for many schools or districts stored together in one system or by one provider.

Centralizing records can simplify management but makes the store a larger target.

See also: PowerSchool Data Breach, Data Breach

docs.title: Change Agent
docs.text:
A person who deliberately works to bring about change within an organization by influencing others' decisions and actions.

Example: An instructional coach hired to help teachers move to the morning-afternoon model.

See also: Opinion Leader, Guiding Coalition

docs.title: Change Fatigue
docs.text:
Exhaustion, cynicism, and disengagement that develop when people face too many changes, too often, without seeing results.

Example: Teachers greet a new initiative with "this too shall pass" after five programs in four years.

See also: Coherence Framework, Teacher Burnout

docs.title: Change Stage
docs.text:
The middle stage of Lewin's model, in which people learn and try out new behaviors, processes, and ways of thinking.

Example: Teachers run the new morning schedule for a semester with coaching support.

See also: Lewin's Change Model, Implementation Dip

docs.title: Change Versus Transition
docs.text:
Bridges' distinction between change, the external event or new situation, and transition, the internal psychological process people go through to adjust to it.

Example: The new schedule starts on September 1 (change), but teachers may take a year to feel at home in it (transition).

See also: Bridges' Transition Model

docs.title: Change Vision
docs.text:
A clear, concise description of the future a change effort aims to create, used to guide decisions and motivate people, the third of Kotter's steps.

Example: "By 2029 every student will finish core academics by noon and spend afternoons building, performing, and serving."

See also: Communicating the Vision, Kotter's Eight Steps

docs.title: Changing Teacher Role
docs.text:
The shift in a teacher's main work from delivering content to coaching, mentoring, and facilitating, as adaptive materials take on more of instruction.

Example: A former lecturer now spends mornings coaching small groups and afternoons leading a robotics team.

See also: Teacher as Coach, Learning Guide, Reduced Direct Instruction

docs.title: Charter School
docs.text:
A publicly funded, tuition-free school that operates independently of the local district under a contract, or charter, granting it freedom over methods in exchange for accountability for results.

Example: Unbound Academy is an online charter school in Arizona approved by the state charter board.

See also: Virtual School, Unbound Academy

docs.title: Chatbot
docs.text:
A software program that carries on a conversation with a user in natural language, through text or speech.

See also: Level 4 Chatbot Textbook, Conversational Tutoring

docs.title: Choosing a Change Model
docs.text:
Selecting the model of change, or the combination of models, that fits a particular school's size, culture, history, and type of change.

Example: A small school uses ADKAR to support individual teachers and Kotter's steps to organize the overall plan.

See also: Kotter's Eight Steps, ADKAR Model

docs.title: Classification Framework
docs.text:
A structured scheme that sorts items into defined categories using clear criteria, so different people sort the same item the same way.

See also: Five-Level Textbook Model, SAE J3016 Standard

docs.title: Classroom
docs.text:
The physical or virtual room in which a group of students and one or more adults meet for instruction and learning activities.

See also: School, Direct Instruction

docs.title: Closing or Widening Gaps
docs.text:
The question of whether a change makes the difference in outcomes between groups of students smaller or larger.

A tool that helps everyone on average can still widen gaps if it helps advantaged students more.

See also: Achievement Gap, Equity of Access

docs.title: Clubs and Extracurriculars
docs.text:
Organized activities outside regular academic classes, such as clubs, teams, publications, and student government.

See also: Afternoon Program

docs.title: Coding Club
docs.text:
A group in which students meet to learn programming and build software projects together.

See also: Robotics Club, Clubs and Extracurriculars

docs.title: Cognitive Offloading
docs.text:
Using an external tool or resource to reduce the mental effort a task requires, such as writing a list or asking an AI to solve a problem.

It can free the mind for other work, but it can also prevent the effort that builds learning.

See also: Over-Reliance on AI, Your Brain on ChatGPT

docs.title: Coherence Framework
docs.text:
Fullan and Quinn's model for aligning a school system around a small number of connected priorities, collaborative cultures, deep learning, and shared accountability.

Example: A district drops five unrelated initiatives to focus on the morning-afternoon model and its supports.

See also: Fullan's Educational Change, Change Fatigue

docs.title: Collaboration
docs.text:
Working jointly with others toward a common outcome, sharing ideas, effort, and responsibility.

See also: Teamwork, Shared Goals

docs.title: Combined Assessment Plan
docs.text:
A school's written plan for how its different forms of assessment fit together: what is measured, with what tool, how often, and who sees the results.

Example: Morning mastery data, afternoon teamwork rubrics, portfolios, and required state tests in one plan.

See also: Assessment Redesign, Mastery-Based Assessment

docs.title: Communicating Before Rumors
docs.text:
Telling families and staff about a change before they hear about it elsewhere, because rumors are far harder to correct than a clear first statement.

Example: The principal sends a letter about the pilot the week before it appears on the board agenda.

See also: Family Communication, Community Communication

docs.title: Communicating the Vision
docs.text:
Repeatedly sharing a change vision through every available channel, and through leaders' own behavior, so it is widely understood and accepted.

Example: The principal explains the new model at every staff meeting, family night, and newsletter for a year.

See also: Change Vision, Family Communication

docs.title: Communication Skills
docs.text:
The abilities needed to exchange ideas clearly and effectively with others, including speaking, writing, listening, and reading nonverbal cues.

Example: A student explains her team's design to visiting parents and answers their questions.

See also: Active Listening, Public Exhibition

docs.title: Community Communication
docs.text:
Sharing information about a school's plans and results with the wider public, including residents, local media, businesses, and community groups.

Example: A district hosts a public forum and posts a plain-language summary of its AI pilot online.

See also: Family Communication, Board Presentation

docs.title: Community Partnership
docs.text:
A working relationship between a school and outside organizations, such as businesses, nonprofits, museums, or colleges, that share resources or expertise.

Example: A local theater company sends actors to lead the school's afternoon drama program.

See also: Afternoon Specialist Staff, Service Learning

docs.title: Compatibility
docs.text:
The degree to which an innovation is seen as consistent with the existing values, experiences, and needs of potential adopters.

Example: A tool that works inside the learning management system teachers already use fits their routines.

See also: Five Innovation Attributes

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text:
The degree to which an innovation is seen as difficult to understand and use, which slows its adoption.

See also: Five Innovation Attributes

docs.title: Composite Story
docs.text:
A fictional account assembled from patterns seen in many real situations, with invented characters, used to make an idea concrete.

Example: The story of Maya, an invented student whose day combines experiences reported in many schools.

Contrast with: Real Case Study

See also: Two-Sided Story

docs.title: Compounding Small Changes
docs.text:
The way a series of modest improvements, each building on the last, adds up over time to a large total change.

Example: Improving by one percent a week compounds to about 68 percent better over a year.

See also: Microstrategy, Exponential Growth

docs.title: Compressed Academic Morning
docs.text:
An academic morning shortened to about two to three hours because adaptive materials let students reach expected learning results in less time than whole-class instruction.

Example: A middle school fits math, reading, science, and social studies into a morning ending at 11:30.

See also: Two-to-Three-Hour Learning, Freed-Up School Time

docs.title: Computational Thinking
docs.text:
A problem-solving approach, drawn from computer science, made up of decomposition, pattern recognition, abstraction, and algorithmic thinking.

Example: Students plan a school garden by breaking it into tasks, spotting repeating patterns, ignoring details, and writing step-by-step instructions.

See also: Decomposition, Algorithmic Thinking

docs.title: Compute Scaling
docs.text:
Increasing the amount of computing power used to train or run AI models, which has been a major driver of their improving capability.

Example: A new model trained with ten times the computing of its predecessor that performs noticeably better on benchmarks.

See also: Limits to AI Growth, Data Center Energy

docs.title: Concept Node
docs.text:
A single idea or skill represented as one point in a learning graph.

See also: Learning Graph, Foundational Concept

docs.title: Concerns-Based Adoption Model
docs.text:
A framework, known as CBAM, for understanding and supporting teachers' experience of an innovation, through their stages of concern, levels of use, and innovation configurations.

Example: A coach surveys teachers' concerns before planning the next round of training.

See also: Stages of Concern, Levels of Use, Innovation Configuration

docs.title: Confidently Wrong Answers
docs.text:
Incorrect responses from an AI system delivered with the same fluent, certain tone as correct ones, which makes the errors hard for learners to notice.

Example: Early versions of Khanmigo made arithmetic mistakes while sounding sure of themselves.

See also: AI Hallucination, AI Tutor Failures

docs.title: Conflict Resolution
docs.text:
The process of addressing a disagreement between people in a way that respects each side and reaches an acceptable outcome.

Example: Two team members who want different project topics agree to combine the best parts of both.

See also: Relationship Skills, Perspective Taking

docs.title: Constructionism
docs.text:
A theory of learning, developed by Seymour Papert, that holds people learn especially well when building a tangible, shareable thing, such as a program, model, or machine.

Example: Students learn geometry by programming a robot to draw shapes.

See also: Constructivism, Learning by Building Together

docs.title: Constructivism
docs.text:
A theory of learning, associated with Jean Piaget, that holds people build their own understanding by connecting new experiences to what they already know.

See also: Social Constructivism, Constructionism

docs.title: Content Commoditization
docs.text:
The process by which instructional content becomes so cheap and widely available that it can no longer command a high price on its own.

Example: When several good free algebra textbooks exist, schools stop paying a premium for basic algebra content.

See also: Publisher Disruption, Value Beyond Content

docs.title: Content Creation Cost
docs.text:
The money, time, and expertise required to write, illustrate, review, and produce instructional material.

AI is lowering this cost sharply, which changes the economics of textbooks.

See also: Falling Production Cost, AI-Generated Content

docs.title: Contract Due Diligence
docs.text:
Careful review of a contract's terms, including data ownership, security duties, exit clauses, and payment conditions, before signing.

Example: A district insists on a clause requiring return and deletion of student data if the vendor fails.

See also: Data Ownership, Vendor Evaluation

docs.title: Conversational Tutoring
docs.text:
Instruction delivered through a back-and-forth exchange in natural language, in which the tutor responds to the student's questions and answers.

Example: A student explains her reasoning on a word problem, and the tutor asks a question that points out her mistake.

See also: Level 4 Chatbot Textbook, Socratic Questioning

docs.title: COPPA
docs.text:
The Children's Online Privacy Protection Act, a U.S. federal law that limits how online services collect personal information from children under 13.

See also: FERPA, Responsible AI with Minors

docs.title: Cost Barrier to AI Schools
docs.text:
The price that keeps AI-first school models out of reach for most families.

Example: Alpha School tuition, about 40,000 to 65,000 dollars a year depending on campus, is roughly 2.6 to 4.2 times average U.S. public per-pupil spending.

See also: Affordable Alpha Model, Alpha Tuition Range

docs.title: Cost Modeling
docs.text:
Estimating the costs of a program or design by listing each cost element, assigning values, and calculating totals under different assumptions.

Example: A district models the cost of Level 2, Level 3, and Level 4 options for its 12,000 students over five years.

See also: Total Cost of Ownership, Cost Per Student

docs.title: Cost Per Student
docs.text:
The total cost of a program, product, or service divided by the number of students who use it, usually stated per year.

Example: A 60,000-dollar license for 2,000 students works out to 30 dollars per student per year.

See also: Cost Modeling, Per-Pupil Spending

docs.title: Creative Commons License
docs.text:
One of a family of standard open licenses that let creators state which reuse rights they grant, such as requiring attribution or forbidding commercial use.
