Example: A textbook released under CC BY-NC-SA can be adapted by a school as long as it credits the author, does not sell it, and shares the changes the same way.

See also: Open License, 5R Permissions

docs.title: Creative Confidence
docs.text:
A person's belief in their own ability to come up with ideas and act on them.

Example: A shy student who sees her first comic published in the school magazine starts proposing more projects.

See also: Creativity

docs.title: Creativity
docs.text:
The ability to produce ideas, products, or solutions that are both new and useful or meaningful.

Example: Students invent a new board game that teaches the rules of fractions.

See also: Divergent Thinking, Creative Confidence

docs.title: Critical Thinking
docs.text:
The disciplined process of analyzing, evaluating, and judging information and arguments to reach well-reasoned conclusions.

Example: A student checks the source and evidence behind a viral claim before sharing it.

See also: Evidence Evaluation, Argument Analysis

docs.title: Crossing the Chasm
docs.text:
Moving an innovation from early adopters into mainstream use by delivering a complete, proven solution to one well-chosen group first.

Example: A district makes the adaptive textbook work fully for sixth-grade math before expanding to other grades.

See also: Beachhead Strategy, Whole Product

docs.title: Cultural Artifacts
docs.text:
The visible, tangible features of an organization's culture, such as its buildings, layouts, dress, language, documents, and rituals.

Example: Desks in rows facing the front are an artifact of a lecture-centered culture.

See also: Schein's Culture Model, School Rituals

docs.title: Culture Assessment
docs.text:
A structured examination of an organization's culture, through surveys, interviews, and observation, to understand its artifacts, values, and assumptions.

Example: A school surveys staff and observes meetings before planning a schedule change.

See also: Schein's Culture Model, School Readiness Assessment

docs.title: Culture Change Plan
docs.text:
A written plan for shifting a school's values, norms, and practices to support a new model, with steps, responsibilities, and ways to track progress.

Example: A plan to make classroom visits normal, celebrate afternoon work, and revise hiring to favor coaching skill.

See also: Culture Assessment, Anchoring in Culture

docs.title: Curiosity
docs.text:
The desire to know, explore, or understand something new, which prompts questions and investigation.

Example: A second grader asks why the moon looks different each night and keeps watching it for a month.

See also: Curiosity-Driven Learning, Intrinsic Motivation

docs.title: Curiosity-Driven Learning
docs.text:
Learning in which a student's own questions and interests determine the topics explored and the direction of study.

Example: During a protected curiosity block, a student uses the textbook's learning graph to explore how bridges carry weight.

See also: Curiosity-Led Morning, Student Agency

docs.title: Curiosity-Led Morning
docs.text:
An academic morning that protects time for students to pursue their own questions, alongside the required adaptive work.

Example: After finishing her math goals, a student spends 30 minutes exploring how earthquakes are measured.

See also: Curiosity-Driven Learning, Academic Morning

docs.title: Curriculum
docs.text:
The planned set of content, skills, learning goals, materials, and sequence that a school or course uses to guide what students study and in what order.

Example: A district's eighth-grade science curriculum lists the units, the standards each covers, and the textbook and labs used.

See also: Learning Outcome, Learning Graph

docs.title: Cybersecurity in Schools
docs.text:
The practices and technologies schools use to protect their networks, devices, and data from attack, theft, and damage.

See also: Data Breach, Vendor Risk

docs.title: Dance
docs.text:
The art of expressive, patterned movement of the body, usually to music.

See also: Arts Education

docs.title: Data Breach
docs.text:
An incident in which protected information is accessed, copied, or disclosed by someone not authorized to do so.

Example: The PowerSchool breach in December 2024 exposed records for tens of millions of students and teachers.

See also: PowerSchool Data Breach, Cybersecurity in Schools

docs.title: Data Center Energy
docs.text:
The electricity consumed by the large facilities that house the computers on which AI models and other online services run.

See also: AI Energy Use, Limits to AI Growth

docs.title: Data Governance
docs.text:
The policies, roles, and procedures an organization uses to decide what data it collects, how it is used, who can access it, and how it is protected.

Example: A district data committee approves each new tool and sets how long its data is kept.

See also: Data Retention Policy, Governance Readiness

docs.title: Data Minimization
docs.text:
The principle of collecting and keeping only the personal data needed for a specific, stated purpose.

Example: An adaptive math book stores which concepts are mastered but not the student's home address or browsing history.

See also: Data Governance, Trust Paradox

docs.title: Data Ownership
docs.text:
The question of who holds rights over data and may decide how it is used, shared, or deleted.

Example: A contract states that student data belongs to the district and families, not to the vendor.

See also: Student-Controlled Data, Contract Due Diligence

docs.title: Data Portability
docs.text:
The ability to move one's data from one system or provider to another in a usable, standard format.

Example: A student who changes districts takes her learning record with her and the new school's system can read it.

See also: Interoperability Standards, Vendor Lock-In

docs.title: Data Retention Policy
docs.text:
A rule stating how long each kind of data is kept and how and when it is deleted.

See also: Data Governance, Data Minimization

docs.title: David Game College
docs.text:
A London school that in 2024 opened what was described as the UK's first GCSE class taught mainly by AI, with students supported by learning coaches instead of traditional teachers.

It shows the AI-first idea spreading, and raises the same question as Alpha: how much comes from software and how much from the adults.

See also: Learning Guide, AI-First School

docs.title: Decomposition
docs.text:
Breaking a complex problem or task into smaller, more manageable parts that can be solved one at a time.

Example: A team splits planning a school fair into booths, schedule, budget, and publicity.

See also: Computational Thinking, Pattern Recognition

docs.title: Design Over Raw AI Power
docs.text:
The principle that how an AI tutor is designed, such as whether it gives hints or answers, matters more for learning than how capable the underlying model is.

Example: The same model hurt or helped Turkish students depending only on whether guardrails were in place.

See also: Guided AI vs Open AI, Turkish High School Study, Harvard Physics AI Tutor

docs.title: Detailed Learning History
docs.text:
A fine-grained record of a student's learning activity over time, such as every answer, attempt, hint, and time spent.

Example: A record showing that a student tried a slope problem four times over two days before getting it right.

See also: Learning Record, Privacy Inflection Point

docs.title: Detector False Positives
docs.text:
Cases in which an AI-writing detector wrongly labels human-written work as AI-generated.

Example: A student who wrote her essay herself is accused of cheating because the detector flagged it.

See also: AI Cheating Detector, Bias Against ELL Writers

docs.title: Device Access
docs.text:
Whether each student has a working device with a browser and a usable screen, at school and, where homework is involved, at home.

Example: A district finds that one in eight students shares a single phone with siblings at home.

See also: Digital Divide, Internet Connectivity

docs.title: Diffusion of Innovations
docs.text:
Everett Rogers' theory of how, why, and at what rate new ideas and technologies spread through a group of people over time.

Example: A new reading program used by two teachers, then a grade level, then the whole district.

See also: Technology Adoption Curve, Five Innovation Attributes

docs.title: Digital Divide
docs.text:
The gap between people who have reliable access to devices, internet, and digital skills and people who do not.

See also: Device Access, Internet Connectivity

docs.title: Digital Textbook
docs.text:
A textbook delivered in electronic form for reading on a computer, tablet, or phone.

A digital format alone does not make a textbook interactive or adaptive.

See also: PDF Textbook, Intelligent Textbook

docs.title: Direct Instruction
docs.text:
A teaching approach in which the teacher explicitly presents content, models skills, and leads guided practice, with students mostly receiving information in a set sequence.

The book predicts that adaptive textbooks will take over much of the time now spent on direct instruction.

See also: Lecture-Based Teaching, Reduced Direct Instruction

docs.title: Direct the Rider
docs.text:
The Switch framework element of giving people's rational side clear direction, through specific behaviors, examples of success, and a clear destination.

Example: "This week, use the dashboard for ten minutes each morning to form your coaching groups."

See also: Switch Framework, Bright Spots

docs.title: Directed Acyclic Graph
docs.text:
A network of points connected by one-way arrows in which it is impossible to follow the arrows and return to a starting point.

Learning graphs use this structure so that no concept is, through a chain, its own prerequisite.

See also: Learning Graph, Learning Dependency

docs.title: Divergent Thinking
docs.text:
Generating many different possible ideas or solutions to an open question, rather than converging on one correct answer.

See also: Creativity

docs.title: Doubling Time
docs.text:
The length of time it takes a quantity that is growing exponentially to become twice as large.

Example: With a doubling time of five months, a quantity grows about 5.3 times in one year.

See also: Five-Month Doubling, Exponential Growth

docs.title: Driving Question
docs.text:
The open-ended, meaningful question that frames a project and guides students' investigation.

Example: "How can we make our playground safer for younger children?"

See also: Project-Based Learning

docs.title: Early Adopters
docs.text:
The group that takes up an innovation soon after the innovators, often respected opinion leaders whose choices others watch.

Example: A well-regarded department head who pilots the new textbook in her classes and shares results.

See also: Opinion Leader, Early Majority

docs.title: Early Majority
docs.text:
The large group that adopts an innovation after seeing it proven by early adopters, deliberate and practical in its choices.

Example: Teachers who sign up for the second year of a pilot after seeing their colleagues' results.

See also: Pragmatist Buyers, The Chasm

docs.title: Early Visible Results
docs.text:
Outcomes of a change that appear soon and can be seen by others, which build confidence and support.

Example: A student exhibition at the end of the first term of afternoon projects.

See also: Short-Term Wins, Observability

docs.title: EdTech Hype Waves
docs.text:
The repeated pattern in which new educational technologies are promised to transform schools, attract heavy investment, and then deliver less than claimed.

Example: Film, television, laptops, and tablets each arrived with promises of a learning revolution.

See also: History of EdTech, Hype Cycle

docs.title: Education
docs.text:
The organized process of helping people acquire knowledge, skills, values, and habits, carried out through teaching, study, practice, and experience, in formal institutions or informal settings.

Example: A district's education mission covers reading and math, but also citizenship, health, and the ability to work with others.

See also: Learning, School, K-12 Education

docs.title: Education Policy
docs.text:
The laws, regulations, funding rules, and official guidelines set by governments and school boards that shape how schools operate and what they teach.

Example: A state law setting minimum instructional minutes per year is an education policy that affects schedule redesign.

See also: Level-Specific Policy, Policy Embedding

docs.title: Educational Equity
docs.text:
The condition in which every student receives the resources, opportunities, and support needed to reach their potential, regardless of background or circumstance.

The book's central equity question is whether the morning-afternoon model can be offered to all students at a public school's budget.

See also: Equity of Access, Digital Divide

docs.title: Educational Technology
docs.text:
Hardware, software, and digital resources used to support teaching, learning, and school administration.

Example: Interactive whiteboards, learning management systems, adaptive math programs, and AI tutors are all educational technology.

See also: History of EdTech, EdTech Hype Waves

docs.title: Effect Size
docs.text:
A standardized number expressing how large a difference between two groups is, often in standard deviation units, so results can be compared across studies.

Example: An effect size of 0.3 means the average tutored student scored about three-tenths of a standard deviation above the average untutored student.

See also: Learning Gains, Bloom's Two-Sigma Problem

docs.title: El Sistema
docs.text:
A youth orchestra program founded in Venezuela and now active worldwide that uses group music-making to build discipline, belonging, and community among young people.

Example: A district partners with a local El Sistema-inspired program to run an afternoon orchestra.

See also: Ensemble Music, Belonging

docs.title: Elementary School Model
docs.text:
The version of the morning-afternoon structure designed for young children, with short adaptive sessions, close adult supervision, and much hands-on and play-based activity.

Example: First graders use the adaptive reading program in 15-minute sessions between read-alouds and centers.

See also: Grade-Level Design

docs.title: Embedded Simulation
docs.text:
An interactive model placed directly within a textbook page that students can manipulate to see how a system behaves.

Example: A predator-prey simulation inside an ecology chapter where students change birth rates and watch populations change.

See also: MicroSim, Browser-Based Simulation

docs.title: Empathy
docs.text:
The ability to understand and share the feelings of another person.

See also: Perspective Taking, Social-Emotional Learning

docs.title: Endings and Losses
docs.text:
The first phase of Bridges' model, in which people let go of old ways, roles, and identities and may grieve what they lose.

See also: Bridges' Transition Model

docs.title: Energy-Efficient Learning
docs.text:
The design principle of choosing the approach that achieves a learning goal with the least computing, which also lowers cost, environmental footprint, and dependence on a connection.

Example: Serving prewritten explanations and reserving live chat for stuck students cuts energy use sharply.

See also: AI Energy Use, Selective Chatbot Use

docs.title: Ensemble Music
docs.text:
Music performed by a group of musicians playing or singing together, such as a choir, band, or orchestra.

Each player has to listen to and adjust to the others, which builds coordination and belonging.

See also: Music Education, El Sistema

docs.title: Equity of Access
docs.text:
Whether all students, regardless of income, location, disability, or language, can actually use a program or resource.

Example: A district checks that students with visual impairments can use every MicroSim with a screen reader.

See also: Educational Equity, Digital Divide

docs.title: Espoused Values
docs.text:
The goals, values, and beliefs an organization states publicly, which may or may not match how people actually behave.

Example: A mission statement promising "every child known by name" in a school where counselors serve 500 students each.

See also: Schein's Culture Model, Basic Assumptions

docs.title: Estonia AI Leap
docs.text:
Estonia's national program, launched in 2025, giving secondary students and teachers access to AI learning tools along with teacher training, building on the country's earlier school-technology success.

It shows a school system adopting AI on purpose, with a plan, training, and public support.

See also: National AI Adoption, Capacity Building

docs.title: Evaluating Result Claims
docs.text:
The habit of testing any statement about what a school, program, or product achieved, by checking evidence level, effect size, who reported it, and whether it was peer reviewed, before believing or repeating it.

Example: A board asks where Unbound Academy students started before accepting a claim that they learn 2.8 times faster.

See also: Self-Reported Results, Independent Evaluation, Preprint

docs.title: Evidence Evaluation
docs.text:
Judging the quality, relevance, and reliability of information offered to support a claim.

Example: A student weighs a peer-reviewed study more heavily than a product's own website.

See also: Critical Thinking, Evaluating Result Claims

docs.title: Evidence-Based Practice
docs.text:
An approach to decisions in which educators choose methods and programs that have been shown, through rigorous research, to improve student outcomes.

Example: A district chooses a tutoring program because two independent randomized studies showed reading gains.

See also: Randomized Controlled Trial, Evaluating Result Claims

docs.title: Exponential Growth
docs.text:
Growth in which a quantity increases by a constant factor over each equal period of time, so that it doubles repeatedly and rises faster and faster.

Example: A horizon of 1 hour that doubles every five months becomes 2, 4, 8, and then 16 hours over twenty months.

Contrast with: Linear Growth

See also: Doubling Time

docs.title: Falling AI Costs
docs.text:
The trend of the price for a given level of AI performance declining steeply over time.

Example: A task that cost several dollars of computing to run through an AI model a few years ago costs a few cents today.

See also: AI Inference Cost, Falling Production Cost

docs.title: Falling Production Cost
docs.text:
The decline in the cost of creating instructional content as AI tools take over much of the drafting, coding, and formatting work.

Example: An interactive textbook that might once have cost hundreds of thousands of dollars can now be produced by a small team.

See also: Content Creation Cost, Content Commoditization

docs.title: Family Communication
docs.text:
The regular, two-way exchange of information between a school and its students' families.

Example: A monthly family night where parents try the adaptive textbook and ask questions.

See also: Communicating Before Rumors, Family Trust

docs.title: Family Trust
docs.text:
The confidence that parents and guardians have that a school will protect their child and use the child's data only in ways they understand and accept.

Example: inBloom closed after parents pushed back, showing what happens when family trust is not built first.

See also: Trust Paradox, inBloom

docs.title: Fear of Job Loss
docs.text:
Worry among staff that a new technology or model will eliminate or shrink their positions.

Example: Teachers ask whether adaptive textbooks mean the district will hire fewer of them.

See also: Self Concerns, Teacher Union

docs.title: Feedback Loop
docs.text:
A cycle in which the result of an action returns to influence the same action, either strengthening it (reinforcing) or counteracting it (balancing).

Example: Early success raises teachers' confidence, which leads to more use of the tool, which brings more success.

See also: Systems Thinking, Causal Loop Diagram

docs.title: FERPA
docs.text:
The Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act, a U.S. federal law that protects the privacy of student education records and gives parents, and students at age 18, rights over them.

See also: COPPA, Student Data Privacy

docs.title: Finland's Phenomenon Learning
docs.text:
Finland's practice of having students study real-world topics across several subjects at once, often in groups, as part of its national curriculum.

It is one of the book's examples of an afternoon model that already works.

See also: Phenomenon-Based Learning, Collaboration

docs.title: Five Innovation Attributes
docs.text:
Rogers' five characteristics that affect how quickly an innovation is adopted: relative advantage, compatibility, complexity, trialability, and observability.

Example: A tool that is clearly better, fits current routines, is simple, can be tried for a week, and shows visible results spreads fast.

See also: Relative Advantage, Trialability

docs.title: Five-Level Textbook Model
docs.text:
McCreary's framework, modeled on the SAE J3016 driving-automation levels, that classifies textbooks into five levels: static, interactive, adaptive, chatbot, and autonomous AI.

It gives schools a shared vocabulary for buying decisions, policy, and expectations.

See also: Level 1 Static Textbook, Level Classification, SAE J3016 Standard

docs.title: Five-Month Doubling
docs.text:
The book's planning figure for AI progress: the 50 percent time horizon of leading AI models has been doubling about every five months, based on METR's measurements.

The exact estimate varies with the models and period measured, so the book treats it as a planning figure, not a constant of nature.

Example: Over a four-year planning window, about ten doublings would multiply the task horizon roughly a thousandfold if the trend held.

See also: METR, Doubling Time, Trend Extrapolation

docs.title: Forecast Uncertainty
docs.text:
The range of possible outcomes around a prediction, reflecting doubt about the data, the model, and whether past trends continue.

Example: If the doubling time is really seven months instead of five, the horizon in four years is much shorter than the central estimate.

See also: Prediction Failure Scenario, Planning Under Uncertainty

docs.title: Formative Assessment
docs.text:
Checking of student understanding during learning, used to adjust teaching and give feedback rather than to assign a final grade.

Example: A three-question exit ticket at the end of class that tells the teacher who needs help tomorrow.

Contrast with: Summative Assessment

docs.title: Foundational Concept
docs.text:
A concept in a learning graph that has no prerequisites within the course and serves as a starting point for later concepts.

See also: Concept Node, Prerequisite Concept

docs.title: Free Textbook
docs.text:
A textbook available to students and schools at no charge, often because it is openly licensed or funded by a government or foundation.

See also: Open Educational Resource, Universal Textbook Access

docs.title: Freed-Up School Time
docs.text:
The hours of the school day released when academic work takes less time, which a school then has to plan to use well.

Example: A school gains about three hours each afternoon and fills them with projects, arts, and sports.

See also: Pro-Social Afternoon, Unstructured Afternoon Drift

docs.title: Full Personalization
docs.text:
Instruction in which content, sequence, pace, examples, and style are all fitted to one individual student.

Example: Two students studying the same topic see different explanations, examples, and practice sets.

See also: Level 5 Autonomous Textbook, Personalized Pacing

docs.title: Fullan's Educational Change
docs.text:
Michael Fullan's body of work on how change happens in schools and school systems, stressing the meaning of change for teachers, capacity building, and coherence.

Example: A district focuses on a few connected priorities and invests in teacher skill instead of launching many initiatives.

See also: Coherence Framework, Capacity Building, Implementation Dip

docs.title: Gap Filling
docs.text:
Identifying and teaching the specific earlier concepts a student missed, so they can succeed with current material.

Example: The system traces a student's algebra errors back to negative numbers and assigns a short review there.

See also: Learning Gap, Learning Graph

docs.title: GDPR
docs.text:
The General Data Protection Regulation, the European Union law that governs how personal data is collected, used, and stored, with strong rights for individuals.

See also: FERPA, Data Minimization

docs.title: Generate Once Serve Many
docs.text:
A delivery model in which AI helps create content one time, people review it, and the finished content is then served to every student as ordinary web pages.

The costly creation step happens once, while the cheap serving step happens many times.

Example: A set of MicroSims written once with AI is used by a million students without any further AI cost.

Contrast with: Real-Time Content Generation

See also: Low-Cost Adaptive Design

docs.title: Generative AI
docs.text:
Artificial intelligence that produces new content, such as text, images, audio, or code, in response to a prompt.

See also: Large Language Model, AI-Generated Content

docs.title: Governance Readiness
docs.text:
The extent to which a school or district has the policies, roles, skills, and processes in place to manage student data and AI tools responsibly before adopting them.

Example: A district with no data-retention policy is not ready to adopt a Level 3 textbook.

See also: Data Governance, School Readiness Assessment

docs.title: Grade-Level Design
docs.text:
Adapting the structure and balance of the school day to the developmental needs of students at a particular age or grade band.

Example: Younger children get shorter screen sessions and more play, while older students get longer independent projects.

See also: Elementary School Model, Middle School Model, High School Model

docs.title: Graduated Regulation
docs.text:
Rules that impose stronger requirements as a technology's capability and risk increase, rather than treating every product the same.

Example: A district requires a privacy review only for products at Level 3 and above.

See also: Level-Specific Policy

docs.title: Grammar of Schooling
docs.text:
Historians David Tyack and Larry Cuban's term for the stable, taken-for-granted structures of schools, such as age-graded classes, periods, subjects, and grades, that resist reform.

Example: A school adopts adaptive software but keeps every student in fixed 50-minute periods by age.

See also: Reform Without Real Change, Industrial-Era School Model

docs.title: Graphic Novel Scene
docs.text:
A short sequence of comic-style panels, with drawings and dialogue, that tells part of a story visually.

Example: A six-panel scene showing a student stuck on a problem, getting a hint from a tutor, and solving it.

See also: Illustrated Story, Storytelling

docs.title: Growth of Level 2 Textbooks
docs.text:
The increasing number of interactive textbooks being published, driven by AI tools that make simulations, learning graphs, and quizzes cheap to create.

Example: A teacher builds a free interactive textbook for her course in a summer using AI tools.

See also: Level 2 Interactive Textbook, Intelligent Textbook Movement

docs.title: Guided AI vs Open AI
docs.text:
The contrast between a tutor designed with guardrails for a learning purpose and an unrestricted general-purpose chatbot, even when both run on the same underlying model.

Example: The same GPT-4 model hurt exam scores when open and caused little harm when restricted to hints.

See also: Design Over Raw AI Power, Open Chatbot Access

docs.title: Guiding Coalition
docs.text:
A group with enough authority, expertise, credibility, and leadership to lead a change effort, the second of Kotter's steps.

Example: A team of the principal, two respected teachers, a parent leader, and a union representative.

See also: Kotter's Eight Steps, Change Agent

docs.title: Hands-On Learning
docs.text:
Learning through physically doing, making, or manipulating materials, rather than only reading or listening.

Example: Students learn about circuits by wiring a battery, switch, and bulb.

See also: Maker Space, Constructionism

docs.title: Harvard Physics AI Tutor
docs.text:
A 2024-2025 randomized study (Kestin et al.) in which Harvard introductory physics students using a carefully designed AI tutor learned more, in less time, than students in an instructor-led active-learning class.

Its lesson is that a tutor built on proven teaching practices can make a shorter academic morning work.

See also: AI Tutor, Design Over Raw AI Power

docs.title: High School Model
docs.text:
The version of the morning-afternoon structure designed for teenagers, with more independent academic work and afternoons that may include internships, advanced projects, and community service.

Example: Eleventh graders finish academics by late morning and spend afternoons on internships and capstone projects.

See also: Grade-Level Design

docs.title: High Tech High
docs.text:
A network of public charter schools in San Diego known for project-based learning, in which students work in teams on real projects and present them at public exhibitions.

It shows the pro-social afternoon is already proven in practice.

See also: Project-Based Learning, Public Exhibition

docs.title: Higher-Order Thinking
docs.text:
Mental work at the upper levels of Bloom's Taxonomy, such as analyzing, evaluating, and creating, that goes beyond recalling or restating information.

Example: Students compare two news reports of the same event and judge which one gives stronger evidence.

See also: Critical Thinking, Bloom's Taxonomy

docs.title: Hints Instead of Answers
docs.text:
A tutoring design in which the AI responds to a stuck student with a clue or question that points toward the next step, rather than giving the solution.

In the Turkish study this design removed most of the harm that open AI access caused.

See also: AI Guardrails, Productive Struggle

docs.title: Hiring for New Roles
docs.text:
Recruiting and selecting staff for positions created or reshaped by a change, using criteria that match the new work.

Example: A school interviews teacher candidates by watching them coach a small group.

See also: Staffing Model, Changing Teacher Role

docs.title: History of EdTech
docs.text:
The record of technologies introduced into schools over time, such as radio, film, television, computers, the internet, and tablets, and how each met or fell short of its promises.

Example: Television was promised in the 1950s to transform classrooms, yet most lessons stayed teacher-led.

See also: EdTech Hype Waves, Reform Without Real Change

docs.title: Holistic Plus Micro Change
docs.text:
The combination of a whole-organization plan, covering vision, coalition, schedule, and policy, with a continuing stream of microstrategies that carry it out person by person.

The large plan gives direction and removes structural obstacles, while the small actions build skills, trust, and habits.

See also: Whole-Organization Change, Microstrategy

docs.title: Human Connection
docs.text:
A relationship or bond of understanding, care, and trust between people.

Example: A mentor who has known a student for three years notices when something is wrong at home.

See also: Belonging, Skills That Need People

docs.title: Human Working Time
docs.text:
The time a skilled person typically needs to complete a given task, used as the yardstick for measuring how long a task is.

Example: Writing and testing a small data-cleaning script might take an experienced programmer about 45 minutes of human working time.

See also: Task Horizon

docs.title: Hype Cycle
docs.text:
Gartner's model of how expectations for a new technology rise to an inflated peak, fall into disillusionment, and then recover gradually to a stable level of real productivity.

Example: Interactive whiteboards were praised, then criticized as underused, then settled into ordinary use.

See also: Peak of Inflated Expectations, Trough of Disillusionment, EdTech Hype Waves

docs.title: IEEE Learning Standards
docs.text:
Standards for learning technology developed by committees of the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers, covering topics such as learning objects, metadata, and learner records.

See also: Interoperability Standards, xAPI

docs.title: Illustrated Story
docs.text:
A story told through text combined with pictures that show key moments, characters, or settings.

See also: Graphic Novel Scene, Storytelling

docs.title: Immediate Feedback
docs.text:
Information about the correctness or quality of a response given right after the response, so the learner can adjust before errors become habits.

Example: A MicroSim shows a student at once that her predicted pendulum period was too long and why.

See also: Formative Assessment, Adaptive Learning

docs.title: Impact Concerns
docs.text:
Later CBAM concerns focused on how an innovation affects students and how it could be improved.

Example: "Are my English learners benefiting as much as the others?"

See also: Stages of Concern

docs.title: Implementation Dip
docs.text:
A temporary drop in performance and confidence that commonly occurs when people first use a new practice, before improvement appears.

Example: Test scores slip in the first semester of the new schedule and recover by year's end.

See also: Managing Expectations, Neutral Zone

docs.title: IMS Global Standards
docs.text:
Education technology specifications, now maintained by the organization 1EdTech, that define how learning tools, platforms, and data systems connect and share information.

See also: Interoperability Standards

docs.title: inBloom
docs.text:
A roughly 100 million dollar, Gates Foundation-funded project to store and share student data across states, which closed in 2014 after parents pushed back over privacy.

Its lesson is that any learning-record system needs family trust and clear data-ownership rules from the start.

See also: Family Trust, Data Ownership, Learning Record Store

docs.title: Independent Evaluation
docs.text:
An assessment of a program's results carried out by researchers or organizations with no financial or reputational stake in the outcome.

Example: A university research team, not the vendor, measures a reading program's effect in 20 schools.

Contrast with: Self-Reported Results

See also: Program Evaluation

docs.title: Industrial-Era School Model
docs.text:
The pattern of schooling that took shape in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, organized around age-based grades, fixed bell schedules, uniform pacing, and teacher-led instruction to large groups.

Example: A high school where every ninth grader moves between rooms at the sound of a bell and covers the same chapter on the same day.

See also: Age-Based Grade Levels, Bell Schedule, Grammar of Schooling

docs.title: Informed Consent
docs.text:
Agreement given by a person, or a parent for a child, after receiving a clear explanation of what will happen, including what data is collected, how it is used, and the risks.

Example: A plain-language form explains the tutoring pilot's data use and lets families opt in or out.

See also: Family Trust, Student-Controlled Data

docs.title: Innovation
docs.text:
An idea, practice, or object that is perceived as new by the person or group considering it.

See also: Diffusion of Innovations

docs.title: Innovation Configuration
docs.text:
A description, usually a map, of an innovation's essential components and, for each, the range of ways it may be carried out from ideal to unacceptable.

It exists because two teachers can both say they use a program while doing very different things.

See also: Concerns-Based Adoption Model, Levels of Use

docs.title: Innovators
docs.text:
The first, small group of people to take up a new idea, usually venturesome and willing to accept risk and failure.

See also: Early Adopters, Technology Adoption Curve

docs.title: Instructional Coaching
docs.text:
Ongoing, job-embedded support in which an experienced educator helps teachers improve through modeling, observation, feedback, and reflection.

Example: A coach co-teaches a lesson, then debriefs with the teacher about what worked.

See also: Professional Development, Capacity Building

docs.title: Intelligent Textbook
docs.text:
A digital textbook that goes beyond fixed text by adding interactive, adaptive, or AI-driven features such as simulations, learning graphs, progress tracking, or conversational tutoring.

Example: An online geometry book with MicroSims on each page and a learning graph that suggests the next concept to study.

See also: Five-Level Textbook Model, Level 2 Interactive Textbook

docs.title: Intelligent Textbook Movement
docs.text:
The growing effort, which began in earnest in 2025, to produce open, interactive, and adaptive textbooks with the help of AI.

Example: Authors and teachers publishing free Level 2 textbooks built with MicroSims and learning graphs.

See also: Intelligent Textbook, Growth of Level 2 Textbooks

docs.title: Interactive Visualization
docs.text:
A chart, diagram, or graphic that responds to user input, such as clicking, hovering, or dragging, to reveal or change information.

See also: MicroSim, Embedded Simulation

docs.title: Internet Connectivity
docs.text:
Whether a student or school has a reliable connection to the internet fast enough for the learning tools in use.

Example: A rural school whose bandwidth slows to a crawl when every class goes online at once.

See also: Offline Access, Digital Divide

docs.title: Interoperability Standards
docs.text:
Agreed technical specifications that let products from different makers exchange data and work together.

Example: A standard lets a MicroSim launch inside any compliant LMS and return a score.

See also: IMS Global Standards, IEEE Learning Standards, xAPI

docs.title: Intrinsic Motivation
docs.text:
The drive to do an activity because it is interesting, enjoyable, or meaningful in itself, rather than for grades, rewards, or to avoid punishment.

Example: A student who keeps reading about volcanoes at home because she wants to know why they erupt.

See also: Curiosity, Student Engagement

docs.title: K-12 Education
docs.text:
The system of primary and secondary schooling that runs from kindergarten through twelfth grade, typically serving children from about age five to about age eighteen.

See also: Education, Age-Based Grade Levels

docs.title: Khanmigo
docs.text:
Khan Academy's AI tutor, launched in 2023, built to guide students with questions rather than give answers and rolled out in many districts; early versions made math mistakes and some students used it less than expected.

Its lesson is that careful design still meets the reality of classroom use.

See also: Socratic Questioning, Level 4 Chatbot Textbook

docs.title: Kotter's Eight Steps
docs.text:
John Kotter's ordered sequence for leading organizational change: create urgency, build a guiding coalition, form a vision, communicate it, remove obstacles, generate short-term wins, build on change, and anchor it in culture.

Example: A superintendent uses the steps as the outline of a three-year change plan.

See also: Sense of Urgency, Guiding Coalition, Short-Term Wins

docs.title: Laggards
docs.text:
The last group to adopt an innovation, often tied to traditional practices and suspicious of change.

Their concerns can point to real problems that deserve an answer.

See also: Late Majority, Resistance to Change

docs.title: Large Language Model
docs.text:
A machine learning system trained on very large amounts of text to predict likely next words, which allows it to answer questions, write, summarize, and hold conversations.

Example: The GPT-4 model used in the Nigeria tutoring pilot is a large language model.

See also: Generative AI, Chatbot, AI Hallucination

docs.title: Late Majority
docs.text:
The large group that adopts an innovation only after most others have, often skeptical and moved by necessity or peer pressure.

See also: Laggards, Early Majority

docs.title: LAUSD Ed Chatbot
docs.text:
An AI chatbot named "Ed" that Los Angeles Unified School District commissioned from the startup AllHere in 2024, committing about 6 million dollars, which failed when the company collapsed within months.

Its lesson is that rushed purchasing and reliance on one unproven vendor put students and their data at risk.

See also: AllHere Collapse, Rushed Procurement Risk

docs.title: LAUSD iPad Rollout
docs.text:
Los Angeles Unified's 2013 plan, budgeted at about 1.3 billion dollars, to give every student an iPad with Pearson curriculum, cancelled amid technical problems, weak curriculum, and a contracting scandal.

Its lesson is that buying devices before planning the teaching wastes money and public trust.

See also: Why School Reforms Fail, Procurement

docs.title: Learning
docs.text:
A lasting change in a person's knowledge, skills, or understanding that results from experience, study, practice, or instruction.

See also: Learning Outcome, Learning Gains

docs.title: Learning Analytics
docs.text:
The collection, analysis, and reporting of data about learners and their activity, used to understand and improve learning and the settings in which it occurs.

Example: A report showing that most students in a unit stall on the same three concepts.

See also: Learning Record Store, Student Progress Dashboard

docs.title: Learning by Building Together
docs.text:
Learning that happens as a group designs and makes something real, so that students teach, question, and correct one another during the work.

Example: A robotics team learns gear ratios while arguing over why its robot is too slow.

See also: Social Constructionism, Project-Based Learning

docs.title: Learning Dependency
docs.text:
A relationship in which understanding one concept requires first understanding another, shown as an arrow in a learning graph.

Example: "Multiplication" has a dependency on "repeated addition."

See also: Prerequisite Concept, Learning Graph

docs.title: Learning Gains
docs.text:
The measured increase in a student's or group's knowledge or skill between two points in time, usually shown by comparing pre-test and post-test scores.

Example: Students scoring 45 percent on a September fractions test and 75 percent in November show a 30-point gain.

See also: Effect Size, Learning Outcome

docs.title: Learning Gap
docs.text:
A difference between what a student is expected to know at a point in their schooling and what the student actually knows, often caused by missed or misunderstood earlier material.

Example: A ninth grader struggling with algebra because he never mastered negative numbers in sixth grade.

See also: Gap Filling, Achievement Gap

docs.title: Learning Graph
docs.text:
A network of the concepts in a course, connected by arrows that show which concepts depend on which, used to plan instruction and suggest what to study next.

Example: A math learning graph shows "equivalent fractions" pointing to "adding fractions with unlike denominators."

See also: Concept Node, Learning Dependency, Directed Acyclic Graph

docs.title: Learning Guide
docs.text:
An adult who supports students' motivation, effort, and progress and runs workshops and projects, rather than lecturing, as in AI-first schools.

Example: Alpha School's adult guides support students during the morning and lead afternoon workshops.

See also: Alpha Adult Guides, Changing Teacher Role

docs.title: Learning Management System
docs.text:
Software that schools use to deliver course materials, assignments, and grades, and to organize communication between teachers and students.

See also: Interoperability Standards, Learning Record Store

docs.title: Learning Organization
docs.text:
Peter Senge's term for an organization in which people continually expand their capacity, learn together, and adapt as a group.

Example: A school where teams review student data each week and adjust their practice together.

See also: Senge's Five Disciplines, Team Learning

docs.title: Learning Outcome
docs.text:
A statement of what a student will be able to know or do after completing a lesson, unit, or course, written so that it can be observed and assessed.

Example: "Students will be able to compare two fractions with unlike denominators and explain their reasoning."

See also: Bloom's Taxonomy, Curriculum

docs.title: Learning Path
docs.text:
An ordered sequence of concepts or activities that a student follows to reach a learning goal, consistent with the dependencies in a learning graph.

Example: A path from "ratios" through "unit rates" and "percent" to "percent increase and decrease."

See also: Path Recommendation, Next-Concept Selection

docs.title: Learning Record
docs.text:
The stored collection of xAPI statements about one learner or one activity, forming a history of learning events over time.

Example: Everything Maya did in her math book over the semester, in order.

See also: Learning Record Store, Mastery Data

docs.title: Learning Record Store
docs.text:
A system that receives, stores, and returns xAPI statements about learners' activities.

The book proposes it as the place where student progress lives, under rules that let students and families control the data.

See also: xAPI, Learning Record, Student-Controlled Data

docs.title: Lecture-Based Teaching
docs.text:
A form of instruction in which an instructor talks to a group of students, who listen and take notes with limited interaction, for most of a class period.

Example: A high school history class where the teacher speaks from slides for 40 of the 50 minutes.

Contrast with: Project-Based Learning, Teacher as Facilitator

docs.title: Legitimate Concern
docs.text:
An objection to a change that rests on a real risk or problem and should shape the plan.

Example: A parent asks how the school will protect her child's data, exposing a gap in the vendor contract.

See also: Responding with Empathy, Resistance to Change

docs.title: Lesson From a Case
docs.text:
The transferable point that a case teaches about situations beyond itself.

Example: From inBloom: student data projects fail without the trust of families from the start.

See also: Real Case Study, Risk-and-Response Framework

docs.title: Level 1 Static Textbook
docs.text:
A textbook with fixed content and no interactivity, such as a traditional print book or a PDF.

See also: Print Textbook, Level 2 Interactive Textbook

docs.title: Level 2 Cost Per Student
docs.text:
The yearly cost per student of providing an interactive textbook served as ordinary web pages, which is very low because hosting static pages is nearly free.

Example: The book's illustration uses about 1.80 dollars per student for content and hosting under the penny-per-day target.

See also: Penny-Per-Day Vision, Level 3 Cost Per Student

docs.title: Level 2 Interactive Textbook
docs.text:
A textbook that adds interactive features, such as MicroSims, learning graphs, embedded simulations, and recommended learning paths, without storing individual student records.

Example: An online physics book where students drag sliders to change a ramp's angle and watch the motion change.

See also: MicroSim, Level 3 Adaptive Textbook

docs.title: Level 3 Adaptive Textbook
docs.text:
A textbook that changes the content and sequence it presents based on each student's goals and recorded progress, which requires storing student records.

It marks the privacy inflection point.

See also: Privacy Inflection Point, Adaptive Learning

docs.title: Level 3 Cost Per Student
docs.text:
The yearly cost per student of an adaptive textbook, which adds the cost of storing and securing student records, governance, and privacy compliance to the interactive content.

Example: A district adds the cost of a Learning Record Store and a privacy review to its Level 2 budget.

See also: Level 2 Cost Per Student, Level 4 Cost Per Student

docs.title: Level 4 Chatbot Textbook
docs.text:
A textbook that offers conversational tutoring through a chatbot built on a large language model, in addition to adaptive features.

Example: A student types "why does this step work?" and a tutor built into the book explains it with a hint.

See also: Conversational Tutoring, AI Tutor

docs.title: Level 4 Cost Per Student
docs.text:
The yearly cost per student of a chatbot textbook, which adds the ongoing cost of running a large language model for each student conversation.

Example: A district finds that live chat for every student costs far more than Level 3, so it limits chat to students who are stuck.

See also: AI Inference Cost, Selective Chatbot Use

docs.title: Level 5 Autonomous Textbook
docs.text:
A textbook that generates content in real time and fully personalizes instruction for each student without a fixed prewritten text.

Example: A system that writes a new explanation, example, and simulation tailored to one student's interests on the spot.

See also: Real-Time Content Generation, Full Personalization

docs.title: Level Adoption Timeline
docs.text:
An estimate of when products at each level become available and widely used in schools.

Example: Level 2 textbooks are already appearing in growing numbers, while Level 5 products are expected later.

See also: Growth of Level 2 Textbooks, Levels 3 to 5 on the Horizon

docs.title: Level Classification
docs.text:
The act of assigning a textbook or AI product to one of the five levels according to the capabilities it actually delivers.

Example: A reviewer places a product at Level 2 because it has simulations but stores no student records.

See also: Product Level Assessment, Five-Level Textbook Model

docs.title: Level Terminology Precision
docs.text:
The discipline of using the level names exactly as defined, so that a claim of a given level means the same thing wherever it is made.

Example: A district policy refuses to call a product "adaptive" unless it changes content from stored student records.

See also: Shared Vocabulary, AI-Powered Marketing Claims

docs.title: Level-Specific Policy
docs.text:
A school or district rule that sets different requirements for products at different levels of the five-level model.

Example: A policy requiring any Level 3 or higher product to pass a privacy and data-governance review before use.

See also: Graduated Regulation, Procurement Criteria

docs.title: Levels 3 to 5 on the Horizon
docs.text:
The book's description of adaptive, chatbot, and autonomous AI textbooks as existing in early form today and expected to become widely available over the next several years.

Example: A district notes that a few adaptive math products exist now and plans its privacy policy before more arrive.

See also: Level Adoption Timeline, Level 3 Adaptive Textbook

docs.title: Levels of Driving Automation
docs.text:
The numbered categories in SAE J3016 that describe how much of the driving task a vehicle performs, from human-only driving to fully self-driving.

They gave the car industry a shared vocabulary, graduated regulation, and realistic expectations while the technology changed quickly.

See also: SAE J3016 Standard, Shared Vocabulary

docs.title: Levels of Use
docs.text:
The CBAM scale describing how a person actually uses an innovation, from non-use and preparation through routine use to refinement and renewal.

Example: An observer finds a teacher at a mechanical level, following the manual step by step.

See also: Concerns-Based Adoption Model, Innovation Configuration

docs.title: Lewin's Change Model
docs.text:
Kurt Lewin's three-stage model of change: unfreezing current habits, moving to new ones, and refreezing the new habits so they last.

Example: A school builds a case for change, pilots a new schedule, and then writes it into policy.

See also: Unfreeze Stage, Change Stage, Refreeze Stage

docs.title: Life-Skills Workshop
docs.text:
A structured session that teaches practical abilities for everyday adult life, such as budgeting, cooking, public speaking, or first aid.

Example: Alpha School devotes afternoon time to life-skills workshops led by adult guides.

See also: Afternoon Program, Alpha School

docs.title: Limits to AI Growth
docs.text:
Factors that could slow or stop the improvement of AI, such as limits on computing, energy, training data, money, or regulation.

Example: A shortage of power for new data centers could slow the trend in task horizons.

See also: Compute Scaling, Prediction Failure Scenario

docs.title: Linear Growth
docs.text:
Growth in which a quantity increases by the same fixed amount in each equal period of time, producing a straight line on an ordinary graph.

Contrast with: Exponential Growth

docs.title: Log-Scale Chart
docs.text:
A chart with one axis on a logarithmic scale, on which steady exponential growth appears as a straight line.

Example: METR's chart of task horizons over time looks like a straight rising line because its vertical axis is logarithmic.

See also: Logarithmic Scale, Exponential Growth

docs.title: Logarithmic Scale
docs.text:
A scale on which each equal step represents multiplication by the same factor, such as 1, 10, 100, 1,000, rather than addition of the same amount.

See also: Log-Scale Chart

docs.title: Long-Running Task
docs.text:
A task that takes a skilled person many hours or days of continuous, multi-step work, requiring planning and error correction along the way.

Example: Designing, writing, and testing a complete unit of interactive lessons is a long-running task.

See also: AI Agent, Task Horizon

docs.title: Low-Cost Adaptive Design
docs.text:
The book's arrangement of static pages, browser simulations, a learning graph, xAPI records, and a Learning Record Store, with AI used mainly to create content once, to personalize learning cheaply.

Example: A district delivers adaptive math to 12,000 students for a few dollars each per year.

See also: Adaptation Without Live AI, Generate Once Serve Many, Affordable Alpha Model

docs.title: Machine Learning
docs.text:
A branch of artificial intelligence in which computer systems improve at a task by finding patterns in data rather than by following rules written by a programmer.

See also: Artificial Intelligence, Large Language Model

docs.title: Maker Space
docs.text:
A room or area equipped with tools and materials where students design, build, and repair physical objects.

Example: A space with 3D printers, hand tools, cardboard, and electronics kits used for afternoon projects.

See also: Hands-On Learning, Constructionism

docs.title: Managing Expectations
docs.text:
Communicating realistically about what a change will deliver, when, and with what difficulties, so people are not discouraged by setbacks.

Example: A principal tells families in advance that results may dip before they rise.

See also: Implementation Dip, Realistic Expectations

docs.title: Mastery Data
docs.text:
Evidence, drawn from a student's stored learning record, of which concepts the student has demonstrated they know.

Adaptation depends on it.

See also: Learning Record, Mastery Threshold

docs.title: Mastery Learning
docs.text:
An approach in which students move to a new topic only after demonstrating a set level of understanding of the current one, with extra time and help given as needed.

Example: A student retakes a different version of a quiz until she scores at least 80 percent before starting the next unit.

See also: Mastery Threshold, Bloom's Two-Sigma Problem

docs.title: Mastery Threshold
docs.text:
The level of performance a student needs to reach to be considered as having learned a concept, such as a minimum score or a number of correct answers in a row.

Example: "Four of five correct on two separate days" is the threshold for each concept in a math book.

See also: Mastery Learning, Mastery Data

docs.title: Mastery-Based Assessment
docs.text:
Assessment that judges whether a student has reached a defined level of understanding on each skill or concept, rather than averaging scores over time.

Example: A report card lists each math concept as "mastered" or "in progress" instead of a single letter grade.

See also: Mastery Learning, Seat Time

docs.title: Matching Strategy to Adopter
docs.text:
Selecting a strategy that fits a person's category on the adoption curve, such as offering early adopters a pilot and late majority members proven results.

Example: Innovators get early access to new tools, while the late majority get a visit to a successful classroom.

See also: Technology Adoption Curve, Matching Strategy to Concern

docs.title: Matching Strategy to Concern
docs.text:
Selecting a microstrategy that answers the specific stage of concern a person actually holds.

Example: A teacher worried about her job gets a conversation about her new role, not another training on the software.

See also: Stages of Concern, Matching Strategy to Adopter

docs.title: Mental Models
docs.text:
Deeply held internal pictures of how the world works that shape how people interpret events and decide what to do.

Example: A teacher who believes "learning happens when I am talking" resists reducing lecture time.

See also: Basic Assumptions, Senge's Five Disciplines

docs.title: METR
docs.text:
An independent research organization (Model Evaluation and Threat Research) that measures what AI systems can do, best known for tracking how long a task, in human working time, AI can complete.

Its finding that this task horizon doubles about every five months is the evidence behind the book's forecast.

See also: Task Horizon, 50 Percent Time Horizon, Five-Month Doubling

docs.title: Microschool
docs.text:
A very small school, often with fewer than 150 students and mixed-age groups, that emphasizes personalized learning and close relationships with a few adults.

Example: Twelve families in a town share a converted storefront where two guides support 30 children of different ages.

See also: AltSchool, Learning Guide

docs.title: MicroSim
docs.text:
A small, focused, browser-based interactive simulation that teaches one concept, designed to be embedded in a textbook page.

Example: A MicroSim with a slider for interest rate that shows how a savings balance grows over 20 years.

See also: Embedded Simulation, Browser-Based Simulation

docs.title: Microstrategy
docs.text:
A small, specific, low-cost action aimed at helping one person or a small group take the next step in a change.

Example: Inviting a hesitant teacher to watch a colleague's ten-minute coaching session.

See also: Holistic Plus Micro Change, Shrinking the First Step

docs.title: Middle School Model
docs.text:
The version of the morning-afternoon structure designed for early adolescents, balancing growing independence in the morning with strong social and exploratory afternoons.

Example: Seventh graders set weekly mastery goals and rotate through clubs every six weeks.

See also: Grade-Level Design

docs.title: Morning Screen-Time Limits
docs.text:
Caps a school sets on how much of the academic morning is spent on a screen and on how long a student works on one without a break.

Example: A school allows no more than about two hours of screen work, with a movement break every 25 to 30 minutes.

See also: Screen Time, Summit Learning

docs.title: Morning-Afternoon Model
docs.text:
The school structure at the core of this book: an academic morning of adaptive, mastery-based learning followed by an afternoon of pro-social activity with other people.

Example: Students work in adaptive textbooks until 11:30 and then rotate through theater, robotics, and sports.

See also: Academic Morning, Pro-Social Afternoon, AI-Native School Day

docs.title: Motivate the Elephant
docs.text:
The Switch framework element of engaging people's emotions, so they feel the need for change and believe they can succeed.

Example: Teachers watch a video of a once-bored student proudly presenting her afternoon project.

See also: Switch Framework, Shrinking the First Step

docs.title: Music Education
docs.text:
Instruction in performing, creating, listening to, and understanding music.

See also: Ensemble Music, Arts Education

docs.title: National AI Adoption
docs.text:
The adoption of AI in education across an entire country's school system, led by national policy.

Example: Estonia's AI Leap paired AI tools with teacher training and built on the country's earlier success with school technology.

See also: Estonia AI Leap, Education Policy

docs.title: Neutral Zone
docs.text:
The middle phase of Bridges' model, a confusing in-between period when the old way is gone but the new way is not yet comfortable.

Example: The first months of a new schedule when routines are unclear and staff feel unsettled.

See also: Bridges' Transition Model, Implementation Dip

docs.title: New Beginnings
docs.text:
The final phase of Bridges' model, in which people take on the new identity, energy, and sense of purpose the change brings.

See also: Bridges' Transition Model

docs.title: Next-Concept Selection
docs.text:
Choosing which concept a student should study next by checking which concepts in the learning graph have all their prerequisites mastered.

Example: Once "ratios" and "division" are mastered, the system offers "unit rates."

See also: Path Recommendation, Learning Graph

docs.title: Nigeria AI Tutoring Pilot
docs.text:
A 2024 World Bank six-week after-school program in Edo State, Nigeria, in which students practiced English with a GPT-4-based tutor while teachers were present, producing large reported gains at very low cost.

Its lesson is that low-cost AI tutoring, with a teacher in the room, can help where resources are scarce.

See also: AI Tutor, Benefits of AI-First Schools

docs.title: Observability
docs.text:
The degree to which the results of an innovation are visible to others.

Example: Students' finished projects displayed in the hallway let other teachers see what the new afternoon produced.

See also: Five Innovation Attributes, Early Visible Results

docs.title: Offline Access
docs.text:
The ability to use learning materials without a live internet connection, for example by downloading pages and simulations in advance.

Example: A student downloads her textbook chapters at school and works on them at home with no internet.

See also: Internet Connectivity, Static Website

docs.title: One-on-One Tutoring
docs.text:
Instruction in which a single tutor works with a single student, adjusting explanations, pace, and practice to that student.

See also: Bloom's Two-Sigma Problem, AI Tutor

docs.title: Open Chatbot Access
docs.text:
Giving students unrestricted use of a general-purpose AI chatbot that will answer any question, including by supplying full solutions.

Example: Students in one arm of the Turkish study could ask the chatbot to solve each practice problem for them.

Contrast with: AI Guardrails

See also: Guided AI vs Open AI

docs.title: Open Educational Resource
docs.text:
A teaching or learning material released under a license that allows anyone to use, adapt, and share it for free.

Example: A free, openly licensed biology textbook that a teacher can download, edit for her class, and repost.

See also: Open License, 5R Permissions

docs.title: Open License
docs.text:
A legal permission from a copyright holder that grants the public the right to use, copy, modify, and share a work under stated conditions.

See also: Creative Commons License, Open Educational Resource

docs.title: OpenBook QR Score
docs.text:
A 0 to 100 rating for open textbooks, from the companion book OER Evaluator, built from ten metrics worth ten points each, five for quality and five for reusability.

Example: A book reported as "QR 65 (Q 32 / R 33)" earned 32 quality points and 33 reusability points.

See also: Quality Subscore, Reusability Subscore, Rising Quality Scores

docs.title: Opinion Leader
docs.text:
A person whose views and behavior informally influence others in a group, so that their adoption of an idea encourages others.

Example: A respected veteran teacher whose endorsement persuades colleagues to try the new textbook.

See also: Early Adopters, Teacher Champion

docs.title: Organizational Change
docs.text:
The process by which an organization alters its structures, practices, culture, or goals.

Example: A school moving from a seven-period day to a morning-afternoon model with new staff roles.

See also: Whole-Organization Change, Lewin's Change Model

docs.title: Organizational Culture
docs.text:
The shared values, beliefs, assumptions, and habits that shape how people in an organization think and behave.

See also: School Culture, Schein's Culture Model

docs.title: Over-Reliance on AI
docs.text:
A pattern in which a person depends on AI so much that they stop building or using their own skills and judgment.

Example: A student who can solve equations only with a chatbot open fails the test given without it.

See also: Cognitive Offloading, Turkish High School Study

docs.title: Parent and Family
docs.text:
The parents, guardians, and other caregivers responsible for a student, who are partners with the school in the child's education and decisions about the child's data.

Example: A family receives a plain-language letter explaining what data the adaptive textbook collects and who can see it.

See also: Family Trust, Family Communication

docs.title: Path Recommendation
docs.text:
A suggestion of which concept or activity a student should study next, based on the order of ideas in a learning graph.

At Level 2 the suggestion depends only on the graph; at Level 3 it also uses the student's record.

See also: Learning Path, Next-Concept Selection

docs.title: Pattern Recognition
docs.text:
Noticing similarities, trends, or regularities among problems or data that help predict outcomes or reuse earlier solutions.

Example: A student notices that every multiple of 9 has digits that add up to a multiple of 9.

See also: Computational Thinking, Abstraction

docs.title: PDF Textbook
docs.text:
A digital textbook distributed as a fixed-layout PDF file that reproduces the printed page with no interactivity.

See also: Level 1 Static Textbook, Digital Textbook

docs.title: Peak of Inflated Expectations
docs.text:
The stage of the hype cycle when publicity and enthusiasm for a technology exceed what it can actually deliver.

Example: Headlines claim an AI tutor will replace teachers within a year.

See also: Hype Cycle, Trough of Disillusionment

docs.title: Peer Observation
docs.text:
A practice in which teachers watch each other teach in order to learn, share ideas, and give supportive feedback.

Example: A teacher visits a colleague's coaching session and borrows her method for grouping students.

See also: Professional Learning Community, Instructional Coaching

docs.title: Penny-Per-Day Vision
docs.text:
The book's cost target of about one cent per student per school day for interactive textbook content and hosting, or roughly 1.80 dollars per student over a 180-day year.

Example: A district of 10,000 students would spend about 18,000 dollars a year on content and hosting at that rate.

See also: Level 2 Cost Per Student, Universal Textbook Access

docs.title: Per-Pupil Spending
docs.text:
The total operating expenditure of a school or district divided by the number of students it serves, used to compare costs across schools and systems.

The book uses the U.S. public average of roughly 15,600 dollars per pupil as the benchmark against AI-first school tuition.

See also: Cost Per Student, Cost Barrier to AI Schools

docs.title: Performance Assessment
docs.text:
Assessment in which students show what they know by completing a real task or producing a product, rather than choosing answers.

Example: Students design and run an experiment and defend their conclusions before a panel.

See also: Portfolio Assessment, Public Exhibition

docs.title: Personal Mastery
docs.text:
Senge's discipline of continually clarifying what one wants to achieve and building the skills to achieve it.

See also: Senge's Five Disciplines, Self-Awareness

docs.title: Personalized Pacing
docs.text:
Adjusting how fast each student moves through material according to how quickly that student masters it.

Example: One student finishes the fractions unit in a week while another takes three, and both reach mastery.

See also: Self-Paced Learning, Adaptive Learning

docs.title: Personally Identifiable Data
docs.text:
Information that identifies a specific person directly, such as a name or ID number, or indirectly when combined with other information.

Example: A birth date plus a school and grade can be enough to identify a single child.

See also: Student Data, FERPA

docs.title: Perspective Taking
docs.text:
Understanding a situation from another person's point of view, including their thoughts, feelings, and reasons.

Example: In a debate, a student argues the side she disagrees with and comes to understand why others hold it.

See also: Empathy, Conflict Resolution

docs.title: Phenomenon-Based Learning
docs.text:
An approach in which students study a real-world event or topic as a whole, drawing on several subjects at once, often in groups.

Example: Students study climate change through its science, economics, geography, and politics in one unit.

See also: Finland's Phenomenon Learning, Project-Based Learning

docs.title: Pilot Classroom
docs.text:
A single classroom where a new practice or tool is tried first, under observation, before wider use.

Example: One sixth-grade class uses the adaptive textbook for a semester while others continue as usual.

See also: Pilot Program, Trialability

docs.title: Pilot Goals
docs.text:
The specific outcomes a trial is meant to test or achieve, stated in advance.

Example: "Students reach grade-level mastery in math in three hours a day or less, with no drop in state test scores."

See also: Pilot Program, Success Measures

docs.title: Pilot Governance
docs.text:
The roles, decision rules, oversight, and reporting arrangements that direct a trial and decide when to adjust, continue, or stop it.

Example: A steering group of parents, teachers, and administrators reviews data each quarter with authority to halt the trial.

See also: Pilot Program, Pilot Risk Checklist

docs.title: Pilot Program
docs.text:
A limited, time-bound trial of a new practice or product in a few settings, used to learn what works before deciding on wider use.

Example: Two schools try the morning-afternoon schedule for one year while the district measures results.

See also: Pilot Goals, Scaling a Pilot, Pilot Classroom

docs.title: Pilot Risk Checklist
docs.text:
A list of known risks a school reviews before and during a trial, with planned responses for each.

Example: Items include screen time, data privacy, vendor stability, afternoon quality, equity of access, and family communication.

See also: Pilot Program, Risk Mitigation

docs.title: Planning Under Uncertainty
docs.text:
Making decisions that remain sound across a range of possible futures, rather than betting everything on a single forecast.

Example: A district pilots the morning-afternoon model in two schools, so it gains whether or not AI improves as fast as predicted.

See also: Prediction Failure Scenario, Pilot Program

docs.title: Planning Window
docs.text:
The span of time over which a decision has to hold up, such as the years a purchase, schedule, or training commitment will be in use.

Example: A district buying laptops it will keep for four years has a four-year planning window for that decision.

See also: Three-to-Four-Year Forecast, Planning Under Uncertainty

docs.title: Plateau of Productivity
docs.text:
The stage of the hype cycle when a technology's real benefits are understood and it is used widely in practical ways.

See also: Hype Cycle

docs.title: Policy Embedding
docs.text:
Writing a new practice into formal policies, budgets, job descriptions, and procedures, so it no longer depends on particular individuals.

Example: The board adopts the morning-afternoon schedule as district policy and funds it in the base budget.

See also: Sustaining Change, Refreeze Stage

docs.title: Portfolio Assessment
docs.text:
Evaluating a student's learning through a collection of their work gathered over time, often with reflections on growth.

Example: A student presents a year's worth of writing drafts, projects, and reflections at a spring conference.

See also: Performance Assessment, Combined Assessment Plan

docs.title: Positive Deviance
docs.text:
A method for finding individuals or groups who get better results than their peers with the same resources, learning what they do differently, and spreading it.

Example: A district studies why one under-resourced school's students gain more on the adaptive textbook than others.

See also: Bright Spots

docs.title: PowerSchool Data Breach
docs.text:
A December 2024 breach at PowerSchool, one of the largest student information system vendors, that exposed records for tens of millions of students and teachers.

It makes the Level 3 privacy threshold concrete: the more centralized student records are, the bigger the target, so minimizing and distributing data reduces harm.

See also: Centralized Student Records, Data Breach, Privacy Inflection Point

docs.title: Pragmatist Buyers
docs.text:
Mainstream adopters who want proven results, references from people like them, and a complete solution before committing.

Example: A principal who asks, "Which schools like mine are using this, and what happened?"

See also: Early Majority, The Chasm

docs.title: Prediction Assumptions
docs.text:
The conditions that need to remain true for a forecast to come true, stated openly so they can be checked.

Example: The forecast assumes the doubling trend continues, costs keep falling, and families trust the tools.

See also: Prediction Failure Scenario, Trend Extrapolation

docs.title: Prediction Failure Scenario
docs.text:
A specific, described way a forecast could turn out wrong, used to test whether a plan still works if it happens.

The book names three: the trend stalls, the benchmarks mislead, and the tools arrive but trust does not.

See also: Prediction Assumptions, Planning Under Uncertainty

docs.title: Preprint
docs.text:
A research paper shared publicly before it has completed formal peer review in a journal.

Example: The "Your Brain on ChatGPT" study and the five-level textbook paper were both released as preprints.

See also: Evaluating Result Claims, Your Brain on ChatGPT

docs.title: Prerequisite Concept
docs.text:
An idea or skill that a student needs to understand before a later idea or skill can be learned successfully.

In a learning graph, prerequisites are the concepts that an arrow points from.

See also: Learning Dependency, Learning Graph

docs.title: Principal
docs.text:
The administrator who leads a single school, responsible for its staff, instruction, student well-being, operations, and relationship with families.

Example: A principal who rewrites the master schedule to create a two-hour afternoon project block.

See also: School Administrator, Change Agent

docs.title: Print Textbook
docs.text:
A textbook produced on paper and bound as a physical book.

See also: Level 1 Static Textbook, Digital Textbook

docs.title: Prior Knowledge
docs.text:
What a student already knows and can do before encountering new material, which shapes how easily and accurately the new material is understood.

Example: A student who already understands multiplication will find area problems easier than one who does not.

See also: Prerequisite Concept, Learning Gap

docs.title: Privacy Inflection Point
docs.text:
The step from Level 2 to Level 3 in the five-level model, where a textbook moves from needing almost no student data to needing detailed learning histories.

From this point on, privacy laws, governance duties, and bias checks apply.

Example: A district can adopt a Level 2 book quickly but runs a full privacy review before adopting a Level 3 book.

See also: Level 3 Adaptive Textbook, Detailed Learning History

docs.title: Private School Tuition
docs.text:
The fee that families pay a privately run school for enrollment, which funds most of the school's operating costs.

Example: Alpha School's yearly tuition ranges from about 40,000 dollars at its original Austin campus to about 65,000 dollars at newer campuses.

See also: Alpha Tuition Range, Cost Barrier to AI Schools

docs.title: Pro-Social Activity
docs.text:
A structured group activity designed to build skills such as cooperation, communication, empathy, and leadership through working with other people.

Example: A mural project where students plan, divide, and paint a wall together.

See also: Pro-Social Behavior, Activity-Skill Matching

docs.title: Pro-Social Afternoon
docs.text:
The second part of the AI-native school day, in which students work with other people on projects, arts, sports, service, and other activities that build human skills.

Example: After a morning of adaptive math and reading, students spend the afternoon rehearsing a play and building a garden.

See also: Morning-Afternoon Model, Skills That Need People

docs.title: Pro-Social Behavior
docs.text:
Voluntary actions intended to benefit other people, such as helping, sharing, cooperating, and comforting.

Example: An older student who stays after practice to help a younger teammate learn a drill.

See also: Pro-Social Activity, Empathy

docs.title: Procurement
docs.text:
The process by which a school or district selects, purchases, and contracts for goods and services.

See also: Procurement Criteria, Vendor Evaluation

docs.title: Procurement Criteria
docs.text:
The specific requirements and standards used to judge products and vendors during purchasing.

Example: Criteria include the product's verified level, privacy terms, data export, accessibility, and cost per student.

See also: Level-Specific Policy, Vendor Evaluation

docs.title: Product Level Assessment
docs.text:
The process a school follows to place a product at a level: gathering documentation and a demonstration, testing what it does for students, identifying its highest defining capability, and recording the result.

Example: A review team finds that a product marketed as "adaptive" does not store progress and records it as Level 2.

See also: Level Classification, Vendor Level Claim

docs.title: Productive Struggle
docs.text:
Effortful work on a problem that is challenging but within reach, in which persistence and mistakes lead to deeper understanding.

AI tools that hand over answers can remove this struggle, which is one reason guardrails matter.

See also: Hints Instead of Answers, Cognitive Offloading

docs.title: Professional Development
docs.text:
Structured learning opportunities that help educators build knowledge and skills for their work.

Example: A summer workshop on running small-group coaching sessions with mastery data.

See also: Instructional Coaching, Staff AI Literacy

docs.title: Professional Learning Community
docs.text:
A group of educators who meet regularly to examine student work and data, share practices, and improve teaching together.

Example: Sixth-grade teachers meet every Wednesday to review mastery data and plan next week's coaching.

See also: Team Learning, Peer Observation
