docs.title: Program Evaluation
docs.text:
The systematic collection and analysis of evidence to judge whether a program is carried out as planned and achieves its intended outcomes.

Example: An outside evaluator compares pilot and non-pilot schools on mastery, attendance, and family satisfaction.

See also: Independent Evaluation, Success Measures

docs.title: Progress Tracking
docs.text:
Recording and displaying what a student has completed and mastered over time, so the student and adults can see advancement toward goals.

Example: A dashboard shows a student has mastered 42 of 60 concepts in the unit.

See also: Student Progress Dashboard, Mastery Data

docs.title: Project-Based Learning
docs.text:
An approach in which students learn by working over an extended period on a complex, real-world question or challenge, ending in a product or presentation.

Example: Students spend six weeks designing a plan to reduce food waste in the cafeteria and present it to the principal.

See also: Driving Question, Public Exhibition, High Tech High

docs.title: Public Exhibition
docs.text:
An event at which students present their completed work to an audience beyond their teacher, such as families, community members, or experts.

Example: An evening where eighth graders show their solar-powered models to parents and local engineers.

See also: Project-Based Learning, Performance Assessment

docs.title: Public School Funding
docs.text:
The money that governments, mainly local, state, and federal, provide to operate public schools, covering staff, buildings, materials, transportation, and services.

Example: A district's budget combines local property taxes, state aid based on enrollment, and federal grants for special education.

See also: Per-Pupil Spending, Budget Reallocation

docs.title: Publisher Business Model
docs.text:
The way a textbook company earns revenue, traditionally by charging for each copy or license of content that is costly to create and protected by copyright.

Example: A publisher charges per student per year for access to its online math curriculum.

See also: Textbook Publisher, Value Beyond Content

docs.title: Publisher Disruption
docs.text:
The pressure on traditional textbook companies as AI-made, low-cost, and open content undercuts their main product.

Example: A publisher's sales fall when districts adopt free interactive textbooks, and it shifts to selling training and assessment services.

See also: Content Commoditization, Value Beyond Content

docs.title: Quality Subscore
docs.text:
The half of the OpenBook QR Score, from 0 to 50, formed by summing five metrics that show how well a resource helps learners learn.

Example: A book with clear writing and good practice questions but no accessibility descriptions might earn a 35 of 50.

See also: OpenBook QR Score, Reusability Subscore

docs.title: Randomized Controlled Trial
docs.text:
A study in which participants are assigned by chance to a group that receives an intervention or to a comparison group that does not, so differences in outcomes can be attributed to the intervention.

Example: The Turkish high school study randomly assigned students to open AI access, guarded AI access, or no AI.

See also: Effect Size, A/B Testing

docs.title: Real Case Study
docs.text:
An account of an actual school, program, or study, based on reported facts and named sources, analyzed to draw lessons.

Example: The inBloom shutdown, described with its funding, closure, and lesson about family trust.

See also: Case Study Method, Composite Story

docs.title: Real-Time Content Generation
docs.text:
The production of new instructional text, examples, problems, or media at the moment a student needs them, rather than writing them in advance.

Example: A system creates a fresh word problem about soccer for a student who just said she likes soccer.

See also: Level 5 Autonomous Textbook, Generate Once Serve Many

docs.title: Realistic Expectations
docs.text:
Beliefs about what a technology can and cannot do that match its actual, demonstrated capabilities.

Example: Parents understand that a Level 2 textbook offers simulations but will not hold a conversation with their child.

See also: Managing Expectations, Hype Cycle

docs.title: Redesign Not Policing
docs.text:
The principle that a school responds to AI by changing what and how it assesses, rather than by trying to catch students with detection software.

Example: A teacher replaces a take-home report with an in-class presentation and questions.

See also: Assessment Redesign, Detector False Positives

docs.title: Reduce the Negatives
docs.text:
The book's goal of identifying the harms AI-first schooling can cause and taking specific steps to prevent or limit them.

Example: A school caps morning screen time and protects afternoon group activities to avoid the Summit Learning backlash.

See also: Strengthen the Positives, Risk Mitigation

docs.title: Reduced Direct Instruction
docs.text:
A smaller share of the school day spent on teacher-led presentation to the whole class, made possible when adaptive materials deliver much of the content.

Example: A teacher gives a ten-minute mini-lesson instead of a 45-minute lecture, then coaches small groups.

See also: Direct Instruction, Changing Teacher Role

docs.title: Reform Without Real Change
docs.text:
The pattern in which an innovation is adopted in name but leaves the actual work of teaching unchanged.

Example: The adaptive software is running on every laptop, and the teacher's lecture goes on as before.

See also: Grammar of Schooling, Why School Reforms Fail

docs.title: Refreeze Stage
docs.text:
The final stage of Lewin's model, in which new behaviors are stabilized through policies, structures, and routines so they become the new normal.

Example: The board writes the morning-afternoon schedule into district policy and the hiring plan.

See also: Lewin's Change Model, Policy Embedding

docs.title: Relationship Skills
docs.text:
The abilities to build and keep healthy connections with others, including communicating, cooperating, resolving conflict, and asking for or offering help.

Example: A student apologizes to a teammate after a disagreement and they agree on how to work together.

See also: Social-Emotional Learning, Conflict Resolution

docs.title: Relative Advantage
docs.text:
The degree to which an innovation is seen as better than the idea or practice it replaces.

See also: Five Innovation Attributes

docs.title: Removing Obstacles
docs.text:
Clearing structures, policies, or practices that block people from acting on a change vision.

Example: The district waives a seat-time rule so students can earn credit by showing mastery.

See also: Kotter's Eight Steps, Shape the Path

docs.title: Resistance to Change
docs.text:
Opposition, reluctance, or passive non-cooperation by people asked to change how they work.

It often signals real concerns that deserve attention, not simply stubbornness.

See also: Sources of Resistance, Legitimate Concern

docs.title: Responding with Empathy
docs.text:
Answering resistance by first listening to and acknowledging people's feelings and concerns, before explaining or persuading.

Example: A principal says, "I hear that you're worried about losing your classroom; let's talk about what your role would be."

See also: Legitimate Concern, Empathy

docs.title: Responsible AI with Minors
docs.text:
The design and use of AI systems for children with added protections for privacy, safety, and development, recognizing that children cannot fully judge risks or consent for themselves.

Example: A tutor for young students that keeps no chat logs beyond the session and never asks for personal details.

See also: Age-Appropriate AI Design, COPPA

docs.title: Retrieval Practice
docs.text:
A learning strategy in which students recall information from memory, for example through quizzes or flashcards, which strengthens long-term retention more than rereading.

Example: A student closes the book and writes down everything she remembers about photosynthesis before checking.

See also: Spaced Practice, Formative Assessment

docs.title: Reusability Subscore
docs.text:
The half of the OpenBook QR Score, from 0 to 50, formed by summing five metrics that show how easily others can find, change, and reuse a resource.

Example: A book in editable web format with an open license and good metadata earns more of these points than a locked PDF.

See also: OpenBook QR Score, 5R Permissions

docs.title: Rising Quality Scores
docs.text:
The trend of open textbooks improving on measures such as the OpenBook QR Score, because AI makes several of the measured improvements cheap.

Example: An author uses AI to add image descriptions and practice questions, raising a book's score in a week.

See also: OpenBook QR Score, Textbook Quality

docs.title: Risk Mitigation
docs.text:
Action taken to lower the likelihood or impact of a possible harm, by avoiding, reducing, transferring, or accepting it.

Example: A district reduces breach risk by storing only mastery data and requiring encryption in its vendor contract.

See also: Risk-and-Response Framework, Pilot Risk Checklist

docs.title: Risk-and-Response Framework
docs.text:
A four-column table that reads each case as the benefit it shows, the risk it also shows, what the school did or could do in response, and the lesson.

Example: Turkish study: benefit, better practice scores; risk, lower exam scores; response, hints instead of answers; lesson, design matters.

See also: Lesson From a Case, Risk Mitigation

docs.title: Risks of AI-First Schools
docs.text:
The possible harms of AI-centered schools, such as over-reliance on AI, excessive screen time, privacy breaches, bias, high cost, and weak afternoon programs.

Example: Summit Learning drew student walkouts over long hours on screens and too little teacher contact.

See also: Benefits of AI-First Schools, Reduce the Negatives

docs.title: Robotics Club
docs.text:
A group in which students design, build, and program robots, often for team competitions.

Example: A high school team that builds a robot to pick up and stack blocks for a regional contest.

See also: Coding Club, Learning by Building Together

docs.title: Rushed Procurement Risk
docs.text:
The danger that buying a product quickly, without full evaluation, leads to poor value, security gaps, or failure.

Example: LA Unified's fast commitment to AllHere's chatbot ended when the company collapsed within months.

See also: LAUSD Ed Chatbot, Contract Due Diligence

docs.title: S-Curve of Adoption
docs.text:
The pattern in which cumulative adoption of an innovation rises slowly at first, then rapidly, then levels off as it approaches saturation.

Example: Internet access in U.S. schools rose slowly, then quickly, then flattened near full coverage.

See also: Technology Adoption Curve, Exponential Growth

docs.title: SAE J3016 Standard
docs.text:
The SAE International standard that defines levels of driving automation for motor vehicles, from no automation to full automation.

The five-level textbook model is modeled on it.

See also: Levels of Driving Automation, Five-Level Textbook Model

docs.title: Scaling a Pilot
docs.text:
Expanding a successful trial to more classrooms, schools, or students while keeping the conditions that made it work.

Example: After one successful year, the district adds four schools and trains their staff with the pilot teachers' help.

See also: Pilot Program, Building on Change

docs.title: Schedule Redesign
docs.text:
Reorganizing how time in the school day, week, or year is divided among subjects, activities, and staff.

Example: A middle school replaces seven periods with a morning academic block and an afternoon project block.

See also: Block Scheduling, Bell Schedule

docs.title: Schein's Culture Model
docs.text:
Edgar Schein's model describing organizational culture in three layers: visible artifacts, espoused values, and deeper basic assumptions.

Example: A school's posters (artifacts) say it values innovation (espoused value), but staff assume mistakes are punished (basic assumption).

See also: Cultural Artifacts, Espoused Values, Basic Assumptions

docs.title: School
docs.text:
An institution that brings students together under the supervision of trained adults for a planned program of instruction and development over a defined schedule.

This book asks what a school is for once much of instruction can be delivered by adaptive software.

See also: AI-Native School, School Day, School Culture

docs.title: School Administrator
docs.text:
A professional who manages the operations, staff, budget, and policies of a school or district, such as a principal, assistant principal, or superintendent.

Example: An assistant superintendent for curriculum who oversees textbook adoptions across the district.

See also: Principal, School Board

docs.title: School Board
docs.text:
An elected or appointed group of community members that governs a school district, setting policy, approving budgets, and hiring the superintendent.

Example: A school board votes to approve a one-year pilot of an adaptive textbook in two middle schools.

See also: Board Presentation, School Board Recommendation

docs.title: School Board Recommendation
docs.text:
The document and presentation in which a leader asks the board to decide whether to approve a pilot, a contract, or a scale-up.

Example: A superintendent recommends a one-year pilot in two schools, with costs, risks, success measures, and a stop rule.

See also: Board Presentation, School Board

docs.title: School Culture
docs.text:
The shared values, beliefs, norms, traditions, and relationships that shape how people in a particular school work, learn, and treat one another.

Example: A school where teachers routinely visit each other's classes and share lesson plans.

See also: Organizational Culture, Shared Beliefs and Norms

docs.title: School Day
docs.text:
The daily span of time during which students attend school, divided into periods or blocks for instruction, meals, breaks, and other activities.

The book argues that the traditional six-to-eight-hour day can be split into a short academic morning and a pro-social afternoon.

See also: AI-Native School Day, Bell Schedule, Schedule Redesign

docs.title: School Readiness Assessment
docs.text:
A structured review of whether a school has the infrastructure, staff skills, policies, culture, and community support needed before adopting a major change.

Example: A checklist covering Wi-Fi capacity, device counts, privacy policy, teacher training, and family support.

See also: Adoption Readiness, Governance Readiness

docs.title: School Rituals
docs.text:
Repeated ceremonies and practices that express and reinforce a school's identity and values.

Example: A Friday morning assembly where students are recognized for kindness.

See also: Cultural Artifacts, School Culture

docs.title: Screen Time
docs.text:
The amount of time a person spends using a device with a display, such as a computer, tablet, phone, or television.

The book notes that screen time lumps very different activities together, but long daily totals were a key complaint in the Summit Learning backlash.

See also: Morning Screen-Time Limits, Summit Learning

docs.title: Seat Time
docs.text:
The amount of time a student spends present in a class, used as the measure of progress or credit instead of demonstrated learning.

Example: A student earns credit for algebra after attending 120 hours of class, even if a test shows she has not mastered half the topics.

See also: Carnegie Unit, Mastery-Based Assessment

docs.title: Selective Chatbot Use
docs.text:
Reserving a live AI tutor for moments where it adds the most value, such as a student who is still stuck after several honest attempts, rather than making it the default for every interaction.

Example: The chat button appears only after a student misses the same problem type three times.

See also: Level 4 Cost Per Student, Energy-Efficient Learning

docs.title: Self Concerns
docs.text:
Early CBAM concerns focused on how an innovation will affect the person personally, such as their job, time, or competence.

Example: "Will I still be needed if students learn from the textbook?"

See also: Stages of Concern, Fear of Job Loss

docs.title: Self-Awareness
docs.text:
The ability to recognize one's own emotions, thoughts, strengths, limits, and values, and how they affect behavior.

Example: A student notices she gets frustrated when rushed and asks for a minute before presenting.

See also: Social-Emotional Learning, Personal Mastery

docs.title: Self-Paced Learning
docs.text:
Learning in which each student moves through material at their own speed, spending more time where needed and moving ahead once a skill is shown.

Example: Two students in the same class are on different units of math because each advances after passing a mastery check.

See also: Personalized Pacing, Mastery Learning

docs.title: Self-Reported Results
docs.text:
Outcome claims made by the organization that runs or sells a program, without verification by an outside party.

Self-reports are not necessarily false, but the reporter has an interest in a favorable result.

Contrast with: Independent Evaluation

See also: Vendor Level Claim

docs.title: Senge's Five Disciplines
docs.text:
The five practices Peter Senge says build a learning organization: personal mastery, mental models, shared vision, team learning, and systems thinking.

See also: Learning Organization, Systems Thinking, Personal Mastery

docs.title: Sense of Urgency
docs.text:
A widely shared recognition that change is needed now, the first of Kotter's steps.

Example: A principal shares evidence that students spend much of the day on material they already know.

See also: Kotter's Eight Steps, Unfreeze Stage

docs.title: Service Learning
docs.text:
An approach that combines community service with classroom learning and reflection, so students meet real needs while building academic and civic skills.

Example: Students test the water quality of a local creek and report their findings to the city council.

See also: Community Partnership, Project-Based Learning

docs.title: Shape the Path
docs.text:
The Switch framework element of changing the environment, routines, and structures so the desired behavior becomes easier.

Example: Setting the adaptive textbook as the default homepage on every student laptop.

See also: Switch Framework, Removing Obstacles

docs.title: Shared Beliefs and Norms
docs.text:
The beliefs held in common by members of a group and the unwritten rules for behavior that follow from them.

Example: An unspoken rule that teachers do not enter each other's rooms uninvited.

See also: School Culture, Basic Assumptions

docs.title: Shared Goals
docs.text:
Objectives that all members of a group understand, accept, and work toward together.

Example: A science team agrees its goal is a working water filter that cleans a cup of muddy water in five minutes.

See also: Teamwork, Shared Vision

docs.title: Shared Vision
docs.text:
A picture of the future that members of an organization hold in common and are committed to creating.

Example: Staff, parents, and students agree they want "mornings with AI, afternoons with each other."

See also: Change Vision, Senge's Five Disciplines

docs.title: Shared Vocabulary
docs.text:
A set of terms whose meanings all parties in a field agree on, so that statements and claims mean the same thing to everyone.

Example: When a vendor and a school both say "Level 3," they agree the product stores student records to adapt content.

See also: Level Terminology Precision, Five-Level Textbook Model

docs.title: Short-Term Wins
docs.text:
Visible, unambiguous early successes that show a change effort is working and build momentum.

Example: A pilot classroom's reading gains shared at a staff meeting after the first quarter.

See also: Early Visible Results, Building on Change

docs.title: Shrinking the First Step
docs.text:
Making the first action in a change so small that doing it is easy and refusing seems unreasonable.

Example: Instead of "adopt the new model," a leader asks a teacher to "try this ten-minute activity once."

See also: Motivate the Elephant, Microstrategy

docs.title: Skills AI Teaches Well
docs.text:
Abilities with clear standards for correct work that can be practiced many times in small steps with instant, specific feedback, such as arithmetic, grammar, vocabulary, and coding syntax.

Example: An adaptive system drilling multiplication facts and giving immediate correction.

Contrast with: Skills That Need People

docs.title: Skills That Need People
docs.text:
Abilities that can be developed only through interaction with others, because another person is part of what is being learned, such as negotiating, persuading a real audience, resolving conflict, and noticing how someone feels.

Example: A student can read about teamwork alone but can only practice it with a team.

Contrast with: Skills AI Teaches Well

See also: Pro-Social Afternoon

docs.title: Social Constructionism
docs.text:
Building understanding by creating shared, tangible products together with others, combining Papert's emphasis on making with the social learning of a group.

Example: A team designs and builds a model city, negotiating each choice along the way.

See also: Learning by Building Together, Constructionism

docs.title: Social Constructivism
docs.text:
A theory of learning, associated with Lev Vygotsky, that holds understanding develops through interaction with other people and the shared language and culture of a group.

Example: Students reach a better explanation of a science result by debating it in small groups.

See also: Zone of Proximal Development, Constructivism

docs.title: Social-Emotional Learning
docs.text:
The process through which students develop the skills to understand and manage emotions, set goals, show empathy, build relationships, and make responsible decisions.

Example: A weekly advisory session where students practice naming their feelings and resolving disagreements.

See also: Self-Awareness, Relationship Skills

docs.title: Socratic Questioning
docs.text:
A teaching method in which a tutor leads a student to understanding through a sequence of questions that prompt the student to examine and reason, rather than by telling.

See also: Hints Instead of Answers, Khanmigo

docs.title: Software Is Not the Model
docs.text:
The lesson that adaptive software alone does not reproduce a school model's results without the culture, adults, community, and afternoon program around it.

Example: Unbound Academy used Alpha's software online without in-person afternoons, and its results did not carry over; AltSchool's technology did not outlast its schools.

See also: Unbound Academy, AltSchool

docs.title: Sources of Resistance
docs.text:
The underlying reasons people oppose a change, such as fear of loss, lack of understanding, past bad experiences, disagreement with goals, or overload.

Example: A teacher opposes the new schedule because a previous reform cost her two years of extra work and then vanished.

See also: Resistance to Change, Change Fatigue

docs.title: Spaced Practice
docs.text:
A study strategy in which practice on a skill or topic is spread out over time, with gaps between sessions, rather than crowded into one session.

Example: An adaptive textbook brings back fraction problems two days, one week, and one month after a student first masters them.

See also: Retrieval Practice

docs.title: Sports and Athletics
docs.text:
Organized physical activities and competitions that build fitness, skill, and discipline.

See also: Team Sports

docs.title: Staff AI Literacy
docs.text:
The understanding that teachers, administrators, and other school staff need about what AI tools can and cannot do, and how to use them responsibly with students.

Example: All staff complete training on spotting AI hallucinations and on the district's data rules.

See also: AI Literacy, Professional Development

docs.title: Staffing Model
docs.text:
The plan for which roles a school employs, how many of each, and how their time is assigned across students and activities.

Example: A school employs academic coaches for the morning and a mix of teachers and part-time specialists for the afternoon.

See also: Afternoon Specialist Staff, Hiring for New Roles

docs.title: Stages of Concern
docs.text:
The CBAM sequence of feelings and questions people have about an innovation, moving roughly from self concerns to task concerns to impact concerns.

Example: A teacher first asks "What will this mean for my job?", later "How do I fit it in?", and finally "Is it helping students?"

See also: Self Concerns, Task Concerns, Impact Concerns

docs.title: Stakeholder
docs.text:
Any person or group with an interest in, or influence over, a change.

Example: Students, teachers, parents, administrators, board members, unions, and local employers are stakeholders in a schedule redesign.

See also: Stakeholder Engagement, Stakeholder Adoption Map

docs.title: Stakeholder Adoption Map
docs.text:
A simple chart listing each interested group, where it stands on the adoption curve, and what its main concerns are, used to plan engagement.

Example: A map shows parents of high achievers as early majority worried about rigor, and the union as late majority worried about jobs.

See also: Stakeholder, Technology Adoption Curve, Matching Strategy to Adopter

docs.title: Stakeholder Engagement
docs.text:
Involving interested people and groups in planning and carrying out a change, so they shape it, understand it, and support it.

Example: A design committee of teachers, parents, and students helps plan the afternoon program.

See also: Stakeholder, Student Voice

docs.title: Standardized Testing
docs.text:
Assessment in which all test takers answer the same or equivalent questions under the same conditions and are scored the same way, so results can be compared across students, schools, and years.

See also: Summative Assessment, Achievement Gap

docs.title: Stanford Detector Study
docs.text:
A 2023 study by Weixin Liang and colleagues at Stanford finding that popular AI-writing detectors often wrongly flagged essays by non-native English writers as AI-generated.

Its lesson is that fighting AI can create equity problems, so schools redesign assignments instead of relying on detection.

See also: Bias Against ELL Writers, Redesign Not Policing

docs.title: Static Website
docs.text:
A website made of prebuilt pages that are delivered to every visitor exactly as stored, without being generated by a server program for each request.

Example: An intelligent textbook built with MkDocs and published as static pages on GitHub Pages.

See also: Web Page Hosting, Generate Once Serve Many

docs.title: Storytelling
docs.text:
Using narratives about people and events to explain ideas, convey values, and persuade.

This book uses real and composite stories to show both the benefits and risks of AI-first schools.

See also: Real Case Study, Composite Story

docs.title: Strengthen the Positives
docs.text:
The book's goal of deliberately reinforcing and spreading the benefits that AI-first schooling can bring.

Example: A school that sees gains from guided tutoring extends it to more subjects.

See also: Reduce the Negatives, Benefits of AI-First Schools

docs.title: Structured Afternoon
docs.text:
An afternoon with clear goals for each activity, a planned sequence, trained adults, and regular reflection, so students know what they are doing and why.

Example: A robotics block with a weekly build goal, a coach, and a five-minute reflection at the end.

Contrast with: Unstructured Afternoon Drift

See also: Afternoon Program Quality

docs.title: Student
docs.text:
A person enrolled in a school or course of study who is expected to acquire knowledge and skills under the guidance of teachers and other adults.

See also: Student Agency, Student Voice

docs.title: Student Agency
docs.text:
A student's capacity and opportunity to make meaningful choices about what, how, and when they learn, and to take responsibility for those choices.

Example: A student picks which of three science projects to pursue and sets her own weekly mastery goals.

See also: Student Goal Setting, Student Voice

docs.title: Student Boredom
docs.text:
A state of low interest and restlessness that arises when learning tasks feel too easy, too hard, repetitive, or disconnected from a student's interests.

Example: A student who already understands percentages sits through a week of lessons on them and stops paying attention.

Contrast with: Student Engagement, Curiosity

docs.title: Student Data
docs.text:
Any information collected about a student, including identity, enrollment, grades, attendance, learning activity, and behavior.

See also: Personally Identifiable Data, Student Data Privacy

docs.title: Student Data Privacy
docs.text:
The protection of student information from collection, use, or disclosure beyond what is necessary, lawful, and agreed to by families.

Example: A district contract forbids a vendor from selling or using student data for advertising.

See also: FERPA, Data Governance, Privacy Inflection Point

docs.title: Student Engagement
docs.text:
The degree of attention, interest, effort, and emotional investment that a student brings to learning activities.

Example: Students who keep working on a bridge design through lunch because they want to see whether it holds show high engagement.

See also: Intrinsic Motivation, Student Boredom

docs.title: Student Goal Setting
docs.text:
The process in which a student, often with an adult, chooses specific learning targets and a timeline for reaching them.

Example: A student sets a goal to master all ten linear-equation concepts by the end of the month.

See also: Student Agency, Progress Tracking

docs.title: Student Progress Dashboard
docs.text:
A visual display that summarizes a student's mastery, activity, and progress toward goals for the student, teachers, or families.

Example: A screen showing which concepts a student has mastered in green and which need review in yellow.

See also: Progress Tracking, Learning Analytics

docs.title: Student Voice
docs.text:
Students' views, preferences, and input on their education, and the opportunities they have to influence decisions.

Example: The Summit Learning walkouts showed students telling their districts what was wrong with long hours on screens.

See also: Student Walkouts, Student Agency

docs.title: Student Walkouts
docs.text:
Protests in which students leave class or school; in this book, the 2018-2019 Brooklyn walkouts against Summit Learning over long screen hours and too little contact with teachers.

The lesson for leaders is to listen to student voice before it turns into protest.

See also: Summit Learning, Student Voice

docs.title: Student-Controlled Data
docs.text:
An arrangement in which students, and their families for younger students, decide who can view, use, or keep their learning records.

Example: A family grants a summer tutoring program access to the child's mastery data for three months.

See also: Data Ownership, Learning Record Store

docs.title: Success Measures
docs.text:
The indicators, set in advance, used to judge whether a program met its goals.

Example: Mastery rates, attendance, family satisfaction, and teamwork rubric scores.

See also: Pilot Goals, Program Evaluation

docs.title: Summative Assessment
docs.text:
An evaluation given at the end of a unit, course, or year to measure what students have learned, usually recorded as a grade or score.

Contrast with: Formative Assessment

See also: Standardized Testing

docs.title: Summit Learning
docs.text:
A personalized-learning platform backed by Facebook engineers and rolled out to many schools, which in 2018 and 2019 drew student walkouts in Brooklyn and family protests in Kansas over screen time and little teacher contact.

Its lesson is that the AI morning needs to stay short and the afternoon truly with people.

See also: Student Walkouts, Morning Screen-Time Limits

docs.title: Sustaining Change
docs.text:
Keeping a new practice in place and improving over years, after initial enthusiasm, funding, and leadership attention fade.

Example: A school keeps its afternoon program running after the principal who started it leaves.

See also: Policy Embedding, Anchoring in Culture

docs.title: Switch Framework
docs.text:
Chip and Dan Heath's model of change, which says lasting change requires directing the rational mind (the Rider), motivating the emotional mind (the Elephant), and shaping the environment (the Path).

Example: A principal gives clear steps, shares a moving student story, and rearranges the schedule to make the change easier.

See also: Direct the Rider, Motivate the Elephant, Shape the Path

docs.title: Systems Thinking
docs.text:
A way of understanding a situation by looking at how its parts interact over time, including feedback and delays, rather than at each part alone.

Example: A board sees that cutting arts programs lowered attendance, which lowered funding, which led to further cuts.

See also: Feedback Loop, Causal Loop Diagram

docs.title: Task Concerns
docs.text:
CBAM concerns focused on the practical management of an innovation, such as time, logistics, and materials.

Example: "How do I run coaching groups while the rest of the class works?"

See also: Stages of Concern

docs.title: Task Horizon
docs.text:
The length of task, measured in how long it takes a skilled human, that an AI system can complete successfully.

Example: If a model reliably finishes tasks that take an expert one hour, its task horizon is about one hour.

See also: 50 Percent Time Horizon, Human Working Time

docs.title: Task Success Rate
docs.text:
The share of attempted tasks that an AI system completes correctly, usually reported as a percentage.

See also: 50 Percent Time Horizon

docs.title: Teacher
docs.text:
A professional who plans learning experiences, explains ideas, guides practice, assesses progress, and supports the growth of students.

In an AI-native school the teacher's role shifts from lecturer toward coach, mentor, and facilitator.

See also: Changing Teacher Role, Teacher as Coach, Teacher Workload

docs.title: Teacher as Coach
docs.text:
A teacher role focused on helping students set goals, practice, and improve through specific feedback and encouragement, much as a sports coach does.

Example: A teacher reviews a student's mastery data and helps her plan how to tackle her weakest concept.

See also: Changing Teacher Role, Teacher as Mentor

docs.title: Teacher as Facilitator
docs.text:
A teacher role focused on organizing activities, resources, and group processes so students learn through their own work and discussion.

Example: A teacher sets up a project, assigns team roles, and steps in only when groups get stuck.

See also: Changing Teacher Role, Project-Based Learning

docs.title: Teacher as Mentor
docs.text:
A teacher role built on a long-term relationship in which the adult guides and supports a student's growth as a person as well as a learner.

Example: An advisory teacher who stays with the same students for three years.

See also: Teacher as Coach, Human Connection

docs.title: Teacher Burnout
docs.text:
A state of emotional, physical, and mental exhaustion in teachers caused by prolonged stress, high workload, and limited support, often leading to reduced effectiveness or leaving the profession.

Example: A district notices that a third of its new teachers leave within three years, citing exhaustion.

See also: Teacher Workload, Change Fatigue

docs.title: Teacher Champion
docs.text:
A teacher who supports an innovation early, uses it well, and helps colleagues adopt it through example and encouragement.

Example: A respected math teacher who runs the pilot and invites others to visit her classroom.

See also: Opinion Leader, Pilot Classroom

docs.title: Teacher Union
docs.text:
An organization that represents teachers in bargaining with school districts over pay, working conditions, and job protections.

See also: Union Engagement, Fear of Job Loss

docs.title: Teacher Workload
docs.text:
The total amount of work required of a teacher, including teaching, planning, grading, communicating with families, meetings, and administrative duties.

Example: A teacher who spends six hours each weekend grading essays has a heavy workload that AI-assisted feedback could reduce.

See also: Teacher Burnout, AI Coaching Teachers

docs.title: Teaching Thinking with AI
docs.text:
Using AI tutors and tools to help students practice thinking skills, such as breaking down problems and evaluating evidence, rather than only to deliver content.

Example: An AI tutor asks a student to split a word problem into steps before solving any of them.

See also: Computational Thinking, Skills AI Teaches Well

docs.title: Team Learning
docs.text:
The process by which a group develops its shared capacity through dialogue, reflection, and joint practice.

Example: A grade-level team meets weekly to watch videos of each other's coaching and discuss what worked.

See also: Professional Learning Community, Learning Organization

docs.title: Team Problem Solving
docs.text:
The process in which a group defines a problem, generates options, chooses a solution, and tests it together.

Example: A team whose model car keeps veering left tests the wheels one by one to find the cause.

See also: Applying Thinking on Teams, Collaboration

docs.title: Team Roles
docs.text:
The distinct responsibilities assigned to members of a group, such as leader, recorder, builder, or presenter, so work is divided and coordinated.

See also: Teamwork

docs.title: Team Sports
docs.text:
Sports in which players work together as a team toward a shared objective against an opposing team.

See also: Sports and Athletics, Teamwork

docs.title: Teamwork
docs.text:
The coordinated effort of a group whose members take on different roles and depend on each other to reach a common goal.

See also: Collaboration, Team Roles, Teamwork Rubric

docs.title: Teamwork Rubric
docs.text:
A scoring guide that describes levels of performance on collaboration skills, such as contributing, listening, resolving conflict, and meeting commitments.

Example: Students and coaches rate each team member from "beginning" to "exemplary" on five teamwork criteria.

See also: Teamwork, Afternoon Program Quality

docs.title: Technology Adoption Curve
docs.text:
A bell-shaped model dividing adopters of a new technology into innovators, early adopters, early majority, late majority, and laggards, according to when they take it up.

Example: A principal sorts her staff along the curve to plan who to invite to a pilot first.

See also: S-Curve of Adoption, Innovators

docs.title: Textbook
docs.text:
A book or organized set of materials written to teach a subject, arranged in a sequence for use by students in a course.

See also: Print Textbook, Intelligent Textbook

docs.title: Textbook Price
docs.text:
The amount a school or student pays to buy or license a textbook or its digital access.

See also: Free Textbook, Cost Per Student

docs.title: Textbook Publisher
docs.text:
A company that develops, produces, markets, and sells textbooks and related instructional materials to schools and students.

See also: Publisher Business Model, Publisher Disruption

docs.title: Textbook Quality
docs.text:
The degree to which a textbook is accurate, clear, well organized, accessible, aligned to learning goals, and effective at helping students learn.

Example: A review team checks a book for factual errors, readability, and whether its practice questions match the standards.

See also: OpenBook QR Score, Quality Subscore

docs.title: The Chasm
docs.text:
Geoffrey Moore's term for the gap between early adopters, who accept an incomplete product for its promise, and the early majority, who want a proven, complete solution.

Example: An AI tutor loved by a few enthusiastic teachers stalls when ordinary classrooms find it hard to set up.

See also: Crossing the Chasm, Pragmatist Buyers

docs.title: Theater
docs.text:
The art of performing stories live before an audience through acting, speech, movement, and staging.

Example: A school play in which students act, build sets, run lights, and manage the stage.

See also: Arts Education, Teamwork

docs.title: Three-to-Four-Year Forecast
docs.text:
The book's central prediction that within three to four years almost every student will have access to a free, high-quality, interactive textbook that adapts to their needs.

Example: A board planning a schedule change for 2029 uses this forecast to ask what the morning should look like by then.

See also: AI Prediction for Schools, Planning Window

docs.title: Total Cost of Ownership
docs.text:
The full cost of a technology over its life, including purchase, setup, training, support, maintenance, data handling, and eventual replacement or exit.

Example: A cheap tablet program becomes expensive once cases, repairs, management software, and replacement in year four are included.

See also: Cost Modeling, Vendor Lock-In

docs.title: Trend Extrapolation
docs.text:
Forecasting future values by extending a pattern observed in past data, on the assumption that the pattern continues.

Example: Extending the five-month doubling line on a log-scale chart to estimate AI task horizons in 2029.

See also: Forecast Uncertainty, Prediction Assumptions

docs.title: Trialability
docs.text:
The degree to which an innovation can be tried on a limited basis before committing to it fully.

Example: A teacher tries one MicroSim in one lesson before deciding whether to use more.

See also: Five Innovation Attributes, Pilot Classroom

docs.title: Trough of Disillusionment
docs.text:
The stage of the hype cycle when a technology fails to meet inflated expectations and interest falls sharply.

Example: After early failures, a district cancels its AI pilot and stops talking about AI altogether.

See also: Hype Cycle, Plateau of Productivity

docs.title: Trust Paradox
docs.text:
The tension in personalized learning that the system needs more student data to serve students well, yet families share more only when they trust it, and trust grows when the system holds back.

The book's resolution is to collect little, say what is held, and build trust through consistent action.

Example: A school that asks for less data at first gains families' confidence and later earns permission for more.

See also: Family Trust, Data Minimization

docs.title: Turkish High School Study
docs.text:
A 2024 Wharton study (Bastani et al.) in which Turkish high school students with open GPT-4 access did better on practice but about 17 percent worse on later unaided exams, while a hints-only version removed most of the harm.

It is the book's thesis in one experiment: design determines whether AI helps or hurts.

See also: Hints Instead of Answers, Guided AI vs Open AI, Design Over Raw AI Power

docs.title: Tutor CoPilot
docs.text:
A 2024 Stanford study of a tool that gave human tutors live AI suggestions during sessions, which improved student mastery, especially for the least experienced tutors, at small cost per tutor.

Its lesson is that AI that makes people better at helping students works well.

See also: AI Coaching Teachers, Teacher as Coach

docs.title: Two-Sided Story
docs.text:
A short composite narrative that shows, in one story, a benefit growing stronger and a risk being reduced, along with the school's response.

Example: A story of one day in an AI-native school in which a student nearly over-relies on the tutor and a coach redirects her.

See also: Composite Story, Risk-and-Response Framework

docs.title: Two-to-Three-Hour Learning
docs.text:
The claim, central to the book, that students using interactive adaptive textbooks can reach today's learning results in two to three hours of academic work a day.

Example: A school plans its academic morning around two and a half hours of mastery-based work.

See also: Compressed Academic Morning, 2 Hour Learning

docs.title: Unbound Academy
docs.text:
A free online Arizona charter school for grades 4-8, approved by a 4-3 state board vote, that uses Alpha's 2 Hour Learning software without in-person afternoons or adult guides; reported early proficiency was below state averages.

Its lesson is that the morning software alone is not the whole model.

See also: 2 Hour Learning, Software Is Not the Model, Virtual School

docs.title: Unfreeze Stage
docs.text:
The first stage of Lewin's model, in which an organization loosens the habits, beliefs, and routines that hold the present way in place, by showing a gap and building psychological safety.

Example: Staff study their own data showing students bored through hours of repeated lessons.

See also: Lewin's Change Model, Sense of Urgency

docs.title: Union Engagement
docs.text:
Working with a teachers' union early and openly on the design and terms of a change.

Example: The district invites union leaders onto the planning committee for the new schedule.

See also: Teacher Union, Stakeholder Engagement

docs.title: Universal Textbook Access
docs.text:
The condition in which every student can use a high-quality textbook for every course, regardless of family income or school budget.

Example: A state provides free interactive textbooks for all core high school subjects to every public school student.

See also: Penny-Per-Day Vision, Equity of Access

docs.title: Unstructured Afternoon Drift
docs.text:
The slide of afternoon time into unplanned free time, passive supervision, or screens, in which adults watch students but nothing is taught.

The book calls it the main risk of the whole model.

Contrast with: Structured Afternoon

See also: Freed-Up School Time

docs.title: Value Beyond Content
docs.text:
What remains worth paying for once instructional content is cheap, such as quality assurance, alignment to standards, teacher support, assessment, data services, and integration.

Example: A district pays a vendor for teacher training and alignment reviews while using free open textbooks.

See also: Publisher Business Model, Whole Product

docs.title: Vendor Evaluation
docs.text:
Assessing a supplier's product, financial stability, track record, security, and terms before buying from it.

Example: A district checks a startup's funding, references, and security audit before signing.

See also: Vendor Risk, Contract Due Diligence

docs.title: Vendor Level Claim
docs.text:
A company's own statement of which level its product belongs to.

Because the vendor has an interest in the claim, schools test it through product level assessment instead of accepting it.

See also: Product Level Assessment, Self-Reported Results

docs.title: Vendor Lock-In
docs.text:
A situation in which a school becomes so dependent on one supplier's product, data formats, or contracts that switching is costly or impractical.

Example: A district cannot change platforms because years of student records exist only in one vendor's format.

See also: Data Portability, Total Cost of Ownership

docs.title: Vendor Risk
docs.text:
The possibility that a supplier will fail, mishandle data, change terms, or otherwise harm the school that depends on it.

Example: The collapse of AllHere left LA Unified with an unfinished chatbot and questions about student data.

See also: Vendor Evaluation, AllHere Collapse

docs.title: Virtual School
docs.text:
A school that delivers instruction mainly or entirely online, with students learning from home or another location instead of attending a physical building.

Example: A statewide virtual school where students log in each morning to video lessons and online assignments.

See also: Charter School, Unbound Academy

docs.title: Visual Arts
docs.text:
Art forms created mainly to be seen, such as drawing, painting, sculpture, photography, and design.

See also: Arts Education

docs.title: Web Browser
docs.text:
A software application, such as Chrome, Safari, Edge, or Firefox, used to find, display, and interact with pages on the World Wide Web.

See also: Browser-Based Simulation, Static Website

docs.title: Web Page Hosting
docs.text:
The service of storing web pages on a server connected to the internet so that browsers can retrieve them.

See also: Static Website, Level 2 Cost Per Student

docs.title: Whole Product
docs.text:
The complete set of products and services a buyer needs to get the promised result, including training, support, integration, and content, beyond the core technology.

Example: An adaptive textbook plus teacher training, LMS integration, a privacy agreement, and help-desk support.

See also: Crossing the Chasm, Value Beyond Content

docs.title: Whole-Organization Change
docs.text:
Change that alters an organization's structures, roles, culture, and practices together, rather than one part at a time.

Example: A school redesigns its schedule, staffing, assessment, and culture to adopt the morning-afternoon model.

See also: Holistic Plus Micro Change, Organizational Change

docs.title: Why School Reforms Fail
docs.text:
The book's synthesis of recurring causes of failed reforms: technology before pedagogy, the grammar of schooling absorbing change, trust not built, and rushed or poorly governed adoption.

Example: The LA Unified iPad rollout started with devices instead of a teaching plan.

See also: Reform Without Real Change, Grammar of Schooling

docs.title: xAPI
docs.text:
The Experience API, a standard for recording learning activities as simple statements that can be stored and shared across different software systems.

Example: A MicroSim sends a record each time a student completes a challenge, which any compliant store can accept.

See also: xAPI Statement, Learning Record Store

docs.title: xAPI Statement
docs.text:
A single record of a learning event, written in the form "actor, verb, object," such as "Maya completed the fractions quiz."

Example: "Student 4471 answered question 3 of the slope MicroSim correctly at 9:42 a.m."

See also: Actor Verb Object, xAPI

docs.title: Your Brain on ChatGPT
docs.text:
A 2025 MIT Media Lab study, released as a preprint, in which students who wrote essays with ChatGPT showed lower brain engagement on EEG and remembered less of their writing than those who wrote alone.

It is small, but it supports placing writing, debate, and making in the people-centered afternoon.

See also: Cognitive Offloading, Preprint

docs.title: Zone of Proximal Development
docs.text:
Vygotsky's term for the range of tasks a learner cannot yet do alone but can do with help from a more skilled person.

Example: A student who cannot yet balance a chemical equation alone succeeds when a peer reminds her to count atoms on each side.

See also: Social Constructivism, Productive Struggle

docs.title: AI-First Stories
docs.text:
This book uses stories to show that moving to an AI-first school has real benefits and real risks. Our goal is to strengthen the positives and reduce the negatives. This appendix collects the real cases the chapters draw on. Each story is labeled as positive, cautionary, or both-sided, and each ends with the lesson it teaches.

Check the facts before citing

Many of these stories are still unfolding, and the figures come from news coverage, preprints, and the schools' own claims. Before a chapter quotes a number, check it against the original source and note the date.

docs.title: Nigeria AI Tutoring Pilot
docs.text:
Positive · 2024 · World Bank

In a six-week after-school program in Edo State, Nigeria, students used a GPT-4-based tutor to practice English while teachers were in the room. The World Bank team reported large learning gains for a very small cost per student.

Lesson: Low-cost AI tutoring, with a teacher present, can help students in places with few resources. This supports the book's claim that AI-first learning does not have to be a luxury.

docs.title: Harvard Physics AI Tutor
docs.text:
Positive · 2024–2025 · Kestin et al.

In a randomized study in an introductory Harvard physics course, students who used a carefully designed AI tutor learned more, in less time, than students in an active-learning class led by an instructor. The tutor was built on proven teaching practices instead of being an open chatbot.

Lesson: A well-designed AI tutor can make the shorter academic morning work. Design matters more than raw AI power.

docs.title: Tutor CoPilot
docs.text:
Positive · 2024 · Stanford University

Tutor CoPilot gave human tutors live AI suggestions during their sessions instead of replacing them. Students' mastery improved, the weakest tutors improved the most, and the cost per tutor for a year was small.

Lesson: AI works well when it makes people better at helping students. This supports the book's picture of the teacher as a coach.

docs.title: Estonia's AI Leap
docs.text:
Positive · 2025 · Estonia (TI-Hüpe)

Estonia launched a national program giving secondary students and teachers access to AI learning tools, along with teacher training. It builds on the country's earlier success bringing computers into schools.

Lesson: A school system can adopt AI on purpose, with a plan, training, and public support. This is a useful example for the change-management chapters.

docs.title: Unbound Academy
docs.text:
Cautionary · 2025– · Arizona

Unbound Academy is a free, online charter school for grades 4–8 that uses Alpha School's 2 Hour Learning software. The Arizona State Board for Charter Schools approved it by a 4–3 vote. A board slideshow reportedly showed 10% proficiency in math and 28% in English Language Arts, below state averages. The school had projected 90%+ within two to three years, and separately claims students learn 2.8 times faster on its own growth tests. The reports do not say where students started, so it is unclear how much they grew.

Lesson: This is the key story to pair with Alpha. The morning software alone is not the whole model. When the program moves online and opens to everyone without in-person afternoons and adult guides, the results do not carry over automatically.

docs.title: The LA Unified Chatbot "Ed"
docs.text:
Cautionary · 2024 · Los Angeles Unified School District

LA Unified committed about $6 million to the startup AllHere for an AI chatbot called "Ed" and spent about $3 million of it. The company collapsed within months of launch. In November 2024 its founder was charged with defrauding investors of nearly $10 million. In 2026 the FBI searched the superintendent's home and office in an investigation reported to be connected to AllHere; he has not been charged with a crime.

Lesson: Rushed purchasing, depending on one vendor, and sending student data to an unproven company all put students at risk. Schools need procurement rules, such as those based on the five-level model, before they buy AI products.

docs.title: AltSchool
docs.text:
Cautionary · 2013–2019 · Silicon Valley

AltSchool raised more than $170 million to build a network of "personalized learning" microschools run on its own software. It closed its schools within a few years and shifted to selling software.

Lesson: Personalization led by technology, without a lasting school culture and community, does not last.

docs.title: Summit Learning
docs.text:
Cautionary · 2018–2019 · Brooklyn and Kansas

Summit Learning, a personalized-learning platform backed by Facebook engineers, was rolled out to many schools. Students walked out in Brooklyn and families protested in Kansas, complaining about long hours on screens and too little contact with teachers.

Lesson: This is the clearest real example of the screen-time risk. An AI morning must stay short, and the afternoon must be truly with other people.

docs.title: inBloom
docs.text:
Cautionary · 2014

inBloom was a $100 million, Gates Foundation-funded project to store and share student data across states. It closed after parents pushed back over privacy.

Lesson: Any xAPI and Learning Record Store system needs the trust of families from the start, with clear rules about who owns and controls student data.

docs.title: PowerSchool Data Breach
docs.text:
Cautionary · December 2024

A breach at PowerSchool, one of the largest student information system vendors, exposed records for tens of millions of students and teachers.

Lesson: Level 3 textbooks and higher need student records. The more centralized those records are, the bigger the target. This makes the level 3 privacy threshold concrete.

docs.title: LA Unified iPad Rollout
docs.text:
Cautionary · 2013 · Los Angeles Unified School District

LA Unified began a $1.3 billion plan to give every student an iPad loaded with Pearson curriculum. The plan was cancelled amid technical problems, weak curriculum, and a scandal over how the contract was awarded.

Lesson: Buying devices before having a plan for teaching wastes money and public trust.

docs.title: Alpha School
docs.text:
Both-sided · 2014– · Austin and other cities

Alpha School students spend about two hours a day on adaptive academic software and the rest of the day on life-skills workshops and projects led by adult guides. Tuition ranges from about $40,000 a year at the original Austin campus to about $65,000 a year at newer campuses in Boston, Miami, and New York.

Lesson: The morning-and-afternoon structure can work, but at private-school prices. The book asks how to offer the same structure to every student using open intelligent textbooks, MicroSims, learning graphs, xAPI, and a Learning Record Store instead of costly live AI.

docs.title: David Game College
docs.text:
Both-sided · 2024 · London

David Game College opened what was described as the UK's first GCSE class taught mainly by AI. Students work with AI learning platforms and are supported by learning coaches instead of traditional teachers.

Lesson: It shows the AI-first idea spreading beyond the United States. It also shows the same open question as Alpha: how much of the result comes from the software and how much from the adults around it.

docs.title: The Turkish High-School Study
docs.text:
Both-sided · 2024 · Bastani et al., Wharton

In a study at a high school in Turkey, students given open GPT-4 access did much better on practice problems. On later exams taken without AI, however, they did about 17% worse than students who never had access. A second version with guardrails, which gave hints instead of answers, removed most of the harm.

Lesson: This is the book's thesis in one experiment. The same AI can help or hurt depending on how it is designed. It also supports the book's low-cost design: guided, structured adaptation is safer than an open chatbot.

docs.title: "Your Brain on ChatGPT"
docs.text:
Both-sided · 2025 · MIT Media Lab

In this study, students who wrote essays with ChatGPT showed lower brain engagement in EEG readings and remembered less of what they had written than students who wrote on their own. The study was small and is still a preprint.

Lesson: It supports the risk of students handing their thinking over to AI, and shows why the book puts writing, debate, and making things into the afternoon.

docs.title: Khanmigo
docs.text:
Both-sided · 2023– · Khan Academy

Khanmigo is an AI tutor built specifically for learning. It guides students with questions instead of giving answers, and it has been rolled out in many school districts. Early versions made math mistakes, and students in some districts used it less than expected.

Lesson: Even careful design meets the reality of how classrooms actually use a tool. A level 4 chatbot is not automatically better than a well-built level 2 or level 3 textbook.

docs.title: AI Cheating Detectors
docs.text:
Cautionary · 2023 · Liang et al., Stanford

A Stanford study found that popular AI-writing detectors often wrongly flagged essays by non-native English writers as written by AI.

Lesson: Fighting AI can create its own equity problems. Schools should redesign assignments instead of relying on detection.

docs.title: The Non-AI Afternoon
docs.text:
Positive · ongoing

The pro-social afternoon does not need to be invented from scratch. These programs already show it working:

  • High Tech High (San Diego): project-based learning, where students work in teams on real projects and present them in public exhibitions
  • Finland's phenomenon-based learning: students study real-world topics across subjects, often in groups
  • El Sistema (Venezuela and worldwide): youth orchestras that use group music-making to build discipline, belonging, and community

Lesson: The afternoon half of the AI-native school day is already proven. AI frees the time; these models show how to use it.

docs.title: Chapters
docs.text: This textbook is organized into 23 chapters covering 532 concepts from the learning graph.

docs.title: Chapter Overview
docs.text:
1. The Building Blocks of Schools, Students, and Learning - This chapter introduces the core vocabulary of schools, students, teachers, and learning theory — education, curriculum, learning outcomes, the school day, direct instruction, spaced and retrieval practice, Bloom's Taxonomy, and formative assessment.
  2. Evidence, Motivation, and the Stakeholders of Schooling - This chapter covers how educators judge what works — evidence-based practice, randomized controlled trials, effect size, and case study methods — alongside the motivational side of learning: curiosity, boredom, engagement, and productive struggle.
  3. School Structures, Equity, and the Industrial-Era Legacy - This chapter examines the structural and historical scaffolding of the school system: the bell schedule, the Carnegie unit, seat time, age-based grade levels, and the industrial-era school model, alongside achievement and equity gaps and alternatives like charter, virtual, and microschools.
  4. Measuring AI Capability: The METR Task-Horizon Studies - This chapter introduces artificial intelligence, machine learning, and large language models, then explains how METR measures AI capability through the task-horizon studies — benchmark task suites, the 50% time horizon, and human working time as the unit of measurement.
  5. Projecting AI Growth: Doubling Curves, Limits, and Uncertainty - This chapter teaches readers to project the METR task-horizon trend forward: reading a logarithmic scale, the five-month doubling time, and the difference between linear and exponential growth.
  6. The Five-Level Model of Intelligent Textbooks - This chapter presents the book's central organizing idea: the five-level model of intelligent textbooks, adapted from the SAE J3016 levels for self-driving cars.
  7. Content Economics and Open Educational Resources - This chapter covers the economics behind falling content-creation costs: open educational resources, open licenses, the OpenBook QR Score, content commoditization, and how publisher business models are changing as AI makes level 1 and level 2 content cheap to produce.
  8. Tracking Mastery: xAPI, Learning Record Stores, and MicroSims - This chapter introduces the technical building blocks that let a textbook adapt to a student without a live AI model: xAPI, Learning Record Stores, mastery data, learning analytics, and MicroSims, together with student-controlled, portable learning data.
  9. Learning Graphs, Interoperability Standards, and Access at Scale - This chapter covers learning graphs as directed acyclic graphs of concept nodes, the interoperability standards (IMS Global, IEEE) that let these pieces work across products, and the practical requirements of delivering content at scale: device access, connectivity, offline access, and a "generate once, serve many" delivery model.
  10. Student Privacy and Data Governance - This chapter covers the level-3 privacy inflection point: why adaptive and higher-level textbooks need detailed student data, and what that triggers — FERPA, COPPA, GDPR, data governance, and algorithmic bias auditing — illustrated by the inBloom shutdown and the PowerSchool data breach.
  11. Mastery Learning and the Case for a Compressed Morning - This chapter makes the case for a shorter academic morning: adaptive and mastery learning, personalized pacing, Bloom's two-sigma problem, one-on-one tutoring, and what AI tutors do well, alongside the critical- and computational-thinking skills a compressed morning is meant to protect time for.
  12. AI Guardrails: Teaching Thinking Without Over-Reliance - This chapter covers how an AI tutor should be designed rather than just how powerful it is: guardrails, hints instead of answers, Socratic questioning, and the risk of cognitive offloading and over-reliance, alongside the specific thinking skills (decomposition, pattern recognition, abstraction, algorithmic thinking) AI can teach well.
  13. Social Learning and Human Skills - This chapter introduces social constructionism and constructivism as the theoretical basis for the pro-social afternoon, along with the specific human skills it targets: collaboration, teamwork, communication, empathy, creativity, and social-emotional learning.
  14. The Pro-Social Afternoon - This chapter covers what fills the pro-social afternoon in practice: the arts, sports, clubs, maker spaces, service learning, and project-based learning, with proven models such as High Tech High, phenomenon-based learning, and El Sistema, plus the risk of an unstructured afternoon.
  15. Technology Adoption and the Diffusion of Innovation - This chapter introduces the technology adoption curve: Rogers' diffusion of innovations, the five innovation attributes, adopter categories from innovators to laggards, the chasm between early adopters and the early majority, and the hype cycle.
  16. Organizational Change Models - This chapter names the major organizational change models used later in the book — Kotter's eight steps, Lewin's unfreeze-change-refreeze, ADKAR, Bridges' transition model, Schein's culture model, Senge's learning organization, Fullan's educational change, and the Concerns-Based Adoption Model — along with organizational and school culture.
  17. Leading Change: Vision, Culture, and Early-Stage Concerns - This chapter goes deeper into the early stages of leading change: Lewin's unfreezing, Kotter's guiding coalition and shared vision, Bridges' endings and losses, Schein's levels of culture, and the first stages of ADKAR and the Concerns-Based Adoption Model.
  18. Sustaining Change: Systems Thinking and National Adoption - This chapter completes the change models with their later, sustaining stages: Senge's systems thinking and mental models, the later stages of ADKAR and CBAM, Bridges' new beginnings, the "grammar of schooling," and Estonia's national AI Leap as a whole-system example.
  19. Microstrategies for Leading Change - This chapter covers the concrete, next-week moves that make change stick: teacher champions, pilot classrooms, bright spots, shrinking the first step, professional learning communities, and engaging stakeholders — including resistance, family communication, and the changing role of the teacher from lecturer to coach and mentor.
  20. Designing the AI-Native School Day - This chapter covers redesigning the school day itself: the morning-afternoon model, scheduling and staffing, the changing teacher role, and grade-level design choices for a real AI-native school.
  21. Implementing the AI-Native Model Responsibly - This chapter covers putting the model into practice responsibly: safe procurement, avoiding vendor lock-in, equity and access, redesigning assessment instead of policing it, and measuring whether a pilot is actually working.
  22. AI-First Case Studies I: Promise and Peril - This chapter presents a first set of real cases that show both the promise and the peril of AI-first schools: Alpha School, the Turkish high school chatbot study, the Harvard physics AI tutor, and the risk-and-response framework used to weigh them.
  23. AI-First Case Studies II: Lessons for Practice - This chapter presents a second set of cases focused on lessons for practice: AltSchool, Summit Learning, the Los Angeles iPad rollout and "Ed" chatbot, and other cautionary and positive examples, closing with how to evaluate result claims and make a recommendation to a school board.

docs.title: How to Use This Textbook
docs.text:
Work through the chapters in order. Each chapter's concepts depend only on concepts introduced in earlier chapters, so completing chapters sequentially ensures every prerequisite has already been covered. The Part structure of the course description groups these 23 chapters into five broader parts plus a closing set of case studies.

Note: Each chapter includes a list of concepts covered. Make sure to complete prerequisites before moving to advanced chapters.

docs.title: The Building Blocks of Schools, Students, and Learning
Summary
docs.text: This chapter introduces the core vocabulary of schools, students, teachers, and learning theory — education, curriculum, learning outcomes, the school day, direct instruction, spaced and retrieval practice, Bloom's Taxonomy, and formative assessment. It gives readers the shared terms the rest of the book builds on, with no AI yet in the picture. After completing it, readers can describe how a traditional classroom and school day work today.
