docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
The vocabulary in this chapter describes a school system that works, often well, within a hard constraint: one teacher, one pace, many students, fixed time.

  • Education is the organized effort; learning is the lasting change inside the learner. Strong performance on today's test is not the same as learning.
  • A school does many jobs besides academic instruction, and any redesign of the school day must still do all of them.
  • Every student arrives at a different starting point, while a classroom gives one teacher less than two minutes per student per period for individual attention.
  • A curriculum exists in three versions (intended, enacted, attained), and precise learning outcomes with observable verbs are how you tell the three apart.
  • Bloom's Taxonomy classifies outcomes by the kind of thinking they ask for, and higher-order thinking (analyze, evaluate, create) depends on a strong base of the lower levels.
  • Direct instruction is effective for novices but paces the whole room together, which turns ordinary differences in readiness into learning gaps.
  • Self-paced learning and student agency answer the one-pace problem in different ways (speed versus choice) and both need structure to work.
  • Formative assessment uses evidence during learning to change what happens next; spaced practice and retrieval practice turn performance into lasting learning.
  • Educational technology has repeatedly been oversold when bolted onto an unchanged school day; it matters when it changes which learning job is done and by whom.
  • Public school funding comes from local, state, and federal sources, and per-pupil spending of roughly $15,000 a year, about $83 a school day in our example, is the baseline any new model will be compared against.

You can now describe how a school works

You just built the vocabulary to describe a traditional school day from the per-pupil budget down to a single hinge question — and to spot exactly where one pace for 28 students leaves learning on the table. Chapter 2 asks who has a stake in changing that, and why. One step at a time, together.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: The Building Blocks of Schools, Students, and Learning
docs.text: Test your understanding of the core vocabulary of schools, students, teachers, and learning science with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. How does this chapter distinguish education from learning?
docs.text:
1. Education happens in school, while learning happens only at home
  2. Education is an organized, intentional effort; learning is a lasting change inside the learner
  3. Education measures what students know; learning is the process of teaching them
  4. Education and learning are synonyms that differ only in how formal the setting is
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The chapter defines education as an organized, intentional effort to help people acquire knowledge and skills, and learning as a relatively lasting change in knowledge or skill that happens inside the learner. Each can occur without the other: a forgotten lecture is education with little learning, and a child touching a hot stove learns with no education. Education is not limited to school, so the first option is wrong, and the chapter says outright the two words are not synonyms.

Concept Tested: Education and Learning

See: Education and Learning: Two Words That Are Not Synonyms

docs.title: 2. In the three versions of a curriculum, which one describes what students actually learn and can show?
docs.text:
1. The intended curriculum
  2. The enacted curriculum
  3. The adopted curriculum
  4. The attained curriculum
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The attained curriculum is what students actually learn and can demonstrate. The intended curriculum is what the documents say students should learn, and the enacted curriculum is what teachers actually teach. Every gap between the three is a place where learning leaks out, as in the unit-rates example where a standard looked fully covered on paper but was only partly learned. "Adopted curriculum" is not one of the three versions.

Concept Tested: Curriculum

See: Curriculum

docs.title: 3. Which of the following is the strongest learning outcome by the chapter's standards?
docs.text:
1. Students will compare two primary sources and identify three points of disagreement
  2. Students will understand the main causes and consequences of the Civil War
  3. Students will appreciate how poets use figurative language in their work
  4. Students will learn about the major ecosystems of North America
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. A strong learning outcome names an observable action, specific content, and a way to tell whether the learner succeeded. "Compare two primary sources and identify three points of disagreement" passes the watch-them-do-it test. The other three use understand, appreciate, and learn about, verbs that cannot be observed directly, so a teacher or a piece of software could not check them.

Concept Tested: Learning Outcome

See: Learning Outcome

docs.title: 4. Which statement about higher-order thinking matches the chapter?
docs.text:
1. It covers the Remember, Understand, and Apply levels of Bloom's Taxonomy
  2. It is reserved for advanced students who have finished the lower levels for good
  3. It depends on a large store of remembered and understood knowledge
  4. It is the kind of thinking most classroom assignments already exercise
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Higher-order thinking refers to analyzing, evaluating, and creating, and the chapter stresses that it depends on a strong base of lower-level knowledge: you cannot critique a historical argument without knowing the history. The first option names the lower-order levels. The chapter warns against reading the taxonomy as a ladder climbed once, and it notes that most assignments sit at the Remember and Apply levels, not the higher ones.

Concept Tested: Higher-Order Thinking

See: Higher-Order Thinking

docs.title: 5. What is a learning gap, as the chapter defines it?
docs.text:
1. The difference between what a student is expected to know and what the student actually knows
  2. The time that passes between teaching a lesson and testing it on a summative exam
  3. The difference between a student's reading level and the student's mathematics level
  4. The number of school days a student misses during the year because of illness or absence
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. A learning gap is the difference between what a student is expected to know or do, as defined by learning outcomes, and what the student actually knows or can do. The chapter shows that gaps compound, because each year's lessons assume last year's outcomes were attained. A mismatch between reading and math levels, like Maya's, can reveal a gap, but the gap is measured against expected outcomes, not between two subjects.

Concept Tested: Learning Gap

See: The Learning Gap

docs.title: 6. A teacher gives a five-question quiz mid-unit, records the scores in the gradebook, and starts the next topic the following day regardless of the results. Is this formative assessment by the chapter's definition?
docs.text:
1. Yes, because the quiz was low stakes and happened during the unit
  2. No, because the results did not change what happened next in teaching or learning
  3. Yes, because any quiz given before the final exam counts as formative
  4. No, because formative assessment must use mini whiteboards or hinge questions
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The key phrase in the definition is that evidence is used to adjust teaching and learning while there is still time to act. A quiz is not formative because of its format or timing; it is formative only if the results change what happens next. Here the scores were recorded and ignored. Timing and low stakes alone are not enough, and whiteboards and hinge questions are examples of formative techniques, not requirements.

Concept Tested: Formative Assessment

See: Formative Assessment: Checking Learning While It Happens

docs.title: 7. What is the difference between self-paced learning and student agency?
docs.text:
1. Self-paced learning lets students choose topics; student agency lets them choose speed
  2. Self-paced learning requires computers; student agency requires a project-based school
  3. Self-paced learning and student agency are two names for the same arrangement
  4. Self-pacing concerns speed through a sequence; agency concerns choosing what and how
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The chapter separates the two: self-pacing gives a student control over how fast they move through a fixed sequence, while agency gives a student meaningful choices about what to study, how to study it, and how to show learning. A self-paced program can offer almost no agency, and a project can offer great agency with a fixed deadline. The first option reverses the two ideas, and Keller's 1968 system shows self-pacing does not require computers.

Concept Tested: Self-Paced Learning and Student Agency

See: Student Agency

docs.title: 8. A student has a test in 30 days and time for three short review sessions. Which plan does the research in this chapter predict will produce the strongest retention on test day?
docs.text:
1. Rereading her notes three times back-to-back on the first day
  2. Rereading her notes on days 1, 3, and 7
  3. Closing her notes and writing down what she remembers on days 1, 4, and 12
  4. Highlighting the key terms in her notes on days 28, 29, and 30
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. This plan combines spaced practice (reviews spread over time) with retrieval practice (recalling from memory rather than rereading), and the chapter's worked example predicts it gives the strongest retention of the plans compared. Spaced rereading beats cramming but is weaker than spaced retrieval. Highlighting was rated a low-utility strategy in the Dunlosky review, and the last option clusters reviews into a cram just before the test.

Concept Tested: Spaced Practice and Retrieval Practice

See: Worked Example: Planning Three Reviews

docs.title: 9. A district's annual report includes salaries, supplies, transportation, and the cost of building a new middle school. To calculate per-pupil spending the standard way, what should be left out?
docs.text:
1. The construction cost of the new building
  2. Teacher salaries and benefits
  3. Transportation costs for school buses
  4. The cost of instructional supplies
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Most published per-pupil figures use current spending, which covers day-to-day operations such as salaries, benefits, supplies, and transportation, and excludes construction and debt payments. In the chapter's example, including a new school's construction raised the figure from $15,000 to about $18,333 per student, a misleading number for comparing everyday costs. Salaries, transportation, and supplies are all part of current spending and stay in the calculation.

Concept Tested: Per-Pupil Spending

See: Worked Example: Computing Per-Pupil Spending

docs.title: 10. What lesson does the chapter draw from a century of educational technology waves, from Pressey's testing machine to one-to-one laptops?
docs.text:
1. Technology has consistently failed to improve learning and should be avoided
  2. Technology bolted onto an unchanged school day tends to be absorbed into old habits
  3. Each wave succeeded, but schools could not afford to keep the equipment running
  4. Technology works best when it replaces the teacher's role in the classroom
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The chapter says the lesson is not that technology fails, but that technology alone rarely changes the grammar of schooling, such as age-graded classes, the bell schedule, and the single pace. Larry Cuban documented a pattern of tools being oversold and underused. The tablet example shows the same device can either digitize the old model or change how learning works. The first option overstates the point, and the chapter argues AI should change what teachers do, not replace them.

Concept Tested: Educational Technology

See: Educational Technology

docs.title: References: The Building Blocks of Schools, Students, and Learning
docs.text:
1. Curriculum - Wikipedia - Surveys definitions of curriculum, from planned content to the full set of student experiences, and its history. Useful background for the chapter's distinction between what schools intend to teach and the learning outcomes they measure.

  2. Bloom's taxonomy - Wikipedia - Explains the original 1956 taxonomy and the 2001 revision, from remembering to creating. Gives readers the vocabulary of higher-order thinking that later chapters use to describe what mornings and afternoons should target.

  3. Testing effect - Wikipedia - Summarizes research showing that recalling information strengthens memory more than rereading it, and its link to spaced practice. Grounds the chapter's retrieval practice section in decades of cognitive science.

  4. Taxonomy of Educational Objectives, Handbook I: The Cognitive Domain (1956) - Benjamin S. Bloom (editor) - David McKay Company - The original source of the six-level hierarchy of thinking skills. Bloom's framework gave teachers a shared way to tell recall questions from analysis and creation tasks, which the chapter relies on.

  5. Make It Stick: The Science of Successful Learning (2014) - Peter C. Brown, Henry L. Roediger III, and Mark A. McDaniel - Belknap Press of Harvard University Press - Credited with bringing retrieval practice, spacing, and interleaving to teachers in plain language, and with showing why learning that feels easy often fades fastest.

  6. Organizing Instruction and Study to Improve Student Learning - What Works Clearinghouse, Institute of Education Sciences - A 2007 federal practice guide recommending spaced review and quizzing, each with an evidence rating. Shows school leaders how strongly the research supports the learning strategies this chapter introduces.

  7. The Learning Scientists: Downloadable Materials - The Learning Scientists - Free posters, slides, and bookmarks for six study strategies, including spaced practice and retrieval practice. Practical classroom materials that turn the chapter's learning-science vocabulary into routines students can use.

  8. Retrieval Practice - Pooja K. Agarwal, RetrievalPractice.org - A cognitive scientist's site with over 100 free guides, classroom strategies, and research summaries on retrieval practice. Helps teachers see how low-stakes recall fits into an ordinary class period.

  9. Formative Assessment - Edutopia - A collection of articles and short videos on quick checks for understanding, questioning, and feedback during a lesson. Gives concrete examples of the formative assessment the chapter describes as checking learning while it happens.

  10. Fast Facts: Expenditures - National Center for Education Statistics - Reports average U.S. public school spending per pupil and how it divides among salaries, benefits, and capital costs. Supplies the baseline numbers behind the chapter's section on school funding.

docs.title: Evidence, Motivation, and the Stakeholders of Schooling
Summary
docs.text: This chapter covers how educators judge what works — evidence-based practice, randomized controlled trials, effect size, and case study methods — alongside the motivational side of learning: curiosity, boredom, engagement, and productive struggle. It also introduces the people involved in a school decision: parents, principals, administrators, and school boards. Readers finish able to weigh a claim about an educational intervention and name the stakeholders it affects.

docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: The Building Blocks of Schools, Students, and Learning

docs.title: A Vendor, a Principal, and a Number
docs.text:
On a Tuesday in October, a sales representative visits Lincoln Middle School, the composite school where Maya from Chapter 1 is a seventh grader. The representative hands the principal, Ms. Okafor, a glossy brochure for an AI-assisted math program called MathPath. It says three things: "Effect size of 0.8," "94% of teachers love it," and "Evidence-based." The district is about to decide whether to buy it for every middle school.

Ms. Okafor has three problems at once. She needs to know whether those three claims mean anything. She needs to know whether a program that helps some students will actually engage Maya, who hides her confusion, and Jordan, who is bored. And she needs to know who has to be consulted before anything is bought: the teachers, the families, the district office, the school board.

This chapter gives you the vocabulary to follow her through all three problems. It has three parts: how to judge evidence, how motivation and engagement work, and who the stakeholders of a school decision are. It matters now because AI products will arrive in schools far faster than the research that evaluates them, and the people making the decisions will mostly be educators and board members, not statisticians.

Before you sign anything

By the end of this chapter you'll be able to read a vendor brochure the way a careful principal does, and say which of its claims you'd trust and which you'd test. You'll also know exactly who needs a seat at the table before a school adopts anything new. Let's find the balance between healthy skepticism and open-minded curiosity.

We start with the setting every example in this chapter lives inside.

docs.title: K-12 Education: The Setting
docs.text:
K-12 education is the span of publicly and privately provided schooling from kindergarten (usually age five) through twelfth grade (usually age seventeen or eighteen), roughly thirteen years of schooling. The "K" stands for kindergarten and the "12" for the final high school grade. In the United States it is commonly divided into three bands, though the boundaries differ by district.

Band Typical grades Typical ages Typical structure Elementary K–5 5–11 One teacher for most subjects; one classroom Middle 6–8 11–14 Subject teachers; periods; a bell schedule High 9–12 14–18 Subject teachers; credits toward graduation; electives

Almost every state requires children to attend school for part of this span, though the starting and ending ages vary. K-12 is also the scope of this book. We do not cover preschool, higher education, or corporate training. The reason to keep the scope narrow is that the decision-makers, the money, and the rules that govern K-12 schools differ sharply from those that govern a university.

docs.title: Worked Example: What Thirteen Years Add Up To
docs.text:
A student who attends school from kindergarten through twelfth grade spends, using the Chapter 1 figures of about 180 days a year and about 6.5 hours a day:

\[ 13 \text{ years} \times 180 \text{ days} = 2{,}340 \text{ days} \qquad 2{,}340 \times 6.5 \text{ hours} \approx 15{,}200 \text{ hours} \]

At the Chapter 1 per-pupil figure of about $15,600 a year, the public cost of those thirteen years is about \( 13 \times \$15{,}600 = \$202{,}800 \), or roughly $200,000 per student. Those two numbers, 15,200 hours and $200,000, frame every decision in this book. An idea that saves even ten percent of the hours or improves the use of the money is worth a serious look. An idea that costs more than it returns is not.

docs.title: Evidence-Based Practice: Judging What Works
docs.text:
When a salesperson says a program is "research-based" or "proven," what are they claiming? Often very little. This section defines the terms researchers and policymakers use to separate strong claims from weak ones.

Evidence-based practice is the use of the best available research evidence, combined with professional judgment and knowledge of the local students and setting, to decide what to do. Three parts matter: research evidence about what has worked elsewhere, professional judgment from teachers who know their students, and context such as the students' ages, languages, and prior knowledge. Drop any one of them and the approach fails. Research alone ignores the classroom in front of you. Judgment alone is a collection of habits that may never have been tested.

The phrase gained legal force in the United States through the Every Student Succeeds Act (ESSA) of 2015, which ties some federal school funds to the use of interventions backed by evidence. ESSA defines four levels of evidence, and the What Works Clearinghouse, run by the U.S. Department of Education's Institute of Education Sciences, reviews studies against standards of this kind. This book adds a fifth bin for claims that are not evidence of effect at all.

Level What the evidence looks like Plain-language meaning Strong At least one well-designed, well-implemented experimental study (random assignment) Students were randomly placed in groups, and the program group did better Moderate At least one well-designed quasi-experimental study (a comparison group, but no random assignment) A comparison group existed, but it was chosen, not drawn by lot Promising At least one well-designed correlational study with statistical controls for who chose the program Users did better after adjusting for obvious differences Demonstrates a rationale A logical explanation based on research, with an evaluation planned or under way A good reason to expect it to work, but no results yet No evidence of effect Testimonials, satisfaction surveys, usage counts, uncontrolled before-and-after gains Doesn't show that the program caused learning

A few things stand out. First, the ladder is about the design of the study, not the size of the claim. A modest effect found by random assignment is stronger evidence than a huge effect from a satisfaction survey. Second, the lowest bin is not a criticism of teachers' opinions, which matter for other reasons. It simply says an opinion is not a measurement of learning.

docs.title: Worked Example: Reading the MathPath Brochure
docs.text:
Return to the three claims in Ms. Okafor's brochure and assign each to a level.

Claim Level Why "94% of teachers love it" No evidence of effect A satisfaction survey says teachers like the program, not that students learned more "Evidence-based" Unknown until asked The label alone is not a study; the question is which study, of what design "Effect size of 0.8" Unknown until asked A size means nothing until you know how it was measured and compared

The right next step is not to reject MathPath but to ask three questions of any vendor: Who was compared with whom? How were they chosen? What was measured, and by whom? The next two sections explain why those questions matter.

Three questions for any vendor

Keep these on an index card: "Compared with whom? Chosen how? Measured by whom?" If the answer to the last one is "the vendor," ask for an independent study as well.

docs.title: Randomized Controlled Trials
docs.text:
A randomized controlled trial (RCT) is a study design in which participants are assigned by chance, like a coin flip, to either a treatment group that receives the intervention or a control group that does not, and the two groups are then compared on the same measure. The randomness is the whole point. If assignment is truly by chance, then on average the two groups start out alike in prior knowledge, motivation, family support, and every other factor, including factors nobody thought to measure. Any later difference is then much more likely to be caused by the intervention.

Compare this with letting students choose. In a school that offers an optional AI tutor, the students who sign up are likely to be more motivated, better organized, or have more supportive homes. If those students score higher, you cannot tell whether the tutor helped or whether motivated students would have done well anyway. This problem is called selection bias, and randomization is the main cure for it.

The most famous education RCT in the United States is Project STAR, run in Tennessee from 1985 to 1989. About 11,600 students in kindergarten through third grade were randomly assigned to small classes of 13 to 17 students or regular classes of 22 to 25, and the small classes produced modest but lasting benefits. RCTs are also now appearing in the AI-tutoring literature the course description mentions: the Turkish high school study that found open chatbot access harmed later exam scores, and a Nigerian after-school tutoring pilot with large gains, were both designed as randomized comparisons.

RCTs have limits. They are expensive, slow, and sometimes impossible: you cannot randomly assign children to different school funding levels. They tell you what happened on average in the studied setting, which may not match your school. And a poorly run RCT, with many students dropping out or the control group getting the treatment anyway, can be less trustworthy than its label suggests.

docs.title: Worked Example: A Pilot That Randomizes
docs.text:
Lincoln Middle has 280 seventh graders. Instead of buying MathPath for everyone, Ms. Okafor runs a six-week pilot. A coin flip, done by a computer, assigns 140 students to use MathPath for 30 minutes a day in addition to regular class, and 140 to continue as normal. All 280 take the same 50-point test at the start and again after six weeks. Suppose the results are:

Group Students Mean score at six weeks Standard deviation MathPath (treatment) 140 34 10 Regular class (control) 140 30 10

The treatment group scored four points higher. Is that a real effect or chance? If the groups were drawn by lot, the random wobble in the difference of two group averages is about

\[ 10 \times \sqrt{\tfrac{1}{140} + \tfrac{1}{140}} \approx 1.2 \text{ points}, \]

so a four-point gap is about three times larger than chance alone would usually produce. That makes a real effect likely. But how big is the effect, and is four points a lot? Answering that question is the job of effect size.

docs.title: Effect Size
docs.text:
Effect size is a standardized measure of how large the difference between two groups is, expressed in units of the spread of scores rather than in raw points. The most common form is Cohen's d: the difference between the two group averages divided by the pooled standard deviation. The standard deviation measures how widely students' scores vary around the average, so d tells you how many "typical spreads" the groups differ by.

\[ d = \frac{\bar{x}_{\text{treatment}} - \bar{x}_{\text{control}}}{s_{\text{pooled}}} \]

Standardizing is what lets you compare a 4-point gain on a 50-point test with a 40-point gain on a 500-point test. In the MathPath pilot, \( d = (34 - 30)/10 = 0.4 \).

To make d intuitive, translate it into a percentile. If scores are roughly bell-shaped, then at \( d = 0.4 \) the average treated student scores above about 66 percent of the control group. The table below summarizes a few reference points; each follows from the same bell-curve arithmetic.

Effect size d The average treated student scores higher than this share of the control group 0.0 50% 0.1 54% 0.2 58% 0.4 66% 0.5 69% 0.8 79%

Now the claim "effect size of 0.8" has a meaning: the average student on the program would outscore about four in five students who were not on it. That would be spectacular, and that is exactly why a skeptic should ask whether it is believable.

How big is "big"? Jacob Cohen suggested in 1988 that 0.2 is small, 0.5 medium, and 0.8 large, but he meant these as rough guides for lab psychology. In education, researchers have learned that real interventions, tested on standardized tests in real schools, rarely produce effects that large. Matthew Kraft's 2020 review of education studies suggests that for well-designed studies of standardized achievement, an effect below 0.05 is small, 0.05 to 0.20 is medium, and above 0.20 is large. By that standard, even an effect of 0.2 is a major result, and a claim of 0.8 should prompt questions about the study's design before celebration. John Hattie's widely cited syntheses use 0.40 as a "hinge point" for a worthwhile effect, but that number has drawn criticism because it mixes studies of very different designs and quality.

The sim below lets you see how much the two groups overlap at different effect sizes.

docs.title: Diagram: Effect Size Visualization
docs.text:
Run the Effect Size Visualization MicroSim fullscreen

Effect Size Visualization (reused MicroSim)

Type: microsim sim-id: effect-size-visualizer Library: p5.js Status: Reused Source: https://dmccreary.github.io/statistics-course/sims/effect-size-visualizer/ Source Repo: https://github.com/dmccreary/statistics-course/tree/main/docs/sims/effect-size-visualizer Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: interpret Learning Objective: The learner will interpret Cohen's d values from 0 to 2.0 by describing how much two score distributions overlap at each value.

Reused from the MicroSim catalog (WHAT match score 0.7557).

Significant is not the same as big

Notice that "is the effect real?" and "is the effect large?" are different questions. A huge study can find a real but tiny effect; a tiny study can find a large one by luck. Always ask for both the size and how the groups were formed.

docs.title: Worked Example: Is 0.8 Believable?
docs.text:
Suppose the MathPath brochure's 0.8 comes from a study. Walk through what you would ask:

  1. Design. Was assignment random? If students chose MathPath, selection bias could create a large "effect" with no learning gain at all.
  2. Outcome measure. Was the test the standard state test, or a test the vendor wrote about exactly the skills MathPath practices? A test written to match the program inflates effects.
  3. Time and size. A two-week pilot with 30 students may give a big number that does not hold up in 3,000 students over a year.
  4. Who ran it. An independent evaluator is more credible than the company's own team, which has a stake in the result.

The pilot at Lincoln Middle, with its random assignment, school-wide test, and independent scoring, would produce a number you can trust. That number, 0.4, is lower than 0.8, and it is still a strong result by Kraft's benchmarks.

docs.title: Case Study Method
docs.text:
An RCT answers "did it work, on average?" The case study method answers a different question: how and why did it work, or not work, in a particular place? A case study is an in-depth examination of one or a few real situations, such as a school, a classroom, or a district, using interviews, observation, documents, and data, with attention to the context that numbers leave out. The term also names a teaching method, used in business and law schools, in which students analyze a real case and argue about what to do. This book uses both senses: it studies cases, and it asks you to reason about them.

Cases are strong where RCTs are weak. A case can show that a program worked beautifully in one school because the principal protected teachers' time, and failed in another because the tablets arrived in January. It can surface problems nobody thought to measure. Its weakness is that one story does not prove a general rule: a vivid success may be an exception. The sound approach is to use both. The course description's stories of Alpha School, Unbound Academy, and the Los Angeles "Ed" chatbot are cases; the effect sizes in the research are the statistics; and a careful reader looks for where the two agree.

docs.title: Worked Example: A Case Study of the Pilot
docs.text:
After the MathPath pilot, Ms. Okafor asks a district researcher to do a short case study. The researcher interviews six teachers, observes four classes, and reads the usage logs. The findings:

  • What worked: Students who got stuck received a hint within seconds, and teachers could see on a dashboard who needed help.
  • What did not: In two classrooms the tablets were used only on Fridays, because teachers lacked planning time to use the dashboard.
  • Context: The classrooms with the largest gains had a teacher who stopped the lesson each day to address the most common error the dashboard showed.

The RCT said the program helped on average. The case study says the average hides a difference in how teachers used it. Both are needed to decide what to do next.

The tool below practices the central evaluation skill of this section: matching a claim to the level of evidence behind it.

docs.title: Diagram: Evidence Tier Claim Checker
docs.text:
Run the Evidence Tier Claim Checker MicroSim Fullscreen

Evidence Tier Claim Checker

Type: microsim sim-id: evidence-tier-claim-checker Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: judge Learning Objective: The learner will judge the strength of the evidence behind ten vendor claims by assigning each to one of five evidence levels, correctly placing at least eight of ten on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: evidence-based practice, randomized controlled trial, selection bias, the five evidence levels (Strong, Moderate, Promising, Demonstrates a rationale, No evidence of effect), all defined in the section "Evidence-Based Practice: Judging What Works" above.

Evidence of Mastery: The learner places each of 10 claims in one of five level bins and submits it. A placement is correct when it matches the "Correct level" column in Content. Mastery is 8 of 10 correct on the first attempt. Reading the level definitions is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A large sample makes a claim strong whatever the study design. (2) Teacher satisfaction is evidence of learning. (3) Any before-and-after gain shows the program worked.

Instructional Rationale: Judging is an Evaluate-level act: the learner must apply criteria (how groups were formed) to unfamiliar claims and commit to a verdict. Including a very large self-selected sample and a before-and-after gain forces the learner to rely on design, not on impressive-sounding numbers.

Content:

Five bins, each with its one-line definition shown on request:

Bin Definition shown Strong Random assignment, well designed and well carried out Moderate A comparison group, but no random assignment Promising A correlational study that adjusts for who chose the program Demonstrates a rationale A research-based reason to expect it to work; results not yet in No evidence of effect Testimonials, surveys, usage counts, uncontrolled before-and-after or self-selected comparisons

Ten claims about the fictional program "MathPath":

# Claim shown to the learner Correct level Why (shown as feedback) 1 "In a study where 1,200 students were randomly assigned to MathPath or a control group, the MathPath group gained 0.15 standard deviations more on the state test." Strong Random assignment and a standardized outcome measure. 2 "A district compared 800 MathPath students with 800 matched students who did not use it, matched on prior scores and demographics; MathPath students gained more." Moderate There is a comparison group, but it was chosen, not drawn by lot. 3 "Across 40 schools, students who used MathPath more hours scored higher, after statistical adjustment for prior scores and family income." Promising A correlational study with controls; it still cannot rule out unmeasured differences. 4 "MathPath's design is based on research about spaced and retrieval practice, and an independent evaluation is under way." Demonstrates a rationale A research-based reason to expect it to work, with results still to come. 5 "94% of teachers surveyed said they love MathPath." No evidence of effect A satisfaction survey does not measure learning. 6 "Students in one pilot classroom raised their average score by 12 points from fall to spring." No evidence of effect Students usually gain over a school year; with no comparison group the gain cannot be credited to the program. 7 "Among 12,000 students, those who chose to use the optional MathPath program scored higher than those who did not." No evidence of effect Students who choose a program differ from those who do not, and a large sample does not fix that. 8 "Two separate randomized trials in different states, with 2,000 students in total, found gains of 0.10 and 0.18 standard deviations." Strong Repeated random-assignment results strengthen the case. 9 "A state analysis compared the 30 schools that adopted MathPath with 30 similar schools that did not, using the same tests." Moderate A comparison group of similar schools, but not randomly formed. 10 "MathPath uses mastery learning, which has strong research support in general; no study of MathPath itself has been done." Demonstrates a rationale A sound reason to expect results, but no evidence yet about this product.

Provenance: The five levels follow the chapter section "Evidence-Based Practice: Judging What Works," which summarizes the Every Student Succeeds Act evidence tiers and adds one bin for non-evidence. The claims are illustrative, written for this chapter; the sim must label them "Fictional claims about a fictional program."

Rules: Each claim has exactly one correct level, given in Content. A claim is scored on its first submitted placement only. The score counts first-attempt correct placements out of 10. Mastery is a score >= 8.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads one claim at a time and sees the five bins.
  2. The learner places the claim in a bin and submits it. The sim marks it correct or incorrect and shows the feedback text.
  3. If incorrect, the learner may place the claim again; the second attempt does not change the score. After the second attempt, the correct level and reason are shown.
  4. After all 10 claims, the sim shows the score and lists any misplaced claims with their correct levels.
  5. The learner should notice that claim 7, with 12,000 students, sits in the lowest bin while claim 1, with 1,200, sits in the highest.

Feedback: 10 claims, shuffled once per session, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: [level]. [Why text]." Incorrect: "Not quite. [Why text for the correct answer, without naming the level]." After the second attempt the correct level is revealed and the claim counts as missed. A running score "First-try correct: n of 10" is shown. Final message for a score >= 8: "You can judge a claim by how its comparison was built." For a score < 8: "Review the level definitions and try again; the claims will be reshuffled."

Starting State: Claim 1 of the shuffled order is shown with five empty bins and the score "First-try correct: 0 of 10." The prompt reads "How strong is the evidence behind this claim?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter names five evidence levels in the order Strong, Moderate, Promising, Demonstrates a rationale, No evidence of effect. The chapter states that a large sample does not fix self-selection and that satisfaction surveys do not measure learning. The mastery bar is 8 of 10.

docs.title: Prior Knowledge and Prerequisite Concepts
docs.text:
Evidence tells you whether something works on average. Learning, as Chapter 1 stressed, happens inside one learner at a time, and what that learner already knows shapes everything.

Prior knowledge is the set of facts, skills, concepts, and beliefs a learner already holds when they begin a new lesson. The educational psychologist David Ausubel wrote in 1968 that the single most important factor influencing learning is what the learner already knows, and that teachers should find this out and teach accordingly. That remains one of the best-supported ideas in the field, and it explains much of the learning gap you met in Chapter 1.

Prior knowledge has three effects. It enables new learning: a student who knows what a fraction is can learn to add fractions. It organizes memory: new facts attach to existing ones, which is why experts remember more of a new fact in their field than novices do. And it can mislead: prior knowledge sometimes includes wrong ideas. In a well-known 1987 documentary, A Private Universe, graduates and faculty at Harvard were asked why it is hot in summer and cold in winter, and many confidently explained that the Earth is closer to the Sun in summer, which is wrong. A teacher who does not find out about such beliefs may teach on top of them without correcting them.

A prerequisite concept is a concept that must be understood before another concept can be learned. Prior knowledge is what the student has; a prerequisite is what a given idea requires. A teacher's work is to compare the two. Prerequisites form chains, and the learning graph introduced in Chapter 1 and covered in depth in Chapter 9 is a map of those chains, with every arrow pointing from a concept to what it depends on.

docs.title: Worked Example: Maya's Missing Stair
docs.text:
Maya's difficulty with ratios in seventh grade traces back to a chain of prerequisites in mathematics. The table lists a simplified chain of eight concepts and what each depends on.

# Concept Depends directly on 1 Whole-number multiplication and division none 2 Fractions as parts of a whole none 3 Equivalent fractions 1, 2 4 Adding and subtracting fractions with unlike denominators 3 5 Multiplying and dividing fractions 1, 2 6 Ratios 3 7 Unit rates 5, 6 8 Proportional equations 7

Ms. Rivera sees that Maya fails unit-rate problems (concept 7). Reteaching unit rates again will not help if the gap lies earlier. A short diagnostic gives Maya a few problems on each concept. She passes concepts 1, 2, and 5 but fails concepts 3, 4, and 6. Failing 3 explains the other two: concepts 4 and 6 both depend on equivalent fractions. The problem is not in unit rates, or even ratios; it is two steps down, at equivalent fractions. This is why a diagnosis needs a map and not just a score.

The practical rule is this: the root gap is a failed concept all of whose own prerequisites passed. A failed concept whose prerequisites also failed is a symptom, not the cause. Fix the root gap and the dependent failures often resolve; reteach a symptom and nothing changes. The sim below lets you practice that diagnosis.

docs.title: Diagram: Prerequisite Chain Diagnosis
docs.text:
Run the Prerequisite Chain Diagnosis MicroSim Fullscreen

Prerequisite Chain Diagnosis

Type: graph-model sim-id: prerequisite-chain-diagnosis Library: vis-network Status: Specified Bloom Level: Analyze Bloom Verb: attribute Learning Objective: The learner will attribute a student's failure on a target concept to its root gap by examining a prerequisite map and a set of pass/fail results, correctly identifying the root gap in at least four of five cases.

Template: https://github.com/dmccreary/automating-instructional-design/tree/main/docs/sims/learning-dependency-network

Prerequisites: prior knowledge, prerequisite concept, root gap, the meaning of a dependency arrow (all defined in the section "Prior Knowledge and Prerequisite Concepts" above).

Evidence of Mastery: For each of 5 cases, the learner selects exactly one node as the root gap and submits it. A selection is correct when it matches the "Root gap" column in Content. Mastery is 4 of 5 correct. Selecting nodes to read their descriptions is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) The target concept the student failed is always the place to reteach. (2) Every failed concept needs reteaching. (3) A concept that failed must have a failed prerequisite.

Instructional Rationale: Attributing a failure to a cause requires reading structure, which here is the prerequisite map. Cases include a root gap at the target itself and cases with several dependent failures, so the learner cannot use a single shortcut.

Content:

Eight nodes, each with its name shown on the node and a one-sentence description shown when it is selected:

# Node Description shown 1 Whole-number multiplication and division Multiplying and dividing whole numbers fluently. 2 Fractions as parts of a whole Understanding a fraction as equal parts of one whole. 3 Equivalent fractions Recognizing that different fractions can name the same amount, such as 1/2 and 2/4. 4 Adding and subtracting fractions with unlike denominators Combining fractions after rewriting them with a common denominator. 5 Multiplying and dividing fractions Multiplying and dividing fractions, including by whole numbers. 6 Ratios Comparing two quantities, such as 3 apples for every 2 oranges. 7 Unit rates Finding the amount per one unit, such as price per ounce. 8 Proportional equations Writing and solving equations that relate two proportional quantities.

Nine arrows, each pointing from a concept to a prerequisite it depends on:

From (depends) To (prerequisite) 3 1 3 2 4 3 5 1 5 2 6 3 7 5 7 6 8 7

Five cases. Each shows a student's pass (P) or fail (F) result on every node, and the target concept the student failed in class:

Case Target N1 N2 N3 N4 N5 N6 N7 N8 Root gap Why (shown as feedback) 1 7 P P P P F P F F 5 Node 5 failed while both its prerequisites (1 and 2) passed; nodes 7 and 8 fail because they sit above node 5. 2 8 P P F F P F F F 3 Node 3 failed while its prerequisites (1 and 2) passed; nodes 4, 6, 7 and 8 fail because they depend on 3, directly or through 6. 3 4 P P P F P P P P 4 Node 4 failed while its only prerequisite (3) passed, so the gap is at the target itself. 4 8 P P P P P P F F 7 Node 7 failed while both its prerequisites (5 and 6) passed; node 8 fails because it depends on 7. 5 6 P F F F F F F F 2 Node 2 has no prerequisites and failed; every other failure lies above it.

Provenance: The map is the simplified fractions-to-proportions chain written for this chapter. The pass and fail results are illustrative, and the sim must label them "Illustrative student results."

Rules: The root gap in a case is the failed node whose direct prerequisites all passed (or that has none). Each case has exactly one root gap. The learner selects one node per case. Nodes with no prerequisites (1 and 2) are visually marked as having none. Zoom and reset are available by buttons; mouse-wheel zoom is disabled.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner explores the map, selecting nodes to read their descriptions.
  2. The learner starts the cases. For case 1, the map shows pass/fail marks on every node and highlights the target.
  3. The learner selects the node they judge to be the root gap and submits.
  4. The sim marks the answer, and highlights the correct node and the failed nodes above it.
  5. The learner continues through case 5, then sees the score.
  6. The learner should notice that the target concept is the root gap in only one of the five cases.

Feedback: 5 cases, fixed order, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct. [Why text]." Incorrect, selected a failed node whose prerequisite also failed: "That node failed because something below it failed. Look for a failed node whose prerequisites all passed." Incorrect, selected a passed node: "That node passed, so it is not a gap." After the second wrong attempt, the root gap is highlighted with the Why text. Score "n of 5" is shown at the end.

Starting State: The full map of 8 nodes and 9 arrows is shown with no node selected, and the prompt reads "A student failed one concept. Where should we reteach?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's table lists the same eight concepts and the same dependencies. The chapter defines the root gap as a failed concept all of whose prerequisites passed. The mastery bar is 4 of 5.

docs.title: Lecture-Based Teaching and Immediate Feedback
docs.text: Two ways of teaching that shape most of a student's day deserve their own definitions: how information reaches the student, and how quickly the student hears back.

docs.title: Lecture-Based Teaching
docs.text:
Lecture-based teaching is a mode of instruction in which the teacher presents information orally to the whole class while students mostly listen and take notes. It overlaps with the direct instruction of Chapter 1 but is narrower: direct instruction also includes guided practice, questioning, and checking, whereas a pure lecture is one-way delivery. Lecturing is efficient for the teacher, since one explanation reaches thirty students, and it works well for giving an overview or telling a compelling story. Its weakness is that the teacher cannot see what each listener understood until later.

The best-known synthesis is a 2014 meta-analysis by Scott Freeman and colleagues in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, which pooled 225 studies of undergraduate science, technology, engineering, and mathematics courses. It found that students in courses with active learning, where students answer questions, solve problems, and discuss during class, earned higher exam scores than students in traditional lecture, by about half a standard deviation. Students in lecture were also more likely to fail: about 34 percent compared with about 22 percent. That evidence comes from college STEM courses, so it should be applied to K-12 with care, but the direction matches what teachers see.

The lesson is not "never lecture." It is that a stretch of listening should be short, followed quickly by students doing something with the idea, with the teacher checking. A short explanation followed by practice is the "I do, we do, you do" pattern from Chapter 1.

docs.title: Immediate Feedback
docs.text:
Immediate feedback is information given to a learner about the correctness of a response, and ideally the reason, within seconds or minutes of the response. It is the opposite of delayed feedback, such as homework returned a week later. Immediate feedback was a central feature of the teaching machines of Chapter 1's history, and it is the capability of computers that most clearly beats a single human teacher with thirty students.

The research on timing is more nuanced than "faster is always better." Feedback soon after an error stops a student from practicing a mistake, and it matters most for novices learning procedures, where a wrong step repeated twenty times becomes a habit. But very quick feedback that simply shows the answer can short-circuit thinking: a student who clicks "show answer" at the first hint learns little. The most useful feedback tells the student what to try next rather than what the answer is. This is the idea behind the hint-first guardrails Chapter 12 covers.

docs.title: Worked Example: Two Homework Cycles
docs.text:
Suppose Maya practices ten unit-rate problems. Compare what happens under two feedback timings.

Paper homework Interactive practice with immediate hints When Maya learns she is wrong Five days later, when the paper is returned Within seconds of each problem Problems Maya repeats with the same error All ten (she does not know) About one or two before a hint corrects her What the teacher sees A stack of papers; marks, not reasons A dashboard of which step students miss Risk The error becomes a habit Students click for the answer instead of thinking

Notice that the second column is better only if the hints are designed well. The risk in the last row is real, and it is why how an AI tool gives feedback matters as much as how fast.

A hint ladder keeps the thinking

When you evaluate any practice tool, ask it for help on a problem and count the steps before it shows the answer. A good tool starts with a nudge ("What is the problem asking for?"), moves to a specific hint, and only then explains. If the first click reveals the answer, the feedback is fast but the learning is not.

docs.title: Summative Assessment
docs.text:
Summative assessment, which Chapter 1 contrasted with formative assessment, is a measurement of learning at the end of a period, such as a unit, semester, or year, used to assign a grade, certify mastery, or report results. Familiar examples are final exams, end-of-unit tests, graduation exams, and state accountability tests. Under ESSA, U.S. states must test students in reading and mathematics every year from third through eighth grade and once in high school, and these results are reported to the public by school. The National Assessment of Educational Progress, often called the "Nation's Report Card," samples students nationally to track trends over time.

Summative tests serve real purposes. They give a common yardstick, allow comparison across schools, and are the standard way the RCTs in the previous section measure results. But they have limits. They arrive too late to help the student who took them. They sample only part of what students learn. And when high stakes are attached, they distort behavior: the social scientist Donald Campbell observed in 1979 that the more a quantitative indicator is used for decisions, the more it is subject to pressure that corrupts both the indicator and the process it was meant to monitor. Teachers narrowing the curriculum to what the test covers, or "teaching to the test," is a textbook example.

docs.title: Worked Example: Two Reports on the Same Student
docs.text:
Compare what two assessments tell Ms. Okafor about Maya's math.

End-of-year state test Weekly five-question checks Type Summative Formative When it arrives June, after the school year ends Every Friday What it says about Maya "Below grade-level proficiency" "Missed equivalent-fraction questions four weeks in a row" What the school can do with it Plan next year's programs Intervene this month Risk Too late for Maya; high stakes can narrow teaching Many small tests can feel like constant evaluation

Both are needed: the first tells the school whether the year succeeded, and the second tells the teacher what to fix while there is still time. An AI-native school depends on getting the second kind of data at scale, a theme Chapter 8 develops.

docs.title: Motivation and Engagement
docs.text: Knowing what works is only part of the story. A program that works on paper does nothing for a student who does not engage with it. This part of the chapter defines the words educators use for the emotional and motivational side of learning.

docs.title: Student Engagement
docs.text:
Student engagement is the degree to which students are attentive, interested, and invested in their learning. Researchers Jennifer Fredricks, Phyllis Blumenfeld, and Alison Paris described it in 2004 as having three connected dimensions:

  • Behavioral engagement: participation and effort you can see, such as attending, completing work, and following rules.
  • Emotional engagement: feelings toward school and tasks, such as interest, enjoyment, and a sense of belonging.
  • Cognitive engagement: the mental effort a student invests, such as choosing to work through a hard problem or checking their own understanding.

The three can come apart. A student can look perfectly on task (behavioral) while feeling nothing (emotional) and thinking about lunch (cognitive). Engagement is also not the same as fun: a laughing, busy class may be engaged with the activity but not with the learning goal.

docs.title: Worked Example: Two Students, Three Dimensions
docs.text:
Ms. Rivera observes two students during a unit-rate lesson and records what she sees.

Dimension Maya Jordan Behavioral Sits quietly, copies the examples, turns in work Finishes early, then doodles Emotional Anxious; avoids eye contact; says "fine" when asked Looks relaxed; says "this is easy" Cognitive Copies steps without checking understanding Thinking about something else Overall Looks engaged; is not Looks disengaged; the work is too easy

Both are at risk, in different ways, and only a teacher who looks at all three dimensions would see it. This is a core promise of well-designed adaptive software: data on what a student actually did reveals cognitive engagement that a quiet face hides.

docs.title: Student Boredom
docs.text:
Student boredom is an unpleasant emotional state in which a student finds the activity uninteresting and has difficulty staying attentive. Boredom is one of the most common emotions students report in class. Surveys of high school students over the past two decades have consistently found that a large share say they are bored in class regularly, though exact percentages vary by survey and should be checked at the source before being cited.

Boredom has more than one cause, and this is the key insight. Psychologist Reinhard Pekrun's research on academic emotions shows that boredom can arise when a task is too easy, when it is too hard and the student has given up, or when the student sees no value in it. The behavior looks the same in all three cases, which is why one fix does not suit all.

docs.title: Worked Example: Three Bored Students
docs.text:
In the same classroom, three students show the same behavior: head down, pencil untouched.

Student Why they are bored What helps Jordan Already mastered the material; the work is too easy Move to harder material; skip ahead Maya Lost two lessons ago; has given up Fill the missing prerequisite; shrink the first step Dev Can do it but asks "when will I ever use this?" Connect the topic to something he cares about

Whole-class pacing (Chapter 1) gives all three the same lesson. Individually paced software can respond to the first two, but only a teacher or a good project is likely to answer Dev.

Same face, different cause

A common trap is treating every bored student as lazy or every disengaged student as a behavior problem. Before you act, ask which of three things is going on: too easy, too hard, or not worth it. Each has a different fix, and the wrong fix, like more challenge for a lost student, makes things worse.

docs.title: Intrinsic Motivation
docs.text:
Intrinsic motivation is the drive to do something because it is interesting or satisfying in itself, not for a reward or to avoid punishment. Its counterpart, extrinsic motivation, is doing something for an outside reward such as a grade, a prize, or approval. Edward Deci and Richard Ryan's self-determination theory holds that intrinsic motivation grows when three needs are met: autonomy (a sense of choice), competence (a sense of being able to succeed), and relatedness (a sense of connection to others).

The most famous result in this area is a 1973 experiment by Mark Lepper, David Greene, and Richard Nisbett. Preschoolers who already liked drawing with felt-tip markers were promised a "good player" award for drawing. Later, in free time, those children drew with markers less than children who had not been promised anything. The reward had changed why they drew, from "because it's fun" to "because I get a prize." This pattern is called the overjustification effect. The takeaway is not that rewards are always harmful: for dull tasks they can help. It is that adding a reward to something a student already enjoys can weaken the enjoyment.

docs.title: Worked Example: Points and Badges
docs.text:
A vendor's practice app awards points and badges for every completed problem. Evaluate it against the three needs.

Need Does the app support it? Risk or fix Autonomy Partly: students choose the order of the practice sets Add more choices about what to explore Competence Yes: students see a progress bar and mastery marks Make sure the marks reflect real mastery, not just time spent Relatedness No: students work alone Pair the app with a short weekly discussion with a classmate Overjustification Points may replace the satisfaction of solving Reward progress toward learning goals, and fade the points over time

The lesson: a feature is not good or bad because it is a badge. It is good if it helps students feel capable and in control, and bad if it becomes the reason they work.

docs.title: Curiosity
docs.text:
Curiosity is the desire to learn or know something, usually triggered by noticing a gap in what you know. George Loewenstein's information-gap theory, from 1994, says curiosity is strongest when you know a little about something, enough to realize you do not know the rest. Too little knowledge produces no curiosity, and complete knowledge leaves nothing to be curious about.

Curiosity also helps memory. In a 2014 brain-imaging study, Matthias Gruber, Bernard Gelman, and Charan Ranganath found that people remembered answers to trivia questions they were curious about better than answers to questions they were not, and that curiosity engaged the brain's reward circuits. In practice, a lesson that opens with a puzzle (Why do puddles disappear on a sunny day?) can prepare students to attend to the explanation.

docs.title: Curiosity-Driven Learning
docs.text:
Curiosity-driven learning is an approach in which students pursue their own questions and interests, with the teacher guiding and resourcing rather than dictating the path. It applies the student agency of Chapter 1 to the choice of topic. Examples are inquiry projects, genius hour, and open-ended research questions.

The evidence needs honest handling. Curiosity-driven approaches can build motivation and ownership, and some, like Sugata Mitra's "Hole in the Wall" experiments in India, where children taught themselves from a public computer, drew worldwide attention. But those results have been disputed, and a well-known 2006 paper by Paul Kirschner, John Sweller, and Richard Clark argued that minimally guided instruction is less effective than guided instruction for novices, who lack the prior knowledge to explore well. The consistent finding is that curiosity works best on top of a foundation: students need enough knowledge to have good questions and enough structure to follow them somewhere.

docs.title: Worked Example: Building Curiosity into a Morning
docs.text:
Consider a two-hour morning block that uses adaptive practice for core skills. A school wants to protect time for curiosity without losing the core.

Segment Minutes What students do Core mastery path 90 Adaptive practice with immediate feedback toward grade-level outcomes Curiosity block 30 Each student pursues a question of their own, with a teacher check-in Total 120

The curiosity block is \( 30 / 120 = 25\% \) of the morning. The design holds the core fixed so every student gets the foundation, and still gives every student a protected slot for their own questions. The next chapters return to how this fits the afternoon.

docs.title: Productive Struggle
docs.text:
Productive struggle is the effortful work a student does to make sense of a problem that is challenging but within reach, before being shown how to solve it. It is not the same as frustration, which is struggle with no way forward. Manu Kapur's research on productive failure, begun in 2008, found that students who first tried to solve a hard problem on their own, even failing, understood the underlying concept better afterward than students who were first taught the procedure. This is the classroom version of the desirable difficulty from Chapter 1.

Struggle is productive when four things hold: the task is hard but reachable, the student has some prior knowledge to work with, errors are treated as normal, and the teacher later consolidates what was learned. It becomes unproductive when the task needs knowledge the student lacks, when there is no support, or when failure is punished.

docs.title: Worked Example: A Hint Ladder
docs.text:
A problem asks: "A 6-pack of juice costs $4.50. What is the price per bottle?" A tool offers four levels of help, and each level removes a little of the struggle.

Level What the tool says How much struggle is left 0 Nothing; the student works alone All of it 1 "What is the problem asking you to find?" Almost all; the student still plans 2 "Which quantity do you divide by which?" Some; the plan is narrowed 3 "Divide 4.50 by 6." Little; only the arithmetic remains 4 "The answer is $0.75." None

A tool that jumps to level 4 removes the struggle, and with it the learning. A tool that never goes past level 0 produces frustration. The art is to give the smallest help that keeps the student moving. This is the central design question for AI tutors, and Chapter 12 builds on it.

Struggle is part of the plan

If a problem is hard and you feel stuck, that doesn't mean you're doing it wrong; it often means the learning is happening. You've already learned to separate performance from lasting learning in Chapter 1, and this is the same idea from the inside. Try the next sim and predict first; being wrong on a prediction is a good kind of struggle.

The terms in this section fit together through a single idea: how hard the task is compared with what the student already knows. Before the next sim, here is a simple model that this book uses. Rate the challenge of a task and the student's prior knowledge on the same 1-to-10 scale, and call the difference, challenge minus prior knowledge, the gap. This is a deliberate simplification, inspired by Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi's work on "flow," which found that people are most absorbed when challenge and skill are well matched. The table gives the four states the model predicts. Providing support, such as a hint ladder, lets a student handle one more level of gap before becoming overwhelmed.

Gap (challenge minus prior knowledge) State without support State with support Gap <= −2 Bored Bored −1 <= gap <= 1 Engaged Engaged 2 <= gap <= 3 Productive struggle Productive struggle Gap = 4 Overwhelmed Productive struggle Gap >= 5 Overwhelmed Overwhelmed

docs.title: Diagram: Challenge and Prior Knowledge Zone Explorer
docs.text:
Run the Challenge and Prior Knowledge Zone Explorer MicroSim Fullscreen

Challenge and Prior Knowledge Zone Explorer

Type: microsim sim-id: challenge-knowledge-zone-explorer Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Analyze Bloom Verb: distinguish Learning Objective: The learner will distinguish whether a student is bored, engaged, in productive struggle, or overwhelmed by examining the gap between a task's challenge and the student's prior knowledge and whether support is available, correctly classifying at least five of six scenarios.

Prerequisites: prior knowledge, student boredom, student engagement, productive struggle, the challenge-minus-prior-knowledge gap and its four states (all defined in the section "Motivation and Engagement" above).

Evidence of Mastery: For each of 6 scenarios, the learner commits a prediction of the student's state before the sim reveals it. A prediction is correct when it matches the "Correct state" column in Content. Mastery is 5 of 6 correct. Moving the sliders in exploration mode is not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A bored student is always lazy. (2) Struggle always means the task is too hard. (3) Making a task easier is always the right response to a struggling student.

Instructional Rationale: Distinguishing the four states requires the learner to apply the gap rule to concrete cases, and scenario 5 shows that the same gap produces a different state when support is present. Predicting before the reveal exposes the learner's own mental model.

Content:

Two quantities on a 1-to-10 scale, and one on/off setting:

Quantity Min Max Step Default Unit Task challenge 1 10 1 5 level Student prior knowledge 1 10 1 5 level Support available (hint ladder) off on n/a off n/a

The gap is task challenge minus student prior knowledge. The four states and their definitions, shown in the legend:

State Definition shown Bored The task is too easy for what the student already knows Engaged The task is well matched to what the student knows Productive struggle The task is hard but within reach, so effort pays off Overwhelmed The task is too hard for the student to make progress

Six scenarios:

# Challenge Prior knowledge Support Gap Correct state Why (shown as feedback) 1 3 8 off −5 Bored The task is five levels below what the student knows. 2 6 6 off 0 Engaged Challenge matches knowledge. 3 8 6 off 2 Productive struggle The task is two levels above what the student knows, which is reachable. 4 9 4 off 5 Overwhelmed A gap of 5 is too large to make progress alone. 5 8 4 on 4 Productive struggle Without support a gap of 4 overwhelms, but a hint ladder lets the student keep making progress. 6 5 7 off −2 Bored The task is two levels below what the student knows.

Provenance: The model is illustrative, based on the chapter's challenge-and-knowledge model and inspired by Csikszentmihalyi's flow research. The sim must label it "Illustrative model, not measured data."

Rules: Gap g = challenge − prior knowledge. Without support: g <= −2 is Bored; −1 <= g <= 1 is Engaged; 2 <= g <= 3 is Productive struggle; g >= 4 is Overwhelmed. With support: g <= −2 is Bored; −1 <= g <= 1 is Engaged; 2 <= g <= 4 is Productive struggle; g >= 5 is Overwhelmed. The state is recomputed whenever a slider or the support setting changes.

Learner Activity:

  1. For scenario 1, the sim shows the challenge, prior knowledge, and support setting. The learner chooses a state and submits.
  2. The sim reveals the state, shows the gap, and displays the feedback text.
  3. The learner continues through scenario 6 and sees the score.
  4. Exploration mode then unlocks. The learner moves both sliders and the support setting and watches the state update.
  5. The learner should notice that turning support on changes the state only when the gap is 4.

Feedback: 6 scenarios, fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [state]. [Why text]." Incorrect: "Not quite. The gap is [g]. [Why text]." The correct state is revealed after the single attempt. A running score "n of 6" is shown. Final message for a score >= 5: "You can read the gap between a task and a student." For a score < 5: "Review the four states and try again."

Starting State: Scenario 1 is shown with the sliders locked at the scenario values, the state hidden, and the prompt "How is this student likely to feel about this task?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's table gives the same four states and thresholds for the gap with and without support. The scale is 1 to 10. The mastery bar is 5 of 6.

docs.title: Screen Time
docs.text:
Screen time is the amount of time a person spends using devices with screens, such as tablets, computers, phones, and televisions. It is one of the most common worries families raise about educational technology, and it deserves a straight answer, because the model in this book puts students in front of a screen for part of the morning.

The first point is that "screen time" lumps together very different activities. Watching videos passively, scrolling social media, playing a game, solving practice problems with feedback, and writing a story on a laptop all count as screen time, yet they differ greatly in cognitive demand and in their effects. Researchers increasingly separate what a student does from how long the screen is on.

The second point is that the evidence on harm is weaker and more mixed than headlines suggest. A 2019 analysis of three large datasets by Amy Orben and Andrew Przybylski found that the association between digital technology use and adolescent well-being was very small, explaining well under one percent of the variation. That study was correlational, so it cannot show cause, and other research finds larger effects for specific uses such as late-night social media. On learning, the OECD's PISA 2022 results found that students who were distracted by other students' devices in class scored lower in mathematics, and that moderate use of devices for learning went with higher scores than heavy use. The pattern is consistent: purpose and context matter more than the total.

The balance in this book's design is to be honest about the tradeoff. A two-hour morning on adaptive software is real screen time, and it also replaces hours of passive listening. The afternoon, centered on people, projects, and movement, is largely screen-free.

docs.title: Worked Example: Comparing Two Days
docs.text:
The table compares Maya's screen use in two designs, using illustrative numbers.

Activity Traditional day (minutes on screen) AI-native day (minutes on screen) Whole-class lessons 10 (teacher projector, video clips) 0 Adaptive practice 0 120 Afternoon projects and clubs 0 20 (looking up information, coding club) Homework 30 0 Social media and games at home 120 120 Total 160 260

The AI-native day adds about 100 minutes of school screen time. Whether that is acceptable depends on what it replaces and what Maya does at home. The home figure, the same in both columns, is larger than the school figure in either one, which is why a school that worries about screen time should talk with families about the evening as well as the morning.

Don't judge a screen by its glow

A common trap is adding up all screen minutes as if they were the same. Instead, sort the minutes into passive, social, and active-learning, and ask what each replaced. If the school day adds two hours of interactive practice, give families the breakdown and a plan for breaks, movement, and an off-screen afternoon.

docs.title: The People Involved: Stakeholders of Schooling
docs.text: Every decision in this chapter, from adopting MathPath to changing the schedule, affects different people differently. The term stakeholder names anyone who is affected by or has influence over a decision. This section covers the ones a school leader hears from first.

docs.title: Parent and Family
docs.text:
Parent and family refers to the adults responsible for a child at home: parents, guardians, grandparents, and other caregivers. They are the child's first and longest-lasting educators, and the only stakeholders who know the student across all thirteen years. The education researcher Joyce Epstein described six ways families and schools work together: parenting, communicating, volunteering, supporting learning at home, taking part in decisions, and collaborating with the community.

Research summarized by Anne Henderson and Karen Mapp in 2002 found that family involvement is associated with better attendance, grades, and attitudes, though most of that evidence is correlational: involved families may differ in other ways. What is clear is that families have real concerns about AI in schools, and that those concerns are often legitimate. The most common are screen time, privacy of the child's data, whether the child will still learn to think, and fairness for children with fewer resources at home.

docs.title: Worked Example: A Family Night Handout
docs.text:
Ms. Okafor prepares answers to four common concerns for a parent night about the MathPath pilot.

Concern What the evidence says What the school will do "Too much screen time" Purpose matters more than total minutes; the pilot is 30 active minutes a day Publish the daily schedule; keep afternoons screen-light "What happens to my child's data?" Adaptive software needs records of student work; this raises privacy duties (Chapter 10) Share the vendor's data policy and let families ask questions "Will my child just get the answers?" It depends on the tool's design; hint-first tools protect thinking Show the hint ladder in a demonstration "What if my child falls behind?" Self-paced tools can drift without checks Teachers review progress weekly and call families when a student stalls

Notice that the right-hand column promises actions, not slogans. It is also an example of this book's pattern: name the risk, then say how the school responds.

docs.title: School Administrator and Principal
docs.text:
A school administrator is a staff member who manages a school or school system rather than teaching classes full time. The group includes principals and assistant principals at the school level and, at the district level, the superintendent (the district's chief executive), and directors of curriculum, technology, finance, and special education. Administrators are responsible for budgets, hiring, schedules, safety, compliance with laws, and carrying out the policies the school board sets.

A principal is the administrator who leads a single school. The principal is both the manager and the instructional leader: setting the school's priorities, hiring and supporting teachers, observing classrooms, and being the main point of contact for families. The importance of the role is well documented. A 2021 review by Jason Grissom, Anna Egalite, and Constance Lindsay for the Wallace Foundation found that a more effective principal raises student achievement by about as much as a few additional months of learning, and has a large effect on whether good teachers stay. A principal rarely controls the budget or the district's contracts, but has great control over whether a new idea survives its first year.

docs.title: School Boards
docs.text:
The school board, sometimes called the board of education, is the body of citizens, usually elected, that governs a school district. It typically has five to nine members who set district policy, adopt the annual budget, approve major contracts, and hire and evaluate the superintendent. There are roughly 13,000 school districts in the United States, each with its own board, so the rules and the politics vary a great deal. Board members are often volunteers or paid a small stipend and may have no professional background in education. They hear from every other stakeholder, which makes them the place where a technology decision is finally made public.

The table summarizes who typically holds which kind of decision in a U.S. public school district. Rules differ by state and district, so treat this as a typical pattern.

Stakeholder Typical decisions Typically answers to Teacher Daily lessons, homework, grading Principal Principal School schedule, pilots within the school's budget, hiring Superintendent District administrator District-wide policies, vendor contracts and data agreements, state reporting Superintendent and board School board Budget, large contracts, policy, hiring the superintendent Voters Parent and family Their own child's participation, home learning, consent Themselves; they may elect the board

docs.title: Worked Example: The Path of a Purchase
docs.text:
Follow what happens if Ms. Okafor wants to adopt MathPath. A pilot of one grade within her school's budget is within her authority as principal. A district-wide purchase of $900,000 is not. It needs the district technology director to check the vendor's data agreement, the superintendent to recommend it, and the board to vote in public, where parents may speak. At each step a different stakeholder asks a different question: Are the teachers ready? Is the data safe? Is it worth the money? Is it fair to every child? A leader who prepares for all four questions before the first meeting is far more likely to succeed.

The sim below practices telling which stakeholder holds which decision.

docs.title: Diagram: School Decision Stakeholder Match
docs.text:
Run the School Decision Stakeholder Match MicroSim Fullscreen

School Decision Stakeholder Match

Type: microsim sim-id: school-decision-stakeholder-match Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: classify Learning Objective: The learner will classify ten school decisions by the stakeholder who typically holds the decision, correctly matching at least eight of ten on the first attempt.

Template: https://github.com/dmccreary/atam/tree/main/docs/sims/stakeholder-universe-map

Prerequisites: parent and family, teacher, principal, school administrator, school board, and the typical decision pattern (all defined in the section "The People Involved: Stakeholders of Schooling" above).

Evidence of Mastery: The learner places each of 10 decisions in one of five stakeholder bins and submits it. A placement is correct when it matches the "Correct stakeholder" column in Content. Mastery is 8 of 10 correct on the first attempt. Reading stakeholder descriptions is exploration, not evidence.
