docs.title: The Teacher's Side: Workload and Burnout
docs.text:
Every structure in this chapter lands on teachers, and the people who teach in it carry the weight.

Teacher workload is the total of the work a teacher does in a week, including classroom teaching, planning, grading, communicating with families, meetings, and administrative tasks. Teaching time is a minority of it. A 2022 RAND Corporation survey found that teachers reported working about 53 hours a week on average, roughly nine hours more than other working adults. The unseen tasks, planning and grading, make up much of the difference, as the Chapter 1 arithmetic of feedback for 140 students suggested.

Teacher burnout is a state of emotional, physical, and mental exhaustion caused by prolonged job stress, marked by exhaustion, cynicism, and a reduced sense of accomplishment. Gallup's 2022 survey found K-12 workers reported the highest rate of burnout of any occupation it studied, with about four in ten saying they felt burned out always or very often. Burnout is a main reason teachers leave, and teacher turnover is expensive for schools and harms students.

AI has a stake in both. A 2025 Gallup survey sponsored by the Walton Family Foundation found that teachers who used AI tools weekly reported saving several hours a week, mostly on planning and administrative tasks. That is a real benefit. The risks are also real: AI-generated materials can contain mistakes teachers have to catch, a new dashboard can add to the monitoring burden rather than reduce it, and a tool imposed without teacher input can feel like one more demand.

A time-saving tool can still cost time

Watch for tools that move work rather than remove it, for example a dashboard that tells a teacher about thirty students' needs without telling them what to do. Before adopting anything, ask teachers to track their hours for a week with and without it, and keep the tool only if the total goes down.

docs.title: Worked Example: A Weekly Hours Audit
docs.text:
Ms. Rivera tracks her week before and after a three-week trial of an AI tool that drafts practice problems and summarizes student errors. The hours are illustrative.

Task Before (hours) After (hours) Change Teaching 25 25 0 Planning and preparing materials 10 6 −4 Grading and feedback 9 6 −3 Checking AI output for errors 0 2 +2 Reading the dashboard 0 2 +2 Meetings, family contact, other 9 9 0 Total 53 50 −3

The tool saved seven hours in two categories and added four in two others, a net saving of three hours, about six percent of her week. That is worth having, and it is much smaller than a vendor's headline might suggest. The audit also shows where to improve the tool: a dashboard that takes two hours to read has room to be better.

docs.title: Judging the Quality of Evidence
docs.text:
Chapter 2 taught you to ask how groups in a study were formed. A second set of questions concerns who produced the evidence and whether anyone checked it. This book relies on all three kinds of source defined here, so it is worth knowing how to weigh each.

An independent evaluation is a study conducted by researchers who did not build, sell, or purchase the product being studied and who have no financial or reputational stake in its results. The independence matters because anyone with a stake, even an honest one, is tempted to make decisions about measures, samples, and reporting that favor a good result. A study paid for by a vendor can still be independent if the contract guarantees that the results will be published whatever they show.

Self-reported results are claims about outcomes made by the people who run, build, or sell a program, using data they collected and analyzed themselves. They are not necessarily false, and they may be accurate. But they cannot be checked, and they are produced by someone with an interest. A school reporting that its students grew faster than national norms is a self-report. So is a vendor's white paper.

A preprint is a research paper made publicly available before it has gone through peer review, the process in which independent experts evaluate a manuscript before a journal publishes it. Servers such as arXiv, SSRN, and EdArXiv host preprints. Preprints let findings spread quickly, which matters for fast-moving fields like AI. The cost is that nobody has yet vetted them, so the claims may contain errors. Peer review is imperfect too: it catches many problems and misses others. A preprint is a lead to be read carefully, not a verdict.

The AI forecasts and the five-level model of intelligent textbooks in this book rest partly on preprints, which is why you will see Chapters 4 through 6 say so, and weigh them accordingly.

A quick three-part check

For any result, ask three questions: Who ran the study? Did anyone outside check it? Was there a comparison group? A "no" to all three means treat the claim as a lead, and look for something stronger before you act.

docs.title: Worked Example: Rating Three Sources
docs.text:
Three documents arrive on Ms. Okafor's desk, all about the same program.

Source Who produced it Checked by others? Comparison group? How to treat it A one-page brochure from the vendor The vendor No None; before-and-after only A lead only A preprint from university researchers who randomized 60 classrooms Independent researchers Not yet peer reviewed Yes (random) Use with caution; read the design and watch for review A peer-reviewed article reporting the same randomized trial Independent researchers Yes Yes (random) Reasonable weight

The same study moves from the second row to the third when it is published after review, and the trust it deserves rises. The first source never becomes evidence by being repeated.

docs.title: Diagram: Source Credibility Checker
docs.text:
Run the Source Credibility Checker MicroSim Fullscreen

Source Credibility Checker

Type: microsim sim-id: source-credibility-checker Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: judge Learning Objective: The learner will judge how much weight each of eight sources of evidence about an educational product deserves by applying the independence, review, and comparison-group rules, correctly rating at least seven of eight on the first attempt.

Template: https://github.com/dmccreary/theory-of-knowledge/tree/main/docs/sims/source-credibility-analyzer

Prerequisites: independent evaluation, self-reported results, preprint, peer review, comparison group, and the rule for weight (all defined in the section "Judging the Quality of Evidence" above).

Evidence of Mastery: For each of 8 sources, the learner commits one of three ratings: Lead only, Use with caution, or Reasonable weight. A rating is correct when it matches the "Correct rating" column in Content. Mastery is 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Reading the rule is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A study paid for by a vendor can never be independent. (2) A preprint is the same as a peer-reviewed paper. (3) A comparison to national norms is a comparison group.

Instructional Rationale: Judging requires applying explicit criteria to details of a source. Including a vendor-funded study with guaranteed publication, a government report, and a comparison to national norms makes the learner apply the rule rather than react to labels.

Content:

The rule, shown on request: First, if there is no comparison group of other students studied at the same time, the rating is Lead only. Comparison with national norms does not count as a comparison group. Second, otherwise add one point if the evaluator is independent (did not build, sell, or buy the product, and the results are published whatever they show) and one point if the work has been peer reviewed. A total of 0 is Lead only, 1 is Use with caution, and 2 is Reasonable weight.

Eight sources:

# Source description shown to the learner Correct rating Why (shown as feedback) 1 A vendor white paper in which company analysts compare their users' scores before and after using the product; no other group was studied; not peer reviewed. Lead only No comparison group, and the vendor produced it. 2 A preprint from university researchers who randomly assigned 60 classrooms to the product or a control; posted on EdArXiv; not yet peer reviewed. Use with caution Independent and has a comparison group, but no peer review yet. 3 A peer-reviewed journal article reporting the same randomized trial by the independent university team. Reasonable weight Independent, has a comparison group, and is peer reviewed. 4 A school's own report that its students gained twice the expected growth, compared with national norms; written by the school; no outside review. Lead only National norms are not a comparison group, and the school produced it. 5 A state education department report comparing 30 adopting schools with 30 matched non-adopting schools; the state neither built nor bought the product; not peer reviewed. Use with caution Independent with a comparison group, but not peer reviewed. 6 A research firm paid by the vendor, under a contract that guarantees publication whatever the results, compared 40 matched schools; not peer reviewed. Use with caution The contract guarantees publication, so it counts as independent, and it has a comparison group; it has not been peer reviewed. 7 A peer-reviewed article by a university team, with no financial ties, comparing 5,000 matched students who did and did not use the product. Reasonable weight Independent, has a comparison group, and is peer reviewed. 8 A preprint by the program's own developers reporting a randomized trial; posted on a preprint server; not peer reviewed. Lead only It has a comparison group, but the developers are not independent and it is not peer reviewed.

Provenance: The definitions follow the chapter section "Judging the Quality of Evidence." The sources are fictional, written for this chapter; the sim must label them "Fictional sources."

Rules: Rating = Lead only if there is no comparison group. Otherwise score = independence (1 or 0) + peer review (1 or 0). Score 0 gives Lead only, 1 gives Use with caution, 2 gives Reasonable weight. A source is scored on its first submitted rating only. The score counts first-attempt correct ratings out of 8. Mastery is a score >= 7.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads one source description and the three ratings.
  2. The learner chooses a rating and submits it. The sim marks it correct or incorrect and shows the feedback text.
  3. If incorrect, the learner may choose again; the second attempt does not change the score. After the second attempt, the correct rating and reason are shown.
  4. After all 8 sources, the sim shows the score and lists misrated sources with their correct ratings.
  5. The learner should notice that sources 2 and 3 describe the same study and differ only in review status, and that source 6 is vendor-paid but still independent.

Feedback: 8 sources, shuffled once per session, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: [rating]. [Why text]." Incorrect: "Not quite. [Why text for the correct answer, without naming the rating]." After the second attempt the correct rating is revealed and the source counts as missed. A running score "First-try correct: n of 8" is shown. Final message for a score >= 7: "You can weigh a source by who made it and who checked it." For a score < 7: "Review the rule and try again; the sources will be reshuffled."

Starting State: Source 1 of the shuffled order is shown with the three ratings and the score "First-try correct: 0 of 8." The prompt reads "How much weight does this source deserve?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter defines independent evaluation, self-reported results, and preprint. It states that a vendor-paid study can be independent if publication is guaranteed, and that a preprint has not been peer reviewed. The mastery bar is 7 of 8.

docs.title: Answering Maya's Question
docs.text:
Maya asked why the bell rings. Now there is a real answer. The bell exists because the industrial-era school model needed to move hundreds of children through a building on a common schedule. The fifty-minute period, the grade level, and the Carnegie credit all trace back to the same logic: batch the children, fix the time, measure the hours. That logic solved real problems of scale and still does the job of coordinating a large building.

It also has costs, which are the costs of fixed time and fixed pace. The arithmetic of the 20-student class shows what they are: idle hours for some, unmastered material for others. These costs fall unevenly, which is why the equity question runs through the whole chapter. Alternatives like charter, virtual, and microschools each loosen one piece of the model, with uneven results, and the history of educational technology shows that tools alone rarely loosen the grammar. The new factor this book examines is a technology whose capability keeps improving, which may make it possible to hold mastery fixed and let time vary.

The chapter's story has both sides. The benefit: ideas like mastery-based pacing could reduce wasted hours and close gaps. The risk: tools that save a few hours for teachers while adding others, evidence that comes from vendors rather than independent studies, and gaps that widen if only the best-resourced schools get the best tools. The response is the pair of habits you practiced: match resources to need, and ask who produced the evidence and who checked it.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• The industrial-era school model grouped children into batches, moved them through fixed stages, and coordinated them by clock; each feature solved a real problem and each has a cost.
  • The bell schedule, age-based grade levels, seat time, and the Carnegie unit (120 hours per credit) all treat time and age as stand-ins for learning.
  • In a fixed-length course, some students finish early and wait while others do not finish; in our 20-student example, 535 hours sit idle and 6 students miss mastery.
  • Education policy is made mainly by states and districts; the school board adopts the policies that govern schedules, grading, and data; standardized testing gives a common yardstick but measures only part of learning.
  • An achievement gap is a group difference in results that usually reflects differences in opportunity; educational equity matches resources to need rather than splitting them equally.
  • Learning gains measure growth in standard deviations, which lets you compare an intervention with a typical year, roughly 0.3 in middle school.
  • Charter, virtual, and microschools loosen different parts of the traditional model, with mixed or thin evidence.
  • The history of EdTech shows a century of big promises absorbed into old structures.
  • Teacher workload (about 53 hours a week) and teacher burnout make a teacher's time the scarcest resource; a tool counts only if it reduces net hours.
  • Weigh evidence by who produced it and who checked it: an independent evaluation carries more weight than self-reported results, and a preprint is a lead until peer review.

You can explain why school is built this way

You just traced the bell, the grade level, and the Carnegie credit back to the problems they solved, and learned to weigh a source by who made it and who checked it. Chapter 4 begins Part 1 of the book's argument: how researchers measure what AI can do, and why that measurement matters to schools. One step at a time, together.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: School Structures, Equity, and the Industrial-Era Legacy
docs.text: Test your understanding of why schools are organized the way they are, how equity gaps arise, and how to weigh the quality of evidence with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. How did the Carnegie Foundation define the Carnegie unit in 1906?
docs.text:
1. A passing score on a standardized end-of-course exam in one subject
  2. A set of learning outcomes that a student must master to earn a credit
  3. One semester of attendance in any course approved by the district
  4. 120 hours of class time in one subject over a school year
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The Carnegie unit is a standard measure of a high school course defined as 120 hours of class time in one subject over a school year. It was created to decide pension eligibility and to give colleges a common way to judge transcripts, and most U.S. high schools still award credits this way. It measures time, not mastery, which is why the chapter groups it with seat time as a stand-in for learning rather than a measure of it.

Concept Tested: Carnegie Unit

See: Carnegie Unit

docs.title: 2. What is the main weakness of using seat time to measure instruction?
docs.text:
1. It is difficult for schools to count and audit accurately
  2. A student who already knows the material and a lost student earn the same credit
  3. It requires every student to take a standardized test before advancing
  4. It gives fast learners more credit than slower learners for the same course
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Seat time assumes a fixed number of hours in class produces a fixed amount of learning. The chapter notes that it is simple to count and audit, so the first option reverses its strength. Its weakness is that it is a poor stand-in for learning: a student who already knows the material and a student who is lost both earn the same seat time. Seat time does not involve testing, and it gives everyone the same credit regardless of speed.

Concept Tested: Seat Time

See: Seat Time

docs.title: 3. Which description fits a charter school?
docs.text:
1. A publicly funded school run independently of the district under a results contract
  2. A privately funded school that charges tuition and answers only to its board of trustees
  3. A very small mixed-age school led by one or a few adults in a home or rented space
  4. A district school that delivers all of its instruction online to students at home
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. A charter school is publicly funded and free to students, but it is run independently of the local district under a charter that sets out its mission and results. Its authorizer can close it if it fails to meet the terms. The second option describes a private school, the third describes a microschool, and the fourth describes a virtual school. The chapter notes some virtual schools are run as charters, but online delivery is not what defines a charter.

Concept Tested: Charter School

See: Charter School

docs.title: 4. A school has 45 hours of tutoring for three students who start at different scores. What would an equitable allocation look like, as opposed to an equal one?
docs.text:
1. Give each student 15 hours so that no one receives more tutoring than anyone else
  2. Give all 45 hours to the highest scorer, who is most likely to benefit
  3. Give the most hours to the student furthest from the goal, none to one who met it
  4. Let each student choose how many hours to use until the 45 hours run out
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Educational equity means matching resources to need so each student can reach the same high standard. In the chapter's example, an equitable share gave 30 hours to the student furthest behind, 15 to the middle student, and none to the student already at the goal, bringing everyone to 80. Giving 15 hours to each is equality, which leaves the gaps between students intact and sends hours to a student who has already reached the goal.

Concept Tested: Educational Equity

See: Worked Example: Equal Is Not Equitable

docs.title: 5. A middle school tutoring program produces an effect of 0.10 standard deviations over a year. Typical annual growth in middle school is about 0.3 standard deviations. How should a principal describe the program's impact?
docs.text:
1. As too small to matter, since anything under 0.2 is negligible
  2. As roughly one-third of an additional year of typical growth
  3. As about three additional years of typical growth
  4. As exactly equal to one additional year of typical growth
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Learning gains can be compared with a typical year of growth by dividing: 0.10 / 0.3 is about one-third, or roughly three months of extra learning. The chapter uses this method to show why researchers treat effects of 0.1 and 0.2 as meaningful, so calling it negligible is the tempting mistake. The three-year answer divides the wrong way. The same effect would be worth much less in early elementary grades, where typical growth is near 1.0.

Concept Tested: Learning Gains

See: Worked Example: How Big Is a Gain?

docs.title: 6. Why do many researchers prefer to describe achievement gaps in terms of opportunity?
docs.text:
1. Because test scores no longer show any differences between groups of students
  2. Because opportunity is easier to measure than academic performance on tests
  3. Because federal law requires schools to report opportunity instead of results
  4. Because the word "gap" can suggest the difference lies in the students themselves
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The chapter notes that the word "gap" can mislead by suggesting the difference lies in the students. Most researchers prefer to describe differences in opportunity, such as access to experienced teachers, funding, safe schools, and resources at home, which produce the differences in results. Group differences in scores still exist and have widened in some cases, as the 2022 NAEP results showed, so the first option is false.

Concept Tested: Achievement Gap

See: Achievement Gap

docs.title: 7. What is a preprint?
docs.text:
1. A research paper made public before it has gone through peer review
  2. A vendor's summary of results published alongside a product brochure
  3. A peer-reviewed article that has been accepted but not yet printed
  4. An early draft of a study shared privately with the funding agency
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. A preprint is a research paper made publicly available, on servers such as arXiv, SSRN, or EdArXiv, before peer review. Preprints let findings spread quickly in fast-moving fields like AI, but nobody has yet vetted them, so the chapter calls a preprint a lead rather than a verdict. A vendor summary is a self-reported result, and an accepted article has already passed peer review. The chapter notes the book's AI forecasts rest partly on preprints.

Concept Tested: Preprint

See: Judging the Quality of Evidence

docs.title: 8. A vendor says its AI tool "saves teachers six hours a week." A teacher's weekly audit shows six hours saved on planning and grading, but four new hours spent checking AI output and reading the dashboard. What conclusion does the chapter's reasoning support?
docs.text:
1. The vendor's claim is confirmed, because six hours were saved on planning and grading
  2. The tool should be dropped, because any added task means it increases workload
  3. The net saving is about two hours, and the dashboard is a clear place to improve the tool
  4. The audit is unreliable, because teachers cannot track their own hours accurately
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. The chapter warns that a time-saving tool can move work rather than remove it, and advises keeping a tool only if total hours go down. Six hours saved minus four added is a net saving of two hours, smaller than the headline but still real. As in Ms. Rivera's audit, the added categories show where the tool can improve. Accepting the gross figure ignores the added tasks, and dropping the tool ignores that the total did fall.

Concept Tested: Teacher Workload

See: Worked Example: A Weekly Hours Audit

docs.title: 9. What constraint was the industrial-era school model designed to handle?
docs.text:
1. A surplus of teachers who needed to be assigned to specialized subjects
  2. Parents' demand for a curriculum shaped around each individual child's interests
  3. Federal accountability rules that required annual testing of every student
  4. A scarcity of teachers and information as many new children entered school
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The model took shape between about 1840 and 1920, when growing cities and compulsory attendance laws brought in many children who had never been to school. The challenge was to teach hundreds of children with few teachers and few resources, and age grouping, one teacher per room, a standard curriculum, and a bell schedule were an efficient answer. Federal annual testing came much later, with No Child Left Behind in 2002, and the model left little room for individual interests.

Concept Tested: Industrial-Era School Model

See: The Industrial-Era School Model

docs.title: 10. A vendor pays for a study of its own product. Under what condition can the study still count as an independent evaluation?
docs.text:
1. If the contract guarantees the results will be published whatever they show
  2. If the vendor's own staff collect the data but outside staff write the report
  3. If the results are posted as a preprint before the product is sold
  4. If the vendor reports the results to the school board in a public meeting
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. An independent evaluation is conducted by researchers with no financial or reputational stake in the results. The chapter says a vendor-paid study can still be independent if the contract guarantees publication regardless of the outcome, which removes the temptation to bury bad news. Vendor staff collecting the data keeps a stakeholder in control of measures and samples. Posting a preprint or presenting to a board does not change who produced the evidence.

Concept Tested: Independent Evaluation

See: Judging the Quality of Evidence

docs.title: References: School Structures, Equity, and the Industrial-Era Legacy
docs.text:
1. Carnegie Unit and Student Hour - Wikipedia - Traces how the Carnegie unit made 120 hours of class time the standard measure of a high school credit. Explains the origin of seat time, a structure that mastery-based models must work around.

  2. Achievement gaps in the United States - Wikipedia - Reviews documented gaps in test scores and attainment by race, income, and other factors, and proposed causes. Provides the background for the chapter's discussion of educational equity and learning gains.

  3. Microschool - Wikipedia - Describes very small schools, often mixed-age and personalized, and their growth as an alternative to conventional schools. Useful context for the alternative models the chapter compares, including AI-first private schools.

  4. Tinkering Toward Utopia: A Century of Public School Reform (1995) - David Tyack and Larry Cuban - Harvard University Press - Tyack and Cuban coined the "grammar of schooling," the bells, grades, and age cohorts that resist reform. Their idea explains why industrial-era structures persist and why new models keep reverting to old patterns.

  5. Teachers and Machines: The Classroom Use of Technology Since 1920 (1986) - Larry Cuban - Teachers College Press - Cuban documented the repeated cycle of hype, limited adoption, and disappointment for film, radio, and television in classrooms. His pattern is the lens the chapter uses for reading the history of educational technology.

  6. The Carnegie Unit: A Century-Old Standard in a Changing Education Landscape - Carnegie Foundation for the Advancement of Teaching - A 2015 report from the unit's own creator assessing whether time-based credit still serves students. Shows that even its originator calls seat time a crude proxy for learning.

  7. The Nation's Report Card (NAEP) - National Center for Education Statistics - National and state results from the National Assessment of Educational Progress, with tools to compare student groups. The standard independent source for measuring achievement gaps and learning gains over time.

  8. Public Charter School Enrollment - NCES Condition of Education - Federal data on how charter enrollment has grown, which states allow charters, and the share serving high-poverty communities. Puts numbers behind the chapter's survey of alternatives to traditional schools.

  9. Center for Research on Education Outcomes (CREDO) - Stanford University - Publishes the National Charter School Study comparing charter and traditional public school student growth. An example of independent evaluation, contrasted in this chapter with results that schools report about themselves.

  10. Teachers' job stress has improved to pre-pandemic levels. They're still pretty stressed out. - Chalkbeat - Reports RAND's 2024 State of the American Teacher survey on burnout, 53-hour work weeks, and pay. Documents the teacher workload and burnout problem that AI-native school designs claim to relieve.

docs.title: Measuring AI Capability: The METR Task-Horizon Studies
Summary
docs.text: This chapter introduces artificial intelligence, machine learning, and large language models, then explains how METR measures AI capability through the task-horizon studies — benchmark task suites, the 50% time horizon, and human working time as the unit of measurement. Readers learn how researchers turned the vague question "how capable is AI?" into a number that can be tracked over time.

This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: The Building Blocks of Schools, Students, and Learning

docs.title: "Doubles What?"
docs.text:
At a school board meeting in November, a board member named Mr. Alvarez raises his hand during the technology report. "I keep reading that AI is doubling every few months," he says. "Doubling what? Because my phone's autocorrect doesn't seem twice as smart as it was last spring."

It is the right question, and it is the question this chapter answers. Claims about AI progress are easy to make and hard to check, because "capability" is vague. A chatbot may write a better poem than it did last year and still fail to book a flight. Unless there is a precise yardstick, "AI is getting better" cannot be turned into a plan. A school that is deciding how to schedule a day three or four years from now needs a number it can track.

This chapter gives you the vocabulary and the yardstick. First we define the terms that every conversation about AI uses and often blurs: artificial intelligence, machine learning, large language models, generative AI, and AI agents. Then we meet a research group called METR that built a measurement of AI capability based on a surprising choice of unit, the amount of time a task takes a human. Finally we see why the measurement behaves like exponential growth, and what that implies for the cost of AI in schools.

A yardstick for a moving target

This is the chapter where the book's big prediction first gets a number you can check, instead of a mood. By the end you'll be able to answer Mr. Alvarez's "doubles what?" in one sentence, and say what the answer does and doesn't tell a school. Let's find the balance between taking the curve seriously and not taking it for a promise.

docs.title: A Ladder of Terms: From AI to AI Agents
docs.text:
People use "AI" for everything from a spam filter to a robot in a movie. The terms below form a ladder, each rung a narrower kind of the one above it, and keeping them straight prevents most confusion.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is the field of building computer systems that perform tasks that would normally require human intelligence, such as understanding language, recognizing images, making decisions, and solving problems. The term was coined in 1955 for a summer workshop at Dartmouth College. It is a broad umbrella. A 1990s chess program that searches moves using rules written by programmers is AI, though it learns nothing from data.

Machine learning (ML) is the part of AI in which a system learns patterns from examples instead of following rules a programmer wrote by hand. You show a machine-learning system thousands of emails labeled "spam" or "not spam," and it adjusts itself until it can label new emails. Most of the AI you meet today is machine learning.

Generative AI is machine learning that creates new content, such as text, images, audio, video, or computer code, rather than only labeling or predicting. A spam filter sorts messages; a generative system writes one.

A large language model (LLM) is a generative AI system trained on enormous amounts of text to produce human-like language. It works, roughly, by predicting what text should come next, and doing that at huge scale produces answers, essays, summaries, and code. The chatbots that became widely known after ChatGPT's release in November 2022 are built on LLMs. This book does not explain how LLMs are built inside; what matters here is what they can do.

An AI agent is a system, usually built on an LLM, that pursues a goal by taking a series of actions on its own: planning steps, using tools such as a web browser or a code editor, checking its results, and trying again when something fails. A chatbot answers your question and waits. An agent is told "build a quiz website," and then writes the code, runs it, reads the error messages, and fixes them without further prompting.

docs.title: Worked Example: One Problem at Every Rung
docs.text:
Imagine the same job at each rung of the ladder: finding scam emails for a school office.

Rung How it tackles the job Where it breaks Fixed rule A programmer writes "if the subject contains WINNER, flag it" Misses "You have been selected" and wrongly flags "Winner of the spelling bee" Machine learning The system is shown 10,000 emails already labeled scam or not, and finds the patterns that separate them: sender oddities, link styles, word mixes. It gives each new email a scam score Fails on a new kind of scam unlike anything in its training examples Large language model Asked "Explain in two sentences why this email looks suspicious," it writes a plain-language explanation The explanation can sound confident and be wrong AI agent Told "Check this week's inbox, move the scams to a folder, and send me a summary," it opens the inbox, scores each message, moves the flagged ones, writes the summary, and emails it A mistake in an early step, such as misjudging one sender, can carry through every step after

Each rung does more than the one before and brings a new way to fail. The agent row is the one to remember: because it acts on its own over many steps, an agent's errors can compound, which is why the length of task it can handle reliably, the subject of the rest of this chapter, matters so much.

docs.title: Worked Example: Three Waves of AI
docs.text:
The terms above were not invented at once. Artificial intelligence has risen in waves, and each wave explains why a different rung of the ladder dominates the news at a different time.

Period What people built Rung of the ladder What happened next 1950s Alan Turing asked in 1950 whether machines can think; the 1955 proposal for a Dartmouth summer workshop gave the field its name AI without machine learning Rule-based programs solved puzzles and played checkers, then stalled on messy real-world problems 1970s and late 1980s Expert systems that encoded specialists' rules AI without machine learning Two "AI winters": funding and interest collapsed when the systems proved brittle and costly to maintain 2012 A deep neural network called AlexNet won an image-recognition contest by a wide margin Machine learning Learning from data replaced hand-written rules across vision, speech, and translation 2017 Google researchers published the transformer design behind modern language models Machine learning, toward LLMs Models could be trained on far more text, far faster November 2022 ChatGPT reached the public Large language models, generative AI Mass adoption, and the education questions of this book

Two lessons follow. The current wave is built on machine learning and large language models, not on rules, which is why its behavior is statistical and sometimes wrong in odd ways. And earlier waves ended in winters when expectations outran results, a pattern the hype cycle of Chapter 15 describes.

docs.title: Worked Example: How a Machine Learns a Rule From Counts
docs.text:
"Learning from examples" can sound mysterious, so here is the smallest honest version. A spam filter is shown 1,000 labeled emails, 200 spam and 800 not spam. For three words it counts how often each appears in each group. These counts are illustrative.

Word Share of spam emails containing it Share of non-spam emails containing it How much more likely in spam "free" 60% 3% \( 0.60/0.03 = 20 \) times "winner" 30% 2% \( 0.30/0.02 = 15 \) times "meeting" 5% 50% \( 0.05/0.50 = 0.1 \) times, so 10 times less likely

A new email contains "free," "winner," and "meeting." Before reading it, spam is 200 of 1,000 emails, which is odds of 1 to 4, or 0.25. Multiply the odds by each word's ratio: \( 0.25 \times 20 \times 15 \times 0.1 = 7.5 \), which is odds of 7.5 to 1, or a probability of \( 7.5/8.5 \approx 88\% \) that the email is spam. Nobody wrote a rule saying "free is suspicious." The counts produced it. Real systems use thousands of features and cleverer arithmetic, but the idea is the same, and it shows the weakness too: a scam that uses none of the words the filter has seen gets no help from the counts.

docs.title: Worked Example: What a Language Model Does at Each Step
docs.text:
A large language model produces text one small piece at a time. The pieces are called tokens, which are chunks of text roughly three-quarters of an English word long. At each step the model assigns a probability to every possible next token, picks one, adds it to the text, and repeats. Suppose the text so far is "The capital of France is" and the model's probabilities, which are illustrative, are:

Next token Probability " Paris" 92% " the" 3% " a" 2% " located" 1% anything else 2%

The model almost always continues with " Paris," because that continuation was overwhelmingly common in its training text. Now change the prompt to a question the training text never settled, such as "The mayor of the school district's biggest town is." The probabilities flatten across many plausible names, and the model still picks one, fluently. That is the mechanism behind the hallucination of Chapter 5: the model is always choosing a likely continuation, whether or not a true one exists. It also explains why a model grounded in a vetted document (Chapter 12) behaves better: the document concentrates the probability on supported text.

docs.title: Worked Example: Generative AI Beyond Text
docs.text:
Generative AI covers more than chatbots, and each kind has its own benefit and risk in a school.

Kind of output A school use A benefit A risk and a response Text Drafting practice questions Saves planning time Errors; a teacher reviews every set Images Illustrating a vocabulary card Fast custom visuals Inaccurate details or biased depictions; check against a trusted source Audio Reading a passage aloud in a student's home language Access for English-language learners Wrong pronunciation; ask a fluent speaker to sample it Code A student's first program Quick feedback on errors Students copy code they do not understand; require them to explain it Video A short explainer clip Engagement Realistic fakes; teach students to ask where a clip came from

The table below summarizes the ladder using examples. It adds no new terms; it organizes the five you have just met, plus the case of ordinary software that is not AI at all.

Category What it does Example Not AI Follows a fixed rule A thermostat that switches on at 68°F AI without machine learning Uses rules or search written by programmers A 1990s chess program Machine learning Learns patterns from data to label or predict A spam filter; a model that predicts which students may fail a course Generative AI Creates new content A tool that draws a picture from a description Large language model Generative AI for language A chatbot that answers a teacher's question in paragraphs AI agent Takes multi-step actions toward a goal using tools A system that writes, runs, and fixes code to build a website

The nesting is the key idea. Every LLM is generative AI, every generative system is machine learning, and every machine-learning system is AI, but not the other way around. The sim below lets you practice sorting examples.

Six categories, shown as nested regions from outside in (Not AI sits outside all the others), each with its definition shown on selection:

Category Definition shown Not AI Software that follows a fixed rule and does nothing that requires intelligence AI without machine learning A system that performs an intelligent task using rules or search written by programmers Machine learning A system that learns patterns from examples in order to label or predict Generative AI A machine-learning system that creates new content, such as images or audio Large language model A generative AI system trained on text to produce language AI agent A system built on a language model that takes multi-step actions with tools toward a goal

Eight examples:

Not AI It follows one fixed rule and does not do anything that requires intelligence. 2 A 1990s chess program that scores positions using rules its programmers wrote. AI without machine learning It plays chess, an intelligent task, but nothing was learned from data. 3 An email filter trained on millions of messages labeled spam or not spam. Machine learning It learned a pattern from past data to predict; it does not create content. 5 A tool that draws a new picture from a sentence describing it. Provenance: Definitions follow the chapter section "A Ladder of Terms: From AI to AI Agents." The examples are illustrative, written for this chapter.

Rules: Each example has exactly one correct category: the narrowest category whose definition it meets. An example is scored on its first submitted placement only. The score counts first-attempt correct placements out of 8. Mastery is a score >= 7.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees one example at a time and the six categories.
  2. The learner places the example and submits. The sim marks it correct or incorrect and shows the feedback text.
  3. If incorrect, the learner may place it again; the second attempt does not change the score. After the second attempt, the correct category and reason are shown.
  4. After all 8 examples, the sim shows the score and lists misplaced examples with their correct categories.
  5. The learner should notice that examples 3 and 4 use machine learning for different purposes and land in the same category, and that examples 7 and 8 both use a language model and differ only in whether they take actions.

Feedback: 8 examples, shuffled once per session, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: [category]. [Why text]." Incorrect: "Not quite. [Why text for the correct answer, without naming the category]." After the second attempt the correct category is revealed and the example counts as missed. A running score "First-try correct: n of 8" is shown. Final message for a score >= 7: "You can place AI systems on the ladder." For a score < 7: "Review the definitions and try again; the examples will be reshuffled."

Starting State: The nested regions are shown with example 1 of the shuffled order, the score "First-try correct: 0 of 8," and the prompt "Which is the narrowest category that fits this system?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter names six categories in the order Not AI, AI without machine learning, Machine learning, Generative AI, Large language model, AI agent. The chapter states that every LLM is generative AI and every generative system is machine learning. The mastery bar is 7 of 8.

docs.title: AI in Education
docs.text:
AI in education is the use of artificial intelligence to support teaching, learning, and school administration. The uses fall into three groups. For students, AI can act as a tutor, give feedback on writing or problem solving, explain a concept several ways, or adapt practice to what a student knows. For teachers, it can draft lesson plans, create practice problems, translate materials, and help with grading and feedback. For administrators, it can assist with scheduling, forecasting enrollment, and analyzing records. AI in education has a longer history than the current excitement suggests, since the intelligent tutoring systems of the 1980s and the adaptive math software of the 2000s were also AI. What changed after 2022 is that LLMs made flexible conversation and content generation cheap and widely available.

A majority of U.S. teachers surveyed in 2025 reported using AI tools in some way, and many students use chatbots on their own, whether or not their school permits it. UNESCO's 2023 guidance on generative AI in education recommended that governments set a minimum age for classroom use, suggesting 13, and stressed that teachers and students need to understand how the tools work before relying on them.

The Chapter 2 evidence habits apply here from the start. Some AI-in-education results are strongly positive and others are negative, and the difference often comes from how the tool is designed, a theme the course description names and Chapter 12 develops.

docs.title: Worked Example: Three Uses, Three Tradeoffs
docs.text:
Here is how the benefit, risk, and response pattern looks for three uses at Lincoln Middle School.

Use Benefit Risk Response A student tutor that answers math questions Immediate help at 8 p.m. when no teacher is available Students may ask for answers instead of thinking Choose a tool that gives hints first; Ms. Rivera reviews logs weekly (Chapter 12) A teacher tool that drafts practice problems Saves planning time Problems may contain errors or be too easy The teacher checks every set before use A district tool that flags students at risk of failing Earlier support for students who need it Biased predictions; privacy of student records Audit the tool for bias; limit who sees the flags (Chapter 10)

The row for each use states what could go wrong and what the school does about it. That habit, naming the tradeoff and the response together, is the one this book asks you to keep.

docs.title: Measuring What AI Can Do
docs.text:
Back to Mr. Alvarez's question. To say AI is "doubling," you first have to say what is being measured. The next three terms set up that question.

AI capability is the range and difficulty of tasks an AI system can perform successfully. It is not a single quantity: a system may be superb at translation and poor at planning a trip. Because capability is multi-dimensional, measuring it requires choosing specific tasks and a way to score them.

The unevenness is not a small caveat. In a 2023 field experiment, researchers from Harvard Business School and Boston Consulting Group gave consultants realistic tasks, some with access to GPT-4 and some without. On tasks inside what the AI did well, consultants with AI finished about 12 percent more tasks, about 25 percent faster, with much higher rated quality. On a task chosen to sit just outside that range, consultants using AI were about 19 percentage points less likely to reach the correct answer than those working alone, because the AI's confident output led them astray. The authors called this a "jagged technological frontier": the edge of what AI does well is not a smooth line, and from the outside it is hard to tell which side of it a task falls on. For a teacher, the implication is that a tool's average ability says little about its ability on the task in front of you.

An AI benchmark is a standardized set of tasks or questions used to measure and compare AI systems, much as a standardized test, which you met in Chapter 3, compares students. A benchmark fixes the questions and the scoring so that results from different systems and different years can be compared. Well-known benchmarks include multiple-choice exams on general knowledge, collections of grade-school math word problems, and sets of real software bugs to fix.

Benchmarks have a typical life story. A new benchmark is hard, and the best systems score low. Within a few years, systems improve until they score near the maximum, and the benchmark stops telling anyone anything. This is called saturation. Benchmarks also suffer from contamination, in which questions or answers leak into a model's training data so the system appears to reason when it is recalling. The pressure on benchmark designers is constant: they must keep inventing harder tests, and a score of 92 percent on an old test is hard to compare with 40 percent on a new one.

A benchmark task suite is the particular collection of tasks that a benchmark runs. A good suite has tasks of many difficulties and lengths, each with a clear way to decide whether it was done correctly. How a suite is built determines what the benchmark can and cannot say.

docs.title: Worked Example: A Benchmark Runs Out of Room
docs.text:
The table shows the best score reached each year on a hypothetical benchmark of 1,000 questions. These numbers are illustrative.

Year Best score Gain over the previous year 2019 12% n/a 2021 35% 23 points in two years 2022 62% 27 points 2023 85% 23 points 2024 94% 9 points 2025 96% 2 points

Through 2023 the benchmark tracks real progress. By 2025 it cannot: a two-point gain could be a real improvement, or a few lucky answers, or a few questions whose answers leaked into training data. Once the best systems score 96 percent there is no room to show further growth, and the benchmark's designers must write a new, harder test. Scores on the old and new tests cannot be placed on one scale. A measure that never hits a ceiling, such as "how long a task, in hours, can the system finish," avoids this trap, and that is the design choice behind the rest of the chapter.

The saturation problem is what METR set out to avoid.

docs.title: METR and the Task-Horizon Idea
docs.text:
METR (pronounced "meter") stands for Model Evaluation and Threat Research. It is a nonprofit research organization based in Berkeley, California, that studies the autonomous capabilities of advanced AI systems, including whether they could carry out tasks that would pose risks. It describes itself as independent of the AI developers it evaluates. In March 2025 METR published a paper titled Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Tasks, which is one of the core references of this book. The paper was released as a preprint, so in the sense of Chapter 3 it was a public draft that had not yet been through peer review when it appeared; that is a reason to hold its specific numbers loosely and its broad pattern more firmly.

METR's central idea is to measure capability with a natural unit, time, instead of a test score. The idea needs three more definitions.

Human working time is the amount of time a skilled human professional, working without distractions, needs to complete a task correctly. METR obtained it by hiring skilled people to do each task while a clock ran, and recording how long they took. A task that takes a skilled person two minutes to complete has a human working time of two minutes. A task that takes a full working day has a human working time of about eight hours. The key point is that human working time is a measure of how hard the task is for people, and it is the same whether an AI or a person eventually does it.

A task success rate is the fraction of attempts at a task, or at a set of similar tasks, that an AI system completes correctly. Running a model ten times on a task and succeeding on seven gives a success rate of 70 percent. METR runs each model many times on each task, since AI systems do not behave identically each time.

A task horizon is the length of task, measured in human working time, that an AI system can complete at a stated level of success. It answers the question, "how long a task can this AI handle?" Putting the three ideas together gives METR's key number.

The 50 percent time horizon is the task length, in human working time, at which an AI system succeeds about half the time. Tasks shorter than the horizon are mostly completed, and tasks longer than it mostly fail. If a model has a 50 percent time horizon of one hour, it completes about half of the one-hour tasks and fewer of the longer ones. METR chose 50 percent because it is the middle of the transition from "usually works" to "usually fails," which makes it a stable point to measure. The price of that choice, as we will see, is that 50 percent is a coin flip, not a reliable worker.

docs.title: Worked Example: One Task, Three Human Times
docs.text: Human working time is not a single fixed number, since skilled people vary. Suppose METR times three professionals on the same task and records 22, 35, and 48 minutes. A single value is needed, and the choice matters: the average is \( (22 + 35 + 48)/3 = 35 \) minutes, and the middle value, the median, is also 35. Had one person gotten distracted and taken 120 minutes, the average would jump to \( (22 + 35 + 120)/3 \approx 59 \) minutes while the median would stay at 35, which is why a robust summary such as the median, or the geometric mean for times that differ by large factors, is the safer choice. The practical point for a reader is that every "task length" in a horizon chart is itself an estimate with a spread, and a careful study says how it was chosen.

docs.title: How the Number Is Produced
docs.text:
The procedure has six steps, and understanding them is the best protection against misreading the result.

  1. Assemble a benchmark task suite. METR combined several suites of tasks, roughly 170 in all, mostly in software engineering, cybersecurity, and reasoning, with lengths from a few seconds to about eight hours or more. Examples include fixing a configuration error, writing a function that passes tests, and improving the speed of a program.
  2. Time skilled humans on each task. This gives each task its human working time.
  3. Run the AI model on every task, several times.
  4. Record the task success rate for each task.
  5. Fit a curve that relates the chance of success to the human working time of the task. Success is high for short tasks and falls as tasks get longer.
  6. Read off the length at which the curve crosses 50 percent. That is the 50 percent time horizon.

The leading model METR tested in the March 2025 paper, Claude 3.7 Sonnet, had a 50 percent time horizon of roughly 50 minutes. That is the starting point for the projections later in this chapter.

docs.text:

How METR Measures a Task Horizon

Type: workflow sim-id: metr-measurement-workflow Library: Mermaid Status: Specified Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: explain Learning Objective: The learner will explain the six steps that turn AI task results into a 50 percent time horizon, correctly answering at least four of five questions about the steps.

Prerequisites: benchmark task suite, human working time, task success rate, task horizon, 50 percent time horizon (all defined in the section "METR and the Task-Horizon Idea" above).

Evidence of Mastery: After exploring the six steps, the learner answers five multiple-choice questions. An answer is correct when it matches the "Correct option" column in Content. Mastery is 4 of 5 correct. Opening a step to read its description is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) The horizon measures how long the AI takes to run. (2) A 50 percent horizon means the AI is reliable on tasks up to that length. (3) The task suite is a single test with one score.

Instructional Rationale: Explaining a process is strongest when the learner can say what each step produces and what the next step needs. Questions that depend on the order and the unit of measure make the learner use the process, not recite it.

Content:

Six steps shown in order as a flow from step 1 to step 6, each with a description revealed on selection:

Step Name Description shown 1 Assemble a benchmark task suite Gather roughly 170 tasks, from seconds to hours long, each with a clear way to check whether it was done correctly. 2 Time skilled humans Skilled professionals do each task while a clock runs, giving its human working time. 3 Run the AI model The AI attempts every task several times. 4 Record the task success rate For each task, record the fraction of attempts that succeeded. 5 Fit a success curve Fit a curve showing how the chance of success falls as human working time grows, on a logarithmic scale. 6 Read off the horizon The task length at which the curve crosses 50 percent is the 50 percent time horizon.

Five questions, each with four options in the order shown:

# Question Options Correct option Why (shown as feedback) 1 In the task-horizon measure, what is the unit that says how long a task is? A. The seconds the AI takes to run; B. The human working time the task needs; C. The number of lines of code written; D. The number of tokens the AI produces B Human working time measures how hard the task is for people, whoever does it. 2 A model has a 50 percent time horizon of 2 hours. What does that mean? A. It succeeds on every task up to 2 hours; B. It runs for 2 hours at a time; C. It succeeds about half the time on tasks that take a skilled human about 2 hours; D. It is 50 percent as capable as a human C The horizon is the task length at which the success rate is about half. 3 Which step comes immediately after skilled humans are timed? A. Fit a success curve; B. Run the AI model on every task several times; C. Assemble the task suite; D. Read off the horizon B The AI's results must exist before success rates can be recorded or fitted. 4 A model attempts a 10-minute task 10 times and succeeds 9 times. What is the task success rate? A. 10 percent; B. 50 percent; C. 90 percent; D. 9 minutes C Success rate is successes divided by attempts: 9 divided by 10 is 90 percent. 5 Why is a human's working time used instead of the AI's running time? A. AI running time cannot be measured; B. Human time gives a common yardstick for how hard a task is, and AI running time depends on hardware; C. Humans are always faster; D. It makes the numbers larger B A task's difficulty for people is the same across models and years, while AI run time depends on hardware and changes quickly.

Provenance: The six steps and the figure of roughly 170 tasks summarize METR (2025), Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Tasks (preprint), as presented in the chapter. The sim must label the figures "As described in a 2025 preprint."

Rules: Steps are shown in the fixed order 1 to 6. The questions are asked in the order shown, one attempt each, and the options are shown in the order listed. A question is correct when the selected option equals the correct option. Mastery is a score >= 4.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner selects each of the six steps in turn to read its description.
  2. The learner starts the questions. Question 1 appears with its four options.
  3. The learner selects an option and submits. The sim marks it correct or incorrect and shows the feedback text.
  4. The learner continues through question 5 and sees the score.
  5. The learner should notice that the unit of the horizon, human time, appears in both step 2 and step 6.

Feedback: 5 questions, fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct. [Why text]." Incorrect: "Not quite. [Why text]." The correct option is revealed after the attempt. A running score "n of 5" is shown. Final message for a score >= 4: "You can explain how a time horizon is produced." For a score < 4: "Review the six steps and try again."

Starting State: The six steps are shown as a flow with no step selected, and the prompt reads "How do you turn a pile of AI test results into one number?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states six steps, roughly 170 tasks, task lengths from seconds to about eight hours or more, and that the horizon is read where the success curve crosses 50 percent.

A ruler made of time

Think of the task horizon as a ruler marked in human minutes and hours instead of test points. That choice is what lets the ruler keep working as AI improves: a score of 95 percent on a test is a ceiling, but "tasks that take a person a day" is a mark you can keep moving up.

docs.title: Worked Example: Reading a Success Curve
docs.text:
Suppose a model attempts tasks of six lengths, many times each, and the success rates are as follows. These numbers are illustrative; they follow a smooth curve of the kind METR fits.

Human working time of the task Task success rate 1 minute 98% 4 minutes 94% 15 minutes 80% 60 minutes 50% 240 minutes (4 hours) 20% 960 minutes (16 hours) 6%

Reading the table, the success rate crosses 50 percent at 60 minutes, so this model's 50 percent time horizon is one hour. A second number is also visible: the success rate is 80 percent at 15 minutes, so the 80 percent time horizon is 15 minutes, four times shorter than the 50 percent one. In METR's real data the 80 percent horizon was also several times shorter than the 50 percent horizon. This matters for schools: a tool that succeeds half the time on one-hour tasks succeeds only four times in five on tasks a quarter that long.

Three questions for any headline

When a headline quotes a task horizon, ask: At what success rate, 50 or 80 percent? On what kind of tasks? Measured when? A "four-hour horizon" at 50 percent on software tasks is a very different claim from a four-hour assistant a teacher can trust.

The shape of the curve in the table, success falling steadily as tasks lengthen, is a simplified model with a stated rule: the chance of success is \( 1/(1 + t/H) \), where \( t \) is the task's human working time and \( H \) is the 50 percent horizon. The sim below lets you try it.

Task Horizon Curve Explorer

Type: microsim sim-id: task-horizon-curve-explorer Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: calculate Learning Objective: The learner will calculate a model's chance of completing tasks of different human working times from its 50 percent time horizon, to within 2 percentage points, and identify the task length at which the chance reaches 80 percent.

Template: https://github.com/dmccreary/tracking-ai-course/tree/main/docs/sims/ai-task-horizons

Prerequisites: human working time, task success rate, task horizon, 50 percent time horizon, and the success rule P = 1/(1 + t/H) (all defined in the section "METR and the Task-Horizon Idea" above).

Evidence of Mastery: Before the horizon can be changed, the learner commits three answers: (Q1) the chance of success on a 15-minute task for a model with H = 60 minutes; (Q2) the task length at which that model's chance is 80 percent; (Q3) the chance of success on a 60-minute task for a later model with H = 240 minutes. An answer is correct when it is within ±2 percentage points (Q1, Q3) or ±1 minute (Q2) of the value in Content. Mastery is 3 of 3 correct. Moving the horizon afterward is exploration.

Misconceptions: (1) A model with a 1-hour horizon is reliable on all tasks up to 1 hour. (2) Success drops to zero just past the horizon. (3) The 80 percent horizon is about the same as the 50 percent horizon.

Instructional Rationale: Applying a stated rule to specific values makes the meaning of the horizon concrete. Committing to calculations first and then exploring other horizons shows how the whole curve shifts as the horizon grows, and why reliability and horizon are different things.

Content:

The success rule: P = 1 / (1 + t/H), where t is the task's human working time in minutes and H is the model's 50 percent time horizon in minutes.

Model horizon H: min 15, max 960, step 15, default 60, unit minutes.

Six reference tasks:

Task Human working time t (minutes) A 1 B 4 C 15 D 60 E 240 F 960

Check values for H = 60:

t (minutes) Chance of success 1 98% 4 94% 15 80% 60 50% 240 20% 960 6%

Answers: Q1 = 80%; Q2 = 15 minutes (the 80 percent horizon is H/4); Q3 = 80% (60 minutes with H = 240 gives 1/(1 + 0.25)).

Provenance: The rule is a simplified model written for this chapter, in the spirit of the success curves METR fits. The sim must label it "Simplified illustrative model, not METR data."

Rules: P = 1/(1 + t/H), shown as a percent rounded to the nearest whole number. The 80 percent horizon is the t for which P = 0.8, which equals H/4. The 50 percent horizon is H. The curve is drawn on a logarithmic horizontal axis from 1 minute to 960 minutes.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads the rule and the six tasks, and answers Q1, Q2, and Q3 as predictions.
  2. The learner submits. The sim checks the answers and shows the curve for H = 60 with the six tasks marked.
  3. The learner moves the horizon from 15 to 960 minutes. The curve and the six success rates update at once.
  4. The learner should notice that the 50 percent point sits at H and the 80 percent point sits at a quarter of H, and that no task is ever certain.

Feedback: Three questions, fixed order, two attempts each. Q1 correct: "Yes: 1/(1 + 15/60) is 0.80." Q1 incorrect: "Divide the task length by the horizon, add 1, then take the reciprocal." Q2 correct: "Yes: the 80 percent point is a quarter of the horizon." Q2 incorrect: "Find the t where t/H equals 0.25." Q3 correct: "Yes: 1/(1 + 60/240) is 0.80." Q3 incorrect: "A longer horizon means the same 60-minute task is relatively shorter." After the second wrong attempt, the answer and its working are shown. A score "n of 3" is shown.

Starting State: The horizon is locked at 60 minutes, the six tasks are listed without success rates, and the prompt reads "How likely is this model to finish each task?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's worked example uses task lengths of 1, 4, 15, 60, 240, and 960 minutes, a 50 percent horizon of 60 minutes, and an 80 percent horizon of 15 minutes.

docs.title: Worked Example: Estimating a Horizon From Noisy Data
docs.text:
Real success rates do not land exactly on 50 percent, so the horizon has to be estimated between two measured points. Suppose a second model produces these results, which are illustrative.

Human working time Task success rate 2 minutes 95% 8 minutes 82% 30 minutes 61% 120 minutes 33% 480 minutes 12%

The 50 percent point lies between 30 minutes (61 percent) and 120 minutes (33 percent). Because task length is spread over a very wide range, the interpolation is done on the logarithm of the time, not on the time itself. The success rate falls 28 points between the two measured lengths, and 50 percent is 11 of those 28 points down from 61, a fraction of \( 11/28 \approx 0.39 \) of the way along. The two lengths differ by a factor of \( 120/30 = 4 \), so the horizon is

\[ 30 \times 4^{0.39} \approx 30 \times 1.72 \approx 52 \text{ minutes}. \]

A reader who interpolated on the plain number line would have placed the point 39 percent of the way from 30 to 120, at about 65 minutes, a 25 percent overestimate. The method matters because the whole argument of the chapter rests on reading a number off a curve. It is also a reminder that the headline figure carries a margin of error, which METR reports as a range.

docs.title: Long-Running Tasks and AI Agents
docs.text:
A long-running task is a task that needs many steps over an extended period, from hours to days, so that early mistakes can compound and the worker must plan, track progress, and recover from errors. Teaching examples are grade thirty essays and write feedback (about five hours), design and prepare a two-week unit with materials (a few days), and build an interactive classroom simulation (a few days). Long-running tasks matter because most valuable work is long-running, and the early AI systems were good at short bursts only.

An AI agent, defined earlier, is the kind of system that can attempt a long-running task, since it can keep working through many steps. This is why the horizon matters for schools: a system with a horizon of a few minutes can answer a student's question, and a system with a horizon of a few hours can walk a student through a multi-step project, check each step, and report to a teacher. The table gives illustrative educational tasks and human working times to make the idea concrete. These times are rough estimates, written for this chapter, and METR's own tasks are software tasks, so the table is an analogy and not a measurement.

Educational task Rough human working time Answer a student's factual question 1 minute Write feedback on one paragraph 5 minutes Draft a quiz of ten questions with an answer key 30 minutes Grade thirty short essays with written comments 5 hours Plan a two-week unit with materials and assessments 20 hours Build and test an interactive classroom simulation 40 hours

docs.title: Worked Example: Why Long Tasks Are Harder Than Short Ones
docs.text:
A long task is a chain of steps, and an agent has to get every step right, or notice and repair its mistakes. Suppose each step succeeds independently with some probability, and the task succeeds only if all the steps do. Then the chance of finishing is the per-step success rate multiplied by itself once per step. The table shows the result for three per-step reliabilities.

Steps in the task 90% per step 95% per step 99% per step 5 59% 77% 95% 10 35% 60% 90% 20 12% 36% 82% 50 0.5% 8% 61%

An agent that is right 95 times in 100 at each step finishes a twenty-step task only about 36 percent of the time. To complete it 80 percent of the time, each step would need to succeed about 98.9 percent of the time, since \( 0.8^{1/20} \approx 0.989 \). This is one reason the 80 percent horizon sits well below the 50 percent horizon, and why a rising horizon means more than "smarter": it means more reliable at every step, and better at noticing and recovering from errors. The model is simple, since real steps are not independent and good agents retry, but it shows why reliability is the quantity to watch.

A coin flip is not a colleague

A common trap is hearing "can do tasks that take a human two hours" and picturing a reliable assistant. A 50 percent horizon means the tool fails about half the time at that length, and the 80 percent horizon is much shorter. For anything a student or family will rely on, plan on a human check, and ask which horizon the vendor is quoting.

docs.title: Exponential Growth and Doubling Time
docs.text:
METR's headline finding concerns how the horizon changes over time. To state it you need two more terms.

Exponential growth is growth in which a quantity increases by a constant percentage or constant factor in each period, rather than by a constant amount. A savings account earning 5 percent a year grows slowly at first and then much faster, because each year's interest is earned on a larger balance. The distinctive feature of exponential growth is that it starts slowly and then becomes enormous, which human intuition is poor at tracking. Chapter 5 contrasts it with linear growth and explains how to read it on a chart.

The doubling time is the length of time it takes a quantity growing exponentially to double. If a quantity has a doubling time of five months, it is twice as large after five months, four times as large after ten, eight times after fifteen, and so on. The number of doublings that have happened is the elapsed time divided by the doubling time, and each doubling multiplies the quantity by two:

\[ \text{value after } t \text{ months} = \text{starting value} \times 2^{t/T} \]

where \( T \) is the doubling time in months. The formula is the whole of the arithmetic you need for the rest of the chapter.

Exponents feel slippery for everyone

If exponents make you nervous, you're in good company; human intuition is built for steady, additive change. You already did similar arithmetic in Chapter 1 when you divided a budget by a day count. Here, just keep doubling a number on paper (1, 2, 4, 8, 16) until the pattern feels solid, then read the table below.

METR found that the 50 percent time horizon of leading AI models has been growing exponentially. This book uses five-month doubling, a doubling time of about every five months, as its planning figure for the task horizon. The estimated doubling time depends on which models and which period are measured, so treat "about five months" as a planning figure and not a constant of nature. Chapter 5 returns to the sensitivity of forecasts to this number.

docs.title: Worked Example: Doubling Time as a Monthly Growth Rate
docs.text: People often meet growth as a percentage and doubling time as a period, so it helps to convert between them. If a quantity doubles every 5 months, it grows by a constant factor \( g \) each month with \( g^5 = 2 \), so \( g = 2^{1/5} \approx 1.149 \). The horizon therefore grows about 14.9 percent a month. Over a year the factor is \( 1.149^{12} = 2^{12/5} \approx 5.3 \), a gain of about 430 percent. A quick check is the "rule of 70": the doubling time in periods is about 70 divided by the percentage growth per period, and \( 70/14.9 \approx 4.7 \) months, close to the true 5. A bank account at 5 percent a year doubles in about 14 years by the same rule. Seen as a monthly rate, five-month doubling sounds like a steady 15 percent, and seen as a yearly factor it sounds like a five-fold annual jump, which are the same fact described two ways.

docs.title: Worked Example: What Five-Month Doubling Implies
docs.text:
Start from a 50 percent horizon of 50 minutes in early 2025 and apply five-month doubling. This is an illustration of the arithmetic, not a forecast.

Months from start Doublings (t/5) Growth factor \( 2^{t/5} \) Horizon 0 0 1 50 minutes 12 2.4 5.3 about 4.4 hours 24 4.8 27.9 about 23 hours 36 7.2 147 about 122 hours, roughly 15 eight-hour workdays 48 9.6 776 about 647 hours, roughly 81 workdays

The table shows why "three to four years" is the book's planning window. In three years the horizon grows by about a factor of 147, from under an hour to about three weeks of full-time human work. In four years it is about 776 times larger, or about four months of work. The growth after the first year looks small next to the growth in the last year, which is the signature of exponential growth.

The result depends heavily on the doubling time. If the doubling time were ten months instead of five, the horizon after 36 months would be \( 50 \times 2^{3.6} \approx 606 \) minutes, about ten hours rather than 122, a result twelve times smaller. A forecast with an exponential in it is only as good as its doubling time.

Count the doublings, not the months

The trick for reading any exponential claim is to ask how many doublings fit in the time. Five months per doubling gives about 2.4 doublings a year, so a factor of about 5 per year and about 147 in three years. Small changes in the doubling time swing the answer enormously, so always ask where the number comes from.

docs.title: AI Inference Cost
docs.text:
Capability is only half of what a school needs to know. The other half is price.

AI inference cost is the cost of running an already-trained AI model to produce an answer, as distinct from the large one-time cost of training the model. Inference is what happens each time a student sends a question and the model replies. It is typically priced per token, a small chunk of text, roughly three-quarters of an English word. Providers quote a price per million tokens, counting both the text sent in and the text generated.

Inference costs have been falling fast. The Stanford AI Index 2025 reported that the cost of querying a model with the performance of GPT-3.5 dropped from about $20 per million tokens in November 2022 to about $0.07 per million tokens in October 2024, more than a 280-fold decrease in under two years. That is about nineteen-fold a year. Two cautions apply. The fall describes a fixed level of capability: the cheapest way to reach the performance of an older model gets cheaper, while the most capable models still cost more. And prices depend on providers' pricing decisions, which can change.

For schools, falling inference cost is what makes AI tutoring something a public school could afford, as opposed to something only a tuition-funded private school could. The arithmetic is short.

docs.title: Worked Example: What a Token Costs in Everyday Terms
docs.text:
Prices per million tokens are hard to picture. A token is about three-quarters of an English word, so 1,000 words is roughly 1,333 tokens. A student asks a tutor to explain a concept in a 100-word question (about 133 tokens) and receives a 1,500-word explanation (about 2,000 tokens), for 2,133 tokens in all.

Price per million tokens Cost of this one exchange Cost of 1,000 such exchanges $20.00 (November 2022) about $0.043 about $43 $2.00 (an illustrative stronger-model price) about $0.004 about $4.30 $0.07 (October 2024, GPT-3.5-level) about $0.00015 about $0.15

At the 2022 price, a classroom of 28 students each asking one such question would cost about $1.20. At the 2024 price it is about four-tenths of a cent. The long, detailed answer matters more than the short question, because the model's output is usually priced higher than its input and is longer. A design that asks the tutor for short hints, as Chapter 12 recommends, is therefore cheaper as well as better for learning.

docs.title: Worked Example: Cost per Student per Year
docs.text:
Suppose a tutoring session uses about 20,000 tokens, such as forty exchanges of about 500 tokens, and a student has one session per school day for 180 days. The year's total is \( 20{,}000 \times 180 = 3{,}600{,}000 \) tokens, or 3.6 million. The cost for that year at each price is:

Price per million tokens Cost per student per year Cost per student per day $20.00 (November 2022) $72.00 $0.40 $0.07 (October 2024) about $0.25 about $0.0014

At the 2024 price, a 28-student class costs about \( 28 \times \$0.25 = \$7 \) a year, and a 12,000-student district about $3,000, against per-pupil spending of roughly $15,600 per student from Chapter 1. At the 2022 price, the same district would have paid about $864,000. A 280-fold price drop turns a luxury into a rounding error, which is the economic fact behind the "pennies per student per day" idea in the course description. The caution: this is a GPT-3.5-level model, and a stronger tutor costs more per token, so Chapter 7 returns to costs with the full picture.
