docs.text:
Run the AI Cost per Student Calculator MicroSim Fullscreen

AI Cost per Student Calculator

Type: microsim sim-id: ai-cost-per-student-calculator Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: calculate Learning Objective: The learner will calculate the yearly AI inference cost per student from tokens per session, sessions per day, school days, and price per million tokens, to within one cent, in three of three challenges.

Template: https://github.com/dmccreary/economics-course/tree/main/docs/sims/opportunity-cost-calculator

Prerequisites: AI inference cost, token, price per million tokens (all defined in the section "AI Inference Cost" above).

Evidence of Mastery: The learner commits answers to three challenges before the controls are unlocked. An answer is correct when it is within ±$0.01 of the value in Content. Mastery is 3 of 3 correct. Using the controls afterward is exploration.

Misconceptions: (1) Cost depends only on the number of sessions. (2) Cheaper models are always worse. (3) The cost of a capable AI tutor is out of reach for a public school.

Instructional Rationale: Calculating cost from four inputs builds fluency with the units and makes the effect of a 280-fold price change tangible. Exploring afterward lets the learner see which input matters most.

Content:

The cost formula: cost per student per year = tokens per session × sessions per day × school days × price per million tokens ÷ 1,000,000.

Inputs:

Input Min Max Step Default Unit Tokens per session 5,000 100,000 5,000 20,000 tokens Sessions per school day 1 5 1 1 sessions School days per year 150 200 10 180 days Price per million tokens 4 choices $0.07 dollars

The four prices: $20.00 (the November 2022 price for GPT-3.5-level performance as reported by the Stanford AI Index 2025), $2.00 (illustrative), $0.20 (illustrative), and $0.07 (the October 2024 price as reported by the same source).

Three challenges:

# Tokens per session Sessions per day School days Price per million Correct cost per student per year Working shown as feedback 1 20,000 1 180 $20.00 $72.00 20,000 × 1 × 180 = 3,600,000 tokens; 3.6 × $20.00 = $72.00. 2 20,000 1 180 $0.07 $0.25 3.6 million tokens × $0.07 = $0.252, which is about $0.25. 3 40,000 2 180 $0.20 $2.88 40,000 × 2 × 180 = 14,400,000 tokens; 14.4 × $0.20 = $2.88.

Provenance: The two reported prices come from the Stanford AI Index 2025 as summarized in the chapter; the sim must show the source and label the $2.00 and $0.20 prices "Illustrative." The session sizes are illustrative, and the sim must say they apply to a GPT-3.5-level model.

Rules: Annual tokens = tokens per session × sessions per day × school days. Cost = annual tokens ÷ 1,000,000 × price. Costs are shown to the cent, and to the tenth of a cent when under $1 per student per year. A district total is shown for an enrollment of 12,000 students, which is the Chapter 1 example district.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner answers challenges 1, 2, and 3 as calculations and submits them.
  2. The sim checks the answers and unlocks the controls.
  3. The learner changes the inputs. The yearly cost, the daily cost, and the district total update at once.
  4. The learner compares the cost at $20.00 and at $0.07 for the same usage.
  5. The learner should notice that price per token changes the result far more than any realistic change in usage.

Feedback: Three challenges, fixed order, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: $[value]. [Working text]." Incorrect: "Not quite. Check the units: the price is per million tokens." After the second wrong attempt the value and working are shown. A score "n of 3" is shown.

Starting State: Challenge 1 is shown with its inputs locked, and the prompt reads "What does one year of AI tutoring cost per student?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's worked example uses 20,000 tokens per session, one session per day, 180 days, 3.6 million tokens a year, prices of $20.00 and $0.07, costs of $72.00 and about $0.25, a 12,000-student district, and per-pupil spending of about $15,600.

docs.title: Answering "Doubles What?"
docs.text:
Mr. Alvarez's question now has an answer: the thing that is doubling is the length of task, measured in human working time, that a leading AI system completes about half the time. It is a specific, measured quantity, and it is not "intelligence" in general.

That answer also shows what the number does not say. It is measured on mostly software tasks, which may be cleaner than the messy tasks of a classroom. It is a 50 percent figure, so reliable performance is at a much shorter horizon. The doubling time is an estimate that depends on the models and period measured. And the main source is a preprint, not yet a settled finding. A board member who takes the curve seriously and holds these limits in mind is better placed than one who dismisses it or treats it as a promise.

The story has the benefit and risk this book always pairs. The benefit: if horizons keep growing, AI systems could eventually coach students through multi-step projects and take hours of routine work from teachers. The risks: tools that fail half the time at their advertised length; students who hand their thinking over to systems whose reliability they cannot judge; and a forecast that, by itself, tells a school nothing about whether a particular product helps a particular child. The response is the combination this book recommends: use the trend to plan, use independent evidence to buy, and keep a person in the loop wherever reliability matters.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Artificial intelligence is the broad field; machine learning learns from data; generative AI creates content; a large language model generates language; an AI agent takes multi-step actions toward a goal.
  • AI in education serves students, teachers, and administrators, and the gap between good and harmful results often depends on how the tool is designed.
  • AI capability is multi-dimensional; an AI benchmark and its benchmark task suite make it measurable, but benchmarks saturate and can be contaminated.
  • METR measures capability in a natural unit: human working time, the time a skilled person needs. The task success rate at each length gives a curve, and the task horizon is the length where it crosses a chosen level.
  • The 50 percent time horizon is a coin flip, not a reliable worker; the 80 percent horizon is several times shorter.
  • A long-running task needs many steps over hours or days, which is the kind of work an AI agent attempts.
  • Exponential growth adds a constant factor per period; the doubling time sets the factor, and value after \( t \) months is the starting value times \( 2^{t/T} \).
  • Five-month doubling is this book's planning figure: from 50 minutes, it implies about 23 hours after two years and about 122 hours after three, but a doubling time twice as long would give a result twelve times smaller.
  • AI inference cost for a fixed capability level fell more than 280-fold from November 2022 to October 2024, which is why AI tutoring could become affordable for public schools.

You can answer 'doubles what?'

You just learned to name what METR measures, read a task horizon, and explain what five-month doubling means for a three-year plan, along with the limits that come with it. Chapter 5 teaches you to read this kind of curve on a logarithmic chart and to say what could bend it. One step at a time, together.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: Measuring AI Capability: The METR Task-Horizon Studies
docs.text: Test your understanding of AI terminology, how METR measures AI capability with task horizons, and what five-month doubling implies with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. Which statement about the nesting of AI terms is correct?
docs.text:
1. Every machine-learning system is generative AI, but not every LLM is machine learning
  2. Every large language model is generative AI, but not every machine-learning system is generative
  3. Every AI system learns from data, but not every AI system uses rules written by programmers
  4. Every AI agent is a chatbot, but not every chatbot is built on a large language model
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The chapter's key idea is the nesting: every LLM is generative AI, every generative system is machine learning, and every machine-learning system is AI, but not the other way around. A spam filter is machine learning without being generative. The third option is false because a 1990s chess program using hand-written rules is AI that learns nothing from data. An agent differs from a chatbot because it takes multi-step actions on its own.

Concept Tested: Artificial Intelligence

See: A Ladder of Terms: From AI to AI Agents

docs.title: 2. In METR's studies, what is human working time?
docs.text:
1. The time an AI model takes to finish a task when run on a standard computer
  2. The average time a typical student would need to complete a school assignment
  3. The time a skilled professional needs to complete a task correctly, without distractions
  4. The number of hours a human reviewer spends checking an AI system's output for errors
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. METR hired skilled people to do each task while a clock ran, so human working time measures how hard the task is for people. It stays the same whether an AI or a person eventually does the task, which is what makes it a usable unit. It is not the AI's own running time, and it is measured on skilled professionals, not typical students. Review time is a separate cost the chapter does not use as the unit.

Concept Tested: Human Working Time

See: METR and the Task-Horizon Idea

docs.title: 3. Why did METR measure AI capability in units of human working time instead of a benchmark test score?
docs.text:
1. Because test scores cannot be computed for AI systems that use language
  2. Because human working time is cheaper to collect than benchmark scores
  3. Because benchmark scores always favor the AI developer that wrote the test
  4. Because a time-based measure does not hit a ceiling the way a saturated test does
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Benchmarks follow a typical life story: they start hard, systems improve until scores approach the maximum, and the test stops telling anyone anything. Scores on old and new tests cannot be placed on one scale. A measure such as "how long a task, in hours, can the system finish" never hits a ceiling, so the ruler keeps working as AI improves. Contamination is a real benchmark problem, but the chapter does not say all scores favor the developer.

Concept Tested: AI Benchmark

See: Worked Example: A Benchmark Runs Out of Room

docs.title: 4. A model's success rates are 96% on 2-minute tasks, 80% on 10-minute tasks, 50% on 40-minute tasks, and 20% on 160-minute tasks. What are its 50 percent and 80 percent time horizons?
docs.text:
1. 40 minutes and 10 minutes
  2. 40 minutes and 160 minutes
  3. 10 minutes and 40 minutes
  4. 80 minutes and 50 minutes
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The 50 percent time horizon is the task length at which the model succeeds about half the time, here 40 minutes. The 80 percent horizon is the length at which it succeeds four times in five, here 10 minutes, four times shorter. The third option swaps the two. The last option confuses success rates with task lengths. As the chapter notes, the reliable horizon sits well below the 50 percent one.

Concept Tested: 50 Percent Time Horizon

See: Worked Example: Reading a Success Curve

docs.title: 5. A vendor tells a principal its AI agent "has a four-hour task horizon." What does the chapter suggest the principal should understand by that claim?
docs.text:
1. The agent will reliably complete any school task that takes a teacher four hours
  2. The agent can work continuously for four hours before it needs to be restarted
  3. At 50 percent, it fails about half of four-hour tasks; its reliable horizon is shorter
  4. The agent completes four-hour tasks in a small fraction of the time a human needs
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. A 50 percent horizon is a coin flip, not a reliable worker: the tool fails about half the time at that length, and the 80 percent horizon is several times shorter. The chapter advises asking at what success rate, on what kind of tasks, and when the figure was measured. METR's tasks are mostly software tasks, so the first option overstates the claim. The horizon describes task length in human time, not how long the agent runs or how fast it works.

Concept Tested: Task Horizon

See: Long-Running Tasks and AI Agents

docs.title: 6. Suppose a leading model has a 50 percent time horizon of 2 hours today, and the horizon keeps doubling about every five months. What would the horizon be after 20 months?
docs.text:
1. About 10 hours
  2. About 32 hours
  3. About 16 hours
  4. About 80 hours
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Twenty months divided by a five-month doubling time gives four doublings, and \( 2 \times 2^4 = 32 \) hours. The 10-hour answer treats the growth as linear, adding two hours per period instead of doubling. The 16-hour answer counts only three doublings. The chapter's advice is to count the doublings, not the months, because exponential growth multiplies by a constant factor each period.

Concept Tested: Five-Month Doubling

See: Exponential Growth and Doubling Time

docs.title: 7. Agent A succeeds 95 percent of the time on each step, and Agent B succeeds 99 percent of the time. On a 20-step task, A finishes about 36 percent of the time and B about 82 percent. What does this comparison show?
docs.text:
1. Long tasks are impossible for any agent, since every agent fails most twenty-step tasks
  2. The difference is too small to matter, because both agents are right on almost every step
  3. Agent A is the better choice for long tasks, because it gives up sooner when steps fail
  4. Small gains in per-step reliability produce large differences on long, multi-step tasks
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. When a task succeeds only if every step does, the per-step rate is multiplied by itself once per step, so errors compound. A four-point gain in per-step reliability more than doubles the chance of finishing. The chapter uses this to explain why the 80 percent horizon sits well below the 50 percent horizon and why a rising horizon means more reliable work at every step. Agent B finishes most twenty-step tasks, so the first option is false.

Concept Tested: Long-Running Task

See: Worked Example: Why Long Tasks Are Harder Than Short Ones

docs.title: 8. What did the "jagged technological frontier" study of consultants using GPT-4 show?
docs.text:
1. AI improved consultants' work on every task, but by different amounts
  2. AI helped only the least experienced consultants and slowed down the experts
  3. AI helped on tasks inside its range but hurt accuracy just outside it
  4. AI performed the same on all tasks, so the frontier was smooth and predictable
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. On tasks inside what the AI did well, consultants with AI finished more tasks, faster, at higher quality. On a task just outside that range, consultants using AI were about 19 percentage points less likely to reach the correct answer, because confident AI output led them astray. The edge of AI ability is jagged and hard to see from outside, so a tool's average ability says little about the task in front of you. The first option misses the harm outside the frontier.

Concept Tested: AI Capability

See: Measuring What AI Can Do

docs.title: 9. A student uses about 3.6 million tokens of AI tutoring over a school year. At the October 2024 price of about $0.07 per million tokens for GPT-3.5-level performance, what is the cost per student per year?
docs.text:
1. About $72.00
  2. About $0.25
  3. About $2.52
  4. About $25.20
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Multiply 3.6 million tokens by $0.07 per million: \( 3.6 \times 0.07 \approx \$0.25 \) per student per year. The $72 answer uses the November 2022 price of $20 per million tokens. The other two shift the decimal point. The chapter cautions that this price applies to a GPT-3.5-level model; stronger tutors cost more per token, so the full cost picture returns in Chapter 7.

Concept Tested: AI Inference Cost

See: Worked Example: Cost per Student per Year

docs.title: 10. At a board meeting, a presenter projects that the AI task horizon will grow about 147-fold in three years. A board member asks what would most change that forecast. Which answer best reflects the chapter?
docs.text:
1. The number of schools and districts that adopt AI tools during the three years
  2. The price per million tokens that AI providers charge schools and districts
  3. The success rate METR uses, since a 50 percent figure is always too optimistic
  4. The doubling time, since ten-month doubling would make the result twelve times smaller
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The 147-fold figure comes from 7.2 doublings at five months each over 36 months. The chapter shows that with a ten-month doubling time the horizon after three years would be about ten hours instead of 122, roughly twelve times smaller, and concludes that a forecast with an exponential in it is only as good as its doubling time. The success-rate choice changes the level of the horizon, not its growth factor. Prices and adoption do not drive the capability curve.

Concept Tested: Doubling Time

See: Worked Example: What Five-Month Doubling Implies

docs.title: References: Measuring AI Capability: The METR Task-Horizon Studies
docs.text:
1. Artificial intelligence - Wikipedia - A broad overview of AI's goals, methods, history, and risks. Gives readers the top rung of the chapter's ladder of terms, from artificial intelligence down to machine learning, language models, and agents.

  2. Machine learning - Wikipedia - Explains how systems learn patterns from data instead of following hand-written rules, with the main families of methods. Clarifies the step between AI in general and the large language models the chapter measures.

  3. Large language model - Wikipedia - Covers how large language models are trained on text, how they generate responses, and their known limitations. Background for understanding the chatbots and AI agents whose task horizons METR tracks.

  4. Artificial Intelligence: A Guide for Thinking Humans (2019) - Melanie Mitchell - Farrar, Straus and Giroux - Mitchell is known for explaining why benchmark scores can overstate what AI understands. Her careful treatment of benchmarks helps readers see why METR measured capability in human working time instead of test scores.

  5. Co-Intelligence: Living and Working with AI (2024) - Ethan Mollick - Portfolio - Mollick introduced the "jagged frontier," the idea that AI is strong at some tasks and weak at others of similar difficulty. The image explains why a single task-horizon number needs careful interpretation.

  6. Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Tasks - METR - METR's plain-language summary of the task-horizon study, showing how a logistic curve finds the task length where a model succeeds half the time. The primary source for this chapter's central measurement.

  7. Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Software Tasks - Kwa, West, Becker, et al., arXiv - The full research paper behind the METR study, detailing the benchmark task suites, human baseline timings, and limitations. For readers who want the methods and caveats behind the 50 percent time horizon.

  8. Task-Completion Time Horizons of Frontier AI Models - METR - METR's reference page listing 50 percent and 80 percent time horizons for frontier models, with an FAQ on what the measure does and does not mean. Helps readers avoid common misreadings of the task-horizon figure.

  9. Trends in AI - Epoch AI - A dashboard tracking growth in training compute, hardware performance, costs, and data centers, each with doubling times. Places the METR trend alongside the other exponential measurements that drive AI capability.

  10. Elements of AI - University of Helsinki and MinnaLearn - A free, self-paced introduction to what AI is and what it can and cannot do, requiring no math or programming. A good starting point for educators new to the chapter's terms.

docs.title: Projecting AI Growth: Doubling Curves, Limits, and Uncertainty
Summary
docs.text: This chapter teaches readers to project the METR task-horizon trend forward: reading a logarithmic scale, the five-month doubling time, and the difference between linear and exponential growth. It also covers what could slow the trend, forecast uncertainty, AI inference cost, and energy use, so readers can hold the prediction and its limits at the same time. Readers finish able to read a log-scale chart and state the assumptions behind a multi-year AI forecast.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: The Building Blocks of Schools, Students, and Learning
  • Chapter 4: Measuring AI Capability: The METR Task-Horizon Studies

docs.title: "Why Should the Line Keep Going?"
docs.text:
A month after the board meeting in Chapter 4, Mr. Alvarez returns with a harder question. "Fine, the horizon doubles about every five months. But a line on a chart is not a law of physics. Why should it keep going for three more years? And what do we do if it doesn't?"

A skeptical teacher, Mr. Dang, adds his own: "I've heard 'this will change everything' about film strips, computers, and tablets. Why is this different?"

Both questions are fair, and this chapter answers them without taking sides. It teaches how to read the kind of chart these claims come with, how to project it, how far a projection can honestly be trusted, and how a school can make decisions that hold up whether the trend continues, slows, or stops. The goal is to hold the prediction and its limits in your head at once.

A forecast you can plan with

This chapter is about being useful under uncertainty: you'll learn to read a doubling chart, name the assumptions behind a multi-year forecast, and choose moves that make sense even if it's wrong. Let's find the balance between planning for a curve and not betting the school on it.

docs.title: Linear Versus Exponential Growth
docs.text:
Chapter 4 introduced exponential growth. To see why it behaves so differently from the growth people expect, compare it with its opposite.

Linear growth is growth by a constant amount in each period: a plant that grows two centimeters every week, or a savings jar that gains ten dollars every month. On a chart it is a straight line, and its rate of change never changes. People find linear growth intuitive, because it matches most of everyday life.

The contrast with exponential growth, which gains a constant factor in each period, is the heart of the argument. Start both from the 50-minute horizon of Chapter 4. The linear version adds 50 minutes every five months, which is 10 minutes a month. The exponential version doubles every five months.

Months Linear (adds 10 min per month) Exponential (doubles every 5 months) 0 50 minutes 50 minutes 12 170 minutes (2.8 hours) about 4.4 hours 24 290 minutes (4.8 hours) about 23 hours 36 410 minutes (6.8 hours) about 122 hours 48 530 minutes (8.8 hours) about 647 hours

At 12 months the two are nearly the same, so early data cannot tell them apart. By 36 months the exponential value is about 18 times the linear one, and by 48 months about 73 times. This is the reason people who correctly understand a doubling trend sound alarmed to people who are extrapolating a straight line: they are not disagreeing about the facts so much as about the shape.

docs.title: Worked Example: Two Students, Two Vocabularies
docs.text: Maya and Jordan each start with 50 vocabulary words. Maya learns 10 new words a month (linear). Jordan's method doubles his word count every five months (exponential, as a thought experiment). After a year Maya knows 170 and Jordan knows about 264; Jordan looks only about 55 percent ahead. After three years Maya knows 410 and Jordan about 7,350. A teacher who checked in after one year and extrapolated a straight line for Jordan would have predicted about 690 words at year three (a straight line through 50 and 264 reaches about 690 at 36 months), off by a factor of more than ten. The shape of the curve, not the early numbers, determines the future.

docs.title: Reading a Logarithmic Chart
docs.text:
Exponential data is awkward to draw. On an ordinary chart the early values are squashed against the bottom while the last few shoot off the top. The usual fix is to change the scale.

A logarithmic scale is an axis on which equal distances represent equal multiples rather than equal amounts. On an ordinary (linear) axis the gridlines might read 0, 100, 200, 300. On a logarithmic axis they read 1, 10, 100, 1,000: each gridline is ten times the one before. In the common base-ten version, the distance between 1 and 10 is the same as between 10 and 100, and the same as between 100 and 1,000.

A log-scale chart is a chart that uses a logarithmic scale on one axis, normally the vertical one, with time on the horizontal axis. Its useful property is that a quantity growing at a constant doubling time plots as a straight line. The steepness of the line tells you the growth rate: a steep line means a short doubling time, and a flatter line a longer one. Equal steps up the chart are equal numbers of doublings, so you can count them.

Three rules help you read one:

  • Check the axis first. If the labels go 1, 10, 100, 1,000, you are looking at a log scale, and a line that rises steadily is exponential growth, not a gentle trend.
  • Straight means constant doubling. A line that bends upward on a log chart is growth getting faster than exponential, and a line that bends downward means growth is slowing.
  • Distance is a ratio. The gap between two points tells you how many times larger the later value is, not how much larger.

Count the gridlines

On a base-ten log chart, every gridline you climb is a tenfold increase, and every gridline contains a little over three doublings (since \( 2^{3.32} \approx 10 \)). So two gridlines up is a factor of 100 in about six or seven doublings, which at five months each is about thirty-three months.

docs.title: Worked Example: Reading the Horizon Chart
docs.text:
On a log-scale chart of the Chapter 4 projection, suppose the vertical axis is labeled 1 minute, 10 minutes, 100 minutes, 1,000 minutes, 10,000 minutes (about a week of work), and 100,000 minutes. The line starts at 50 minutes, between the first two gridlines, and crosses 10,000 minutes at about 38 months. You can check this: \( 50 \times 2^{38/5} \approx 50 \times 194 \approx 9{,}700 \) minutes. The gap between 50 and 10,000 is a factor of 200, which is about 7.6 doublings, which at five months each is 38 months. Reading a log chart means translating distance into doublings and doublings into time.

The sim below, reused from another book in this series, plots the same exponential data on a linear and a logarithmic axis so you can see the straightening effect for yourself.

docs.title: Diagram: Linear Versus Semi-Log Plot of Exponential Data
docs.text:
Run the Linear vs Semi-Log Plot MicroSim fullscreen

Linear vs Semi-Log Plot of Exponential Data (reused MicroSim)

Type: microsim sim-id: semilog-linearization Library: p5.js Status: Reused Source: https://dmccreary.github.io/pre-calc/sims/semilog-linearization/ Source Repo: https://github.com/dmccreary/pre-calc/tree/main/docs/sims/semilog-linearization Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: compare Learning Objective: The learner will compare how the same exponential data looks on a linear axis and on a logarithmic axis, and explain why it plots as a straight line on the logarithmic one.

Reused from the MicroSim catalog (WHAT match score 0.782). The source sim's own lesson page is unfinished, but its main.html runs as described.

Logs trip up almost everyone

If a log scale feels backwards at first, that's normal; most of us learned charts where equal steps mean equal amounts. You already read two kinds of scale in Chapter 1 when you compared minutes and dollars. Try the sim above with the slider on one value and watch which axis the line straightens on.

docs.title: Projecting the Trend
docs.text:
Now we can state the forecast and its logic.

Trend extrapolation is the practice of extending a pattern observed in past data into the future, on the assumption that the forces that produced the pattern will continue. It is the most common forecasting method, since it needs no theory, only a line. Its strength is that, over short spans, the future often resembles the recent past. Its weakness is that it fails exactly when the forces behind the pattern change, which is when the forecast matters most.

History offers both successes and failures. Moore's law, Gordon Moore's 1965 observation that the number of transistors on a chip doubles at a steady interval, which he revised in 1975 to about every two years, held for decades and shaped an entire industry. It also slowed as chips approached physical limits. Many other exponential-looking trends turned out to be the early part of an S-curve: growth that accelerates, then levels off as it runs into a ceiling. The adoption of any new technology follows an S-curve, with the exponential phase lasting until the market is saturated.

A planning window is the span of time over which a decision has to hold up: the years a purchase, schedule, or training commitment will be in use. Schools plan in windows of about three to five years. Device fleets are replaced every three to five years, textbook adoptions last five to seven, and a kindergartner who starts in 2026 graduates in 2039. A forecast is useful only to the extent it covers the planning window of the decision it informs.

The book's central projection is the three-to-four-year forecast: applying five-month doubling to the task horizon over the next three to four years. From a start of about 50 minutes in early 2025, the Chapter 4 arithmetic gives a horizon of roughly 122 hours after three years and 647 hours after four. These figures are central estimates, not promises; the next section shows how wide the honest range around them is.

docs.title: Worked Example: When Could AI Build a Textbook Chapter?
docs.text:
Suppose a skilled team needs about 40 hours of human working time to write one chapter of an interactive textbook with its simulations. When does the 50 percent horizon cross 40 hours, which is 2,400 minutes? Solve \( 50 \times 2^{t/5} = 2{,}400 \):

\[ 2^{t/5} = 48 \qquad \frac{t}{5} = \log_2 48 \approx 5.6 \qquad t \approx 28 \text{ months} \]

So on the central trend the horizon passes 40 hours about 28 months after early 2025, around mid-2027. But a 50 percent horizon means the system finishes such a chapter correctly only half the time. If reliable output requires the 80 percent horizon, which in Chapter 4's simple model is a quarter of the 50 percent horizon, the 50 percent horizon must reach 160 hours, or 9,600 minutes:

\[ 2^{t/5} = 192 \qquad \frac{t}{5} = \log_2 192 \approx 7.6 \qquad t \approx 38 \text{ months} \]

That is about three years, mid-2028. This is the reasoning behind the book's prediction that interactive textbooks will become cheap and widely available within three to four years: not a guess about "intelligence," but arithmetic on a measured trend with a stated reliability bar.

docs.title: Forecast Uncertainty
docs.text:
Forecast uncertainty is the range of outcomes a forecast could reasonably turn out to have, which grows the further into the future the forecast looks. A single number, such as "122 hours," conceals that range. An honest forecast gives a range and says what it depends on.

The main source of uncertainty in an exponential forecast is the doubling time, because it sits in the exponent. Using an illustrative range of four to six months around the five-month planning figure:

Doubling time Horizon after 36 months Horizon after 48 months 4 months about 427 hours about 3,413 hours 5 months about 122 hours about 647 hours 6 months about 53 hours about 213 hours 10 months (trend halves in speed) about 10 hours about 23 hours

A shift of one month either way moves the three-year answer by a factor of about two or three, and the two ends of the range, four and six months, differ by a factor of eight. A trend that slows to half speed produces a three-year horizon about twelve times smaller than the central one. These are the same arithmetic as the Chapter 4 formula, applied to different inputs, and they show why precision about the doubling time matters more than precision about the starting value.

Uncertainty has other sources too: the measurement itself (a preprint on one set of tasks), whether horizons on benchmark tasks match horizons on messy real-world work, and whether progress on the 50 percent horizon carries over to the reliability that matters.

Don't mistake a line for a law

A common trap is reading a trend line as a guarantee, in either direction: "it will certainly happen" or "it's obviously hype." Instead, ask what the line assumes, how far it extends past the data, and how much the answer changes if the doubling time shifts by a month. If the answer swings by a factor of eight, say so in the plan.

The sim below lets you try these sensitivities yourself.
