docs.title: Level 1: Static Textbooks
docs.text:
A Level 1 static textbook is a textbook with fixed content and no response to the learner. Print and PDF textbooks are the standard examples. At most they add navigation aids, such as a table of contents, bookmarks, and text search, which help the reader move around but do not respond to what the reader does.

Level 1 is by far the most common level in use today. Its strengths are real: it is cheap to produce and copy, works everywhere, needs no student data, and raises no privacy questions. Its limits are the ones listed above: one pace, one path, no feedback.

docs.title: Level 2: Interactive Textbooks
docs.text:
A Level 2 interactive textbook is a textbook whose content responds to the learner's actions: the learner changes something and the page changes in return. It does not need to know who the learner is, and it stores nothing about them between visits. Because it needs no student records, it carries essentially none of the privacy burden of the higher levels, which is what makes Level 2 the sweet spot of the book's low-cost design.

Four features characterize Level 2.

An embedded simulation, which this book calls a MicroSim, is a small interactive model inside the page, running in the browser with no server, in which the learner changes inputs and watches the result. The sims in this book, such as the effect-size visualizer of Chapter 2 and the task-horizon explorer of Chapter 4, are embedded simulations.

Self-check quizzes give immediate feedback on answers, using the idea from Chapter 2 that quick feedback prevents practicing mistakes.

A learning graph, covered in Chapter 9, maps each concept and the concepts it depends on. At Level 2 it is a fixed map the textbook author made, shared by every reader.

Path recommendation is a suggestion, based on the learning graph, of what concept to read or practice next, such as "you opened Ratios; first review Equivalent Fractions." At Level 2 the recommendation depends on what the learner says they know or what they clicked, within a single visit. It does not require a saved record of the learner.

docs.title: Worked Example: A Level 2 Page in Action
docs.text: A student opens a page on unit rates in a Level 2 textbook. She drags a slider for the price of a pack of juice and the bottle count, and the page recomputes the price per bottle. She answers a self-check question and is told immediately that she divided in the wrong order, with a hint. At the bottom the page says, "If equivalent fractions are shaky, try this review." Every other student who opens the page sees the same content. When she closes the browser, the page remembers nothing. The textbook responded to her, and it never needed to know her name.

docs.title: The Intelligent Textbook Movement and the Growth of Level 2
docs.text:
The intelligent textbook movement is the growing effort, from researchers, open-education authors, and developers, to build textbooks that go beyond static pages. Research workshops on intelligent textbooks have met alongside the major conferences on AI in education for several years, and the movement began in earnest in 2025, when AI tools made it practical for a single author to produce a complete interactive textbook.

The growth of Level 2 textbooks is the most visible result. Because a Level 2 textbook is made of ordinary web pages and small simulations, it costs little to host and nothing to copy, and AI authoring tools lower the cost of writing it. Dozens of open Level 2 textbooks, and hundreds of reusable MicroSims, now exist in the catalog that supports this book's own tooling, and the number is rising quickly. As Chapter 7 explains, this is the economic force that makes Level 2 content cheap and often free.

docs.title: Worked Example: What Drives the Movement
docs.text:
The intelligent textbook movement did not begin because a single tool appeared. Several forces arrived together, and understanding them helps predict where it goes.

Force What changed Why it matters Authoring cost AI tools made it practical for one person to draft chapters and simulations (Chapter 7) A Level 2 book no longer needs a publisher's team Open licenses Creative Commons let authors share and remix Content and simulations can be reused legally Reusable MicroSims Small browser-based simulations can be embedded anywhere A good sim is written once and used in many books Standards xAPI, LTI, and open formats Books can plug into schools' existing systems Hosting Static sites on free or cheap hosts Distribution costs almost nothing Demand Teachers and families want more than a PDF There is a ready audience

None of these requires a large language model in front of every student. That is part of why the movement can spread at the low cost the book argues for.

docs.title: Worked Example: Growth Through Reuse
docs.text:
Level 2 growth is helped by an effect that print never had: an interactive element built for one book can be reused in another. This book is a small example. Of its 78 simulation blocks, 13 are reused from existing books and 65 are new specifications, so about 17 percent of its interactive elements were free to adopt. Suppose, as an illustration, that building a simulation from scratch takes about 8 hours and adapting an existing one takes about 1 hour, at $50 an hour.

Scenario Simulations reused Hours saved Cost saved This book today 13 of 78 \( 13 \times 7 = 91 \) \( 91 \times \$50 = \$4,550 \) A catalog twice as rich: 40 percent reuse 31 of 78 \( 31 \times 7 = 217 \) $10,850

The more sims exist, the more any new book can borrow, which lowers the cost of the next book. That feedback is the reinforcing loop of Chapter 18 applied to content, and it is a main reason the Level 2 supply keeps growing.

Check for the reset test

Here's a quick way to tell Level 2 from Level 3: change something on the page, then reload it. If the page forgets you, it's Level 2. If it remembers where you were, what you got wrong, or what you should do next, it's keeping a record about you, and that's Level 3.

docs.title: Level 3: Adaptive Textbooks
docs.text:
A Level 3 adaptive textbook is a textbook that changes what it shows each student based on a stored record of that student's goals and progress. The defining step from Level 2 is memory about an individual: the system keeps a record of what each student has done and mastered and uses it to choose what comes next.

Two features define Level 3.

Progress tracking is the recording of what a student has read, attempted, and mastered over time, kept in a store tied to that student. It is the foundation of adaptation: without a record, nothing can adapt. Chapter 8 explains how a standard called xAPI and a Learning Record Store make this possible while keeping the data under the student's and family's control.

Student goal setting is the student's stating of what they want to achieve, such as passing a particular exam, mastering a unit by a date, or following an interest, which the system uses to shape the path. It builds on the student agency of Chapter 1 by giving the student a voice in the plan.

An adaptive textbook might use simple rules, such as "if the student scored below 80 percent on the last three questions, review the prerequisite," or a statistical model that estimates mastery. Neither requires a large language model. Adaptive math platforms existed long before ChatGPT, and by this model's definition they are Level 3.

Level 3 is the privacy inflection point. Below it, a textbook needs almost no student data. At Level 3 and above, it needs detailed learning histories, which brings in the privacy laws, the governance duties, and the checks for bias that Chapter 10 covers. This is the same step as the jump from Level 2 to Level 3 in the car model, where the system takes control and liability questions begin.

Personalization has a price in privacy

Here's the tradeoff at the heart of this book: the more a textbook adapts to a child, the more it has to know about that child. That is not a reason to avoid Level 3. It is a reason to decide, before adopting one, exactly what is kept, by whom, and for how long.

docs.title: Worked Example: What the Record Contains
docs.text:
After a month, the record for Maya in a Level 3 math textbook holds the following. The values are illustrative.

Item in the record Example value What the system does with it Goal "Be ready for the unit test on March 12" Plans backwards from the date Mastery of each concept Equivalent fractions: 40%; Ratios: 25% Sends her back to equivalent fractions Time on each page 4 minutes on unit rates Flags that she may have skipped the practice Errors made Divided in the wrong order, 6 times Selects practice on the specific mistake Last visit Yesterday, 7:40 p.m. Schedules a review of older material

Each row is useful, and each row is also personal data about a child. Ms. Okafor should ask for every item in this kind of table: What is stored? Who sees it? When is it deleted?

docs.title: Level 4: Chatbot Textbooks
docs.text:
A Level 4 chatbot textbook is a textbook that adds a conversational AI, usually built on a large language model, which students can talk to about the material. The chatbot, defined in Chapter 5, can answer questions, rephrase an explanation, and respond to a student's own words, ideally by drawing on the textbook's content so that its answers match what the course teaches.

Conversational tutoring is instruction carried out through dialogue: the tutor asks questions, listens to the student's answers, gives hints, and adjusts its next question to the response. It imitates what a good human tutor does and is the reason one-to-one tutoring has been so effective in the research (Chapter 11). A well-designed conversational tutor does not hand over answers. It asks "what is the problem asking you to find?" and lets the student do the thinking, which is the hint ladder of Chapter 2.

A common example is Khan Academy's Khanmigo, launched in 2023 as a tutoring assistant layered on a platform that already tracked student progress. By this model's definitions it is a Level 4 chat tutor on top of a Level 3 platform. This classification is the book's reading of the product, and the vendor may describe it differently.

docs.title: Worked Example: Anatomy of a Good Tutoring Conversation
docs.text:
Conversational tutoring is built from a small number of moves. Here is a short dialogue, with each tutor move named, using the juice problem from earlier chapters.

Turn What is said Tutor move 1 Maya: "I don't get unit rates." Tutor: "When you read 'price per bottle,' what is it asking you to find?" Clarification question; hint level 1 2 Maya: "How much one bottle costs?" Tutor: "Yes. What do you know about the 6-pack?" Confirms; narrows the plan 3 Maya: "It costs $4.50, and has 6 bottles. Do I multiply?" Tutor: "Try it: if you multiply, what do you get, and does it fit the story?" Probes an assumption; lets her test it 4 Maya: "27. No, the pack is only $4.50, so it must be divide." Self-correction, with no answer given 5 Maya: "0.75." Tutor: "How could you check that?" Asks for evidence 6 Maya: "0.75 times 6 is 4.50." Tutor: "Exactly. Now try 8 pencils for $2.00." Confirms; transfers to a new problem

The tutor never states the answer and never says "wrong." It asks six questions, one of which Maya answers by checking her own work. The dialogue is also a test for any product: a tutor that cannot do this, or that does it only when the student volunteers the right answer, is a chatbot with a teaching label.

docs.title: Worked Example: Two Chat Tutors, Same Question
docs.text:
Maya types, "What's the price per bottle if 6 bottles cost $4.50?" Compare two Level 4 designs.

Answer-first tutor Hint-first tutor Reply "Divide $4.50 by 6. The answer is $0.75." "What is the problem asking you to find? Which number is the total, and which is the count?" Maya's reply "ok" "The total is $4.50 and the count is 6, so... divide?" Next move Moves to the next problem "Good. Which goes first, 4.50 or 6? Try it and tell me what you get." What Maya practiced Copying an answer Identifying the quantities and choosing the operation Risk She cannot repeat this on the test The tutor takes longer, and a frustrated student may give up

Both tutors are Level 4. The second is the one the evidence of Chapter 2 favors, and the Turkish high-school study the course description mentions found that this design difference mattered more than the power of the model. The remedy for the second design's risk is not to drop the hints but to add support: after two honest tries the tutor offers a worked example of a different problem.

Level 4 adds the new risks of Chapter 5: hallucination, and students asking for answers instead of thinking. It also adds a per-conversation computing cost. It needs guardrails: hint-first behavior, limits on age and topic, and logs that teachers can review. Chapter 12 develops these.

docs.title: Level 5: Autonomous AI Textbooks
docs.text:
A Level 5 autonomous textbook is a textbook that the AI generates and adapts for each student on its own, in real time, without a human author creating the content in advance. Where a Level 4 chatbot answers questions about a textbook someone wrote, a Level 5 system writes the textbook itself for the student in front of it.

Two features define Level 5.

Real-time content generation is the creation of explanations, examples, exercises, simulations, and assessments at the moment a student needs them, rather than their selection from a library prepared in advance.

Full personalization is adaptation of the content along every relevant dimension at once: the student's goals, prior knowledge, pace, interests, language, reading level, and accessibility needs. A Level 3 textbook changes the order of prepared content; a fully personalized Level 5 textbook changes the content itself.

docs.title: Worked Example: A Level 5 Lesson for Maya
docs.text:
Suppose Maya's record says she is weak on equivalent fractions, loves drawing, and reads two grades above level. A Level 3 textbook would select the prepared equivalent-fractions lesson from a library. A Level 5 system would instead write one: an explanation that uses the area of drawn tiles, since she likes drawing, at her reading level, with six new practice problems built around her recent errors, and a short simulation made on the spot to let her slide a fraction bar. No human wrote that lesson, and no human has read it before she does. The benefit is a lesson no library could contain. The risk is that nobody has checked it. If the explanation has a small error, Maya learns the error. That is why the safeguard table below puts human review of generated lessons first at Level 5.

Level 5 is where the arithmetic of Chapter 5 matters. Writing and checking a chapter-sized lesson with simulations takes tens of hours of human work, so a system that could do it reliably needs a task horizon well beyond one day at high reliability. On the book's central trend that point is about three years away, and the doubts of Chapter 5 apply fully. Level 5 also has the largest verification problem: when no one has reviewed the content in advance, someone has to ensure it is accurate, appropriate, and free of bias.

The table summarizes the five levels. Each row restates what you have just read; use it as a reference.

Level Name What it adds What it needs to know about the student Main new risk 1 Static Nothing beyond fixed content Nothing One pace for everyone 2 Interactive Responds to actions: simulations, quizzes, graph, paths Nothing stored Poorly built or inaccurate simulations 3 Adaptive Adapts to goals and progress A stored record of each student Privacy, bias, data breaches 4 Chatbot Conversation about the material The record plus the conversation Hallucination; answers instead of thinking 5 Autonomous Generates the textbook itself per student Everything above, in real time Unreviewed content; loss of human oversight

docs.title: Levels 3 to 5 on the Horizon and the Adoption Timeline
docs.text:
A level adoption timeline is an estimate of when products at each level become available and widely used. The book's prediction (Chapter 5) is that within three to four years almost every student could have access to a free, high-quality interactive textbook. Level 2 textbooks are already being published in growing numbers, and Levels 3 to 5 on the horizon describes the rest: levels that exist in early form or in the lab and are not yet routine.

Level Status as this book is written What would have to be true for wide adoption 1 Dominant Already widespread 2 Growing quickly; often free Authors and schools adopt open Level 2 textbooks 3 Available in adaptive platforms, mostly commercial Privacy governance and standards such as xAPI become routine 4 Early products; fast-moving Guardrails and independent evidence of benefit 5 Not yet reliable Long-task reliability, content verification, and public trust

On the central trend of Chapter 5, the horizon needed to write and check a lesson at 80 percent reliability is reached around mid-2028, which would make Level 5 technically plausible about three years out, with trust and regulation likely to arrive later. This is a projection with all the caveats of the last chapter, not a schedule.

docs.title: Diagram: Product Level Classifier
docs.text:
Run the Product Level Classifier MicroSim Fullscreen

Product Level Classifier

Type: microsim sim-id: product-level-classifier Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: judge Learning Objective: The learner will judge the level of eight fictional learning products by assigning each the highest defining capability it delivers, and will identify whether the vendor's claimed level is an overclaim, accurate, or an underclaim, correctly assigning at least seven of eight levels on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: the five levels and their defining capabilities, the rule that a product's level is the highest defining capability it actually delivers, vendor level claim, AI-powered marketing claim (all defined in the sections on the five levels and below).

Evidence of Mastery: For each of 8 products, the learner assigns a level from 1 to 5 and submits it. An assignment is correct when it equals the "Actual level" in Content. Mastery is 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Reading the level definitions is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) "AI-powered" means a high level. (2) An adaptive textbook must use a large language model. (3) A chat box added to a static book makes it autonomous.

Instructional Rationale: Judging a claim requires the learner to compare a described set of features with the level definitions. Including a no-AI adaptive product, an underclaim, and an overclaim based on "personalized" or "autonomous" wording makes the learner apply the definition, not the marketing language.

Content:

The level definitions, shown on request:

Level Defining capability 1 Fixed content; no response to the learner 2 Responds to the learner's actions; stores nothing about the learner 3 Adapts using a stored record of each student's goals and progress 4 Adds conversational tutoring about the material 5 Generates the textbook content itself for each student in real time

Eight fictional products:

# Product and description shown Vendor's claimed level Actual level Why (shown as feedback) 1 ClearPage Digital Edition: a PDF textbook with bookmarks, searchable text, and a hyperlinked glossary. Marketed as an "AI-powered interactive textbook." 2 1 Bookmarks, search, and links do not respond to what the learner does; the content is fixed. 2 SimBook Physics: a web textbook with 20 embedded simulations where students move sliders, and self-check quizzes with immediate feedback. Every student sees the same pages and nothing is saved. Marketed as "interactive." 2 2 It responds to actions and stores nothing about the learner. 3 PathFinder Biology: SimBook-style pages plus a concept map that recommends the next section from what the student clicks during the visit. No accounts and no records. Marketed as "personalized learning." 3 2 Recommending a path from a single visit's clicks is Level 2; nothing is stored about the student. 4 AdaptiveMath: student accounts store every answer, and software chooses the next problem using fixed rules based on the student's mastery record. No language model. Marketed as "AI-powered adaptive learning." 3 3 It adapts from a stored record, which is Level 3; no language model is needed. 5 TutorBook: AdaptiveMath's features plus a chat window where a language model answers questions about the lesson, drawing on the textbook, with a hints-first rule. Marketed as "Level 4." 4 4 It adds conversational tutoring on top of the adaptive record. 6 WriteAssist: TutorBook's features, and the chat can also write a new practice problem when asked. The sequence of lessons is still the authors' fixed chapters. Marketed as "fully autonomous." 5 4 The textbook itself is not generated for each student; extra practice problems do not make it Level 5. 7 InstantText: each night the system reads each student's record and writes the next day's lesson text, examples, and exercises for that student; teachers may review them. Marketed as "Level 5." 5 5 It generates the textbook content itself for each student. 8 FlashPro: a flashcard app with a fixed deck. It stores each user's responses and schedules the next card from them. Marketed as "interactive." 2 3 It adapts from a stored record, so it is Level 3 with the privacy duties that come with it.

Provenance: The level definitions follow the chapter section "The Five Levels at a Glance." The products are fictional, written for this chapter; the sim must label them "Fictional products."

Rules: Each product has exactly one actual level, given in Content. A product is scored on its first submitted level only. After the assignment is revealed, the sim states "Overclaim" when the claimed level is greater than the actual level, "Accurate" when equal, and "Underclaim" when less. The score counts first-attempt correct levels out of 8. Mastery is a score >= 7.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads one product description and the vendor's claimed level.
  2. The learner assigns a level from 1 to 5 and submits it. The sim marks it correct or incorrect and shows the feedback text and the overclaim, accurate, or underclaim label.
  3. If incorrect, the learner may assign again; the second attempt does not change the score. After the second attempt, the correct level and reason are shown.
  4. After all 8 products, the sim shows the score and a summary of how many claims were overclaims, accurate, and underclaims.
  5. The learner should notice that three of the eight claims overclaim, one underclaims, and one product with no AI model is classed at Level 3.

Feedback: 8 products, shuffled once per session, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: Level [n]. [Why text]." Incorrect: "Not quite. [Why text for the correct answer, without naming the level]." After the second attempt the correct level is revealed and the product counts as missed. A running score "First-try correct: n of 8" is shown. Final message for a score >= 7: "You can see past the marketing to the level." For a score < 7: "Review the five definitions and try again; the products will be reshuffled."

Starting State: Product 1 of the shuffled order is shown with its description and claimed level, the score "First-try correct: 0 of 8," and the prompt "What level is this product, really?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that a product's level is the highest defining capability it actually delivers to students in use. The chapter's table gives the same five definitions. Three claims overclaim (products 1, 3, 6), one underclaims (product 8), and four are accurate. The mastery bar is 7 of 8.

docs.title: Using the Levels to Evaluate Products and Claims
docs.text:
The levels become a working tool when you apply them to real products and real marketing. This section defines the terms used in that work.

Level classification is the act of assigning a product to one of the five levels according to the capabilities it actually delivers. Product level assessment is the fuller process a school follows to do so, and it has four steps: gather the product's documentation and a demonstration; test what the product does for students, not what the brochure says; identify the highest defining capability delivered; and record what student data it needs at that level. The checklist for a product level assessment asks:

  1. Does the product do anything but show fixed content? If not, it is Level 1.
  2. Does it respond to the learner's actions on the page? If so, it is at least Level 2.
  3. Does it keep a record of each student and change what it shows from that record? If so, it is at least Level 3.
  4. Can a student hold an open conversation with it about the material? If so, it is at least Level 4.
  5. Does it generate the textbook content itself, for each student, in real time? If so, it is Level 5.

Level terminology precision is the discipline of using the level names exactly as defined, so that a claim of "Level 3" means one thing wherever it is made. Precision protects buyers, and it matters because the common marketing words do not map to levels.

AI-powered marketing claims are product descriptions that use "AI-powered," "intelligent," "personalized," or "adaptive" without saying what the system does or what data it uses. They are common and uninformative. "AI-powered" can describe a PDF with a chat box, a simple adaptive scheduler with no AI model, or a fully generative system. Because the level depends on capability and not on whether an AI model is inside, "AI-powered" is neither necessary nor sufficient for any level.

A vendor level claim is a vendor's statement of the level of its own product. It is a self-report in the sense of Chapter 3: the vendor has an interest in the claim. The right response is not to reject it but to test it using the product level assessment, and to ask for a demonstration of each defining capability. The usual error is an overclaim, in which a vendor states a level above what the product delivers, and the sim above gave you practice spotting them. An underclaim, in which a product delivers more than it admits, matters too, because a vendor that does not realize it stores student records may also not be protecting them.

'AI-powered' is not a level

A common trap is accepting "AI-powered" or "personalized" as if it described capability. Instead, ask four things: what does it do for the student, using what data, stored where, and for how long? The answers place the product on the ladder and tell you what protections it needs.

docs.title: Worked Example: The Three Emails
docs.text:
Return to Ms. Okafor's three emails and apply the checklist after a demonstration of each.

Email says What the demo shows Highest capability delivered Level What to ask next "AI-powered interactive textbook" Web pages with simulations and quizzes; no logins Responds to actions; stores nothing 2 Are the simulations accurate and accessible? Who reviews them? "Adaptive, personalized learning platform" Student accounts; software picks the next problem from past answers; no chat Adapts from a stored record 3 What is stored, where, for how long, and has it been audited for bias? "Autonomous AI textbook" A chat box beside fixed chapters; the same chapter order for everyone Conversation about fixed content 4 How are hallucinations handled? Does it give hints or answers? Is the log reviewable?

None of the three is the highest-level claim the marketing suggested, and the third is two levels below its claim. The framework did not reject any of them. It told Ms. Okafor which questions to ask each one.

docs.title: Graduated Regulation and Level-Specific Policy
docs.text:
The SAE standard supported graduated regulation: rules that get stricter as a system takes on more responsibility. The same approach suits textbooks, because the risks change from level to level. A rule strict enough for Level 5 is wasteful at Level 1, and a rule written for Level 1 is dangerous at Level 5.

A level-specific policy is a school or district policy that sets different requirements for products at different levels. It is the practical result of the model. For example, a policy might say that any product at Level 3 or above must pass a privacy and data-governance review before use. This book recommends the following minimum safeguards. They are recommended practice, not legal requirements, and the real legal duties, such as FERPA and COPPA, are the subject of Chapter 10.

Safeguard First required at Reason Accessibility check of every page (screen reader, keyboard) Level 1 Every student must be able to use the product Independent accuracy check of simulations by a subject expert Level 2 Interactive models can mislead if they are wrong Review of how student records are stored, who sees them, and when they are deleted Level 3 The product now holds personal data Parent notice and consent process for collecting student learning data Level 3 Families have a right to know and to decide Bias audit of how the system chooses next steps for different groups Level 3 Adaptive choices can treat groups unequally Hint-first rules and logging for the chat tutor, reviewed weekly Level 4 Chat can give answers and can hallucinate Age limit and supervision rules for open-ended chat Level 4 Open conversation with minors needs boundaries Human review of AI-generated lessons before students see them Level 5 No author has checked the content in advance

Each safeguard keeps applying at higher levels, so a Level 4 product needs the Level 1, 2, and 3 safeguards as well.

docs.title: Diagram: Level-Specific Safeguard Matcher
docs.text:
Run the Level-Specific Safeguard Matcher MicroSim Fullscreen

Level-Specific Safeguard Matcher

Type: microsim sim-id: level-specific-safeguard-matcher Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: apply Learning Objective: The learner will apply the level-specific policy by choosing the lowest level at which each of eight safeguards should first be required, correctly matching at least seven of eight on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: the five levels, level-specific policy, graduated regulation (all defined in the chapter sections above).

Evidence of Mastery: For each of 8 safeguards, the learner chooses a level from 1 to 5 and submits it. A choice is correct when it equals the "First required at" level in Content. Mastery is 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Reading the level definitions is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) All safeguards should apply at every level from the start. (2) Privacy review is needed only for chatbots. (3) A product with no AI model needs no data governance.

Instructional Rationale: Applying a graduated policy means matching a risk to the capability that first creates it. Items such as the privacy review, which first applies to a product with no AI model, force the learner to link safeguards to capability, not to the amount of AI.

Content:

Eight safeguards:

# Safeguard shown to the learner First required at Why (shown as feedback) 1 Accessibility check of every page for screen readers and keyboard use 1 Every student must be able to use any textbook, whatever its level. 2 Independent accuracy check of the simulations by a subject expert 2 Interactive models first appear at Level 2 and can mislead if they are wrong. 3 Review of how student records are stored, who sees them, and when they are deleted 3 Level 3 is the first level that keeps records about individual students. 4 Parent notice and consent process for collecting student learning data 3 Collecting individual learning data begins at Level 3. 5 Bias audit of how the system chooses next steps for different groups of students 3 The system first makes individualized choices at Level 3. 6 Hint-first rules and weekly review of the chat tutor's logs 4 Open conversation first appears at Level 4. 7 Age limit and supervision rules for open-ended chat 4 Open conversation with minors first appears at Level 4. 8 Human review of AI-generated lessons before students see them 5 Content is first generated without an author's prior review at Level 5.

Provenance: The safeguards and levels follow the chapter section "Graduated Regulation and Level-Specific Policy" and are recommended practice written for this book, not legal requirements. The sim must say so.

Rules: Each safeguard has exactly one correct first-required level, given in Content. A safeguard is scored on its first submitted choice only. The score counts first-attempt correct choices out of 8. Mastery is a score >= 7. After each answer the sim states that the safeguard also applies to every higher level.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees one safeguard at a time and the five levels.
  2. The learner chooses the lowest level at which it should first be required and submits. The sim marks it and shows the feedback text.
  3. If incorrect, the learner may choose again; the second attempt does not change the score. After the second attempt, the correct level and reason are shown.
  4. After all 8, the sim shows the score and a stacked view of the safeguards required at each level.
  5. The learner should notice that three safeguards first apply at Level 3, more than at any other level, and that none depends on whether a product contains an AI model.

Feedback: 8 safeguards, shuffled once per session, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: Level [n]. [Why text]." Incorrect: "Not quite. [Why text for the correct answer, without naming the level]." After the second attempt the correct level is revealed and the item counts as missed. A running score "First-try correct: n of 8" is shown. Final message for a score >= 7: "You can match safeguards to levels." For a score < 7: "Review where each risk first appears and try again."

Starting State: Safeguard 1 of the shuffled order is shown with the five levels, the score "First-try correct: 0 of 8," and the prompt "At what level should this first be required?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's safeguard table lists the same eight safeguards at levels 1, 2, 3, 3, 3, 4, 4, and 5. The chapter states that each safeguard keeps applying at higher levels. The mastery bar is 7 of 8.

docs.title: Setting Realistic Expectations
docs.text:
The last idea borrowed from the SAE standard is realistic expectations: making clear what each level can and cannot do today, so that buyers neither expect too much nor dismiss what works. A Level 2 textbook is not a tutor, and a Level 4 chatbot is not a trained teacher. Equally, a school that dismisses Level 2 as "just web pages" misses the best value for money in the model.

A useful summary for a school leader is to match the level to the job. Level 2 is excellent for explaining ideas, practicing skills with feedback, and letting students explore simulations, at very low cost and with no privacy burden. Level 3 earns its added burden when a school needs to track mastery and personalize pacing at scale. Level 4 adds the most when a student is stuck and needs a patient conversation, provided guardrails are in place. Level 5 is a promising direction that should be watched, tested in small pilots, and independently evaluated before anyone relies on it.

Five levels, one question at a time

If five levels and thirty-odd terms feel like a lot, start with one habit: for any product, ask "what does it do, using what data?" You already used a simpler version of that question in Chapter 2 when you asked "compared with whom, chosen how?" Everything else in this chapter hangs off that one question.

docs.title: Back to the Three Emails
docs.text:
Ms. Okafor now has a plan. She replied to each vendor with the same four questions: what does your product do for the student, using what data, stored where, and for how long? She asked for a demonstration of each defining capability, and she told the vendors she would classify the product herself. The Level 2 vendor needed nothing further except an accessibility check. The Level 3 vendor was invited to a privacy review. The "autonomous" vendor, whose product turned out to be a Level 4 chat tutor, was asked about its hallucination controls and given a pilot, not a district contract.

The story shows both sides. The benefit is clear: the levels let a school buy the right thing, at the right price, with the right protections, and avoid paying a Level 4 price for a Level 1 product. The risk is that a framework can create false confidence: a level is a statement about capability, not quality, and a product can sit at any level and still be a poor one. The response is to treat the level as the first question and the independent evidence of Chapter 2 as the second.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• A textbook can be print, digital, or PDF; a PDF textbook is a print textbook on a screen, with fixed content for every reader.
  • An intelligent textbook uses software to respond, adapt, converse, or generate; it does not have to contain AI.
  • A classification framework creates a shared vocabulary; the SAE J3016 standard and its levels of driving automation gave cars a shared vocabulary, graduated regulation, and realistic expectations, and the textbook model borrows all three.
  • The five-level textbook model: Level 1 static, Level 2 interactive, Level 3 adaptive, Level 4 chatbot, Level 5 autonomous. A product's level is the highest defining capability it actually delivers.
  • Level 2 adds embedded simulations, self-check quizzes, learning graphs, and path recommendation, with nothing stored about the student; the intelligent textbook movement and the growth of Level 2 textbooks make it cheap and often free.
  • Level 3 adds progress tracking and student goal setting, and is the privacy inflection point because it keeps records about individuals.
  • Level 4 adds conversational tutoring through a chatbot; Level 5 adds real-time content generation and full personalization.
  • The level adoption timeline has Levels 3 to 5 on the horizon, with Level 5 plausible technically around three years out on the central trend but dependent on reliability and trust.
  • Apply the four steps of product level assessment; level terminology precision matters because AI-powered marketing claims say nothing about level, and a vendor level claim is a self-report to be tested.
  • Level-specific policy matches safeguards to the level where each risk first appears: accessibility at Level 1, simulation accuracy at Level 2, records and bias audits at Level 3, chat guardrails at Level 4, human review of generated lessons at Level 5.

You can place any product on the ladder

You just learned all five levels, the logic borrowed from self-driving cars, and the four-step assessment that sees through "AI-powered." That's the book's central tool, and everything from here builds on it. Chapter 7 asks what each level costs, and why Level 2 is heading toward free. One step at a time, together.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: The Five-Level Model of Intelligent Textbooks
docs.text: Test your understanding of the five-level model, the SAE ideas it borrows, and how to classify products and match safeguards to each level with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. Which level of the five-level model is defined by changing what each student sees based on a stored record of that student's goals and progress?
docs.text:
1. Level 2, interactive textbook
  2. Level 4, chatbot textbook
  3. Level 5, autonomous textbook
  4. Level 3, adaptive textbook
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. A Level 3 adaptive textbook keeps a record of what each student has done and mastered and uses it to choose what comes next. The defining step up from Level 2 is memory about an individual: a Level 2 textbook responds to actions on the page but stores nothing between visits. Level 4 adds conversation and Level 5 adds real-time content generation, but stored-record adaptation is what first appears at Level 3.

Concept Tested: Level 3 Adaptive Textbook

See: Level 3: Adaptive Textbooks

docs.title: 2. The book borrows three lasting effects of the SAE J3016 standard for self-driving cars. What are they?
docs.text:
1. Lower prices, faster adoption, and fewer accidents
  2. A shared vocabulary, graduated regulation, and realistic expectations
  3. Federal funding, vendor certification, and independent testing
  4. Full automation, liability insurance, and a single national rule
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. J3016 gave the auto industry a shared vocabulary for "self-driving" claims, supported graduated regulation in which rules get stricter as the system takes on more responsibility, and set realistic expectations by making clear that Level 5 remained a goal while Level 2 systems were on the road. The textbook model borrows all three. A single national rule for all levels is the opposite of graduated regulation.

Concept Tested: SAE J3016 Standard

See: The SAE Levels: A Model from Self-Driving Cars

docs.title: 3. Why does the chapter call Level 2 the sweet spot of the book's low-cost design?
docs.text:
1. It is the only level that uses a large language model to explain concepts
  2. It tracks each student's mastery without needing any student accounts
  3. It responds to learners' actions but stores nothing, so it has almost no privacy burden
  4. It is the level most commercial vendors already sell to large school districts
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. A Level 2 interactive textbook responds through embedded simulations, self-check quizzes, a learning graph, and path recommendations, but it does not need to know who the learner is and stores nothing between visits. That means essentially none of the privacy burden of higher levels, and ordinary web pages cost little to host and nothing to copy. Tracking mastery requires a stored record, which is Level 3, and Level 2 needs no language model.

Concept Tested: Level 2 Interactive Textbook

See: Level 2: Interactive Textbooks

docs.title: 4. A demo shows web pages with simulations and quizzes, plus a chat box that answers students' questions about the fixed chapters. Everyone gets the same chapter order, and no student records are kept. At what level should the principal classify it?
docs.text:
1. Level 4, because students can hold an open conversation about the material
  2. Level 2, because no student records are stored between visits
  3. Level 5, because the AI writes new answers in real time for each student
  4. Level 3, because the chat box adapts its replies to each question
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The checklist asks whether a student can hold an open conversation with the product about the material; if so, it is at least Level 4. Like the "autonomous" product in Ms. Okafor's emails, a chat box beside fixed chapters is a Level 4 chatbot textbook. Level 5 requires generating the textbook content itself for each student, not answering questions about prepared chapters. Responding to a question is not the stored-record adaptation that defines Level 3.

Concept Tested: Level Classification

See: Using the Levels to Evaluate Products and Claims

docs.title: 5. The chapter says Level 3 is the "privacy inflection point." What makes it parallel to Level 3 in the SAE car levels?
docs.text:
1. At both, the product first becomes affordable for most ordinary buyers
  2. At both, a human must supervise the system at every moment
  3. At both, the system stops working outside a defined area
  4. At both, the system takes on a new responsibility that changes the rules
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. For cars, Level 3 is where the system takes primary control, so liability questions arise. For textbooks, Level 3 is where the system begins to track individual learning, so privacy laws, governance duties, and bias checks come in. The chapter calls this the reason the framework is more than a metaphor: the level at which the system takes on a new kind of responsibility is the level at which the rules must change. Constant human supervision describes SAE Level 2.

Concept Tested: Five-Level Textbook Model

See: Worked Example: Mapping the Car Levels to Textbook Levels

docs.title: 6. A district's level-specific policy follows the chapter's recommended safeguards. A school wants to adopt a Level 4 chatbot textbook. Which safeguards apply?
docs.text:
1. Every safeguard from Levels 1 through 4, from accessibility to chat guardrails
  2. Only the Level 4 safeguards: hint-first rules, logging, and age limits for chat
  3. Only the privacy review and consent process, since chat products store records
  4. Only human review of AI-generated lessons, since chat output is generated by AI
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The chapter says each safeguard keeps applying at higher levels, so a Level 4 product needs the Level 1, 2, and 3 safeguards as well: accessibility checks, simulation accuracy checks, records review, parent consent, and a bias audit, plus hint-first rules, logging, and age limits for chat. Applying only the Level 4 rules is the tempting mistake. Human review of generated lessons is first required at Level 5, where the system writes the content itself.

Concept Tested: Level-Specific Policy

See: Graduated Regulation and Level-Specific Policy

docs.title: 7. How does full personalization at Level 5 differ from adaptation at Level 3?
docs.text:
1. Level 3 changes the content itself; Level 5 changes only the order of lessons
  2. Level 3 changes the order of prepared content; Level 5 changes the content itself
  3. Level 3 needs no student data; Level 5 needs only the student's reading level
  4. Level 3 requires a chatbot; Level 5 works without any language model at all
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. A Level 3 textbook selects and orders prepared content from a library based on a student's record. A Level 5 system generates explanations, examples, exercises, and simulations on the spot, adapting along every dimension at once: goals, prior knowledge, pace, interests, language, reading level, and accessibility needs. The first option reverses the two. Level 3 does require stored student data, and it needs no chatbot; adaptive math platforms using simple rules existed long before ChatGPT.

Concept Tested: Full Personalization

See: Level 5: Autonomous AI Textbooks

docs.title: 8. A board member argues that only products labeled "AI-powered" should be considered intelligent textbooks. Why does the chapter's framework reject this reasoning?
docs.text:
1. Because AI-powered products are banned from classrooms until they reach Level 5
  2. Because intelligent textbooks are defined by being printed with interactive features
  3. Because levels depend on capability delivered, and some need no AI model
  4. Because the label "AI-powered" applies only to Level 1 and Level 2 products
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. The level depends on what the product actually does for students, not on whether an AI model is inside, so "AI-powered" is neither necessary nor sufficient for any level. A Level 2 textbook can do its work with careful design and simple software, and a Level 3 platform can adapt with simple rules. Meanwhile "AI-powered" can describe a PDF with a chat box. The chapter treats such marketing claims as uninformative and tells buyers to ask what the product does, using what data.

Concept Tested: AI-Powered Marketing Claims

See: Using the Levels to Evaluate Products and Claims

docs.title: 9. According to the chapter, what determines a product's level?
docs.text:
1. The most advanced feature listed in the vendor's brochure or website
  2. The highest defining capability the product delivers to students in use
  3. The price per student, since higher levels cost more to build
  4. Whether the product contains a large language model or a simpler AI model
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The rule that makes classification workable is that a product's level is the highest defining capability it actually delivers to students in use, not the highest one in its brochure. A product level assessment tests what the product does in a demonstration. Brochure features are vendor self-reports to be tested, and price and the presence of an AI model do not set the level; the chapter warns that "AI-powered" is not a level.

Concept Tested: Product Level Assessment

See: The Five Levels at a Glance

docs.title: 10. A vendor describes its product as "just a simple Level 2 interactive book." During a demo, a teacher reloads a page and the product remembers which problems the student got wrong last week. What should the school conclude?
docs.text:
1. The product is Level 2 as claimed, since remembering errors is a navigation aid
  2. The product is Level 1, since it shows the same problems to every student
  3. The vendor has overclaimed, so the school should reject the product outright
  4. The product keeps student records, so it is Level 3 and needs a privacy review
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The chapter's reset test says that if a page remembers where you were or what you got wrong after a reload, it is keeping a record about you, which is Level 3. This is an underclaim, and the chapter notes it matters because a vendor that does not realize it stores student records may also not be protecting them. The product therefore needs the Level 3 safeguards, including a review of storage, access, and deletion. The vendor understated the level rather than overclaiming it.

Concept Tested: Vendor Level Claim

See: Using the Levels to Evaluate Products and Claims

docs.title: References: The Five-Level Model of Intelligent Textbooks
docs.text:
1. Textbook - Wikipedia - Covers the history, economics, and formats of textbooks, from print to digital and open textbooks. Background for the chapter's starting point, the print and PDF textbooks that sit at Level 1.

  2. Self-driving car - Wikipedia - Describes autonomous vehicles and the SAE J3016 levels of driving automation, from no automation to full automation. Shows the model the five-level textbook framework borrows its structure from.

  3. Intelligent tutoring system - Wikipedia - Explains computer tutors that model student knowledge and adapt instruction, with their history and research results. Context for the adaptive Level 3 and conversational Level 4 textbooks.

  4. Brave New Words: How AI Will Revolutionize Education (and Why That's a Good Thing) (2024) - Salman Khan - Viking - Khan describes the design of Khanmigo, a chatbot tutor that asks guiding questions instead of giving answers. His account illustrates conversational tutoring and the promise and limits of Level 4 textbooks.

  5. Building Intelligent Interactive Tutors: Student-Centered Strategies for Revolutionizing E-Learning (2009) - Beverly Park Woolf - Morgan Kaufmann - Woolf explains how tutors combine a student model, a domain model, and a teaching model to adapt instruction. Her framework clarifies what makes a Level 3 adaptive textbook different from Level 2.

  6. A Five-Level Classification Framework for Intelligent Textbooks: Lessons from Autonomous Vehicle Standards - Dan McCreary, EdArXiv - The December 2025 preprint that adapts SAE J3016 to define five textbook levels for procurement and level-specific policy. The primary source for this chapter's framework.

  7. The Five Levels of Intelligent Textbooks - Intelligent Textbooks site - A short web summary of each level, from static to autonomous, noting that Level 3 is where student data tracking begins. Useful as a quick reference when classifying a product.

  8. Khanmigo - Khan Academy - The product page for Khan Academy's AI tutor and teaching assistant, which guides students toward answers. A real-world Level 4 example readers can examine when practicing level classification.

  9. ASSISTments - ASSISTments - A free nonprofit math practice platform that gives students instant feedback and hints and gives teachers real-time reports. A concrete example for testing where an interactive or adaptive product falls on the five-level scale.

  10. OpenStax - Rice University - Free, openly licensed, peer-reviewed textbooks available online and as PDFs. A widely used example of digital textbooks at Levels 1 and 2, useful as a baseline when comparing products.

docs.title: Content Economics and Open Educational Resources
Summary
docs.text: This chapter covers the economics behind falling content-creation costs: open educational resources, open licenses, the OpenBook QR Score, content commoditization, and how publisher business models are changing as AI makes level 1 and level 2 content cheap to produce. Readers finish able to use the OpenBook QR Score to compare two open textbooks and explain why AI is commoditizing basic textbook content.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: The Building Blocks of Schools, Students, and Learning
  • Chapter 4: Measuring AI Capability: The METR Task-Horizon Studies
  • Chapter 5: Projecting AI Growth: Doubling Curves, Limits, and Uncertainty
  • Chapter 6: The Five-Level Model of Intelligent Textbooks

docs.title: "What Will It Cost Per Student?"
docs.text:
At the district's budget meeting, the finance director, Mr. Patel, asks the question every board member eventually asks: "Fine, it's a good idea. What will it cost per student, per year, all in?" Behind him sits a binder with a $900,000 proposal from a publisher for a district-wide digital math program, and beside it a librarian's printout of a free open textbook that covers the same grades.

The two items on the table are not obviously comparable. One is a product with a price. The other is free, and nobody can say what "free" leaves out. To answer Mr. Patel, a school leader needs to understand three things: why content that once cost a publisher a great deal to produce is becoming cheap, what makes a free textbook good and reusable, and where the money goes at each of the five levels of Chapter 6.

The answer is more surprising than "it's all free." Content is becoming nearly free, but devices, teacher training, and data protection are not, and the biggest costs in a digital classroom are often the ones that never appear on a software invoice.

Follow the money, not the hype

This chapter lets you answer a finance director with numbers: what content costs to make, what a free textbook really offers, and what each level of textbook costs per student. You'll also learn to score a free textbook for quality and reusability in a few minutes. Let's find the balance between the savings that are real and the costs that hide.

docs.title: Why Textbook Content Costs What It Does
docs.text:
A textbook publisher is a company that commissions, edits, produces, markets, and distributes textbooks and related materials. The large publishers serving U.S. schools and colleges, such as Pearson, McGraw Hill, Cengage, and Houghton Mifflin Harcourt, grew over many decades by solving a hard problem: assembling expert authors, editors, designers, reviewers, and a sales force to put a reliable book in every classroom.

Content creation cost is the total cost of producing a textbook's content before a single copy is sold: author and subject-expert time, editing, fact-checking and review, design and illustration, simulations and assessments, accessibility work, and production. For a traditional textbook this cost is large and mostly up-front, which is why publishers needed to sell many copies at a high price to recover it. After the book is finished, producing one more copy costs almost nothing in digital form, so the economics are those of fixed cost: the first copy is expensive, and every later copy is nearly free.

A publisher business model is the way a publisher earns money from that content. The classic model is to sell a new edition every few years at a high price, rely on the fact that the person who chooses the book (a professor or a district) is not the person who pays (a student or a taxpayer), and sell updated editions so that used copies lose value. Later models added digital subscriptions, bundled "inclusive access" fees charged with tuition, and adaptive homework platforms sold alongside the book.

Textbook price is what the buyer pays. The College Board estimates that the average undergraduate's annual budget for books and supplies is about $1,300, a figure that has made textbook cost a long-running political issue in higher education. In K-12, districts pay, usually through adoption cycles of five to seven years, and the cost is part of the per-pupil spending of Chapter 1.

docs.title: Worked Example: Anatomy of a Textbook's Cost
docs.text:
The table gives an illustrative breakdown for one chapter of a traditional textbook with its simulations and assessments, using round numbers chosen to show where the effort goes. The hours and hourly cost are assumptions, not industry data.

Task Hours of skilled work per chapter Cost at $50 per hour Drafting the text 30 $1,500 Designing and building the simulations 25 $1,250 Writing practice questions and assessments 10 $500 Expert review and fact-checking 8 $400 Editing, accessibility, and production 7 $350 Total 80 $4,000

For a 20-chapter book the content cost in this illustration is about $80,000, before marketing and sales. Notice that the largest items, drafting and building simulations, are exactly the tasks that AI is getting better at, which leads to the next section.

docs.title: Worked Example: Why Publishers Revise Every Few Years
docs.text:
The classic business model depends on a sales pattern. A new edition sells to a wave of buyers, then a used market forms, and sales fall each year until the next edition resets them. Suppose a college textbook priced at $150 sells the following numbers of new copies over a four-year edition. The figures are illustrative.

Year of the edition New copies sold Revenue 1 10,000 $1,500,000 2 6,000 $900,000 3 3,500 $525,000 4 2,000 $300,000 Total 21,500 $3,225,000

Sales fall by 80 percent from year 1 to year 4, which is why a publisher releases a new edition even when the subject has not changed: the revision restarts the curve. Now suppose a quarter of the adopting instructors switch to a free open textbook of comparable quality. Revenue drops to 75 percent of the total, or $2,418,750, a loss of $806,250 per edition, and the publisher cannot cut its fixed costs of authors, editors, and sales staff by the same fraction. A business built on high price and a four-year cycle is under pressure from content that costs nothing to copy and can be revised weekly, which is the content commoditization of the next sections.

docs.title: Worked Example: The Person Who Chooses Is Not the Person Who Pays
docs.text:
Textbook price has been hard to discipline because the usual purchasing roles are split.

College K-12 Who chooses the book The instructor A district committee, usually for several years Who pays The student Taxpayers, through the district What the chooser sees Quality and convenience Quality, alignment to standards, and the sales presentation What limits the price The used and rental market The district budget and procurement rules Why this favors high prices The chooser does not feel the cost A multi-year adoption locks in the choice

An instructor who assigns a $150 book bears none of its cost. Open textbooks change the incentive by removing the price from the decision, and a district that applies the scorecard of Chapter 20 puts the price back in front of the chooser.

docs.title: AI and Falling Production Costs
docs.text:
AI-generated content is text, images, simulations, quizzes, and other learning materials produced mainly by an AI system, typically a large language model (Chapter 4), from a prompt or an outline, and then reviewed and edited by a person. The people review it because of the hallucination problem of Chapter 5.

Falling production cost is the decline in the cost of producing content as AI takes over parts of the work. It follows from the two trends of earlier chapters: the task horizon is growing, so AI can complete longer jobs such as a whole chapter, and the price per token is falling, so each job costs less to run. The human role shifts from writing every sentence to specifying, reviewing, and correcting.

docs.title: Worked Example: The Same Chapter, AI-Assisted
docs.text:
Take the 80-hour chapter above and suppose AI generates the first draft of the text, the practice questions, and the first version of each simulation, while a skilled person specifies, reviews, tests, and fixes.

Task Hours of skilled work, AI-assisted Cost at $50 per hour Specifying the chapter and prompts 3 $150 Reviewing and editing the draft 6 $300 Testing and fixing the simulations 5 $250 Expert review and fact-checking 5 $250 Accessibility check and production 3 $150 Total skilled work 22 $1,100 AI computing for generation n/a about $20

The illustrative cost falls from about $4,000 to about $1,120 per chapter, a fall of about 72 percent, and for a 20-chapter book from about $80,000 to about $22,400. Two cautions apply. First, the saving depends on the review step: skipping it moves the cost into errors that students learn. Second, the assumptions are illustrative, and an author who measures their own hours will find different values.

docs.title: Worked Example: How Much Review Is Enough?
docs.text:
AI-generated content can carry errors, and review catches some of them. The more a reviewer does, the fewer errors remain and the more it costs. Suppose an AI draft of one chapter contains 6 errors on average (an assumed figure), and consider four ways to produce the chapter, with the costs of the Chapter 7 illustration.

Approach Review Errors caught (assumed) Errors left Cost per chapter AI draft, no review None 0% 6.0 about $20 AI draft, spot check 2 hours 40% 3.6 about $120 AI draft, expert review and fact-checking 11 hours 90% 0.6 about $570 Written by hand, then edited 80 hours 95% of a smaller base about 0.2 about $4,000

The first row is cheapest and leaves ten times as many errors as the third. The jump from spot check to expert review costs about $450 and removes three errors, or about $150 per error avoided. For content that students will rely on, that is a reasonable price. The table also shows a property of the whole economics: the AI draft cost is tiny, and what matters is how much human judgment you buy afterward. The figures are assumptions, and a school can measure its own: count the errors an expert finds in a sample of AI drafts.

docs.title: Worked Example: The Floor Under Falling Costs
docs.text:
Falling AI prices make generation nearly free. They do not make a chapter free, because human review dominates the cost. Suppose generation costs $20 per chapter today and its price falls nineteen-fold a year, as in Chapter 4, while review stays at $1,100.

Year Generation cost Review cost Total per chapter 0 $20.00 $1,100 $1,120 1 $1.05 $1,100 $1,101 2 $0.06 $1,100 $1,100

A thousandfold fall in the AI cost lowers the total by under 2 percent. The cost floor is human time. The real prospect for further savings is better tools that cut review hours: halving the 22 hours of skilled work in the earlier example to 11 would bring the chapter to about $550. This is why the book's cost claims rest on review practices as well as on AI prices.

Cheap to write is not cheap to trust

A common trap is counting the generation cost and forgetting the review cost. A draft that costs $20 to produce can still cost students dearly if no one checks it. Always budget reviewer time, and treat AI-generated content as a draft until a subject expert has read it.

AI-generated content also raises a rights question. In the United States, courts and the Copyright Office have so far held that a work produced entirely by an AI system, without human authorship, is not eligible for copyright. Human choices in selecting, arranging, and editing can be protected. For open resources the point cuts both ways: material no one owns is easy to share, but a school cannot assume it can license purely AI-generated material, and it should check the terms of the AI tool that produced it.

docs.title: Open Educational Resources
docs.text:
An open educational resource (OER) is a teaching, learning, or research material, in any medium, that is in the public domain or released under an open license that allows others to access, use, adapt, and share it at no cost or with minimal restrictions. The idea was formalized at a 2002 UNESCO forum and endorsed in UNESCO's 2012 Paris Declaration and 2019 Recommendation on OER. Well-known examples include OpenStax, which Rice University launched in 2012 to publish free peer-reviewed college textbooks; the CK-12 Foundation, which offers free K-12 materials; and K-12 curricula such as Illustrative Mathematics.

The word open is the one that matters. A free textbook is one that students can use at no cost. Free is a statement about price, and open is a statement about permissions. A free PDF that you may read but not edit, translate, or share is free and not open. An open textbook is free and carries a license that grants permissions, so teachers can fix errors and adapt it to their own students. Many open textbooks are also free, and this chapter uses "free open textbook" for the combination.

An open license is a copyright license by which the owner grants the public advance permission to use a work in specified ways, so that no one needs to ask. The most widely used family is the Creative Commons licenses.

A Creative Commons license is one of a set of standard open licenses, published by the nonprofit Creative Commons, that combine four elements: BY (attribution: give credit), SA (share-alike: share adaptations under the same terms), NC (non-commercial: no commercial use), and ND (no derivatives: share only unchanged copies). The six main licenses are:

License Elements What it allows CC BY Attribution Almost anything, if you credit the author CC BY-SA Attribution, share-alike Adaptations allowed if shared under the same license CC BY-NC Attribution, non-commercial Adaptations allowed for non-commercial use only CC BY-NC-SA Attribution, non-commercial, share-alike Non-commercial adaptations under the same license CC BY-ND Attribution, no derivatives Sharing unchanged copies only CC BY-NC-ND Attribution, non-commercial, no derivatives The most restrictive: unchanged, non-commercial sharing only

The book you are reading uses CC BY-NC-SA, which is why it carries the non-commercial label in its footer.

docs.title: The 5R Permissions
docs.text:
The 5R permissions, described by the education researcher David Wiley, are the five things an open license lets you do. They are the working test of whether something is truly open:

  1. Retain: make, own, and control copies of the work, such as downloading and archiving it.
  2. Reuse: use the work in its original form in many settings, such as a class or a website.
  3. Revise: adapt, edit, translate, or reformat the work.
  4. Remix: combine the work with other materials to create something new.
  5. Redistribute: share copies of the original or your changed version with others.

The licenses in the table grant the 5Rs to different degrees. CC BY grants all five. A no-derivatives license withholds revise and remix. A non-commercial license limits what a school may do if it also sells a course. A school choosing a textbook should check which of the five it needs, and the sim below, reused from the companion book OER Evaluator, practices matching classroom actions to permissions.

docs.text:
The six Creative Commons licenses grant the 5R permissions to different degrees. The table shows what each allows. NC means non-commercial and SA means share-alike.

License Retain Reuse Revise Remix Redistribute Conditions CC BY Yes Yes Yes Yes Yes Credit the author CC BY-SA Yes Yes Yes Yes Yes Credit; share adaptations under the same license CC BY-NC Yes Yes Yes Yes Yes, non-commercially Credit; no commercial use CC BY-NC-SA Yes Yes Yes Yes Yes, non-commercially Credit; no commercial use; same license CC BY-ND Yes Yes No No Unchanged copies only Credit CC BY-NC-ND Yes Yes No No Unchanged, non-commercial Credit; no commercial use

A free textbook, as defined earlier, is about price, and an open one is about this table. Three cases show the difference.

The textbook Free to read? Open? Why A PDF posted free on a publisher's site, "all rights reserved" Yes No You may read it, but not edit, translate, or share it An OpenStax textbook under CC BY Yes Yes All five permissions with credit A textbook under CC BY-ND Yes Partly You can share it unchanged, but cannot adapt it

docs.title: Worked Example: Can We Combine These?
docs.text:
A district wants to build one course from several open sources. Combining works is called remixing, and the licenses must be compatible. The following reflects the general rules; the Creative Commons compatibility chart and the district's counsel settle real cases.

Combination Allowed? The result must be licensed as CC BY with CC BY Yes CC BY or any license that keeps credit CC BY with CC BY-SA Yes CC BY-SA CC BY with CC BY-NC Yes CC BY-NC, so it may not be sold CC BY-SA with CC BY-NC-SA No, in general Each requires adaptations to carry its own license, which cannot both be satisfied CC BY-ND with anything Not as an adaptation The no-derivatives work cannot be changed or merged

A district that plans to sell a course, or that wants its own teachers to adapt freely, should prefer CC BY and CC BY-SA sources and avoid NC and ND ones. The book you are reading uses CC BY-NC-SA, which is a good choice for its author's goals and a limit on certain reuses, and the example shows why the choice of license is itself a design decision.

License check in thirty seconds

Before a school adapts an open textbook, find the license in the footer and ask one question: "Will we need to edit it, combine it, or hand out our version?" If the answer is yes, a BY or BY-SA license is safest. NC and ND can block exactly the things teachers most want to do.

docs.title: The OpenBook QR Score: Judging an Open Textbook
docs.text:
A free textbook is only useful if it is good and if others can reuse it. Textbook quality is the degree to which a textbook helps learners learn: whether it is accurate, aligned with the learning outcomes it claims, readable, accessible to all students, and gives learners practice with feedback. Quality is a matter of judgment, which is why different reviewers using different checklists reach different conclusions. A repeatable method was needed.

The OpenBook QR Score, developed in the author's companion book OER Evaluator, is that method. It scores a resource on ten metrics worth ten points each, for a total from 0 to 100. Five metrics measure quality and five measure reusability, and the score is reported with both halves, as in "QR 65 (Q 32 / R 33)." The letters stand for Quality and Reusability.

Quality (up to 50 points) Reusability (up to 50 points) Accuracy and currency Open license Alignment to learning outcomes Modularity Readability Metadata Accessibility Editable source Practice with feedback Portability

The quality subscore is the sum of the five quality metrics, from 0 to 50, and shows how well the resource helps learners learn. (The OER Evaluator calls it the quality subtotal.) The reusability subscore is the sum of the five reusability metrics, from 0 to 50, and shows how easily others can find, change, and reuse the resource. The five reusability metrics in plain terms: an open license clearly grants permissions; modularity means the parts can be lifted out and used alone; metadata is structured descriptive information that lets people and software find the resource; an editable source means the original files, not just a finished copy, are available; and portability means the content works across devices and platforms.

The total places a resource in a band: Excellent (90 to 100), Good (75 to 89), Fair (50 to 74), Weak (25 to 49), and Poor (0 to 24). A band is a quick label and not an adoption decision, and a bare total can hide a weak half, which is why the score is always reported with both subscores.

docs.title: Worked Example: Comparing Two Open Textbooks
docs.text:
A school is choosing between two free open algebra textbooks. A reviewer scores each on the ten metrics. These scores are illustrative.

Metric Open Algebra FreeMath Complete Accuracy and currency 9 6 Alignment to learning outcomes 8 6 Readability 8 7 Accessibility 7 5 Practice with feedback 8 6 Quality subscore (Q) 40 30 Open license 6 9 Modularity 6 8 Metadata 5 7 Editable source 7 7 Portability 8 7 Reusability subscore (R) 32 38 Total 72 68 OpenBook QR Score QR 72 (Q 40 / R 32) QR 68 (Q 30 / R 38)

Both books fall in the Fair band, and the totals differ by only four points. The halves tell the story: Open Algebra is the better book to hand students tomorrow, while FreeMath Complete is the better raw material for a district that wants to adapt, combine, and republish. Neither total alone would reveal that. The sim below, reused from the same companion book, lets you practice the calculation from metric scores to subscores, total, and band.

Reused from the author's companion book OER Evaluator, whose index marks it as built. Its terms "subtotal" and "adoption decision" correspond to this chapter's "subscore" and to the choice of whether to adopt.

Read the two halves, not just the total

Notice how two books with nearly the same total can be good for different jobs. A single number hides which half is weak, which is why a careful buyer always asks for Q and R separately. This is the same lesson as the effect-size habit of Chapter 2: the headline number is where you start asking questions.

docs.title: Reading Q and R Together
docs.text:
The two subscores do different jobs, and plotting each resource on a grid of Q against R makes the decision visible. Splitting each axis at its midpoint of 25 (an illustrative threshold) gives four regions.

Region Q R What it means A sensible use High quality, high reuse At least 25 At least 25 Good for students and easy to adapt Adopt, and contribute improvements High quality, low reuse At least 25 Under 25 Good, but hard to change or find Use as is; ask the author for open source files Low quality, high reuse Under 25 At least 25 Weak, but easy to rework Raw material: improve it Low quality, low reuse Under 25 Under 25 Weak and hard to change Skip it

The sim below, from the companion book OER Evaluator, lets you place resource profiles in the four regions.
