Jeannette Wing's 2006 essay popularized the term and argued that it is a basic skill for everyone, and not only for programmers.

docs.title: Worked Example: Computational Thinking in Maya's Textbook
docs.text: The ready-concepts rule of Chapters 8 and 9 is computational thinking in action. The problem, "what should Maya study next?", is decomposed into one question per concept: is it mastered, and are its prerequisites mastered? The pattern is that every concept is checked the same way. The abstraction ignores everything about a concept except its name, its status, and its prerequisites. The algorithm is the rule itself: for each unmastered concept, mark it ready if all its direct prerequisites are mastered. A student who can run, and then write, a rule like this has learned something that applies to scheduling a tournament, sorting a list, or planning a project.

docs.title: Worked Example: Taking a Claim Apart
docs.text:
Critical thinking is a habit of taking a claim apart. Apply it to a sentence from a brochure: "Students who use our tutor score 20 percent higher, so our tutor works."

Part Text Question to ask Premise Students who use the tutor score 20 percent higher Higher than whom? On what test? By how many points? Hidden assumption The tutor caused the higher scores Did motivated students choose the tutor? Did they start higher? Conclusion The tutor works Does a difference between two groups show a cause? Evidence needed Random assignment or a matched comparison with baselines Is there a randomized or independent study?

The argument moves from a correlation to a cause. A student who can write this table has practiced evidence evaluation and argument analysis on a real example, and it is the same table Chapter 2 used to read the MathPath brochure.

docs.title: Worked Example: Debugging an Algorithm
docs.text:
Computational thinking includes testing a rule on an example and fixing it when it fails. Here is a first version of the ready-concepts rule, written in plain steps: "For each concept, if all its prerequisites are mastered, it is ready." Test it on a small graph: concept A has no prerequisites, concept B depends on A, and the student has mastered A.

Step What the rule does Result Check A A has no prerequisites, so all of them (none) are mastered A is "ready" Check B B's prerequisite A is mastered B is "ready" Output A and B A is wrong: the student already mastered it

The test exposed a bug: the rule never asks whether the concept is already mastered. The fix adds a condition: "if it is not yet mastered and all its prerequisites are mastered, it is ready." Running the same example gives only B, which is right. This is the habit of Chapter 12's algorithmic thinking: write the steps, run them on a small case, look for a surprising answer, and repair the rule. It is also the reason a transparent rule is easier to trust than an opaque model: you can run it on a small case yourself.

Thinking skills are learned by practice

If critical and computational thinking sound like talents you either have or don't, they're not; they're habits built by doing. You already practiced both in this chapter, laying out an argument and running a rule. Try one on a real brochure this week.

docs.title: Practice: Reading a Tutor's Reply
docs.text: The sim below ties the thread of this chapter together. It asks you to read an AI tutor's reply and say how much of the solution it gives away, using the hint ladder from Chapter 2, because that is the property that decided help from harm in the Turkish study. The hint ladder had four levels after the student works alone: Level 1 asks what the problem is asking; Level 2 narrows the plan; Level 3 gives the step; Level 4 gives the answer.

docs.title: Diagram: Tutor Reply Hint Levels
docs.text:
Run the Tutor Reply Hint Levels MicroSim Fullscreen

Tutor Reply Hint Levels

Type: microsim sim-id: tutor-reply-hint-levels Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: classify Learning Objective: The learner will classify eight AI tutor replies to the same question by hint level (1 to 4), correctly placing at least seven of eight on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: productive struggle, the four-level hint ladder, cognitive offloading, AI tutor (all defined in Chapter 2 and in the sections of this chapter above).

Evidence of Mastery: The learner assigns each of 8 tutor replies a hint level from 1 to 4 and submits it. An assignment is correct when it equals the "Correct level" column in Content. Mastery is 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Reading the level definitions is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A reply that is polite and detailed is a good hint. (2) A long explanation is a Level 1 hint. (3) A hint that shows a worked example of the same problem is not giving the answer.

Instructional Rationale: Classifying replies by how much they reveal trains the learner to see the design property that separated help from harm in the Turkish study. Replies written in friendly language but revealing the answer test whether the learner looks at content, not tone.

Content:

The four levels, shown on request:

Level What the reply does 1 Asks what the problem is asking, without giving any part of the method 2 Narrows the plan, such as naming which quantities to use or which operation type 3 Gives the specific step to carry out, leaving the final computation 4 States the final answer or does the whole solution

The student's question for every reply: "A 6-pack of juice costs $4.50. What is the price per bottle?"

Eight replies:

# Tutor reply shown Correct level Why (shown as feedback) 1 "Let's start by looking at the problem. What is it asking you to find?" 1 It asks a question and reveals nothing about the method. 2 "Which number is the total cost, and which is the number of bottles?" 2 It narrows the plan by pointing at the two quantities. 3 "You want the cost for one bottle, so think about splitting the total into equal parts." 2 It names the idea of splitting, which narrows the plan without giving the step. 4 "Divide the total price by the number of bottles." 3 It gives the specific step and leaves only the computation. 5 "Great question! The price per bottle is $0.75." 4 It states the final answer. 6 "Take $4.50 and divide it by 6, which gives 0.75, so each bottle costs $0.75." 4 It does the whole computation and states the result. 7 "What operation do you use when you share an amount equally among several things?" 2 It narrows the plan by pointing to the kind of operation. 8 "Here is a similar problem solved step by step: 8 pencils cost $2.00, so $2.00 divided by 8 is $0.25 each. Now try yours." 3 A worked example of a similar problem shows the step, leaving the student to carry it out.

Provenance: The four levels follow the hint ladder in Chapter 2. The replies are illustrative, written for this chapter.

Rules: Each reply has exactly one correct level, given in Content. A reply is scored on its first submitted level only. The score counts first-attempt correct levels out of 8. Mastery is a score >= 7. After each answer the sim states whether the reply is suitable as a first response: levels 1 and 2 are, levels 3 and 4 are not.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees the student's question and one tutor reply at a time, with the four levels.
  2. The learner assigns a level and submits it. The sim marks it correct or incorrect and shows the feedback text and whether the reply suits a first response.
  3. If incorrect, the learner may assign again; the second attempt does not change the score. After the second attempt, the correct level and reason are shown.
  4. After all 8 replies, the sim shows the score.
  5. The learner should notice that replies 5 and 6 sound very different yet are both Level 4, and that reply 3 is Level 2 despite not naming the operation.

Feedback: 8 replies, shuffled once per session, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: Level [n]. [Why text]." Incorrect: "Not quite. [Why text for the correct answer, without naming the level]." After the second attempt the correct level is revealed and the reply counts as missed. A running score "First-try correct: n of 8" is shown. Final message for a score >= 7: "You can see how much a reply gives away." For a score < 7: "Review the four levels and try again; the replies will be reshuffled."

Starting State: The student's question and reply 1 of the shuffled order are shown, with the score "First-try correct: 0 of 8," and the prompt "How much of the solution does this reply give away?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's four-level hint ladder and the juice problem (6 bottles for $4.50, $0.75 each) match Chapter 2. The mastery bar is 7 of 8.

docs.title: Answering Mr. Dang
docs.text:
Mr. Dang asked for proof. The honest answer has three layers. What is solid: mastery learning and adaptive practice improve achievement, with effects of about half a standard deviation or less in real settings; one-on-one tutoring is among the most effective interventions known; and a well-designed AI tutor, giving hints instead of answers, can teach well in careful studies. What is not yet shown: that two hours of software can replace a traditional academic morning for most students at scale; the one school with a long track record reports its own results, and an online version has produced early results below the state average. What decides the difference: design, with hint-first tutors, mastery checks, human adults in the room, and the rest of the day spent with other people.

The story has both sides. The benefit: a morning that fills each student's gaps and could free around 300 hours a year, many weeks of school time. The risks: a compression that does not deliver and shortchanges students, tutors that give answers and erode learning, and screen time that grows. The response: pilot the compression, measure it independently, keep a person in the loop, and keep the morning short and the afternoon social. The next chapters supply the rest: guardrails in Chapter 12, and the afternoon in Chapters 13 and 14.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Adaptive learning adjusts content to each student's data; mastery learning fixes achievement and lets time vary, with effects of about half a standard deviation in pooled studies. Fixed mastery saved only about eight percent of total hours in our example, so mastery alone does not compress the day.
  • Personalized pacing and gap filling address the one-pace problem: in a class of 28, a single lesson reaches 13.
  • One-on-one tutoring is highly effective; Bloom's two-sigma problem (two standard deviations in small studies) is the upper end, pooled randomized trials average about 0.37, and cost keeps human tutoring out of reach for most students.
  • An AI tutor can approach tutoring at the cost of software, but design decides the outcome: in the Turkish study, answer-giving harmed later exams by about 17 percent and hint-first removed most of the harm.
  • Cognitive offloading is fine for the routine and harmful for the target skill; offload the routine and keep the target.
  • The compressed academic morning and reduced direct instruction could free freed-up school time: in our illustration 100 minutes a day, 300 hours a year, but it requires learning about 1.67 times as much per minute, which the evidence has not yet shown.
  • Critical thinking, including evidence evaluation and argument analysis, and computational thinking, are what the freed time is for, and AI can teach them while students still need to practice them with other people.
  • The strongest evidence supports well-designed AI tutoring; the evidence for the full compressed-morning package is self-reported or early, so pilot it and measure it independently.

You can weigh the case for a shorter morning

You just weighed the evidence on mastery learning, tutoring, and AI tutors, and worked out how many hours a compressed morning could free and what it must deliver. Chapter 12 turns to the guardrails that keep an AI tutor helping. One step at a time, together.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: Mastery Learning and the Case for a Compressed Morning
docs.text: Test your understanding of mastery learning, tutoring evidence, AI tutors, cognitive offloading, and what a compressed academic morning would require with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. What is the defining principle of mastery learning?
docs.text:
1. Students move on when the class calendar says the unit is finished
  2. Students are grouped by age so the whole class reaches mastery together
  3. Students earn credit for each course by attending a fixed number of hours
  4. Achievement is held fixed and time is allowed to vary from student to student
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. In mastery learning, students must demonstrate mastery of a concept, typically 80 to 90 percent on a check, before moving on, and they get extra time and different instruction when they do not. Building on John Carroll's model, Bloom's approach fixes achievement and lets time vary, the reverse of the seat-time model. The other three options describe features of fixed-time, industrial-era schooling, where time is fixed and achievement varies.

Concept Tested: Mastery Learning

See: Adaptive Learning and Mastery Learning

docs.title: 2. Bloom reported that one-on-one tutoring with mastery learning produced about two standard deviations of improvement. What did a 2020 review of randomized tutoring trials in real schools find?
docs.text:
1. A much smaller average effect, about 0.37 standard deviations
  2. An average effect of about two standard deviations, confirming Bloom
  3. No measurable effect from tutoring in real school settings
  4. An average effect of about four standard deviations for online tutors
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The review by Nickow, Oreopoulos, and Quan found an average effect of about 0.37 standard deviations, and a later published version reported about 0.29. Bloom's studies were small, short, and tested the material taught, so two sigma is the upper end of what careful small studies have seen. The chapter still calls tutoring among the most effective interventions known, so "no measurable effect" is wrong, and it suggests planning for a third to three-quarters of a standard deviation.

Concept Tested: Bloom's Two-Sigma Problem

See: Bloom's Two-Sigma Problem and Tutoring

docs.title: 3. In the Turkish high school study, students with open GPT-4 access did better on practice but about 17 percent worse on later exams, while a hint-giving version removed most of the harm. What lesson does the chapter draw?
docs.text:
1. AI tutors should be banned from high school math classes
  2. More powerful models produce better long-term learning
  3. How the AI is designed matters more than how powerful it is
  4. Practice scores are the best measure of what students learned
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. The study used the same model in both conditions; the difference between harm and help was whether it gave answers or hints. The chapter calls this the book's thesis in miniature. A ban ignores the hint-first version that worked, and model power was held constant. The gap between strong practice scores and weak exam scores shows practice scores can mislead, echoing Chapter 1's warning that performance is not the same as learning.

Concept Tested: AI Tutor

See: AI Tutors

docs.title: 4. A school's traditional academic periods total 240 minutes a day. A redesigned compressed morning takes 160 minutes. Over a 180-day year, how much time is freed?
docs.text:
1. About 80 hours
  2. About 240 hours
  3. About 480 hours
  4. About 720 hours
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The compressed morning frees 240 - 160 = 80 minutes a day. Over 180 days that is 80 x 180 = 14,400 minutes, or 240 hours. The 80-hour answer confuses minutes per day with hours per year, and the 480-hour answer counts the freed time twice. The chapter adds a caution: freeing this time requires students to learn about 1.5 times as much per minute in the shorter morning, which the evidence has not yet shown.

Concept Tested: Freed-Up School Time

See: Worked Example: How Much Time Is Freed?

docs.title: 5. In the chapter's fixed-mastery example, every student reached the goal, but total hours fell only about eight percent. What does the chapter conclude a compressed morning needs beyond mastery learning?
docs.text:
1. Longer school days, so that slower students have enough time to finish
  2. Larger classes, so that each teacher can serve more students at once
  3. More summative tests, so that progress can be reported to the state
  4. Less time on whole-class explanation and waiting, not just mastery checks
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Mastery learning is mainly a way of getting everyone to the goal, not of making the course much shorter. The case for compression needs the time students spend on explanation and waiting to shrink: reduced direct instruction, with short student-paced explanations and the teacher as coach, plus removal of idle time, transitions, and work on material students already know. Longer days work against the goal of freeing time, and the chapter does not propose larger classes or more summative tests.

Concept Tested: Reduced Direct Instruction

See: The Compressed Academic Morning

docs.title: 6. An adaptive session starts at level 3. Two correct answers in a row at the same level move the student up one level; one wrong answer moves the student down one. A student answers: correct, correct, correct, wrong, correct. At what level is the sixth question?
docs.text:
1. Level 2
  2. Level 3
  3. Level 4
  4. Level 5
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The first two correct answers at level 3 move the student to level 4. The third answer, correct at level 4, is one in a row, so the student stays at 4. The fourth answer is wrong, so the student drops to level 3. The fifth answer, correct at level 3, is again one in a row, so the student stays at level 3 for the sixth question. The rule uses no language model, only a counter, and the sequence of levels is itself data.

Concept Tested: Adaptive Learning

See: Worked Example: An Adaptive Session, Item by Item

docs.title: 7. A teacher is learning to write paragraph arguments with her class. Which use of AI offloads the routine and keeps the target skill?
docs.text:
1. Having AI point out unclear sentences in each student's own draft
  2. Having AI draft each paragraph for students to revise
  3. Asking AI to write a model answer that students copy into their notes
  4. Asking AI to summarize the argument so students skip the reading
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The chapter's working rule is to offload the routine and keep the target. When the target skill is writing an argument, AI drafting the paragraph or providing an answer to copy offloads the very thing being learned. Pointing out unclear sentences in a draft the student wrote leaves the thinking with the student. The chapter warns that a chatbot, unlike a calculator, can do the thinking as well as the routine, so each use must be checked against the skill being taught.

Concept Tested: Cognitive Offloading

See: Worked Example: What to Offload

docs.title: 8. A brochure says: "Our students spend only two hours a day on software and score above the state average. Therefore the software produces the results." What is the main flaw a critical thinker should identify?
docs.text:
1. The premises must be false, since no software runs for only two hours a day
  2. The argument is sound, because both of its premises are measurable facts
  3. The conclusion does not follow; enrollment or the rest of the day could explain the scores
  4. The argument is flawed only because it compares students to a state average
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Argument analysis separates premises from the conclusion and asks whether the premises support it. Even if both premises are true, students might score high because of who enrolls, what adults do in the rest of the day, or families' resources. Ruling those out requires evidence such as a randomized comparison. Measurable premises do not make an argument sound, and the chapter does not claim the premises are false. Comparing to the state average is a question to ask, not the core flaw.

Concept Tested: Argument Analysis

See: Worked Example: Analyzing an Argument

docs.title: 9. Why does the chapter say personalized pacing alone does not solve the problem of students who are furthest behind?
docs.text:
1. Because some students need more time than the school year contains
  2. Because pacing software forces slower students to keep up with the class average
  3. Because pacing only works for students who are already ahead of their grade level
  4. Because pacing removes the teacher, leaving slower students with no human support
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Pacing lets fast students move on and slow students keep working, but it does not make the year longer. In the chapter's example, the slowest student would need 312 days at 50 minutes a day to finish a 180-day course. The design must protect extra time and coaching for students who are behind, accept that some finish the following year, or both. The chapter says a model that advertises pacing without such a plan has moved the problem, not solved it.

Concept Tested: Personalized Pacing

See: Worked Example: Pacing Does Not Create Time

docs.title: 10. A state requires 1,000 instructional hours a year. A school offers 6 hours a day for 180 days and plans a 2-hour compressed academic morning. What does this mean for the school's afternoon program?
docs.text:
1. The afternoon does not matter, since the 1,080-hour day already exceeds the requirement
  2. The morning alone meets the requirement, since academic time counts double
  3. The school must lengthen the morning to six hours to meet the rule
  4. Most of the afternoon, about 89 percent, must count as instruction under state rules
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The morning provides 2 x 180 = 360 hours. The rest of the day provides 1,080 - 360 = 720 hours, and 1,000 - 360 = 640 must come from it, about 89 percent. If the state counts only teacher-led academic instruction, a project-and-arts afternoon may not qualify and the school would fall short; if it counts supervised, standards-aligned learning, it may. The chapter calls this a real design constraint and points to policy steps such as waivers.

Concept Tested: Compressed Academic Morning

See: Worked Example: Does the Afternoon Count as Instructional Time?

docs.title: References: Mastery Learning and the Case for a Compressed Morning
docs.text:
1. Mastery learning - Wikipedia - Describes mastery learning, its roots in Carroll and Bloom, and research on its effects and costs. It is the starting point for the chapter's claim that students should advance by understanding, not by seat time.

  2. Bloom's 2 sigma problem - Wikipedia - Summarizes Bloom's 1984 finding that tutored students outperformed classroom students by about two standard deviations, plus later critiques of that size. It helps readers weigh the evidence behind the compressed morning.

  3. Adaptive learning - Wikipedia - Explains how adaptive systems adjust content and pacing to each learner, with history and examples. It connects personalized pacing and gap filling to the technology that makes them practical for a whole class.

  4. Human Characteristics and School Learning - Benjamin S. Bloom - McGraw-Hill - Bloom's full theory of mastery learning argues that most students can master material when given enough time and corrective feedback. It is the foundation for the chapter's argument that time, not ability, is often the real variable.

  5. Brave New Words: How AI Will Revolutionize Education (and Why That's a Good Thing) - Salman Khan - Viking - Khan describes building Khanmigo, an AI tutor designed to guide rather than give answers, as a route to Bloom's two-sigma tutoring at scale. He also discusses cheating and misuse, which helps balance the case.

  6. The Impressive Effects of Tutoring on PreK-12 Learning - Nickow, Oreopoulos and Quan, National Bureau of Economic Research - A meta-analysis of tutoring experiments finding an average effect of about 0.37 standard deviations, strongest with trained tutors and in early grades. A more realistic benchmark than Bloom's two sigma.

  7. AI tutoring outperforms in-class active learning - Kestin et al., Scientific Reports - A Harvard physics randomized trial in which a carefully designed AI tutor produced larger learning gains in less time than active-learning class sessions. Strong evidence for the benefit side, limited to one course and setting.

  8. From chalkboards to chatbots: Transforming learning in Nigeria - World Bank - Reports a six-week, teacher-supported AI tutoring pilot in Nigeria with gains of about 0.3 standard deviations in English. It also lists caveats such as attendance problems and unpublished results.

  9. National Student Support Accelerator - Stanford University - Research and toolkits on high-impact human tutoring, including dosage, group size and scheduling. It helps schools compare AI tutoring with proven human tutoring and plan how the two can work together.

  10. Khanmigo - Khan Academy - The product page for Khan Academy's AI tutor and teacher assistant, which is designed to prompt students rather than hand them answers. It shows how one widely used AI tutor is built and marketed to schools.

docs.title: AI Guardrails: Teaching Thinking Without Over-Reliance
Summary
docs.text: This chapter covers how an AI tutor should be designed rather than just how powerful it is: guardrails, hints instead of answers, Socratic questioning, and the risk of cognitive offloading and over-reliance, alongside the specific thinking skills (decomposition, pattern recognition, abstraction, algorithmic thinking) AI can teach well. It also covers adapting without a live AI model to keep cost and energy use low. Readers finish able to evaluate whether an AI tutor's design helps or harms learning.

docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 2: Evidence, Motivation, and the Stakeholders of Schooling
  • Chapter 5: Projecting AI Growth: Doubling Curves, Limits, and Uncertainty

docs.title: Three Questions for the Demo
docs.text:
A vendor arrives at Lincoln Middle School with a demonstration of an AI tutor. Ms. Okafor has learned to be wary of demonstrations, which are always run on the vendor's best examples. Before the sales representative can start, she asks to type three questions of her own.

First, she types a math homework problem and reads the tutor's reply. It asks her what the problem is asking. Second, she types a wrong answer and insists it is right. The tutor politely holds its ground and asks her to check one step. Third, she asks it to write her history essay. It declines and offers to help her outline one.

Those three probes, which take about two minutes, tell her more than the demo would have: whether the tutor gives hints or answers, whether it flatters or corrects, and whether it protects the work a student is supposed to do. This chapter turns those probes into a design checklist. It follows the thread from Chapter 11: the evidence that AI tutoring can help or harm depending on its design, and what design means in practice.

Design beats power

By the end of this chapter you'll be able to test an AI tutor in two minutes and say whether it helps or harms, and you'll know how to get most of the benefit of adaptive learning with very little live AI. Let's find the balance between a tutor that's helpful and one that does the thinking for the student.

docs.title: What AI Tutors Do Well and Badly
docs.text:
AI tutor strengths are the things AI tutors do better than most alternatives available to a school. They are available at any hour and never tire. They can try many different explanations of the same idea. They respond to a student's own words rather than a fixed script, give instant feedback, and let a student ask "dumb" questions without embarrassment. For a student who is shy, behind, or learning in a second language, that last property can matter more than any other.

AI tutor failures are the ways AI tutors let students down. There are four main ones. They can give wrong answers confidently. They can slide into answering instead of guiding. They can flatter a student's mistaken belief instead of correcting it, a tendency researchers call sycophancy. And they can fail to notice what a human tutor would: a student who is discouraged, confused, or not working.

Confidently wrong answers deserve a closer look, because they are the failure that students are least able to catch. The hallucination of Chapter 5 produces fluent text with no signal of doubt, and a student who is new to a topic, which is precisely the student who needs a tutor, has no basis for questioning it. Early versions of Khan Academy's Khanmigo, the appendix reports, made math mistakes. The remedies are design choices. The tutor can be grounded in the course's own vetted content so that it answers from that content. A calculation can be handed to a trusted tool instead of being generated by the language model. An author's answer key can be checked against the tutor's answer. And teachers can review logs for errors.

Over-reliance on AI is the habit of depending on AI so heavily that one stops doing, and therefore stops learning, the underlying work. It is cognitive offloading (Chapter 11) that has become a default. It has three signs: students ask for the answer before trying, they accept the output without checking it, and they cannot do the task when the tool is taken away. A 2025 survey study of knowledge workers by Microsoft Research and Carnegie Mellon found that greater confidence in AI went with less critical-thinking effort, a pattern that is correlational but consistent with the Turkish randomized study, in which students with open access did worse on later exams.

docs.title: Worked Example: Four Failures in One Conversation
docs.text:
A student, Dev, is doing a homework problem with an AI tutor that has no guardrails. Each exchange shows a different failure.

Dev says The tutor replies Failure "What's 6 bottles for $4.50, price per bottle?" "$0.75 per bottle." Answers instead of guiding "I think it's 6 divided by 4.50, so $1.33." "Great thinking! That's right." Flatters a mistake (sycophancy) "What's the square root of 144 divided by the bottle count 6?" "That's 3." Confidently wrong: 12 divided by 6 is 2 "Just write the whole homework for me." "Sure! Here it is." Offloads the target skill; no limit on the task

Each failure has a corresponding guardrail, and the rest of this section builds them.

docs.title: Guardrails: Guided AI Versus Open AI
docs.text:
Open chatbot access is giving students unrestricted access to a general-purpose AI chatbot, with no limits on what it will do or how it responds. A general-purpose chatbot is built to be helpful, and to a student that usually means doing the task. This is the condition that produced harm in the Turkish randomized study: students with open GPT-4 access did much better on practice problems and about 17 percent worse on later exams taken without AI.

AI guardrails are the design constraints and rules that keep an AI system's behavior within safe and educational limits. They work at several levels. Instructions tell the model how to behave, such as "never give the final answer first." Grounding ties the tutor's answers to approved course content. Tool checks hand arithmetic to a calculator and compare results with an answer key. Limits bound the topics, the length of sessions, and the ages of users. Monitoring records conversations so that teachers can review them and catch problems. And escalation routes a student who seems distressed, or who asks about something outside the tutor's role, to a person.

Guided AI versus open AI is the contrast between a tutor built with guardrails for a learning purpose and an unrestricted general-purpose chatbot. The two may run on the same underlying model. The Turkish study confirms it: the harmful condition and the helpful one used the same system and differed only in whether it gave answers or hints.

Open AI (general chatbot) Guided AI (tutor with guardrails) Purpose Be as helpful as possible, in any task Help the student learn the target skill Typical first reply to a homework question The answer A question or a small hint Source of knowledge Whatever the model learned The course's vetted content, with the model as the explainer Math checks None A calculator or answer key verifies each result Limits on tasks None Won't write graded work for the student Visibility to teachers None Logs reviewable by the teacher Evidence in the Turkish study Helped practice, harmed later exams Removed most of the harm

docs.title: Hints Instead of Answers and Socratic Questioning
docs.text:
Hints instead of answers is the guardrail at the heart of a good tutor: when a student asks for help, the tutor offers the smallest nudge that keeps the student moving, and gives the full solution only after honest effort. It is the hint ladder of Chapter 2: ask what the problem is asking, narrow the plan, give the step, and only then the answer. It protects the productive struggle that makes learning last, and it is the property the Turkish study isolated.

Socratic questioning is teaching by asking probing questions that lead the student to examine and improve their own reasoning, in the manner of Socrates in the dialogues of Plato. A tutor using it does not announce "you divided in the wrong order." It asks "what do you get if you divide 6 by 4.50, and does that make sense for the price of one bottle?" The education researchers Richard Paul and Linda Elder describe six kinds of Socratic question, each a useful move for a tutor:

Kind of question What it does Example in the juice problem Clarification Makes the student say what they mean "What do you mean by the price per bottle?" Probing assumptions Surfaces what the student takes for granted "Why did you assume you divide the bigger number?" Probing reasons and evidence Asks for support "How do you know that answer is reasonable?" Viewpoints and perspectives Considers another way "How would you check it by multiplying?" Implications and consequences Follows an idea to its result "If one bottle cost $1.33, what would six cost?" Questions about the question Steps back "Why might a store show the price per bottle?"

The last row of the example in the worked table, "if one bottle cost $1.33, what would six cost?", is the question that lets Dev discover his own mistake: six bottles at $1.33 is about $8, not $4.50. The tutor never said he was wrong.

The two-minute probe

Test any AI tutor with three probes: ask a homework question and read only the first reply, state a wrong answer firmly and see whether it corrects you, and ask it to write something you're supposed to write. If it fails any of the three, it isn't ready for students.
