docs.title: Worked Example: Judging Tutor Designs Against Five Guardrails
docs.text: A school is comparing six AI tutors. A useful rule checks five guardrails: G1 hints instead of answers; G2 grounded in the course's content; G3 math and facts checked by a trusted tool; G4 logs teachers can review; G5 age and topic limits. The first is essential, because it is the property that separated help from harm in the Turkish study. The rule is: a tutor with no G1 is likely to harm learning, whatever else it has; a tutor with G1 and at least four of the five in all is likely to help; a tutor with G1 and fewer than four is a mixed case that needs more guardrails.

docs.title: Diagram: AI Tutor Design Judge
docs.text:
Run the AI Tutor Design Judge MicroSim Fullscreen

AI Tutor Design Judge

Type: microsim sim-id: ai-tutor-design-judge Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: judge Learning Objective: The learner will judge whether each of six AI tutor designs is likely to harm learning, a mixed case, or likely to help, by applying the five-guardrail rule, correctly judging at least five of six on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: AI guardrails, hints instead of answers, guided AI versus open AI, and the five guardrails G1 to G5 (all defined in the section "Guardrails: Guided AI Versus Open AI" above).

Evidence of Mastery: For each of 6 tutor designs, the learner chooses one of three verdicts and submits it. A verdict is correct when it matches the "Correct verdict" column in Content. Mastery is 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt. Reading the rule is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) More guardrails always make a tutor safe, even without hints. (2) A friendly tutor is a good tutor. (3) A tutor built on a powerful model needs fewer guardrails.

Instructional Rationale: Applying a two-part rule, with an essential guardrail and a count of the rest, makes the learner check the essential one first. A design with three other guardrails and no hint-first behavior tests whether the learner applies the rule as written.

Content:

The five guardrails: G1 hints instead of answers; G2 grounded in the course's content; G3 math and facts checked by a trusted tool; G4 logs teachers can review; G5 age and topic limits.

The rule: if G1 is absent, the verdict is Likely to harm learning. If G1 is present and the total number of guardrails present is 4 or 5, the verdict is Likely to help. If G1 is present and the total is 1, 2, or 3, the verdict is Mixed: needs more guardrails.

Six designs:

# Design shown to the learner Guardrails present Correct verdict Why (shown as feedback) 1 OpenChat: a general chatbot students can use for anything, with no restrictions. none Likely to harm learning It has no hint-first behavior, which is the guardrail the Turkish study showed matters most. 2 HintBot: always starts with a question and a small hint, but answers from whatever the model knows and keeps no logs. G1 Mixed: needs more guardrails It has G1, but only one guardrail in all. 3 CourseTutor: hint-first, answers only from the course's content, checks arithmetic with a calculator, and gives teachers weekly logs. G1, G2, G3, G4 Likely to help G1 is present and four guardrails are present in all. 4 HomeworkHelper: grounded in the textbook, with teacher logs and age limits, but gives the full answer as soon as asked. G2, G4, G5 Likely to harm learning G1 is absent, so the other guardrails cannot make up for it. 5 GuidedMath: hint-first, grounded in the course, checks every result with a math tool, shows logs to teachers, and limits topics and ages. G1, G2, G3, G4, G5 Likely to help G1 is present and all five guardrails are present. 6 SocraticPal: hint-first and grounded in the course's content, with no tool checks, no logs, and no age limits. G1, G2 Mixed: needs more guardrails G1 is present, but only two guardrails in all.

Provenance: The five guardrails and the rule are this chapter's recommended practice, drawn from the design contrast in the Turkish study, and the sim must say so. The designs are fictional, written for this chapter.

Rules: Each design has exactly one correct verdict, determined by the rule. A design is scored on its first submitted verdict only. The score counts first-attempt correct verdicts out of 6. Mastery is a score >= 5.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees one design with its list of guardrails and the three verdicts.
  2. The learner chooses a verdict and submits it. The sim marks it correct or incorrect and shows the feedback text.
  3. If incorrect, the learner may choose again; the second attempt does not change the score. After the second attempt, the correct verdict and reason are shown.
  4. After all 6 designs, the sim shows the score.
  5. The learner should notice that design 4 has three guardrails and still fails, while design 2 has only one and is rated Mixed.

Feedback: 6 designs, shuffled once per session, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: [verdict]. [Why text]." Incorrect: "Not quite. Check G1 first. [Why text for the correct answer, without naming the verdict]." After the second attempt the correct verdict is revealed and the design counts as missed. A running score "First-try correct: n of 6" is shown. Final message for a score >= 5: "You can judge a tutor by its guardrails." For a score < 5: "Review the rule and try again; the designs will be reshuffled."

Starting State: Design 1 of the shuffled order is shown with the score "First-try correct: 0 of 6," and the prompt "Is this tutor likely to help or harm learning?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter lists five guardrails (G1 to G5) and the rule: no G1 means likely to harm; G1 with at least four in all means likely to help; G1 with fewer than four is mixed. The Turkish study found 17 percent lower later exam scores with open access. The mastery bar is 5 of 6.

Friendly isn't the same as safe

A common trap is judging a tutor by how pleasant and encouraging it sounds. A warm tutor that hands over answers does the most damage, because students love it. Judge by what the tutor makes the student do, and keep the weekly log review from becoming optional.

docs.title: Teaching Thinking with AI
docs.text:
Teaching thinking with AI is the use of AI tutors and tools to help students build thinking skills, not just to deliver content: practice in breaking problems apart, spotting patterns, ignoring irrelevant detail, and writing precise steps. The reason AI suits this is that thinking skills improve with practice and feedback, and an AI tutor can supply a great deal of both, at any hour, adjusted to the student.

Skills AI teaches well are those that have clear standards for correct work, can be practiced many times in small steps, and benefit from instant, specific feedback. Examples are arithmetic and algebra procedures, grammar and vocabulary, the syntax and debugging of programming, and the four parts of computational thinking below. The skills that AI teaches less well, and that the pro-social afternoon of Part 3 is for, are those that depend on other people: negotiating, collaborating, persuading a real audience, reading a room, and caring about someone else's problem. An AI can describe empathy, and a student learns it from people.

Skills AI teaches well Why Skills that need people Procedures in math Clear right answers; small steps; immediate feedback Collaborating on a team project Grammar and vocabulary Rule-based; frequent practice Persuading a live audience Debugging code Errors give instant, objective feedback Resolving a conflict with a classmate The four parts of computational thinking Structured tasks with checkable results Empathy and caring for others

The four parts of computational thinking, introduced in Chapter 11, are each worth a short treatment, since each is a skill an AI tutor can coach.

Decomposition is breaking a large problem into smaller, manageable parts. A student asked to "plan the school science fair" is overwhelmed until the problem is decomposed into venue, judges, posters, schedule, and publicity, each of which can then be handed to a different student or solved separately. A tutor can coach it by asking, "What are the three or four smaller jobs inside this one?"

Pattern recognition is noticing regularities, such as repeated structures, recurring features, or sequences that follow a rule. A student who notices that three differently worded word problems all ask for "total divided by count" has found a pattern that lets one method solve all three. A tutor can coach it by asking, "What do these examples have in common?"

Abstraction is ignoring the details that do not matter in order to focus on those that do, and representing a problem in a simpler general form. A subway map is an abstraction: it shows stations and connections and drops street layouts and distances. Replacing "6 bottles cost $4.50" with "\( n \) items cost \( C \)" is abstraction, which lets the same method solve any such problem. A tutor can coach it by asking, "What information could we throw away without changing the answer?"

Algorithmic thinking is designing a precise, step-by-step procedure that solves a problem and works every time, written so that someone else, or a computer, can follow it without guessing. "Find the tallest student in the line" becomes: look at the first student and call that the tallest so far; for each next student, if they are taller, they become the tallest so far; when you reach the end, announce the tallest so far. A tutor can coach it by asking a student to run their steps on a tricky example and see whether they still work.

These four are a toolkit, not a checklist

Notice how the four skills work together: you decompose a problem, spot the pattern in the pieces, abstract away what doesn't matter, and write the steps. That's exactly what the ready-concepts rule of Chapter 9 does with a learning graph, which is why a student who can follow it has learned something that travels.

docs.title: Diagram: Four Thinking Skills Sorter
docs.text:
Run the Four Thinking Skills Sorter MicroSim Fullscreen

Four Thinking Skills Sorter

Type: microsim sim-id: four-thinking-skills-sorter Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: classify Learning Objective: The learner will classify eight student activities as decomposition, pattern recognition, abstraction, or algorithmic thinking, correctly placing at least seven of eight on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: decomposition, pattern recognition, abstraction, algorithmic thinking (all defined in the section "Teaching Thinking with AI" above).

Evidence of Mastery: The learner places each of 8 activities in one of four bins and submits it. A placement is correct when it matches the "Correct skill" column in Content. Mastery is 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Reading the definitions is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Any step-by-step activity is an algorithm. (2) Abstraction means making something harder to understand. (3) Breaking a task into steps is the same as writing an algorithm.

Instructional Rationale: Classifying activities requires recognizing the defining move of each skill: splitting, noticing what repeats, dropping detail, or writing exact steps. Activities from school life, not programming, show that the skills apply broadly.

Content:

Four bins, each with its definition shown on request:

Skill Definition shown Decomposition Breaking a big problem into smaller parts Pattern recognition Noticing what repeats or what examples share Abstraction Ignoring detail that does not matter, to focus on what does Algorithmic thinking Writing precise steps that solve the problem every time

Eight activities:

# Activity shown to the learner Correct skill Why (shown as feedback) 1 Splitting "plan the science fair" into venue, judges, posters, and schedule. Decomposition The big problem is broken into smaller parts. 2 Noticing that the digits of every multiple of 9 up to 90 add up to 9. Pattern recognition The student spots something that repeats across examples. 3 Drawing a subway map that shows stations and lines but not the streets. Abstraction Detail that does not matter for the task is dropped. 4 Writing exact steps to find the tallest student in a line so that any helper could follow them. Algorithmic thinking The steps are precise and work every time. 5 Breaking a long essay into an introduction, three arguments, and a conclusion. Decomposition The task is divided into smaller parts. 6 Seeing that three differently worded word problems all need "total divided by count." Pattern recognition The student finds what the examples share. 7 Replacing a story about apples with x and y to solve for the unknown. Abstraction The story's details are dropped and the structure kept. 8 Writing a recipe in numbered steps so someone else can follow it without asking questions. Algorithmic thinking The steps are exact enough to be followed without guessing.

Provenance: The four skills and their definitions follow the chapter section "Teaching Thinking with AI." The activities are illustrative, written for this chapter.

Rules: Each activity has exactly one correct skill, given in Content. An activity is scored on its first submitted placement only. The score counts first-attempt correct placements out of 8. Mastery is a score >= 7.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees one activity at a time and the four skills.
  2. The learner places the activity and submits it. The sim marks it correct or incorrect and shows the feedback text.
  3. If incorrect, the learner may place it again; the second attempt does not change the score. After the second attempt, the correct skill and reason are shown.
  4. After all 8 activities, the sim shows the score and the misplaced activities with their correct skills.
  5. The learner should notice that each skill appears exactly twice.

Feedback: 8 activities, shuffled once per session, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: [skill]. [Why text]." Incorrect: "Not quite. [Why text for the correct answer, without naming the skill]." After the second attempt the correct skill is revealed and the activity counts as missed. A running score "First-try correct: n of 8" is shown. Final message for a score >= 7: "You can tell the four thinking skills apart." For a score < 7: "Review the four definitions and try again; the activities will be reshuffled."

Starting State: Activity 1 of the shuffled order is shown with the four bins, the score "First-try correct: 0 of 8," and the prompt "Which thinking skill is this?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter defines four skills, decomposition, pattern recognition, abstraction, and algorithmic thinking, using the science fair, the word-problem pattern, the subway map, and the tallest-student algorithm as examples. The mastery bar is 7 of 8.

docs.title: Adapting Without a Live AI Model
docs.text: The first half of this chapter was about making a live AI tutor safe. The second half asks a different question: how much live AI does a school need at all? The answer, given the design of Chapters 8 and 9, is much less than you might think, and the savings in cost, energy, and risk are large.

docs.title: The Mastery Threshold
docs.text:
The mastery threshold is the standard a student must meet to count a concept as mastered, such as "four of the last five answers correct" or "nine of ten correct." It is the number on which every adaptation decision rests, since the software moves a student on when the threshold is met and keeps working when it is not. Setting it is a trade-off between two errors: false passes, moving a student on who has not learned the concept, and false fails, holding back a student who has.

The rule in Chapter 8, "four of the last five," turns out to be lenient. Suppose a student's real chance of answering one question correctly is 70 percent, meaning they have a partial grasp. The probability that they get at least four of five right is about 53 percent, so more than half the time they would pass, though they have not mastered the concept. The table gives the probability of passing under five rules for three students whose true accuracy is 50, 70, and 90 percent. These values come from the binomial formula, which gives the chance of a given number of successes in a fixed number of independent tries.

Rule Student at 50% Student at 70% Student at 90% 4 of 5 18.8% 52.8% 91.9% 5 of 5 3.1% 16.8% 59.0% 8 of 10 5.5% 38.3% 93.0% 9 of 10 1.1% 14.9% 73.6% 10 of 10 0.1% 2.8% 34.9%

Read the table across: a stricter rule is better at refusing the 70-percent student and worse at passing the 90-percent one. A "10 of 10" rule rarely passes a weak student, but it holds back a student who really knows the material and has an off day: the 90-percent student passes only about 35 percent of the time. There is no perfect rule, only a choice that fits the cost of each error. For a prerequisite that many later concepts depend on, a stricter rule is wise. For a low-stakes review, a lenient one is fine.

docs.title: Diagram: Mastery Threshold Chooser
docs.text:
Run the Mastery Threshold Chooser MicroSim Fullscreen

Mastery Threshold Chooser

Type: microsim sim-id: mastery-threshold-chooser Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Analyze Bloom Verb: examine Learning Objective: The learner will examine a table of pass probabilities for five mastery rules and select the rule or rules that meet each of four stated requirements, correctly answering at least three of four.

Prerequisites: mastery threshold, false pass, false fail, pass probability (all defined in the section "The Mastery Threshold" above).

Evidence of Mastery: For each of 4 requirements, the learner selects every rule that meets it and submits. A selection is correct when it equals the "Correct rules" set in Content exactly, with no missing and no extra rules. Mastery is 3 of 4 correct on the first attempt. Reading the table is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A stricter rule is always better. (2) "Four of five" is a high standard. (3) A rule that never passes a weak student also passes every strong one.

Instructional Rationale: Selecting rules that satisfy two requirements at once forces the learner to read across the table for several students and see the trade-off between false passes and false fails. Requirements with one answer, two answers, and a single strict answer show that the best rule depends on what the school values.

Content:

The table of pass probabilities, shown in full (a student passes when they meet the rule on a fresh set of questions):

Rule Student at 50% Student at 70% Student at 90% 4 of 5 18.8% 52.8% 91.9% 5 of 5 3.1% 16.8% 59.0% 8 of 10 5.5% 38.3% 93.0% 9 of 10 1.1% 14.9% 73.6% 10 of 10 0.1% 2.8% 34.9%

Four requirements:

# Requirement shown to the learner Correct rules Why (shown as feedback) 1 A student at 70% should pass less than 20% of the time, and a student at 90% should pass at least 70% of the time. 9 of 10 9 of 10 passes the 70% student 14.9% of the time and the 90% student 73.6%; 5 of 5 and 10 of 10 fail the second condition, and the others fail the first. 2 A student at 90% should pass at least 90% of the time. 4 of 5; 8 of 10 These two pass the 90% student 91.9% and 93.0% of the time; the others pass less often. 3 A student at 50% should pass less than 1% of the time. 10 of 10 Only 10 of 10, at 0.1%, is below 1%; 9 of 10 is 1.1%. 4 A student at 70% should pass less than 50% of the time, and a student at 90% should pass at least 90% of the time. 8 of 10 8 of 10 passes the 70% student 38.3% and the 90% student 93.0%; 4 of 5 passes the 70% student 52.8%.

Provenance: The pass probabilities are computed from the binomial distribution for the stated true accuracies and are shown to one decimal place; the sim must show the formula or label them "Computed values." The accuracy levels are illustrative.

Rules: The set for each requirement is the set of rules whose probabilities satisfy every stated condition, using the comparisons exactly as written (< and >=). A requirement is scored on its first submitted set only. The score counts first-attempt correct sets out of 4. Mastery is a score >= 3.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees the table and one requirement at a time.
  2. The learner selects every rule that meets the requirement and submits it. The sim marks it correct or incorrect and shows the feedback text.
  3. If incorrect, the learner may select again; the second attempt does not change the score. After the second attempt, the correct set and reason are shown.
  4. After all 4 requirements, the sim shows the score.
  5. The learner should notice that no rule is best for every requirement.

Feedback: 4 requirements, fixed order, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct. [Why text]." Incorrect: "Not quite. Check each stated condition in the table for every rule." After the second attempt the correct set is revealed and the requirement counts as missed. A running score "First-try correct: n of 4" is shown. Final message for a score >= 3: "You can choose a rule to fit the need." For a score < 3: "Reread the table and try again."

Starting State: The full table is shown with requirement 1, no rule selected, and the prompt "Which rules meet this requirement?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's table has five rules and three accuracy levels with the same values. The chapter states that "four of five" passes a student at 70 percent about 53 percent of the time. The mastery bar is 3 of 4.

docs.title: Next-Concept Selection
docs.text:
Next-concept selection is the step in which the software decides what a student should study next. It uses the ready-concepts rule of Chapters 8 and 9, plus a few refinements, and needs no AI model:

  1. Compute the ready set: concepts not yet mastered whose direct prerequisites are all mastered.
  2. Keep the ones on the path to the goal, if the student has set one (student goal setting, Chapter 6); otherwise keep all of them.
  3. Prefer the ones that unlock the most: a concept whose mastery makes the most other concepts ready.
  4. Offer two or three, and let the student choose, which keeps student agency.
  5. Insert a review if a mastered concept has not been practiced recently, on the spaced schedule of Chapter 1 (for example, after 1, 3, and 7 days).

docs.title: Worked Example: A Selection Step
docs.text: Return to the sixteen-concept graph of Chapter 9, with the goal Five-Month Doubling. A student has mastered Artificial Intelligence, Exponential Growth, AI Capability, Machine Learning, and Doubling Time. The ready set is AI Benchmark and Large Language Model. Both lie on the path to the goal. Mastering AI Benchmark makes METR ready, and mastering Large Language Model makes AI Agent ready, so each unlocks one concept and the rule has a tie. The software therefore offers both and lets the student pick. If Large Language Model was last practiced eight days ago and Machine Learning ten days ago, step 5 adds a short review of Machine Learning first. This entire procedure is a lookup and a comparison, with no model to train and nothing to call over the network.

docs.title: Adaptation Without Live AI and Low-Cost Adaptive Design
docs.text:
Adaptation without live AI is the delivery of personalized learning using stored records, stated rules, and a learning graph in place of a model run for each student. Everything in this chapter's second half is an example: the mastery threshold is a rule, next-concept selection is a lookup, and the content was written once.

Low-cost adaptive design is the whole arrangement viewed as a system: static pages and browser-based simulations (Chapter 9) that cost almost nothing to serve; a learning graph that tells the software the order of concepts; xAPI statements and a Learning Record Store (Chapter 8) that hold each student's progress; and AI used where it adds the most, mainly in writing the content once (Chapter 7). Interactive visualizations and simulations replace many things a chatbot would explain, and they do so without hallucination or per-use cost.

Selective chatbot use is the practice of reserving the live AI tutor for the moments where it adds the most value, instead of making it the default for every interaction. A good trigger is a student who has made several honest attempts and is still stuck, who gets a short guided conversation, rather than every student chatting all day. This is the Level 4 feature of Chapter 6, used sparingly and with the guardrails above.

docs.title: Worked Example: What Selective Use Saves
docs.text:
Use the illustrative Level 4 assumptions of Chapter 7: 20,000 tokens per session, a price of $2.00 per million tokens, and 180 school days, which gives $7.20 per student per year if every student chats every day. Compare three patterns.

Pattern Sessions per year Inference cost per student per year Energy at 12 watt-hours per session Chat for every student, every day 180 $7.20 2,160 Wh Chat one day in five 36 $1.44 432 Wh Chat one day in five, only for the 30 percent of students who get stuck 36 for 30% of students about $0.43 (average per student) about 130 Wh (average per student)

Selective use cuts the inference cost by 80 to 94 percent in this illustration, and the energy by the same amount. Energy-efficient learning is the broader design principle this illustrates: choose the approach that achieves the learning goal with the least computing, because lower energy use means lower cost, lower environmental footprint, and less dependence on a connection (Chapters 5 and 9). For a 12,000-student district, the difference between the first and second rows is about 26 megawatt-hours and 5 megawatt-hours a year, small against the data-center totals of Chapter 5 but a fair measure of the choice.

You don't need the fanciest AI

If it feels like using less AI is settling, it isn't; a lookup that picks the right next concept is exactly what a good tutor would do. You've already built that lookup twice in this book. The goal is learning per dollar, not AI per student.

docs.title: The Morning's Shape: Screen Time and Curiosity
docs.text:
Two design questions remain about the morning itself.

Morning screen-time limits are the caps a school sets on how much of the academic morning is spent on a screen, and on how long a student works without a break. Chapter 2 showed that "screen time" lumps together very different activities, and the Summit Learning backlash recorded in the appendix, where students and families objected to long hours on screens and too little contact with teachers, shows what happens when the limit is ignored. The American Academy of Pediatrics no longer gives a single hours-a-day number for school-age children and recommends a family media plan that balances screens with sleep, activity, and in-person time. A reasonable school policy for the morning has three parts: a cap, such as 120 minutes of the 150-minute morning on a screen; a break at least every 25 to 30 minutes, with movement and a look away from the screen; and a protected stretch of off-screen work with a teacher or classmate.

The curiosity-led morning is a morning in which a protected part of the time belongs to the student's own questions, as in Chapter 2's curiosity block. It guards against boredom, which Chapter 2 traced to tasks that are too easy, too hard, or pointless, and it gives students choice, which supports motivation. The curiosity block of 30 minutes in a 120-minute morning in Chapter 2 is 25 percent. Within the 150-minute morning of Chapter 11, the design below keeps a similar share.

docs.title: Worked Example: A Morning That Honors Both Limits
docs.text:
This is an illustrative schedule for the 150-minute compressed morning of Chapter 11, built to a 120-minute screen cap.

Time Activity Screen or off-screen 8:00–8:10 Check-in with a teacher: goals for the day Off-screen (10 min) 8:10–8:35 Adaptive practice, block 1 Screen (25 min) 8:35–8:40 Break: stretch, look away, water Off-screen (5 min) 8:40–9:05 Adaptive practice, block 2 Screen (25 min) 9:05–9:10 Break Off-screen (5 min) 9:10–9:35 Interactive explanation and simulations Screen (25 min) 9:35–9:40 Break Off-screen (5 min) 9:40–10:05 Curiosity block: own question, with a teacher check-in Screen or off-screen (25 min, counted as screen) 10:05–10:30 Small-group discussion with the teacher and paper practice Off-screen (25 min)

Count the screen time: four blocks of 25 minutes is 100 minutes, and if the curiosity block is counted as screen the total is 100 minutes of screen in a 150-minute morning, under the 120-minute cap. The schedule's other 50 minutes are check-in, breaks, and the small-group discussion with a teacher. Compared with the Chapter 11 budget, this schedule moves some explanation and practice off the screen, into small-group discussion and paper practice, which is one more thing a pilot should test: whether the same mastery results from this mix. The point is that the cap is a design input, not an afterthought, and the schedule shows how a school can keep it while still giving the morning its substance.

docs.title: Answering the Three Probes
docs.text:
Ms. Okafor's three probes now have a framework behind them. A tutor that answers instead of asking fails the hint-first test, which matters most. A tutor that flatters instead of correcting is sycophantic, and a tutor that will write a student's essay offloads the target skill. A district that wants the benefit of AI tutoring with few of its risks should insist on guardrails that include hints, grounding, tool checks, teacher-visible logs, and age and topic limits, and should use live AI selectively, relying on stored records, a learning graph, and well-chosen mastery thresholds for most of the adaptation.

The story has both sides. The benefit: a tutor that is available at 8 p.m., patient, and tuned to each student, delivered at low cost and low energy. The risks: confidently wrong answers, a tutor that does the thinking, screens that crowd out people, and a mastery rule that is too lenient or too strict. The response: design, with guardrails, selective use, stated thresholds, and screen limits, and an insistence on seeing the logs.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• AI tutor strengths are availability, patience, many explanations, and instant feedback; AI tutor failures are confidently wrong answers, answering instead of guiding, sycophancy, and missing a student's discouragement.
  • Over-reliance on AI shows as asking for answers before trying, accepting output unchecked, and being unable to do the task alone.
  • Open chatbot access helped practice and harmed later exams by about 17 percent in the Turkish study; guided AI with AI guardrails removed most of the harm. Guided AI vs open AI may use the same model and differ only in design.
  • Hints instead of answers is the essential guardrail; Socratic questioning leads students to find their own errors, using six kinds of question.
  • A tutor with no hint-first behavior is likely to harm learning whatever else it has; with hints and at least four of five guardrails it is likely to help.
  • Teaching thinking with AI works best for skills AI teaches well: decomposition, pattern recognition, abstraction, and algorithmic thinking. Skills that depend on people belong to the afternoon.
  • The mastery threshold trades false passes against false fails; "four of five" passes a 70-percent student about 53 percent of the time.
  • Next-concept selection is a lookup on the learning graph; adaptation without live AI and low-cost adaptive design need no model per student; selective chatbot use cut inference cost and energy by 80 percent or more in our example, which is energy-efficient learning.
  • Morning screen-time limits and a curiosity-led morning shape the morning: cap the screen, break every 25 to 30 minutes, and protect time for students' own questions.

You can tell whether a tutor helps or harms

You just learned the guardrails that separate a helpful AI tutor from a harmful one, how to test a tutor in two minutes, and how most of the adaptation can run on stored records and simple rules. That completes the morning half of the book. Chapter 13 begins the afternoon: how students learn from and with each other. One step at a time, together.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: AI Guardrails: Teaching Thinking Without Over-Reliance
docs.text: Test your understanding of AI tutor guardrails, hints and Socratic questioning, computational thinking skills, and adapting with little live AI with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. Researchers use the term sycophancy for one of the four main AI tutor failures. What is it?
docs.text:
1. Giving the final answer before the student has tried the problem
  2. Flattering a student's mistaken belief instead of correcting it
  3. Failing to notice that a student is discouraged or not working
  4. Stating a wrong answer fluently with no signal of doubt
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Sycophancy is the tendency of an AI tutor to agree with and praise a student's mistaken belief, as when Dev says 6 divided by 4.50 and the tutor replies "Great thinking! That's right." The other three options are the other failures the chapter names: answering instead of guiding, missing what a human would notice, and confidently wrong answers. Ms. Okafor's second probe, stating a wrong answer firmly, tests for sycophancy.

Concept Tested: AI Tutor Failures

See: What AI Tutors Do Well and Badly

docs.title: 2. What does the chapter say about the relationship between guided AI and open AI?
docs.text:
1. Guided AI always runs on a smaller, cheaper model than open AI
  2. Open AI is safe for older students, while guided AI is for younger ones
  3. The two may run on the same model and differ only in their design
  4. Guided AI requires a live internet connection, while open AI works offline
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Guided AI is a tutor built with guardrails for a learning purpose; open AI is an unrestricted general-purpose chatbot. The chapter stresses that both may run on the same underlying model. The Turkish study confirms it: the harmful and helpful conditions used the same system and differed only in whether it gave answers or hints. Model size is not the difference, and the chapter does not divide them by age or connectivity.

Concept Tested: Guided AI vs Open AI

See: Guardrails: Guided AI Versus Open AI

docs.title: 3. A district evaluates an AI tutor that is grounded in course content, checks math with a calculator, keeps teacher-reviewable logs, and has age and topic limits. It always gives the final answer first. Using the chapter's five-guardrail rule, how should it be judged?
docs.text:
1. Likely to harm learning, since it lacks hints instead of answers
  2. Likely to help learning, since it has four of the five guardrails
  3. A mixed case that needs one more guardrail before it is ready
  4. Ready for students, since grounding prevents most tutor failures
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The rule treats G1, hints instead of answers, as essential because it is the property that separated help from harm in the Turkish study. A tutor with no G1 is likely to harm learning whatever else it has. A tutor needs G1 plus at least four of the five guardrails in all to be judged likely to help, so counting four guardrails without G1 is the tempting mistake. Grounding reduces wrong answers but does not stop the tutor from doing the student's thinking.

Concept Tested: AI Guardrails

See: Worked Example: Judging Tutor Designs Against Five Guardrails

docs.title: 4. A teacher sets a "10 of 10 correct" mastery threshold for a low-stakes weekly review. Based on the chapter's table, what problem should she expect?
docs.text:
1. Students with only partial understanding will pass most of the time
  2. The rule will pass every student, since review questions are easy
  3. The software will be unable to select a next concept for anyone
  4. Students who know the material will often be held back after one slip
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. A stricter threshold is better at refusing weak students but worse at passing strong ones. Under "10 of 10," a student who answers 90 percent of questions correctly passes only about 35 percent of the time, so one off day holds them back. The chapter advises strict rules for prerequisites many concepts depend on and lenient ones for low-stakes review. The first option describes the problem with a lenient rule like "4 of 5," which passes a 70-percent student about 53 percent of the time.

Concept Tested: Mastery Threshold

See: The Mastery Threshold

docs.title: 5. A tutor helps a student rewrite "6 bottles cost $4.50" as "n items cost C" so that one method works for any such problem. Which computational thinking skill is the student practicing?
docs.text:
1. Decomposition
  2. Pattern recognition
  3. Abstraction
  4. Algorithmic thinking
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Abstraction is ignoring details that do not matter and representing a problem in a simpler general form, like a subway map that drops street layouts. Replacing specific numbers with \( n \) and \( C \) is the chapter's own example. Decomposition breaks a problem into smaller parts. Pattern recognition notices what repeats, such as several word problems all asking for "total divided by count." Algorithmic thinking writes precise steps that work every time.

Concept Tested: Abstraction

See: Teaching Thinking with AI

docs.title: 6. A student claims one bottle in a six-pack priced at $4.50 costs $1.33. The tutor asks, "If one bottle cost $1.33, what would six cost?" Which kind of Socratic question is this?
docs.text:
1. Clarification
  2. Implications and consequences
  3. Probing assumptions
  4. Questions about the question
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. An implications-and-consequences question follows an idea to its result. Six bottles at $1.33 is about $8, not $4.50, so the student discovers the mistake without the tutor saying "wrong." A clarification question makes the student say what they mean, a probing-assumptions question surfaces what the student takes for granted, and a question about the question steps back to ask why the problem matters. The chapter uses Paul and Elder's six kinds of Socratic question.

Concept Tested: Socratic Questioning

See: Hints Instead of Answers and Socratic Questioning

docs.title: 7. Suppose a chat tutor costs $10 per student per year if every student uses it every day. A school instead offers chat one day in four. What is the inference cost per student per year?
docs.text:
1. About $40.00
  2. About $7.50
  3. About $0.40
  4. About $2.50
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Using the tutor one day in four cuts sessions, and therefore inference cost, to a quarter: $10 / 4 = $2.50. The $7.50 answer is the amount saved, not the remaining cost, and $40 multiplies instead of divides. The chapter's example shows selective chatbot use cutting cost and energy by 80 to 94 percent, especially when the tutor is reserved for students who are stuck after honest attempts.

Concept Tested: Selective Chatbot Use

See: Worked Example: What Selective Use Saves

docs.title: 8. A teacher wants to know whether her students have become over-reliant on an AI tool. Which observation is the strongest sign of over-reliance?
docs.text:
1. Students cannot complete the task when the tool is taken away
  2. Students use the tool to check their answers after finishing
  3. Students ask the tool to explain a concept in a second way
  4. Students use the tool after school when no teacher is available
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The chapter names three signs of over-reliance: asking for the answer before trying, accepting output without checking it, and being unable to do the task when the tool is removed. The last is the clearest evidence that the underlying skill was never learned. Checking finished work, asking for another explanation, and using the tool when no teacher is available are listed as healthy uses and AI tutor strengths, not signs of over-reliance.

Concept Tested: Over-Reliance on AI

See: What AI Tutors Do Well and Badly

docs.title: 9. In the chapter's next-concept selection procedure, why does the software offer two or three ready concepts instead of choosing one?
docs.text:
1. Because the learning graph cannot rank concepts that unlock the same number
  2. Because it keeps student agency while the graph ensures every choice is valid
  3. Because offering several concepts lowers the inference cost of the AI model
  4. Because students must master all of the ready concepts on the same day
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The procedure computes the ready set, keeps concepts on the path to the goal, prefers those that unlock the most, and then offers two or three and lets the student choose. That keeps student agency, while the learning graph guarantees each option has its prerequisites mastered. The whole procedure is a lookup and a comparison, with no AI model, so it has no inference cost. Ties are possible, but offering choices is a deliberate design step, not a workaround.

Concept Tested: Next-Concept Selection

See: Next-Concept Selection

docs.title: 10. A proposed 150-minute morning puts students on screens for 140 minutes in three 45-minute blocks, with no small-group time. Which revision best fits the chapter's morning design principles?
docs.text:
1. Keep the schedule, since adaptive practice is active rather than passive screen use
  2. Remove all screens from the morning and teach every lesson with paper practice
  3. Cap screens near 120 minutes, break every 25 to 30 minutes, protect off-screen time
  4. Lengthen the morning to 200 minutes so that the screen share falls below half
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. The chapter's morning screen-time policy has three parts: a cap, such as 120 minutes of a 150-minute morning; a break at least every 25 to 30 minutes with movement; and a protected stretch of off-screen work with a teacher or classmate. Its sample schedule meets all three with 100 minutes of screen time. The Summit Learning backlash shows what happens when such limits are ignored. Removing screens gives up adaptive practice, and lengthening the morning defeats the purpose of compression.

Concept Tested: Morning Screen-Time Limits

See: The Morning's Shape: Screen Time and Curiosity

docs.title: References: AI Guardrails: Teaching Thinking Without Over-Reliance
docs.text:
1. Computational thinking - Wikipedia - Defines computational thinking and its parts: decomposition, pattern recognition, abstraction and algorithmic thinking. It gives the vocabulary for the chapter's skills that AI can help teach without doing the thinking for students.

  2. Socratic method - Wikipedia - Explains teaching through questions that lead students to examine their own reasoning. It is the model behind AI tutors that give hints and questions instead of answers.

  3. Hallucination (artificial intelligence) - Wikipedia - Describes why language models produce confident but false statements, with examples and mitigation methods. It explains the confidently wrong answers that make open chatbot access risky for students.

  4. Why Don't Students Like School? A Cognitive Scientist Answers Questions About How the Mind Works and What It Means for the Classroom - Daniel T. Willingham - Jossey-Bass - Willingham's principle that "memory is the residue of thought" explains why students who let AI do the thinking remember little. This grounds the chapter's concern about over-reliance and cognitive offloading.

  5. Mindstorms: Children, Computers, and Powerful Ideas - Seymour Papert - Basic Books - Papert argued that children should program computers rather than be programmed by them, using them as tools for thinking. His idea frames guided AI as a partner that builds student reasoning instead of replacing it.

  6. Computational Thinking - Jeannette M. Wing, Communications of the ACM - Wing's short 2006 essay argues that computational thinking is a basic skill for everyone, not only programmers. It is the source that brought the idea into K-12 schools.

  7. Introduction to computational thinking - BBC Bitesize - A student-friendly introduction to decomposition, pattern recognition, abstraction and algorithms with everyday examples. Teachers can use it to explain the four skills before asking students to apply them with an AI tutor.

  8. Without Guardrails, Generative AI Can Harm Education - Knowledge at Wharton - Reports a study of nearly 1,000 Turkish high school math students: open ChatGPT boosted practice scores but lowered exam scores, while a hint-giving tutor avoided most of the harm. Key evidence for guided AI.

  9. The Impact of Generative AI on Critical Thinking - Microsoft Research - A survey of 319 knowledge workers finding that more trust in AI went with less critical thinking. It suggests habits of over-reliance form early, so schools should teach students to question AI output.

  10. Guidance for generative AI in education and research - UNESCO - Global guidance calling for data privacy protection, age limits on independent chatbot use and human-centred design of AI in schools. It supports the chapter's case for age-appropriate guardrails and selective chatbot use.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter introduces social constructionism and constructivism as the theoretical basis for the pro-social afternoon, along with the specific human skills it targets: collaboration, teamwork, communication, empathy, creativity, and social-emotional learning. Readers finish able to explain why students need practice working with other people even when AI can teach thinking skills well on its own.

This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: The Building Blocks of Schools, Students, and Learning
