docs.title: Opinion Leaders and Change Agents
docs.text: Two roles in Rogers' theory explain how an idea moves from one category to the next. An opinion leader is a member of a social system whom others look to for advice and information about innovations. Opinion leaders influence through informal respect, not authority, and they are often people who are close to the norm of the group and well connected, and not necessarily the most innovative. In a school, the teacher whom colleagues ask "have you tried this?" is an opinion leader. A change agent is a person who works, on behalf of an organization, to influence the adoption of an innovation in a desired direction. Instructional coaches, technology integrators, and principals are change agents. The most effective change agents work with and through opinion leaders, since an outsider's recommendation counts for less than a trusted colleague's.

docs.title: Worked Example: Choosing a Messenger
docs.text:
Ms. Okafor wants to bring the early majority along. She considers two teachers to demonstrate the Level 2 textbook at the district meeting.

Candidate Profile How colleagues see them Verdict Mr. Park An innovator who tries every new tool and presents at conferences "He'll try anything; it won't work for the rest of us" Poor messenger for the early majority Ms. Rivera A respected veteran, cautious, who adopted only after she saw it work and changed her mind publicly "If she says it helps, it helps" An opinion leader; the right messenger

The tempting choice is the enthusiast. The right choice is the person whose endorsement the early majority will believe, which is a decision about trust and not about technical skill.

Pick the respected skeptic

When you need peers to believe a pilot worked, put the most respected cautious colleague on stage, not the biggest enthusiast. A skeptic who changed their mind is worth ten champions.

docs.title: The Chasm
docs.text:
The author and consultant Geoffrey Moore, in his 1991 book Crossing the Chasm, argued that Rogers' curve hides a gap. The two groups on either side of the first boundary want different things, and the usual ways of winning the first group do not work on the second.

The chasm is the gap, between the early adopters and the early majority, that an innovation must cross to become widely used. Early adopters, whom Moore calls visionaries, are willing to accept a new product that is incomplete and risky because they see a chance for a big payoff. Pragmatist buyers make up the early majority. They want a solid, proven product that fits into how they already work, and they take their cue from references, from other pragmatists like themselves. They do not want to be the first, and they will not take a risk for a vision. Because early adopters cannot give pragmatists what they need, and pragmatists will not buy until others like them do, many innovations that thrive with the first 16 percent of adopters stall completely at the gap.

Crossing the chasm is the work of moving an innovation from the early adopters to the early majority. Two ideas from Moore's strategy matter most for schools.

A beachhead strategy is the choice to concentrate all effort on winning one narrow, well-defined group first, in the way an army lands on one beach before advancing, instead of spreading effort thinly across everyone. Moore's image is the D-Day landing in Normandy. In a school system, a beachhead might be "seventh-grade math at one or two schools," where the new approach is made to work completely, visibly, and with reference stories, before expanding to every subject.

A whole product is the complete solution a pragmatist needs, including everything around the core product that makes it work in practice: the training, the integration with existing systems, the support, the instructions, and the answers to the worries about privacy and safety. Pragmatists do not buy a "technology"; they buy something that works on Monday morning. For a school, the whole product of a Level 2 textbook includes login and learning-management-system integration (Chapter 9), accessibility, teacher training, a plan for students without devices, and a family communication plan.

docs.title: Worked Example: Lincoln's Chasm
docs.text:
The district has about 64 teachers in the innovator and early-adopter groups, and Ms. Okafor's pilot reached six of them. Here is what the chasm looks like in her situation, and what crossing it means.

Early adopters (the pilot) Early majority (the other 136 teachers) What they want A chance to try something new and make it work Proof it works, ease, and support Who they listen to Their own vision and conference talks Colleagues like them, in schools like theirs What the pilot offered An unfinished tool and a lot of help from Ms. Okafor Not yet: no training package, no integration, no references Beachhead to choose Seventh-grade math in two more schools, with the full package Whole product to build Single sign-on, a one-hour training, a parent letter, an accessibility check, a plan for students without home devices

The pilot was not wasted. It produced the reference stories of Ms. Rivera and a set of lessons about what the whole product must include. But expanding it unchanged to every school would be crossing the chasm by hope.

docs.title: Diagram: Choose the Move to Cross the Chasm
docs.text:
Run the Choose the Move to Cross the Chasm MicroSim Fullscreen

Choose the Move to Cross the Chasm

Type: microsim sim-id: choose-chasm-crossing-move Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: apply Learning Objective: The learner will apply Moore's chasm ideas by choosing, for each of six situations, the move that best helps an innovation cross from early adopters to the early majority, correctly choosing at least five of six on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: the chasm, pragmatist buyers, crossing the chasm, beachhead strategy, whole product, opinion leader (all defined in the sections "Adopter Categories and the Adoption Curve" and "The Chasm" above).

Evidence of Mastery: For each of 6 situations, the learner selects one of four moves and submits it. A choice is correct when it matches the "Best move" column in Content. Mastery is 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt. Reading the move definitions is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) More features will persuade pragmatists. (2) Spreading effort across every group is safer than focusing. (3) Enthusiasm from innovators proves the product is ready for everyone.

Instructional Rationale: Choosing the best move for a situation requires diagnosing what the pragmatists lack: a focus, a complete solution, a trusted reference, or proof. Distractors that sound reasonable but target the wrong group force the learner to apply the ideas, not recognize the vocabulary.

Content:

Four moves shown for every situation:

Move Definition shown Choose a beachhead Focus all effort on one narrow, well-defined group and make the innovation work completely there first Build the whole product Add the training, integration, support, and safeguards that make it work in practice Use a trusted reference Let a respected peer from a similar setting tell the story Add more features Extend what the product can do for the most enthusiastic users

Six situations:

# Situation shown to the learner Best move Why (shown as feedback) 1 A district rolled a new tool out to all 40 schools at once, and a little support went to each, so none of them has a visible success. Choose a beachhead Spreading thin produced no visible success; focus on one group first. 2 Teachers like the tool but say, "It doesn't connect to our login system and there is no training, so we can't use it." Build the whole product Pragmatists need integration and training, not more interest. 3 A skeptical veteran teacher at another school asks, "Has anyone like me made this work?" Use a trusted reference Pragmatists trust peers who are like them. 4 Enthusiasts are asking for five new advanced features, but the early majority says it cannot adopt without training, a simple sign-in, and a support line. Build the whole product Pragmatists need a complete, supported solution, not more features. 5 Principals say they would adopt if only there were a one-page plan for parents, a privacy review, and an accessibility check. Build the whole product These are parts of the whole product around the core tool. 6 The early majority teachers at the neighboring school say they would try it if a colleague they respect had already made it work in a similar class. Use a trusted reference The decisive factor is a respected peer's experience.

Provenance: The moves follow Moore's Crossing the Chasm as summarized in the chapter. The situations are illustrative, written for this chapter.

Rules: Each situation has exactly one best move, given in Content. A situation is scored on its first submitted choice only. The score counts first-attempt correct choices out of 6. Mastery is a score >= 5. The move "Add more features" is never the best move in this set.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads one situation and sees the four moves.
  2. The learner selects a move and submits it. The sim marks it correct or incorrect and shows the feedback text.
  3. If incorrect, the learner may choose again; the second attempt does not change the score. After the second attempt, the correct move and reason are shown.
  4. After all 6 situations, the sim shows the score.
  5. The learner should notice that "add more features" is never the right answer for the early majority, and that building the whole product is the best move in three of the six situations.

Feedback: 6 situations, shuffled once per session, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: [move]. [Why text]." Incorrect: "Not quite. Ask what the early majority is missing. [Why text for the correct answer, without naming the move]." After the second attempt the correct move is revealed and the situation counts as missed. A running score "First-try correct: n of 6" is shown. Final message for a score >= 5: "You can pick the move that crosses the chasm." For a score < 5: "Review the four moves and try again; the situations will be reshuffled."

Starting State: Situation 1 of the shuffled order is shown with the four moves, the score "First-try correct: 0 of 6," and the prompt "Which move best helps this innovation cross the chasm?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter defines the chasm as the gap between early adopters and the early majority, and names the beachhead strategy, the whole product, and trusted references as the moves for crossing it. The mastery bar is 5 of 6.

docs.title: The Hype Cycle and Educational Technology
docs.text:
Technologies do not spread in a smooth line. They attract attention in bursts. The hype cycle, a model developed by the research firm Gartner in the mid-1990s, describes the typical pattern of expectations about a new technology over time, in five stages:

  1. Innovation trigger: a breakthrough or product launch sparks interest.
  2. Peak of inflated expectations: publicity builds, success stories are repeated, and expectations exceed what the technology can do. The peak of inflated expectations is the point of maximum hype.
  3. Trough of disillusionment: the technology fails to meet the inflated expectations, interest fades, and early projects are abandoned. The trough of disillusionment is the low point of confidence.
  4. Slope of enlightenment: a smaller group continues experimenting and learns what the technology is actually good for.
  5. Plateau of productivity: the technology is understood, its benefits are realized, and it is adopted for what it does well. The plateau of productivity is steady, useful adoption.

The hype cycle is a useful description and not a scientific law. Academic reviews have found limited evidence that technologies follow it reliably, and Gartner's placements are judgments. Its value is as a reminder that expectations and reality diverge in a predictable direction early on, and that the disappointment of the trough is not necessarily the end of the technology.

EdTech hype waves are the repeated cycles of hype and disappointment that educational technology has gone through, each with its own peak and trough. The history of Chapter 3 gave several: film in 1913, teaching machines in the 1950s, classroom computers in the 1980s, interactive whiteboards, and one-to-one tablets, such as the Los Angeles iPad rollout of 2013, which was cancelled after technical problems, weak curriculum, and a scandal over the contract. The most recent clear wave before AI was the massive open online course. The New York Times called 2012 "the year of the MOOC," and universities rushed to join. By 2013, the Udacity founder Sebastian Thrun was quoted saying that the product was "lousy" for many students, and completion rates for the free courses were often under ten percent. MOOCs did not vanish. They settled into a useful niche in professional and continuing education.

(Bloom level: Understand. Bloom verb: explain.)

docs.title: Worked Example: Where Is Generative AI?
docs.text:
The table places events in the story of generative AI in schools on the hype cycle. It is a reading of the evidence, and you should expect reasonable people to disagree about the exact stage.

Event Stage Why ChatGPT released in November 2022 Innovation trigger A breakthrough product sparks wide interest 2023 predictions that AI tutors would replace teachers; schools ban, then rush to adopt Peak of inflated expectations Expectations well beyond what studies show Reports of tutors giving wrong answers, students offloading thinking, a vendor collapsing after a large district purchase Toward the trough Real failures meet the inflated claims Randomized studies showing guided tutors help and open access harms Slope of enlightenment Experiments clarify what works and why Guided AI built into ordinary tools, with guardrails Plateau of productivity (not yet reached) The settled, useful use

The important implication for a school: if the hype cycle is a fair picture, the schools that gain most are the ones that neither join the peak nor flee the trough. They learn during the trough, with small pilots, so that they are ready when the slope arrives.

Disappointment is data, not a verdict

Notice what the trough of disillusionment really is: the moment when claims meet evidence. Some technologies fall out of use there, and others, like MOOCs, find their real job. A school that watches the trough closely learns what is genuinely useful, and learns it cheaply.

Misconceptions: (1) The trough means a technology has failed. (2) The peak is when a technology is most useful. (3) Every technology follows the cycle exactly.

Instructional Rationale: Classifying events by the pattern of expectations they show, rather than by the technology's quality, makes the learner use the cycle as a lens. Events from different technologies show the same shape recurring.

Content:

Five stages with definitions on request:

Stage Definition shown Innovation trigger A breakthrough or launch sparks interest Peak of inflated expectations Publicity and expectations exceed what the technology can do Trough of disillusionment Failures meet the inflated expectations and interest falls Slope of enlightenment Experiments clarify what the technology is good for Plateau of productivity The technology is understood and used for what it does well

Eight events:

# Event shown to the learner Correct stage Why (shown as feedback) 1 In November 2012 a major newspaper calls the year "the year of the MOOC," and universities rush to offer free online courses. Peak of inflated expectations Publicity and expectations are at their highest. 2 In 2013 a leading MOOC founder says that much of the product is "lousy," and completion rates are often under ten percent. Trough of disillusionment Failures meet the inflated expectations. 3 Online courses settle into a useful niche in professional and continuing education, with clear uses. Plateau of productivity The technology is understood and used for what it does well. 4 In 2013 a large district announces a plan to give every student a tablet. Peak of inflated expectations A large rollout is announced on the strength of expectations. 5 The tablet plan is cancelled after technical problems, weak curriculum, and a contract scandal. Trough of disillusionment The failures meet the inflated expectations. 6 A general-purpose AI chatbot is released to the public in November 2022 and attracts enormous attention. Innovation trigger A breakthrough product sparks interest. 7 Randomized studies show a guided AI tutor helps and open chatbot access harms later exam scores. Slope of enlightenment Experiments clarify what works and why. 8 A few teachers, after the 1980s computer boom, continue experimenting with computers for programming and writing and develop effective practices. Provenance: The stages follow the Gartner hype cycle as described in the chapter. Rules: Each event has exactly one correct stage, given in Content. An event is scored on its first submitted placement only. The score counts first-attempt correct placements out of 8. Mastery is a score >= 7.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees one event at a time and the five stages.
  2. The learner places the event and submits it. The sim marks it correct or incorrect and shows the feedback text.
  3. If incorrect, the learner may place it again; the second attempt does not change the score. After the second attempt, the correct stage and reason are shown.
  4. After all 8 events, the sim shows the score and the events arranged along the cycle.
  5. The learner should notice that the MOOC and the tablet stories follow the same shape, and that the trough is followed by learning, not only abandonment.

Feedback: 8 events, shuffled once per session, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: [stage]. [Why text]." Incorrect: "Not quite. [Why text for the correct answer, without naming the stage]." After the second attempt the correct stage is revealed and the event counts as missed. A running score "First-try correct: n of 8" is shown. Final message for a score >= 7: "You can read the hype cycle in a story." For a score < 7: "Review the five stages and try again; the events will be reshuffled."

docs.title: Adoption Readiness
docs.text:
Adoption readiness is the degree to which a person, school, or district is prepared to adopt a particular innovation. It has two sides. One is the innovation's readiness, as the five attributes measure: how advantageous, compatible, simple, trialable, and observable it appears. The other is the organization's readiness: whether it has the devices, connectivity, time, training, leadership support, and trust that adoption needs, and whether its culture is open to change. A strong innovation in an unready school stalls, and a mediocre one in a ready school can succeed for the wrong reasons.

A practical readiness check asks six questions of a school before a pilot:

  1. Does the innovation score well on the five attributes for our teachers?
  2. Do teachers have the time and training to try it?
  3. Do students have the devices and connectivity (Chapter 9)?
  4. Do we have the privacy and governance basics in place for its level (Chapter 10)?
  5. Is there an opinion leader willing to try it and be honest about it?
  6. Is the principal ready to protect the pilot from other demands?

docs.title: Worked Example: A Barrier Diagnosis
docs.text:
The district's second school, Eastside, tries the same Level 2 textbook, and after a month only two of fifteen teachers are using it. The principal collects the reasons teachers give.

What teachers say Which attribute is the barrier "It doesn't fit our pacing guide, which says what to teach each week." Compatibility "I couldn't figure out how to log the students in." Complexity "I'm not sure it's better than the book we have." Relative advantage "I'd try it, but the district says we must commit for a year." Trialability "I don't know anyone who has used it; I've never seen it in a classroom." Observability

Five teachers, five different attributes. The fix is therefore not a single push, such as more training, but a targeted response to each: align the textbook with the pacing guide, simplify the sign-in, share Maya's results, offer a one-unit trial, and invite colleagues to visit Ms. Rivera's classroom. The attributes make the diagnosis specific.

Mastery is 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Reading the attribute definitions is exploration, not evidence.

Instructional Rationale: Attributing a comment to an attribute requires reading the reason behind it, such as a fit problem, a difficulty problem, or a visibility problem. Comments that sound alike but differ in cause, such as "doesn't fit my schedule" and "too hard to use," make the learner separate the attributes.

Five attributes with definitions on request:

Attribute Definition shown Relative advantage Perceived as better than what it replaces Compatibility Consistent with existing values, practices, and needs Complexity Perceived as difficult to understand and use Trialability Can be tried on a limited basis Observability Results are visible to others

Eight comments:

# Teacher comment shown to the learner Barrier attribute Why (shown as feedback) 1 "It doesn't match the weekly pacing guide I am required to follow." Compatibility It conflicts with an existing requirement. 2 "I spent an hour and still couldn't get the students logged in." Relative advantage The benefit over the current practice is not clear. 4 "I'd try it for a unit, but the contract is for three years with no exit." Trialability It cannot be tried on a limited basis. 5 "I've never seen a class using it, so I can't picture how it would go." Observability The results are not visible to the teacher. 6 "It would mean giving up the group discussions that I believe in." Compatibility It conflicts with a practice the teacher values. 7 "The sign-in, the settings, and the dashboard are too much to learn." Complexity It is perceived as too complicated. 8 "Nobody in our school can tell me what difference it made." Observability The benefit is not visible to others.

Provenance: Definitions follow the chapter section "The Five Innovation Attributes" and Rogers (2003). The comments are illustrative, written for this chapter.

Rules: Each comment has exactly one barrier attribute, given in Content. A comment is scored on its first submitted placement only. The score counts first-attempt correct placements out of 8. Mastery is a score >= 7.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees one comment at a time and the five attributes.
  2. The learner places the comment and submits it. The sim marks it correct or incorrect and shows the feedback text.
  3. If incorrect, the learner may place it again; the second attempt does not change the score. After the second attempt, the correct attribute and reason are shown.
  4. After all 8 comments, the sim shows the score and the misplaced comments with their correct attributes.
  5. The learner should notice that two comments each point to compatibility, complexity, and observability, and that none of them is a matter of willingness.

Feedback: 8 comments, shuffled once per session, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: [attribute]. [Why text]." Incorrect: "Not quite. [Why text for the correct answer, without naming the attribute]." After the second attempt the correct attribute is revealed and the comment counts as missed. A running score "First-try correct: n of 8" is shown. Final message for a score >= 7: "You can name the barrier behind a comment." For a score < 7: "Review the five attributes and try again; the comments will be reshuffled."

Starting State: Comment 1 of the shuffled order is shown with the five attributes, the score "First-try correct: 0 of 8," and the prompt "Which attribute is the barrier?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter lists five attributes (relative advantage, compatibility, complexity, trialability, observability) and the Eastside barrier diagnosis. The mastery bar is 7 of 8.

docs.title: Estonia: A System Adopting on Purpose
docs.text: One real case shows a whole system working with these ideas. The book's AI-First Stories appendix describes Estonia's AI Leap (in Estonian, TI-Hüpe), a national program launched in 2025 that gives secondary students and teachers access to AI learning tools, along with teacher training. It builds on Estonia's earlier success bringing computers and programming into its schools. By the terms of this chapter, the strategy has several of the right features: it began with a defined group (a beachhead of older students and their teachers), it paired the tool with training (part of a whole product), it had the backing of a national government (a change agent), and it built on a record of earlier success (compatibility and credibility). The program is new and its results are not yet known, so it is a useful model of method and not yet proof of effect.

docs.title: Answering the Question from the Other Principal
docs.text:
Ms. Okafor's colleague asked why her result for six teachers should work for his forty. The answer from this chapter is that it will not automatically, and that the reasons are knowable. The innovation has to look good on the five attributes to his teachers. The early majority at his school need proof from people like them, so an opinion leader, not an enthusiast, should carry the story. The pilot must be turned into a whole product with training, support, and integration, and the first expansion should be a beachhead, with a few schools and one grade, instead of everyone at once. And the district should expect a trough: some early enthusiasm will fade, and what remains will be what works.

The story has both sides. The benefit: a clear method for getting a good idea past the first sixteen percent of adopters. The risks: mistaking early adopters' enthusiasm for general readiness, rolling out too widely and too fast, riding the hype and then abandoning a useful tool at the trough, and treating hesitant teachers as the problem. The response: diagnose the attributes, pick a beachhead, build the whole product, choose the right messengers, and treat the trough as a learning period.

Don't mistake the first 16 percent for everyone

A common trap is reading a pilot's success as proof of readiness for the whole system, when the pilot was run by people who wanted to try it. Instead, ask what the early majority will need that the pilot did not provide, such as training, integration, references, and a trial that doesn't lock them in, and plan for that before you scale.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• An innovation is anything perceived as new; diffusion of innovations is its spread through channels, over time, in a social system, and it moves through trust in peers more than through announcements.
  • The five innovation attributes, relative advantage, compatibility, complexity, trialability, and observability, predict much of the speed of spread and diagnose a stall.
  • The technology adoption curve has innovators (2.5%), early adopters (13.5%), the early majority (34%), the late majority (34%), and laggards (16%); the S-curve of adoption is the cumulative form, with the steepest part in the early majority.
  • Opinion leaders persuade by respect, and change agents work through them; pick the respected skeptic as messenger.
  • The chasm lies between early adopters and the early majority; pragmatist buyers want proof and a whole product. Crossing the chasm works through a beachhead strategy and trusted references.
  • The hype cycle, with its peak of inflated expectations, trough of disillusionment, and plateau of productivity, describes expectations over time; EdTech hype waves have repeated, from MOOCs to tablets, and the trough is a time to learn.
  • Adoption readiness has an innovation side and an organization side; diagnose a stall by attribute, not by blaming people.

You can say why a good idea stalls

You just learned how innovations spread, how to score them on five attributes, why they stall at the chasm, and how to ride the hype cycle without being thrown by it. Chapter 16 widens the lens from a technology to a whole organization and the models of how organizations change. One step at a time, together.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: Technology Adoption and the Diffusion of Innovation
docs.text: Test your understanding of how innovations spread, the five innovation attributes, adopter categories, the chasm, and the hype cycle with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. In Rogers' adopter categories, what share of adopters do innovators and early adopters make up together?
docs.text:
1. About 2.5 percent
  2. About 34 percent
  3. About 16 percent
  4. About 50 percent
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Innovators are 2.5 percent and early adopters 13.5 percent, for a combined 16 percent. The early majority and late majority are 34 percent each, and laggards are 16 percent. The cumulative shares at the end of each category are 2.5, 16, 50, 84, and 100 percent. The 16 percent point matters because Moore's chasm lies right after it, where many innovations that thrive with the first adopters stall.

Concept Tested: Technology Adoption Curve

See: Adopter Categories and the Adoption Curve

docs.title: 2. Which of Rogers' five innovation attributes is the degree to which an innovation can be tried on a limited basis before committing?
docs.text:
1. Trialability
  2. Observability
  3. Compatibility
  4. Relative advantage
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Trialability is the degree to which an innovation can be tried on a limited basis, such as a free Level 2 textbook used with one class for one unit. A three-year district contract has low trialability. Observability is whether results are visible to others, compatibility is fit with existing values and practice, and relative advantage is whether it is perceived as better than what it replaces.

Concept Tested: Trialability

See: The Five Innovation Attributes

docs.title: 3. Why do many innovations stall at the chasm between early adopters and the early majority?
docs.text:
1. Because early adopters lose interest once a product becomes popular with others
  2. Because the early majority cannot afford the products that early adopters can buy
  3. Because laggards actively campaign against new products at that point
  4. Because pragmatists want peer proof and a whole product, which visionaries can't give
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Geoffrey Moore argued that early adopters, the visionaries, accept incomplete and risky products for a chance at a big payoff. The early majority are pragmatist buyers who want a solid, proven product that fits how they already work, and they take their cue from other pragmatists. Because each group wants something different, the usual ways of winning visionaries do not work on pragmatists. Cost and laggard opposition are not the mechanism Moore describes.

Concept Tested: The Chasm

See: The Chasm

docs.title: 4. A teacher explains why she has not tried a new adaptive tool: "The vendor requires two full days of training before I can even open it." Which innovation attribute is the barrier?
docs.text:
1. Observability
  2. Complexity
  3. Relative advantage
  4. Compatibility
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Complexity is the degree to which an innovation is perceived as difficult to understand and use, and it works against adoption. The chapter gives exactly this case: a teacher who must attend a two-day training before opening the software has met high complexity. Observability would be "I've never seen it used," relative advantage would be "I'm not sure it's better," and compatibility would be "it doesn't fit our pacing guide."

Concept Tested: Complexity

See: Worked Example: A Barrier Diagnosis

docs.title: 5. A principal needs a teacher to present pilot results so that cautious colleagues will try a new tool. Who is the better messenger, according to the chapter?
docs.text:
1. The teacher who tries every new tool first and presents at national conferences
  2. The district technology director, who has the most technical knowledge
  3. A respected, cautious veteran who adopted only after seeing it work
  4. The vendor's representative, who knows the product's features best
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. An opinion leader influences through informal respect, not authority, and is often close to the group's norm. The early majority want proof from people like them, so a respected skeptic who changed her mind is the right messenger. The chapter calls the enthusiast the tempting choice and a poor messenger, because colleagues think "he'll try anything; it won't work for the rest of us." Technical knowledge and a vendor's pitch count for less than a trusted colleague's word.

Concept Tested: Opinion Leader

See: Worked Example: Choosing a Messenger

docs.title: 6. According to the chapter, how should a school treat the trough of disillusionment in the hype cycle?
docs.text:
1. As a time to learn with small pilots about what the technology is good for
  2. As proof that the technology has failed and should be abandoned by schools
  3. As a signal to buy at scale while vendors are offering low prices
  4. As a stage that only affects technologies with no real classroom benefits
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The trough is the moment when claims meet evidence. Some technologies fall out of use there, and others, like MOOCs, find their real job. The chapter says the schools that gain most neither join the peak nor flee the trough; they learn during it with small pilots so they are ready when the slope of enlightenment arrives. Abandoning the technology confuses disappointment with a verdict, and buying at scale ignores what the trough teaches.

Concept Tested: Trough of Disillusionment

See: Worked Example: Where Is Generative AI?

docs.title: 7. A district has 600 teachers. Using Rogers' percentages, how many teachers are in the early majority?
docs.text:
1. About 81
  2. About 300
  3. About 96
  4. About 204
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The early majority is 34 percent of adopters, and 0.34 x 600 = 204 teachers. About 81 would be the 13.5 percent of early adopters, about 96 would be the 16 percent of innovators and early adopters combined (or laggards), and 300 is the cumulative count at the 50 percent point, the end of the early majority. The chapter's 400-teacher example shows the early majority is a different audience that needs proof, simplicity, and trusted colleagues.

Concept Tested: Early Majority

See: Worked Example: A District of 400 Teachers

docs.title: 8. How does the chapter distinguish an opinion leader from a change agent?
docs.text:
1. An opinion leader is paid by a vendor; a change agent works for the school board
  2. An opinion leader persuades by respect; a change agent works for an organization
  3. An opinion leader always adopts first; a change agent always adopts last
  4. An opinion leader sets district policy; a change agent trains new teachers
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. An opinion leader is a member of a social system whom others look to for advice, influencing through respect rather than authority. A change agent, such as an instructional coach, technology integrator, or principal, works on behalf of an organization to influence adoption in a desired direction. The chapter says the most effective change agents work through opinion leaders. Opinion leaders are not necessarily the most innovative, so they do not always adopt first.

Concept Tested: Change Agent

See: Opinion Leaders and Change Agents

docs.title: 9. After a successful six-teacher pilot of a Level 2 textbook in seventh-grade math, a superintendent proposes rolling it out to every school and every subject next fall. Which plan best fits the chapter's analysis?
docs.text:
1. Pick a beachhead, such as one grade in two more schools, and build the whole product
  2. Proceed with the full rollout, since the pilot proves the district is ready
  3. Wait until every teacher in the district volunteers before expanding
  4. Expand to every subject but only in the pilot school, so its teachers can lead
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The pilot was run by innovators and early adopters, so its success does not prove the early majority is ready. Moore's beachhead strategy concentrates effort on one narrow group and makes the approach work completely before expanding. Pragmatists also need a whole product: single sign-on, short training, a parent letter, an accessibility check, and a plan for students without devices. A full rollout is crossing the chasm by hope, and waiting for every volunteer ignores the late majority and laggards.

Concept Tested: Beachhead Strategy

See: Worked Example: Lincoln's Chasm

docs.title: 10. A district scores a Level 2 open textbook at 21 of 25 on the five innovation attributes and a Level 4 chat tutor at 13, mainly because the tutor is low on compatibility, complexity, and trialability. What does this comparison predict?
docs.text:
1. The chat tutor will spread faster, since its relative advantage is the highest
  2. Both will spread at the same rate, since the attributes do not affect adoption
  3. The textbook should spread quickly; the tutor slowly, with more groundwork
  4. The textbook will stall at the chasm, since free products lack a whole product
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Rogers found the five attributes account for roughly half or more of the variation in adoption rates. The chapter's illustrative scores predict that the Level 2 textbook, which fits existing lessons and is free to try, should spread quickly, while the Level 4 tutor, which raises privacy and cheating concerns and needs a privacy review before trial, should spread slowly. The scores are judgments, but they force a school to say why it expects spread or stall. The tutor's relative advantage was scored lower, not higher.

Concept Tested: Five Innovation Attributes

See: Worked Example: Scoring Two Innovations

docs.title: References: Technology Adoption and the Diffusion of Innovation
docs.text:
1. Diffusion of innovations - Wikipedia - Covers Rogers' theory of how new ideas spread, including the five innovation attributes, adopter categories, opinion leaders, and the S-curve. It is the backbone of this chapter's vocabulary.

  2. Technology adoption life cycle - Wikipedia - Describes the bell curve of innovators, early adopters, early majority, late majority, and laggards, and notes Moore's chasm between the first groups. It helps readers place teachers on the adoption curve.

  3. Gartner hype cycle - Wikipedia - Explains the five phases from technology trigger to plateau of productivity and summarizes criticism that few technologies follow the full cycle. Useful for judging generative AI claims with appropriate skepticism.

  4. Diffusion of Innovations (5th ed.) - Everett M. Rogers - Free Press - Rogers' synthesis of decades of diffusion studies, credited with the five attributes (relative advantage, compatibility, complexity, trialability, observability) and the adopter categories. It explains why a good innovation can still spread slowly.

  5. Crossing the Chasm (3rd ed.) - Geoffrey A. Moore - HarperBusiness - Moore's argument that pragmatist buyers will not follow visionaries without a whole product and peer references, and that a beachhead strategy wins them. It explains why pilot success with enthusiasts rarely spreads district-wide.

  6. Diffusion of Innovations (TheoryHub) - Newcastle University - A plain-language review of Rogers' theory, covering attributes, the innovation-decision process, the S-curve, critical mass, and criticisms such as pro-innovation bias. A balanced short reference for leadership teams.

  7. Quaking Up with Geoffrey Moore - strategy+business - A free profile of Moore and his adoption frameworks, from Crossing the Chasm onward, and how they apply to established organizations. It adds context for the chasm, pragmatists, and whole-product ideas in the chapter.

  8. Top Ed-Tech Trends of 2013: MOOCs and Anti-MOOCs - Hack Education (Audrey Watters) - A critic's account of MOOCs sliding from the peak of inflated expectations into the trough of disillusionment. It is a concrete recent example of an edtech hype wave.

  9. The Recurring Cycle of Hype and Despair Around Ed Tech - Punya Mishra - Traces repeated edtech promises, from 1930s talking pictures to MOOCs, and argues they fail when they focus on the tool rather than teaching. A useful caution for AI adoption plans.

  10. AI Leap (TI-Hüpe) - AI Leap Foundation, Estonia - Describes Estonia's national program pairing teacher training, a guided AI learning app, and independent evaluation by the University of Tartu. It is the chapter's main example of a system adopting on purpose.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter names the major organizational change models used later in the book — Kotter's eight steps, Lewin's unfreeze-change-refreeze, ADKAR, Bridges' transition model, Schein's culture model, Senge's learning organization, Fullan's educational change, and the Concerns-Based Adoption Model — along with organizational and school culture. Readers finish able to name each model and what it is used for before studying any one in depth.
