docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: The Building Blocks of Schools, Students, and Learning
  • Chapter 6: The Five-Level Model of Intelligent Textbooks
  • Chapter 15: Technology Adoption and the Diffusion of Innovation

docs.title: Too Many Models, One School
docs.text:
After the district meeting, Ms. Okafor's phone fills with advice. The superintendent's office sends a link to an article on "Kotter's eight steps." A consultant recommends "ADKAR." A teacher, who took a course last year, writes that what the staff needs is "Lewin, and especially the refreezing part." A board member says the real issue is "culture," and that "you can't change a school without changing its culture."

Everyone is right, in a way, and she is overwhelmed. Each person has named a real model, built by serious researchers and used for decades, and each model sees the problem from a different angle. The trouble is that there are many of them, they use overlapping words, and it is not clear which one to use when.

This chapter is a map. It names each of the major models, says in a sentence what it is for, and shows how to tell which to reach for. It does not teach any one in depth. Chapter 17 does that for the early stages of change, and Chapters 18 and 19 for the later stages and for small, practical moves. The goal here is that when Ms. Okafor's phone fills up again, she can sort the advice into a toolbox.

A map before the tools

This chapter doesn't ask you to master eight models; it asks you to know what each is for, so you pick the right one for the question in front of you. By the end you'll be able to name each model and say when it earns its place. Let's find the balance between using the research and not drowning in it.

docs.title: What Organizational Change Is
docs.text:
Organizational change is the process by which an organization moves from its current way of working to a different one, whether in structure, technology, processes, people, or culture. In a school, moving from a six-period day to a morning-and-afternoon design, or adopting a Level 3 textbook, is organizational change, since it alters what many people do each day, and not only what one person does.

The research on change makes three points that apply to every model below. Change is planned and emergent: leaders set a direction, and the people doing the work reshape it as they go. Change is emotional: it brings loss, uncertainty, and anxiety alongside opportunity. And change is slow: culture and habits, not technology, set the pace. You will often see the claim that "70 percent of change efforts fail," repeated in books and talks. The figure is poorly sourced, and a 2011 review by Mark Hughes found no solid evidence for it. What the research does support is that many large change efforts fall short of their goals, and that the usual reasons are about people, not technology.

docs.title: Worked Example: Is This Change Organizational?
docs.text:
Change Organizational change? Why One teacher tries a new simulation in her own class No (an individual practice change) Only one person's work changes Six teachers in one school pilot the Level 2 textbook Small A group's routines change The district adopts Level 3 textbooks and changes the schedule Yes Structures, roles, schedules, and culture all change The district hires a new superintendent Not by itself A change of person is not a change of how work is done

The last row is worth remembering. Replacing a leader is easy to do and rarely changes an organization unless the way of working changes.

docs.title: The Models at a Glance
docs.text:
Eight models and ideas do most of the work in education change. Each is introduced here with its author, its central idea, and the question it answers best.

Kotter's eight steps is a model of leading large-scale change, from John Kotter of Harvard Business School, first published in 1995 and expanded in his 1996 book Leading Change. It gives eight steps in order: establish a sense of urgency, form a guiding coalition, create a vision, communicate the vision, remove obstacles, create short-term wins, build on the change, and anchor the changes in the culture. It answers the question what should leaders do, and in what order? Chapters 17 and 18 take the steps in two halves.

Lewin's change model, from the psychologist Kurt Lewin in 1947, describes change as three stages: unfreeze the current way of doing things, change to the new way, and refreeze so that the new way becomes stable. It answers what are the basic phases of any change? and is the oldest and simplest model on the list. It also gave the field the idea of forces for and against change.

The ADKAR model, from Jeff Hiatt of the firm Prosci, published in 2006, is a model of change at the level of the individual. It has five elements, each of which a person needs in order to change: Awareness of the need, Desire to take part, Knowledge of how to change, Ability to do it, and Reinforcement to sustain it. It answers where is this person stuck? and is useful because it points at a specific missing element.

Bridges' transition model, from William Bridges in 1991, separates change (the external event, such as a new schedule) from transition (the internal, psychological process of adjusting to it). Transition runs through three phases: an ending, a neutral zone of confusion, and a new beginning. It answers how are people feeling, and what do they need now? and it is the model that takes loss seriously.

Schein's culture model, from Edgar Schein of MIT, describes the culture of an organization at three levels: the visible artifacts, the stated values, and the unseen basic assumptions beneath them. It answers why does the organization resist what it says it wants? and explains why change efforts that alter only the visible surface fail.

Senge's learning organization, from Peter Senge's 1990 book The Fifth Discipline, describes an organization that continually expands its capacity to create the results it wants, built from five disciplines. It answers how do we become a place that keeps improving, instead of running one change after another?

Fullan's educational change, from Michael Fullan, a Canadian researcher of school reform, applies change research specifically to schools. It stresses that change succeeds through a school's people and culture, that the early period of any change brings a dip in performance, and that coherence across a system matters. It answers what is different about changing a school?

The Concerns-Based Adoption Model (CBAM), developed by Gene Hall, Shirley Hord, and colleagues at the University of Texas in the 1970s, was built specifically to track how teachers adopt new practices. It examines three things: the concerns a teacher has about the change, how the teacher actually uses the innovation, and what the innovation looks like in practice. It answers where is each teacher, and what do they need next?

Model Level it works at The question it answers Where it goes deeper Kotter's eight steps The whole organization, led from the top What should leaders do, in order? Chapters 17 and 18 Lewin's three stages Any change What are the basic phases? Chapter 17 ADKAR The individual Where is this person stuck? Chapter 17 Bridges' transition model The individual's feelings What do people need during transition? Chapter 17 Schein's culture model The organization's culture Why do we resist what we say we want? Chapter 17 Senge's learning organization The organization's capacity How do we keep learning? Chapter 18 Fullan's educational change Schools and systems What is distinctive about school change? Chapter 18 CBAM The teacher Where is each teacher, and what next? Chapters 17 and 19

docs.title: Worked Example: Sorting the Advice
docs.text:
Return to Ms. Okafor's four pieces of advice and place each in the table.

Advice she received Model What it is good for here "Follow Kotter's eight steps" Kotter A sequence for the district's leaders to follow "Use ADKAR" ADKAR Finding which teachers lack awareness, desire, knowledge, or ability "Lewin, especially refreezing" Lewin Making sure the new practice sticks after the pilot "It's about culture" Schein, Fullan Seeing why the school's habits resist the new schedule

None of the four conflicts with the others. They are tools for different jobs: Kotter for leaders' sequence, ADKAR for individuals, Lewin for the shape of the whole change, and Schein for what lies beneath. She does not have to choose one.

docs.title: Diagram: Name That Change Model
docs.text:
Run the Name That Change Model MicroSim Fullscreen

Name That Change Model

Type: microsim sim-id: name-that-change-model Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: classify Learning Objective: The learner will classify eight school change situations by the model that best addresses them, correctly placing at least seven of eight on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: Kotter's eight steps, Lewin's change model, ADKAR, Bridges' transition model, Schein's culture model, Senge's learning organization, Fullan's educational change, the Concerns-Based Adoption Model (all defined in the section "The Models at a Glance" above).

Evidence of Mastery: The learner places each of 8 situations in one of eight model bins and submits it. A placement is correct when it matches the "Best model" column in Content. Mastery is 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Reading the model summaries is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) One model fits every change problem. (2) The models compete and only one is right. (3) A model for individuals can be used to diagnose a culture.

Instructional Rationale: Matching a situation to a model requires finding the question the situation is really asking: sequence, phase, individual gap, feelings, culture, learning capacity, school-specific dynamics, or teacher concerns. One situation per model makes each model's distinctive question stand out.

Content:

Eight models with their one-line question, shown on request:

Model Question it answers Kotter's eight steps What should leaders do, and in what order? Lewin's change model What are the basic phases of a change? ADKAR Where is this individual stuck? Bridges' transition model How are people feeling, and what do they need now? Schein's culture model Why does the organization resist what it says it wants? Senge's learning organization How do we become a place that keeps learning? Fullan's educational change What is distinctive about changing a school, and why does it dip first? CBAM Where is each teacher, in concerns and in use?

Eight situations:

# Situation shown to the learner Best model Why (shown as feedback) 1 A principal wants a plan for the first months of a change: build a team of respected leaders, create urgency, and plan some quick wins. Kotter's eight steps It is a leader's ordered plan for large-scale change. 2 A district leader asks how to think about the phases of the change: loosening old habits, moving to the new practice, and making it stable. Lewin's change model Unfreeze, change, and refreeze are Lewin's three stages. 3 A coach wants to know, for one teacher, whether the missing piece is awareness, desire, knowledge, ability, or reinforcement. ADKAR It locates the missing element for an individual. 4 Teachers are grieving the loss of the lecturer role and are in a confusing in-between period. Bridges' transition model It addresses endings, the neutral zone, and new beginnings. 5 The school says it values collaboration, but in practice classroom doors stay closed and no one expects otherwise. Schein's culture model The stated value and the underlying assumption disagree. 6 The district wants to become a place where teams learn continuously and see the whole system. Senge's learning organization It describes an organization that keeps building its capacity to learn. 7 In the first term of the pilot, scores fell before they rose, and leaders are worried the change is failing. Fullan's educational change It names the implementation dip and expects it. 8 A coach wants to know how each teacher feels about the change and how they actually use it in class. CBAM It tracks teachers' concerns and their level of use.

Provenance: The models and their questions follow the chapter section "The Models at a Glance." The situations are illustrative, written for this chapter.

Rules: Each situation has exactly one best model, given in Content, and each model has exactly one situation. A situation is scored on its first submitted placement only. The score counts first-attempt correct placements out of 8. Mastery is a score >= 7.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees one situation at a time and the eight models.
  2. The learner places the situation and submits it. The sim marks it correct or incorrect and shows the feedback text.
  3. If incorrect, the learner may place it again; the second attempt does not change the score. After the second attempt, the correct model and reason are shown.
  4. After all 8 situations, the sim shows the score and the misplaced situations with their correct models.
  5. The learner should notice that each model is best for a different kind of question.

Feedback: 8 situations, shuffled once per session, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: [model]. [Why text]." Incorrect: "Not quite. Ask what question the situation is really asking. [Why text for the correct answer, without naming the model]." After the second attempt the correct model is revealed and the situation counts as missed. A running score "First-try correct: n of 8" is shown. Final message for a score >= 7: "You can match a model to a change problem." For a score < 7: "Review the eight questions and try again; the situations will be reshuffled."

Starting State: Situation 1 of the shuffled order is shown with the eight models, the score "First-try correct: 0 of 8," and the prompt "Which model best addresses this situation?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter names eight models and the one-sentence question each answers, as in the table. The mastery bar is 7 of 8.

docs.title: Culture: Organizational and School
docs.text:
Organizational culture is the set of shared beliefs, values, assumptions, and habits of behavior that characterize an organization, often summarized as "the way we do things here." It is mostly invisible to the people inside it, because it feels like common sense. A new employee notices it quickly, since it is the unwritten rules: how decisions are really made, who may disagree with whom, and what is rewarded.

School culture is the organizational culture of a school: its shared beliefs and norms about teaching and learning, its rituals and routines, its expectations of students and staff, and the way adults treat each other. Researchers such as Terrence Deal and Kent Peterson have found that a school's culture strongly shapes whether reforms take hold. It is the deeper form of what Tyack and Cuban called the grammar of schooling in Chapter 1: the age-graded classroom, the bell schedule, and the closed classroom door are cultural as well as structural. A school whose culture holds that teaching is a private act will resist collaborative afternoon teams however well they are designed.

docs.title: Worked Example: Culture in Two Schools
docs.text:
Two schools adopt the same Level 2 textbook with the same training.

School A School B Staff norm Teachers share lesson plans and observe each other Teachers work alone; closed doors are respected What happens to the new textbook Teachers swap tips; use spreads in weeks Each teacher decides privately; use stays with the first few adopters After a semester Most teachers use it About one in five use it

The software and the training were identical. The difference was culture, which is why the books on change spend so much time on it, and why Chapter 17 takes up Schein's model.

docs.title: Learning Organizations
docs.text:
A learning organization is an organization that continually expands its capacity to create the results it truly wants, in which people keep learning how to learn together. Peter Senge popularized the idea. It is the opposite of a school that runs one change initiative after another, none lasting, because nobody learns from the last one.

Senge's five disciplines are the practices that build a learning organization:

  1. Personal mastery: each person's commitment to continual growth and to what they truly care about.
  2. Mental models: surfacing and questioning the deeply held assumptions that shape how we see things.
  3. Shared vision: building a picture of the future that people truly want, instead of one imposed on them.
  4. Team learning: groups that think and learn together, with dialogue and not debate.
  5. Systems thinking: seeing the whole system and the connections among its parts, rather than isolated events. Senge called it the fifth discipline because it integrates the others.

The learning organization is the destination of the change models: the point is not a single successful change but a school that handles change well. Chapter 18 treats systems thinking in depth.

docs.title: Fullan, the Implementation Dip, and CBAM
docs.text:
Fullan's educational change is the body of work by Michael Fullan on how change really happens in schools. Three of his ideas recur in this book. Change succeeds through people: the knowledge, skill, and commitment of the teachers who carry it out, not through plans on paper. Change takes time: several years, and not a school year. And change needs coherence: the many initiatives in a school and district have to fit together, since a school asked to do twelve unrelated things will do none of them well.

The implementation dip is the temporary drop in performance and confidence that happens when people begin to use an innovation that requires new skills and new understanding. Fullan described it from many school reform efforts: before the new practice becomes fluent, people are worse at it than they were at the old one. The dip is not a sign of failure. It is the price of learning a skill, and a leader who panics at the first low result and abandons the effort stops just before the payoff. The absence of a dip can itself be a warning, because it may mean that nothing really changed.

docs.title: Worked Example: A Dip in the Data
docs.text:
Lincoln Middle tracks the share of unit-test questions that students answer correctly in the pilot classes. These numbers are illustrative.

Month Share correct 0 (baseline) 70% 1 68% 2 64% 3 63% 4 65% 5 68% 6 71% 9 76% 12 78%

Performance falls from 70 to 63 percent by month 3, a drop of 7 points, or 10 percent of the baseline, then recovers past the baseline at month 6 and reaches 78 percent by month 12. A leader who looked only at months 1 to 3 would call the pilot a failure. One who knows about the implementation dip sees an ordinary shape and prepares teachers and families for it in advance.

The Concerns-Based Adoption Model is the model that lets a leader see where each teacher is. It was created because early studies showed that schools often assumed teachers had adopted a new practice when many had barely begun. CBAM looks at the concerns a teacher holds, which move from "What is this?" and "How will this affect me?" toward "How is it affecting students?" and "How can we do better together?" It also looks at the teacher's level of use, from not using the innovation at all, through awkward mechanical use, to routine and refined use. Chapters 17 and 19 apply it in detail.

The ADKAR model gives the matching view of the individual: Awareness, Desire, Knowledge, Ability, and Reinforcement. Taken in order, they say that a person who does not know why the change is needed (no awareness) will not want it (no desire), and a person who wants it but does not know how (no knowledge) cannot do it (no ability), and without reinforcement will slide back.

docs.title: Worked Example: Two Teachers, Two Diagnoses
docs.text:
Ms. Rivera and a colleague, Mr. Hale, both are struggling with the new textbook.

Ms. Rivera Mr. Hale What they say "I want to use it, but I can't get the students' logins to work" "I don't see why we're changing; the old book worked" ADKAR diagnosis Has awareness and desire; lacks ability (a technical problem) Lacks awareness of the need and desire What helps A coach who fixes the logins today A conversation about the evidence, and visits to a classroom that is using it

The same symptom, "not using it," has two different causes. A leader who gives both teachers more training treats one and ignores the other.

Match the help to the missing piece

When a teacher isn't using a new tool, ask which of the five ADKAR pieces is missing before offering help. Training fixes missing knowledge and ability; it does nothing for missing awareness or desire, and those need a different kind of conversation.

docs.title: Managing Expectations
docs.text:
Managing expectations is the practice of setting, and repeatedly resetting, what people believe the change will deliver and how soon. It draws together three earlier ideas: the hype cycle of Chapter 15, which shows that early expectations run ahead of results; the implementation dip, which shows that results fall before they rise; and the realistic expectations of Chapter 6, which says to describe what each level of textbook can and cannot do.

A leader who promises that the new model will be easy and quick sets the school up for disappointment at the first low result, because the promise and the dip collide. A leader who says in advance, "We expect a dip in the first few months, here is what it will look like, and here is how we will know it is normal," makes the dip part of the plan. This is partly a matter of honesty and partly of trust, since a leader whose predictions come true is believed the next time.

docs.title: Worked Example: Two Letters to Families
docs.text:
Ms. Okafor drafts two versions of the letter to parents before the pilot begins.

Draft 1 Draft 2 Promise "Your child's math scores will go up this semester." "We expect scores to dip slightly in the first two to three months as students and teachers learn the new approach, then recover. We will report every month." What happens at month 3 Scores are down; families feel misled; trust falls Scores are down as predicted; families see the plan is working Effect on the pilot Pressure to stop early Support to continue

She sends Draft 2. It is less exciting and it is far more likely to survive month 3.

docs.title: Diagram: Is This a Normal Dip?
docs.text:
Run the Is This a Normal Dip? MicroSim Fullscreen

Is This a Normal Dip?

Type: microsim sim-id: is-this-a-normal-dip Library: Chart.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: judge Learning Objective: The learner will judge whether each of three pilot performance series shows a normal implementation dip, an unusually deep or late dip, or no dip, applying the stated rule, and correctly judging all three.

Prerequisites: implementation dip, managing expectations, the rule for a normal dip (all defined in the section "Fullan, the Implementation Dip, and CBAM" above).

Evidence of Mastery: For each of 3 monthly series, the learner commits a judgment and also the month of the lowest point, before the sim reveals the correct answers. A judgment is correct when it matches the "Correct judgment" column in Content. Mastery is 3 of 3 judgments correct. Viewing a chart afterward is exploration.

Misconceptions: (1) Any drop below baseline means the pilot is failing. (2) No drop means the pilot is going well. (3) A dip that lasts a year is normal.

Instructional Rationale: Judging a series against explicit thresholds requires reading three numbers from the data: the depth, the time of the low point, and the time of recovery. The no-dip series tests whether the learner understands that a missing dip can signal shallow change.

Content:

The rule shown: A normal dip has its lowest point in months 2 to 4, is no deeper than 15 percent of the baseline, and is back at or above the baseline by month 8. A dip that is deeper than 15 percent, that bottoms after month 4, or that has not recovered by month 8 is "Deep or late: investigate." A series that never falls below 97 percent of the baseline is "No dip: check whether practice really changed."

Baseline for all three series: 70 (percent correct at month 0).

Three series, by month 0 to 12:

Month Series A Series B Series C 0 70 70 70 1 68 69 70 2 64 63 70 3 63 58 71 4 65 55 70 5 68 54 71 6 71 56 70 7 73 58 71 8 75 60 70 9 76 62 71 10 77 63 70 11 78 64 71 12 78 65 71

Answers:

Series Lowest point (month, value) Depth as share of baseline Recovery to baseline Correct judgment Why (shown as feedback) A month 3, 63 10.0% month 6 Normal dip The low is in months 2 to 4, the depth is under 15 percent, and recovery comes before month 8. B month 5, 54 22.9% not by month 12 Deep or late: investigate The low comes after month 4, the depth is over 15 percent, and it has not recovered by month 8. C none below 70 0% not applicable No dip: check whether practice really changed It never falls below 97 percent of the baseline, which can mean the practice did not really change.

Provenance: The data and thresholds are illustrative, written for this chapter, and the sim must label them "Illustrative data and rule, not research findings." The idea of the dip is from Fullan.

Rules: Depth = (baseline − lowest value) ÷ baseline. The lowest point is the month with the smallest value (first such month if tied). Recovery month = the first month at or above the baseline after the lowest point. The judgments follow the rule shown in Content. A normal dip needs all three conditions. Series C is judged "No dip" when its minimum is >= 0.97 × baseline.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads the rule and the three series charts.
  2. For each series, the learner commits the month of the lowest point and a judgment, and submits them.
  3. The sim reveals the depth, the lowest point, and the recovery month, and marks each judgment correct or incorrect with the feedback text.
  4. The learner should notice that series C looks the safest and is the one the rule flags for a different reason.

Feedback: Three series, fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [judgment]. [Why text]." Incorrect: "Not quite. Check the depth, the month of the low point, and the recovery month against the rule. [Why text for the correct answer, without naming the judgment]." The correct judgment is revealed after the attempt. A score "n of 3" is shown. Final message for 3 of 3: "You can tell a normal dip from a warning sign." Otherwise: "Review the rule and try again."

Starting State: The three charts are shown with the rule, no answers entered, and the prompt "Is each pilot on a normal path?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's worked example (series A) has a baseline of 70, a low of 63 at month 3, a depth of 10 percent, and recovery at month 6, with 78 at month 12. The chapter states that the absence of a dip can itself be a warning. The mastery bar is 3 of 3.

Don't judge a pilot by month two

A common trap is reading a first low result as proof the change doesn't work, and stopping just before the recovery. Instead, say in advance what a normal dip looks like, how deep and how long, and check the actual numbers against that. A pilot that is far outside the normal range deserves investigation, not abandonment by reflex.

docs.title: Putting the Map to Use
docs.text:
Ms. Okafor now has a toolbox. For the leaders' sequence she uses Kotter's eight steps. For the teacher who does not want the change, she uses ADKAR. For feelings of loss among veterans, Bridges, in Chapter 17. For the culture of closed doors, Schein. For the long-term aim of a school that keeps learning, Senge. For the first-term dip, Fullan. For tracking where each teacher is, CBAM. She does not apply all of them at once, and she knows which question each answers.

The story has both sides. The benefit: decades of research on change, in a form a busy principal can use. The risks: model overload, applying a model's vocabulary without its substance, treating a framework as a guarantee, and forgetting that these models describe people, who surprise. The response is to start with the question and choose the model that fits it, to expect a dip, and to keep checking with the teachers themselves.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Organizational change alters how many people work; replacing a leader is not by itself a change, and the "70 percent of change efforts fail" figure is poorly sourced.
  • Kotter's eight steps give leaders an ordered plan; Lewin gives three phases (unfreeze, change, refreeze); ADKAR diagnoses the individual; Bridges addresses feelings of loss; Schein reveals culture; Senge aims at a learning organization; Fullan speaks to schools; CBAM tracks teachers.
  • Organizational culture is "the way we do things here," and school culture decides whether a reform takes hold: identical training produced very different results in two schools.
  • A learning organization builds Senge's five disciplines: personal mastery, mental models, shared vision, team learning, and systems thinking.
  • The implementation dip is a temporary fall in performance as people learn a new practice; a normal dip bottoms early and recovers, and the absence of one may mean shallow change.
  • Managing expectations means saying in advance what the dip will look like, which makes it part of the plan and protects trust.
  • Match the model to the question; the models are tools for different jobs, not rivals.

You can sort the advice into a toolbox

You just learned what each major change model is for, how culture decides whether a reform takes hold, and why a first-term dip is normal and worth planning for. Chapter 17 digs into the early stages of leading change: urgency, coalitions, vision, losses, and concerns. One step at a time, together.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: Organizational Change Models
docs.text: Test your understanding of the major organizational change models, school culture, the implementation dip, and managing expectations with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. What are the three stages of Kurt Lewin's change model?
docs.text:
1. Awareness, desire, and reinforcement
  2. Unfreeze, change, and refreeze
  3. Ending, neutral zone, and new beginning
  4. Urgency, coalition, and vision
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Lewin's 1947 model describes change as unfreezing the current way of doing things, changing to the new way, and refreezing so the new way becomes stable. It is the oldest and simplest model in the chapter and also gave the field the idea of forces for and against change. The first option draws on ADKAR, the third is Bridges' transition model, and the fourth names Kotter's first three steps.

Concept Tested: Organizational Change

See: The Models at a Glance

docs.title: 2. What are the five elements of the ADKAR model?
docs.text:
1. Analysis, Design, Knowledge, Assessment, Review
  2. Artifacts, Dialogue, Knowledge, Assumptions, Results
  3. Action, Data, Kindness, Adoption, Reflection
  4. Awareness, Desire, Knowledge, Ability, Reinforcement
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Jeff Hiatt's ADKAR model, published by Prosci in 2006, describes what an individual needs to change: Awareness of the need, Desire to take part, Knowledge of how to change, Ability to do it, and Reinforcement to sustain it. Taken in order, a person without awareness will not want the change, and one with desire but no knowledge cannot do it. Its value is that it points at the specific missing element for one person.

Concept Tested: ADKAR Model

See: The Models at a Glance

docs.title: 3. Schein describes organizational culture at three levels. Why does his model explain the failure of change efforts that alter only the visible surface?
docs.text:
1. Because unseen basic assumptions beneath artifacts and values keep shaping behavior
  2. Because visible artifacts are the deepest level and cannot be changed by leaders
  3. Because stated values always match what people actually do day to day
  4. Because culture changes automatically once a new principal or leader is hired
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Schein's levels are the visible artifacts, the stated values, and the unseen basic assumptions beneath them. Change efforts that alter only artifacts, such as a new schedule or a new tool, leave the assumptions in place, and those assumptions keep driving behavior. That is why an organization can resist what it says it wants. Artifacts are the surface level, not the deepest. The chapter also notes that replacing a leader is not by itself a change in how work is done.

Concept Tested: Organizational Culture

See: The Models at a Glance

docs.title: 4. A teacher says, "I believe in the new textbook and want to use it, but I don't know how to set up the mastery checks." Using ADKAR, what is missing, and what kind of help fits?
docs.text:
1. Awareness; a conversation about the evidence for the change
  2. Desire; a visit to a classroom where the textbook is working well
  3. Knowledge; training or coaching on how to set up the checks
  4. Reinforcement; public recognition for teachers who use the textbook
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. The teacher has awareness and desire but lacks knowledge of how to do it. The chapter's tip is to match the help to the missing piece: training fixes missing knowledge and ability, while missing awareness or desire needs a different kind of conversation. A talk about evidence or a classroom visit is what Mr. Hale, who did not see the need, required. Reinforcement comes after a person can already do the new practice.

Concept Tested: ADKAR Model

See: Worked Example: Two Teachers, Two Diagnoses

docs.title: 5. What distinction is at the center of Bridges' transition model?
docs.text:
1. Between leaders who plan a change and teachers who carry it out
  2. Between short-term wins and long-term anchoring of change in culture
  3. Between change as an outside event and transition as inner adjustment
  4. Between innovators who adopt early and laggards who adopt last
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. William Bridges separates change, the external event such as a new schedule, from transition, the internal psychological process of adjusting to it. Transition runs through an ending, a neutral zone of confusion, and a new beginning. The chapter calls it the model that takes loss seriously, answering "how are people feeling, and what do they need now?" Short-term wins and anchoring are Kotter's steps, and innovators and laggards come from Rogers.

Concept Tested: Organizational Change

See: The Models at a Glance

docs.title: 6. In a new reading program, the share of questions answered correctly falls from 72 percent at baseline to 66 percent by month 3, then climbs back to 73 percent by month 6. At month 3, a board member proposes ending the program. What does the chapter's reasoning support?
docs.text:
1. End the program, since any drop below baseline shows the change has failed
  2. Replace the teachers, since a dip shows they lack the needed skills
  3. Restart the program from the beginning with a different vendor and plan
  4. Continue, since a temporary dip while people learn new skills is normal
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Fullan's implementation dip is the temporary drop in performance and confidence when people begin using an innovation that requires new skills. It is the price of learning, not a sign of failure, and a leader who abandons the effort at the first low result stops just before the payoff. The pattern here, falling early and recovering past baseline, is the ordinary shape. The chapter adds that a pilot far outside the normal range deserves investigation, not reflexive abandonment.

Concept Tested: Implementation Dip

See: Worked Example: A Dip in the Data

docs.title: 7. A principal wants to know where each teacher is in adopting a new practice, from "What is this?" to "How can we do better together?", and what each needs next. Which model was built for that question?
docs.text:
1. The Concerns-Based Adoption Model
  2. Kotter's eight steps
  3. Lewin's three stages
  4. Senge's learning organization
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. CBAM, developed by Gene Hall, Shirley Hord, and colleagues in the 1970s, was built specifically to track how teachers adopt new practices. It looks at the concerns a teacher holds, which move from "What is this?" toward "How can we do better together?", and at the teacher's level of use, from not using to refined use. Kotter gives leaders an ordered sequence, Lewin describes the phases of any change, and Senge describes an organization that keeps learning.

Concept Tested: Concerns-Based Adoption Model

See: Fullan, the Implementation Dip, and CBAM

docs.title: 8. Why did Peter Senge call systems thinking "the fifth discipline"?
docs.text:
1. Because it was the last discipline he discovered in his research
  2. Because it integrates the other four disciplines into a whole
  3. Because it is the easiest discipline for new teams to learn
  4. Because it replaces personal mastery once a team is formed
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Senge's five disciplines are personal mastery, mental models, shared vision, team learning, and systems thinking. Systems thinking means seeing the whole system and the connections among its parts rather than isolated events, and Senge called it the fifth discipline because it integrates the others. Together they build a learning organization, one that continually expands its capacity to create the results it wants instead of running one initiative after another.

Concept Tested: Senge's Five Disciplines

See: Learning Organizations

docs.title: 9. Two schools adopt the same Level 2 textbook with identical training. After a semester, most teachers at School A use it, but only about one in five at School B do. Teachers at School A share plans and observe each other; teachers at School B work alone behind closed doors. What best explains the difference?
docs.text:
1. School B's teachers received weaker training than School A's teachers
  2. School culture, since shared norms decide whether a reform spreads
  3. The textbook was better suited to School A's students than to School B's
  4. School B's principal failed to follow Kotter's eight steps in order
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The software and the training were identical, so the difference was culture, "the way we do things here." At School A, teachers swapped tips and use spread in weeks; at School B, each teacher decided privately and use stayed with the first few adopters. Researchers such as Deal and Peterson find that school culture strongly shapes whether reforms take hold. The scenario rules out training differences, and nothing indicates the students or Kotter's sequence differed.

Concept Tested: School Culture

See: Worked Example: Culture in Two Schools

docs.title: 10. A principal is drafting a letter to families before a pilot begins. Which approach best reflects the chapter's guidance on managing expectations?
docs.text:
1. Promise that scores will rise this semester, to build excitement for the pilot
  2. Say nothing about results, so that families are not disappointed later
  3. Describe only the technology, since families care most about the tools
  4. Say scores may dip for two to three months before recovering, and report monthly
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Managing expectations means setting, and resetting, what people believe a change will deliver and how soon. A leader who promises quick gains sets up a collision between the promise and the implementation dip, and trust falls at the first low result. A letter that predicts the dip and commits to regular reports makes the dip part of the plan, so when it arrives families see the plan working. Silence avoids the problem only until results appear.

Concept Tested: Managing Expectations

See: Worked Example: Two Letters to Families

docs.title: References: Organizational Change Models
docs.text:
1. Change management - Wikipedia - Surveys the major change models, including Lewin's three steps, Kotter's eight steps, and Prosci's ADKAR. It gives readers one place to compare the models this chapter maps before later chapters apply them.

  2. Organizational culture - Wikipedia - Defines organizational culture, including Schein's description of shared basic assumptions, and reviews how culture is studied and changed. It supports the chapter's section on organizational and school culture.

  3. Learning organization - Wikipedia - Explains the learning organization concept and Senge's five disciplines: systems thinking, personal mastery, mental models, shared vision, and team learning. It previews ideas developed in Chapters 17 and 18.

  4. Leading in a Culture of Change (Revised Edition) - Michael Fullan - Jossey-Bass - Fullan names the implementation dip, the drop in performance and confidence when people meet an innovation that needs new skills. Knowing the dip is normal keeps leaders from abandoning a reform too early.

  5. The Fifth Discipline: The Art and Practice of the Learning Organization (Revised Edition) - Peter M. Senge - Doubleday/Currency - Senge's book introduced the five disciplines and argued that systems thinking ties the others together. It gives schools a model for continually learning rather than running one-time initiatives.

  6. CBAM: The Concerns-Based Adoption Model - American Institutes for Research - Overview of CBAM's three diagnostic tools: Innovation Configurations, Stages of Concern, and Levels of Use. It shows how leaders can match support to each teacher instead of relying on training alone.

  7. Michael Fullan - Michael Fullan - Fullan's site offers free handouts, articles, and a Professional Capital survey on educational change. It is a direct source for the educational-change thinking summarized in this chapter.

  8. What Makes a School a Learning Organisation? - OECD Education Working Paper 137 (Kools and Stoll) - Proposes seven action-oriented dimensions of a school as a learning organisation, from shared vision to learning-focused leadership. It translates Senge's business-oriented idea into school terms.

  9. How Principals Affect Students and Schools - Wallace Foundation - Synthesizes 219 studies on principal effects, including building a productive climate and promoting collaboration. It links school culture, a core idea in this chapter, to student and teacher outcomes.

  10. School Culture - Edutopia - A collection of practitioner articles and videos on belonging, teacher well-being, routines, and onboarding. It offers concrete examples of the visible behaviors and rituals that make up a school's culture.

docs.title: Leading Change: Vision, Culture, and Early-Stage Concerns
Summary
docs.text: This chapter goes deeper into the early stages of leading change: Lewin's unfreezing, Kotter's guiding coalition and shared vision, Bridges' endings and losses, Schein's levels of culture, and the first stages of ADKAR and the Concerns-Based Adoption Model. Readers finish able to apply these early-stage tools to diagnose where a school is at the start of a change effort.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 2: Evidence, Motivation, and the Stakeholders of Schooling
  • Chapter 13: Social Learning and Human Skills
  • Chapter 15: Technology Adoption and the Diffusion of Innovation
  • Chapter 16: Organizational Change Models

docs.title: Monday Morning at Lincoln
docs.text:
The pilot has run for a semester, the results are good, and the board has approved a district-wide plan. On Monday, Ms. Okafor stands in front of 400 teachers at a district gathering and realizes that she has been assuming something she has not checked. She has been assuming they are ready.

They are not, and not because anyone is difficult. A veteran teacher near the back is quietly wondering whether the lectures he has refined over twenty years are about to be declared worthless. A young teacher is excited and a little afraid of looking foolish. A department chair is calculating how the new schedule will affect her team's planning time. A teacher who missed the earlier meetings has not heard of the plan at all.

This chapter is about the beginning of a change effort: getting people ready. Chapter 16 mapped the models. Here the models are applied to the early work, using the stages of each that matter most at the start. The theme is that readiness is a human condition more than a technical one, with a diagnosis for each person and a different kind of help for each.

Start with people, not the plan

This chapter is about the first stretch of a change: creating urgency, building a team, painting a vision, and listening to what people feel and worry about. You'll leave able to diagnose where a school stands at the start and choose a first move that fits. Let's find the balance between moving with purpose and bringing people with you.

docs.title: Lewin: Unfreeze, Change, Refreeze
docs.text:
Lewin's change model describes change in three stages, and it gives the first overall shape to the work. Kurt Lewin proposed it in 1947. His central image is a block of ice: to give it a new shape you must first melt it, then reshape it, then freeze it again.

The unfreeze stage is the preparation of an organization for change by loosening the habits, beliefs, and routines that hold the present way in place. People do not change while they are comfortable. Unfreezing creates motivation by showing a gap between how things are and how they should be, and by building enough psychological safety that people can let go. The change stage is the period of actually moving to the new way of working: learning, trying, making mistakes, and adjusting. It is uncertain and uncomfortable, and it is where the implementation dip of Chapter 16 lives. The refreeze stage is the stabilization of the new way so that it becomes the normal way, supported by policies, routines, rewards, and habits so that people do not slide back.

Lewin also gave the field a tool for the unfreezing stage, force field analysis. It pictures any situation as a balance between driving forces, which push toward change, and restraining forces, which push against it. Lewin's most useful insight is practical: pushing harder on the driving forces tends to raise the restraining forces too, as people dig in, whereas reducing the restraining forces lets change happen with less tension.

Critics note that the three-stage picture can mislead in a world where change never stops. In schools, where one reform follows another, "refreezing" can become ossifying. A modern reading treats refreezing lightly: make the new practice stable, while keeping a habit of learning and adjusting, which is Senge's learning organization from Chapter 16.

docs.title: Worked Example: A Force Field for the Compressed Morning
docs.text:
Ms. Okafor lists the forces and scores each from 1 (weak) to 5 (strong). The scores are illustrative judgments.

Driving forces Strength Restraining forces Strength Evidence of learning gaps in the data 4 Culture of closed doors 4 Potential relief from teacher workload 3 Fear of job loss 3 Free open textbooks 3 Privacy concerns 3 Leadership support 4 Students without home devices 4 Total 14 Total 14

The forces balance exactly at 14 and 14, which is why the effort feels stuck. A leader could push the driving forces harder, with more urgency and more pressure, and the restraining forces would probably grow. Lewin's advice is to reduce the restraining forces instead. Suppose the school lends devices (restraining force from 4 to 1) and completes a privacy review (from 3 to 1). The restraining total falls to \( 4 + 3 + 1 + 1 = 9 \), and the net is \( 14 - 9 = +5 \) in favor of change, without turning up any pressure on teachers.

docs.title: Diagram: Force Field Balance
docs.text:
Run the Force Field Balance MicroSim Fullscreen

Force Field Balance

Type: microsim sim-id: force-field-balance Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: calculate Learning Objective: The learner will calculate the total driving force, the total restraining force, and the net force for a change situation, before and after reducing two restraining forces, correctly answering three of three questions.

Prerequisites: force field analysis, driving force, restraining force, unfreeze stage (all defined in the section "Lewin: Unfreeze, Change, Refreeze" above).

Evidence of Mastery: Before the controls unlock, the learner commits three answers: (Q1) the total driving force; (Q2) the total restraining force after the device force is reduced to 1 and the privacy force to 1; (Q3) the net force after those reductions. An answer is correct when it equals the value in Content. Mastery is 3 of 3 correct. Changing the strengths afterward is exploration.

Misconceptions: (1) The way to overcome resistance is to push harder. (2) A balanced situation is stable and safe. (3) All forces are equally easy to change.

Instructional Rationale: Calculating totals before and after a reduction makes the arithmetic of Lewin's advice visible: lowering a restraining force by 3 improves the net exactly as raising a driving force by 3 would, without adding pressure. Committing to the answers first ties the learner's expectation to the numbers.

Content:

Eight forces, each with a strength from 1 to 5 (min 1, max 5, step 1), with the starting values:

Force Kind Starting strength Evidence of learning gaps in the data Driving 4 Potential relief from teacher workload Driving 3 Free open textbooks Driving 3 Leadership support Driving 4 Culture of closed doors Restraining 4 Fear of job loss Restraining 3 Privacy concerns Restraining 3 Students without home devices Restraining 4

Net force = total driving − total restraining. Starting totals: driving 14, restraining 14, net 0.

Answers: Q1 = 14; Q2 = 9 (4 + 3 + 1 + 1); Q3 = +5.

Provenance: The forces and strengths are illustrative, written for this chapter, and the sim must label them "Illustrative judgments." Force field analysis is from Kurt Lewin.

Rules: Total driving = sum of the driving strengths; total restraining = sum of the restraining strengths; net = driving − restraining. When any strength changes, totals and net update at once. A net of 0 is shown as "balanced," a positive net as "favors change," and a negative net as "favors the status quo."

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner answers Q1, Q2, and Q3 and submits them.
  2. The sim checks the answers and unlocks the controls.
  3. The learner changes strengths. A balance bar shows the totals and the net.
  4. The learner should notice that lowering a restraining force by 3 moves the net exactly as much as raising a driving force by 3.

Feedback: Three questions, fixed order, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: [value]. [Working text]." Incorrect: "Not quite. Add the strengths on each side, then subtract." After the second wrong attempt the value and working are shown. A score "n of 3" is shown.

Starting State: The eight forces are shown at their starting values, balanced at 14 and 14, with the prompt "How could the school tip the balance without adding pressure?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's worked example has driving forces of 4, 3, 3, and 4 (total 14), restraining forces of 4, 3, 3, and 4 (total 14), and reductions of the device force from 4 to 1 and the privacy force from 3 to 1, giving a restraining total of 9 and a net of +5.

docs.title: Kotter: From Urgency to Anchoring
docs.text:
John Kotter's eight steps give leaders a sequence. The sequence matters because Kotter's research found that organizations often skipped early steps, such as building urgency, in their hurry to reach later ones, and the skipped steps came back to cause failure. Here are the eight, with what each means for a school.

Sense of urgency is the shared belief, among enough people, that change is needed now and that staying the same is riskier than changing. Without it, people have no reason to do the hard work. Urgency is not panic: it comes from facing real facts, such as Chapter 1's finding that in a class of 28 only 13 students are in reach of a single lesson. Kotter argued that a large majority of leaders must be honestly convinced before going further.

A guiding coalition is a group of people with enough power, credibility, expertise, and trust to lead the change. In a school it should include the principal, respected teachers, a union representative, a family representative, and technical staff, and it should include voices that are skeptical. A coalition made only of enthusiasts will not be believed by the rest.

A change vision is a clear, compelling picture of the future the change is meant to create, simple enough to explain in a few minutes. The book's own vision is "mornings with AI, afternoons with each other." A good vision says what will be different for students, and why it is worth the difficulty. Communicating the vision is repeating it through every channel and in actions as well as words, far more often than seems necessary, because people hear it through the noise of their own concerns. Kotter observed that leaders typically under-communicate by a large factor.

Removing obstacles is clearing the barriers, in structures, systems, and skills, that stand between people and the change: a bell schedule that blocks the afternoon, a contract term that blocks a new role, a login system that does not work, a supervisor who undermines the effort. Lewin's lesson applies here: removing a barrier is more effective than pushing people over it.

Short-term wins are visible, unambiguous successes achieved early, which show that the effort is working and build momentum. They need to be real, visible, and clearly linked to the change. A pilot classroom's gains, a student exhibition, or a teacher's saved evening count. Building on change is using the credibility from early wins to take on bigger problems, instead of declaring victory too soon. Kotter treated premature victory as one of the most common mistakes. Anchoring in culture is making the new way of working part of "the way we do things here," by embedding it in hiring, orientation, evaluation, schedules, and stories, so that it survives the departure of its champions.

The image has no text; 10 numbered callouts supply every label.

Story balance: the benefit is a clear order of work; the two hazards show skipping steps and declaring victory too soon, and their tips give the response, Lewin's refreeze paired with Kotter's anchoring.

docs.title: Worked Example: Kotter at Lincoln
docs.text:
Step What Lincoln did What it looked like Sense of urgency Shared the data that 13 of 28 students are in reach of one lesson A staff meeting discussion of the learning-gap chart Guiding coalition Recruited a veteran, a union representative, a parent, and the tech director A team of seven that meets weekly Change vision Wrote "Mornings with AI, afternoons with each other" One sentence on the staff room wall and in family letters Communicating the vision Repeated it at every meeting and family night The principal's weekly note includes one line on progress Removing obstacles Fixed logins, adjusted the bell schedule for the pilot, lent devices A list of obstacles the team resolves each month Short-term wins Shared pilot gains and held a student exhibition at eight weeks A celebration night for families Building on change Added two grades and a second school A second pilot using the first as a reference Anchoring in culture Wrote the model into hiring, orientation, and the calendar New teachers are shown the pilot in their first week

The steps are in order for a reason. A vision announced without urgency is ignored, and a vision with no coalition has no one to carry it.

docs.title: Diagram: Which Kotter Step Is This?
docs.text:
Run the Which Kotter Step Is This? MicroSim Fullscreen

Which Kotter Step Is This?

Type: microsim sim-id: which-kotter-step Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: classify Learning Objective: The learner will classify eight leadership actions by the Kotter step each carries out, correctly placing at least seven of eight on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: the eight steps (sense of urgency, guiding coalition, change vision, communicating the vision, removing obstacles, short-term wins, building on change, anchoring in culture), all defined in the section "Kotter: From Urgency to Anchoring" above.

Evidence of Mastery: The learner places each of 8 actions in one of eight step bins and submits it. A placement is correct when it matches the "Correct step" column in Content. Mastery is 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Reading the step definitions is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Steps can be done in any order. (2) Communicating the vision is a single announcement. (3) A win means the change is finished.

Instructional Rationale: Classifying actions requires recognizing the purpose each step serves, not just its name. Actions that sound similar, such as sharing results (short-term wins) and adding grades (building on change), make the learner distinguish purposes.

Content:

Eight steps with one-line definitions shown on request:

Step Definition shown Sense of urgency Enough people believe change is needed now Guiding coalition A group with the power and trust to lead the change Change vision A clear picture of the future the change creates Communicating the vision Repeating the vision in many ways and actions Removing obstacles Clearing barriers in structures, systems, and skills Short-term wins Early, visible successes Building on change Using early success to take on bigger problems Anchoring in culture Making the new way part of the normal way

Eight actions:

# Action shown to the learner Correct step Why (shown as feedback) 1 The principal shares data that only 13 of 28 students are in reach of a typical lesson and invites staff to discuss it. Sense of urgency It builds a shared belief that change is needed. 2 She recruits a respected veteran, a union representative, a parent, and the technology director into a leadership team. Guiding coalition It assembles a group with credibility and power to lead. 3 The team writes one sentence: "Mornings with AI, afternoons with each other." Change vision It states a clear picture of the future. 4 The vision is repeated at every staff meeting, in newsletters, and at family nights. Communicating the vision It repeats the vision through many channels. 5 The district adjusts the bell schedule and fixes the login problem that blocked teachers. Removing obstacles It clears barriers in structures and systems. 6 After eight weeks, the team shares the pilot class's gains at a student exhibition. Short-term wins It shows an early, visible success. 7 Instead of declaring victory, the team uses the results to add two more grades and a second school. Building on change It uses early success to take on more. 8 Hiring criteria, new-teacher orientation, and the school calendar are updated to reflect the new model. Anchoring in culture It makes the change part of the normal way.

Provenance: The steps follow Kotter (1996) as described in the chapter. The actions are illustrative, written for this chapter.

Rules: Each action has exactly one correct step, given in Content, and each step has exactly one action. An action is scored on its first submitted placement only. The score counts first-attempt correct placements out of 8. Mastery is a score >= 7.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees one action at a time and the eight steps.
  2. The learner places the action and submits it. The sim marks it correct or incorrect and shows the feedback text.
  3. If incorrect, the learner may place it again; the second attempt does not change the score. After the second attempt, the correct step and reason are shown.
  4. After all 8 actions, the sim shows the score and the steps in order.
  5. The learner should notice that the eight actions, in order, tell the story of one change effort.

Feedback: 8 actions, shuffled once per session, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: [step]. [Why text]." Incorrect: "Not quite. [Why text for the correct answer, without naming the step]." After the second attempt the correct step is revealed and the action counts as missed. A running score "First-try correct: n of 8" is shown. Final message for a score >= 7: "You can see which step an action serves." For a score < 7: "Review the eight steps and try again; the actions will be reshuffled."

Starting State: Action 1 of the shuffled order is shown with the eight steps, the score "First-try correct: 0 of 8," and the prompt "Which step does this action carry out?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's worked example lists the same eight actions in order, with 13 of 28 students in reach, a team of seven, and a pilot celebration at eight weeks. The mastery bar is 7 of 8.

Don't declare victory at the first win

A common trap is celebrating a good pilot as if the change were done, then moving attention elsewhere. Old habits return. Use the win to push into the next grade or school, and keep going until the new way is in hiring, scheduling, and the way new teachers are welcomed.

docs.title: Vision as a Shared Thing: Senge's Shared Vision and Personal Mastery
docs.text:
Kotter says a vision should be clear and communicated. Peter Senge adds a harder point: a vision that is only announced is not shared. Shared vision, one of Senge's five disciplines, is a picture of the future that people throughout the organization truly hold and want, built through conversation and not handed down. The difference is between compliance, in which people go along with what they were told, and commitment, in which they want it. Compliance produces the minimum and fades when the leader leaves. Commitment produces initiative. A principal can write a vision statement in an afternoon, but a shared vision takes months of listening, in which teachers' hopes shape the picture.

Personal mastery, another of Senge's disciplines, is each person's commitment to their own continual growth and to what they truly care about. It matters for change because an organization learns only as fast as its people do, and because people who are growing, and not being merely managed, bring energy and honesty to the work. A school that wants teachers to become coaches, as the book proposes, needs to support the teacher's own development as a person, not only to train them on a tool.

docs.title: Worked Example: Compliance or Commitment?
docs.text:
Two principals announce the same vision. A teacher's reactions differ.

Principal A Principal B How the vision was made Written by the principal and emailed Built over six weeks in small-group conversations with teachers, students, and parents A veteran teacher's reaction "Another thing from the office; I'll do what's required" "Some of my own ideas are in it; I want to see it work" Behavior after six months Minimum use; some quiet resistance Teachers propose improvements Type Compliance Commitment

The extra five weeks of conversation produced the difference. It is slower at the start and much faster after.

docs.title: Bridges: Endings and Losses
docs.text:
William Bridges made a distinction that changes how a leader sees resistance. The change is the external event, such as a new schedule; the transition is the internal psychological process of coming to terms with it. A leader can announce the change on Monday, but the transition takes much longer. Bridges' transition model describes the transition as having three phases, which the next chapter covers fully, and it begins with the one leaders most often skip.

Endings and losses are the first phase of a transition, in which people must let go of the old way and grieve what the change takes from them. Bridges argued that every change, even a welcome one, involves loss, and that people cannot begin anything new until they have an ending. The losses are often not the obvious ones. A teacher losing the lecture format may lose her identity as an expert, the competence she has built, her routines, her relationships with colleagues in the old structure, and her sense of control. Leaders who skip the ending and talk only about the exciting new beginning are puzzled when people do not respond.

docs.title: Worked Example: A Loss Inventory
docs.text:
Ms. Okafor meets with the seventh-grade math team and lists what the compressed morning takes from them.

Kind of loss What a teacher might feel Identity "I am the person who explains this well to a whole class" Competence "I was good at this, and now I'm a beginner again" Routines "Fifty minutes of my own lesson, five times a day, is gone" Relationships "I'm no longer at the front; will students still need me?" Control "The software decides the pace now" Meaning "Why did I spend years learning something that's being replaced?"

She does not argue with any of it. She acknowledges each, asks the team what part of their craft they most want to keep, and builds that into the new role: the coach who knows exactly when a student needs a human explanation. Naming the losses is what lets the team start to look ahead.

docs.title: Schein: Culture Beneath the Surface
docs.text:
Schein's culture model describes an organization's culture in three layers. At the surface are artifacts: what you can see and hear, such as the building, the schedule, the dress, the language, and the rituals. In the middle are espoused values: what the organization says it believes, such as "we value collaboration." At the base are basic assumptions: the unspoken, taken-for-granted beliefs that really drive behavior, such as "a good teacher works alone." When the values people state disagree with the assumptions they hold, the assumptions win, which explains why reforms announced at the level of artifacts and values often fail. Chapter 18 treats the three levels and culture assessment in detail.

Two kinds of cultural material show up early in a change and are worth naming now. Shared beliefs and norms are the beliefs held in common and the unwritten rules for behavior: that teachers do not enter each other's rooms uninvited, that parents are informed and not consulted, that the schedule is not to be touched. School rituals are the repeated, symbolic events and routines that express and reinforce a school's culture: morning announcements, assemblies, awards, staff meetings, the first day and the last. Rituals matter to change in two ways. They are a source of resistance when a change disrupts a cherished one. And they are a tool, because a new ritual, such as a student exhibition night, builds the new culture in the open.

docs.title: Worked Example: Reading a School's Culture Quickly
docs.text:
Ms. Okafor lists what she sees at Lincoln and where it points.

Level What she sees at Lincoln What it suggests Artifact Classroom doors are closed; the staff room is silent at lunch Teaching is private Espoused value The mission says "collaborative learning community" The school says it values collaboration Basic assumption (inferred) New teachers are told "close your door and do your own thing" The deeper rule is that autonomy outranks collaboration Ritual The only whole-staff event is a Friday announcement Information flows down, not across

The gap between the stated value and the assumption tells her where the plan will meet resistance: collaborative afternoon teams will clash with the real rule. She plans to open doors through low-risk peer visits, not mandates.

docs.title: ADKAR: The First Three Elements
docs.text:
The ADKAR model, introduced in Chapter 16, gives each person's path through a change in five elements. The first three are the early-stage ones, and they are the ones a leader must secure before training can help.

ADKAR Awareness is a person's understanding of why the change is needed and what will happen if it does not occur. Awareness is created by honest, repeated communication of the reasons and the evidence, not by an announcement of what will happen. ADKAR Desire is a person's wish to take part and support the change. It is the hardest element to create, because it cannot be ordered. It grows from the person's own motives: what the change means for them, their trust in leadership, their values, and their sense of being heard. ADKAR Knowledge is knowing how to change: what to do differently, and the skills and information to do it. Knowledge is what training and job aids supply, and it is useless without awareness and desire.

Element The person's question What builds it A sign it is missing Awareness "Why are we doing this?" Honest explanation of the reasons and the evidence "I don't see why we're changing" Desire "Do I want to take part?" Involvement, listening, sponsors, addressing "what's in it for me" "I understand why, but I don't want to" Knowledge "How do I do it?" Training, examples, job aids "I'm willing, but I don't know where to start"

docs.title: Worked Example: Reading Three Teachers
docs.text:
Teacher says Missing element First move "I wasn't at the meeting; what is this about?" Awareness A short, direct explanation with the data "I get it, but my job is to lecture. I don't want to change." Desire A listening conversation about what they fear and value "I'd like to try it, but I don't know how the dashboard works." Knowledge A 20-minute demonstration and a one-page guide

Training the first two would waste their time. Chapter 18 returns to Ability and Reinforcement.

docs.title: CBAM: Concerns at the Start
docs.text:
The Concerns-Based Adoption Model (CBAM), introduced in Chapter 16, begins with the observation that teachers going through a change move through predictable concerns, and that leaders help most by answering the concern a person actually has. Stages of concern are the seven kinds of concern, labeled 0 to 6, that people have about an innovation as they get to know it: awareness (0), informational (1), personal (2), management (3), consequence (4), collaboration (5), and refocusing (6). A person may have several at once, and concerns usually move from earlier to later stages as the person gains experience. The stages are measured with a questionnaire, the Stages of Concern Questionnaire, and an interview.

Self concerns are the first three stages, in which the person's concern is about themselves in relation to the innovation:

  • Stage 0, awareness: little concern or involvement. "I'm not thinking about this."
  • Stage 1, informational: a wish to know more about what it is. "What exactly is it, and how does it work?"
  • Stage 2, personal: concern about what it will mean for oneself. "How will this affect me? Will I be able to do it? Will I be judged?"

Concerns of the first three stages are not signs of resistance. They are the natural start of anyone's learning, and they need answers, not persuasion. A person at stage 2 who is told "it will be great for the students" has not been answered, since the question was about themselves. Chapter 18 covers the later stages, which are about the task (stage 3) and about impact on students and on colleagues (stages 4 to 6).

An innovation configuration is a description, usually a map, of what an innovation looks like in practice, listing its essential components and, for each, the range of ways it may be carried out from the ideal to the unacceptable. It exists because two teachers can both say they are "using the new textbook" while doing very different things. An innovation configuration map defines what the school means by "using it," so that a leader can see whether the innovation is actually happening.

docs.title: Worked Example: An Innovation Configuration Map
docs.text:
An illustrative map for the adaptive morning, with three components.

Component Ideal Acceptable Unacceptable Pacing Students move at their own pace, with teacher check-ins Students move at their own pace, with little teacher contact Whole class forced to move at one pace Mastery checks Mastery rule applied; teacher reviews each dashboard flag Mastery rule applied; teacher reviews weekly Students move on regardless of mastery Teacher dashboard Used daily to pull small groups Used weekly Never opened

With this map, "using it" is no longer a yes or no. A teacher who lets students pace themselves but never opens the dashboard is acceptable on one component and unacceptable on another. The map tells the coach exactly where to help.

Three stages with one-line meanings shown on request:

Stage Meaning shown Awareness Little concern or involvement; it is not on the person's mind Informational A wish to know more about what it is and how it works Personal Concern about what it will mean for oneself

# Teacher statement shown to the learner Correct stage Suggested response (shown as feedback) 1 "I've heard something about a new textbook, but it isn't really on my radar." Awareness Acknowledge the timing and offer a brief note for later. 3 "What exactly is a Level 2 textbook, and what does it do?" Informational Provide a clear description and a demonstration. 4 "Can someone explain how the learning graph chooses the next concept?"
