Rules: Each statement has exactly one correct stage, given in Content, and each stage has exactly two statements. A statement is scored on its first submitted choice only. The score counts first-attempt correct choices out of 6. Mastery is a score >= 5.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads one statement and sees the three stages.
  2. The learner selects a stage and submits it. The sim marks it correct or incorrect and shows the suggested response.
  3. If incorrect, the learner may choose again; the second attempt does not change the score. After the second attempt, the correct stage is shown.
  4. After all 6 statements, the sim shows the score.
  5. The learner should notice that none of the six statements is resistance, and that each is answered by information, not persuasion.

Feedback: 6 statements, shuffled once per session, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: [stage]. [Suggested response]." Incorrect: "Not quite. Ask whether the person wants to know what it is, how it affects them, or is not yet thinking about it. [Suggested response for the correct stage]." After the second attempt the correct stage is revealed and the statement counts as missed. A running score "First-try correct: n of 6" is shown. Final message for a score >= 5: "You can hear the concern behind a statement." For a score < 5: "Review the three stages and try again; the statements will be reshuffled."

Starting State: Statement 1 of the shuffled order is shown with the three stages, the score "First-try correct: 0 of 6," and the prompt "What kind of concern is this?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter defines stages 0, 1, and 2 as the self concerns and states that they are not signs of resistance. The mastery bar is 5 of 6.

docs.title: Lewin's Refreeze and Kotter's Anchoring Revisited
docs.text:
The early stages end where the late ones begin. Lewin's refreeze and Kotter's anchoring in culture say the same thing in different words: a change has not happened until it is part of the normal way of working. The two ideas bring this chapter's themes together. Unfreezing needs urgency, a coalition, and a vision that people share. The change stage needs obstacles removed and early wins. Refreezing, or anchoring, needs the new way to be written into hiring, routines, and rituals.

A change isn't done until it's ordinary

Notice how the two models agree: the finish line is not the launch, it's the day nobody calls it "the new way" anymore. That's why rituals matter. A new ritual, like an exhibition night, turns a change into a tradition people defend.

docs.title: Diagnosing Where a School Stands
docs.text:
Ms. Okafor's Monday morning now has a diagnostic. For the district as a whole she asks whether there is urgency, a coalition, a vision, and obstacles that have been cleared. For the culture she reads artifacts, stated values, and the assumptions beneath them. For each group of teachers she asks which ADKAR element is missing and which concern they hold. In the room of 400, she now sees the veteran at the back grieving a loss, the young teacher at stage 2 worrying about being judged, the department chair weighing the schedule, and the teacher who has not heard at all, who lacks awareness.

The story has both sides. The benefit: early-stage tools that tell a leader where to start with each group and each person. The risks: moving to the new vision before people have grieved the old one, mistaking early questions for resistance, announcing a vision no one shares, and building on a culture that contradicts the plan. The response: listen first, diagnose by person and by stage, answer the question each person is actually asking, and treat the culture as something to read before you try to change it.

Answer the question they asked

When a teacher asks "Will I be evaluated on this?", resist the urge to reply "it's great for kids." Answer the question about them first, directly and honestly. People can hear about students only after their own concern has been heard.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Lewin's change model has three stages: the unfreeze stage (create motivation, loosen habits), the change stage (learning and the dip), and the refreeze stage (stabilize). Force field analysis shows that reducing restraining forces beats pushing driving forces.
  • Kotter's steps, in order: a sense of urgency, a guiding coalition, a change vision, communicating the vision, removing obstacles, short-term wins, building on change, and anchoring in culture.
  • A shared vision is built with people and produces commitment; a vision that is only announced produces compliance. Personal mastery is the growth of each person.
  • Bridges distinguishes change from transition; endings and losses come first, and leaders who skip them are puzzled by the lack of response.
  • Schein's culture model reads artifacts, espoused values, and basic assumptions; shared beliefs and norms and school rituals are early clues and tools.
  • ADKAR Awareness, Desire, and Knowledge are the first three elements; training only helps when the first two are present.
  • Stages of concern begin with self concerns (awareness, informational, personal), which are not resistance and need answers; an innovation configuration map defines what "using it" means.

You can diagnose the start of a change

You just learned the early stages of five change models, built a force field and a loss inventory, and learned to hear the concern behind a teacher's question. That's the start of change done thoughtfully. Chapter 18 follows the change through its middle and late stages and into systems thinking. One step at a time, together.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: Leading Change: Vision, Culture, and Early-Stage Concerns
docs.text: Test your understanding of the early stages of leading change, from urgency and vision to losses, culture, and teachers' first concerns, with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. In Kotter's eight steps, which step comes first?
docs.text:
1. Form a guiding coalition
  2. Create a change vision
  3. Generate short-term wins
  4. Establish a sense of urgency
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Kotter's sequence begins with a sense of urgency, the shared belief that change is needed now and that staying the same is riskier. The steps then run through guiding coalition, change vision, communicating the vision, removing obstacles, short-term wins, building on change, and anchoring in culture. Kotter found organizations often skipped early steps like urgency in their hurry, and the skipped steps came back to cause failure. A vision announced without urgency is ignored.

Concept Tested: Sense of Urgency

See: Kotter: From Urgency to Anchoring

docs.title: 2. In the Concerns-Based Adoption Model, which stages make up the "self concerns"?
docs.text:
1. Management, consequence, and collaboration
  2. Awareness, informational, and personal
  3. Consequence, collaboration, and refocusing
  4. Informational, management, and consequence
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Self concerns are the first three of the seven stages of concern: awareness (0), informational (1), and personal (2). In these stages, the person's concern is about themselves in relation to the innovation, such as "What is it?" and "How will this affect me?" Management (3) is about the task, and consequence, collaboration, and refocusing (4 to 6) are about impact on students and colleagues. The chapter stresses that self concerns are not resistance and need answers, not persuasion.

Concept Tested: Self Concerns

See: CBAM: Concerns at the Start

docs.title: 3. A school's force field analysis scores the driving forces at a total of 13. Its restraining forces are students without devices (5), fear of job loss (4), privacy concerns (3), and closed-door culture (2). The school lends devices, cutting that force to 2, and completes a privacy review, cutting that force to 1. What is the net balance now?
docs.text:
1. About +4 in favor of change
  2. About -1 against change
  3. About +9 in favor of change
  4. About 0, still evenly balanced
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The restraining forces start at 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 = 14, giving a net of 13 - 14 = -1 against change. After the changes they are 2 + 4 + 1 + 2 = 9, so the net is 13 - 9 = +4 in favor of change. The -1 answer is the starting balance, and +9 confuses the restraining total with the net. Lewin's point is that reducing restraining forces tips the balance without adding pressure on teachers.

Concept Tested: Lewin's Change Model

See: Worked Example: A Force Field for the Compressed Morning

docs.title: 4. What is Lewin's most useful practical insight from force field analysis?
docs.text:
1. Driving forces always outweigh restraining forces once a leader fully commits
  2. Restraining forces disappear on their own after the refreeze stage
  3. Pushing on driving forces raises resistance; reducing restraining forces works better
  4. A change effort should begin only when the driving forces total twice the restraining forces
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Force field analysis pictures a situation as a balance between driving forces toward change and restraining forces against it. Lewin's insight is that pushing harder on the driving forces tends to raise the restraining forces as people dig in, while reducing restraining forces lets change happen with less tension. The chapter echoes this under Kotter's step of removing obstacles: removing a barrier is more effective than pushing people over it. The other options are not claims Lewin made.

Concept Tested: Unfreeze Stage

See: Lewin: Unfreeze, Change, Refreeze

docs.title: 5. A teacher says, "I understand the data and why we're doing this, but my job is to lecture, and I don't want to change." What is the best first move according to ADKAR?
docs.text:
1. A listening conversation about what the teacher fears and values
  2. A short, direct explanation of the data behind the change
  3. A 20-minute demonstration of the dashboard and a one-page guide
  4. A formal evaluation of the teacher's lecture-based instruction
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The teacher has awareness of why the change is needed but lacks desire, the hardest element to create because it cannot be ordered. Desire grows from the person's own motives, trust in leadership, values, and a sense of being heard, so the first move is a listening conversation. Explaining the data again targets awareness, which is already present. A demonstration targets knowledge, which the chapter says is useless without awareness and desire.

Concept Tested: ADKAR Desire

See: Worked Example: Reading Three Teachers

docs.title: 6. According to Bridges, why are leaders who talk only about an exciting new beginning often puzzled when staff do not respond?
docs.text:
1. Because staff have not yet received enough technical training
  2. Because the new beginning is usually announced too late in the school year
  3. Because staff respond only to urgency, not to positive messages
  4. Because people cannot begin anew until they have an ending for what they lose
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Bridges distinguishes the external change from the internal transition, which begins with endings and losses. Every change, even a welcome one, involves loss, and the losses are often not obvious: identity as an expert, hard-won competence, routines, relationships, control, and meaning. Leaders who skip the ending are puzzled by the lack of response. In the chapter's loss inventory, Ms. Okafor acknowledges each loss and builds what teachers most want to keep into their new role.

Concept Tested: Endings and Losses

See: Bridges: Endings and Losses

docs.title: 7. At a staff meeting, a teacher asks, "Will I be evaluated on this? What if I can't do it?" Which stage of concern is this, and how should a leader respond?
docs.text:
1. Stage 4, consequence; explain the expected effect on student learning
  2. Stage 2, personal; answer the question about the teacher directly and honestly
  3. Stage 0, awareness; send the teacher information about the plan
  4. Stage 5, collaboration; pair the teacher with a colleague to coordinate
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The teacher is asking how the change will affect them, which is stage 2, personal, one of the self concerns. The chapter warns that a person at stage 2 told "it will be great for the students" has not been answered, since the question was about themselves. The chapter's tip is to answer the question about them first, directly and honestly; people can hear about students only after their own concern has been heard. Responding with student impact addresses stage 4.

Concept Tested: Stages of Concern

See: CBAM: Concerns at the Start

docs.title: 8. What is the difference between a vision that is announced and a shared vision, in Senge's terms?
docs.text:
1. An announced vision is long and detailed; a shared vision fits on one line
  2. An announced vision comes from the board; a shared vision comes from the principal
  3. An announced vision yields compliance; a shared vision, built together, yields commitment
  4. An announced vision is written down; a shared vision is never put in writing
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. A shared vision is a picture of the future that people throughout the organization truly hold, built through conversation rather than handed down. Compliance produces the minimum and fades when the leader leaves; commitment produces initiative. In the chapter's example, the principal who built the vision over six weeks with teachers, students, and parents got proposed improvements, while the one who emailed it got minimum use. Length and who writes it are not the distinction.

Concept Tested: Shared Vision

See: Worked Example: Compliance or Commitment?

docs.title: 9. A school's mission statement says it is a "collaborative learning community," but new teachers are told, "Close your door and do your own thing." A principal plans collaborative afternoon teams. Using Schein's model, what should she expect, and what fits as a response?
docs.text:
1. The mission statement will carry the plan, so she can mandate teams right away
  2. Teachers will welcome teams, since the school already values collaboration
  3. Resistance will come only from new teachers, so she should focus on them
  4. The hidden assumption will win, so she should open doors through low-risk peer visits
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Schein's model separates artifacts, espoused values, and basic assumptions. The mission is an espoused value; the advice to new teachers reveals the basic assumption that autonomy outranks collaboration. When stated values and assumptions disagree, the assumptions win, so the plan will meet resistance at that point. The chapter's response is to open doors through low-risk peer visits rather than mandates. The first two options mistake the stated value for the real culture.

Concept Tested: Schein's Culture Model

See: Worked Example: Reading a School's Culture Quickly

docs.title: 10. Using the chapter's innovation configuration map, a coach observes that a teacher lets students move at their own pace with little teacher contact but never opens the teacher dashboard. What should the coach conclude?
docs.text:
1. Acceptable on pacing, unacceptable on the dashboard, so help should target the dashboard
  2. The teacher is fully using the innovation, since students work at their own pace
  3. The teacher is not using the innovation at all, so the coach should start over with training
  4. The teacher is ideal on every component, since the students appear engaged
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. An innovation configuration map lists an innovation's essential components and, for each, the range from ideal to unacceptable. In the chapter's map, self-pacing with little teacher contact is acceptable, while a dashboard that is never opened is unacceptable. "Using it" is no longer a yes or no, and the map tells the coach exactly where to help. The second and third options treat use as all-or-nothing, which is the problem the map was designed to solve.

Concept Tested: Innovation Configuration

See: Worked Example: An Innovation Configuration Map

docs.title: References: Leading Change: Vision, Culture, and Early-Stage Concerns
docs.text:
1. Kurt Lewin - Wikipedia - Biography of the social psychologist associated with unfreeze, change, refreeze, including evidence that the three-step model took final form after his death. It helps readers use the model with appropriate caution.

  2. Force-field analysis - Wikipedia - Explains Lewin's method of listing the forces driving and restraining a change. It supports the chapter's worked example of a force field for the compressed morning.

  3. Edgar Schein - Wikipedia - Describes Schein's three levels of culture: artifacts and behaviors, espoused values, and shared basic assumptions. It is the basis for the chapter's guidance on reading a school's culture quickly.

  4. Leading Change - John P. Kotter - Harvard Business Review Press - Kotter's eight-stage process, from establishing a sense of urgency and a guiding coalition to anchoring change in culture. Its list of common leadership errors explains why many school reforms stall early.

  5. Managing Transitions: Making the Most of Change (4th ed.) - William Bridges with Susan Bridges - Da Capo Lifelong Books - Bridges separates external change from the internal transition people go through, and starts every transition with an ending. His loss inventory helps leaders name what teachers are giving up.

  6. The 8-Step Process for Leading Change - Kotter Inc. - Lists and explains Kotter's eight steps, from creating urgency to instituting change, and notes their later evolution into "accelerators." A compact reference for the chapter's Kotter at Lincoln example.

  7. Bridges Transition Model - William Bridges Associates - Describes endings, the neutral zone, and new beginnings, and the difference between change and transition. It supports the chapter's section on endings and losses.

  8. The Prosci ADKAR Model - Prosci - Defines the five ADKAR elements, with Awareness, Desire, and Knowledge as the early stages this chapter covers. It helps leaders diagnose why an individual teacher has not yet moved.

  9. Stages of Concern - American Institutes for Research - Explains the seven Stages of Concern, from unconcerned and informational to refocusing, and how to assess them. It grounds the chapter's focus on teachers' early self concerns.

  10. Innovation Configurations - American Institutes for Research - Describes how to build an Innovation Configuration map that shows ideal, acceptable, and unacceptable versions of a practice. It supports the chapter's worked example on mapping the AI-native model.

docs.title: Sustaining Change: Systems Thinking and National Adoption
Summary
docs.text: This chapter completes the change models with their later, sustaining stages: Senge's systems thinking and mental models, the later stages of ADKAR and CBAM, Bridges' new beginnings, the "grammar of schooling," and Estonia's national AI Leap as a whole-system example. Readers finish able to choose a change model suited to a school's size, culture, and history, and to read a simple causal loop diagram.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: The Building Blocks of Schools, Students, and Learning
  • Chapter 15: Technology Adoption and the Diffusion of Innovation
  • Chapter 16: Organizational Change Models
  • Chapter 17: Leading Change: Vision, Culture, and Early-Stage Concerns

docs.title: A Year Later
docs.text:
A year after the district-wide launch, Ms. Okafor visits a classroom at Eastside Elementary. The software is on every device, the dashboard is open, and the lesson looks, to a casual visitor, like the new model. Then she watches for ten minutes. The students are all on the same page at the same pace. The teacher is lecturing from the front while the software runs, unattended, behind her. The reform is in the room. The change is not.

It is the oldest failure in school reform and the reason this chapter exists. Chapters 16 and 17 covered getting a change started. This chapter covers the stretch where most changes quietly fail: the middle, when the excitement has faded, the first wins are old news, the confusing in-between is hard, and the pressure has moved on to the next initiative. It completes each model with its later stages and then steps back to the view that helps most at this point: seeing the school as a system.

Where changes quietly stall

This chapter is about the middle and the long run of a change: the awkward in-between, the practice that has to become real, and the system that pushes back. You'll learn to tell a reform that's merely in the room from one that has changed the work, and to read a simple diagram of how a school's forces interact. Let's find the balance between starting strong and finishing for real.

docs.title: Bridges, Completed: Neutral Zone and New Beginnings
docs.text:
Chapter 17 introduced Bridges' distinction and his first phase. Change versus transition is the distinction between the external event, a new schedule or tool, which can happen on a date, and the internal psychological process of adjusting to it, which takes as long as it takes. Change is a situation, and transition is a process. A leader who treats them as one issues a date and expects people to be ready on it.

The neutral zone is the middle phase of a transition: the old way has ended and the new way is not yet comfortable. People are confused, anxious, and less productive, and morale often dips. Bridges called it a time of both danger and opportunity: people may withdraw or leave, and they may also be unusually creative, because the old rules no longer bind them. Leaders cannot skip it, and they help by providing temporary structure, communicating often, setting short-term goals, and treating the confusion as normal.

New beginnings are the third phase, in which people take on a new identity and purpose and the new way becomes their own. Bridges named four things leaders must supply to start a new beginning, the four P's: the purpose behind the change, a picture of what the outcome looks and feels like, a plan for getting there, and a part for each person to play. The last is the most neglected. A teacher who knows the plan but not her own role cannot begin.

docs.title: Worked Example: Three Phases for a Veteran Teacher
docs.text: Phase What Mr. Hale experiences What helps Ending He misses the whole-class explanations he built over twenty years Acknowledge the loss; ask which part of his craft to keep Neutral zone He is unsure of his role; he is sometimes lecturing, sometimes coaching Temporary routines, a weekly check-in, no pressure to be fluent New beginning He leads small-group sessions and is proud of a student breakthrough Purpose, picture, plan, and a named part to play: "reading lead for the small groups"

docs.title: ADKAR, Completed: Ability and Reinforcement
docs.text:
The first three ADKAR elements, awareness, desire, and knowledge, are about readiness. The last two are about sustaining.

ADKAR Ability is the demonstrated capacity to put the change into practice. Knowing how and being able to do it are different, as anyone who has read about swimming and then entered the water knows. Ability comes from practice, coaching, time, and permission to be imperfect. It is the element where the implementation dip of Chapter 16 appears, and the gap between knowledge and ability is where many well-trained teachers stall. ADKAR Reinforcement is what keeps the change in place after it begins: recognition, feedback, accountability, and the removal of the old way. Without reinforcement, people drift back to the familiar. It corresponds to Lewin's refreeze and Kotter's anchoring.

Element The person's question What builds it A sign it is missing Ability "Can I actually do it?" Practice, coaching, time, tolerance for mistakes "I know how, but I can't get it to work in my class" Reinforcement "Will this last, and is it noticed?" Recognition, feedback, accountability, removing the old way "It went well for a month, then everything went back"

docs.title: CBAM, Completed: Task and Impact Concerns, and Levels of Use
docs.text:
Chapter 17 introduced the first three of CBAM's stages of concern, the self concerns. The remaining four are the ones that appear once a teacher starts using the innovation.

Task concerns are the concerns of stage 3, management: how to organize time, materials, and logistics in order to use the innovation. "How do I fit this into my fifty minutes? What do I do when the logins fail?" They are practical and they dominate the first months of use. Impact concerns are the concerns of stages 4 to 6: consequence (stage 4), whether students are benefiting; collaboration (stage 5), how to work with colleagues to increase the benefit; and refocusing (stage 6), ideas for improving or replacing the innovation with something better. A teacher with impact concerns is the leader's best asset, and a leader who answers task concerns well lets teachers move on to them.

Levels of use is CBAM's second dimension: it describes what a person does with the innovation, in eight levels. They run from nonuse (0), through orientation (I, learning about it) and preparation (II, getting ready), to mechanical use (III, short-term, disjointed, focused on getting each step right), routine (IVA, stable use with little change), refinement (IVB, varying the use to increase impact), integration (V, combining efforts with colleagues), and renewal (VI, re-evaluating and seeking major modifications). Where the stages of concern describe what a person feels, the levels of use describe what a person does, and the two can be different: a teacher may be at mechanical use while holding impact concerns.

Stage of concern Kind Typical statement 0 Awareness, 1 Informational, 2 Personal Self "What is it? How will it affect me?" 3 Management Task "How do I fit this in? Why does the login fail?" 4 Consequence, 5 Collaboration, 6 Refocusing Impact "Are students better off? How can we do this better together?"

docs.title: Worked Example: Reading Three Teachers
docs.text:
Teacher says Stage of concern Level of use "I use it every day but I'm always behind and scrambling to keep up." Task (3) Mechanical (III) "My students who were stuck are moving, and I want to see whether the others are too." Impact: consequence (4) Routine (IVA) "Three of us are comparing dashboards to decide how to change the morning." Impact: collaboration (5) Integration (V)

A coach who answers the first teacher with a lecture on student outcomes has answered a question she has not yet asked. What she needs is help with the logistics.

docs.title: Diagram: What Level of Use Is This?
docs.text:
Run the What Level of Use Is This? MicroSim Fullscreen

What Level of Use Is This?

Type: microsim sim-id: what-level-of-use Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: classify Learning Objective: The learner will classify eight teacher behaviors by CBAM level of use, correctly placing at least seven of eight on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: the eight levels of use (nonuse, orientation, preparation, mechanical, routine, refinement, integration, renewal), defined in the section "CBAM, Completed" above.

Evidence of Mastery: The learner places each of 8 behaviors in one of eight level bins and submits it. A placement is correct when it matches the "Correct level" column in Content. Mastery is 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Reading the level definitions is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Higher levels are better in all cases. (2) Level of use and stage of concern are the same. (3) A teacher who uses the tool every day is at a high level.

Instructional Rationale: Classifying a behavior requires attention to what the teacher does and why, not whether they use the tool. Pairs of behaviors that both involve daily use but differ in fluency and in collaboration make the learner see the differences among levels.

Content:

Eight levels, each with a one-line description shown on request:

Level Description shown 0 Nonuse No involvement and no plan to be involved I Orientation Learning about the innovation and deciding whether to use it II Preparation Getting ready to use it for the first time III Mechanical use Using it in a short-term, disjointed way, focused on each step IVA Routine Using it in a stable way with few changes IVB Refinement Varying the use to increase its impact on students V Integration Combining efforts with colleagues for collective impact VI Renewal Re-evaluating the innovation and seeking major modifications or alternatives

Eight behaviors:

# Behavior shown to the learner Correct level Why (shown as feedback) 1 The teacher has not looked at the new textbook and has no plan to. 0 Nonuse There is no involvement and no plan. 2 The teacher attends a demonstration and reads a guide, but has not decided whether to use it. I Orientation The teacher is learning about it and deciding. 3 The teacher has booked training and is setting up logins for next month. II Preparation The teacher is getting ready for first use. 4 The teacher uses it every day but works through each step with the guide beside her and often loses track. III Mechanical use Use is disjointed and focused on each step. 5 The teacher's use is smooth and unchanged from week to week. IVA Routine Use is stable with few changes. 6 The teacher notices that some students stall at one concept and changes how she uses the dashboard to catch them sooner. IVB Refinement She varies her use to increase impact. 7 Three teachers compare dashboards weekly and redesign the morning together. V Integration They combine efforts with colleagues. 8 The teacher decides the textbook no longer meets her students' needs and starts designing a different approach. VI Renewal She re-evaluates and seeks major changes or alternatives.

Provenance: The eight levels follow the Concerns-Based Adoption Model (Hall and Hord), as described in the chapter. The behaviors are illustrative, written for this chapter.

Rules: Each behavior has exactly one correct level, given in Content, and each level has exactly one behavior. A behavior is scored on its first submitted placement only. The score counts first-attempt correct placements out of 8. Mastery is a score >= 7.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees one behavior at a time and the eight levels.
  2. The learner places the behavior and submits it. The sim marks it correct or incorrect and shows the feedback text.
  3. If incorrect, the learner may place it again; the second attempt does not change the score. After the second attempt, the correct level and reason are shown.
  4. After all 8 behaviors, the sim shows the score and the levels in order.
  5. The learner should notice that behaviors 4 and 5 both describe daily use, yet sit at different levels.

Feedback: 8 behaviors, shuffled once per session, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: [level]. [Why text]." Incorrect: "Not quite. Ask what the teacher is doing and how fluently. [Why text for the correct answer, without naming the level]." After the second attempt the correct level is revealed and the behavior counts as missed. A running score "First-try correct: n of 8" is shown. Final message for a score >= 7: "You can read a level of use from a behavior." For a score < 7: "Review the eight levels and try again; the behaviors will be reshuffled."

Starting State: Behavior 1 of the shuffled order is shown with the eight levels, the score "First-try correct: 0 of 8," and the prompt "What level of use is this?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter lists eight levels of use from nonuse (0) to renewal (VI). The mastery bar is 7 of 8.

docs.title: Culture, Assessed
docs.text:
Chapter 17 introduced Schein's three levels. They deserve a closer look now, since culture is what pulls a change back.

Cultural artifacts are the visible and audible products of a culture: the building, the layout of rooms, the schedule, the dress code, the posters, the language people use, the rituals they perform. They are easy to observe and hard to interpret, since the same artifact can mean different things in different places. Espoused values are the goals, philosophies, and ideals that an organization says it holds, found in mission statements, speeches, and how people explain themselves. Basic assumptions are the deepest layer: the unconscious, taken-for-granted beliefs about how the world works that shape perception and behavior and are rarely discussed. They are what people would be shocked to hear questioned. Schein's central claim is that the assumptions drive behavior, so that when stated values and assumptions disagree, the assumptions win.

Culture assessment is the process of finding out what a school's culture actually is, using observation, documents, interviews, and surveys, and especially by looking for gaps between the layers. A simple four-step version: gather artifacts by walking through and watching; compare them with the espoused values in the mission and in conversation; infer the assumptions where the two disagree by asking "why do we do it this way?" repeatedly; and decide which assumptions will help and which will hinder the change.

Team learning, one of Senge's five disciplines, is the capacity of a group to think together and to produce results beyond what any member could alone. It uses dialogue, a free flow of meaning in which people explore ideas without trying to win, as distinct from discussion, in which positions are defended. Culture assessment works best as a team-learning exercise, since people see their own assumptions only when others show them.

Mental models, another of Senge's disciplines, are the deeply held pictures and assumptions about how the world works that shape what we see and do. They are the individual form of what Schein calls basic assumptions. A teacher's mental model that "students learn when I explain" will shape how she uses an adaptive textbook whatever the training says. Surfacing and testing mental models is how a school finds the beliefs that stand between it and a new practice.

docs.title: Worked Example: Sorting Observations
docs.text:
Observation Layer Why Classroom doors are closed during lessons Artifact It is a visible fact The mission says "collaborative learning community" Espoused value It is what the school says New teachers are told "shut your door and do your own thing" Artifact (a spoken norm) pointing to an assumption It reveals what is really believed "Good teaching is something you do alone" (inferred) Basic assumption It is unspoken and taken for granted A teacher declines a colleague's offer to visit, saying "I'm fine on my own" Artifact pointing to an assumption It shows the assumption in action

The assumption, not the mission, predicts how the school will react to collaborative afternoon teams.

docs.title: Diagram: Artifact, Value, or Assumption?
docs.text:
Run the Artifact, Value, or Assumption? MicroSim Fullscreen

Artifact, Value, or Assumption?

Type: microsim sim-id: artifact-value-or-assumption Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Analyze Bloom Verb: distinguish Learning Objective: The learner will distinguish eight statements about a school as cultural artifacts, espoused values, or basic assumptions, correctly placing at least seven of eight on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: cultural artifacts, espoused values, basic assumptions, culture assessment (all defined in the section "Culture, Assessed" above).

Evidence of Mastery: The learner places each of 8 statements in one of three bins and submits it. A placement is correct when it matches the "Correct layer" column in Content. Mastery is 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Reading the layer definitions is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) The mission statement describes the culture. (2) A visible practice is the same as a belief. (3) Basic assumptions can be read off the walls.

Instructional Rationale: Distinguishing the layers requires deciding whether a statement can be observed, is stated, or is only inferred. Statements that look alike, such as a stated value and the behavior that contradicts it, make the learner separate what is said from what is believed.

Content:

Three layers with definitions shown on request:

Layer Definition shown Cultural artifact Something visible or audible that you can observe directly Espoused value A belief or goal the organization states Basic assumption An unspoken, taken-for-granted belief, usually inferred from behavior

Eight statements:

# Statement shown to the learner Correct layer Why (shown as feedback) 1 Staff meetings begin with the principal reading announcements for twenty minutes. Cultural artifact It is an observable practice. 2 The school's mission statement says, "Every student can succeed." Espoused value It is a stated belief. 3 Teachers assume that struggling students lack effort, and rarely ask whether the lesson was clear. Basic assumption It is an unspoken belief inferred from behavior. 4 The hallway has trophies in the front case and student art in the back corridor. Cultural artifact It is something visible. 5 At open house, the principal says, "We value collaboration among teachers." Espoused value It is a stated value. 6 Everyone in the building takes for granted that the principal makes decisions and teachers carry them out. Basic assumption It is a taken-for-granted belief no one states. 7 The school day is divided into fifty-minute periods separated by bells. Cultural artifact It is observable structure. 8 The handbook states that "parents are partners in education." Espoused value It is a stated belief.

Provenance: The three layers follow Schein's culture model, as described in the chapter. The statements are illustrative, written for this chapter.

Rules: Each statement has exactly one correct layer, given in Content. A statement is scored on its first submitted placement only. The score counts first-attempt correct placements out of 8. Mastery is a score >= 7.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees one statement at a time and the three layers.
  2. The learner places the statement and submits it. The sim marks it correct or incorrect and shows the feedback text.
  3. If incorrect, the learner may place it again; the second attempt does not change the score. After the second attempt, the correct layer and reason are shown.
  4. After all 8 statements, the sim shows the score.
  5. The learner should notice that the espoused values and the basic assumptions in the set point in different directions.

Feedback: 8 statements, shuffled once per session, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: [layer]. [Why text]." Incorrect: "Not quite. Ask whether it can be observed, is stated, or can only be inferred. [Why text for the correct answer, without naming the layer]." After the second attempt the correct layer is revealed and the statement counts as missed. A running score "First-try correct: n of 8" is shown. Final message for a score >= 7: "You can tell the layers of culture apart." For a score < 7: "Review the three layers and try again; the statements will be reshuffled."

Starting State: Statement 1 of the shuffled order is shown with the three layers, the score "First-try correct: 0 of 8," and the prompt "Which layer of culture is this?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter defines three layers (cultural artifacts, espoused values, basic assumptions) and the principle that assumptions win when they disagree with stated values. The mastery bar is 7 of 8.

docs.title: Why Reforms Stall
docs.text:
The grammar of schooling, the phrase of David Tyack and William Tobin, popularized with Larry Cuban in Chapter 1, names the persistent regularities in how schools divide time and space, sort students into age-graded classes, assign them to separate classrooms, and split knowledge into subjects. Tyack and Tobin asked in 1994 why such a structure had been so hard to change, and they showed that it is deeply embedded in the expectations of teachers, parents, and policymakers, so that reforms that disturb it are absorbed or rejected.

Reform without real change is the pattern in which an innovation is adopted in name but leaves the actual work of teaching unchanged. It is the Eastside classroom: the software is running and the lecture goes on. The historian Larry Cuban documented it across a century of technology in schools, summed up in his phrase "oversold and underused," and in an earlier book as "tinkering toward utopia." The reasons are the ones in this chapter: reforms that do not touch the grammar of schooling, the basic assumptions of the culture, or the daily work of teachers get absorbed. The test of a real change is whether the practice is different, which is why the innovation configuration of Chapter 17 matters.

Change fatigue is the weariness and cynicism that people feel when one change initiative follows another with no time to absorb any. The organizational researcher Eric Abrahamson called the pattern "repetitive change syndrome." In schools it takes the form of teachers who say, "This too shall pass," because past initiatives did. Change fatigue is an argument for focus: fewer changes, kept longer, and a leader who finishes what she starts.

Whole-organization change is change that affects an entire organization at once, its structure, culture, and routines, as distinct from a change that affects one team. The compressed morning with a pro-social afternoon is whole-organization change, since it alters the schedule, the roles of every adult, and the daily experience of every student. Whole-organization change is slower and riskier than a pilot and cannot be completed by decree. It requires every tool in Chapters 16 to 18, and usually a combination of the large-scale plan and the small-scale moves of Chapter 19.

docs.title: Worked Example: Is It Real?
docs.text:
Sign Reform without real change Real change What the classroom looks like Software on, teacher lecturing Students at their own pace; teacher with a small group What the dashboard shows Logged in, little activity Mastery moving; teacher using flags What teachers say "I put it on while I teach" "I use it to decide who to pull aside" Level of use Orientation or mechanical Routine or refinement Effect after a year Same scores, lower trust Gains and higher teacher confidence

In the room isn't the same as in the work

A common trap is counting logins and device use as proof that a change has happened. Instead, watch what teachers and students actually do, and compare it with the innovation configuration. A school can have 100 percent adoption on the dashboard and no change in practice.

docs.title: Seeing the System
docs.text:
Systems thinking, the fifth of Senge's disciplines, is the practice of seeing a situation as a whole, with its connected parts, feedback, and delays, and not as a series of separate events. It asks, "What structure produces this behavior?" instead of "Who is to blame?" The environmental scientist Donella Meadows made the approach accessible in her book Thinking in Systems. Its value in schools is that many problems are produced by the way the parts interact: a policy that helps one group harms another, a fix works briefly and then fails, an effort in one place causes a problem somewhere else.

A feedback loop is a chain of cause and effect that circles back, so that a change in one element eventually influences itself. There are two kinds. A reinforcing loop amplifies: more of something leads to still more of it, whether a virtuous spiral or a vicious one. A balancing loop resists: it pushes the system toward a goal or limit and counteracts change. Success breeding confidence breeding more success is reinforcing. A thermostat is balancing, and so is an organization's resistance to being pushed too fast.

A causal loop diagram is a picture of a system's feedback loops: the variables are named, arrows show causal links, and each arrow carries a sign. A plus (+) means the two variables move in the same direction (more of one leads to more of the other), and a minus (−) means they move in opposite directions. Reading a loop is easy: count the minus signs around it. An even number (including zero) makes the loop reinforcing (R), and an odd number makes it balancing (B). Delays, where the effect takes time to appear, are marked with two short lines across the arrow.

docs.title: Worked Example: Two Loops in a Rollout
docs.text:
Lincoln's rollout contains two loops. The first is reinforcing.

Link Sign Meaning Student results → Teacher confidence + Better results raise confidence Teacher confidence → Quality of use + Confident teachers use it better Quality of use → Student results + Better use improves results

There are zero minus signs, so the loop is reinforcing: success feeds itself, and so does failure, in the other direction. The second loop is balancing.

Link Sign Meaning Rollout speed → Teacher overload + Faster rollout means more work Teacher overload → Resistance + More overload means more resistance Resistance → Rollout speed − More resistance slows the rollout

There is one minus sign, an odd number, so the loop is balancing: pushing the rollout faster raises resistance that pushes back. A leader who sees only the first loop will accelerate and be surprised by the second. The two together explain why the Chapter 17 advice to remove obstacles works better than adding pressure.

docs.title: Diagram: Reinforcing or Balancing?
docs.text:
Run the Reinforcing or Balancing? MicroSim Fullscreen

Reinforcing or Balancing?

Type: causal-loop sim-id: reinforcing-or-balancing Library: vis-network Status: Specified Bloom Level: Analyze Bloom Verb: distinguish Learning Objective: The learner will distinguish six causal loops from school change as reinforcing or balancing by counting the minus signs around each, correctly classifying at least five of six on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: feedback loop, reinforcing loop, balancing loop, causal loop diagram, the rule that an even number of minus signs makes a loop reinforcing and an odd number makes it balancing (all defined in the section "Seeing the System" above).

Evidence of Mastery: For each of 6 loops, the learner selects Reinforcing or Balancing and submits it. A selection is correct when it matches the "Correct type" column in Content. Mastery is 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt. Reading the rule is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Reinforcing means good and balancing means bad. (2) A loop with a minus sign cannot be reinforcing. (3) The number of variables decides the type.

Instructional Rationale: Applying the counting rule to concrete school loops makes the learner read link signs and count them, and avoids judging by the sound of the variables. A vicious reinforcing loop and a balancing loop that protects trust show that the type is about structure, not about desirability.

Content:

The rule shown: count the minus signs around the loop; even (including zero) is Reinforcing, odd is Balancing.

Six loops, each shown as a ring of variables with signed links:

# Loop (variable, sign of the link to the next variable) Minus signs Correct type Why (shown as feedback) 1 Student results (+) → Teacher confidence (+) → Quality of use (+) → Student results 0 Reinforcing Zero minus signs is even, so the loop amplifies success. 2 Rollout speed (+) → Teacher overload (+) → Resistance (−) → Rollout speed 1 Balancing One minus sign is odd, so the loop resists being pushed. 3 Family trust (+) → Willingness to share data (+) → Quality of personalization (+) → Family trust 0 Reinforcing Zero minus signs is even; trust and good personalization feed each other. 4 Data collected (+) → Breach risk (−) → Family trust (+) → Data allowed (+) → Data collected 1 Balancing One minus sign is odd; more data raises breach risk, which lowers family trust, which limits the data allowed. 5 Teacher workload (+) → Burnout (+) → Absences (+) → Teacher workload 0 Reinforcing Zero minus signs is even; the loop is a vicious cycle. 6 Screen time (+) → Family complaints (+) → Pressure to cut screen time (−) → Screen time 1 Balancing One minus sign is odd; complaints push screen time back down.

Convention for reading the table: the sign in parentheses after a variable is the sign of the link from that variable to the next one in the ring, and the last variable links back to the first. In loop 4, more breach risk means less family trust, so that link is a minus.

Provenance: The rule follows the standard convention for causal loop diagrams, as described in the chapter. The loops are illustrative, written for this chapter, and the sim must label them "Illustrative loops."

Rules: Type = Reinforcing if the number of minus signs around the loop is even (0, 2, ...) and Balancing if it is odd. Each loop has exactly one correct type, given in Content. A loop is scored on its first submitted answer only. The score counts first-attempt correct answers out of 6. Mastery is a score >= 5. Zoom and reset are by buttons; mouse-wheel zoom is disabled.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees one loop drawn as a ring with signed arrows and the two types.
  2. The learner counts the minus signs, selects a type, and submits it. The sim marks it correct or incorrect and shows the feedback text.
  3. If incorrect, the learner may choose again; the second attempt does not change the score. After the second attempt, the correct type and reason are shown.
  4. After all 6 loops, the sim shows the score and the count of minus signs in each loop.
  5. The learner should notice that three loops are reinforcing and three are balancing, and that loop 5 is reinforcing even though it is harmful.

Feedback: 6 loops, shuffled once per session, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: [type]. [Why text]." Incorrect: "Not quite. Count the minus signs around the whole loop. [Why text for the correct answer, without naming the type]." After the second attempt the correct type is revealed and the loop counts as missed. A running score "First-try correct: n of 6" is shown. Final message for a score >= 5: "You can read a loop." For a score < 5: "Review the counting rule and try again; the loops will be reshuffled."

Starting State: Loop 1 of the shuffled order is shown with the two types, the score "First-try correct: 0 of 6," and the prompt "Is this loop reinforcing or balancing?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's worked example uses loop 1 (student results, teacher confidence, quality of use) as reinforcing and loop 2 (rollout speed, teacher overload, resistance) as balancing. The counting rule is even for reinforcing and odd for balancing. The mastery bar is 5 of 6.

docs.title: Coherence and Capacity
docs.text:
Two ideas from Michael Fullan, with Joanne Quinn, address how a whole system sustains change.

The coherence framework is a model, from Fullan and Quinn's 2016 book, of the four elements that, together, make the parts of a school or district pull in one direction: focusing direction (a small number of clear priorities), cultivating collaborative cultures (teams that learn together), deepening learning (improving what happens in classrooms), and securing accountability (internal responsibility first, external second). It addresses the change-fatigue problem directly: a system asked to do twelve unconnected things will do none well, and coherence is the discipline of fewer, connected priorities.

Capacity building is the development of the knowledge, skills, resources, and motivation of people, individually and collectively, so that they can carry out and sustain a change. Fullan distinguishes it from simply demanding results. A district that tells teachers to adopt a new model, and measures them on it, without investing in their ability, has set a target and built no capacity. Capacity building is the long-run form of ADKAR Ability and Knowledge, applied to the whole system.

docs.title: Choosing a Change Model and a National Example
docs.text:
Choosing a change model is the work of selecting the model, or the combination, that fits a particular school's size, culture, history, and the type of change. No model is best for everything. A short guide follows.

If the school... Lean on Because Is small, with a strong collegial culture CBAM, ADKAR, and peer routines Individual concerns and conversations can steer the change Is large or a district Kotter's steps, with CBAM for monitoring A sequence and a structure for many people Has a closed-door culture Schein, Senge The culture is the main obstacle and must be surfaced Has a history of failed reforms Bridges, change fatigue, capacity building People need their losses and the past honored Is under time pressure Kotter for the plan, ADKAR for individuals Speed needs a sequence and fast diagnosis

National AI adoption is the adoption of AI in education by an entire country's school system, led by national policy. It tests every idea in this chapter at the largest scale, and two recent cases show different outcomes. In Estonia, the AI Leap program (Chapter 15) paired the tools with teacher training and built on the country's record of earlier success with school technology, and it is an example of a coherent, capacity-building approach whose results are still unfolding. South Korea offers a contrasting example: in 2025 the government introduced AI-powered digital textbooks in many schools, and, as reported, strong objections from teachers and parents about the pace, screen time, privacy, and workload led the legislature within months to reclassify them as supplementary materials rather than official textbooks. The details of both cases should be checked against current reporting. The contrast, a rollout built with training and trust against a rapid mandate that met resistance, is the lesson of the whole chapter.

The system pushes back in proportion to the push

Notice what the balancing loop of the rollout says: the harder you push, the harder the system pushes back. A national rollout that outruns teachers' capacity meets exactly that resistance. Going slower on the push and faster on the capacity is often the faster route.

docs.title: Answering the Eastside Classroom
docs.text:
Ms. Okafor's visit to Eastside now has a diagnosis. The reform is in the room and not in the work: teachers are at orientation or mechanical use, still holding task concerns, in the neutral zone of a transition no one acknowledged. The culture assumes lecturing is teaching. The rollout was fast, which raised resistance. Capacity, not just training, was missing, and nothing reinforced the new practice.

The story has both sides. The benefit: tools that tell a leader why a change has stalled and what to do in each case. The risks: declaring success at adoption, pushing speed that the system pushes back against, changing too many things, and imposing a national or district plan without building capacity. The response is to measure practice and not logins, to expect and honor the neutral zone, to read the culture, to build capacity, and to focus on fewer priorities for longer.

Slow is allowed

If a year of work seems to have produced a reform that's only in the room, don't despair; that's the ordinary middle of a real change, and you now have the tools to read it. Pick one classroom, one concern, one loop, and work on that.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Change versus transition: change is an event and transition is an inner process; Bridges' neutral zone is a confusing, necessary middle, and new beginnings need purpose, picture, plan, and part.
  • ADKAR Ability needs practice and coaching, and ADKAR Reinforcement needs recognition and feedback to prevent sliding back.
  • CBAM's task concerns (stage 3) and impact concerns (stages 4 to 6) follow the self concerns; levels of use describe what a teacher does, from nonuse to renewal.
  • Cultural artifacts, espoused values, and basic assumptions are assessed together; culture assessment looks for gaps, mental models are the individual form, and team learning surfaces them.
  • The grammar of schooling explains reform without real change; change fatigue follows a pile of initiatives; whole-organization change needs the whole toolbox.
  • Systems thinking uses feedback loops and the causal loop diagram: an even number of minus signs makes a loop reinforcing, an odd number makes it balancing.
  • The coherence framework and capacity building aim a system at fewer, connected priorities and the people to carry them out.
  • Choosing a change model depends on size, culture, history, and time; national AI adoption shows both a coherent approach (Estonia) and a rapid mandate that met resistance (South Korea, as reported).

You can tell a real change from a reform in the room

You just learned how to carry a change through the neutral zone and the practice gap, to read a culture and a feedback loop, and to tell real change from adoption in name only. Chapter 19 gets practical: concrete moves a leader can make next week. One step at a time, together.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: Sustaining Change: Systems Thinking and National Adoption
docs.text: Test your understanding of the later stages of change, culture assessment, systems thinking, and national AI adoption with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. Bridges named four things leaders must supply for a new beginning. What are they?
docs.text:
1. Pressure, praise, policy, and pay
  2. Pilot, proof, publicity, and permanence
  3. Purpose, picture, plan, and part
  4. People, process, products, and priorities
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Bridges' four P's are the purpose behind the change, a picture of what the outcome looks and feels like, a plan for getting there, and a part for each person to play. The chapter calls the last the most neglected: a teacher who knows the plan but not her own role cannot begin. In the worked example, Mr. Hale's new beginning includes a named part, "reading lead for the small groups." The other options are not Bridges' list.

Concept Tested: New Beginnings

See: Bridges, Completed: Neutral Zone and New Beginnings

docs.title: 2. In CBAM, which stages of concern are the impact concerns?
docs.text:
1. Consequence, collaboration, and refocusing (stages 4 to 6)
  2. Awareness, informational, and personal (stages 0 to 2)
  3. Management only, the task concern (stage 3)
  4. Informational and management (stages 1 and 3)
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Impact concerns are stages 4 to 6: consequence (are students benefiting?), collaboration (how can we work with colleagues to increase the benefit?), and refocusing (how could we improve or replace the innovation?). Stages 0 to 2 are self concerns, and stage 3, management, is the task concern about time, materials, and logistics. The chapter says a teacher with impact concerns is a leader's best asset, and answering task concerns well lets teachers move on to them.

Concept Tested: Impact Concerns

See: CBAM, Completed: Task and Impact Concerns, and Levels of Use

docs.title: 3. A causal loop diagram links three variables in a circle. Two of the three arrows carry a minus sign, and one carries a plus sign. What kind of loop is it?
docs.text:
1. Balancing, because it contains at least one minus sign
  2. Reinforcing, because it has an even number of minus signs
  3. Balancing, because it has more minus signs than plus signs
  4. Neither, because loops with mixed signs cannot be classified
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The chapter's rule is to count the minus signs around a loop: an even number, including zero, makes it reinforcing, and an odd number makes it balancing. Two minus signs is even, so the loop is reinforcing. Two opposite-direction links cancel out, so a change still feeds back on itself in the same direction. The first and third options use rules the chapter does not give; any loop can be classified by this count.

Concept Tested: Causal Loop Diagram

See: Seeing the System

docs.title: 4. A district reports 100 percent of classrooms logging in to its new adaptive software. Why does the chapter warn that this may still be reform without real change?
docs.text:
1. Because login data are usually incorrect and should not be collected
  2. Because full adoption always brings a dip that hides the real gains
  3. Because the software only counts teachers, not students, as its active users
  4. Because real change means practice differs, not just that the tool is running
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Reform without real change is when an innovation is adopted in name but the actual work of teaching stays the same, as in the Eastside classroom where the software ran unattended while the teacher lectured. Larry Cuban documented this across a century as "oversold and underused." The chapter says a school can have 100 percent adoption on the dashboard and no change in practice, so leaders should watch what teachers and students do and compare it with the innovation configuration.

Concept Tested: Reform Without Real Change

See: Why Reforms Stall

docs.title: 5. A teacher says, "I use the new textbook every day, but I'm always scrambling to keep up and the logins keep failing." What stage of concern and level of use does this suggest, and what should a coach offer?
docs.text:
1. Impact concern and refinement; a discussion of student outcomes data
  2. Self concern and nonuse; an introduction to what the textbook is
  3. Task concern and mechanical use; practical help with the logistics
  4. Collaboration concern and integration; time to plan with colleagues
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. The teacher uses the innovation daily but in a scrambling, step-by-step way, which matches mechanical use (level III), and the worry about fitting it in and failing logins is a task concern (stage 3, management). The chapter warns that a coach who answers this teacher with a lecture on student outcomes has answered a question she has not yet asked. She needs help with logistics. She is already using the textbook, so nonuse does not fit.

Concept Tested: Levels of Use

See: Worked Example: Reading Three Teachers

docs.title: 6. What does Bridges' neutral zone describe, and how can leaders help during it?
docs.text:
1. A pause before the change is announced; leaders should keep plans secret
  2. The confusing middle after the old way ends; leaders give temporary structure
  3. The final phase when the change is complete; leaders should celebrate and move on
  4. A period when no one is affected by the change; leaders need do nothing at all
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The neutral zone is the middle phase of a transition: the old way has ended and the new one is not yet comfortable. People are confused, anxious, and less productive, and morale often dips. Bridges called it a time of danger and opportunity, since people may withdraw but may also be unusually creative. Leaders cannot skip it; they help with temporary structure, frequent communication, short-term goals, and treating the confusion as normal. New beginnings, not the neutral zone, are the final phase.

Concept Tested: Neutral Zone

See: Bridges, Completed: Neutral Zone and New Beginnings

docs.title: 7. A superintendent leads a district where three reforms in five years were dropped, and teachers say, "This too shall pass." Using the chapter's guide to choosing a change model, which approach should she lean on?
docs.text:
1. Bridges' transition model, attention to change fatigue, and capacity building
  2. Kotter's eight steps alone, moving quickly to show real strength this time
  3. A rapid mandate with external accountability for every teacher
  4. Rogers' adopter categories, to identify the laggards and replace them
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The chapter's guide says a school with a history of failed reforms should lean on Bridges, change fatigue, and capacity building, because people need their losses and the past honored. Change fatigue, which Abrahamson called "repetitive change syndrome," is an argument for fewer changes kept longer. Moving fast or imposing a mandate risks triggering the balancing loop of resistance. The book treats laggards' concerns with respect rather than as people to replace.

Concept Tested: Choosing a Change Model

See: Choosing a Change Model and a National Example

docs.title: 8. How does Fullan and Quinn's coherence framework address change fatigue?
docs.text:
1. By adding new initiatives each year so that staff stay energized
  2. By replacing internal responsibility with external accountability
  3. By letting each school choose its own unrelated priorities
  4. By focusing a system on a small number of clear, connected priorities
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The coherence framework has four elements: focusing direction on a small number of clear priorities, cultivating collaborative cultures, deepening learning, and securing accountability with internal responsibility first and external second. A system asked to do twelve unconnected things will do none of them well, so coherence is the discipline of fewer, connected priorities. Adding initiatives is the cause of change fatigue, and the framework puts internal responsibility ahead of external accountability.

Concept Tested: Coherence Framework

See: Coherence and Capacity

docs.title: 9. A district's rollout is slower than planned, so a leader orders schools to speed it up. The rollout contains a loop in which rollout speed raises teacher overload (+), overload raises resistance (+), and resistance slows the rollout (−). What does systems thinking predict?
docs.text:
1. The rollout will speed up steadily, since the loop is reinforcing
  2. The loop will stop working once the leader issues the order
  3. Pushing harder raises resistance; reducing overload works better
  4. Resistance will fall, since faster rollouts end the uncomfortable middle sooner
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. The loop has one minus sign, an odd number, so it is balancing: pushing the rollout faster raises overload and resistance, which push the rollout back. A leader who sees only the reinforcing loop of success will accelerate and be surprised. The chapter concludes that the system pushes back in proportion to the push, and that going slower on the push and faster on capacity, such as removing obstacles and reducing overload, is often the faster route.

Concept Tested: Feedback Loop

See: Worked Example: Two Loops in a Rollout

docs.title: 10. The chapter contrasts Estonia's AI Leap with South Korea's 2025 AI digital textbooks, as reported. What lesson does it draw?
docs.text:
1. A rollout built on training and trust beats a rapid mandate that outruns capacity
  2. National programs always fail, so AI adoption should be left to individual teachers
  3. Larger countries adopt AI faster because they have bigger national technology budgets
  4. Digital textbooks succeed only when they replace printed textbooks entirely
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Estonia paired AI tools with teacher training and built on earlier success with school technology, a coherent, capacity-building approach whose results are still unfolding. In South Korea, as reported, objections from teachers and parents about pace, screen time, privacy, and workload led the legislature within months to reclassify AI textbooks as supplementary materials. The chapter calls this contrast the lesson of the whole chapter. It does not say national programs always fail, and it notes both cases should be checked against current reporting.

Concept Tested: National AI Adoption

See: Choosing a Change Model and a National Example

docs.title: References: Sustaining Change: Systems Thinking and National Adoption
docs.text:
1. Systems thinking - Wikipedia - Introduces systems thinking as a focus on wholes, relationships, and feedback, with roots in the work of Forrester, Meadows, and Senge. It frames the chapter's view of a school as a system.

  2. Causal loop diagram - Wikipedia - Explains how variables, links, and reinforcing or balancing feedback loops are drawn and read. It supports the chapter's worked example mapping two loops in an AI rollout.

  3. Mental model - Wikipedia - Describes mental models as internal pictures of how the world works and connects them to single- and double-loop learning. It helps explain why teachers' beliefs about school can block a reform.

  4. Thinking in Systems: A Primer - Donella H. Meadows (edited by Diana Wright) - Chelsea Green Publishing - Meadows' primer on stocks, flows, feedback loops, and leverage points. Her plain examples show why pushing harder on one part of a system often produces resistance.

  5. Tinkering Toward Utopia: A Century of Public School Reform - David Tyack and Larry Cuban - Harvard University Press - Tyack and Cuban coined the "grammar of schooling," the lasting structures such as grade levels and fixed periods. It explains why reforms are often absorbed without real change.

  6. Leverage Points: Places to Intervene in a System - The Donella Meadows Project - Meadows' essay ranking twelve places to intervene in a system, from parameters up to goals and paradigms. It helps leaders choose changes that last rather than surface fixes.

  7. Causal Loop Construction: The Basics - The Systems Thinker - A step-by-step guide to choosing variables, labeling links, and identifying reinforcing and balancing loops. A practical companion for drawing the chapter's causal loop diagrams.

  8. Using "Fixes That Fail" to Get Off the Problem-Solving Treadmill - The Systems Thinker - Daniel Kim explains how quick fixes create long-term problems and offers steps to find higher-leverage action. It sheds light on change fatigue and reform without real change.

  9. Levels of Use - American Institutes for Research - Describes the eight Levels of Use, from nonuse through routine and refined use to renewal. It supports the chapter's completion of CBAM and its worked example reading three teachers.

  10. National Assembly Passes Bill to Switch AI-Driven Textbooks into 'Education Materials' - The Korea Times - Reports South Korea's August 2025 law downgrading AI digital textbooks to optional materials after concerns about teacher resistance, screen time, and literacy. It is the chapter's contrast case to Estonia.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter covers the concrete, next-week moves that make change stick: teacher champions, pilot classrooms, bright spots, shrinking the first step, professional learning communities, and engaging stakeholders — including resistance, family communication, and the changing role of the teacher from lecturer to coach and mentor. Readers finish able to choose a microstrategy suited to a specific teacher's stage of concern.

This chapter builds on concepts from:

docs.title: What Do I Do on Monday?
docs.text:
After a year of frameworks, Ms. Okafor's assistant principal, Mr. Santos, says what she has been thinking. "I understand Kotter. I understand the neutral zone. But it's Sunday night. What do I actually do tomorrow?"

It is a fair challenge to everything in the last three chapters. Models describe change. They do not, on their own, tell a leader what to say to a nervous teacher in the hallway on Monday morning. This chapter turns to the small, concrete moves that do. They are cheap, they can start next week, and they work by changing what individual people experience, one at a time.

The chapter ties the models of Chapters 16 to 18 to practical moves and fits each move to a person's situation: a teacher's stage of concern, a group's place on the adoption curve. It covers teachers, then families, the union, the board, and students, since a school's change belongs to all of them. Along the way it treats resistance as information, not as an obstacle to be overcome.

From frameworks to Monday morning

This chapter is the "what do I do tomorrow" chapter: small moves, matched to the person in front of you. You'll finish able to choose a first step for a particular teacher, family, or union representative. Let's find the balance between a bold plan and a modest first step.

docs.title: Microstrategies and the Big Plan
docs.text:
A microstrategy is a small, concrete action that a leader or teacher can take now, in a few minutes or hours, which moves one person or one group a little closer to adopting a change. Examples are inviting a colleague to watch a lesson, asking a teacher to try one ten-minute activity, or sharing one student's work at a staff meeting. A microstrategy does not require a budget line or a committee.

Holistic plus micro change is the combination of a whole-organization plan (the vision, the coalition, the schedule, the policies of Chapters 16 to 18) with a continuing stream of microstrategies that carry it out person by person. Each does what the other cannot. The large plan gives direction and removes structural obstacles, and the microstrategies build the skills, trust, and habits that no plan can order. A school with only the plan has a policy that is ignored. A school with only microstrategies has pleasant moments that never add up.

docs.title: Worked Example: Plan and Moves Together
docs.text: Part of the change Large-scale plan Microstrategies that carry it out Teachers adopt the Level 2 textbook Board approves it; schedule changed; training budget A teacher champion shows a lesson; a colleague visits; the coach helps with logins Families accept the new morning District policy on data; a family handbook A short phone call from the teacher; a parent night with a demonstration The afternoon runs well Staffing plan; partnership agreements A weekly debrief ritual; one student exhibition at the end of the first month

docs.title: The Switch Framework
docs.text:
A useful organizing model for microstrategies comes from Chip and Dan Heath's 2010 book Switch: How to Change Things When Change Is Hard. The Switch framework uses an image: a rider sitting on an elephant, on a path. The rider is the rational, planning side of a person. The elephant is the emotional side, much stronger, and the part that tires of effort and balks. The path is the situation around them. A change succeeds when all three are addressed, since a clear-headed rider cannot steer a reluctant elephant, and a willing elephant still struggles on a rocky path.

Direct the rider is the set of moves that give the rational side clarity: with the bright spots, a script of the critical moves, and a picture of the destination. Motivate the elephant is the set of moves that engage emotion: finding the feeling, shrinking the change, and growing people's identity. Shape the path is the set of moves that change the situation so that the right behavior is easier: tweaking the environment, building habits, and rallying the herd.

Part What it is Tactics A school example Direct the rider Clarity for the thinking mind Follow the bright spots; script the critical moves; point to the destination A one-page script for the first week; a picture of exhibition night Motivate the elephant Energy for the feeling mind Find the feeling; shrink the change; grow your people A student's breakthrough story; "try one ten-minute activity"; "we are coaches" Shape the path An easier route Tweak the environment; build habits; rally the herd A login that works first time; a standing weekly check; "most of the school is already doing it"

The most important lesson of the framework is diagnostic. When a change stalls, ask which of the three is the problem. A teacher who "doesn't know what to do" needs a rider fix, a teacher who "knows but doesn't care" needs an elephant fix, and a teacher who "wants to, but the login keeps failing" needs a path fix. More of the wrong kind of help does nothing.

docs.title: Diagram: The Rider, the Elephant and the Path
docs.text:

The Rider, the Elephant and the Path
