docs.title: Diagram: Rider, Elephant, or Path?
docs.text:
Run the Rider, Elephant, or Path? MicroSim Fullscreen

Rider, Elephant, or Path?

Type: microsim sim-id: rider-elephant-path Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: classify Learning Objective: The learner will classify nine change tactics as directing the rider, motivating the elephant, or shaping the path, correctly placing at least eight of nine on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: the Switch framework, direct the rider, motivate the elephant, shape the path, and the nine tactics (all defined in the section "The Switch Framework" above).

Evidence of Mastery: The learner places each of 9 tactics in one of three bins and submits it. A placement is correct when it matches the "Correct part" column in Content. Mastery is 8 of 9 correct on the first attempt. Reading the definitions is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Giving people information is always enough. (2) Emotion is an obstacle to change. (3) Changing the environment is not really leading.

Instructional Rationale: Classifying a tactic requires identifying whom it is aimed at: the thinking mind, the feeling mind, or the situation. Three tactics per part ensure the learner sees the full set and not one favorite.

Content:

Three bins with definitions on request:

Part Definition shown Direct the rider Give the thinking mind clarity about what to do and where it leads Motivate the elephant Engage feeling and identity so people want to act Shape the path Change the situation so that the right behavior is easier

Nine tactics:

# Tactic shown to the learner Correct part Why (shown as feedback) 1 Find the classroom where students like yours already thrive with the tool and copy what that teacher does. Direct the rider Following a bright spot gives clear, proven direction. 2 Give teachers a one-page script for the first week: what to click and what to say on days one to five. Direct the rider Scripting the critical moves removes ambiguity. 3 Show a vivid picture of the exhibition night that the freed afternoons will make possible. Direct the rider Pointing to the destination clarifies where the change leads. 4 Share a story of a student's breakthrough so that teachers feel why this matters. Motivate the elephant Finding the feeling engages emotion. 5 Ask each teacher to try one ten-minute activity this week. Motivate the elephant Shrinking the change makes it feel doable. 6 Invite teachers to see themselves as learning coaches, not lecturers. Motivate the elephant Growing people's identity builds motivation. 7 Fix the single sign-on so the login works on the first try. Shape the path Tweaking the environment removes friction. 8 Add a standing fifteen-minute dashboard check to the weekly team meeting. Shape the path Building a habit makes the behavior routine. 9 Make visible that most teachers in the neighboring school already use it. Shape the path Rallying the herd makes the behavior the norm.

Provenance: The framework follows Heath and Heath (2010), as described in the chapter. The tactics are illustrative, written for this chapter.

Rules: Each tactic has exactly one correct part, given in Content, and each part has exactly three tactics. A tactic is scored on its first submitted placement only. The score counts first-attempt correct placements out of 9. Mastery is a score >= 8.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees one tactic at a time and the three parts.
  2. The learner places the tactic and submits it. The sim marks it correct or incorrect and shows the feedback text.
  3. If incorrect, the learner may place it again; the second attempt does not change the score. After the second attempt, the correct part and reason are shown.
  4. After all 9 tactics, the sim shows the score and the tactics grouped by part.
  5. The learner should notice that three of the tactics change nothing about people and everything about the situation.

Feedback: 9 tactics, shuffled once per session, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: [part]. [Why text]." Incorrect: "Not quite. Ask whom the tactic is aimed at: the thinking mind, the feeling mind, or the situation. [Why text for the correct answer, without naming the part]." After the second attempt the correct part is revealed and the tactic counts as missed. A running score "First-try correct: n of 9" is shown. Final message for a score >= 8: "You can tell which part of the change a tactic serves." For a score < 8: "Review the three parts and try again; the tactics will be reshuffled."

Starting State: Tactic 1 of the shuffled order is shown with the three parts, the score "First-try correct: 0 of 9," and the prompt "Which part of the change does this tactic serve?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter names nine tactics, three per part, as in the table. The mastery bar is 8 of 9.

docs.title: Bright Spots and Positive Deviance
docs.text:
Bright spots are examples of success already happening within the system, which can be studied and copied. Instead of asking "what's wrong and how do we fix it?" a leader asks "where is this already working, and what are those people doing?" Positive deviance is the same idea as a method: finding individuals or groups who achieve better results than their peers with the same resources, and spreading what they do. The best-known case is from Vietnam in the 1990s, when Jerry Sternin of Save the Children looked for children who were well-nourished in poor villages and found that their mothers added small shrimp, crabs, and sweet-potato greens to meals and fed the children several small meals a day. Spreading those practices, which were free and already local, reduced malnutrition, and the villagers owned them because they were their own.

In a district, a bright spot is a classroom where the new tool is working with students like yours, run by a teacher with your constraints. Copying what that teacher does is more believable and cheaper than importing a practice from a conference.

docs.title: Teacher Champions and Pilot Classrooms
docs.text:
A teacher champion is a respected teacher who tries a change early, shares honestly how it goes, and helps colleagues. Chapter 15's advice was to choose the respected skeptic who changed their mind, not the biggest enthusiast. A champion needs support: protected time, a reduced load elsewhere, and recognition, since the risk of burning out the first adopter is real. A champion who is asked to do everything stops being a model and becomes a cautionary tale.

A pilot classroom is a single classroom, or a small number, in which a change is tried carefully before it spreads, with a baseline, a plan, support, and a way to measure results. A good pilot has a volunteer teacher, one clear goal, a start and end date (six to eight weeks is common), a baseline measure taken before it starts, support from a coach, a data-privacy plan, and an agreed plan for sharing what is learned. Where possible it is designed like the randomized pilot of Chapter 2, so that its results can be believed by skeptics.

Early visible results are the quick, concrete, easily seen outcomes that a pilot or champion produces, shared widely, which convince others that the change works. They have to be real and related to the change: hours of grading saved, a count of students who mastered a concept, a student's work shown at a staff meeting. They are Kotter's short-term wins, made specific.

docs.title: Worked Example: A Pilot Plan on One Page
docs.text:
Element Lincoln's plan for the afternoon-project pilot Teacher Ms. Rivera, a volunteer, and a champion Scope One seventh-grade section of 28 students Goal Test whether teams of four with defined roles complete a project better than a comparison section Duration Six weeks Baseline A teamwork rubric scored in week 0 for both sections Support A coach one hour a week; a half-day of planning time Measure The same rubric at week 6, scored by a second teacher who does not know which section is which Early visible result A student exhibition at week 6 Sharing A fifteen-minute talk at a staff meeting, with a student presenter

The plan fits on a page and could begin next Monday.

docs.title: Shrinking the First Step and Compounding Small Changes
docs.text:
Shrinking the first step is the practice of making the first action so small that doing it is easy and even a little silly to refuse. Instead of "adopt the new model," a leader asks for "try this ten-minute activity once." It works on the elephant: a small step costs little effort, produces a success, and shifts how the person sees themselves ("I'm someone who tries this"). It also supplies information for the rider, since the person now knows something real about the change.

Compounding small changes is the way a series of small improvements, each modest, adds up to a large one, because each builds on the one before. If a teacher improves some skill by one percent a week, the improvements multiply. Over 52 weeks they compound to \( 1.01^{52} \approx 1.68 \), about 68 percent better than the start, which is more than 52 percent, the simple sum. The illustration is deliberately simple, and real skills do not improve at a constant rate, but the principle holds: small, repeated steps beat large, rare ones, because they are more likely to be done at all.

docs.title: Worked Example: A Ladder of First Steps
docs.text:
For a teacher with a personal concern ("Will I be able to do this?"), the leader offers steps that grow slowly.

Week Step Time required 1 Open the textbook page and try one simulation yourself 10 minutes 2 Use one simulation with one class for the warm-up 10 minutes 3 Add one self-check question and read the results 15 minutes 4 Look at the dashboard together with the coach 20 minutes 6 Run one full lesson in the new format 50 minutes

The teacher has done a full lesson by week 6 without ever being asked to "adopt the new model." Each step was small enough to finish.

Ask for the smallest step that counts

When someone hesitates, don't argue for the big change. Ask for the smallest step that would still tell them something real, such as one ten-minute activity. A step small enough to say yes to is worth more than a bold request that gets "let me think about it."

docs.title: Coaching, Observation, and Learning Communities
docs.text:
Professional development is the ongoing learning of teachers and other staff to improve their practice. Research on what works, summarized by Laura Desimone, finds five features of effective professional development: a content focus tied to what teachers teach, active learning in place of listening to lectures, coherence with other goals and with teachers' needs, sufficient duration over weeks or months, and collective participation by groups of teachers from the same school. A single day of training with a binder is the weakest form and, unfortunately, the most common.

Staff AI literacy is the knowledge and skill staff need to understand what AI tools are, judge when to use them and when not to, evaluate their output, and protect student data (Chapters 5, 10, and 12). It is a part of professional development, and an early one, because teachers who do not understand the tools cannot guide students in using them well, and teachers who do not understand the risks cannot answer families' questions.

Instructional coaching is a form of professional development in which a trained colleague works with a teacher one-on-one or in small groups over time: observing, modeling, planning, giving feedback, and helping the teacher try new practices. It is the best-supported form of professional development. A 2018 review of 60 studies by Matthew Kraft, David Blazar, and Dylan Hogan found that coaching improved teachers' instruction by about half a standard deviation and student achievement by about 0.18 standard deviations, with larger effects for coaching that was in person and not too widely spread. It addresses the task concerns of CBAM (Chapter 18) and the ability element of ADKAR, because it supplies practice and feedback in the teacher's own classroom.

Peer observation is the practice in which teachers watch each other teach, for learning and not for evaluation, usually with a short conversation before and after. Its power is observability, one of Rogers' five attributes (Chapter 15): teachers see the change working in a real room with real students. It must be safe, so it works best with a protocol, such as the observer looking for one thing the host asked about, and with a firm rule that what is seen is not used to evaluate.

A professional learning community (PLC) is a group of teachers who meet regularly to improve student learning together by examining evidence and sharing practice. The educators Richard DuFour and Robert Eaker built the model around a focus on learning, a collaborative culture, and attention to results. A PLC works through four questions: What do we want students to learn? How will we know when they have learned it? What will we do if they have not? What will we do if they already have? These four questions are mastery learning (Chapter 11) in a team routine, and the dashboards of Chapters 8 and 9 supply the evidence for the second question.

docs.title: Worked Example: A Fifteen-Minute PLC Routine
docs.text:
Lincoln's seventh-grade math team meets weekly for fifteen minutes, using the dashboard.

Minutes Step Question 0–3 Look at the class mastery heatmap (Chapter 8) Which concept has a dark column? 3–8 Share what is working for students who got it What did the bright spot do? 8–12 Plan for students who haven't Who will we pull aside, and with what? 12–15 Plan for students who already know it What will they do with the extra time?

The routine takes no extra time that the team does not already spend, and it turns the dashboard into a decision.

docs.title: Matching the Strategy to the Person
docs.text:
Most of the chapter so far lists tools. This section is about choosing among them.

Matching strategy to concern is selecting a microstrategy that answers the CBAM stage of concern (Chapters 17 and 18) that a person actually holds. Matching strategy to adopter is selecting a strategy that fits the person's category on the adoption curve (Chapter 15). Together they say that the right move depends on who and where.

Person's concern Typical statement Microstrategy that fits Informational (stage 1) "What does it actually look like?" Peer observation; a pilot-classroom visit Personal (stage 2) "Will I be able to do this?" Shrink the first step; a private demonstration Task (stage 3) "How do I fit it in? The logins fail." Instructional coaching; fix the obstacle Consequence (stage 4) "Are students better off?" Share early visible results; examine data in a PLC Collaboration (stage 5) "How can we improve it together?" A professional learning community; peer observation Adopter category What they respond to Microstrategy that fits Innovators Permission and resources to try Give them a pilot classroom and a small budget Early adopters Strategic vision and a chance to lead Make them champions; ask for their input on the plan Early majority Proof from peers and a smooth path Peer observation; a champion's story; remove obstacles Late majority Reassurance and pressure from norms Make the practice visible and routine; mandatory basics with support Laggards Respect and no surprises Listen to their concerns; give time; do not shame

Choose the Microstrategy

Type: microsim sim-id: choose-the-microstrategy Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: apply Learning Objective: The learner will apply the matching tables by choosing the microstrategy that best fits each of eight teacher situations, correctly choosing at least seven of eight on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: the six microstrategies and the matching of strategy to concern and to adopter (all defined in the sections above and in "Matching the Strategy to the Person").

Evidence of Mastery: For each of 8 situations, the learner selects one of six microstrategies and submits it. A choice is correct when it matches the "Best microstrategy" column in Content. Mastery is 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Reading the matching tables is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) The same microstrategy works for every teacher. (2) More training solves every concern. (3) A mandate is a strategy.

Instructional Rationale: Choosing a microstrategy requires diagnosing the person's concern first and then selecting the move that answers it. Situations with similar topics but different concerns, such as seeing it versus managing logistics, force the learner to diagnose before choosing.

Content:

Six microstrategies with a one-line description shown on request:

Microstrategy Description shown Teacher champion A respected colleague shares honestly how it went Pilot classroom Try it in one class, with a baseline and a plan, before committing Instructional coaching A trained colleague works with the teacher over time Shrink the first step Ask for one very small first action Peer observation Watch a colleague teach, for learning, not evaluation Professional learning community A team meets weekly to examine evidence and plan

Eight situations:

# Situation shown to the learner Best microstrategy Why (shown as feedback) 1 A teacher with an informational concern says, "I want to see what this looks like in a real class." Peer observation Seeing it in a colleague's room answers the question directly. 2 A teacher with a personal concern is overwhelmed by the whole plan and says, "I can't do all that." Shrink the first step A very small first action makes it doable. 3 A teacher with a task concern spends every Monday fighting logins and organizing the lesson. Instructional coaching A coach can help with the logistics in the teacher's own classroom. 4 Early-majority teachers say they will believe it when a respected colleague tells them how it went. Teacher champion They trust peers like themselves. 5 A principal wants to test the model in one class for six weeks, with a baseline, before committing the school. Pilot classroom It is a careful trial before spreading. 6 Teachers with impact concerns want to improve their results by working with colleagues on the evidence. Professional learning community A weekly team routine examines evidence and plans together. 7 A teacher in the implementation dip says, "I'm worse at this than I was before." Instructional coaching Practice and feedback in the teacher's room carry people through the dip. 8 A late-majority teacher says, "Show me data from a classroom in our own building." Pilot classroom A local pilot supplies results from a similar setting.

Provenance: The matching follows the chapter's tables. The situations are illustrative, written for this chapter.

Rules: Each situation has exactly one best microstrategy, given in Content. A situation is scored on its first submitted choice only. The score counts first-attempt correct choices out of 8. Mastery is a score >= 7.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads one situation and sees the six microstrategies.
  2. The learner selects one and submits it. The sim marks it correct or incorrect and shows the feedback text.
  3. If incorrect, the learner may choose again; the second attempt does not change the score. After the second attempt, the correct microstrategy and reason are shown.
  4. After all 8 situations, the sim shows the score.
  5. The learner should notice that two situations call for coaching and two for a pilot, for different reasons.

Feedback: 8 situations, shuffled once per session, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: [microstrategy]. [Why text]." Incorrect: "Not quite. First ask what concern the person has. [Why text for the correct answer, without naming the microstrategy]." After the second attempt the correct microstrategy is revealed and the situation counts as missed. A running score "First-try correct: n of 8" is shown. Final message for a score >= 7: "You can match the move to the person." For a score < 7: "Review the matching tables and try again; the situations will be reshuffled."

Starting State: Situation 1 of the shuffled order is shown with the six microstrategies, the score "First-try correct: 0 of 8," and the prompt "Which microstrategy best fits this teacher?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter lists six microstrategies and matches them to stages of concern and adopter categories. The mastery bar is 7 of 8.

docs.title: Resistance, Concerns, and Job Fears
docs.text:
Resistance to change is opposition, active or passive, to a proposed change. It is usually treated as a problem, and the research suggests a different view: resistance is often information. In a 2009 article, Jeffrey Ford and Laurie Ford argued that resistance can be a resource, since people who push back often see real problems that the leaders do not.

Sources of resistance are the reasons people resist, and they are worth sorting, because each calls for a different response:

  • Loss of identity, competence, routines, or status (Chapter 17).
  • Uncertainty: not knowing what the change means.
  • Lack of trust in the leaders or the process, often from past failed reforms.
  • Disagreement on substance: a belief that the proposal is wrong.
  • Workload and capacity: no time or support to do it.
  • Poor communication: not having been told, or having been told too late.

A legitimate concern is a worry about a change that has a real basis in evidence or experience, and which the leader should take seriously and address. Many of the concerns teachers and families raise about AI, such as student privacy (Chapter 10), over-reliance (Chapter 12), screen time (Chapter 2), thin evidence (Chapter 11), and unequal access (Chapter 3), are legitimate. Treating them as resistance to be overcome throws away the people who have noticed the real risks.

Fear of job loss is the worry that the change will make a teacher's job unnecessary. It is perhaps the strongest concern, and it deserves a straight answer, not a slogan. The honest answer, based on the design of this book, is that the model changes teachers' work and does not remove the need for it: the afternoon needs more adults who can coach, facilitate, and debrief, and the morning needs a coach who knows when a student needs a human explanation. The Stanford study of Tutor CoPilot, described in the AI-First Stories appendix, found that AI worked best when it helped human tutors do better, and not when it replaced them. A leader should not promise what she cannot guarantee, but she can say what the plan assumes, and put it in writing.

Responding with empathy is meeting a concern by first understanding and acknowledging it, and only then responding with information or options. It has four moves: listen without interrupting, acknowledge the feeling and the reason ("That's a real worry, and it makes sense given what you've seen before"), ask a question to understand more, and respond with facts, options, or a commitment. It is active listening (Chapter 13) applied to change.

docs.title: Worked Example: Four Replies to a Worried Teacher
docs.text:
A teacher says, "I'm afraid this means my job won't exist in five years."

Reply Kind Effect "You're overreacting; nobody is losing their job." Dismissive Closes the conversation; trust falls "That's not what the plan says." Defensive Argues with the feeling; no acknowledgment "Don't worry, everything will be fine." Reassurance without substance Sounds kind and answers nothing "That's a real worry, and it makes sense. Here is what the plan assumes about teachers' roles, and what we can and can't promise. What would you want in writing?" Empathic and substantive Acknowledges, informs, and asks

docs.title: Diagram: Empathy or Not?
docs.text:
Run the Empathy or Not? MicroSim Fullscreen

Empathy or Not?

Type: microsim sim-id: empathy-or-not Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: classify Learning Objective: The learner will classify eight replies to a worried teacher as dismissive, defensive, reassurance without substance, or empathic and substantive, correctly placing at least seven of eight on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: responding with empathy, legitimate concern, fear of job loss (all defined in the section "Resistance, Concerns, and Job Fears" above).

Evidence of Mastery: The learner places each of 8 replies in one of four bins and submits it. A placement is correct when it matches the "Correct kind" column in Content. Mastery is 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Reading the definitions is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Reassurance is the same as empathy. (2) Facts alone answer a worry. (3) Disagreeing is always defensive.

Instructional Rationale: Classifying replies shows the learner that kind-sounding replies can be empty and that factual replies can be defensive. Two replies per kind, on the same statement, make the distinction concrete.

Content:

The statement every reply answers: a teacher says, "I'm afraid this means my job won't exist in five years."

Four bins with definitions on request:

Kind Definition shown Dismissive Tells the person the worry is unfounded or silly Defensive Argues with the worry or restates the plan without acknowledging the feeling Reassurance without substance Offers comfort with no facts, options, or commitments Empathic and substantive Acknowledges the concern and then offers facts, options, or a commitment

Eight replies:

# Reply shown to the learner Correct kind Why (shown as feedback) 1 "You're overreacting; that's ridiculous." Dismissive It tells the teacher the worry is silly. 2 "That's not what the plan says. Read the document." Defensive It argues with the worry without acknowledging it. 3 "Don't worry, it'll all work out." Reassurance without substance It comforts without any facts or commitments. 4 "That's a real worry. The plan assumes more adult coaches in the afternoon, and I'll put in writing what I can and can't promise. What would you like included?" Empathic and substantive It acknowledges, informs, and asks. 5 "Nobody is going to lose their job, so there's nothing to discuss." Dismissive It closes the conversation and promises more than can be known. 6 "We've been over this at three meetings." Defensive It points to past explanation instead of hearing the worry. 7 "I understand, I'm sure you'll be fine." Reassurance without substance It sounds kind and offers nothing concrete. 8 "It makes sense you'd worry given past cuts. Here are the roles the model needs and how we will support you in moving into them; let's meet next week to look at your schedule." Empathic and substantive It acknowledges the reason, gives facts and support, and offers a next step.

Provenance: The four kinds follow the chapter section "Resistance, Concerns, and Job Fears." The replies are illustrative, written for this chapter.

Rules: Each reply has exactly one correct kind, given in Content, and each kind has exactly two replies. A reply is scored on its first submitted placement only. The score counts first-attempt correct placements out of 8. Mastery is a score >= 7.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees the teacher's statement and one reply at a time, with the four kinds.
  2. The learner places the reply and submits it. The sim marks it correct or incorrect and shows the feedback text.
  3. If incorrect, the learner may place it again; the second attempt does not change the score. After the second attempt, the correct kind and reason are shown.
  4. After all 8 replies, the sim shows the score.
  5. The learner should notice that only the empathic and substantive replies both acknowledge the worry and offer something concrete.

Feedback: 8 replies, shuffled once per session, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: [kind]. [Why text]." Incorrect: "Not quite. Ask whether the reply acknowledges the worry and then offers something concrete. [Why text for the correct answer, without naming the kind]." After the second attempt the correct kind is revealed and the reply counts as missed. A running score "First-try correct: n of 8" is shown. Final message for a score >= 7: "You can tell empathy from reassurance." For a score < 7: "Review the four kinds and try again; the replies will be reshuffled."

Starting State: The teacher's statement and reply 1 of the shuffled order are shown with the four kinds, the score "First-try correct: 0 of 8," and the prompt "What kind of reply is this?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's worked example lists four kinds of reply (dismissive, defensive, reassurance without substance, empathic and substantive) to the same statement about job loss. The mastery bar is 7 of 8.

Don't promise what you can't guarantee

A common trap is answering job fears with "nobody will lose their job." It feels kind, and if the promise cannot be kept it destroys trust. Say what the plan assumes, what you can commit to in writing, and what you don't know yet.

docs.title: Stakeholders: Families, Unions, the Board, and Students
docs.text: A stakeholder is any person or group with an interest in, or influence over, a change (Chapter 2). Stakeholder engagement is the practice of involving stakeholders in planning and carrying out a change, so that they shape it, understand it, and support it. A stakeholder adoption map is a simple chart that lists each stakeholder group and records where it stands on the adoption curve and what its main concern is, so that the leader can plan a move for each.

docs.title: Worked Example: A Stakeholder Adoption Map
docs.text: Stakeholder Where they stand Main concern First move Teachers in the pilot Innovators and early adopters Support and recognition Make them champions Other teachers Early and late majority Workload; "will it work for my students?" Peer observation; a coach Families Mixed; many pragmatists Screen time, privacy, "will my child still learn to think?" A parent night; a handout (Chapter 8) The teacher union Cautious Workload, evaluation, job security, data use Early meeting and written assurances The school board Pragmatist buyers Cost, evidence, risk A short, honest board presentation Students Often early adopters Fairness; voice Ask them; use their feedback

docs.title: Families and the Community
docs.text: Family communication is the regular, two-way exchange of information between the school and students' families. For a change like this one it needs to be early, specific, and honest, and it needs to go both ways. Communicating before rumors is the discipline of telling families and staff about a change before they hear about it elsewhere, because rumors, once started, are far harder to correct than a clear statement is to make. A leader who waits for the plan to be perfect lets the rumor mill write it. Silence is read as secrecy. Community communication extends the same practice to the wider community: local newspapers, community groups, employers, and neighbors without children in the school, whose taxes and goodwill the school depends on.

docs.title: Worked Example: A Communication Calendar
docs.text: When What Who Channel Six weeks before What is planned and why; what is not yet decided All families Letter and a parent meeting Four weeks before A demonstration of the textbook and the hint-first tutor Interested families An evening open house Two weeks before What data is collected and who sees it (Chapter 8's handout) All families A one-page summary and a Q and A Month 2 of the pilot Honest results, including the dip All families A short monthly update Ongoing Questions and concerns Anyone A phone line and an email address with a promised reply time

docs.title: Unions, the Board, and Students
docs.text:
A teacher union is an organization that represents teachers in negotiating pay, working conditions, and policies with their employer, and in many districts it holds contractual rights that bear directly on a change: the length of the work day, class size, evaluation, and what teachers can be required to do. In the United States the main unions are the National Education Association and the American Federation of Teachers, and both have engaged with AI: the NEA has adopted a policy statement on AI in education, and in 2025 the AFT launched a national academy to train teachers in AI with support from several technology companies. Union engagement is the practice of involving the union early and as a partner: sharing plans before they are final, asking for its concerns, and agreeing on how workload, evaluation, and data will be handled, often in a written memorandum. A union that has been consulted can be a champion. One that learns of a change from the newspaper will oppose it, with good reason.

A board presentation is the report to the school board, whose approval and budget a change depends on. It works best when it is short, honest, and organized around the board's questions: what are we trying to do, what is the evidence, what will it cost, what are the risks and how will we manage them, and how will we know if it is working? A board hears from every stakeholder, so a presentation that names the concerns and the responses earns more trust than one that sells.

Student voice is the participation of students in decisions that affect them: giving opinions, shaping choices, and sometimes sharing in the decisions themselves. Roger Hart's 1992 "ladder of participation" describes eight rungs, from tokenism, where students are decoration, to projects in which young people initiate and share decisions with adults. Students are the people most affected by an AI-native school, and often the quickest to notice what is not working, such as a confusing interface, or a tutor that hands over answers. A leader who asks them gets information no one else has.

Everyone with a stake sees a different school

Notice how the same plan looks different from each seat: the teacher sees workload, the parent sees screens and privacy, the union sees contracts, the board sees cost, and the student sees whether it's fair. A leader's job is to hold all five views at once, which is why a stakeholder map is worth drawing.

docs.title: Back to Monday
docs.text:
Mr. Santos's question now has an answer, and it is a list of five things: pick one teacher and ask for one small step; walk one skeptic into a colleague's classroom; fix the one obstacle that has been blocking the logins; write the first honest letter to families, including the dip; and call the union representative before the board meeting. None of it needs a budget, and all of it is matched to a person.

The story has both sides. The benefit: moves small enough to start tomorrow and matched to what each person needs. The risks: treating microstrategies as a replacement for the plan, wearing out the champion, calling legitimate concerns resistance, promising what can't be kept, and leaving stakeholders to find out from rumors. The response is the combination in this chapter: the large plan with the small moves, a diagnosis before each move, empathy before information, and the families, the union, and the students at the table from the start.

Small moves are real leadership

If a hallway conversation or a ten-minute classroom visit feels too small to count as leading a change, remember the compounding arithmetic: small steps taken often beat big ones taken rarely. Pick one person and one move this week.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• A microstrategy is a small action that moves one person; holistic plus micro change combines the whole-organization plan with a stream of microstrategies.
  • The Switch framework: direct the rider (bright spots, script the critical moves, point to the destination), motivate the elephant (find the feeling, shrink the change, grow identity), and shape the path (tweak the environment, build habits, rally the herd). Diagnose which one is stalled.
  • Bright spots and positive deviance find success already in the system; a teacher champion and a pilot classroom produce early visible results.
  • Shrinking the first step and compounding small changes make change doable; 1 percent a week for 52 weeks compounds to about 68 percent.
  • Professional development works with content focus, active learning, coherence, duration, and collective participation; staff AI literacy comes early; instructional coaching, peer observation, and a professional learning community have the strongest support.
  • Matching strategy to concern (CBAM stage) and to adopter (adoption category) chooses the move.
  • Resistance to change has sources; a legitimate concern deserves a response; fear of job loss needs an honest answer, not a slogan; responding with empathy comes before information.
  • Stakeholder engagement with a stakeholder adoption map covers family communication (communicating before rumors, community communication), union engagement with the teacher union, a board presentation, and student voice.

You can name your Monday move

You just learned the small, concrete moves that carry a change, how to match each move to the person in front of you, and how to treat resistance as information. That completes Part 4 on culture and change. Chapter 20 puts it all together in the design of an AI-native school day. One step at a time, together.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: Microstrategies for Leading Change
docs.text: Test your understanding of the small, concrete moves that make change stick and how to match each one to the person and stakeholder in front of you with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. What are the three parts of the Heaths' Switch framework?
docs.text:
1. Unfreeze the habit, change the practice, refreeze the routine
  2. Direct the rider, motivate the elephant, shape the path
  3. Build awareness, create desire, reinforce the change
  4. Find the champion, run the pilot, scale the results
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Chip and Dan Heath picture a rider (the rational, planning side) on an elephant (the stronger emotional side) on a path (the situation). Directing the rider gives clarity, motivating the elephant engages emotion, and shaping the path makes the right behavior easier. A change succeeds when all three are addressed. The first option is Lewin's model, the third draws on ADKAR, and the fourth lists microstrategies rather than the framework.

Concept Tested: Switch Framework

See: The Switch Framework

docs.title: 2. What is positive deviance?
docs.text:
1. A teacher who openly refuses to adopt a new practice at all
  2. An effect in which early success leads to unrealistic expectations
  3. A method of importing proven practices from other countries
  4. Spreading the practices of people who beat their peers with the same resources
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Positive deviance looks for individuals or groups who achieve better results than their peers with the same resources, then spreads their practices. In the best-known case, Jerry Sternin of Save the Children found that mothers of well-nourished children in poor Vietnamese villages added small shrimp, crabs, and sweet-potato greens to meals, and spreading these free, local practices reduced malnutrition. The chapter notes this is more believable and cheaper than importing practices from outside, which is what the third option describes.

Concept Tested: Positive Deviance

See: Bright Spots and Positive Deviance

docs.title: 3. A teacher says, "I want to use the new textbook, and I know what to do, but the student logins keep failing." In the Switch framework, what kind of fix does this call for?
docs.text:
1. Direct the rider, with a script of the first week's moves
  2. Motivate the elephant, with a student's breakthrough story
  3. Shape the path, by fixing the login so it works the first time
  4. Grow identity, by telling the teacher "we are coaches now"
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. The chapter's diagnostic says a teacher who "doesn't know what to do" needs a rider fix, one who "knows but doesn't care" needs an elephant fix, and one who "wants to, but the login keeps failing" needs a path fix. This teacher has both clarity and motivation; the situation is the obstacle. The chapter warns that more of the wrong kind of help does nothing, so a script or a motivating story would miss the real problem.

Concept Tested: Shape the Path

See: The Switch Framework

docs.title: 4. Why does shrinking the first step work, according to the chapter?
docs.text:
1. A tiny step costs little, brings a success, and shifts how people see themselves
  2. A tiny step lets the leader skip the training and support the change would otherwise need
  3. A tiny step guarantees the person will adopt the full model within a week
  4. A tiny step keeps the change secret until the plan is ready to announce
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Shrinking the first step makes the first action so small that it is easy, even a little silly, to refuse, such as "try this ten-minute activity once." It works on the elephant: low effort, a quick success, and a new self-image ("I'm someone who tries this"). It also gives the rider real information about the change. In the ladder of first steps, the teacher reaches a full lesson by week 6 without ever being asked to "adopt the new model." It is not a substitute for support or a guarantee.

Concept Tested: Shrinking the First Step

See: Shrinking the First Step and Compounding Small Changes

docs.title: 5. A teacher improves one teaching skill by 2 percent a week for 26 weeks, with each week building on the last. About how much better is the skill at the end, and how does that compare with simply adding the weekly gains?
docs.text:
1. About 26 percent, the same as adding the weekly gains
  2. About 52 percent, the same as adding the weekly gains
  3. About 40 percent, less than adding up the weekly gains
  4. About 67 percent, more than adding the weekly gains
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Compounding multiplies the gains: \( 1.02^{26} \approx 1.67 \), or about 67 percent better. Simply adding 2 percent for 26 weeks gives 52 percent, which is less, because compounding builds each gain on the one before. The chapter's own example, 1 percent a week for 52 weeks, compounds to about 68 percent versus a sum of 52. It cautions that real skills do not improve at a constant rate, but small, repeated steps beat large, rare ones because they are more likely to be done.

Concept Tested: Compounding Small Changes

See: Shrinking the First Step and Compounding Small Changes

docs.title: 6. What did the 2018 review by Kraft, Blazar, and Hogan find about instructional coaching?
docs.text:
1. Coaching had no measurable effect on instruction or student achievement
  2. Coaching improved instruction by about 0.5 SD and achievement by about 0.18 SD
  3. Coaching worked only when delivered online to large groups of teachers
  4. Coaching improved achievement by about two standard deviations, matching tutoring
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The review of 60 studies found that coaching improved teachers' instruction by about half a standard deviation and student achievement by about 0.18 standard deviations, with larger effects for in-person coaching that was not spread too widely. The chapter calls coaching the best-supported form of professional development, because it supplies practice and feedback in the teacher's own classroom and addresses CBAM task concerns and ADKAR ability. The third option reverses the finding about delivery.

Concept Tested: Instructional Coaching

See: Coaching, Observation, and Learning Communities

docs.title: 7. A teacher who has heard about the new morning model asks, "But what does it actually look like in a real classroom?" Which microstrategy best matches this concern?
docs.text:
1. Share early visible results in a professional learning community
  2. Schedule instructional coaching to fix logistics problems
  3. Arrange a peer observation or a visit to a pilot classroom
  4. Ask the teacher to lead a planning team for the next pilot
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. "What does it actually look like?" is an informational concern, stage 1 in CBAM. The chapter's matching table pairs it with peer observation or a pilot-classroom visit, which supply observability, one of Rogers' five attributes. Sharing results in a PLC fits a consequence concern (stage 4), coaching on logistics fits a task concern (stage 3), and leading a planning team suits a collaboration concern or an early adopter. Matching the move to the concern is the point.

Concept Tested: Matching Strategy to Concern

See: Matching the Strategy to the Person

docs.title: 8. A group of parents raises concerns about student privacy and over-reliance on AI. How does the chapter suggest a leader should treat these concerns?
docs.text:
1. As legitimate concerns that may point to real risks the leaders have not seen
  2. As resistance to be overcome with a stronger presentation of the benefits
  3. As a sign that the parents lack awareness and need more training
  4. As concerns to be addressed only after the program has launched
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Jeffrey Ford and Laurie Ford argued that resistance can be a resource, because people who push back often see real problems leaders do not. A legitimate concern has a real basis in evidence or experience. The chapter lists privacy, over-reliance, screen time, thin evidence, and unequal access as legitimate concerns about AI, and warns that treating them as resistance throws away the people who noticed the real risks. Waiting until after launch ignores the advice to communicate before rumors.

Concept Tested: Legitimate Concern

See: Resistance, Concerns, and Job Fears

docs.title: 9. A veteran teacher says, "I'm afraid this means my job won't exist in five years." Which principal reply best reflects the chapter's guidance?
docs.text:
1. "Don't worry. Nobody here is going to lose their job, I promise."
  2. "That's a fair worry. Here's what the plan says about your role, and what I can promise."
  3. "You're overreacting. The plan clearly says that teachers will still be needed here."
  4. "Let's talk about it later, once the pilot results come in this spring."
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Responding with empathy means listening, acknowledging the feeling and its reason, asking to understand more, and then giving facts, options, or a commitment. The chapter's model reply does this and adds what the plan assumes, what can and cannot be promised, and what the teacher would want in writing. A blanket promise feels kind but destroys trust if it cannot be kept. Calling the teacher an overreactor is dismissive, and postponing leaves the fear unanswered.

Concept Tested: Fear of Job Loss

See: Worked Example: Four Replies to a Worried Teacher

docs.title: 10. A superintendent wants to wait until the AI-native plan is fully finished before telling the teacher union or families, so that she can "present a polished plan." What does the chapter's analysis predict, and what should she do instead?
docs.text:
1. The polished plan will win support, so waiting is the safest approach
  2. Families will not notice the change, so only the union needs early notice
  3. The union has no role in schedule changes, so only the families need to be told
  4. Rumors and opposition are likely; she should share drafts early and agree terms in writing
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The chapter says to communicate before rumors, because rumors are far harder to correct than a clear early statement, and silence is read as secrecy. A leader who waits for the plan to be perfect lets the rumor mill write it. Union engagement means sharing plans before they are final, asking for concerns, and agreeing on workload, evaluation, and data, often in a written memorandum. A union that learns of a change from the newspaper will oppose it, with good reason; unions often hold contractual rights over the work day.

Concept Tested: Union Engagement

See: Stakeholders: Families, Unions, the Board, and Students

docs.title: References: Microstrategies for Leading Change
docs.text:
1. Positive Deviance - Wikipedia - Explains the strength-based approach of finding people who already solve a shared problem better than their peers with the same resources. It is the research idea behind this chapter's "bright spots" and teacher-champion microstrategies.

  2. Professional Learning Community - Wikipedia - Describes how teams of teachers learn together from their own daily practice. Useful background for the chapter's coaching, peer observation, and learning-community moves that help a staff build AI literacy together.

  3. Change Management - Wikipedia - Surveys the discipline of preparing and supporting people through organizational change, including common models and the reasons change efforts fail. Gives context for treating resistance as information rather than as an obstacle.

  4. Switch: How to Change Things When Change Is Hard - Chip Heath and Dan Heath - Broadway Books - The Heaths are credited with the Switch framework: direct the rider (clear steps), motivate the elephant (feelings), and shape the path (the environment). The chapter's bright spots and shrinking the first step come straight from this book.

  5. Instructional Coaching: A Partnership Approach to Improving Instruction - Jim Knight - Corwin Press - Knight is credited with the partnership model of coaching, in which the coach treats teachers as equal professionals who make their own choices. It explains why coaching, not mandates, moves hesitant teachers toward new classroom practice.

  6. AI Guidance for Schools Toolkit - TeachAI - A free toolkit from Code.org, ETS, ISTE, Khan Academy and the World Economic Forum with sample policies, a staff and family presentation deck, and engagement advice. Practical material for the stakeholder and family-communication moves in this chapter.

  7. What Is a "Professional Learning Community"? - ASCD (Richard DuFour) - DuFour's widely cited article sets out three ideas: focus on learning, work in teams, and hold yourselves accountable for results. It shows what a real learning community looks like, as opposed to a meeting with a new name.

  8. The Effect of Teacher Coaching on Instruction and Achievement: A Meta-Analysis - Annenberg Institute, Brown University - Kraft, Blazar and Hogan pool 60 causal studies and find clear effects of coaching on teaching and smaller effects on achievement. They warn that effects shrink as programs grow, a caution for scaling coaching.

  9. AFT to Launch National Academy for AI Instruction - American Federation of Teachers - The July 2025 announcement of a union-led AI training academy funded by Microsoft, OpenAI and Anthropic. It shows a teacher union shaping AI training, which matters for the chapter's union-engagement and job-fear discussion.

  10. Positive Deviance Collaborative - Positive Deviance Collaborative - The home of the positive deviance approach, with guides, tools and case studies, including education projects. Helpful for leaders who want a structured way to find and spread the practices of a school's own bright spots.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter covers redesigning the school day itself: the morning-afternoon model, scheduling and staffing, the changing teacher role, and grade-level design choices for a real AI-native school. Readers finish able to draft a daily schedule that pairs a morning adaptive-learning block with afternoon pro-social activities.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 3: School Structures, Equity, and the Industrial-Era Legacy
  • Chapter 6: The Five-Level Model of Intelligent Textbooks
  • Chapter 10: Student Privacy and Data Governance
  • Chapter 11: Mastery Learning and the Case for a Compressed Morning

docs.title: The Blank Bell Schedule
docs.text:
The board has approved a one-year pilot, and Ms. Okafor sits down on a Saturday morning with a blank sheet of paper and the school's current bell schedule. Six periods, four lunches, a bus that leaves at 3:05, a union contract that says what a teacher's day is, and a state rule about instructional minutes. Somewhere on the page she has to draw a morning with adaptive learning and an afternoon with projects, arts, and teams, and make it fit a building that was designed for something else.

Everything in the earlier parts of the book converges on this page. The evidence for a shorter morning (Chapter 11), the afternoon that fills the freed time (Chapter 14), the guardrails (Chapter 12), the privacy duties (Chapter 10), the culture and the people (Chapters 15 to 19) all have to become a schedule, a staffing plan, an assessment system, a purchase, and a pilot. This chapter is the design chapter. It takes each in turn and ends with the questions a school must answer before it starts.

From ideas to a schedule

This chapter turns the whole book into a draft school day, a staffing plan, and a pilot. By the end you'll be able to sketch a day for your own school and name the decisions that have to be made before it runs. Let's find the balance between an ambitious design and one a real building can carry.

docs.title: AI-First and AI-Native
docs.text:
Two terms need separating, since the field uses them loosely. An AI-first school is a school that puts AI technology at the center of how it delivers instruction, often described by the amount of AI software the students use. Alpha School, whose students spend about two hours a day on adaptive academic software, with the rest of the day in life-skills workshops and projects led by adult guides, is the best-known example, and the AI-First Stories appendix tells both its story and the cautionary tale of Unbound Academy, which used the same software without the in-person afternoons.

An AI-native school is the design this book proposes: a school built around a pedagogy and a purpose first, and then equipped with the AI that serves it. In an AI-native school the starting question is what students need, which is mastery of the academic core and practice with people, and AI is used where it does that job best, with guardrails, at the lowest level that works (Chapter 6), and usually without a live model per student (Chapter 12). The difference matters because "AI-first" describes a tool, and the tool alone is not the model, as the contrast between Alpha and Unbound shows.

AI-first school AI-native school (this book) Starting point The technology The learning goals and the people Typical AI use A central part of the day, often at a high level The minimum level that does the job; live AI used selectively The afternoon Varies; sometimes absent Required, structured, pro-social Evidence standard Often the school's own reports Independent evidence, with a pilot Main risk Technology without culture Under-resourcing the afternoon

The morning-afternoon model is the structure at the core of the AI-native school: an academic morning of adaptive, mastery-based learning, followed by an afternoon of pro-social activity with other people. The AI-native school day is the day that results, with the particular schedule, the screen limits (Chapter 12), the curiosity block (Chapter 2), and the afternoon program (Chapter 14) fitted together.
