docs.title: The AI-Native School Day by Grade
docs.text:
The design is not the same for a six-year-old and a sixteen-year-old. Young children need more play, movement, and adult attention and much less screen time. Older students need more academic depth, credits, and preparation for what follows. The table gives an illustrative design for four grade bands. Every number is a starting point for a school to adjust, not a finding.

Grade band Academic morning Cap on screen time in the morning Afternoon emphasis K–2 About 90 minutes About 30 minutes Play, movement, music, hands-on projects, stories 3–5 About 120 minutes About 75 minutes Projects, arts, sports, simple clubs, service with older buddies 6–8 About 150 minutes About 120 minutes Projects with public exhibitions, clubs, arts, life-skills workshops 9–12 About 180 minutes, with seminars and labs counted About 120 minutes Capstone projects, internships and community partnerships, ensembles, service

For the youngest children the main message is restraint. National pediatric guidance has for years recommended limits on screen time for young children and emphasized play and interaction, so the K–2 morning is mostly adult-led and hands-on, with a short adaptive block for reading and number practice. High school adds the constraint of credits and external exams, and the Carnegie unit of Chapter 3, so the 180-minute morning there includes teacher-led seminars and laboratory work that do not run on a screen.

docs.title: Schedule Redesign
docs.text: Schedule redesign is the rebuilding of a school's daily and weekly timetable to carry the new model. It begins from the fixed constraints that Ms. Okafor listed: bus routes, lunch service, teacher contracts, state rules on instructional time (which in many states require a minimum number of hours or days, and which a school should check, since some states allow waivers for innovation), and the building's rooms. Good schedule redesign negotiates these constraints one at a time instead of ignoring them.

docs.title: Worked Example: A Middle School Day
docs.text:
This is an illustrative schedule for a middle school of 280 students, built to the 6–8 row above: a 150-minute morning with a 120-minute screen cap, then a project-and-people afternoon.

Time Block Screen? 7:50–8:00 Arrival and advisory check-in with a coach No 8:00–8:40 Adaptive math Yes (40 min) 8:40–8:45 Break: stretch, look away No 8:45–9:25 Adaptive reading and writing Yes (40 min) 9:25–9:30 Break No 9:30–10:10 Science and social studies: interactive pages and simulations Yes (40 min) 10:10–10:15 Break No 10:15–10:30 Small-group coaching with the teacher No 10:30–11:00 Movement and snack No 11:00–12:00 Project block (driving question, teams) Some 12:00–12:40 Lunch No 12:40–1:40 Arts, ensembles, or sports No 1:40–2:40 Clubs, life-skills workshops, or service learning Some 2:40–3:00 Reflection, exhibition preparation, dismissal No

The academic morning is 150 minutes, of which 120 is on a screen, matching the cap. The afternoon contains 200 minutes of programming (project, arts or sports, clubs and workshops, and reflection), arranged in four blocks. The bus still leaves at 3:05.

docs.title: Staffing Model
docs.text: A staffing model is the plan for which adults are present, in which roles, in what numbers, at each part of the day. The morning and afternoon need different staffing. In the morning, an adult coach with a section of 28 students moves among them, checks the dashboard, and pulls small groups. In the afternoon, programs need smaller groups, since the SAFE practices of Chapter 14 depend on an adult who can structure, observe, and debrief. A common target for project and arts blocks is one adult for 15 to 20 students.

docs.title: Worked Example: Adult Hours for the 280-Student School
docs.text:
Compare the adult hours needed for the traditional day and the AI-native day for 280 students, using sections of 28 for the illustration (real pupil-to-teacher ratios in the United States are lower, about 15 to 1, because teachers also have planning periods and non-classroom duties, so these figures show the shape of the change and not a budget).

Traditional AI-native Morning 10 sections × 150 min of teaching = 1,500 adult-minutes 10 sections × 150 min of coaching = 1,500 adult-minutes Afternoon 10 sections × 240 min of teaching = 2,400 adult-minutes 14 groups of 20 × 200 min of programming = 2,800 adult-minutes Total per day 3,900 adult-minutes = 65 adult-hours 4,300 adult-minutes = about 71.7 adult-hours

The AI-native day needs about 10 percent more adult-hours in this illustration, not fewer. The change is in what the adults do: coaching and facilitating instead of lecturing. The model does not save on staff. Its savings come from elsewhere, such as content and curriculum (Chapter 7), and what it buys is a day in which every adult hour is spent on a person. The cost depends on who fills the afternoon slots, since teachers, specialists, trained paraprofessionals, and community partners cost different amounts and bring different strengths.

docs.title: The Changing Teacher Role
docs.text:
The changing teacher role is the shift in what teachers do in an AI-native school, from presenting content to the whole class toward guiding, coaching, and supporting individual students and groups. The educator Alison King put the idea in a 1993 phrase, "from sage on the stage to guide on the side." It is easy to say and hard to do, and it must not be mistaken for "teachers matter less." A teacher's expertise, in what students find difficult, how to explain it differently, and how to notice a student in trouble, matters more when software has taken over the routine delivery.

Four overlapping roles describe the new work.

Teacher as coach is the role of helping students set goals, practice, and improve, with specific feedback and encouragement, as a sports coach does. Teacher as mentor is the role of a longer-term relationship in which an adult offers guidance, advice, and support for a student's growth as a person as well as a learner: the advisory teacher who knows a student for years. Teacher as facilitator is the role of structuring group learning, setting up the task, asking the questions that deepen thinking, and stepping back so students do the work. A learning guide is the term some AI-first schools, including Alpha School, use for the adult who supports students' motivation, effort, and progress in place of delivering content. A guide may not be a subject expert, and that is a design choice with risks: a student who needs a human explanation of a hard concept needs a person who can give one.

docs.title: Worked Example: How a Teacher's Week Changes
docs.text:
An illustrative comparison of how Mr. Hale spends his instructional time, in percent.

Activity Traditional week AI-native week Whole-class lecture and explanation 50 5 Supervising practice 20 0 Small-group and one-to-one coaching 5 30 Project and afternoon facilitation 0 30 Mentoring and advisory 0 10 Planning and preparation 10 15 Grading and feedback 15 5 Other 0 5 Total 100 100

Lecturing and supervised practice, 70 percent of the week, fall to 5 percent, and coaching, facilitation, and mentoring, none of which is lecture, rise to 70 percent. The shift is large, and it is why Chapters 17 and 19 spent so long on losses, concerns, coaching, and champions. The plan asks the teacher to give up a great deal of what they know how to do.

Same adults, different work

Notice what the staffing arithmetic and the time table say together: the model needs roughly as many adults, doing nearly the opposite work. That's why it's a change in the teacher's identity, not a cut in teachers, and why that conversation has to be honest from the start.

docs.title: Assessment Redesign
docs.text:
Assessment redesign is the rebuilding of how a school measures and reports learning so that it fits the new model. In the traditional design most assessment is by tests and grades at the end of units. The AI-native design has two sources of evidence: mastery data from the morning (Chapter 8), which is continuous and automatic, and evidence from the afternoon, which is performances, products, and portfolios. Redesign also has to answer the integrity question that AI raises (below).

Mastery-based assessment is assessment in which a student advances after demonstrating mastery of a concept, usually against a stated threshold, with opportunities to try again, in place of earning a grade at a fixed time. It uses the mastery rule and the thresholds of Chapter 12. Reports describe what a student has mastered, and not a letter grade for a period. The Mastery Transcript Consortium, founded in 2017, is one effort to build transcripts on this basis.

Performance assessment is assessment in which students show what they can do by carrying out a meaningful task, such as presenting, building, performing, or defending a position, and a rubric is used to score it. The public exhibition of Chapter 14 is a performance assessment. Its strength is that it measures the skills that tests do not, such as communication and collaboration. Its challenge is reliability: different scorers can disagree, so scorers need training, shared rubrics, and some double scoring.

Portfolio assessment is assessment based on a collection of a student's work over time, selected and reflected on by the student, which shows growth and the quality of what the student can do. In New York State, a consortium of schools has for years used performance tasks and portfolios in place of most state exams under a waiver, which makes it one of the best-known examples.

docs.title: Worked Example: What Goes in a Student's Record
docs.text:
Evidence Source What it shows Concept mastery summary (dashboard) Morning, automatic Which of 120 concepts are mastered, and when Project portfolio with reflections Afternoon, student-curated The quality of work and the student's growth Public exhibition score (rubric, two scorers) Afternoon, performance Communication and teamwork, with reliability checks Teacher mentor narrative Advisory Character, effort, and growth

No single piece is the whole picture. The set is a fuller portrait than a grade, and each piece comes with the checks, such as thresholds, double scoring, and reflection, that keep it trustworthy.

docs.title: Academic Integrity and the Detector Problem
docs.text:
Academic integrity is the commitment of a school community to honesty in learning and assessment: doing one's own work and giving credit for the work of others. AI has made the old rules unclear, since a chatbot can write an essay in seconds. The response has two parts, which together are better than either alone: redesign the work so that cheating is less useful, and set clear rules for when AI is allowed.

Redesign means that important assessments are done in person, in class; that process evidence, such as drafts, notes, and revision history, is part of the work; that students explain or defend their work orally; and that tasks are personal and local, so a generic answer does not fit. Clear rules mean saying, for each task, whether AI is not allowed, allowed for certain steps, or allowed with disclosure. A simple "traffic light" works: red for no AI (an in-class writing sample), yellow for AI in specific ways (brainstorming, feedback on a draft, with notes on what was used), and green for AI as a full tool with disclosure (a research project).

An AI cheating detector is software that claims to tell whether a piece of text was written by an AI system. They are tempting, since they promise to restore the old system. The evidence is against relying on them. In July 2023, OpenAI withdrew its own AI text classifier because of its low accuracy. Detector false positives are the cases in which the detector wrongly labels human-written work as AI-written. Even a small false-positive rate produces a lot of wrongly accused students when applied to thousands of essays, and the harm falls on the accused student, who must prove they did their own work.

Bias against ELL writers is the finding that AI detectors are more likely to flag the writing of English-language learners as AI-generated. A 2023 study by Weixin Liang and colleagues at Stanford tested seven popular detectors on essays written by non-native English speakers for the TOEFL exam, and found that, on average, more than half were wrongly labeled as AI-generated, while essays by U.S. eighth graders, who are native speakers, were classified almost perfectly. One explanation is that detectors often look for text that is highly predictable, and writers working in a second language tend to use simpler, more predictable wording. An approach that wrongly accuses the students who already face the greatest barriers has a clear equity problem (Chapter 3), and it is one reason the AI-First Stories appendix advises redesigning assignments instead of relying on detection.

docs.title: Worked Example: How Many Accusations Are False?
docs.text:
Suppose a school runs a detector on 10,000 essays. Five percent, 500, were actually written with AI, and the detector catches 80 percent of them. It wrongly flags 1 percent of the human-written essays, a rate that sounds small.

Number Essays written by AI 500 Human-written essays 9,500 AI essays correctly flagged (80%) 400 Human essays wrongly flagged (1%) 95 Total flagged 495 Share of flagged essays that are false accusations 95 ÷ 495 ≈ 19%

About one in five accusations is wrong even with a favorable detector. Now add the equity problem. Suppose 10 percent of the human-written essays, 950, are by English-language learners, and the detector wrongly flags 20 percent of them, while it still flags 1 percent of the other 8,550.

Wrong flags ELL writers: 950 × 20% 190 Other writers: 8,550 × 1% 85.5 Total wrong flags 275.5 ELL writers' share of the wrong flags 190 ÷ 275.5 ≈ 69% Share of all flagged essays that are false: 275.5 ÷ (400 + 275.5) about 41%

Students who are 10 percent of the human writers receive about 69 percent of the false accusations, and about two in five accusations are false. The numbers are illustrative, and they show how a modest-looking error rate, combined with a bias, produces a serious injustice.

docs.title: Diagram: False Accusations Calculator
docs.text:
Run the False Accusations Calculator MicroSim Fullscreen

False Accusations Calculator

Type: microsim sim-id: false-accusations-calculator Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: calculate Learning Objective: The learner will calculate how many human-written essays an AI detector wrongly flags, the share of flagged essays that are false accusations, and the share of false flags that fall on English-language learners, correctly answering three of three questions.

Prerequisites: AI cheating detector, detector false positives, bias against ELL writers (all defined in the section "Academic Integrity and the Detector Problem" above).

Evidence of Mastery: Before the controls unlock, the learner commits three answers: (Q1) the share of flagged essays that are false accusations when the false-positive rate is 1 percent for all writers; (Q2) the number of wrong flags among English-language learners when their false-positive rate is 20 percent; (Q3) the English-language learners' share of all wrong flags in that case. An answer is correct when it is within the tolerance in Content. Mastery is 3 of 3 correct. Using the controls afterward is exploration.

Misconceptions: (1) A 1 percent false-positive rate means 1 percent of accusations are wrong. (2) A detector's errors fall evenly on all students. (3) A small subgroup cannot account for most of the false flags.

Instructional Rationale: Calculating from counts, not from rates alone, shows how base rates and subgroup bias turn a small error rate into many false accusations. Committing to answers first, then exploring other rates, lets the learner see which inputs matter most.

Content:

Inputs and defaults:

Input Min Max Step Default Unit Essays checked 1,000 20,000 1,000 10,000 essays Share written by AI 0 50 1 5 percent Detector catches AI essays (sensitivity) 50 100 5 80 percent False-positive rate, most writers 0 10 1 1 percent Share of human essays by ELL writers 0 30 5 10 percent False-positive rate, ELL writers 0 50 5 20 percent

Rules shown: AI essays = essays × share written by AI. Human essays = essays − AI essays. True flags = AI essays × sensitivity. ELL essays = human essays × ELL share; other essays = human essays − ELL essays. Wrong flags = ELL essays × ELL false-positive rate + other essays × most-writers rate. Share of flags that are false = wrong flags ÷ (true flags + wrong flags). ELL share of wrong flags = ELL wrong flags ÷ wrong flags.

Check values at the defaults, with a 1 percent rate for all writers (ELL rate set to 1): AI essays 500, human essays 9,500, true flags 400, wrong flags 95, false share 19.2 percent.

Check values at the defaults with the 20 percent ELL rate: ELL essays 950, other essays 8,550, ELL wrong flags 190, other wrong flags 85.5, total wrong flags 275.5, false share 40.8 percent, ELL share of wrong flags 69.0 percent.

Answers: Q1 = 19.2% (±0.5); Q2 = 190 (±1); Q3 = 69.0% (±0.5).

Provenance: The numbers are illustrative, written for this chapter, and the sim must label them "Illustrative, not the performance of any real detector." The 20 percent ELL rate is chosen to illustrate the direction of the finding in the 2023 Stanford study, which reported higher rates.

Rules: All results are computed from the inputs above and shown to one decimal place for percentages and the nearest tenth for counts. When the total flags are zero, the false share is shown as "no flags."

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner answers Q1, Q2, and Q3 and submits them.
  2. The sim checks the answers and unlocks the controls.
  3. The learner changes the inputs. The counts and shares update at once.
  4. The learner should notice that lowering the share of essays written by AI makes the false share of flags rise sharply, and that the ELL share of wrong flags depends on the ELL false-positive rate.

Feedback: Three questions, fixed order, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: [value]. [Working text]." Incorrect: "Not quite. Work from counts: flagged essays are true flags plus wrong flags." After the second wrong attempt the value and working are shown. A score "n of 3" is shown.

Starting State: The defaults are shown with the results hidden, and the prompt reads "If the detector wrongly flags only 1 percent of human essays, how many accusations are false?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's worked example uses 10,000 essays, 5 percent by AI, 80 percent sensitivity, a 1 percent false-positive rate (95 wrong flags of 495, about 19 percent), then 950 ELL essays at 20 percent (190 wrong flags), a total of 275.5, an ELL share of about 69 percent, and about 41 percent of all flags being false.

Don't let a detector be the judge

A common trap is treating a detector's score as proof, and accusing a student on it. Instead, redesign the assessment so that you can see the student's process, talk with them about the work, and use a detector, if at all, only as a reason to ask a question and never as the answer.

docs.title: Equity of Access
docs.text:
Equity of access is the principle that every student has the devices, connectivity, supports, and opportunities to take full part in the new model, whatever their family's income, location, language, or disability. The design that has been described could narrow gaps by giving every student a patient tutor and a rich afternoon, or widen them if only well-resourced students benefit (Chapter 3). Five commitments help to keep it on the narrowing side.

  • Devices and connectivity: a school device for every student, loaner or take-home devices where homework needs them, and offline access (Chapter 9) for students without reliable internet.
  • Accessibility: content that works with screen readers and keyboards, captions, and supports for students with disabilities.
  • Language: supports for English-language learners, such as bilingual content and tools that do not penalize non-native writing.
  • A free afternoon: no fees for afternoon programs and transportation so that every student can take part, since a program that costs money recreates the gap.
  • Equitable partnerships: deliberately seeking community partners for schools that have few nearby, so that enrichment does not cluster where families are already advantaged.

docs.title: Procurement and Vendor Evaluation
docs.text:
Procurement is the formal process by which a school or district buys goods and services, governed by purchasing laws and board policy: defining the need, soliciting proposals or bids, evaluating them, awarding a contract, and managing it. It is where a good plan can be undone by a bad purchase. The Los Angeles "Ed" chatbot, described in the appendix, is the cautionary case: the district committed about $6 million to a startup, spent about $3 million, and the company collapsed within months of launch. The lesson the appendix draws is that schools need procurement rules before they buy AI products.

Procurement criteria are the standards a district sets in advance for what a product must meet in order to be bought. This book's earlier chapters supply most of them. The five levels (Chapter 6) give a vocabulary for the requirement: "we need a Level 2 textbook, not a Level 4 chatbot." The criteria also include independent evidence of effect (Chapter 2), privacy and data governance appropriate to the level (Chapter 10), guardrails for any tutor (Chapter 12), the interoperability standards of Chapter 9 (LTI, OneRoster, xAPI), the total cost of ownership (Chapter 7), and, among those, the value beyond content a vendor provides. Vendor evaluation is the use of the criteria to assess a particular vendor and its product: reviewing its documents, testing the product, checking references, and judging its financial and security health (vendor risk, Chapter 10).

docs.title: Worked Example: A Weighted Scorecard
docs.text:
Lincoln's district uses a scorecard with seven criteria and weights that sum to 100. Each vendor is scored from 1 (poor) to 5 (excellent) on each criterion. The weighted score is the sum of weight × score ÷ 5, so a perfect vendor would score 100. A knockout rule adds that a score of 2 or below on privacy or on vendor viability stops the purchase until the problem is resolved.

Criterion Weight Vendor A score Vendor B score Independent evidence of effect 20 4 3 Privacy and data governance 20 5 3 Level and capability fit 15 3 5 Guardrails for the AI tutor 15 4 3 Standards and interoperability 10 3 5 Total cost of ownership 10 4 3 Vendor viability (finances, references) 10 2 5

Vendor A's weighted score is \( 20 \times 4/5 + 20 \times 5/5 + 15 \times 3/5 + 15 \times 4/5 + 10 \times 3/5 + 10 \times 4/5 + 10 \times 2/5 = 16 + 20 + 9 + 12 + 6 + 8 + 4 = 75 \). Vendor B's is \( 12 + 12 + 15 + 9 + 10 + 6 + 10 = 74 \). Vendor A scores higher on total, and the knockout rule stops it, because its viability score is 2. This is the Ed lesson in a rule: a strong product from a company that may not survive is a risk the total does not show, so the district asks Vendor A to resolve the viability concern, with financial statements and an exit plan, before it can proceed. Meanwhile Vendor B may proceed to a pilot.

docs.title: Diagram: Vendor Scorecard
docs.text:
Run the Vendor Scorecard MicroSim Fullscreen

Vendor Scorecard

Type: microsim sim-id: vendor-scorecard Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: calculate Learning Objective: The learner will calculate the weighted scores of two vendors from criterion scores and weights, and apply the knockout rule to decide which vendor may proceed, correctly answering three of three questions.

Prerequisites: procurement criteria, vendor evaluation, weighted scoring, the knockout rule (all defined in the section "Procurement and Vendor Evaluation" above).

Evidence of Mastery: Before the controls unlock, the learner commits three answers: (Q1) Vendor A's weighted score; (Q2) Vendor B's weighted score; (Q3) which vendor may proceed under the knockout rule. An answer is correct when it equals the value in Content. Mastery is 3 of 3 correct. Changing the scores afterward is exploration.

Misconceptions: (1) The highest total score always wins. (2) A weak score on one criterion can be offset by strong scores elsewhere. (3) Weights are the same as scores.

Instructional Rationale: Calculating the weighted totals shows how close the two vendors are, and applying the knockout rule shows that some criteria must be passed whatever the total. Committing to the answers first ties the learner's expectation to the numbers.

Content:

Seven criteria with weights (sum 100):

Criterion Weight Independent evidence of effect 20 Privacy and data governance 20 Level and capability fit 15 Guardrails for the AI tutor 15 Standards and interoperability 10 Total cost of ownership 10 Vendor viability 10

Scores, each from 1 to 5 (min 1, max 5, step 1):

Criterion Vendor A Vendor B Independent evidence of effect 4 3 Privacy and data governance 5 3 Level and capability fit 3 5 Guardrails for the AI tutor 4 3 Standards and interoperability 3 5 Total cost of ownership 4 3 Vendor viability 2 5

Rules shown: weighted score = the sum over criteria of (weight × score ÷ 5), out of 100. Knockout rule: a vendor with a score of 2 or below on privacy and data governance, or on vendor viability, may not proceed until the problem is resolved.

Answers: Q1 = 75; Q2 = 74; Q3 = Vendor B (Vendor A is knocked out by a viability score of 2, though its total is higher).

Provenance: The criteria, weights, and scores are illustrative, written for this chapter, and the sim must label them "Illustrative scorecard." The criteria come from Chapters 2, 6, 7, 9, 10, and 12.

Rules: Weighted score = sum of (weight × score ÷ 5), shown to the nearest whole number. A vendor is knocked out when its privacy or viability score is <= 2. When both vendors are knocked out, the sim says "Neither vendor may proceed." When one or both change a score, totals and knockout status update at once.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner answers Q1, Q2, and Q3 and submits them.
  2. The sim checks the answers and unlocks the controls.
  3. The learner changes scores. Totals, a bar comparison, and the knockout status update at once.
  4. The learner should notice that raising Vendor A's viability score from 2 to 3 lets it proceed, and that Vendor A would then be the higher-scoring choice.

Feedback: Three questions, fixed order, two attempts each. Q1 and Q2 correct: "Correct: [value]. [Working text]." Q1 and Q2 incorrect: "Not quite. Multiply each weight by its score, divide by 5, and add." Q3 correct: "Correct: Vendor B. Vendor A has the higher total but a viability score of 2." Q3 incorrect: "Check the knockout rule for privacy and viability." After the second wrong attempt the answer and working are shown. A score "n of 3" is shown.

Starting State: The two vendors' scores are shown with the totals hidden, and the prompt reads "Which vendor should the district move forward with?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's worked example uses seven criteria with weights of 20, 20, 15, 15, 10, 10, and 10, Vendor A's total of 75, Vendor B's total of 74, and the knockout rule applied to Vendor A's viability score of 2.

docs.title: Readiness and Pilots
docs.text:
School readiness assessment is the review of whether a school is prepared to start the new model, drawing together the readiness checks of earlier chapters: governance readiness (Chapter 10), adoption readiness (Chapter 15), staff AI literacy (Chapter 19), and the capacity to run the schedule and staffing above. It asks: are the privacy basics in place for the level we plan to use? Do the attributes of the innovation fit our teachers? Do teachers know enough about AI to guide students and answer families? Do we have the devices and connectivity? Is there an opinion leader to carry the story and a principal ready to protect the pilot? A school that answers "no" to several should fix them, or stay at a lower level, before it starts.

A pilot program is a limited, planned trial of the new model, in one grade, one school, or a few classrooms, designed to find out whether it works and what it needs before it spreads. It extends the pilot classroom of Chapter 19 to the scale of a program. Pilot goals are the specific, measurable outcomes the pilot is meant to achieve, written before it begins, together with the rule for deciding what to do next. A pilot without stated goals cannot fail, and so cannot teach anything. Good goals are specific, measured against a baseline, include more than test scores, and are paired with a decision rule.

docs.title: Worked Example: A Pilot Decision Rule
docs.text:
Lincoln's pilot for one grade of 140 students states five goals and a rule in advance.

Goal Baseline Target Measured by Learning gain on the state-aligned test Comparison section At least 0.15 standard deviations higher Independent scorer Teacher workload 53 hours a week (Chapter 3) No more than 2 hours higher Weekly time log Family satisfaction n/a At least 70 percent satisfied Survey Privacy n/a No serious incident Incident log No group harmed Comparison section No subgroup more than 0.1 standard deviations lower Subgroup analysis

The rule: scale if all five goals are met; stop if there is a serious privacy incident or any subgroup is more than 0.1 standard deviations lower than the comparison; otherwise extend the pilot a semester and fix what was missed. The rule means the decision is made on the evidence, not on the mood of the room.

docs.title: Diagram: Scale, Extend, or Stop?
docs.text:
Run the Scale, Extend, or Stop? MicroSim Fullscreen

Scale, Extend, or Stop?

Type: microsim sim-id: scale-extend-or-stop Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: judge Learning Objective: The learner will judge whether each of six pilot results leads to scaling, extending, or stopping by applying the stated decision rule, correctly judging at least five of six on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: pilot program, pilot goals, decision rule (all defined in the section "Readiness and Pilots" above).

Evidence of Mastery: For each of 6 pilot results, the learner selects Scale, Extend, or Stop and submits it. A selection is correct when it matches the "Correct decision" column in Content. Mastery is 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt. Reading the rule is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A high test gain is enough to scale. (2) A pilot that misses one goal has failed. (3) A privacy incident can be offset by learning gains.

Instructional Rationale: Applying a stated rule to varied results requires checking the stop conditions first, then the scale conditions, so the learner practices decision discipline and not impression.

Content:

The rule shown: Stop if there is a serious privacy incident, or if any subgroup is more than 0.1 standard deviations below the comparison. Otherwise, Scale if all of these hold: gain >= 0.15 standard deviations, teacher workload increase <= 2 hours a week, family satisfaction >= 70 percent. Otherwise, Extend.

Six results (no serious privacy incident and no harmed subgroup unless stated):

# Pilot result shown to the learner Correct decision Why (shown as feedback) 1 Gain 0.20 SD; workload +1 hour; satisfaction 78%; no incident; no harmed subgroup. Scale All conditions are met and no stop condition applies. 2 Gain 0.12 SD; workload +1 hour; satisfaction 80%; no incident; no harmed subgroup. Extend The gain is below 0.15; no stop condition applies. 3 Gain 0.25 SD; workload +3 hours; satisfaction 75%; no incident; no harmed subgroup. Extend Workload is above the 2-hour limit. 4 Gain 0.30 SD; workload 0 hours; satisfaction 85%; a serious privacy incident occurred. Stop A serious privacy incident is a stop condition, whatever the gains. 5 Gain 0.18 SD overall, with English-language learners 0.15 SD below the comparison; workload +1 hour; satisfaction 74%; no incident. Stop A subgroup is more than 0.1 SD below the comparison, which is a stop condition. 6 Gain 0.16 SD; workload +2 hours; satisfaction 65%; no incident; no harmed subgroup. Extend Satisfaction is below 70 percent; the other conditions are met.

Provenance: The rule and the results are illustrative, written for this chapter, and the sim must say that real thresholds should be set by each district.

Rules: Check the stop conditions first. Stop if a serious privacy incident occurred or any subgroup is more than 0.1 SD below the comparison. If neither, Scale if gain >= 0.15 SD and workload increase <= 2 hours and satisfaction >= 70 percent; otherwise Extend. Each result has exactly one correct decision, given in Content. A result is scored on its first submitted decision only. The score counts first-attempt correct decisions out of 6. Mastery is a score >= 5.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads one pilot result and sees the three decisions.
  2. The learner selects a decision and submits it. The sim marks it correct or incorrect and shows the feedback text.
  3. If incorrect, the learner may choose again; the second attempt does not change the score. After the second attempt, the correct decision and reason are shown.
  4. After all 6 results, the sim shows the score.
  5. The learner should notice that the two largest gains, results 4 and 5, lead to a stop.

Feedback: 6 results, shuffled once per session, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: [decision]. [Why text]." Incorrect: "Not quite. Check the stop conditions first. [Why text for the correct answer, without naming the decision]." After the second attempt the correct decision is revealed and the result counts as missed. A running score "First-try correct: n of 6" is shown. Final message for a score >= 5: "You can let the rule decide." For a score < 5: "Review the rule and try again; the results will be reshuffled."

Starting State: Result 1 of the shuffled order is shown with the three decisions, the score "First-try correct: 0 of 6," and the prompt "What does the rule say to do?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's pilot rule has a gain target of 0.15 SD, a workload limit of 2 hours, a satisfaction target of 70 percent, and stop conditions of a serious privacy incident or a subgroup more than 0.1 SD below the comparison. The mastery bar is 5 of 6.

docs.title: Answering the Blank Page
docs.text:
Ms. Okafor's Saturday has an output. She has a grade-band design, a schedule that fits the bus, a staffing sketch that needs about the same number of adults doing different work, an assessment record with mastery data and portfolios, a rule for AI and integrity that avoids detectors, a list of equity commitments, a procurement scorecard, a readiness check, and a pilot with a decision rule written in advance. The pilot is for one grade, for one year, and the rule decides in advance whether it continues.

The story has both sides. The benefit: a school day designed from what students need, with each part traceable to evidence in this book. The risks: a plan that outruns the building and the people, an afternoon starved of adults, assessment that quietly reverts to the old test, an integrity policy built on faulty detectors, a purchase made without criteria, and a pilot that cannot fail. The response is a sequence of smaller commitments: stay at the lowest level that works, pilot before scaling, write the decision rule first, and keep the equity commitments non-negotiable.

A draft is enough to start

If drawing a whole school day from scratch feels like too much, draft one grade band and one week; the schedule above took one Saturday. Your first draft will be wrong in useful ways, and the pilot is there to find them.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• An AI-first school is defined by its technology; an AI-native school by its learning goals and people, using the morning-afternoon model; the AI-native school day varies by grade band, with less screen time for the youngest.
  • Schedule redesign works within real constraints; the 280-student example needed about 10 percent more adult-hours, so the staffing model changes what adults do, not how many are needed.
  • The changing teacher role moves from lecturing to teacher as coach, teacher as mentor, and teacher as facilitator; a learning guide is not necessarily a subject expert, which is a design risk.
  • Assessment redesign combines mastery-based assessment, performance assessment, and portfolio assessment, each with checks for reliability.
  • Academic integrity is best served by redesigning assignments and setting clear rules; an AI cheating detector produces detector false positives, with bias against ELL writers, so about two in five flags can be false in our illustration.
  • Equity of access needs devices, accessibility, language support, a free afternoon, and equitable partnerships.
  • Procurement criteria and vendor evaluation, with a weighted scorecard and a knockout rule, prevent a repeat of the Ed chatbot; a school readiness assessment checks the school before a pilot program with written pilot goals and a decision rule.

You can draft an AI-native school day

You just turned the whole book into a schedule, a staffing plan, an assessment record, a procurement scorecard, and a pilot with a rule that decides in advance. That's a design a school can actually test. Chapter 21 covers implementing it responsibly, and Chapters 22 and 23 return to the real stories. One step at a time, together.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: Designing the AI-Native School Day
docs.text: Test your understanding of how to design an AI-native school day, from schedules and staffing to assessment, integrity, procurement, and pilots, with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. How does this book distinguish an AI-native school from an AI-first school?
docs.text:
1. It uses more hours of AI software each day than an AI-first school does
  2. It is always a private school, while an AI-first school is always public
  3. It starts from learning goals and people, then adds the AI that serves them
  4. It uses no AI in the morning and relies on teachers for instruction
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. An AI-first school puts AI technology at the center of instruction and is often described by how much AI students use. An AI-native school starts with a pedagogy and purpose, mastery of the academic core and practice with people, and uses AI where it does that job best, at the lowest level that works and with guardrails. The chapter's point is that "AI-first" describes a tool, and the tool alone is not the model, as the contrast between Alpha School and Unbound Academy shows.

Concept Tested: AI-Native School

See: AI-First and AI-Native

docs.title: 2. In the chapter's 280-student staffing illustration, how does the AI-native day compare with the traditional day in adult hours?
docs.text:
1. About half as many, since the software handles most instruction
  2. About 10 percent more, with adults coaching and facilitating, not lecturing
  3. Exactly the same, with no change in what the adults do each day
  4. About twice as many, which makes the model unaffordable
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The illustration gives about 65 adult-hours a day for the traditional schedule and about 71.7 for the AI-native one, roughly 10 percent more, because afternoon programs need groups of about 15 to 20 per adult. The model does not save on staff; the change is in what adults do. Its savings come from elsewhere, such as content. The chapter notes the figures show the shape of the change, not a budget, since real pupil-to-teacher ratios are lower.

Concept Tested: Staffing Model

See: Worked Example: Adult Hours for the 280-Student School

docs.title: 3. A school runs an AI detector on 20,000 essays. Four percent were written with AI, and the detector catches 75 percent of those. It wrongly flags 2 percent of human-written essays. About what share of all flagged essays are false accusations?
docs.text:
1. About 2 percent
  2. About 25 percent
  3. About 61 percent
  4. About 39 percent
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. There are 800 AI essays, and the detector flags 600 of them. There are 19,200 human essays, and 2 percent, 384, are wrongly flagged. Total flags are 600 + 384 = 984, and 384 / 984 is about 39 percent false. The 2 percent answer confuses the false-positive rate with the share of accusations that are false, and 61 percent is the share that are correct. The chapter shows how a small-sounding error rate produces many wrongly accused students.

Concept Tested: Detector False Positives

See: Worked Example: How Many Accusations Are False?

docs.title: 4. What did the 2023 Stanford study by Liang and colleagues find about AI detectors and English-language learners?
docs.text:
1. More than half of non-native writers' TOEFL essays were wrongly flagged as AI
  2. Detectors flagged native and non-native writers at about the same low rate overall
  3. Detectors were more accurate on non-native writers because their wording is simpler
  4. Detectors caught nearly all AI essays, so their bias was acceptable in practice
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The study tested seven popular detectors and found that, on average, more than half of TOEFL essays written by non-native English speakers were wrongly labeled as AI-generated, while essays by U.S. eighth graders were classified almost perfectly. One explanation is that detectors look for predictable text, and second-language writers tend to use simpler, more predictable wording. That simplicity causes the false flags rather than better accuracy. The chapter calls this a clear equity problem and advises redesigning assignments instead of relying on detection.

Concept Tested: Bias Against ELL Writers

See: Academic Integrity and the Detector Problem

docs.title: 5. Using the chapter's weighted scorecard (weights 20, 20, 15, 15, 10, 10, 10 for evidence, privacy, level fit, guardrails, standards, total cost, and viability), a vendor scores 3, 2, 4, 4, 5, 4, and 4. What is the outcome?
docs.text:
1. A score of 70, so the vendor proceeds directly to a district contract
  2. A score of 80, so the vendor proceeds to a one-grade pilot
  3. A score of 70, but the knockout rule stops the purchase because privacy scored 2
  4. A score of 52, so the vendor is rejected permanently by the district
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. The weighted score is the sum of weight times score divided by 5: 12 + 8 + 12 + 12 + 10 + 8 + 8 = 70. The knockout rule says a score of 2 or below on privacy or on vendor viability stops the purchase until the problem is resolved, so this vendor cannot proceed regardless of its total. The chapter applies the rule to Vendor A's viability score, calling it the Ed chatbot lesson in a rule: the total does not show some risks. A knockout pauses the purchase; it is not a permanent rejection.

Concept Tested: Procurement Criteria

See: Worked Example: A Weighted Scorecard

docs.title: 6. A one-grade pilot uses the chapter's five goals and decision rule. Results: learning gain of 0.18 standard deviations over the comparison section, teacher workload up 3 hours a week, 75 percent family satisfaction, no privacy incident, and no subgroup more than 0.1 standard deviations lower. What does the rule say to do?
docs.text:
1. Scale, since the learning gain beat the 0.15 target
  2. Stop, since one of the five goals was missed
  3. Scale, since no privacy incident occurred and families are satisfied
  4. Extend the pilot a semester and fix the workload problem
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The rule is to scale only if all five goals are met, stop if there is a serious privacy incident or a subgroup is more than 0.1 standard deviations lower, and otherwise extend a semester and fix what was missed. Workload rose by 3 hours against a limit of no more than 2, so not all goals were met, but neither stop condition applies. Scaling on the learning gain alone ignores the rule written in advance, which exists so that the decision rests on evidence, not the mood of the room.

Concept Tested: Pilot Goals

See: Worked Example: A Pilot Decision Rule

docs.title: 7. A teacher is applying the chapter's "traffic light" rules for AI use. Which pairing of task and rule fits the chapter's examples?
docs.text:
1. In-class writing sample: green, AI as a full tool with disclosure
  2. Research project: green, AI as a full tool with disclosure
  3. Brainstorming for an essay: red, no AI allowed
  4. Research project: red, no AI allowed
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The chapter's traffic light sets red for no AI, as in an in-class writing sample; yellow for AI in specific ways, such as brainstorming or feedback on a draft with notes on what was used; and green for AI as a full tool with disclosure, as in a research project. Clear rules for each task, together with redesigning work so process evidence and oral explanation are part of it, serve academic integrity better than detection. The other pairings reverse the chapter's examples.

Concept Tested: Academic Integrity

See: Academic Integrity and the Detector Problem

docs.title: 8. A school plans to staff its academic morning with "learning guides" who support motivation and progress but are not subject experts. What design risk does the chapter identify?
docs.text:
1. Guides will cost more than certified teachers, raising the budget
  2. Guides cannot legally supervise students during the school day
  3. A student who needs a human explanation of a hard concept may not get one
  4. Guides will make the morning longer, cutting into the afternoon
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. A learning guide, the term some AI-first schools such as Alpha School use, supports students' motivation, effort, and progress in place of delivering content. The chapter calls the choice of non-expert guides a design choice with risks: a student who needs a human explanation of a hard concept needs a person who can give one. It stresses that a teacher's expertise matters more, not less, once software handles routine delivery. The chapter does not claim guides cost more or are legally barred.

Concept Tested: Learning Guide

See: The Changing Teacher Role

docs.title: 9. A district's new afternoon program charges a $150 activity fee per semester and offers no transportation. Analyzed against the chapter's equity commitments, what is the main problem?
docs.text:
1. The fee is too low to cover partner costs, so programs will be weak
  2. Fees are acceptable as long as the morning software is free to all students
  3. Transportation is needed only for students in the K-2 grade band
  4. A program that costs money recreates the gap; it should be free with transport
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. One of the chapter's five equity-of-access commitments is a free afternoon: no fees for afternoon programs and transportation so every student can take part, because a program that costs money recreates the gap. The model could narrow gaps by giving every student a patient tutor and a rich afternoon, or widen them if only well-resourced students benefit. A free morning does not make up for an afternoon only some families can afford, which is why the second option fails.

Concept Tested: Equity of Access

See: Equity of Access

docs.title: 10. A school board weighs two proposals. Proposal 1 is a district-wide AI-first model with four hours a day of adaptive software, supported by a vendor's self-reported results. Proposal 2 is a one-year AI-native pilot in one grade with written goals, an independent scorer, a decision rule, and equity commitments. Which judgment is best supported by the chapter?
docs.text:
1. Proposal 1, because more AI time each day produces faster learning gains
  2. Proposal 2, because it tests the model independently and decides the next step in advance
  3. Proposal 1, because district-wide adoption avoids the cost of running a pilot
  4. Neither, because AI should not be used in schools until it is fully proven
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The chapter recommends staying at the lowest level that works, piloting before scaling, writing the decision rule first, and keeping equity commitments non-negotiable. Proposal 2 does all of these and uses independent evidence, which the AI-native design requires; Proposal 1 relies on self-reported results and commits the whole district at once, the pattern the Ed chatbot case warns against. More AI time is not evidence of benefit, and the book does not argue for waiting until AI is fully proven; it argues for careful pilots.

Concept Tested: Pilot Program

See: Readiness and Pilots

docs.title: References: Designing the AI-Native School Day
docs.text:
1. Blended Learning - Wikipedia - Explains how schools combine online learning with face-to-face teaching, including rotation and flex models. The morning-afternoon model is one form of blended learning, so this article gives readers the wider family of designs.

  2. Authentic Assessment - Wikipedia - Describes assessment through realistic tasks that ask students to use what they know, rather than recall it. It is the basis for the chapter's performance, portfolio and mastery-based assessment ideas, which are harder to complete with AI.

  3. Artificial Intelligence Content Detection - Wikipedia - Covers software that tries to identify AI-written text and notes it is often unreliable. It reports studies showing detectors wrongly flag non-native English writers, the evidence behind the chapter's warning about detector false positives.

  4. Understanding by Design (Expanded 2nd Edition) - Grant Wiggins and Jay McTighe - ASCD - Wiggins and McTighe are credited with backward design: decide what students should understand, then the evidence that would show it, and only then plan lessons. This is the logic of redesigning assessment rather than policing AI use.

  5. Blended: Using Disruptive Innovation to Improve Schools - Michael B. Horn and Heather Staker - Jossey-Bass - Horn and Staker are credited with the widely used catalog of blended-learning models, such as station rotation and flex. Their models help leaders see the scheduling, staffing and room choices behind an AI-native day.

  6. Blended Learning Models - Clayton Christensen Institute - Short descriptions and examples of seven blended-learning models, from station rotation to enriched virtual. A quick reference when drafting a schedule that pairs a morning adaptive block with afternoon group work.

  7. GPT Detectors Are Biased Against Non-Native English Writers - arXiv (Liang, Yuksekgonul, Mao, Wu and Zou, Stanford) - The 2023 study that found popular AI detectors often label non-native English writing as AI-generated. The authors caution against using detectors in schools, which supports the chapter's equity concerns.

  8. Guidance for Generative AI in Education and Research - UNESCO - UNESCO's first global guidance on generative AI in schools, recommending data protection, age limits and a human-centered approach to teaching. Useful for checking a school-day design against international norms.

  9. AI and Education Policy 101: Lessons from Early Adopters - Center on Reinventing Public Education - Reports how early-adopter districts write AI policy, starting from a court case over a student penalized for AI use. Its principles on academic integrity and stakeholder input apply directly to this chapter.

  10. AI Literacy: A Framework to Understand, Evaluate, and Use Emerging Technology - Digital Promise - A framework and strategies for building AI literacy for students and teachers in PK-12 settings. It helps define what teachers in their new coach and facilitator roles need to know.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter covers putting the model into practice responsibly: safe procurement, avoiding vendor lock-in, equity and access, redesigning assessment instead of policing it, and measuring whether a pilot is actually working. Readers finish able to write procurement criteria and a success-measures plan for a school considering the model.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 2: Evidence, Motivation, and the Stakeholders of Schooling
  • Chapter 7: Content Economics and Open Educational Resources
  • Chapter 10: Student Privacy and Data Governance
  • Chapter 19: Microstrategies for Leading Change
