docs.title: The Contract on the Desk
docs.text:
Two months before the pilot, Ms. Okafor gets a call from the district's purchasing office. A vendor, whose product the district liked, has sent a 38-page contract, and the vendor's representative has mentioned that the price is good "through the end of the month." The purchasing officer, who is not a lawyer, asks whether the school is ready to sign.

Chapter 20 gave her a scorecard and a pilot rule. This chapter covers what happens after the decision to proceed: reading the contract, resisting the clock, governing the pilot, measuring honestly, scaling at a sustainable speed, watching who is helped and who is left behind, paying for it, staffing it, and making it last. The theme is the one the title says: responsibly. A good plan can be undone in any of these steps, and the failures in this book's AI-First Stories appendix, the Los Angeles chatbot and the iPad rollout among them, mostly happened here, in the implementation, and not in the idea.

Where good plans get tested

This chapter is about the unglamorous middle: contracts, pilots, measures, budgets, and staffing. You'll finish with checklists you can use on a real purchase and a real pilot. Let's find the balance between moving fast enough to help students and slowly enough to protect them.

docs.title: Rushed Procurement Risk
docs.text: Rushed procurement risk is the danger that pressure to buy quickly, from hype, a vendor's deadline, an expiring budget, or fear of falling behind, leads a school to skip the checks that protect it. The pattern is familiar. Federal pandemic-relief funds (ESSER), which had to be spent by 2024, pushed many districts to buy technology quickly. The Los Angeles "Ed" chatbot, from the book's appendix, shows the cost: the district committed about $6 million to a startup and spent about $3 million before the company collapsed within months of launch. The remedy is a rule applied every time: no purchase before the criteria of Chapter 20 are met, whatever the deadline. A price that is only good until the end of the month is a reason for more caution, and a good vendor will extend it for a district that is doing due diligence.

docs.title: Contract Due Diligence
docs.text:
Contract due diligence is the careful review of a contract, and of the vendor behind it, before signing. It is the step that turns the privacy and governance principles of Chapter 10 into legal obligations. A district should have the contract read by someone qualified, usually counsel, with a checklist of the terms that matter most for an AI product:

  • Data ownership and use: the district and families own the data; the vendor may use it only to provide the service, and may not use identifiable student data to train its own models or for marketing.
  • Breach notice: a fixed deadline, such as 72 hours, for telling the district about a breach.
  • Deletion: data is deleted on termination, within a stated time, with written confirmation.
  • Subprocessors: a list of any other companies that will handle the data, with notice of changes.
  • Portability: the right to export the data in a standard format at any time.
  • Price and term: caps on renewal increases, no automatic multi-year renewal, and a right to terminate for convenience.
  • Accessibility and standards: commitments to accessibility and to the interoperability standards of Chapter 9.
  • Model changes: notice before the underlying AI model or its behavior changes materially.

Many districts use a shared template for the data terms, such as the National Data Privacy Agreement developed through the Student Data Privacy Consortium, so that each district does not negotiate from scratch.

docs.title: Worked Example: Reading Eight Clauses
docs.text:
Ms. Okafor and the district's counsel mark up eight clauses from the 38-page contract.

Clause Verdict Why "Vendor may use identifiable student data to improve and train its own AI models." Red flag A use beyond providing the service (Chapter 10) "Data is deleted within 60 days of termination, with written confirmation." Acceptable A stated deadline and proof "Vendor will notify the district of any breach within 72 hours." Acceptable A firm deadline "Vendor will notify the district of a breach 'in a timely manner.'" Needs change No deadline can be enforced "Price may rise by any amount at renewal; the contract renews automatically for three years." Needs change No cap and automatic multi-year commitment "The district owns all student data and may export it in a standard format at any time." Acceptable Ownership and portability "The district may not terminate before the end of the three-year term." Needs change No exit if the vendor fails "Vendor may share student data with unnamed third parties for marketing." Red flag Student data must never be used for advertising

Two red flags end the conversation until they are removed. Three more are fixable and should be negotiated. A vendor that will not change the red flags has answered the due-diligence question.

docs.title: Diagram: Contract Clause Review
docs.text:
Run the Contract Clause Review MicroSim Fullscreen

Contract Clause Review

Type: microsim sim-id: contract-clause-review Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: judge Learning Objective: The learner will judge eight contract clauses from an AI product contract as acceptable, needing change, or a red flag, correctly judging at least seven of eight on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: contract due diligence, vendor lock-in, data ownership, breach notice, deletion, and the contract checklist (all defined in the sections "Buying Responsibly" above and in Chapter 10).

Evidence of Mastery: The learner places each of 8 clauses in one of three categories and submits it. A placement is correct when it matches the "Correct verdict" column in Content. Mastery is 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Reading the checklist is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A vague promise is as good as a stated deadline. (2) Any clause that favors the vendor is a red flag. (3) Student data may be used to train a vendor's models if the vendor says it is anonymous.

Instructional Rationale: Judging a clause requires matching its wording to the checklist, noticing missing deadlines or caps, and separating fixable terms from deal-breakers. Pairs of clauses on the same topic, such as a firm and a vague breach deadline, force attention to wording.

Content:

Three categories with definitions on request:

Category Definition shown Acceptable Protects the district and families as written Needs change Not harmful in intent, but too vague or one-sided; negotiate a fix Red flag Allows a use or risk the district should not accept; remove before signing

Eight clauses:

# Clause shown to the learner Correct verdict Why (shown as feedback) 1 "Vendor may use identifiable student data to improve and train its own AI models." Red flag It allows a use beyond providing the service. 2 "Data is deleted within 60 days of termination, with written confirmation." Acceptable It has a deadline and proof. 3 "Vendor will notify the district of any data breach within 72 hours." Acceptable It sets a firm deadline. 4 "Vendor will notify the district of a breach in a timely manner." Needs change There is no deadline that can be enforced. 5 "Price may rise by any amount at renewal, and the contract renews automatically for three years." Needs change There is no price cap and a long automatic commitment. 6 "The district owns all student data and may export it in a standard format at any time." Acceptable It states ownership and portability. 7 "The district may not terminate before the end of the three-year term for any reason." Needs change There is no exit if the vendor fails or the product disappoints. 8 "Vendor may share student data with unnamed third parties for marketing purposes." Red flag Student data must never be used for advertising or shared with unnamed parties.

Provenance: The categories follow the chapter's contract checklist and Chapter 10. The clauses are fictional, written for this chapter, and the sim must say it is not legal advice.

Rules: Each clause has exactly one correct verdict, given in Content. A clause is scored on its first submitted verdict only. The score counts first-attempt correct verdicts out of 8. Mastery is a score >= 7.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads one clause and sees the three verdicts.
  2. The learner selects a verdict and submits it. The sim marks it correct or incorrect and shows the feedback text.
  3. If incorrect, the learner may choose again; the second attempt does not change the score. After the second attempt, the correct verdict and reason are shown.
  4. After all 8 clauses, the sim shows the score.
  5. The learner should notice that clauses 3 and 4 cover the same topic and receive different verdicts.

Feedback: 8 clauses, shuffled once per session, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: [verdict]. [Why text]." Incorrect: "Not quite. Check for a deadline, a cap, an exit, and any use beyond the service. [Why text for the correct answer, without naming the verdict]." After the second attempt the correct verdict is revealed and the clause counts as missed. A running score "First-try correct: n of 8" is shown. Final message for a score >= 7: "You can read a contract for what protects students." For a score < 7: "Review the checklist and try again; the clauses will be reshuffled."

Starting State: Clause 1 of the shuffled order is shown with the three verdicts, the score "First-try correct: 0 of 8," and the prompt "Is this clause acceptable, does it need a change, or is it a red flag?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's worked example lists the same eight clauses with two red flags, three that need change, and three acceptable. The mastery bar is 7 of 8.

docs.title: Vendor Lock-In
docs.text:
Vendor lock-in is the dependence of a school on one vendor's systems or formats so strongly that switching is prohibitively costly, leaving the vendor in a position to raise prices or reduce quality. It happens when data lives in a proprietary format, when content cannot be moved, when staff are trained only on that product, and when the contract has no exit. The defenses come from earlier chapters. Open standards (xAPI, LTI, OneRoster, Chapter 9) let data and tools move. A contract right to export data in a standard format makes the data portable. Short terms and termination rights limit the commitment. And a fallback matters most of all: an open Level 2 textbook (Chapter 7) is something a district can host itself, so a district that keeps one as a baseline can walk away from any vendor.

Ask 'how do we leave?'

Before signing anything, ask the vendor to explain, in writing, how the district would leave: what data it gets back, in what format, how fast, and at what cost. A vendor who answers easily isn't worried about it. One who hedges has told you something.

docs.title: Pilot Governance
docs.text: Pilot governance is the structure of decision-making and oversight for a pilot: who is accountable, who decides, what data is collected and who may see it, and what stops the pilot. A short governance statement for a pilot names a steering group that includes a teacher, a family representative, the technology and privacy lead, and a principal; limits the vendor's access to the data the pilot needs; sets a data-sharing agreement; sets the stop rules written in advance (Chapter 20); sets a reporting schedule, such as a monthly note to families and staff; and says whether the pilot counts as research. If it does, formal review of the protection of human subjects may be required, and families must be given informed consent.

docs.title: Success Measures and Program Evaluation
docs.text:
Success measures are the specific indicators a pilot or program uses to judge whether it is succeeding. A balanced set covers more than test scores: learning (mastery gains and an independent test), engagement and attendance, teacher time and well-being, equity (results for each subgroup), cost per student, privacy incidents, and student and family experience. Measures should be chosen before the pilot starts, and a mix of leading indicators that move early (such as mastery counts) and lagging indicators that move late (such as annual test results) is useful. The warning from Chapter 2 applies: when a single measure becomes the target it is corrupted, so a set of measures is safer than one.

Program evaluation is the systematic assessment of a program's design, implementation, and results. A common tool is the logic model, which lays out the chain from the resources put in (inputs), through the activities carried out and what they produce directly (outputs), to the results for students (outcomes). Evaluation asks of each link whether it happened and whether the next followed. It should use independent evaluation where possible (Chapter 3), a baseline and a comparison group (Chapter 2), standardized testing for the academic core, and the quality tools of Chapter 14 for the afternoon.

A/B testing is a method in which two versions of something, A and B, are compared by randomly assigning people to each and measuring the difference. It is the randomized controlled trial of Chapter 2 on a small scale, used here to test whether a change helps. The ethical concern, that some students are denied a possibly better version, has a standard answer: delayed access. Everyone gets the new version, but the order is randomized, so the group that starts later serves as the comparison. The companion book OER Evaluator teaches how to run an A/B test on an improved open textbook.

docs.title: Worked Example: A Delayed-Access A/B Test
docs.text:
A school wants to know whether an improved version of an explanation page helps students on a ten-question quiz. It randomly assigns 120 students to the improved version (A) and 120 to the original (B) for one week, and then switches B to the improved version.

Group Students Mean quiz score (out of 10) Standard deviation A: improved page 120 7.9 2.0 B: original page 120 7.4 2.0

The difference is 0.5 points, and the effect size is \( d = (7.9 - 7.4)/2.0 = 0.25 \), a meaningful result by the benchmarks of Chapter 2, from a test that cost nothing but a coin flip and a week. Because everyone then gets the improved page, no student was left out. The result is one study of one page, so the school should check that it holds for another class before generalizing.

docs.title: Scaling Without Breaking
docs.text: Scaling a pilot is the expansion of a successful pilot to more classrooms, schools, or the whole district. Chapter 15 supplied the ideas: choose a beachhead, build the whole product, and expect the chasm. Responsible scaling adds two rules. First, scale only as fast as capacity grows: the number of coaches, the training, and the support must keep pace, or the early majority meets a half-built product. Second, scale in stages with a gate at each: a pilot becomes a grade, then a school, then a feeder pattern, then the district, with the decision rule of Chapter 20 applied at each gate.

docs.title: Worked Example: Coach Capacity as the Speed Limit
docs.text:
Suppose a coach can support about 12 teachers well (an illustrative figure). The number of coaches needed is the number of teachers divided by 12, rounded up.

Stage Teachers Coaches needed Year 1: the pilot and a second school 40 \( \lceil 40/12 \rceil = 4 \) Year 2: all middle schools 150 \( \lceil 150/12 \rceil = 13 \) Year 3: the whole district 400 \( \lceil 400/12 \rceil = 34 \)

The district has to grow from 4 coaches to 34 in three years. If it cannot hire or train that many, the right response is to slow the scaling, not to thin the coaching. The coach, not the technology, is the speed limit.

docs.title: Diagram: Coach Capacity Calculator
docs.text:
Run the Coach Capacity Calculator MicroSim Fullscreen

Coach Capacity Calculator

Type: microsim sim-id: coach-capacity-calculator Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: calculate Learning Objective: The learner will calculate the number of coaches needed for a given number of teachers and coach capacity, and the number of teachers a given number of coaches can support, correctly answering three of three questions.

Prerequisites: scaling a pilot, instructional coaching, coach capacity, rounding up (all defined in the sections "Scaling Without Breaking" above and in Chapter 19).

Evidence of Mastery: Before the controls unlock, the learner commits three answers: (Q1) the coaches needed for 150 teachers at a capacity of 12; (Q2) the coaches needed for 400 teachers at a capacity of 12; (Q3) the largest number of teachers that 8 coaches can support at a capacity of 12. An answer is correct when it equals the value in Content. Mastery is 3 of 3 correct. Using the controls afterward is exploration.

Misconceptions: (1) Coaches needed can be a fraction. (2) Scaling speed depends only on the software. (3) A thinner coach load has no effect.

Instructional Rationale: Calculating with rounding up makes the learner confront the fact that capacity is in whole people. Asking in both directions, teachers to coaches and coaches to teachers, shows that coach capacity sets the speed limit of scaling.

Content:

Rules shown: coaches needed = teachers ÷ capacity, rounded up to the next whole number. Teachers supported = coaches × capacity.

Controls:

Input Min Max Step Default Unit Teachers to support 10 600 10 150 teachers Teachers per coach 6 20 1 12 teachers Coaches available 1 50 1 8 coaches

Check values at capacity 12: 40 teachers need 4 coaches; 150 need 13; 400 need 34.

Answers: Q1 = 13; Q2 = 34; Q3 = 96 teachers.

Provenance: The capacity of 12 teachers per coach is illustrative, written for this chapter, and the sim must label it "Illustrative; set your own." The rounding rule is arithmetic.

Rules: Coaches needed = ceiling(teachers ÷ capacity). Teachers supported = coaches available × capacity. The sim shows the gap between coaches needed and coaches available, and says "Slow the rollout" when coaches available are fewer than coaches needed.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner answers Q1, Q2, and Q3 and submits them.
  2. The sim checks the answers and unlocks the controls.
  3. The learner changes the teachers, the capacity, and the coaches available. The coaches needed, the gap, and the message update at once.
  4. The learner should notice that lowering capacity from 12 to 6 doubles the coaches needed, to the nearest whole coach.

Feedback: Three questions, fixed order, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: [value]. [Working text]." Incorrect: "Not quite. Divide, then round up to a whole coach." After the second wrong attempt the value and working are shown. A score "n of 3" is shown.

Starting State: The defaults are shown with the results hidden, and the prompt reads "How many coaches does a district rollout need?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's worked example uses a capacity of 12 teachers per coach, giving 4 coaches for 40 teachers, 13 for 150, and 34 for 400. The mastery bar is 3 of 3.

docs.title: Digital Divide and Cost Barrier
docs.text:
The digital divide is the gap between those who have ready access to the internet and digital devices and those who do not, which tracks income, geography, and disability. Chapter 9 covered devices and offline access, and Chapter 20 listed the equity commitments. In implementation the divide appears in specifics: a student who cannot finish adaptive practice at home, a family without a reliable connection, an older device that cannot run a simulation. The remedies are specific too: loaner devices, hotspots, offline copies, and community Wi-Fi, supported in recent years by federal programs such as the Emergency Connectivity Fund.

The cost barrier to AI schools is the price that keeps AI-first models out of reach for most families. Alpha School charges about $40,000 a year at its original Austin campus and about $65,000 at newer campuses, against the roughly $15,600 that U.S. public schools spend per pupil (Chapter 2), so tuition is about 2.6 to 4.2 times the public cost. A model that is available only at those prices is a model for the few, and is a reason that the public school version, using open Level 2 and Level 3 textbooks and a structured afternoon, matters.

docs.title: Closing or Widening Gaps
docs.text: A tool that helps everyone on average can still widen gaps if it helps the advantaged more. Closing or widening gaps is the question of whether the change makes the difference between groups of students smaller or larger. The educational psychologist Keith Stanovich named the pattern the Matthew effect, after the saying that those who have get more: students who start ahead gain more from new tools and opportunities. To tell which is happening a school has to measure the gap before and after, for each subgroup, not only the average.

docs.title: Worked Example: Everyone Improves, the Gap Widens
docs.text:
Mean mastery scores for a lower-income group and a higher-income group at two schools, before and after one year.

School Group Before After Gap before Gap after Result 1 Lower-income 62 70 12 9 Closing Higher-income 74 79 2 Lower-income 58 63 14 17 Widening Higher-income 72 80

At School 2 both groups improved, and the average improvement was 6.5 points. A report that said "scores rose" would be true, and the gap grew from 14 to 17 points. At School 1 the lower-income group gained more, and the gap closed. The averages alone would make the two schools look alike.

docs.title: Diagram: Is the Gap Closing?
docs.text:
Run the Is the Gap Closing? MicroSim Fullscreen

Is the Gap Closing?

Type: microsim sim-id: is-the-gap-closing Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Analyze Bloom Verb: differentiate Learning Objective: The learner will differentiate five schools' results as closing, widening, or unchanged gaps by computing the gap before and after, correctly classifying at least four of five on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: closing or widening gaps, the Matthew effect, achievement gap (defined in the section "Equity in Implementation" above and in Chapter 3).

Evidence of Mastery: For each of 5 schools, the learner selects Closing, Widening, or Unchanged and submits it. A selection is correct when it matches the "Correct result" column in Content. Mastery is 4 of 5 correct on the first attempt. Viewing the computed gaps after answering is exploration.

Misconceptions: (1) If both groups improve, the gap must be closing. (2) A larger gain for one group always closes the gap. (3) An unchanged gap means no change in scores.

Instructional Rationale: Differentiating requires computing the gap, not reading the gains. Cases where both groups improve but the gap widens, and cases where both improve equally and the gap is unchanged, make the learner compute.

Content:

The rule shown: gap = higher-income mean − lower-income mean. If the gap after is at least 1 point smaller than before, the result is Closing; at least 1 point larger, Widening; otherwise Unchanged.

Five schools, mean mastery before and after:

School Lower-income before Lower-income after Higher-income before Higher-income after Gap before Gap after Correct result Why (shown as feedback) 1 62 70 74 79 12 9 Closing The gap fell from 12 to 9. 2 58 63 72 80 14 17 Widening Both improved, but the gap rose from 14 to 17. 3 60 66 70 76 10 10 Unchanged Both gained 6 points, so the gap stayed at 10. 4 55 65 70 72 15 7 Closing The lower-income group gained 10 and the other gained 2. 5 64 66 71 79 7 13 Widening The higher-income group gained 8 and the other gained 2.

Provenance: The scores are illustrative, written for this chapter, and the sim must label them "Illustrative data."

Rules: Gap = higher-income mean − lower-income mean. Result = Closing if gap after <= gap before − 1; Widening if gap after >= gap before + 1; otherwise Unchanged. Each school has exactly one correct result, given in Content. A school is scored on its first submitted answer only. The score counts first-attempt correct answers out of 5. Mastery is a score >= 4.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees one school's four numbers and the three results.
  2. The learner computes the gaps, selects a result, and submits it. The sim marks it correct or incorrect and shows the feedback text.
  3. If incorrect, the learner may choose again; the second attempt does not change the score. After the second attempt, the correct result and reason are shown.
  4. After all 5 schools, the sim shows the score and each school's gap before and after.
  5. The learner should notice that in schools 2 and 5 the scores of both groups rose.

Feedback: 5 schools, shuffled once per session, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: [result]. [Why text]." Incorrect: "Not quite. Compute the gap before and after. [Why text for the correct answer, without naming the result]." After the second attempt the correct result is revealed and the school counts as missed. A running score "First-try correct: n of 5" is shown. Final message for a score >= 4: "You can see past the averages to the gap." For a score < 4: "Review the rule and try again; the schools will be reshuffled."

Starting State: School 1 of the shuffled order is shown with its four scores and the three results, the score "First-try correct: 0 of 5," and the prompt "Is the gap between the two groups closing?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's worked example uses schools 1 and 2 with the same numbers (gaps 12 to 9 and 14 to 17). The rule for a closing, widening, or unchanged gap is a change of at least one point. The mastery bar is 4 of 5.

docs.title: Assessment and Integrity in Practice
docs.text:
Redesign not policing is the principle that a school should respond to AI by changing what and how it assesses, not by trying to catch students with detectors. Chapter 20 gave the reasons: detectors produce false accusations, with the heaviest burden on English-language learners, and a redesigned assessment makes AI less useful for cheating while measuring what matters better.

The combined assessment plan is the school's written plan for how the different kinds of assessment fit together: what is measured, with what tool, how often, and who sees it. It pairs the morning's mastery data with the afternoon's evidence and keeps the required state tests (which federal law still mandates, Chapter 2) in their place.

A teamwork rubric is a scoring guide for teamwork in a project, with a small number of criteria and descriptions of performance at each level, so that teachers and students share a picture of what good looks like. Rubrics support the performance assessment of Chapter 20 and are scored by two people on a sample to check agreement.

docs.title: Worked Example: A Combined Assessment Plan and a Teamwork Rubric
docs.text:
What is measured Tool How often Who sees it Concept mastery in the academic core Dashboard mastery data (Chapter 8) Continuous Student, teacher, family Quality of work and growth Portfolio with reflection Each term Student, mentor, family Communication and teamwork Exhibition and a teamwork rubric, two scorers Each project Student, teacher, family Grade-level standards State test Annually (required) School, district, state

An illustrative teamwork rubric, scored from 1 to 4.

Criterion 1: Beginning 2: Developing 3: Proficient 4: Exemplary Contribution Does little of the team's work Does an assigned part Does a fair share and helps others Does a fair share and improves the team's work Listening Interrupts or ignores others Listens but rarely responds Paraphrases and asks questions Draws out quieter members and builds on their ideas Roles and accountability Unclear or avoids a role Fills a role when reminded Fills a role reliably Fills a role and covers gaps without being asked Handling disagreement Avoids it or makes it personal Raises it, but argues positions Discusses interests and reaches agreement Helps the team turn the disagreement into a better solution

A rubric is only as good as the scorers

A common trap is adopting a rubric and trusting every score. Different scorers can read it differently, which makes scores unfair. Have two people score a sample independently, compare, and discuss the differences until they agree on what each level looks like.

docs.title: Grade-Level Models, Scheduling, and Staff
docs.text:
Grade-level design is the adaptation of the AI-native school day to the needs of a particular age group, which Chapter 20 outlined in a table. Three models follow from it.

The elementary school model keeps one home-room teacher with a class for most of the day, which gives young children a stable relationship. The academic morning is short, mostly teacher-led and hands-on, and a brief adaptive block supports reading and number practice. The afternoon is play, movement, music, stories, and projects, often with older students as buddies. The middle school model adds an advisory teacher who follows a student for several years, an adaptive morning of about 150 minutes, and projects with public exhibitions in the afternoon, as in the schedule of Chapter 20. The high school model builds around credits and preparation for what follows: a morning that mixes adaptive work with seminars and laboratories, and an afternoon of capstone projects, internships and dual enrollment with community partners, ensembles, and service.

Block scheduling is the arrangement of the school day into fewer, longer periods, typically 80 to 90 minutes, which may alternate by day or by semester. It suits the new model, since a project, a laboratory, or a studio session needs a long uninterrupted block, and a high school's afternoon is the natural place for it. The costs are fewer class meetings per course, which makes long gaps between meetings of the same class, and the need for teachers to plan activities that fill a long block. The evidence on block scheduling is mixed, so it is a choice about fit and not a proven improvement.

Afternoon specialist staff are the adults, other than classroom teachers, who lead the afternoon: artists, musicians, coaches, makers, coders, and community experts, often part time or contracted. They bring skills that classroom teachers may not have. They also bring requirements: background checks, training in the school's structure (the SAFE practices of Chapter 14) and in safety, and a clear line of supervision. Hiring for new roles is the recruitment of adults for the roles the model needs, such as learning coach, afternoon facilitator, and program lead. The qualities to hire for are facilitation, the ability to build relationships with young people, comfort with technology, and a growth mindset, and the interview should include a demonstration, such as leading a ten-minute activity, since a résumé does not show it.

AI coaching teachers is the use of AI to support teachers in improving their practice, in the way the Tutor CoPilot study in the appendix used it: the AI gave suggestions to human tutors during their sessions. In that study, students' mastery improved, the least experienced tutors improved the most, and the cost per tutor was small. AI coaching can also help with lesson planning, reflection on a recorded lesson, and feedback on classroom talk. It carries the privacy and guardrail concerns of Chapters 10 and 12, since classroom recordings are sensitive, and it should support the teacher's judgment, not replace it or be used to rank teachers.

docs.title: Paying for It
docs.text: Budget reallocation is the shifting of existing money from old uses to new ones, the main way a school pays for the model, since new money is rare. Chapter 7 showed where savings arise: a print-textbook baseline of about $53 per student per year against about $6 to $13 for Level 2 or Level 3 content and training, which for a district of 12,000 students is roughly $490,000 to $570,000 a year. Other sources include ending licenses for content that has an open equivalent, reducing spending on remediation as gaps are closed earlier, and reassigning staff time.

docs.title: Worked Example: Is It Self-Financing?
docs.text:
The afternoon is the main new cost. Suppose a district of 12,000 students needs the equivalent of 20 additional full-time afternoon specialists at an illustrative loaded cost of $60,000 each.

Amount per year Savings: print versus Level 2 content and training (Chapter 7) about $570,000 New cost: 20 afternoon specialists × $60,000 $1,200,000 Gap to fill about $630,000

The savings from content alone do not pay for the afternoon. The honest conclusion is that a district must find the rest by other means: community partners and volunteers, reassigning teacher time from lecturing (the adult-hours of Chapter 20), grants, and phasing the program in. The model is not free. Its claim is narrower: that it can be done within the order of magnitude of public school budgets, which Alpha's tuition of $40,000 to $65,000 shows is not true of every version.

docs.title: Making It Last
docs.text:
Sustaining change is the work of keeping the new way of working in place after the pilot ends and the champions move on. It is the refreeze and anchoring of Chapter 17 applied to the whole model. Policy embedding is making the change part of the formal rules: board policy, the bell schedule, the handbook, job descriptions, hiring practices, budgets, and agreements with the union and with the state. Where a rule gets in the way, such as a seat-time requirement tied to the Carnegie unit (Chapter 3), policy embedding includes seeking the waiver, and some states have allowed competency-based credit to replace seat time.

A culture change plan is a written plan, usually for one to two years, that brings together the change models of Chapters 16 to 19 and aims at the culture itself. It names the culture the school has and the one it wants (Chapter 18's assessment), and sets out actions for each of the main steps.

docs.title: Worked Example: A Twelve-Month Culture Change Plan
docs.text:
Months Focus Models used Main actions 1–2 Ready the ground Kotter (urgency, coalition), CBAM (concerns survey), culture assessment Share the data; form the coalition; read the culture; list losses 3–5 Launch the pilot ADKAR, Bridges, pilot governance Champions; coaching; family communication; one-page pilot plan 6–8 Show results and learn Implementation dip, short-term wins Honest monthly reports; peer observation; exhibition night 9–10 Build the whole product Whole product, capacity building Training package; integration; hiring for new roles 11–12 Embed Anchoring, policy embedding Board policy; hiring practices; schedule; staff orientation

The plan fits on a page, and it names a model at each phase. Each line of it is a commitment, not a hope.

docs.title: Answering the Contract
docs.text:
Ms. Okafor's phone call has an answer. She will not sign by the end of the month. She will send the contract to counsel with the checklist, ask the vendor to remove two red flags and fix three terms, and tell the purchasing officer that a vendor that wants a district's business will extend the date. She will keep an open Level 2 textbook as the fallback, so that the district can leave if it has to. The pilot will have a governance statement, a balanced set of measures chosen in advance, a delayed-access design for the first test, and a decision rule. The scaling will be paced by coach capacity, and the gap data will be reported by subgroup.

The story has both sides. The benefit: a model that is carried out with its protections intact and that can be defended to families, the board, and the press. The risks: a rushed purchase, a locked-in vendor, a pilot that cannot fail, a scale-up that outruns its coaches, a gap that quietly widens, an afternoon with no money, and a change that fades when the champion leaves. The response is the set of habits in this chapter: due diligence before signing, an exit plan, governance and measures before the pilot, capacity-paced scaling, gap monitoring, honest budgets, and embedding in policy.

Responsible means leave-able

Notice the thread through every section: a responsible implementation can be stopped, left, measured, and corrected. A contract you can exit, a pilot with a stop rule, a gap you track, a fallback you host yourself. The things you can't undo are the ones to be most careful about.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Rushed procurement risk skips the checks that protect schools; contract due diligence covers data use, breach notice, deletion, portability, price, term, and model changes. Two red flags end the conversation.
  • Vendor lock-in is prevented with open standards, data export, short terms, and an open Level 2 fallback.
  • Pilot governance sets who decides and what stops the pilot; success measures are a balanced set chosen in advance; program evaluation uses a logic model, independent evaluation, and a comparison; A/B testing with delayed access answers the ethical objection.
  • Scaling a pilot is paced by capacity: 4, 13, and 34 coaches for 40, 150, and 400 teachers at 12 teachers per coach.
  • The digital divide and the cost barrier to AI schools (tuition of $40,000 to $65,000) show why the public model matters; check closing or widening gaps with the gap, not the average.
  • Redesign not policing pairs with a combined assessment plan and a teamwork rubric scored by two raters.
  • Grade-level design gives the elementary school model, middle school model, and high school model; block scheduling suits projects; afternoon specialist staff and hiring for new roles supply the adults; AI coaching teachers supports without replacing.
  • Budget reallocation does not fully pay for the afternoon in our example; sustaining change needs policy embedding and a culture change plan.

You can implement it responsibly

You just learned to read a contract for what protects students, govern and evaluate a pilot, pace a scale-up to coach capacity, watch the gaps, and pay for and sustain the model. That completes the how-to of the book. Chapters 22 and 23 return to the real stories, the ones that worked and the ones that went wrong, and what they teach. One step at a time, together.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: Implementing the AI-Native Model Responsibly
docs.text: Test your understanding of responsible procurement, pilot governance and evaluation, capacity-paced scaling, equity monitoring, and sustaining the model with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. What is vendor lock-in?
docs.text:
1. Dependence on one vendor so strong that switching becomes too costly
  2. A contract clause that guarantees a vendor's price for the full term
  3. A security feature that locks student data so only the vendor can see it
  4. An agreement among vendors not to compete for the same school district
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Vendor lock-in happens when data lives in proprietary formats, content cannot be moved, staff are trained only on one product, and the contract has no exit, leaving the vendor able to raise prices or reduce quality. The defenses are open standards such as xAPI, LTI, and OneRoster, a contract right to export data, short terms with termination rights, and above all a fallback, such as an open Level 2 textbook the district can host itself.

Concept Tested: Vendor Lock-In

See: Vendor Lock-In

docs.title: 2. How does a delayed-access design answer the ethical objection to A/B testing in schools?
docs.text:
1. It lets families choose which version their child receives
  2. It gives the new version only to the students who are furthest behind
  3. It randomizes when each group gets the new version, so all receive it
  4. It tests the new version on teachers before any students see it
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. The objection to A/B testing is that some students are denied a possibly better version. In a delayed-access design, everyone gets the new version, but the order is randomized, so the group that starts later serves as the comparison. In the chapter's example, students were randomly assigned to the improved or original page for one week, and then the original group switched. Letting families choose would reintroduce the selection bias that randomization is meant to remove.

Concept Tested: A/B Testing

See: Success Measures and Program Evaluation

docs.title: 3. During contract due diligence, counsel reviews four clauses in an AI tutoring contract. Which one should be marked as a red flag?
docs.text:
1. "Data is deleted within 60 days of termination, with written confirmation."
  2. "Vendor may use identifiable student data to improve and train its own AI models."
  3. "Vendor will notify the district of any breach within 72 hours."
  4. "The district owns all student data and may export it in a standard format at any time."
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The chapter's due-diligence checklist says the vendor may use data only to provide the service and may not use identifiable student data to train its own models or for marketing. Using it to train the vendor's AI is a use beyond the service, so it is a red flag that ends the conversation until it is removed. The other three clauses are acceptable: a stated deletion deadline with proof, a firm breach-notice deadline, and district ownership with portability.

Concept Tested: Contract Due Diligence

See: Worked Example: Reading Eight Clauses

docs.title: 4. A district plans to scale a program to 250 teachers. If one coach can support about 12 teachers well, how many coaches will the district need?
docs.text:
1. About 12
  2. About 20
  3. About 25
  4. About 21
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The number of coaches is the number of teachers divided by 12, rounded up: 250 / 12 is about 20.8, which rounds up to 21. Rounding down to 20 would leave some teachers without adequate coaching. The chapter's point is that the coach, not the technology, is the speed limit for scaling: if the district cannot hire or train enough coaches, it should slow the scaling rather than thin the coaching.

Concept Tested: Scaling a Pilot

See: Worked Example: Coach Capacity as the Speed Limit

docs.title: 5. After one year, a school's lower-income students rose from a mastery score of 60 to 66, and higher-income students rose from 75 to 84. The principal's report says, "Scores rose for every group." What does the chapter's analysis reveal?
docs.text:
1. Both groups improved, but the gap between them widened from 15 to 18 points
  2. The gap closed, since both groups improved by a similar amount
  3. The program failed, since lower-income students did not reach the higher group
  4. The result cannot be judged without the state test scores for the year
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The gap was 75 - 60 = 15 points before and 84 - 66 = 18 points after, so it widened even though both groups improved. Higher-income students gained 9 points and lower-income students 6. The chapter warns that a tool that helps everyone on average can still widen gaps, the Matthew effect Stanovich described, and that a school must measure the gap for each subgroup before and after, not only the average. The report's statement is true and incomplete.

Concept Tested: Closing or Widening Gaps

See: Worked Example: Everyone Improves, the Gap Widens

docs.title: 6. Why does the chapter favor "redesign not policing" as the response to AI and academic integrity?
docs.text:
1. Because AI detectors are too expensive for most districts to license
  2. Because detectors falsely accuse students, especially English learners
  3. Because students who use AI are always honest about it when asked
  4. Because federal law prohibits schools from using AI detectors on student work
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Redesign not policing means changing what and how a school assesses rather than trying to catch students with detectors. Chapter 20 showed that detectors produce false accusations, with the heaviest burden on English-language learners, while redesigned assessments, such as in-class work, process evidence, and oral defense, make AI less useful for cheating and measure what matters better. The chapter does not rest the case on cost or a legal ban.

Concept Tested: Redesign Not Policing

See: Assessment and Integrity in Practice

docs.title: 7. A school runs a delayed-access A/B test of a revised lesson page. Group A, with the revised page, has a mean quiz score of 8.2; Group B, with the original, has 7.6. Both groups have a standard deviation of 2.4. What is the effect size?
docs.text:
1. About 0.6
  2. About 0.10
  3. About 1.4
  4. About 0.25
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The effect size is the difference in means divided by the standard deviation: (8.2 - 7.6) / 2.4 = 0.6 / 2.4 = 0.25. The 0.6 answer is the raw difference in points, not standardized. As in the chapter's example, an effect of 0.25 is meaningful by the education benchmarks of Chapter 2. The chapter adds that one study of one page should be checked in another class before the school generalizes from it.

Concept Tested: Program Evaluation

See: Worked Example: A Delayed-Access A/B Test

docs.title: 8. A district estimates $400,000 a year in content savings from switching to an open Level 2 textbook. Its afternoon program needs 15 additional specialists at $60,000 each. What conclusion does the chapter's reasoning support?
docs.text:
1. The model is self-financing, since content savings exceed the afternoon cost
  2. The model should be abandoned, since it cannot be paid for from savings
  3. Savings leave a gap of about $500,000 to fill through partners, grants, or phasing
  4. The district should cut the afternoon program to match the content savings exactly
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Fifteen specialists at $60,000 cost $900,000, so the $400,000 in savings leaves a gap of about $500,000. The chapter's worked example reaches the same kind of conclusion: content savings alone do not pay for the afternoon, so a district must find the rest through community partners and volunteers, reassigning teacher time from lecturing, grants, and phasing in. The model's claim is narrower: it can be done within the order of magnitude of public budgets, unlike AI-first tuition of $40,000 to $65,000.

Concept Tested: Budget Reallocation

See: Worked Example: Is It Self-Financing?

docs.title: 9. A vendor's representative tells a purchasing officer that a favorable price is good "through the end of the month," and the district's one-time funds must be spent soon. The 38-page contract has not been reviewed. Which course of action is best justified by the chapter?
docs.text:
1. Decline the deadline, send the contract to counsel, ask for an extension, keep a fallback
  2. Sign now to lock in the price, then negotiate the contract terms after the pilot begins
  3. Sign a shorter version of the contract that omits the data terms to save time
  4. Cancel all AI purchases, since any deadline pressure proves the vendor cannot be trusted
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Rushed procurement risk is the danger that pressure from hype, deadlines, or expiring budgets leads a school to skip its protections; the Los Angeles "Ed" chatbot, which spent about $3 million before the company collapsed, shows the cost. The chapter's rule is no purchase before the criteria are met, whatever the deadline, and says a good vendor will extend a price for a district doing due diligence. Signing first gives up leverage, omitting data terms removes the protections, and cancelling everything overreacts.

Concept Tested: Rushed Procurement Risk

See: Rushed Procurement Risk

docs.title: 10. A district's pilot plan uses one success measure: the state test score at the end of the year. Analyzed against the chapter's guidance on success measures, what is the main weakness?
docs.text:
1. State tests cannot be used in pilots, since they are required for accountability
  2. A single measure is fine, as long as an independent evaluator scores it
  3. A single lagging measure can be corrupted and misses equity, cost, and privacy
  4. The measure should be replaced with a teacher satisfaction survey alone
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. A balanced set of success measures covers learning, engagement and attendance, teacher time and well-being, equity by subgroup, cost per student, privacy incidents, and student and family experience, chosen before the pilot. A mix of leading indicators that move early and lagging ones like annual tests is useful. The chapter applies Chapter 2's warning that when a single measure becomes the target it is corrupted, so a set is safer than one. Replacing the test with one survey repeats the same mistake.

Concept Tested: Success Measures

See: Success Measures and Program Evaluation

docs.title: References: Implementing the AI-Native Model Responsibly
docs.text:
1. Vendor Lock-In - Wikipedia - Explains how customers become tied to one supplier because switching is too costly, with real examples. It names the risk the chapter's contract checks are designed to prevent, such as data export and exit terms.

  2. Digital Divide - Wikipedia - Describes unequal access to and use of digital technology across income, place, race, age and disability. It frames the chapter's question of whether an AI-native model closes or widens achievement gaps.

  3. Program Evaluation - Wikipedia - Covers how to collect and analyze evidence about whether a program meets its goals and gives value for money. Background for the chapter's success measures, comparison groups and decisions about whether to scale a pilot.

  4. Learning to Improve: How America's Schools Can Get Better at Getting Better - Anthony S. Bryk, Louis M. Gomez, Alicia Grunow and Paul G. LeMahieu - Harvard Education Press - The authors are credited with bringing improvement science and Plan-Do-Study-Act cycles to schools. Their "learn fast, fail fast, improve quickly" approach shows how to run a pilot that learns before it scales.

  5. The Checklist Manifesto: How to Get Things Right - Atul Gawande - Metropolitan Books - Gawande is credited with showing that short checklists prevent errors by experts in complex work. His argument supports the chapter's use of due-diligence checklists for contracts, pilots and procurement decisions.

  6. Carnegie Improvement Science Collection - Carnegie Foundation for the Advancement of Teaching - A free library of improvement science tools, including PDSA cycle templates and the 90-Day Cycle Handbook. Practical support for pilot governance and evaluation.

  7. What Works Clearinghouse - Institute of Education Sciences - The federal source for reviews of education research, practice guides and intervention reports. Useful when a vendor makes claims about results, since it shows which kinds of studies count as strong evidence.

  8. Empowering Education Leaders: A Toolkit for Safe, Ethical, and Equitable AI Integration - U.S. Department of Education, Office of Educational Technology (via ERIC) - The October 2024 toolkit on privacy, bias, procurement and planning for AI in schools. Full text is free, and its risk modules match the chapter's due-diligence steps.

  9. Common Sense Privacy Program - Common Sense Media - Publishes evaluations of the privacy policies of education technology products and a set of privacy questions for educators. A practical starting point for checking a vendor's data practices before signing a contract.

  10. What Went Wrong with L.A. Unified's iPad Program? - Government Technology - A 2015 account of the Los Angeles iPad rollout: weak planning, thin teacher training, unfinished curriculum and dependence on one vendor. A clear warning about rushed procurement and scaling before piloting.

docs.title: AI-First Case Studies I: Promise and Peril
Summary
docs.text: This chapter presents a first set of real cases that show both the promise and the peril of AI-first schools: Alpha School, the Turkish high school chatbot study, the Harvard physics AI tutor, and the risk-and-response framework used to weigh them. Readers finish able to analyze a story about AI in schools to find which benefit and which risk it shows.

docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 2: Evidence, Motivation, and the Stakeholders of Schooling
  • Chapter 11: Mastery Learning and the Case for a Compressed Morning
  • Chapter 12: AI Guardrails: Teaching Thinking Without Over-Reliance

docs.title: Why Stories
docs.text:
The board has read the evidence, the design, and the plan. At the last meeting, Mr. Alvarez, who asked "doubles what?" in Chapter 4, says what many people feel after a long presentation. "I follow the argument. But I keep thinking about the schools that already tried this. What happened to them?"

It is the right instinct. Arguments convince the mind, and stories show what an argument looks like when it meets a real school. This chapter and the next turn from theory to cases. They tell the stories of real schools, studies, and products that have tried some version of the model, both where it seemed to work and where it did not, and they use a single framework to read each one.

The cases come from the book's AI-First Stories appendix, which collects them with their sources. The appendix carries a caution that applies here too: many of these stories are still unfolding, and some figures come from news coverage, preprints, and the schools' own claims. Before any number in this chapter is quoted elsewhere, it should be checked against the original source and dated.

What happened to the schools that tried it?

This chapter reads real cases the way the book has taught you to read evidence: with a benefit, a risk, and a response for each. You'll finish able to take any story about AI in schools and say which benefit it shows, which risk, and what the school did about it. Let's find the balance between the promise in the headline and the peril in the footnote.

docs.title: How the Book Uses Stories
docs.text:
Storytelling is the use of narrative to convey information, in which events are linked in time and cause around people, goals, and obstacles. People tend to understand and remember information better when it comes in story form, though the strength of the effect varies and popular claims about it are often exaggerated. This book uses stories in two ways, and it keeps them distinct so that readers never mistake one for the other.

A real case study is an account of an actual school, program, or study, based on reported facts and sources, analyzed to draw lessons (Chapter 2's case study method). Every real case in this book names its source, and says where the figures are uncertain. A composite story is a fictional account assembled from patterns seen in many real situations, with invented characters, used to make an idea concrete. Maya, Jordan, Dev, Ms. Okafor, Ms. Rivera, and Lincoln Middle School are composites. They never claim to be real, and no quotation or outcome attached to them should be taken as a fact about a real person. An illustrated story, which the course description calls for in most chapters, is a story, real or composite, told with images, such as a short graphic-novel scene, to reach readers who learn well visually.

The distinction matters ethically. A composite story is honest when it is labeled, and dishonest when it is passed off as a real case. A real case is honest when it reports what the source says and no more.

docs.title: Worked Example: Real or Composite?
docs.text: Statement Kind How the book treats it "Maya's mother asked how the software knew which fractions her daughter was stuck on." Composite story Invented to illustrate a parent's question "In a Turkish high school study, students given open GPT-4 access did about 17 percent worse on later exams." Real case study Cited to a published study; the figure should be checked against the source "Alpha School charges about $40,000 to $65,000 a year." Real case study Reported tuition, which varies by campus; verify before citing "A teacher at Lincoln Middle said the dashboard saved her an evening." Composite story An invented example

docs.title: A Framework for Reading Cases
docs.text:
Every case in this chapter is read with the same five questions, which give the chapter its shape. The questions follow from the book's stated goal, which the course description puts as strengthening the positives and reducing the negatives.

Benefits of AI-first schools are the gains that the model promises: learning at each student's own pace, and more time for curiosity, the arts, and teamwork. Risks of AI-first schools are the harms it can bring. The course description names seven: screen time, handing thinking over to AI, wrong AI answers, privacy risks, cost and equity gaps, fear of job loss, and unstructured afternoons. Every case is read for which of these it shows.

The risk-and-response framework pairs each risk a story shows with what the school did, or could do, about it. It is a table with four columns: the story's benefit, the risk it also shows, the response, and the lesson. A lesson from a case is the transferable point that the case teaches about something beyond itself.

Strengthen the positives is the half of the goal that builds on what works: protecting and expanding the benefits, such as mastery-based pacing and a structured afternoon. Reduce the negatives is the other half: lowering the likelihood or the harm of each risk. Risk mitigation is the set of actions that do the reducing, and it has four general forms: avoid the risk entirely, reduce its likelihood or harm, transfer it (for example, to an insurer or to a contract), or accept it knowingly. A school chooses among them for each risk.

Risk A typical mitigation Where the book develops it Screen time Cap the screens in the morning; break every 25 to 30 minutes; keep the afternoon off-screen Chapter 12 Handing thinking over to AI Hint-first tutors; assessments that show process Chapters 11, 12, 20 Wrong AI answers Ground the tutor in vetted content; check with tools; teach verification Chapters 5, 12 Privacy Minimize data; governance; contracts Chapters 10, 21 Cost and equity gaps Open Level 2 and 3 content; devices; a free afternoon Chapters 7, 9, 20, 21 Fear of job loss Honest roles, written commitments, coaching Chapter 19 Unstructured afternoon The SAFE practices and trained adults Chapter 14

docs.title: Worked Example: A Story in the Framework
docs.text:
Read the Tutor CoPilot case from the appendix with the four columns.

Benefit Risk also shown Response Lesson Students' mastery improved, and the weakest tutors improved most The risk of over-reliance on AI suggestions; privacy of session data The AI suggested moves to a human tutor, who stayed in charge AI works well when it makes people better at helping students

docs.title: Diagram: Which Benefit or Risk?
docs.text:
Run the Which Benefit or Risk? MicroSim Fullscreen

Which Benefit or Risk?

Type: microsim sim-id: which-benefit-or-risk Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Analyze Bloom Verb: distinguish Learning Objective: The learner will distinguish eight statements drawn from AI-first school stories as one of two benefits or one of six risks, correctly placing at least seven of eight on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: benefits of AI-first schools, risks of AI-first schools, the risk-and-response framework (all defined in the section "A Framework for Reading Cases" above).

Evidence of Mastery: The learner places each of 8 statements in one of eight bins and submits it. A placement is correct when it matches the "Correct bin" column in Content. Mastery is 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Reading the bin definitions is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A story shows only a benefit or only a risk. (2) Any complaint about AI is a privacy risk. (3) A high price is only a cost issue, not an equity issue.

Instructional Rationale: Distinguishing the bins requires reading what each statement says about the effect on students: pace, time for people, screens, thinking, accuracy, data, access, or unstructured time. Statements from different stories test whether the learner uses the framework, not the story's name.

Content:

Eight bins with definitions shown on request:

Bin Definition shown Benefit: own pace Each student moves at their own speed Benefit: time for people More time for curiosity, the arts, and teamwork Risk: screen time Too many hours on screens Risk: handing thinking over Students let AI do the thinking Risk: wrong answers The AI gives incorrect answers Risk: privacy Student data is exposed or misused Risk: cost and equity Price or access leaves some students out Risk: unstructured afternoon Freed time drifts into free time with no plan

Eight statements:

[Why text for the correct answer, without naming the bin]." After the second attempt the correct bin is revealed and the statement counts as missed. docs.title: Case 1: Alpha School
docs.text:
Alpha School is a private school network that began in Austin, Texas, in 2014 and now has campuses in several cities, including Boston, Miami, and New York. Its model is the best-known working example of the morning-and-afternoon design. Students spend about two hours a day on adaptive academic software, a model the school calls 2 Hour Learning, and the rest of the day on life-skills workshops and projects led by adult guides. Two-to-three-hour learning is the broader claim, which this chapter and Chapter 11 examine, that with adaptive software a student can reach a traditional day's academic results in two to three hours.

Alpha adult guides are the adults who lead the afternoon and support students in the morning. They are not classroom lecturers. They support motivation, effort, and progress, and run workshops and projects. This is the learning guide of Chapter 20, and the design raises the question Chapter 20 flagged: when a student needs a human explanation of a difficult idea, is there an adult who can give one?

Alpha tuition range is the cost the schools charge: about $40,000 a year at the original Austin campus and about $65,000 a year at newer campuses in Boston, Miami, and New York. Each figure applies to its campuses, and the higher figure should not be given as the price for every campus.

Framework column Alpha School Benefit A structure that frees most of the day for projects, workshops, and people; adaptive pacing in the morning Risk also shown Cost and equity: the price is about 2.6 to 4.2 times public per-pupil spending of about $15,600; and the results are reported by the school, with no independent evaluation in this book's sources Response The book asks how to offer the same structure to every student, using open Level 2 and Level 3 textbooks, learning graphs, and a structured afternoon in place of costly live AI Lesson The structure can work, at private-school prices

docs.title: Case 2: Unbound Academy and the Software Is Not the Model
docs.text:
Unbound Academy is a free online charter school for grades 4 to 8 in Arizona that uses Alpha School's 2 Hour Learning software. The Arizona State Board for Charter Schools approved it by a 4–3 vote. According to the appendix, a board slideshow reportedly showed about 10 percent of students proficient in math and 28 percent in English language arts, below state averages, against the school's projection of 90 percent or more within two to three years. The school also claims that students learn 2.8 times faster on its own growth tests. The reports do not say where students started, so it is unclear how much they grew.

The lesson of the two cases together is the principle this book calls software is not the model: the same software, used without the adults and the in-person afternoon, did not carry over its results. The software is one part of the model, and the adult guides, the projects, and the people are the others. A school that buys the software and omits the afternoon has bought a fraction of what it saw.

Framework column Unbound Academy Benefit Free to families, which addresses the cost barrier; an adaptive morning Risk also shown The software without the afternoon: early reported results below state averages, with no baseline to judge growth Response Hold claims to the evidence standard of Chapter 2; ask for starting points and independent evaluation Lesson The morning software alone is not the whole model

docs.title: Case 3: The Turkish High School Study
docs.text:
The Turkish high school study, by Hamsa Bastani and colleagues at the Wharton School in 2024, was a randomized field experiment in a Turkish high school. Students practicing mathematics were given either no AI, open access to a GPT-4 chatbot, or a version with guardrails that gave hints instead of answers. The students with open access did much better on the practice problems. On later exams taken without AI, however, they did about 17 percent worse than students who had never had access, and the guardrailed version removed most of that harm.

The lesson is design over raw AI power: the same underlying AI helped or harmed depending on its design, so what matters about an AI tutor is whether it gives hints or answers, not how powerful it is. The study is a randomized comparison, which makes it strong evidence of the direction of the effect, though it covers one school and short-term math, and its size should not be applied to every setting.

Framework column Turkish high school study Benefit Better practice performance with AI help Risk also shown Handing thinking over: worse later exams without AI Response The hint-first version, with guardrails, removed most of the harm Lesson Design matters more than power

docs.title: Case 4: The Harvard Physics AI Tutor
docs.text:
The Harvard physics AI tutor study, by Gregory Kestin and colleagues at Harvard, published in 2025, was a randomized study in an introductory physics course. Students who learned from a carefully designed AI tutor, built on proven teaching practices instead of being an open chatbot, learned more, in less time, than students in an active-learning class led by an instructor. It is the strongest piece of evidence for the claim that a well-designed AI tutor can make a shorter academic morning work.

It is also the study with the most limits to remember: one course, at one university, with college students who are unusually well prepared. Whether the result holds for a middle schooler who is behind in fractions is an open question that only independent studies in those settings can answer.

Framework column Harvard physics AI tutor Benefit Learned more in less time Risk also shown Generalization: one course, one university; privacy and over-reliance remain to be managed Response A tutor designed on proven practices, with guidance and structure Lesson A well-designed tutor can help, and design is the condition

The two studies are one lesson from both ends

Notice how neatly the Turkish and Harvard studies fit together: one shows the harm of an open chatbot and the other the benefit of a designed tutor. Together they say what Chapter 12 argued, that the question to ask of any AI tutor is how it was built.

docs.title: Case 5: Summit Learning
docs.text:
Summit Learning was a personalized-learning platform developed with support from Facebook engineers and rolled out to many schools. In 2018 and 2019 students in Brooklyn walked out, and families in Kansas protested, complaining about long hours on screens and too little contact with teachers. The appendix calls it the clearest real example of the screen-time risk.

The case shows the risk of a model that is technology-led without a human afternoon: students felt isolated, and families lost trust. It is the reason the book keeps the morning short and the afternoon social. It also shows how quickly local trust can fail when students and families are not part of the design (Chapter 19's student voice and communication).

Framework column Summit Learning Benefit Personalized pacing and a platform that many schools adopted Risk also shown Screen time and too little contact with teachers Response (In this case, protest rather than design) a short screen-based morning, a people-centered afternoon, and families and students heard early Lesson A personalized morning must stay short, and the rest of the day must be with other people

docs.title: A Pilot Risk Checklist
docs.text:
A pilot risk checklist is a short list of the main risks that a pilot must be checked against, each with a named response, before the pilot starts. It turns the cases of this chapter into a tool. It has one line for each of the seven risks the course description names.

Risk What the pilot must have Check Screen time A cap on morning screen time and breaks (Chapter 12) A schedule with the cap Handing thinking over to AI Hint-first tutoring and assessments that show process (Chapters 12, 20) A test of the tutor's first reply Wrong AI answers Grounding in vetted content and checks by tools (Chapter 12) A log review plan Privacy Data minimization, governance, and a contract with the checklist terms (Chapters 10, 21) A signed data agreement Cost and equity Devices, a free afternoon, and subgroup monitoring (Chapters 20, 21) A gap report by subgroup Fear of job loss A written statement of the teacher's role and a coaching plan (Chapter 19) A document shared with staff Unstructured afternoon SAFE practices and trained adults (Chapter 14) An afternoon quality rating

docs.title: Worked Example: Finding the Gap in a Plan
docs.text:
A district shows Ms. Okafor a pilot plan. She reads it against the checklist.

Risk The plan says Covered? Screen time "Morning screens capped at 120 minutes, with breaks" Yes Handing thinking over "Tutor gives hints first; assessments include a process portfolio" Yes Wrong answers Nothing No Privacy "Data agreement signed; retention schedule attached" Yes Cost and equity "Loaner devices; subgroup report each term" Yes Fear of job loss "Roles statement shared with staff" Yes Unstructured afternoon "Afternoon rated by the SAFE practices" Yes

The plan is strong, and it has one hole: nothing says what happens when the tutor is wrong. She asks the district to add a log review and a check on the tutor's math before the pilot starts.
