docs.title: What the Cases Say Together
docs.text:
Read together, the five cases say five things. A structure with an adaptive morning and a people-centered afternoon can work, but at private-school prices (Alpha). The software does not carry the results by itself (Unbound). How the AI is designed decides help or harm (Turkey, Harvard). A technology-led personalized model that crowds out people loses trust fast (Summit). And the way to read any such story is to name its benefit, its risk, its response, and its lesson.

The evidence behind them is uneven, which is itself a lesson: the strongest studies, the randomized ones, concern tutors, and the evidence for whole-school models is self-reported or early. The honest reading is that the components have support and the package is still being tested.

The story of this chapter has both sides, like all the stories in this book. The benefit: real cases that make the argument concrete and keep it honest. The risks: reading a case as proof, quoting a figure that has not been checked, and treating a composite as a real person. The response is the framework and the habit: source every real case, label every composite, and pair every benefit with its risk.

A case is a story, not a result

A common trap is treating one vivid case, in either direction, as proof. One school's success doesn't show the model works elsewhere, and one failure doesn't show it can't. Ask what kind of evidence the case rests on, what the source is, and what would have to be true for it to apply to your school.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Storytelling helps understanding, and the book separates the real case study (sourced), the composite story (labeled, fictional), and the illustrated story.
  • The risk-and-response framework reads each case as benefit, risk, response, and lesson from a case, in service of strengthening the positives and reducing the negatives through risk mitigation (avoid, reduce, transfer, accept).
  • The benefits of AI-first schools are own-pace learning and time for people; the risks are screen time, handing thinking over, wrong answers, privacy, cost and equity gaps, fear of job loss, and unstructured afternoons.
  • Alpha School runs 2 Hour Learning with Alpha adult guides, at an Alpha tuition range of about $40,000 to $65,000; Unbound Academy uses the same software without the afternoon, which shows that software is not the model.
  • The Turkish high school study (about 17 percent worse on later exams with open access; hints removed most of the harm) and the Harvard physics AI tutor show design over raw AI power.
  • Summit Learning is the clearest screen-time cautionary case.
  • The pilot risk checklist has one line per risk, and two-to-three-hour learning is a plausible and still unproven claim for the whole package.

You can read a story the way the book does

You just learned to sort real cases from composites, to read each case as a benefit, a risk, a response, and a lesson, and to check a pilot plan against seven risks. Chapter 23 continues with the rest of the stories and their lessons. One step at a time, together.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: AI-First Case Studies I: Promise and Peril
docs.text: Test your understanding of how to read real cases about AI in schools, including Alpha School, Unbound Academy, the Turkish and Harvard studies, and Summit Learning, with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. What tuition does the chapter report for Alpha School?
docs.text:
1. About $40,000 a year in Austin and about $65,000 at newer campuses
  2. About $65,000 a year at every campus in the network
  3. About $15,600 a year, the same as public per-pupil spending
  4. About $40,000 a year at newer campuses and about $65,000 in Austin
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Alpha School charges about $40,000 a year at its original Austin campus and about $65,000 a year at newer campuses such as Boston, Miami, and New York. The chapter stresses that each figure applies to its own campuses and that the higher figure should not be given as the price for every campus. The fourth option reverses the two. Compared with public per-pupil spending of about $15,600, the tuition is about 2.6 to 4.2 times as much.

Concept Tested: Alpha Tuition Range

See: Case 1: Alpha School

docs.title: 2. According to the chapter, when is a composite story, such as the story of Maya and Lincoln Middle School, honest?
docs.text:
1. When its outcomes match the results of a published study
  2. When it includes a real student's name and the name of the school
  3. When it is told with images as an illustrated story
  4. When it is clearly labeled as fiction, not passed off as a real case
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. A composite story is a fictional account assembled from patterns in many real situations, with invented characters, used to make an idea concrete. The chapter says it is honest when labeled and dishonest when passed off as a real case, and that no quotation or outcome attached to a composite should be taken as fact about a real person. Adding a real name would make it misleading. An illustrated story can be real or composite, so images do not decide honesty.

Concept Tested: Composite Story

See: How the Book Uses Stories

docs.title: 3. To manage the risk of a vendor data breach, a district buys cyber insurance and adds a contract clause making the vendor responsible for breach costs. Which form of risk mitigation is this?
docs.text:
1. Avoid
  2. Accept
  3. Transfer
  4. Reduce
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. The chapter names four forms of risk mitigation: avoid the risk entirely, reduce its likelihood or harm, transfer it (for example, to an insurer or through a contract), or accept it knowingly. Insurance and a contract clause shift the cost of a breach to others, which is transfer. Data minimization or multi-factor authentication would reduce the risk, not transfer it. Not using the product at all would avoid it. A school chooses among the four for each risk.

Concept Tested: Risk Mitigation

See: A Framework for Reading Cases

docs.title: 4. Unbound Academy uses Alpha School's 2 Hour Learning software but without the in-person afternoon. What principle does the book draw from comparing the two?
docs.text:
1. Software is not the model: adults, projects, and people produced the results too
  2. Online schools always outperform in-person schools when they use the same software
  3. The software works only when students pay tuition, which raises motivation
  4. Two hours of software is too little, so the morning should be lengthened
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The same software, used without the adult guides and the in-person afternoon, did not carry over its results: Unbound's early reported proficiency was below state averages. The book calls this principle "software is not the model." A school that buys the software and omits the afternoon has bought a fraction of what it saw. The chapter does not claim online schools do better, and it does not attribute the difference to tuition or the length of the morning.

Concept Tested: Software Is Not the Model

See: Case 2: Unbound Academy and the Software Is Not the Model

docs.title: 5. A pilot plan includes a 120-minute morning screen cap, a hint-first tutor, a signed data agreement, loaner devices with subgroup reports, a teacher roles statement, and a weekly review of tutor logs for errors. Checked against the chapter's pilot risk checklist, which risk is not covered?
docs.text:
1. Wrong AI answers
  2. Unstructured afternoon
  3. Handing thinking over to AI
  4. Fear of job loss
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The checklist has one line for each of the seven risks the course description names: screen time, handing thinking over to AI, wrong AI answers, privacy, cost and equity, fear of job loss, and unstructured afternoons. The plan covers the first six, including wrong answers through the log review, but says nothing about the afternoon. The checklist requires the SAFE practices and trained adults, checked with an afternoon quality rating, before the pilot starts.

Concept Tested: Pilot Risk Checklist

See: A Pilot Risk Checklist

docs.title: 6. The Turkish high school study found harm from open chatbot access, while the Harvard physics study found benefit from a designed AI tutor. What does the chapter conclude from reading them together, and what limit applies?
docs.text:
1. AI tutors work for college students but harm high school students, so ages should be separated
  2. More powerful models help and weaker ones harm, so schools should buy the strongest model
  3. Both studies prove a compressed morning works for all students in every setting
  4. How the AI is designed decides help or harm, but each study covers only one setting
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The Turkish study used the same model in each condition, and the hint-first version removed most of the harm; the Harvard tutor was built on proven teaching practices rather than as an open chatbot. Together they show design over raw AI power. Both are randomized, but each has limits: the Turkish study covers one school and short-term math, and the Harvard study one course at one university with well-prepared students. The first option confuses setting with design.

Concept Tested: Design Over Raw AI Power

See: Case 4: The Harvard Physics AI Tutor

docs.title: 7. Reading Summit Learning with the risk-and-response framework, which risk does the case most clearly show?
docs.text:
1. Screen time and too little contact with teachers
  2. Wrong AI answers delivered with confidence
  3. Fear of job loss among teachers
  4. Privacy breaches of student data
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. In 2018 and 2019 students in Brooklyn walked out and families in Kansas protested Summit Learning over long hours on screens and too little contact with teachers. The appendix calls it the clearest real example of the screen-time risk. The case shows a technology-led model without a human afternoon, in which students felt isolated and families lost trust. It is the reason the book keeps the morning short and the afternoon social, and hears students and families early.

Concept Tested: Summit Learning

See: Case 5: Summit Learning

docs.title: 8. A district gives students an open chat tutor for homework. Homework scores rise, but teachers notice that unit test scores without the tutor fall. The district switches to a hint-first tutor and adds in-class assessments that show process. How should this story be entered in the risk-and-response framework?
docs.text:
1. Benefit: lower costs. Risk: privacy. Response: a data agreement. Lesson: contracts.
  2. Benefit: higher scores. Risk: screen time. Response: shorter sessions. Lesson: limits.
  3. Benefit: better homework. Risk: offloaded thinking. Response: hint-first tutor. Lesson: design.
  4. Benefit: time saved. Risk: job loss. Response: a roles statement. Lesson: reassure.
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. The framework has four columns: the story's benefit, the risk it also shows, the response, and the lesson. Here the benefit is better homework performance, the risk is handing thinking over to AI, shown by falling scores without the tool, the response is a hint-first tutor and process-based assessment, and the lesson matches the Turkish study: design matters more than power. The other options name risks the story does not show; in this story, test scores fell rather than rose.

Concept Tested: Risk-and-Response Framework

See: A Framework for Reading Cases

docs.title: 9. Unbound Academy reportedly showed about 10 percent of students proficient in math and 28 percent in English language arts, while claiming students learn 2.8 times faster on its own growth tests. The reports do not say where students started. What can a careful reader conclude?
docs.text:
1. The program clearly works, since students learn 2.8 times faster
  2. The program clearly fails, since proficiency is far below the state average
  3. The program works for English but not for math, based on the two scores
  4. Little about the program's effect, without baselines and independent evaluation
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Proficiency shows where students stand at one moment, not how much they grew, and the reports give no starting points. The 2.8-times figure comes from the school's own growth tests, a self-reported result. The chapter's response is to hold claims to the evidence standard of Chapter 2: ask for starting points and an independent evaluation. Concluding that it clearly works or clearly fails reads more into the figures than they support.

Concept Tested: Unbound Academy

See: Case 2: Unbound Academy and the Software Is Not the Model

docs.title: 10. At a board meeting, a member says, "Alpha School proves the two-hour model works. We should adopt it district-wide next year." Which response is best supported by the chapter's reading of the cases?
docs.text:
1. Agree, since Alpha's success shows the model will work at any price and in any school
  2. Disagree in part: Alpha's results are self-reported, so pilot with independent evaluation
  3. Disagree completely, since Unbound's results prove the model cannot work in public schools
  4. Agree, as long as the district buys the same adaptive software that Alpha uses
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The chapter's honest reading is that the components have support while the package is still being tested: the strongest randomized evidence concerns tutors, and the evidence for whole-school models is self-reported or early. Alpha's results come from the school, with no independent evaluation in the book's sources, and at private-school prices. The chapter warns against treating one vivid case as proof in either direction, so Unbound does not prove failure, and buying the software alone ignores that software is not the model.

Concept Tested: Real Case Study

See: What the Cases Say Together

docs.title: References: AI-First Case Studies I: Promise and Peril
docs.text:
1. Alpha School - Wikipedia - An overview of the private school network founded in Austin in 2014 that uses "2 Hour Learning" software with adult guides. It notes that the school's result claims rely on internal analyses that have not been independently verified.

  2. Intelligent Tutoring System - Wikipedia - Explains computer systems that give learners tailored instruction and feedback, and the long research history behind them. Background for judging the AI tutors in the Turkish and Harvard studies.

  3. Case Study - Wikipedia - Describes the case study as a detailed look at one real organization or event in its setting, with its strengths and limits. It helps readers see what a single school's story can and cannot prove.

  4. Failure to Disrupt: Why Technology Alone Can't Transform Education - Justin Reich - Harvard University Press - Reich is credited with showing that new learning technologies tend to be absorbed into existing school routines and to benefit already-advantaged students. His argument is a lens for reading every case in this chapter.

  5. Oversold and Underused: Computers in the Classroom - Larry Cuban - Harvard University Press - Cuban is credited with documenting the gap between heavy technology spending and modest change in classroom teaching. His work explains why software alone is not the model and why the adults matter.

  6. What Public Schools and Parents Can Learn from a $40,000-a-Year Private School - The 74 - A January 2026 opinion piece on Alpha School's reported growth results and mastery approach. It also lists concerns: high tuition, an advantaged student body, small samples and unlicensed guides. The author discloses an NWEA advisory role.

  7. Inside the $65K "AI-Powered" Private School Coming to Massachusetts - NBC Boston - September 2026 coverage of Alpha's new Greater Boston campuses, where tuition is higher than the original Austin campus. Justin Reich warns that students cannot learn to deliberate with neighbors while alone at a computer.

  8. Tucson Families Join Free AI-Powered Online School - KOLD 13 News - August 2026 report on Unbound Academy, Arizona's online charter that uses a two-hour AI academic block. It notes that several other states rejected the school, and that its learning-speed claims are the school's own.

  9. Without Guardrails, Generative AI Can Harm Education - Knowledge at Wharton - A summary of the Turkish high school math study of about 1,000 students. Unrestricted ChatGPT helped practice but hurt exam scores, while a tutor with guardrails avoided the harm, showing design matters more than raw AI power.

  10. An AI Tutor Helped Harvard Students Learn More Physics in Less Time - KQED MindShift (from The Hechinger Report) - Jill Barshay's account of the Harvard physics AI tutor study, with its caveats: fewer than 200 Harvard students, a carefully designed tutor, and no claim that AI should replace instructors.

docs.title: AI-First Case Studies II: Lessons for Practice
Summary
docs.text: This chapter presents a second set of cases focused on lessons for practice: AltSchool, Summit Learning, the Los Angeles iPad rollout and "Ed" chatbot, and other cautionary and positive examples, closing with how to evaluate result claims and make a recommendation to a school board. Readers finish able to use a past failure or success to write a risk checklist for a new pilot.

docs.title: The Vote
docs.text:
The board will vote next month, and Ms. Okafor has been asked to make a recommendation. She has the evidence, the design, the plan, the contract, and the pilot rule. What she does not yet have is the thing a board member will want most: some sense of what happens to districts that do this badly, and what the ones that did it well had in common.

This final chapter collects the cases that answer that question, and then turns them into practice. It covers the failures, which supply the strongest risk checklist the book can offer, the successes and the both-sided cases, and the habits for reading any claim a vendor or a school makes. It ends with the capstone task of the whole book: writing a recommendation to a school board that is honest about both sides.

As in Chapter 22, the facts come from the book's AI-First Stories appendix and its sources, and the same caution applies: many of these stories are still unfolding, some figures come from news coverage, preprints, and schools' own claims, and several accounts in the appendix are marked as still needing source checks. Before any number here is quoted, check it against the original.

What the failures can teach

This is the book's last chapter, and it's the one that turns stories into a recommendation. You'll read the failures for what they'd have caught with the checklists you already have, then write a board recommendation that names both sides. Let's find the balance between learning from what went wrong and not being frozen by it.

docs.title: The Los Angeles iPad Rollout
docs.text: The LAUSD iPad rollout began in 2013, when the Los Angeles Unified School District started a $1.3 billion plan to give every student an iPad loaded with curriculum from Pearson. The plan was cancelled amid technical problems, weak curriculum, and a scandal over how the contract was awarded. The lesson is that buying devices before having a plan for teaching wastes money and public trust. It is also an edtech hype wave (Chapter 15) in miniature: an announcement at the peak of expectations, and a cancellation in the trough.

docs.title: The Los Angeles "Ed" Chatbot and the AllHere Collapse
docs.text:
A decade later, the same district made a different mistake. The LAUSD Ed chatbot was an AI assistant for students and families, built by a startup called AllHere. The district committed about $6 million to the company and spent about $3 million before the AllHere collapse: the company folded within months of the chatbot's launch. In November 2024, its founder was charged with defrauding investors of nearly $10 million. In 2026, the FBI searched the home and office of the district's superintendent in an investigation reported to be connected to AllHere; as the appendix notes, he has not been charged with a crime. The case is still developing, and the facts should be checked against current reporting.

What is clear from the facts already established is the pattern of rushed procurement risk and vendor risk from Chapters 10 and 21: a large commitment to an unproven company, student data sent to a vendor that did not survive, and no check on the vendor's financial health. The lesson the appendix draws is that schools need procurement rules before they buy AI products, such as those based on the five-level model.

docs.title: AltSchool
docs.text: AltSchool was a network of "personalized learning" microschools in the San Francisco area and elsewhere, launched in 2013 and run on its own software. It raised more than $170 million, closed its schools within a few years, and shifted to selling its software to other schools. Its lesson is that personalization led by technology, without a lasting school culture and community, does not last. It is the Software Is Not the Model principle of Chapter 22 from another direction: even a well-funded team with its own software could not make the model work without the culture around it.

docs.title: Summit Learning and the Student Walkouts
docs.text: Chapter 22 introduced Summit Learning. The student walkouts are the part of that story most relevant to practice: in 2018 and 2019, students in Brooklyn walked out of school and families in Kansas protested, complaining about long hours on screens and too little contact with teachers. The lesson for a school leader is about student voice (Chapter 19): the students themselves told the district, loudly, what was not working, and a school that had asked them earlier would have heard it earlier.

docs.title: inBloom and the PowerSchool Data Breach
docs.text: Two cases concern data (Chapter 10). inBloom was a $100 million project, funded by the Gates Foundation, to store and share student data across states. It closed in 2014 after parents objected on privacy grounds. Its lesson is that any xAPI and Learning Record Store system needs the trust of families from the start, with clear rules about who owns and controls the data. The PowerSchool data breach came in December 2024, when a breach at one of the largest student information system vendors exposed the records of tens of millions of students and teachers. It makes the Level 3 privacy threshold concrete: the more centralized the records, the bigger the target.

docs.title: The Stanford Detector Study
docs.text: The Stanford detector study, by Weixin Liang and colleagues in 2023, found that popular AI-writing detectors often wrongly flagged essays by non-native English writers as written by AI. It is the evidence behind Chapter 20's advice to redesign assignments and not to rely on detection, since fighting AI with detection can create its own equity problem.

docs.title: Worked Example: The Failures and the Practice That Would Have Caught Them
docs.text: Case What failed Practice that would have helped Chapter LAUSD iPad rollout (2013) Devices bought before a teaching plan; a contract scandal A readiness assessment, a pilot, and procurement criteria 20, 21 LAUSD Ed chatbot and AllHere (2024) A large commitment to an unproven vendor Vendor evaluation, a knockout rule on viability, and staged payments 20, 21 AltSchool (2013–2019) Technology without a lasting culture Culture assessment and capacity building 18, 21 Summit Learning (2018–2019) Long screen hours, little contact with teachers Screen limits, a people-centered afternoon, and student voice 12, 14, 19 inBloom (2014) Families did not trust a central data store Informed consent, data ownership, and minimization 10 PowerSchool (2024) One vendor held very many records Minimization, retention limits, and vendor risk checks 10, 21 AI detectors (2023) False accusations, biased against ELL writers Redesign, not policing 20

docs.text:

Which Lesson Does the Failure Teach?

Type: microsim sim-id: which-lesson-does-failure-teach Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: classify Learning Objective: The learner will classify seven real failures as teaching one of seven lessons, correctly matching at least six of seven on the first attempt.

Misconceptions: (1) All the failures show the same mistake. (2) Technology failures are caused by weak technology. (3) A data failure is a security failure only.

Instructional Rationale: Matching each failure to the lesson it teaches requires understanding the cause, not just the name. Cases that look alike, such as the two Los Angeles programs, make the learner separate planning from vendor choice.

Seven lessons, shown as bins. The labels L1 to L7 are for this specification only; the learner sees each lesson's short form.

Lesson Short form L1 Plan the teaching before buying devices L2 Set procurement rules and check a vendor's survival L3 Technology without a lasting culture does not last L4 Listen to students about screens and contact with teachers L5 Earn family trust and make data ownership clear L6 Centralized records are a large target; hold less L7 Redesign assessment instead of relying on detectors

Seven failures:

# Failure shown to the learner Correct lesson Why (shown as feedback) 1 A district announced a $1.3 billion plan to give every student an iPad, and cancelled it amid technical problems and weak curriculum. L1 The devices came before the teaching plan. 2 A district committed about $6 million to an AI chatbot startup that collapsed within months. L2 There were no procurement rules or checks on the vendor's survival. 3 A well-funded network of personalized microschools closed its schools within a few years and sold its software instead. L3 The technology had no lasting culture around it. 4 Students walked out and families protested over long screen hours and too little contact with teachers. Provenance: The cases and lessons come from the book's AI-First Stories appendix and Chapters 10, 20, and 21, and the sim must say "Check figures against the sources." The lessons' short forms are this book's wording.

Rules: Each failure has exactly one correct lesson, given in Content, and each lesson has exactly one failure. A failure is scored on its first submitted placement only. The score counts first-attempt correct placements out of 7. Mastery is a score >= 6.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees one failure at a time and the seven lessons.
  2. The learner places the failure and submits it. The sim marks it correct or incorrect and shows the feedback text.
  3. If incorrect, the learner may place it again; the second attempt does not change the score. After the second attempt, the correct lesson and reason are shown.
  4. After all 7 failures, the sim shows the score and the pairs.
  5. The learner should notice that each failure matches a practice from an earlier chapter.

Feedback: 7 failures, shuffled once per session, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: [lesson]. [Why text]." Incorrect: "Not quite. Ask what caused the failure. [Why text for the correct answer, without naming the lesson]." After the second attempt the correct lesson is revealed and the failure counts as missed. A running score "First-try correct: n of 7" is shown. Final message for a score >= 6: "You can say what each failure teaches." For a score < 6: "Review the seven cases and try again; the failures will be reshuffled."

Starting State: Failure 1 of the shuffled order is shown with the seven lessons, the score "First-try correct: 0 of 7," and the prompt "Which lesson does this failure teach?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's table pairs the iPad rollout, the Ed chatbot, AltSchool, the Summit walkouts, inBloom, the PowerSchool breach, and the AI detectors with the seven lessons in that order. The mastery bar is 6 of 7.

docs.title: Why School Reforms Fail
docs.text:
Why school reforms fail is the question that the failures above answer together. Looking across them, four causes recur. Technology came before pedagogy: the iPad rollout and AltSchool began with the tool, and not with the learning. The grammar of schooling and the culture absorbed the change: a reform that did not alter the work of teaching left the structure in place (Chapter 18). Trust was not built: inBloom and Summit lost the families and students on whom they depended. And the hype outran the evidence: the announcements at the peak of expectations were followed by the trough (Chapter 15). The same four causes are the reason that the book's answer to each is a practice, from culture assessment to student voice to pilots, and not a technology.

The failures were mostly not about the technology

A common trap is reading these cases as "the technology wasn't good enough," which suggests waiting for better technology. Mostly the technology worked as designed; what failed was planning, trust, procurement, culture, and listening. Better AI will not fix those, and the book's checklists will.

docs.title: Cases That Worked and Cases With Both Sides
docs.text:
The positive and both-sided cases show the other half of the pattern, and each has its own limits.

The Nigeria AI tutoring pilot was a six-week after-school program in Edo State, Nigeria, in 2024, in which students used a GPT-4-based tutor to practice English with teachers in the room. The World Bank team reported large learning gains for a very small cost per student. The lesson is that low-cost AI tutoring with a teacher present can help where resources are scarce, and the caution is that it is a short pilot in one setting.

Tutor CoPilot, a Stanford study from 2024, gave human tutors live AI suggestions during their sessions instead of replacing them. Students' mastery improved, the weakest tutors improved the most, and the cost per tutor for a year was small. The lesson is that AI works well when it makes people better at helping students, which supports the AI-coaching-teachers idea of Chapter 21.

The Estonia AI Leap, a 2025 national program, gave secondary students and teachers access to AI learning tools along with teacher training, building on the country's earlier success bringing computers into schools. The lesson is that a school system can adopt AI on purpose, with a plan, training, and public support, though the results are not yet known (Chapter 18).

High Tech High, the San Diego network of project-based charter schools (Chapter 14), shows the pro-social afternoon working as a whole school's design, with driving questions and public exhibitions. Finland's phenomenon learning is the national requirement for multidisciplinary, phenomenon-based modules. El Sistema, the Venezuelan youth orchestra program, is the model of group music-making. Together the three are the proof, the appendix says, that the afternoon half of the AI-native day is already proven. Each has detractors and uneven evidence, as Chapter 14 noted.

The both-sided cases carry a benefit and a risk in one story. David Game College, in London, opened in 2024 what was described as the UK's first GCSE class taught mainly by AI, with learning coaches in place of traditional teachers; it shows the idea spreading, and the same open question as Alpha, which is how much of the result comes from the software and how much from the adults. Khanmigo, Khan Academy's AI tutor, built to guide students with questions and not answers, has been rolled out in many districts since 2023; early versions made math mistakes, and students in some districts used it less than expected, a reminder that even careful design meets the reality of classroom use. Your Brain on ChatGPT, a 2025 MIT Media Lab study, found that students who wrote essays with ChatGPT showed lower brain engagement in EEG readings and remembered less of what they wrote; it was small and is still a preprint, so it supports the risk of handing thinking over without proving its size.

docs.title: Evaluating Result Claims
docs.text:
Evaluating result claims is the habit of testing any statement about what a school, program, or product achieved before believing it or repeating it. It draws together Chapters 2 and 3: the evidence levels, effect sizes, self-reported versus independent results, and preprints. Six questions do most of the work.

Question What it exposes Where did the students start? A result with no baseline says nothing about growth Compared with whom? Without a comparison group, a gain may be ordinary growth Who measured it, and who paid? Self-reported results are produced by someone with a stake Has anyone outside checked it? Peer review or independent evaluation raises trust How big, and for how long? A tiny or very short study may not hold up What was actually measured? Satisfaction or usage is not learning

Apply them to the claims in the cases. Unbound Academy's reported proficiency of 10 percent in math came with no starting point, so it says nothing about how much students grew. Its claim that students learn 2.8 times faster is measured on its own growth tests, which are self-reported. The Nigerian pilot and the Harvard study are randomized, which answers "compared with whom," though each has a short duration and a narrow setting. The MIT study answers "has anyone outside checked it" with "not yet," since it is a preprint with a small sample.

Ask the Right Question

Type: microsim sim-id: ask-the-right-question Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: classify Learning Objective: The learner will classify six result claims by the question that best exposes the weakness in each, correctly matching at least five of six on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: the six questions for evaluating result claims (defined in the section "Evaluating Result Claims" above), and Chapters 2 and 3.

Evidence of Mastery: The learner places each of 6 claims in one of six question bins and submits it. A placement is correct when it matches the "Best question" column in Content. Mastery is 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt. Reading the question list is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Any claim with a number is evidence. (2) One question is enough for every claim. (3) A strong result needs no questions.

Instructional Rationale: Choosing the best question requires finding what is missing from the claim: a starting point, a comparison, an independent measure, an outside check, a size, or the thing measured. Each claim is built to be missing one of these.

Content:

Six questions, shown as bins:

Question Where did the students start? Compared with whom? Who measured it, and who paid? Has anyone outside checked it? How big, and for how long? What was actually measured?

Six claims:

# Claim shown to the learner Best question Why (shown as feedback) 1 "Our students learn 2.8 times faster, according to our own growth tests." Who measured it, and who paid? The school's own tests are self-reported. 2 "Only 10 percent of our students are proficient in math now, but we will reach 90 percent in three years." Where did the students start? Without a starting point, neither the present figure nor the target shows growth. 3 "Our students did very well on the end-of-year exam." Compared with whom? [Why text for the correct answer, without naming the question]." After the second attempt the correct question is revealed and the claim counts as missed. A running score "First-try correct: n of 6" is shown. Final message for a score >= 5: "You can find the question that exposes a claim." For a score < 5: "Review the six questions and try again; the claims will be reshuffled."

docs.title: The Affordable Alpha Model
docs.text: The book's capstone design question is the one Alpha's tuition poses: can the structure of a short adaptive morning and a people-centered afternoon be offered to every student at a public school's budget? The affordable Alpha model is this book's answer, the design that has been built up over the chapters: open Level 2 and Level 3 textbooks and MicroSims instead of costly live AI for every student (Chapters 6 to 9), selective use of a guarded chatbot (Chapter 12), the structured afternoon (Chapter 14), and a governed pilot (Chapters 20 and 21). It keeps what Unbound lacked, the in-person afternoon with adults, and avoids what makes Alpha unaffordable, tuition-level pricing for software and staffing.

docs.title: Worked Example: The Added Cost per Student
docs.text:
The table adds the illustrative figures of earlier chapters for the incremental cost per student per year of a 12,000-student district, with devices already owned.

Item Per student per year Source Level 4 textbook with selective chatbot use, including records, governance, training, and guardrail review $17.24 Chapters 7 and 12 Afternoon specialists: 20 full-time at $60,000 each, for 12,000 students $100.00 Chapter 21 New cost $117.24 Less the print-textbook baseline −$53.33 Chapter 7 Net added cost about $64

Net of the print savings, the model adds about $64 per student per year to a public budget of about $15,600 per student, a rise of about 0.4 percent. Alpha's tuition is $40,000 to $65,000. A fair comparison needs a caution: the tuition pays for an entire school, and the $64 is only the increment on top of existing public spending, so the right comparison is a public school at about $15,664 per student against a private school at $40,000 to $65,000. The figures are illustrative and exclude devices, facilities, and transportation. The model's trade-offs are real: the afternoon staffing is the largest piece, results depend on execution, and nobody has yet shown with independent evidence that this particular package matches the outcomes Alpha reports.

docs.title: Stories That Teach: Two-Sided Stories and Graphic Novel Scenes
docs.text:
Chapter 22 distinguished real cases from composite and illustrated stories. Two forms matter for practice.

A two-sided story is a short composite story that shows, in one narrative, a benefit growing stronger and a risk being reduced, with the school's response. It is the course description's capstone: a story of about 1,500 words about one day in an AI-native school, with a one-page commentary that links it to the risk-and-response framework. It is useful because it makes the framework concrete for families and staff who will not read a table. A graphic novel scene is an illustrated story told in panels, which suits the visual learner, a short scene such as a student, a tutor, and a teacher working through a moment.

docs.title: Worked Example: A Two-Sided Story in Miniature
docs.text:
Maya and the Hint. On Tuesday morning, Maya is stuck on a unit-rate problem and asks the tutor for the answer. The tutor, which gives hints first, asks her what the problem is asking. Annoyed, she tries twice, then gets a hint about which number to divide, and solves it. (The benefit: her own pace and a patient tutor, available when no teacher is.) That afternoon, Ms. Rivera reads the weekly log and sees that on Friday the tutor, because of a configuration slip, gave a student the answer on the first request. (The risk: an answer-giving tutor.) She flags it, the vendor fixes it within a day, and the school adds a check of the tutor's first reply to its weekly routine. (The response.) On Friday Maya presents the problem she solved to her team. (The positive strengthened.)

The four parts, benefit, risk, response, and strengthened positive, are the whole structure. A graphic novel scene would show the same moment as six panels: Maya frowning at the screen, the tutor's question, her second try, the hint, her "oh!", and the team presentation.

docs.title: The Recommendation to the Board
docs.text:
A school board recommendation is the document and presentation in which a leader asks the board to take a decision, here whether to approve the pilot, the contract, or the scale-up. It is the book's last practical task. A good recommendation has seven parts:

  1. The recommendation itself, stated in one sentence, such as "Approve a one-year pilot of the model in two schools, with a written decision rule for scaling."
  2. The case, in three or four sentences: the problem (learning gaps, Chapter 1), the opportunity, and the vision.
  3. The evidence, with its level: what is strong (randomized tutoring studies), what is early or self-reported (whole-school claims), and what is unknown (Chapter 2's questions).
  4. The risks and responses, in the framework's form, using the pilot risk checklist.
  5. The equity analysis: who benefits, who might be left behind, and how gaps will be monitored (Chapter 21).
  6. The cost, with the total cost of ownership and where the money comes from (Chapters 7 and 21).
  7. The decision rule and timeline: what will be measured, when the board will see results, and what would make the district stop, extend, or scale (Chapter 20).

docs.title: Worked Example: A One-Page Recommendation Outline
docs.text:
Part Lincoln's recommendation Recommendation Approve a one-year pilot of the Level 3 morning and the structured afternoon in two schools The case Only 13 of 28 students are reached by one lesson; the model could reach more and free time for people Evidence Randomized studies support designed AI tutors; whole-school claims are self-reported; our pilot will be independently scored Risks and responses The seven-risk checklist, with responses, attached Equity Devices lent; free afternoon; gap reported by subgroup each term Cost About $64 per student net of print savings, plus devices; sources listed Decision rule Scale if gain >= 0.15 SD, workload not up more than 2 hours, satisfaction at least 70 percent; stop on a serious privacy incident or a harmed subgroup

A recommendation is a promise to measure

Notice what the best recommendation does: it doesn't ask the board to believe, it asks the board to test and promises to report honestly. That's the same habit as the whole book, applied to a decision: name the evidence, name the risks, and say in advance what would change your mind.

docs.title: What the Whole Book Comes To
docs.text:
The book began with a prediction: that within three to four years almost every student could have access to a free, high-quality, interactive, adaptive textbook, and that schools would then have to decide what to do with the time that frees. Its answer was mornings with AI, afternoons with each other. Along the way it has said, each time, what the evidence supports and what it does not.

The cases of these last two chapters carry the same two-sided message. The model's components have support: adaptive pacing, mastery learning, well-designed AI tutors, project-based afternoons, and the open, low-cost Level 2 and Level 3 textbooks that make it affordable. The package as a whole is still being tested, the cautionary cases show how it fails when technology comes before people, and nothing in the evidence guarantees success. The book's goal, in the words of the course description, is to strengthen the positives and reduce the negatives, and the way to do that is the one this chapter has practiced: read every story for its benefit and its risk, ask the six questions of every claim, borrow the lessons of the failures, pilot before scaling, and tell families and boards the truth.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• The failures mostly show planning, trust, culture, and procurement failing, not technology: the LAUSD iPad rollout (devices before a teaching plan), the LAUSD Ed chatbot and AllHere collapse (an unchecked vendor), AltSchool (no lasting culture), Student walkouts at Summit Learning (listen to students), inBloom (family trust), the PowerSchool data breach (centralized records), and the Stanford detector study (redesign, not policing).
  • Why school reforms fail: technology before pedagogy, the culture absorbing the change, trust not built, and hype outrunning evidence.
  • The Nigeria AI tutoring pilot, Tutor CoPilot, Estonia's AI Leap, High Tech High, Finland's phenomenon learning, and El Sistema show what can work; David Game College, Khanmigo, and Your Brain on ChatGPT carry a benefit and a risk together.
  • Evaluating result claims uses six questions: where did students start, compared with whom, who measured it, has anyone checked it, how big and how long, and what was measured.
  • The affordable Alpha model adds about $64 per student per year net of print savings in our illustration, against Alpha's $40,000 to $65,000 tuition, with the afternoon staffing as the main cost and the full package still unproven.
  • A two-sided story and a graphic novel scene make the framework concrete; a school board recommendation states the ask, the case, the evidence with its level, the risks and responses, the equity analysis, the cost, and the decision rule.

You've finished the book, and you can make the case

You just learned to read the failures for what they'd have caught, test every claim with six questions, price the affordable model, and write a board recommendation that names both sides. That's the whole book: evidence, design, change, and the honesty to say what's still unknown. One step at a time, together.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: AI-First Case Studies II: Lessons for Practice
docs.text: Test your understanding of what past failures and successes teach, how to evaluate result claims, the affordable Alpha model, and how to make an honest recommendation to a school board with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. What is the main lesson the chapter draws from the 2013 Los Angeles iPad rollout?
docs.text:
1. Tablets are too fragile for daily use by students in large districts
  2. A district should buy devices from several vendors rather than one
  3. Buying devices before having a plan for teaching wastes money and public trust
  4. Curriculum from a single publisher is always weaker than open content
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. LAUSD started a $1.3 billion plan to give every student an iPad loaded with Pearson curriculum, and it was cancelled amid technical problems, weak curriculum, and a scandal over the contract award. The lesson is that buying devices before a teaching plan wastes money and trust. The chapter also calls it an edtech hype wave in miniature, announced at the peak and cancelled in the trough. Its matching practices are a readiness assessment, a pilot, and procurement criteria.

Concept Tested: LAUSD iPad Rollout

See: The Los Angeles iPad Rollout

docs.title: 2. Looking across the failures in this chapter, what does the book conclude about why school reforms fail?
docs.text:
1. The technology was not good enough, so schools should wait for better AI
  2. Mostly not technology: pedagogy came second, trust was not built, hype outran evidence
  3. Reforms fail mainly because teacher unions block them during contract negotiations
  4. Reforms fail because school boards approve far too few pilots each year
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The chapter names four recurring causes: technology came before pedagogy (the iPad rollout, AltSchool), the grammar of schooling and culture absorbed the change, trust was not built (inBloom, Summit), and hype outran the evidence. It warns against reading the cases as "the technology wasn't good enough," which suggests waiting for better technology. Mostly the technology worked as designed; planning, trust, procurement, culture, and listening failed, and better AI will not fix those.

Concept Tested: Why School Reforms Fail

See: Why School Reforms Fail

docs.title: 3. A vendor's brochure says, "92 percent of teachers report that students love our AI tutor." Which of the chapter's six questions most directly exposes the weakness of this claim?
docs.text:
1. Where did the students start?
  2. Compared with whom?
  3. How big, and for how long?
  4. What was actually measured?
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The claim reports teacher satisfaction, and the chapter's sixth question, "What was actually measured?", exposes that satisfaction or usage is not learning. The other questions also matter but do not target the core problem here: a baseline and a comparison group would be needed to judge any gain, yet this claim does not even measure a gain. Chapter 2's evidence levels place satisfaction surveys in the bin of claims that show no evidence of effect.

Concept Tested: Evaluating Result Claims

See: Evaluating Result Claims

docs.title: 4. A district is about to make a large commitment to a young AI startup with an impressive demo. Which practice from the chapter's failure table would most directly have prevented the LAUSD Ed chatbot loss?
docs.text:
1. Screen-time limits and a people-centered afternoon program for students
  2. Vendor evaluation with a viability knockout rule and staged payments
  3. Informed consent and data minimization for every participating family
  4. Redesigning assessments instead of using AI detectors
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The district committed about $6 million to AllHere and spent about $3 million before the company folded within months of launch, with no check on its financial health. The chapter matches this failure to vendor evaluation, a knockout rule on viability, and staged payments, the rushed procurement and vendor risks of Chapters 10 and 21. Screen limits fit Summit Learning, consent and minimization fit inBloom, and assessment redesign fits the detector study.

Concept Tested: AllHere Collapse

See: Worked Example: The Failures and the Practice That Would Have Caught Them

docs.title: 5. Using the chapter's method for the affordable Alpha model, a 12,000-student district estimates $17.24 per student for a Level 4 textbook with selective chatbot use and needs 24 full-time afternoon specialists at $60,000 each. With a print-textbook baseline of $53.33 per student, what is the net added cost per student per year?
docs.text:
1. About $84
  2. About $137
  3. About $120
  4. About $64
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The specialists cost 24 x $60,000 = $1,440,000, or $120 per student for 12,000 students. Adding $17.24 gives a new cost of about $137.24, and subtracting the $53.33 print baseline leaves about $84. The $137 answer forgets the print savings, $120 counts only the specialists, and $64 is the chapter's own figure for 20 specialists. As in the chapter, afternoon staffing is the largest piece of the cost.

Concept Tested: Affordable Alpha Model

See: Worked Example: The Added Cost per Student

docs.title: 6. A district is choosing between an AI system that replaces its small-group human tutors and one that gives those human tutors live suggestions during sessions. Which case from the chapter is most relevant, and what does it suggest?
docs.text:
1. Khanmigo, which suggests that AI tutors should replace human tutors as soon as possible
  2. AltSchool, which suggests that personalized software works best with no adults present
  3. Tutor CoPilot, which suggests AI works well when it makes human tutors better
  4. Your Brain on ChatGPT, which suggests that all AI assistance harms learning
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. In the 2024 Stanford Tutor CoPilot study, human tutors received live AI suggestions instead of being replaced. Students' mastery improved, the weakest tutors improved the most, and the cost per tutor was small. The chapter's lesson is that AI works well when it makes people better at helping students, which supports the AI-coaching-teachers idea of Chapter 21. Khanmigo is a both-sided case, AltSchool shows the failure of technology without culture, and the MIT study is a small preprint.

Concept Tested: Tutor CoPilot

See: Cases That Worked and Cases With Both Sides

docs.title: 7. A parent cites the "Your Brain on ChatGPT" study as proof that AI permanently damages students' thinking. How should a careful reader assess this claim using the chapter?
docs.text:
1. The study is small and still a preprint, so it flags a risk without proving its size
  2. The study is a large randomized trial, so it proves that the harm is permanent
  3. The study found no effect, so the parent's concern has no basis
  4. The study was independently replicated, so it settles the question
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The 2025 MIT Media Lab study found that students who wrote essays with ChatGPT showed lower brain engagement in EEG readings and remembered less of what they wrote. The chapter notes it was small and is still a preprint, so it supports the risk of handing thinking over without proving its size. Applying the six questions, "has anyone outside checked it?" gets "not yet." The parent's concern is legitimate, but "permanent damage" overstates what the evidence shows.

Concept Tested: Your Brain on ChatGPT

See: Evaluating Result Claims

docs.title: 8. The chapter estimates that the affordable Alpha model adds about $64 per student per year, compared with Alpha's $40,000 to $65,000 tuition. What caution does the chapter attach to this comparison?
docs.text:
1. The $64 figure includes devices, facilities, and transportation, so it is overstated
  2. Alpha's tuition is the same at every campus, so a single comparison is fair
  3. The $64 figure has been confirmed by an independent evaluation of the full package
  4. The tuition pays for a whole school, while $64 is an increment on top of public spending
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The chapter cautions that tuition pays for an entire school, while the $64 is only the increment on top of existing public spending, so the fair comparison is a public school at about $15,664 per student against a private school at $40,000 to $65,000. The figures are illustrative and exclude devices, facilities, and transportation, which reverses the first option. Alpha's tuition varies by campus, and no independent evidence yet shows this package matches Alpha's reported outcomes.

Concept Tested: Affordable Alpha Model

See: Worked Example: The Added Cost per Student

docs.title: 9. A teacher drafts a two-sided story: a student solves a hard problem with a hint-first tutor, and later the teacher finds in the log that the tutor gave another student the answer on the first request. The story ends there. Using the chapter's structure, what is missing?
docs.text:
1. The benefit, since the story does not show the tutor helping anyone
  2. The response to the risk and the positive being strengthened
  3. The risk, since the log review shows nothing went wrong
  4. Nothing, since a two-sided story only needs one benefit and one risk
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. A two-sided story shows a benefit growing stronger and a risk being reduced, with the school's response. The chapter's "Maya and the Hint" has four parts: the benefit (a patient tutor at her own pace), the risk (an answer-giving tutor found in the log), the response (the teacher flags it, the vendor fixes it, the school adds a weekly check), and the strengthened positive (Maya presents her solved problem). This draft has the first two and stops before the response and the strengthened positive.

Concept Tested: Two-Sided Story

See: Worked Example: A Two-Sided Story in Miniature

docs.title: 10. A principal must recommend a decision to the board. Draft 1 says: "AI is the future. Alpha School's results prove it works. We should adopt it district-wide." Draft 2 asks for a one-year, two-school pilot; separates randomized tutoring evidence from self-reported whole-school claims; attaches the seven-risk checklist; reports gaps by subgroup; gives a net cost; and states a scale, extend, or stop rule. Which draft better meets the chapter's standard, and why?
docs.text:
1. Draft 1, because boards respond best to a confident vision without any details
  2. Draft 1, because Alpha's results are strong enough to skip a pilot
  3. Draft 2, because it states evidence levels, risks, equity, cost, and a set rule
  4. Neither, because a board recommendation should avoid naming any risks
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. The chapter's school board recommendation has seven parts: the recommendation in one sentence, the case, the evidence with its level, the risks and responses, the equity analysis, the cost, and the decision rule and timeline. Draft 2 includes all of them. Draft 1 treats self-reported results as proof and skips the pilot, the pattern behind several of the chapter's failures. The chapter says the best recommendation asks the board not to believe but to test, and promises to report honestly.

Concept Tested: School Board Recommendation

See: The Recommendation to the Board

docs.title: References: AI-First Case Studies II: Lessons for Practice
docs.text:
1. Altitude Learning (formerly AltSchool) - Wikipedia - The history of AltSchool, the venture-funded personalized-learning school network that closed its schools, rebranded as a software company in 2019, and ceased operations in 2025. A key case of technology arriving before a lasting school culture.

  2. Phenomenon-Based Learning - Wikipedia - Explains the approach in which students study a real topic across subjects, and Finland's 2016 reform that required it alongside subject teaching. Background for the chapter's positive case of Finland's phenomenon learning.

  3. El Sistema - Wikipedia - Describes Venezuela's publicly funded youth orchestra program, founded in 1975, that uses group music-making to build discipline and belonging. The article also notes criticism of its social claims, which makes it a useful two-sided example.

  4. Tinkering Toward Utopia: A Century of Public School Reform - David Tyack and Larry Cuban - Harvard University Press - Tyack and Cuban are credited with the idea of the "grammar of schooling," the lasting structures that absorb reforms. Their work explains why so many of the failures in this chapter changed tools but not teaching.

  5. Teaching Machines: The History of Personalized Learning - Audrey Watters - MIT Press - Watters is credited with tracing today's personalized-learning promises back to the teaching machines of the 1920s to 1960s. Her history helps readers question result claims that sound new but repeat old hopes.

  6. Feds Charge Once-Lauded AllHere AI Founder in $10M Scheme to Defraud Investors - LA School Report (The 74) - November 2024 report on fraud charges against the founder of AllHere, maker of LAUSD's "Ed" chatbot, after the company collapsed. A clear case for vendor viability checks before buying.

  7. PowerSchool Begins Notifying Students and Teachers After Massive Data Breach - TechCrunch - Covers the December 2024 breach of a major student information system, entered through a support account without multi-factor authentication. It shows the risk of one vendor holding records for millions of students.

  8. From Chalkboards to Chatbots: Transforming Learning in Nigeria - World Bank Blogs - Results of the six-week 2024 after-school AI tutoring pilot in Edo State, with teachers present. A randomized evaluation found large English gains at low cost; the authors list open questions about long-term effects.

  9. Tutor CoPilot: A Human-AI Approach for Scaling Real-Time Expertise - arXiv (Wang, Ribeiro, Robinson, Loeb and Demszky, Stanford) - A randomized trial with 900 tutors and 1,800 students in which AI suggestions helped human tutors, especially weaker ones, at about $20 per tutor per year. Tutors also reported some unsuitable suggestions.

  10. Your Brain on ChatGPT - MIT Media Lab - The project page for the 2025 study finding lower brain engagement and weaker recall in students who wrote essays with ChatGPT. It lists its own limits: a small sample, one task, and a preprint not yet peer-reviewed.

docs.title: Learning Graph for AI-Native Schools
docs.text:
Open Learning Graph Viewer Fullscreen

This section contains the learning graph for this textbook. A learning graph is a graph of concepts used in this textbook. Each concept is represented by a node in a network graph. Concepts are connected by directed edges that indicate what concepts each node depends on before that concept is understood by the student.

A learning graph is the foundational data structure for intelligent textbooks that can recommend learning paths. A learning graph is like a roadmap of concepts to help students arrive at their learning goals.

At the left of the learning graph are prerequisite or foundational concepts. They have no outbound edges. They only have inbound edges for other concepts that depend on understanding these foundational prerequisite concepts. At the far right we have the most advanced concepts in the course. To master these concepts you must understand all the concepts that they point to.

Here are other files used by the learning graph.

docs.title: Course Description
docs.text: We use the Course Description as the source document for the concepts that are included in this course. The course description uses the 2001 Bloom taxonomy to order learning objectives.

docs.title: List of Concepts
docs.text: We use generative AI to convert the course description into a Concept List. Each concept is in the form of a short Title Case label with most labels under 32 characters long.

docs.title: Concept Dependency List
docs.text: We next use generative AI to create a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). DAGs do not have cycles where concepts depend on themselves. We provide the DAG in two formats. One is a CSV file and the other format is a JSON file that uses the vis-network JavaScript library format. The vis-network format uses nodes, edges and metadata elements with edges containing from and to properties. This makes it easy for you to view and edit the learning graph using an editor built with the vis-network tools.

docs.title: Course Description Quality Assessment
docs.text:
This report rates the overall quality of the course description for the purpose of generating a learning graph.

  • Course description fields and content depth analysis
  • Validates course description has sufficient depth for generating 300-600 concepts
  • Compares course description against similar courses
  • Identifies content gaps and strengths
  • Suggests areas of improvement View the Course Description Quality Assessment

docs.title: Learning Graph Quality Validation
docs.text:
This report gives you an overall assessment of the quality of the learning graph. It uses graph algorithms to look for specific quality patterns in the graph.

  • Graph structure validation - all concepts are connected
  • DAG validation (no cycles detected)
  • Foundational concepts: 14 entry points
  • Indegree distribution analysis
  • Longest dependency chains
  • Connectivity: percent of nodes connected to the main cluster

View the Learning Graph Quality Validation

docs.title: Concept Taxonomy
docs.text:
In order to see patterns in the learning graph, it is useful to assign colors to each concept based on the concept type. We use generative AI to create about a dozen categories for our concepts and then place each concept into a single primary classifier.

  • A concept classifier taxonomy with approximately 12 categories (+/- 1 or 2)
  • Category organization - foundational elements first, course capstone project ideas last
  • Balanced categories (3.5% - 15% each)
  • All categories under 30% threshold
  • Pedagogical flow recommendations
  • Clear 3-5 letter abbreviations for use in CSV file
  • A Miscellaneous (MISC) category is sometimes added View the Concept Taxonomy

docs.title: Taxonomy Distribution
docs.text:
This reports shows how many concepts fit into each category of the taxonomy. Our goal is a somewhat balanced taxonomy where each category holds an equal number of concepts. We also don't want any category to contain over 30% of our concepts.

  • Statistical breakdown
  • Detailed concept listing by category
  • Visual distribution table
  • Balance verification

View the Taxonomy Distribution Report

docs.title: Gap Analysis
docs.text:
1. Broad audience (−1). The book serves several groups with different needs. This does not block learning graph generation, but chapter writers will need to choose a main reader. Teachers and school leaders are the natural primary audience, with board members, policymakers, and parents as secondary readers.
  2. Case-study topics (−1). Topics such as "Unbound Academy" and "lessons from Tutor CoPilot" are specific examples. In the learning graph, they work best as examples attached to general concepts (for example, Guardrails or AI That Coaches Teachers) rather than as concepts of their own.
  3. Recall of case names (−1). "Name the key case studies and the main lesson of each" is fine for a quiz but adds little to the learning graph.

docs.title: Improvement Suggestions
docs.text:
These are optional; the description is already ready to use.

  1. Add one sentence naming the primary reader (for example, "written mainly for K-12 teachers and school leaders, with sections for board members and parents").
  2. When the learning graph is generated, treat case studies as examples of concepts, not as concepts, unless the case is central (Alpha School and the five-level model are central).
  3. Check the stories written from memory in the AI-First Stories appendix before chapters cite their numbers. Fourteen stories are still marked "Sources still to add."

  • Bloom's coverage: 68 outcomes across all six levels, which suggests foundation, process, judgment, and design concepts.
  • Estimated concept count: 250–350 concepts, well above the 200-concept target.

docs.title: Known Limitations
docs.text:
• Concept coverage is 234 of 532 chapter concepts (44%). Ten questions per chapter cannot reach the 75% target when chapters list 15–35 concepts. The questions focus on each chapter's main ideas: concepts named in the title, given their own section, or shown in bold.
  • The correct option is the longest one in 121 of 230 questions (53%). Most of these are near ties. Six clear cases were fixed by rewording, but a test-wise reader could still find a slight "pick the longest" pattern.
  • Some apply questions use illustrative numbers worked out with the chapter's own method, so they do not repeat the chapter's worked examples. These numbers are invented for the exercise and are not facts.
  • Still-developing cases (South Korea's AI textbooks, the LAUSD/AllHere chatbot, Unbound Academy) keep the chapters' "as reported" wording. These questions should be rechecked when the chapters are updated.
  • Chapter 16 tests Lewin's and Bridges' models, which the learning graph places in Chapter 17. They are tagged with the broader concept "Organizational Change."

docs.title: Recommendations
docs.text:
1. When chapters are revised, rerun the validator and rebuild quiz-bank.json so the bank matches the quizzes.
  2. Raise coverage in concept-heavy chapters (6, 13, 15 and 19) with a second quiz set drawn from quiz-bank.json, or with 12–15 questions per quiz.
  3. Lengthen some distractors in the near-tie questions to remove the slight "pick the longest" cue.
  4. Use quiz-bank.json for LMS export and for practice questions in the chatbot.
