docs.title: Poster Ideas
docs.text:
Ideas for full-page overlay infographic posters.

Each poster is an infographic overlay MicroSim: a text-free background image with an interactive layer of labels on top, built with the shared engines in docs/sims/shared-libs/. There are two engines:

  • Callout (diagram.js) draws numbered markers with leader lines. Use it for one complex scene where small parts need names.
  • Grid (grid-diagram.js) draws large rectangular hover zones. Use it for side-by-side comparisons and posters split into regions.

The first poster, Crossing the Chasm (Chapter 15), is built and is the model for the twelve below. Its background is a hand-built SVG drawn by a Python script, so no text-to-image step is needed. Most posters below can be drawn the same way. A few (marked) would look better painted from an image-prompt.md.

Rules that apply to every poster

  • No text in the image, not even the title. Every word lives in data.json.
  • Exception: grid posters may print column headers in the image, with showLabels: false.
  • Every poster shows a benefit, a risk, and the school's response to the risk (the book's story-balance rule).
  • Any number baked into a zone's facts goes through Phases 1–4 of the verified-infographic guide first, and carries a source_id. Numbers taken from the book's own worked examples cite the chapter instead.
  • Each poster starts at status: scaffold, is embedded in its chapter under a #### Diagram: heading, and is added to nav: and docs/sims/index.md.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
# Poster Chapter Engine sim-id 1 The Factory Day vs. the AI-Native Day 3, 20 Grid factory-vs-ai-native-day 2 Five Levels: Textbooks and Self-Driving Cars 6 Grid five-levels-textbooks-and-cars 3 Seat Time vs. Mastery 3, 11 Grid seat-time-vs-mastery-poster 4 Anatomy of a Learning Record 8 Callout anatomy-of-a-learning-record 5 The Student Record Vault 10 Callout student-record-vault 6 Answer Machine vs. Thinking Tutor 12 Grid answer-machine-vs-thinking-tutor 7 The EdTech Hype Cycle 15 Callout edtech-hype-cycle-overlay 8 The Rider, the Elephant and the Path 19 Callout rider-elephant-path-overlay 9 Kotter's Eight Steps as a Mountain Trail 17 Callout kotter-mountain-trail 10 Schein's Culture Iceberg 17, 18 Callout schein-culture-iceberg 11 What a Textbook Costs per Student 7 Grid textbook-cost-per-student-poster 12 Promise and Peril: Five AI-First Cases 22 Grid promise-and-peril-cases

Several of these share a topic with an existing practice sim, such as seat-time-vs-mastery, where-on-hype-cycle, rider-elephant-path, which-kotter-step, who-may-see-this-record and cost-per-student-by-level. That is deliberate: the poster explains the idea, and the practice sim that follows it in the chapter checks it. To avoid a clash with the existing sim ids, the overlay ids end in -poster or -overlay.

docs.title: 1. The Factory Day vs. the AI-Native Day
docs.text:
Chapters: 3 (Industrial-Era School Model), 20 (Designing the AI-Native School Day) Engine: Grid, two columns, each split into a morning band and an afternoon band (four zones plus two header zones) Why a poster: the whole argument of the book is a comparison between two school days. Seeing them side by side, hour by hour, makes it concrete.

Image: two vertical school-day timelines drawn as buildings in cross-section. - Left, the factory day: identical classrooms stacked like a production line, rows of desks facing the front, a bell on the wall, students grouped by age, and a clock that dominates each room. - Right, the AI-native day: - Morning: small clusters of students at laptops, each at a different point on a winding path, with a coach moving between them. - Afternoon: open spaces with project tables, a garden, a stage and a workshop.

Zones

Zone Summary Facts to show Factory morning Everyone hears the same lesson at the same pace Bell schedule; age-based grade levels; seat time; Carnegie unit Factory afternoon More of the same, by subject Teacher workload and burnout; little time for projects AI-native morning A compressed academic morning, about two to three hours, at each student's own pace Personalized pacing; mastery learning; gap filling; reduced direct instruction AI-native afternoon Freed-up time for people skills Projects, clubs, service, the pro-social afternoon (Ch 14) Teacher, left Lecturer and grader — Teacher, right Coach, mentor, facilitator Changing teacher role (Ch 20)

Story balance: - Benefit: freed-up time. - Risk: too much screen time and isolated students. - Response: morning screen-time limits, and a structured (not empty) afternoon.

To verify: the length of the compressed morning. Use the book's phrasing and cite Chapter 11.

docs.title: 2. Five Levels: Textbooks and Self-Driving Cars
docs.text:
Chapter: 6 (The Five-Level Model of Intelligent Textbooks) Engine: Grid, five columns in two rows (cars on top, textbooks below), so one zone per level per row Why a poster: the chapter's analogy to the SAE driving levels is the key to the model, and it lands best when the two ladders sit side by side.

Image: five columns that rise like a staircase from left to right. - Top row: a car at each level, from a car with a driver's hands on the wheel to a car with no steering wheel at all. - Bottom row: a textbook at each level: - a closed print book - a laptop with a slider and a graph - a laptop with a branching path - a laptop with a chat bubble - a laptop generating pages on the fly - Small column headers "1"–"5" may be printed, with showLabels: false.

Zones (textbook row)

Level Summary Facts 1 Static Fixed content, like print and PDF No interactivity; nothing known about the student 2 Interactive Responds to what the learner does Embedded simulations, quizzes, learning graphs 3 Adaptive Driven by each student's progress Needs stored student records (Ch 8, 10) 4 Chatbot Conversational tutoring Large language models; inference cost (Ch 7) 5 Autonomous Real-time content generation Full personalization; not yet realistic

Story balance: - Benefit: each level adds power. - Risk: each level also adds cost, data and things that can go wrong. Vendors claim a higher level than they deliver. - Response: the chapter's rule that a product's level is the highest capability it delivers in use.

To verify: the SAE level names (cite SAE J3016) and the date of the five-level paper (December 2025 preprint).

docs.title: 3. Seat Time vs. Mastery
docs.text:
Chapters: 3 (Seat Time, Carnegie Unit), 11 (Mastery Learning) Engine: Grid, two columns Why a poster: the difference is about time, and a picture of two students' paths through the same unit makes the hidden gaps visible.

Image: two staircases of the same five concepts (blocks). - Left, seat time: a calendar marches forward and the student climbs on schedule, but some blocks are cracked or missing. The higher blocks wobble on the gaps. - Right, mastery: the student stays on a block until it is solid (a small green check shape, not text), then climbs. Every block is whole, and some students are higher than others.

Zones

Zone Summary Facts Seat time: the calendar Time is fixed; learning varies Carnegie unit; the class moves on together Seat time: the cracked blocks Gaps build up silently Later concepts depend on earlier ones (learning dependency, Ch 8) Mastery: the solid blocks Learning is fixed; time varies Mastery threshold; gap filling Mastery: the spread of students Students finish at different times Personalized pacing; what the class does together instead

Story balance: - Benefit: no hidden gaps. - Risk: students spread far apart, and slow students fall further behind in time. - Response: tutoring and gap filling for those who are stuck, and shared afternoon work that does not depend on pace.

To verify: none; this poster is conceptual.

docs.title: 4. Anatomy of a Learning Record
docs.text:
Chapter: 8 (Tracking Mastery: xAPI and the Learning Record Store) Engine: Callout, top-bottom layout, about 10 callouts Why a poster: the path from a click to a dashboard is invisible to most teachers and parents. A single picture of it answers the chapter's opening question, "How does it know?"

Image: a left-to-right flow: 1. A student at a laptop moving a slider in a MicroSim. 2. A glowing envelope leaves the laptop. The envelope is drawn as three linked tiles, shown only as a person icon, an action icon and an object icon. 3. It travels to a filing-cabinet server (the Learning Record Store). 4. The cabinet feeds a teacher's dashboard with bars. 5. The cabinet also feeds a learning graph whose next node lights up. 6. A small key on a lanyard hangs from the student, standing for student-controlled data.

Callouts: the MicroSim; the xAPI statement; actor; verb; object; result (score); the Learning Record Store; the dashboard (learning analytics); the learning graph choosing the next concept; the key (data portability and student control).

Story balance: - Benefit: the textbook adapts without a live AI model, cheaply. - Risk: a detailed learning history is sensitive data. - Response: data minimization and student-controlled records (links to poster 5).

To verify: the xAPI statement structure (cite the xAPI specification).

docs.title: 5. The Student Record Vault
docs.text:
Chapter: 10 (Student Privacy and Data Governance) Engine: Callout, side-panel layout, about 12 callouts Why a poster: "who may see what" is a set of nested rules that is hard to follow in prose and easy to follow as rings.

Image: - Centre: a student's record as a glowing folder inside a round vault. - Rings: concentric walls, each with a gate. - Innermost ring: the student and the family. - Second ring: the teacher and the school. - Third ring: the district. - Outer ring: the vendors and researchers. - Around the rings: - a crack in the outer wall with papers blowing out (a data breach) - a shredder by one gate (the retention policy) - a small balance scale on a desk (bias auditing)

Callouts: student data vs. personally identifiable data; behavioral data; FERPA (the school's gate); COPPA (the under-13 gate); GDPR (where it applies); data minimization (a small vault); informed consent; the retention-policy shredder; vendor risk; the breach crack; algorithmic bias auditing; the trust paradox.

Story balance: - Benefit: detailed records let a textbook adapt. - Risk: the privacy inflection point, and the inBloom and PowerSchool cases. - Response: governance readiness before adoption.

To verify: the scope of each law, the inBloom and PowerSchool facts, and any numbers about breaches. Run the verified-infographic Phases 1–4.

docs.title: 6. Answer Machine vs. Thinking Tutor
docs.text:
Chapter: 12 (AI Guardrails: Teaching Thinking Without Over-Reliance) Engine: Grid, two columns of three rows (the question, the AI's move, what the student is left with) Why a poster: the same homework question handled two ways shows exactly what a guardrail changes.

Image: two chat conversations on two phones. Speech bubbles hold only shapes and icons, no words. - Left phone, open AI: one big bubble with a finished answer (a checkmark and a neat page). The student leans back, and a small, empty thought cloud floats above them. - Right phone, guided AI: a chain of short bubbles, with a question-mark icon, a lightbulb hint and a smaller question mark. The student is writing on paper, and the thought cloud above them holds four small icons: puzzle pieces (decomposition), a repeating pattern (pattern recognition), a simplified shape (abstraction) and numbered steps (algorithmic thinking).

Zones

Zone Summary Facts Open AI: the move Gives the answer Fast and convenient Open AI: the result Cognitive offloading Over-reliance; confidently wrong answers go unchecked Guided AI: the move Hints instead of answers Socratic questioning; the tutor holds back Guided AI: the result The student does the thinking The four computational-thinking skills The guardrails What makes the right phone different Mastery threshold; selective chatbot use; screen-time limits

Story balance: - Benefit: an AI tutor is patient and always available. - Risk: over-reliance. - Response: guardrails, and the guided-AI design.

To verify: any study figures quoted about tutoring outcomes (run the verified phases, or keep the poster qualitative).

docs.title: 7. The EdTech Hype Cycle
docs.text:
Chapter: 15 (Technology Adoption, the hype-cycle section) Engine: Callout, top-bottom layout, about 11 callouts Why a poster: a century of education technology on one curve is the fastest way to show that the pattern repeats.

Image: a landscape whose skyline is the hype-cycle curve. - The five phases: - a rocket launch at the trigger - a crowded, fireworks-lit peak - a foggy valley at the trough - a gentle staircase up the slope - a calm, productive plateau with a working classroom - Objects placed on the curve, one per technology wave: - an old radio - a classroom TV on a cart - a computer-lab desktop - a laptop cart - a MOOC certificate - a glowing chat bubble for generative AI

Callouts: the five phases (5), plus one per technology wave (6). The wave placements must match the chapter's own hype-cycle table.

Story balance: - Benefit: some technologies do reach the plateau. - Risk: buying at the peak, and abandoning at the trough. - Response: realistic expectations, and staying on the slope of enlightenment, where a small group keeps learning what works.

To verify: the dates and claims for each wave. Run Phases 1–4; Gartner is the source for the curve itself.

docs.title: 8. The Rider, the Elephant and the Path
docs.text:
Chapter: 19 (Microstrategies for Leading Change, the Switch framework) Engine: Callout, side-panel layout, 10 callouts Why a poster: the Heaths' framework is already an image. Drawing it, with each of the nine moves placed in the scene, turns a list into something memorable.

Image: - The rider: a small figure holding a map and pointing ahead. A bright patch of the landscape glows in the distance (a bright spot), and a far-off hilltop shows a school building at the destination. - The elephant: a large elephant, partly tired. A heart shape floats near it, a small step-sized stone sits right in front of its foot (shrink the change), and a team badge hangs on its harness (grow your people). - The path: - a smooth, fenced path with a well-worn groove (build habits) - a signpost with no words (tweak the environment) - a herd of elephants walking ahead (rally the herd)

Callouts: direct the rider (follow the bright spots, script the critical moves, point to the destination); motivate the elephant (find the feeling, shrink the change, grow your people); shape the path (tweak the environment, build habits, rally the herd); plus one overall callout for the three-part idea.

Story balance: - Benefit: each move is small and cheap. - Risk: a clear plan (rider) with no motivation (elephant) stalls. - Response: address all three, and use the chapter's examples, such as "a login that works first time."

To verify: none beyond attribution to Heath and Heath (2010), Switch.

docs.title: 9. Kotter's Eight Steps as a Mountain Trail
docs.text:
Chapter: 17 (Leading Change: Vision, Culture, and Early-Stage Concerns) Engine: Callout, dual-panel layout, 8 step callouts plus 2 risk callouts Why a poster: Kotter's steps are a sequence, and a trail up a mountain shows that skipping one leaves you stranded.

Image: a mountain with a switchback trail and eight camps. 1. A camp with a fire alarm-style flare (urgency) 2. A rope team (the guiding coalition) 3. A telescope pointed at the summit (vision) 4. A signal flag station (communicating) 5. Fallen logs being cleared (removing obstacles) 6. A small flag planted on a ledge (a short-term win) 7. A wider camp with more tents (building on change) 8. A stone cairn at the summit (anchoring in culture)

Two hazards complete the scene: a climber sliding back down a shortcut gully, and a summit cairn that is only half built.

Callouts: the eight steps, using the book's names (sense of urgency, guiding coalition, change vision, communicating the vision, removing obstacles, short-term wins, building on change, anchoring in culture). The two risk callouts are: - Skipping steps: the shortcut gully. - Declaring victory too soon: the half-built cairn.

Story balance: - Benefit: a clear order of work. - Risk: skipping steps, or declaring victory too soon. - Response: Lewin's refreeze and Kotter's anchoring, as the chapter pairs them.

To verify: step names (cite Kotter, Leading Change).

docs.title: 10. Schein's Culture Iceberg
docs.text:
Chapters: 17 (Schein's culture model), 18 (culture assessment) Engine: Callout, side-panel layout, about 9 callouts Why a poster: Schein's three layers are about what you can and cannot see, and an iceberg shows that directly. It also explains why reforms that change only the surface fail.

Image: an iceberg in cross-section, at sea. - Above the water (artifacts): a school building with a bell tower, a printed schedule shape, a trophy case and a crowd at a pep rally (a ritual). - At the waterline (espoused values): a framed mission-statement shape with blank lines, and a banner with no text. - Deep below (basic assumptions): dark, heavy ice with fossil-like shapes, such as a single desk alone in a room ("a good teacher works alone") and a clock fused into the ice ("learning takes a fixed time"). - The reform ship: a small boat labelled with nothing, steering at the visible tip while the hidden mass sits beneath its path.

Callouts: artifacts; school rituals; espoused values; shared beliefs and norms; basic assumptions (two examples); the grammar of schooling; the reform ship ("reform without real change"); culture assessment (a diver with a lamp).

Story balance: - Benefit: culture holds a school together through hard times. - Risk: when stated values and real assumptions disagree, the assumptions win. - Response: assess culture before announcing change, and work on assumptions through small wins.

To verify: none beyond attribution to Schein.

docs.title: 11. What a Textbook Costs per Student
docs.text:
Chapter: 7 (Content Economics and Open Educational Resources) Engine: Grid, four columns (Print, Level 2, Level 3, Level 4) Why a poster: a finance director's question ("What will it cost per student, all in?") has a picture answer: stacked cost blocks, one stack per option. Image: best painted from an image prompt, or built as an SVG with exact block heights.

Image: four stacks of coin-like blocks on a table, with block height proportional to cost. - Print: one tall stack. - Level 2: a tiny stack. - Level 3: a slightly taller stack, with blocks in different colors for records, governance and training. - Level 4: taller again, with an added block glowing like a chat bubble (inference).

A laptop sits behind all four stacks, slightly faded, to show the device cost that is not included.

Zones

Option Per student per year (devices already owned) Facts Print baseline about $53.33 $80 book, six years, four core subjects Level 2 $5.80 Penny-per-day content and hosting ($1.80) plus $4.00 of training Level 3 $12.80 Adds a learning record store ($3.00), privacy governance ($2.00) and $2.00 more training Level 4 $23.00 Adds inference ($7.20 at $2 per million tokens), log review ($1.00) and $2.00 more training The device (faded) about $75 a year $300 laptop over four years

Story balance: - Benefit: content costs collapse. - Risk: hidden costs (devices, training, governance), plus publisher disruption. - Response: total cost of ownership and explicit cost models.

To verify: all figures come from the chapter's illustrative model. Cite Chapter 7 and say "illustrative" in every zone. No web verification is needed unless real prices are added.

docs.title: 12. Promise and Peril: Five AI-First Cases
docs.text:
Chapter: 22 (AI-First Case Studies I: Promise and Peril) Engine: Grid, five columns (one per case) by three rows (benefit, risk, response), 15 zones Why a poster: the chapter's risk-and-response framework is a table. A poster that fills it in for all five cases shows the pattern at a glance, and it is the book's story-balance rule in one picture. Image: best painted.

Image: five vertical panels, each showing a school scene in a consistent flat style: 1. A small private school with guides beside students at laptops (Alpha School) 2. A home screen with a single student and a virtual classroom (Unbound Academy) 3. A Turkish high-school math classroom with two groups, one with open AI and one with a guided tutor (the Turkish study) 4. A university physics lecture hall with students working with an AI tutor (Harvard) 5. A large public-school classroom with students on a learning platform and a mentor checking in (Summit Learning)

In each panel, a green band at the top holds a symbol for its benefit, a red band in the middle a symbol for its risk, and a blue band at the bottom a symbol for its response.

Zones: one per case per row, so 15 in all. Each zone's facts include its source.

Story balance: built into the design. Every case gets all three rows, and a missing response is shown as an empty blue band, not invented.

To verify: everything. Run the verified-infographic Phases 1–4 for every claim: - Alpha School's tuition: about $40,000 at the original Austin campus to about $65,000 at newer campuses. Never give $65,000 for every campus. - The study results. - The Unbound charter decisions. - The Summit Learning history.

Allow asymmetric content where a case has no published evidence for a row.

docs.title: Suggested build order
docs.text:
1. Posters 4, 8, 9 and 10: they can be drawn as SVGs from simple shapes, need no outside facts, and each fills a gap in a chapter with no picture of its main model.
  2. Posters 1, 3 and 6: two-column grid comparisons, quick to build.
  3. Posters 2 and 11: need care with exact figures and level names, but no web research.
  4. Posters 5, 7 and 12: need the verified-infographic research phases first.

docs.title: List of MicroSims for AI-Native Schools
docs.text:
Interactive MicroSims that let you try out the ideas in each chapter: classify real school decisions, run cost and growth calculators, and explore learning graphs. Each one is embedded in its chapter and also works on its own page.

  • Afternoon Program Quality Judge

    Judge six fictional afternoon programs as structured, partly structured, or unstructured by counting the SAFE practices each one includes.

  • AI Cost per Student Calculator

    Calculate the yearly AI inference cost per student from tokens per session, sessions per day, school days, and price per million tokens, then explore how price changes the result.

  • AI Terms Classifier

    Place eight example systems in the narrowest of six nested categories, from Not AI to AI agent.

  • AI Tutor Design Judge

    Judge six fictional AI tutor designs as likely to harm learning, mixed, or likely to help, by applying the five-guardrail rule.

  • Alpha or Unbound?

    Compare Alpha School and Unbound Academy by placing nine facts as true of Alpha only, Unbound only, or both.

  • Anatomy of a Learning Record

    Follow one click from a MicroSim to a teacher's dashboard: the xAPI statement, the Learning Record Store, the learning graph and the student's key.

  • Answer Machine vs. Thinking Tutor

    An interactive grid infographic of the same homework question handled two ways: an open chatbot that gives the answer and leaves the student with nothing to do, and a guided AI tutor that gives hints and leaves the student doing the thinking, with the guardrails that make the difference.

  • Artifact, Value, or Assumption?

    Sort eight statements about a school into Schein's three layers of culture: artifacts, espoused values, and basic assumptions.

  • Ask the Right Question

    Match six result claims to the question that best exposes the weakness in each.

  • Bloom Level Task Sorter

    Sort twelve classroom tasks into the six levels of the revised Bloom's Taxonomy, with a hint and a second try for each task.

  • Building Blocks Concept Map

    Explore how the 21 Chapter 1 concepts depend on one another, then select the direct prerequisites of six concepts on the map.

  • Challenge and Prior Knowledge Zone Explorer

    Predict whether a student is bored, engaged, in productive struggle, or overwhelmed from the gap between task challenge and prior knowledge, then explore the model.

  • Choose the Microstrategy

    Choose the microstrategy that best fits each of eight teacher situations, by diagnosing the concern first.

  • Choose the Move to Cross the Chasm

    Choose, for six situations, the move that best helps an innovation cross the chasm from early adopters to the early majority.

  • Coach Capacity Calculator

    Calculate the number of coaches a rollout needs, rounding up, and the number of teachers a given number of coaches can support.

  • Contract Clause Review

    Judge eight clauses from a fictional AI product contract as acceptable, needing change, or a red flag.

  • Cost per Student by Level

    Calculate the yearly cost per student and the district cost for Level 2, 3, and 4 textbooks from itemized costs, then explore AI usage, token price, and devices.

  • Crossing the Chasm

    Explore Moore's chasm as a landscape shaped like the adoption curve, with 13 callouts for the adopter groups, the whole product, the beachhead and the risk of crossing by hope.

  • Doubling Time Projection Calculator

    Calculate how many months a 50-minute task horizon takes to reach 40 hours for doubling times of 4, 5, and 6 months, then explore other doubling times and targets.

  • The EdTech Hype Cycle

    An interactive infographic of the hype cycle drawn as a landscape, with 11 callouts for the five stages and six waves of educational technology, from film in 1913 to generative AI.

  • Empathy or Not?

    Classify eight replies to a teacher who fears losing their job as dismissive, defensive, reassurance without substance, or empathic and substantive.

  • Equal vs. Equitable Tutoring

    Compare an equal split of 45 tutoring hours with an equitable one by finding the allocation that brings three students to a score of 80.

  • Evidence Tier Claim Checker

    Judge the evidence behind ten fictional vendor claims by placing each in one of five evidence levels, from Strong to No evidence of effect.

  • The Factory Day vs. the AI-Native Day

    An interactive poster of two school buildings in cross-section: the industrial-era factory day on the left and the AI-native day on the right, with six zones for the teacher's role, the morning and the afternoon in each school.

  • False Accusations Calculator

    Calculate how many human-written essays an AI detector wrongly flags, the share of flags that are false, and the share of false flags that fall on English-language learners.

  • Find the Missing Safeguard

    Read six pilot plans against the seven-risk pilot checklist and find the one risk each plan fails to address.

  • Five Levels: Textbooks and Self-Driving Cars

    An interactive grid poster that sets the six SAE J3016 levels of driving automation above the five levels of intelligent textbooks, with the shared Level 3 threshold and the rule for testing a vendor's level claim.

  • Force Field Balance

    Calculate the driving, restraining, and net forces for a school change, before and after reducing two restraining forces, then explore with sliders.

  • Four Thinking Skills Sorter

    Classify eight school activities as decomposition, pattern recognition, abstraction, or algorithmic thinking.

  • Four-Fifths Bias Audit Calculator

    Calculate selection rates and four-fifths ratios for three student groups, decide which groups an audit flags, then change the counts and watch the flags update.

  • Generate Once Versus Generate for Each Student

    Compare the yearly cost of generating a textbook once and serving it to everyone with generating content live for each student, and find the break-even number of students.

  • Governance Readiness Judge

    Judge six fictional districts as not ready, ready for Level 3, or well placed for Level 4 by applying the must-have and should-have rule.

  • Is the Gap Closing?

    Compute the gap between higher-income and lower-income students before and after for five schools, and decide whether each gap is closing, widening, or unchanged.

  • Is This a Normal Dip?

    Judge whether each of three pilot performance series shows a normal implementation dip, a deep or late dip, or no dip, using a stated rule.

  • Is This Data Identifying?

    Classify eight data fields as a direct identifier, identifying in combination, or not identifying.

  • Judging the Evidence for a Shorter Morning

    Judge the strength of the evidence behind eight claims about AI tutoring and the compressed morning, using the five evidence levels from Chapter 2.

  • Kotter's Eight Steps as a Mountain Trail

    Climb Kotter's eight steps for leading change as camps on a switchback trail, with two risks: skipping steps and declaring victory too soon.

  • Learning Graph Viewer

    Interactive viewer for the 532-concept AI-Native Schools learning graph, with search, category filtering, and statistics.

  • Level-Specific Safeguard Matcher

    Choose the lowest of five textbook levels at which each of eight safeguards should first be required.

  • Listening Responses

    Classify eight replies to a nervous teammate as paraphrase, clarifying question, reflecting feeling, advice, or judgment.

  • Mastery Threshold Chooser

    Examine a table of pass probabilities for five mastery rules and select every rule that meets each of four requirements.

  • Match Activity to Skill

    Classify ten afternoon activities by the human skill each one builds most directly: collaboration, communication, empathy, creativity, or computational thinking.

  • METR Measurement Workflow

    Read the six steps that turn AI task results into a 50 percent time horizon, then answer five questions about the steps.

  • Missing Project Element

    Find the one essential project element that each of six fictional project descriptions lacks.

  • Morning Time Budget

    Calculate the minutes, hours, and school days a compressed academic morning frees, and the speedup it requires, then explore the trade-off with sliders.

  • Name That Change Model

    Match each of eight school change situations to the change model that best addresses it.

  • One Lesson, Many Readiness Levels

    Predict where one whole-class lesson should be pitched for a class spread across eight readiness levels, then move the pitch to see who is in reach.

  • Prerequisite Chain Diagnosis

    Trace a student's failure on a fractions-to-proportions prerequisite map back to the root gap in five illustrative cases.

  • Product Level Classifier

    Judge the real level of eight fictional learning products and label each vendor claim an overclaim, accurate, or an underclaim.

  • Promise and Peril: Five AI-First Cases

    An interactive grid poster that reads five AI-first cases (Alpha School, Unbound Academy, the Turkish high school study, the Harvard physics AI tutor and Summit Learning) as a benefit, a risk and a response, with an empty band where no response was found.

  • Ready Concepts Finder

    Select exactly the ready concepts in a 16-concept learning graph for six different sets of mastered concepts.

  • Reinforcing or Balancing?

    Classify six causal loops from school change as reinforcing or balancing by counting the minus signs around each loop.

  • Rider, Elephant, or Path?

    Classify nine change tactics as directing the rider, motivating the elephant, or shaping the path, the three parts of the Switch framework.

  • The Rider, the Elephant and the Path

    Find the nine moves of the Switch framework in one scene: direct the rider, motivate the elephant and shape the path.

  • Scale, Extend, or Stop?

    Apply a pilot decision rule to six pilot results and judge whether each pilot should scale, extend, or stop.

  • Schein's Culture Iceberg

    Explore Schein's three levels of a school's culture as an iceberg, and see why reforms aimed at the visible tip can leave practice unchanged.

  • School Decision Stakeholder Match

    Match ten school decisions to the stakeholder who typically holds them: teacher, principal, district administrator, school board, or family.

  • Schooling and EdTech Timeline

    Explore twenty events in the history of schooling and educational technology from 1848 to 2022, then place eight of them in their eras.

  • Seat Time vs. Mastery

    Calculate how many of twenty students master a fixed-length course and how many hours the early finishers sit idle, then compare with a mastery-based schedule.

  • Seat Time vs. Mastery

    An interactive poster comparing two staircases of the same five concepts: seat time, where the calendar moves the class on and gaps crack the blocks, and mastery learning, where every block is solid but students spread apart in time.

  • Source Credibility Checker

    Rate eight fictional sources of evidence about an education product as Lead only, Use with caution, or Reasonable weight by applying a three-part rule.

  • Spacing and Retrieval Retention Explorer

    Predict which review schedule and method keep the most memory for a day-30 exam, then compare forgetting curves for massed, spaced, and expanding reviews.

  • The Student Record Vault

    An interactive infographic of who may come close to a student's record: a glowing folder inside four walls, for the family, the school, the district and vendors, with 14 callouts for FERPA, COPPA, GDPR, governance practices and the inBloom and PowerSchool cases.

  • Task Horizon Curve Explorer

    Calculate a model's chance of finishing tasks of different lengths from its 50 percent time horizon, then move the horizon and watch the success curve shift.

  • Tutor Reply Hint Levels

    Classify eight AI tutor replies to the same juice-price question by hint level, from 1 (asks a question) to 4 (gives the answer).

  • Vendor Scorecard

    Calculate the weighted scores of two vendors and apply the knockout rule to decide which vendor may proceed.

  • Verify the AI Summary

    Judge whether each of six statements in an AI-written summary is supported by a short source passage.

  • What a Textbook Costs per Student

    An interactive poster that answers a finance director's question with four stacks of cost blocks, print and Levels 2 to 4, drawn to scale, with the faded laptop a school may also have to buy standing behind them.

  • What Level of Use Is This?

    Classify eight teacher behaviors by CBAM level of use, from nonuse to renewal.

  • Where Is It on the Hype Cycle?

    Place eight events from the history of educational technology on the five stages of the hype cycle.

  • Where the Minutes Go in a Traditional School Day

    Estimate how many minutes of an illustrative 425-minute middle-school day are whole-class direct instruction, then reveal a chart of where the minutes go.

  • Which Attribute Is the Barrier?

    Name the innovation attribute that is the barrier behind each of eight teacher comments about a new tool.

docs.title: Afternoon Program Quality Judge
docs.text:
Run the Afternoon Program Quality Judge MicroSim Fullscreen Chapter 14: The Pro-Social Afternoon

To edit the sketch, paste the contents of afternoon-program-quality-judge.js into the p5.js editor and set the editor's p5.js version to 2.x. The learning content is in the CONFIG block at the top of the file.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Freed afternoon time helps students only if it is used well. Durlak, Weissberg, and Pachan (2010) found that after-school programs improved personal and social skills when they followed four practices, known as SAFE:

  • Sequenced: a connected, step-by-step set of activities.
  • Active: students practice the skills actively.
  • Focused: a component devoted to personal or social skills.
  • Explicit: specific, stated skill goals.

The rule in this MicroSim counts the practices: all 4 is Structured, 2 or 3 is Partly structured, and 0 or 1 is Unstructured. A program can be quiet and supervised, or lively and hands-on, and still miss most of the four. The rule is a simple school-level check, not a full quality assessment. The six programs are fictional.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text: Read the program description, then choose one of the three ratings. Press Show SAFE practices to see what each practice means. A wrong first answer gives a hint and lets you choose again, but only the first answer counts toward First-try correct. After six programs, the results screen shows your score and the number of practices in each program.

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:
• Choice buttons: commit an answer. A wrong first answer gives a hint and lets you choose again; only the first answer counts.
  • Show definitions: opens or closes the reference table. Reading it is exploration, not evidence.
  • Next: moves to the next item after feedback. On the results screen, Previous missed and Next missed step through what you missed.
  • Play again: starts a practice run with the items reshuffled. Practice runs do not change the first-run score.

Nothing moves until you act, and the MicroSim does not store your answers.

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Teachers, administrators, school board members, policymakers, and parents.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Structured afternoon, unstructured afternoon drift, afternoon program quality, and the SAFE practices, from the section "Structure Versus Drift" in Chapter 14

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Judge (6 min). Rate the six programs. For each one, tick off S, A, F, and E on paper before you choose.
  2. Compare (3 min). Homework Hall is quiet and Open Gym is noisy. Why do they get the same rating?
  3. Improve (5 min). Pick the Garden Project. Add the two missing practices in one sentence each.

docs.text:
Mastery is 5 of 6 correct on the first try. Only the first answer to each program on the first run counts. Then ask learners to answer these without the MicroSim:

  1. A program has a trained adult, hands-on work, and nothing else. Rating? (Unstructured. Only Active is present.)
  2. Does a supervised program have quality? (Not by itself. Supervision is not one of the four practices.)
  3. A program has Sequenced, Active, and Explicit but no Focused component. Rating? (Partly structured.)

docs.text:
1. A meta-analysis of after-school programs that seek to promote personal and social skills. Durlak, Weissberg, and Pachan (2010), American Journal of Community Psychology. The source of the SAFE practices.
  2. Social emotional learning. Wikipedia. The skills that SAFE programs aim to build.
  3. After-school activity. Wikipedia. The range of after-school programs.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A school that gives every student an AI tutor pays for AI inference: each session uses tokens, and providers charge a price per million tokens. The yearly cost per student is:

cost per student per year = tokens per session × sessions per day × school days × price per million tokens ÷ 1,000,000

Three challenges come first, with the inputs shown but locked. After the third, the controls unlock and the yearly cost, the daily cost, the district total for 12,000 students, and the share of $15,600 per-pupil spending update at once. A bar chart compares the same usage at all four prices.

The $20.00 (November 2022) and $0.07 (October 2024) prices for GPT-3.5-level performance come from the Stanford AI Index 2025. The $2.00 and $0.20 prices are illustrative, and so are the session sizes.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
Nothing moves until you act, and the MicroSim does not store your answers.

  • Your answer box and Check: type a dollar amount for the challenge and press Check (or Enter). Two attempts per challenge; only the first counts toward the score.
  • Next: moves to the next challenge. After challenge 3 it unlocks the controls.
  • Tokens per session: slider from 5,000 to 100,000 in steps of 5,000.
  • Sessions per day: slider from 1 to 5.
  • School days: slider from 150 to 200 in steps of 10.
  • Price per million tokens: menu of $20.00, $2.00, $0.20, and $0.07.
  • Redo challenges and Defaults: start the challenges again, or reset the controls.

Costs are shown to the cent, and to the tenth of a cent when under $1.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner will calculate the yearly AI inference cost per student from tokens per session, sessions per day, school days, and price per million tokens, to within one cent, in three of three challenges. (Bloom level: Apply.)

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Teachers, administrators, school board members, education policymakers, and parents.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • AI inference cost, token, and price per million tokens, from the section "AI Inference Cost" in Chapter 4.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Calculate (6 min). Work the three challenges on paper first, then type each answer. Read the working shown after each one.
  2. Compare (4 min). After the controls unlock, keep the usage fixed and switch between $20.00 and $0.07. How many times larger is the cost at $20.00?
  3. Explore (4 min). At $0.07, raise tokens per session and sessions per day to their maximums. Is the cost still small next to $15,600 per pupil?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim, then check each answer by using it.

  1. A district uses 20,000 tokens per session, 1 session a day, 180 days, at $20.00 per million tokens. What is the yearly cost per student? ($72.00. 3.6 million tokens × $20.00 per million.)
  2. The same usage at $0.07 per million tokens? (About $0.25.)
  3. Which input changed the cost most between 2022 and 2024? (The price per million tokens, which fell more than 280-fold.)
  4. Is a capable AI tutor out of reach for a public school on cost alone? (Not at these prices: inference is a tiny share of per-pupil spending. Other costs, such as training and oversight, still matter.)

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. The 2025 AI Index Report. Stanford HAI. Reports the fall in the price of GPT-3.5-level performance from about $20 to about $0.07 per million tokens.
  2. Large language model. Wikipedia. How language models process text as tokens.
  3. Lexical analysis: tokens. Wikipedia. What a token is in computing.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
The terms artificial intelligence, machine learning, generative AI, large language model, and AI agent form a ladder: each rung is a narrower kind of the one above it. Every large language model is generative AI, and every generative system is machine learning.

The left side shows six categories as nested regions, with Not AI outside them all and AI agent innermost. For each of eight example systems you click the narrowest region that fits and press Submit. Clicking a region also shows its definition.

The examples are illustrative, written for Chapter 4. They are shuffled once per session.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
Nothing moves until you act, and the MicroSim does not store your answers.

  • Nested regions: click a region to select it and read its definition. The innermost region you click is the one selected.
  • Submit: commits your choice. Two attempts per example; only the first counts.
  • Next: moves to the next example; after the eighth it shows your score.
  • Try again: reshuffles the examples and starts over.

Choose the narrowest category whose definition the example meets, not just the one whose topic word sounds right.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner will classify eight example systems into the narrowest of six categories (Not AI, AI without machine learning, Machine learning, Generative AI, Large language model, AI agent), correctly placing at least seven of eight on the first attempt. (Bloom level: Understand.)

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Teachers, administrators, school board members, education policymakers, and parents.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • The terms artificial intelligence, machine learning, generative AI, large language model, and AI agent, from the section "A Ladder of Terms" in Chapter 4.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Read the regions (2 min). Click each region once and read its definition.
  2. Classify (6 min). Place all eight examples. Before you submit, say which defining feature decided your choice: learning from data, creating content, using language, or taking actions.
  3. Discuss (3 min). Why do the spam filter and the course-failure predictor land in the same region? What is the only difference between the chatbot and the quiz-website builder?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim, then check each answer by using it.

  1. A thermostat switches the heat on below 68°F. Which category? (Not AI. It follows one fixed rule.)
  2. A 1990s chess program uses rules its programmers wrote. Which category? (AI without machine learning.)
  3. A tool turns text into new spoken audio. Why is it not a large language model? (It creates audio, not language, so it is Generative AI.)
  4. What makes a system an AI agent rather than a chatbot? (It takes multi-step actions with tools toward a goal, instead of stopping after it answers.)

docs.text:
1. Artificial intelligence. Wikipedia. The field and its history.
  2. Machine learning. Wikipedia. Systems that learn patterns from data.
  3. Generative artificial intelligence. Wikipedia. Systems that create new text, images, and audio.
  4. Intelligent agent. Wikipedia. Agents that act toward goals.

docs.title: AI Tutor Design Judge
docs.text:
Run the AI Tutor Design Judge MicroSim Fullscreen Chapter 12: AI Guardrails: Teaching Thinking Without Over-Reliance

To edit the sketch, paste the contents of ai-tutor-design-judge.js into the p5.js editor and set the editor's p5.js version to 2.x. The learning content is in the CONFIG block at the top of the file.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
This chapter names five guardrails for an AI tutor:

  • G1 hints instead of answers
  • G2 grounded in the course's content
  • G3 math and facts checked by a trusted tool
  • G4 logs teachers can review
  • G5 age and topic limits

G1 comes first. In the Turkish high-school study, open GPT-4 access lowered later exam scores by about 17 percent, while a hint-first version removed most of the harm. So the rule checks G1 before it counts the rest:

  1. G1 absent: Likely to harm learning.
  2. G1 present, 1 to 3 guardrails in all: Mixed: needs more guardrails.
  3. G1 present, 4 or 5 guardrails in all: Likely to help.

The guardrails and the rule are this chapter's recommended practice, drawn from the design contrast in the Turkish study. The six designs are fictional.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text: Read the design and its list of guardrails, then choose one of the three verdicts. Press Show the five guardrails to see what each code means. A wrong first answer gives a hint and lets you choose again, but only the first answer counts toward First-try correct. After six designs, the results screen shows your score and lets you review the designs you missed.

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:
• Choice buttons: commit an answer. A wrong first answer gives a hint and lets you choose again; only the first answer counts.
  • Show definitions: opens or closes the reference table. Reading it is exploration, not evidence.
  • Next: moves to the next item after feedback. On the results screen, Previous missed and Next missed step through what you missed.
  • Play again: starts a practice run with the items reshuffled. Practice runs do not change the first-run score.

Nothing moves until you act, and the MicroSim does not store your answers.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner can judge whether each of six AI tutor designs is likely to harm learning, a mixed case, or likely to help, by applying the five-guardrail rule, correctly judging at least five of six on the first attempt. (Bloom level: Evaluate.)

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Teachers, administrators, school board members, policymakers, and parents.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • AI guardrails, hints instead of answers, guided AI versus open AI, and the five guardrails G1 to G5, from the section "Guardrails: Guided AI Versus Open AI" in Chapter 12

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Judge (6 min). Work through the six designs. Check G1 first, then count all the guardrails.
  2. Compare (3 min). HomeworkHelper has three guardrails and fails. HintBot has one and is Mixed. Explain the difference.
  3. Apply (5 min). Pick an AI tool your school uses or is considering. Which of G1 to G5 does it have? What is its verdict?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Mastery is 5 of 6 correct on the first try. Only the first answer to each design on the first run counts. Then ask learners to answer these without the MicroSim:

  1. A tutor has G2, G3, G4, and G5 but gives answers on request. Verdict? (Likely to harm learning. G1 is absent.)
  2. A tutor has G1 and G4 only. Verdict? (Mixed: needs more guardrails.)
  3. Does a more powerful model need fewer guardrails? (No. The rule looks at the design, not the model.)

docs.text:
1. Generative AI Can Harm Learning. Bastani and colleagues. The Turkish study behind the G1 rule.
  2. Intelligent tutoring system. Wikipedia. How tutoring systems are designed and evaluated.
  3. Retrieval-augmented generation. Wikipedia. One way to ground a tutor in the course's content (G2).
  4. Socratic questioning. Wikipedia. The questioning style behind hint-first tutoring.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Alpha School and Unbound Academy use the same adaptive software, 2 Hour Learning. They are not the same program. Alpha is an in-person private school that charges about $40,000 (Austin) to about $65,000 (newer campuses) a year, and it has an afternoon of workshops and projects led by adult guides. Unbound is a free online charter school in Arizona, approved by a 4–3 vote, with no in-person afternoon.

The MicroSim shows nine facts, one at a time. You decide whether each is true of Alpha only, Unbound only, or both. At the end, the facts are grouped. The shared software is only one fact; the facts that only Alpha has are the people and the afternoon. The pair shows a benefit and a risk. The software lets students move at their own pace, but Unbound, which has the software without the adults and the afternoon, reported early results below state averages. The book's response is that the software is not the model: a school that copies it must also plan the people and the afternoon. Several details are still unfolding, so check them against the sources.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the fact in the white box.
  2. Click the bin you think fits. The button turns blue.
  3. Press Submit. The box below the fact says whether you are right and why.
  4. If you are wrong, the button you chose turns orange. Choose again and press Submit. The second try does not change the score. After a second miss, the right answer turns green.
  5. Press Next to go on. After the last fact, press Finish to see your score, with the facts grouped as Alpha only, Unbound only, and both.
  6. Press Start over at any time to reshuffle and begin again.

Only your first try on each fact counts toward the score. The facts are shuffled each run. Nothing moves until you act, and the MicroSim does not store your answers.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner can compare Alpha School and Unbound Academy by placing nine facts as true of Alpha only, Unbound only, or both, correctly placing at least eight of nine on the first attempt. (Bloom level: Understand.)

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Teachers, school administrators, school board members, education policymakers, and parents.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Alpha School, Unbound Academy, 2 Hour Learning, Alpha adult guides, and "software is not the model," from the sections "Case 1" and "Case 2" in Chapter 22.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Recall (2 min). List what you remember about each school before you start.
  2. Compare (5 min). Place all nine facts. Aim for 8 of 9 on the first try.
  3. Explain (4 min). Using the grouped facts, explain why the same software can lead to different results.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim, then check each answer by using it.

  1. Which school uses the 2 Hour Learning software? (Both.)
  2. Which school has an in-person afternoon led by adult guides? (Alpha only.)
  3. Do the two schools differ only in price? (No. They also differ in delivery (in person or online), the adults, and the afternoon.)

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Alpha School. Wikipedia. Overview of the school and its two-hour model.
  2. What public schools and parents can learn from a $40,000-a-year private school. The 74. A report on Alpha School.
  3. Tucson families join free AI-powered online school. KOLD News. A report on Unbound Academy.

docs.title: Anatomy of a Learning Record
docs.text:
Run the Anatomy of a Learning Record MicroSim Fullscreen Chapter 8: Tracking Mastery: xAPI, Learning Record Stores, and MicroSims

You can add this MicroSim to any web page with this iframe:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/ai-native-schools/sims/anatomy-of-a-learning-record/main.html"
        height="720px"
        width="100%"
        scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Parents and teachers often ask of an adaptive textbook, "How does it know?" This infographic answers with one picture. A student moves a slider in a MicroSim. The page sends a short xAPI statement, drawn as an envelope holding three linked tiles: the actor, the verb and the object, with the result pinned to the corner. The envelope travels to a filing-cabinet server, the Learning Record Store, which keeps each student's learning record.

From the cabinet, two things happen. A teacher's dashboard shows learning analytics across the class, and a learning graph lights up the next concept the student is ready for. No live AI model is involved: the choice is a lookup in a stored record, using a stated rule and a map.

The scene also shows both sides of the story. The open drawer full of folders is the risk: a detailed history of a child's learning is sensitive data. The key on the student's lanyard is the school's response: collect the minimum, and keep the record under the student's and family's control.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
• Explore: hover over a numbered marker or a label to read about that part of the scene. Several callouts include a tip at the bottom.
  • Quiz: click Quiz. The sim names a part of the scene, and you click the marker where it lives. Your score shows next to the buttons.
  • Calibrate (authors): open main.html?edit=true to drag markers, then copy the JSON into data.json.

docs.title: The 11 Callouts
docs.text:
1. MicroSim in the browser: the laptop screen with a slider
  2. xAPI statement: the glowing envelope
  3. Actor: who did it, recorded as a code, not a name
  4. Verb: what they did, such as answered or experienced
  5. Object: the question or simulation they acted on
  6. Result: the optional outcome, such as a score of 0.8
  7. Learning Record Store: the filing-cabinet server
  8. Learning record: the open drawer, a sensitive history
  9. Teacher dashboard: learning analytics across the class
  10. Learning graph: the next ready concept lights up
  11. Student-controlled data: the key on the lanyard

The scene is a text-free SVG made by make-learning-record-svg.py in this folder. The script prints the marker positions used in data.json.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will trace one student action from a MicroSim to a teacher's dashboard, naming the parts of an xAPI statement and the role of the Learning Record Store, and explain how the record is kept under student control.

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Teachers, school leaders and parents.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10 minutes.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (5 minutes): hover over all 11 callouts in number order, following the click from the laptop to the dashboard and the learning graph.
  2. Quiz (3 minutes): run Quiz mode until you can find every callout without hovering first.
  3. Apply (2 minutes): write the statement for one action in your own class as a sentence: who, did what, to what, with what result. Then name one item you would not record, and why.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: The learner finds at least 9 of 11 callouts in Quiz mode and can explain to a parent, in two sentences, what is recorded and who controls it.

  • Experience API - Wikipedia
  • What is Learning Analytics? - Society for Learning Analytics Research
  • Chapter 8: Tracking Mastery - source of the Maya worked examples and the five student-control principles

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
This poster shows one homework question handled two ways. In the middle, a six-pack of juice, a stack of coins and a question mark stand for the question used throughout Chapter 12: a six-pack costs $4.50, so what is the price per bottle? Both tutors may run on the same underlying model. What differs is the design.

On the left, an open chatbot sends one big, finished answer with a checkmark. It is fast and always available, which is the benefit. The student leans back with a blank sheet and an empty thought cloud, which is the risk: over-reliance, where the tool does the thinking and the student cannot do the task without it. On the right, a guided tutor sends a chain of short bubbles, a question, a hint and a smaller question, and the student's last bubble is their own correct answer. That student is writing on paper, and their thought cloud holds the four thinking skills: decomposition, pattern recognition, abstraction and algorithmic thinking. The shield and guard rail at the bottom are the school's response: the guardrails that turn the left phone into the right one.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
• Explore: hover over a panel to see its name, then click it to read a summary and facts. Most facts use the chapter's juice problem and Dev's conversation.
  • Quiz Me: click Quiz Me. The sim asks a question, and you click the panel that answers it. Your score shows next to the buttons.
  • Calibrate (authors): open main.html?edit=true to drag zone corners, then copy the JSON into data.json.

docs.title: The 6 Zones
docs.text:
1. Answer machine: the orange phone of an open AI chatbot, with one big answer bubble, a checkmark and a lightning bolt
  2. Left with: offloading: the student leaning back under an empty, dashed thought cloud
  3. The same question: the juice six-pack, coins and question mark in the center
  4. The guardrails: the shield and guard rail ringed by a book, a calculator, an eye, an hourglass and a padlock
  5. Left with: thinking: the student writing on paper under a thought cloud of four skill icons
  6. Thinking tutor: the teal phone of a guided AI tutor, with a chain of question, hint and attempt bubbles

The image is a text-free SVG made by make-tutor-poster-svg.py in this folder. The script also prints the zone percentages used in data.json.

To practice the ideas on this poster, try the Tutor Reply Hint Levels MicroSim, which rates tutor replies on the four-level hint ladder, and the Four Thinking Skills Sorter, which sorts student activities into the four thinking skills.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text:
The learner will compare an open AI chatbot with a guided AI tutor answering the same homework question, and explain how guardrails change what the student is left with.

Bloom level: Analyze. Bloom verb: compare.

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Teachers, instructional coaches, and school and district leaders choosing or configuring an AI tutor.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10 minutes.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (5 minutes): click the center question first, then the two phones, then the two students. Finish with the guardrails.
  2. Quiz (3 minutes): run Quiz Me until you can answer every question on the first click.
  3. Apply (2 minutes): think of an AI tool your students use now. Which phone does it look like? Which guardrail from the shield would move it to the right side?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: The learner answers at least 6 of 7 quiz questions correctly and can name two guardrails that would make a specific tool behave like the guided tutor.

  • Socratic questioning - Wikipedia

docs.title: Artifact, Value, or Assumption?

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Edgar Schein describes organizational culture in three layers: cultural artifacts you can observe, espoused values the organization states, and basic assumptions that no one states but everyone acts on. You read eight statements about a school and place each in a layer.

Ask one question: can it be observed, is it stated, or can it only be inferred from behavior? In this set the stated values and the basic assumptions point in different directions, which is why assumptions usually win. The statements are illustrative, written for this chapter.

Layer Definition Cultural artifact Something visible or audible that you can observe directly Espoused value A belief or goal the organization states Basic assumption An unspoken, taken-for-granted belief, usually inferred from behavior

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
• Read the statement on the card. The progress strip shows which statement you are on and your running score, "First-try correct".
  • Choose one of the three layers with the buttons. If your first answer is wrong, a hint appears and you choose again. Only your first answer counts toward the score.
  • Show definitions opens a table of the layers. Reading it is exploration, not evidence of mastery.
  • Next moves on after you read the feedback. On the results screen, Previous missed and Next missed page through the ones you missed, and Play again reshuffles the statements for a practice run.

docs.title: Good to Know
docs.text:
• Mastery is 7 of 8 correct on the first try, on the first run. Practice runs give the same feedback but do not change the first-run score.
  • The statements are shuffled once per run. Nothing moves until you act, and the MicroSim does not store your answers.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will distinguish eight statements about a school as cultural artifacts, espoused values, or basic assumptions, correctly placing at least seven of eight on the first attempt. (Bloom level: Analyze.)

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Teachers, school administrators, school board members, education policymakers, and parents.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Cultural artifacts, espoused values, basic assumptions, and culture assessment, from the section "Culture, Assessed" in Chapter 18.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Predict (2 min). Does a school's mission statement describe its culture? Write yes or no and why.
  2. Distinguish (5 min). Place the eight statements. For each, ask whether it is observed, stated, or inferred.
  3. Discuss (3 min). Find a stated value in the set that a basic assumption contradicts. Which one wins in practice?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim, then check each answer by using it.

  1. The school day is divided into fifty-minute periods. Which layer? (Cultural artifact: it is observable structure.)
  2. The handbook says parents are partners. Which layer? (Espoused value: it is a stated belief.)
  3. Can basic assumptions be read off the walls? (No. They are inferred from behavior.)
  4. Is a visible practice the same as a belief? (No. The practice is an artifact; the belief behind it may be an assumption.)

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Organizational culture. Wikipedia. Includes Schein's three levels of culture.
  2. Edgar Schein. Wikipedia. The psychologist who developed the three-layer model.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Schools and vendors make claims about results. Six questions expose most weak claims:

  1. Where did the students start?
  2. Compared with whom?
  3. Who measured it, and who paid?
  4. Has anyone outside checked it?
  5. How big, and for how long?
  6. What was actually measured?

The MicroSim shows six claims, one at a time. Each one is built to be missing one thing: a starting point, a comparison, an independent measure, an outside check, a size, or the thing measured. You pick the question that exposes it. Every claim sounds impressive until the right question is asked. The claims are illustrative, written in the style of real claims.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the claim in the white box.
  2. Click the question you think fits. The button turns blue.
  3. Press Submit. The box below the claim says whether you are right and why.
  4. If you are wrong, the button you chose turns orange. Choose again and press Submit. The second try does not change the score. After a second miss, the right answer turns green.
  5. Press Next to go on. After the last claim, press Finish to see your score, with each claim and its best question.
  6. Press Start over at any time to reshuffle and begin again.

Only your first try on each claim counts toward the score. The claims are shuffled each run. Nothing moves until you act, and the MicroSim does not store your answers.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner can classify six result claims by the question that best exposes the weakness in each, correctly matching at least five of six on the first attempt. (Bloom level: Understand.)

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Teachers, school administrators, school board members, education policymakers, and parents.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • The six questions for evaluating result claims, from the section "Evaluating Result Claims" in Chapter 23, and Chapters 2 and 3.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Recall (2 min). Say the six questions without looking.
  2. Classify (5 min). Match all six claims. Aim for 5 of 6 on the first try.
  3. Apply (5 min). Find a real result claim from a vendor or a news story and ask all six questions of it.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim, then check each answer by using it.

  1. "94 percent of teachers said they love the program." Which question exposes it? (What was actually measured? Satisfaction is not learning.)
  2. Is any claim with a number evidence? (No. A number without a starting point, a comparison, or an outside check proves little.)
  3. "A new preprint shows an AI tutor doubles learning." Which question? (Has anyone outside checked it? A preprint has not been peer reviewed.)

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Preprint. Wikipedia. Research shared before peer review.
  2. Selection bias. Wikipedia. Why results depend on who enrolled.
  3. What Works Clearinghouse. Institute of Education Sciences. Independent reviews of education research.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
The revised Bloom's Taxonomy (Anderson and Krathwohl, 2001) sorts learning outcomes into six levels of thinking: Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyze, Evaluate, and Create. The top three are called higher-order thinking.

This MicroSim shows twelve tasks from different subjects, one at a time, in a shuffled order. You choose the level each task asks for. The tasks mix subjects so you sort by the kind of thinking, not by the topic.

Three traps are built in. The verb alone does not decide the level. A longer or harder task is not always higher. Writing something is not automatically Create.

The tasks are illustrative, written for this chapter.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
• Read the task on the card, then press the level button you think fits.
  • Show definitions opens the one-line definition of each level. Reading it does not count against you.
  • If your first answer is wrong, you get a hint and a second try. Only the first try counts toward your score.
  • After the second try, the correct level and the reason appear. Press Next for the next task.
  • After all twelve tasks, the results screen shows your first-try score. Previous missed and Next missed step through the tasks you missed. Play again reshuffles the tasks for practice.

Mastery is 10 of 12 on the first try. Nothing moves until you choose, and the MicroSim does not store your answers.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner can classify twelve classroom tasks into the six levels of the 2001 revised Bloom's Taxonomy, placing at least 10 of 12 correctly on the first try. (Bloom level: Understand.)

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Teachers, administrators, school board members, policymakers, and parents.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • The six levels of Bloom's Taxonomy and the meaning of higher-order thinking, from Chapter 1.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Predict (2 min). Before you start, write down which level you think "Explain in your own words why ice floats" belongs to, and which level "Compare two accounts of the same battle" belongs to.
  2. Sort (8 min). Work through all twelve tasks. Use Show definitions whenever you are unsure.
  3. Discuss (5 min). Look at the tasks you missed. For each one, name the trap: the verb, the length, or the act of writing.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim.

  1. "Explain why ice floats" and "Compare two accounts of a battle" both ask the student to talk about an idea. Why are they at different levels? (Explaining restates an idea, which is Understand. Comparing breaks two sources into parts and relates them, which is Analyze.)
  2. Is "State the year the Constitution was signed" a higher level because it is a history task? (No. Recalling one fact is Remember.)
  3. Is every writing task Create? (No. Summarizing in writing is Understand. Composing a new story is Create.)

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Bloom's taxonomy. Wikipedia. The original 1956 framework and the 2001 revision.
  2. Bloom's Taxonomy. Vanderbilt University Center for Teaching. The six revised levels with sample verbs and classroom uses.
  3. Higher-order thinking. Wikipedia. Why the top levels are grouped together.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
The 21 concepts in Chapter 1 are not a list of separate vocabulary words. They depend on one another. This map shows those dependencies, taken from the book's own learning graph.

Each arrow points from a concept to a prerequisite it depends on. For example, the arrow from Per-Pupil Spending points to Public School Funding: you need to know where school money comes from before you can divide it per student. This direction is the reverse of many diagrams, which draw arrows from a prerequisite to what it enables.

Four concepts are gold: Education, Learning, Student, and Teacher. They have no prerequisites in this chapter. Every other concept rests on at least one of them.

The quiz asks six questions. For each, you select every direct prerequisite of a highlighted concept: the concepts its own arrows point to, not the ones further down the chain.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
• Explore. Click any concept to read its definition.
  • Press Start quiz. The concept for each question has a purple border.
  • Click concepts to select them (orange). Click again to unselect. Clear selection removes them all.
  • Press Submit. If the answer is wrong, a hint says whether you missed a prerequisite or picked an extra one, and you get a second try. Only the first try counts toward your score.
  • After a correct answer or a second wrong one, the correct prerequisites turn green and the arrows to them are highlighted. Press Next question.
  • After six questions you see your first-try score and any questions you missed.
  • Zoom in, Zoom out, and Reset change the view. You can drag the map to pan. The mouse wheel does not zoom, so the page scrolls normally.

Mastery is 5 of 6 on the first try. The MicroSim does not store your answers.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner can explain which earlier concepts a Chapter 1 concept depends on by selecting its direct prerequisites on the concept map, with at least 5 of 6 questions correct. (Bloom level: Understand.)

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Teachers, administrators, school board members, policymakers, and parents.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • All 21 concepts in Chapter 1, and the meaning of a dependency arrow from the section "Putting the Building Blocks Together."

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Predict (2 min). Before you open the quiz, guess how many direct prerequisites Higher-Order Thinking has. Many people guess three or more because it sounds advanced.
  2. Explore (4 min). Click the four gold concepts. Then trace the chain from Per-Pupil Spending down to Education. How many steps is it?
  3. Quiz (6 min). Answer the six questions. Follow only the arrows that leave the highlighted concept.
  4. Discuss (3 min). Why does this book draw arrows toward prerequisites? What would a teacher do with the map when a student struggles with Learning Gap?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim.

  1. What are the direct prerequisites of Direct Instruction? (Teacher, Learning, and Classroom.)
  2. Higher-Order Thinking sounds advanced. How many direct prerequisites does it have? (One: Bloom's Taxonomy.)
  3. An arrow goes from Learning Gap to Learning Outcome. Which one must a learner understand first? (Learning Outcome. The arrow points to the prerequisite.)
  4. Name the four concepts with no prerequisites. (Education, Learning, Student, and Teacher.)

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Concept map. Wikipedia. Diagrams that show how ideas relate to one another.
  2. Directed acyclic graph. Wikipedia. The kind of graph a learning graph is: arrows with no loops.
  3. Knowledge space. Wikipedia. A model of which concepts a learner must know before others.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
How a student feels about a task depends on the gap between the task's challenge and what the student already knows. Both are rated on a 1-to-10 scale, and the gap is challenge minus prior knowledge.

Gap Without support With support (hint ladder) −2 or less Bored Bored −1 to 1 Engaged Engaged 2 to 3 Productive struggle Productive struggle 4 Overwhelmed Productive struggle 5 or more Overwhelmed Overwhelmed

Support matters at the edge. A gap of 4 overwhelms a student working alone, but a hint ladder keeps the same student making progress.

The MicroSim first gives you six scenarios. For each one you predict the state before it is revealed. After your results, Explore the model opens a map of every challenge and knowledge pair, colored by state, with sliders and a support checkbox.

This is an illustrative model, not measured data. It is based on the chapter's challenge-and-knowledge model and inspired by Csikszentmihalyi's research on flow.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
• Read the scenario: the task challenge, the student's prior knowledge, and whether support is on.
  • Work out the gap, then press the state you predict. Your prediction is final for each scenario.
  • The feedback shows the gap and the reason. Press Next for the next scenario.
  • After all six scenarios, the results screen shows your score. Explore the model opens the map. Move the two sliders and tick Support available to see which pairs change state.
  • Back to results returns to the results screen. Play again starts a practice run.

Mastery is 5 of 6 on the first run. Nothing moves until you choose, and the MicroSim does not store your answers.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner can distinguish whether a student is bored, engaged, in productive struggle, or overwhelmed by examining the gap between task challenge and prior knowledge and whether support is available, with at least 5 of 6 scenarios correct. (Bloom level: Analyze.)

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Teachers, administrators, school board members, policymakers, and parents.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Prior knowledge, student boredom, student engagement, productive struggle, and the four states of the challenge-minus-knowledge gap, from Chapter 2.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Predict (6 min). Work through the six scenarios. Write the gap on paper before you choose a state.
  2. Explore (5 min). Open Explore the model. Set challenge 8 and prior knowledge 4, then tick and untick support. Then try a gap of 3 and a gap of 5. When does support change the state?
  3. Discuss (4 min). A student is overwhelmed by a task with a gap of 4. Name two responses: one that lowers the challenge and one that adds support. Which keeps the learning goal intact?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim.

  1. A task is at level 5 and the student knows level 7. What is the state? (Bored. The gap is −2.)
  2. Does struggle always mean the task is too hard? (No. A gap of 2 or 3 is productive struggle, where effort pays off.)
  3. A gap of 4 overwhelms a student. Is making the task easier the only fix? (No. A hint ladder turns the same gap into productive struggle.)

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Flow (psychology). Wikipedia. Csikszentmihalyi's model of challenge and skill.
  2. Zone of proximal development. Wikipedia. What a learner can do with help but not yet alone.
  3. Instructional scaffolding. Wikipedia. Support that lets a learner work above their current level.
