docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Geoffrey Moore's chasm is the gap between early adopters, who like new things, and the early majority, pragmatists who want a complete solution that people like them already use. Each of six situations shows an innovation stuck at the chasm. You choose the move that best helps it cross: choose a beachhead, build the whole product, use a trusted reference, or add more features.

To choose well, first diagnose what the pragmatists lack: a focus, a complete solution, or a trusted peer. "Add more features" is never the best move in this set. The situations are illustrative, written for this chapter.

Move Definition Choose a beachhead Focus all effort on one narrow, well-defined group and make the innovation work completely there first Build the whole product Add the training, integration, support, and safeguards that make it work in practice Use a trusted reference Let a respected peer from a similar setting tell the story Add more features Extend what the product can do for the most enthusiastic users

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
• Read the situation on the card. The progress strip shows which situation you are on and your running score, "First-try correct".
  • Choose one of the four moves with the buttons. If your first answer is wrong, a hint appears and you choose again. Only your first answer counts toward the score.
  • Show definitions opens a table of the moves. Reading it is exploration, not evidence of mastery.
  • Next moves on after you read the feedback. On the results screen, Previous missed and Next missed page through the ones you missed, and Play again reshuffles the situations for a practice run.

docs.title: Good to Know
docs.text:
• Mastery is 5 of 6 correct on the first try, on the first run. Practice runs give the same feedback but do not change the first-run score.
  • The situations are shuffled once per run. Nothing moves until you act, and the MicroSim does not store your answers.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will apply Moore's chasm ideas by choosing, for each of six situations, the move that best helps an innovation cross from early adopters to the early majority, correctly choosing at least five of six on the first attempt. (Bloom level: Apply.)

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Teachers, school administrators, school board members, education policymakers, and parents.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • The chasm, pragmatist buyers, crossing the chasm, the beachhead strategy, the whole product, and opinion leaders, from the sections "Adopter Categories and the Adoption Curve" and "The Chasm" in Chapter 15.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Predict (2 min). Which move do vendors most often reach for when adoption stalls? Write your guess.
  2. Apply (8 min). Work through the six situations. For each one, say what the early majority is missing before you choose.
  3. Discuss (5 min). Build the whole product is the best move in three of the six situations. Why does it come up so often in schools?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim, then check each answer by using it.

  1. A district gave a little support to all 40 schools at once and none has a visible success. Which move? (Choose a beachhead: focus on one group first.)
  2. Teachers say the tool has no training and does not connect to their login. Which move? (Build the whole product.)
  3. Will more features persuade pragmatists? (No. Pragmatists need a complete, supported solution and a trusted reference.)
  4. A skeptical teacher asks, "Has anyone like me made this work?" Which move? (Use a trusted reference.)

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Crossing the Chasm. Wikipedia. Summary of Moore's book and the chasm idea.
  2. Technology adoption life cycle. Wikipedia. The adopter groups and the gap between early adopters and the early majority.
  3. Diffusion of innovations. Wikipedia. Rogers' theory that Moore builds on.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Chapter 19 describes six microstrategies, small moves a leader can make with one person or one team: a teacher champion, a pilot classroom, instructional coaching, shrinking the first step, peer observation, and a professional learning community. You read eight teacher situations and choose the microstrategy that best fits each one.

Diagnose first: what concern does the person have, and what kind of adopter are they? Then pick the move that answers it. Two situations call for coaching and two for a pilot, for different reasons. The situations are illustrative, written for this chapter.

Microstrategy Description Teacher champion A respected colleague shares honestly how it went Pilot classroom Try it in one class, with a baseline and a plan, before committing Instructional coaching A trained colleague works with the teacher over time Shrink the first step Ask for one very small first action Peer observation Watch a colleague teach, for learning, not evaluation Professional learning community A team meets weekly to examine evidence and plan

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
• Read the situation on the card. The progress strip shows which situation you are on and your running score, "First-try correct".
  • Choose one of the six microstrategies with the buttons. If your first answer is wrong, a hint appears and you choose again. Only your first answer counts toward the score.
  • Show descriptions opens a table of the microstrategies. Reading it is exploration, not evidence of mastery.
  • Next moves on after you read the feedback. On the results screen, Previous missed and Next missed page through the ones you missed, and Play again reshuffles the situations for a practice run.

docs.title: Good to Know
docs.text:
• Mastery is 7 of 8 correct on the first try, on the first run. Practice runs give the same feedback but do not change the first-run score.
  • The situations are shuffled once per run. Nothing moves until you act, and the MicroSim does not store your answers.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will apply the matching tables by choosing the microstrategy that best fits each of eight teacher situations, correctly choosing at least seven of eight on the first attempt. (Bloom level: Apply.)

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Teachers, school administrators, school board members, education policymakers, and parents.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • The six microstrategies and the matching tables in the section "Matching the Strategy to the Person" in Chapter 19.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Predict (2 min). When teachers struggle with a new practice, what do schools usually offer? Write it down.
  2. Apply (8 min). Work through the eight situations. Name the concern before you choose the move.
  3. Discuss (5 min). The two coaching situations call for coaching for different reasons. What are they?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim, then check each answer by using it.

  1. A teacher says, "I want to see what this looks like in a real class." Which microstrategy? (Peer observation.)
  2. A late-majority teacher wants data from a classroom in the same building. Which microstrategy? (Pilot classroom.)
  3. Does more training solve every concern? (No. The move depends on the concern; an overwhelmed teacher needs a smaller first step.)
  4. Is a mandate a microstrategy? (No. A mandate does not answer anyone's concern.)

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Professional learning community. Wikipedia. Teams of teachers who meet to examine evidence and plan.
  2. Concerns-Based Adoption Model (CBAM). SEDL. Archive of the CBAM tools: stages of concern, levels of use, and innovation configurations.
  3. Diffusion of innovations. Wikipedia. Rogers' theory of how innovations spread, including the adopter categories.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Teachers learning a new model need instructional coaches, and a coach can support only so many teachers. Coach capacity sets the speed limit of a rollout.

Coaches needed = teachers ÷ teachers per coach, rounded up. Coaches come in whole people, so 150 teachers at 12 per coach need 12.5 coaches, which means 13. Teachers supported = coaches × teachers per coach. Eight coaches at 12 each support 96 teachers.

The MicroSim starts with three questions. After them, three sliders unlock: teachers to support, teachers per coach, and coaches available. The coaches needed, the gap, and a row of coach squares update at once. When there are fewer coaches than needed, the sim says Slow the rollout. The capacity of 12 is illustrative; set your own.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read Question 1. Type your answer and press Check. Type only the number.
  2. If you are wrong, you get a hint and one more try. After a second miss, the sim shows the answer and the working. Only a first-try answer counts toward the score.
  3. Press Next question. After Question 3, press See the results.
  4. The three sliders unlock. Change them and watch the results update at once.
  5. Defaults puts the inputs back to their starting values. Start over returns to Question 1.

The results stay hidden until you answer the three questions. Nothing moves until you act, and the MicroSim does not store your answers.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner can calculate the number of coaches needed for a given number of teachers and coach capacity, and the number of teachers a given number of coaches can support, correctly answering three of three questions. (Bloom level: Apply.)

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Teachers, school administrators, school board members, education policymakers, and parents.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Scaling a pilot, instructional coaching, coach capacity, and rounding up, from the section "Scaling Without Breaking" in Chapter 21 and from Chapter 19.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Calculate (5 min). Answer the three questions. Round up where you must.
  2. Explore (4 min). Lower teachers per coach from 12 to 6. What happens to the coaches needed?
  3. Plan (5 min). Set the sliders for your own district. How many teachers can the next phase of the rollout include?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim, then check each answer by using it.

  1. 400 teachers at 12 per coach. How many coaches? (400 ÷ 12 = 33.3, rounded up to 34.)
  2. Can the coaches needed be a fraction? (No. A coach is a whole person, so always round up.)
  3. Does buying more software licenses speed up the rollout? (Not if coaches are the limit. The rollout can go only as fast as coaches can support teachers.)

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. The effect of teacher coaching on instruction and achievement. Kraft, Blazar, and Hogan. A meta-analysis of coaching studies.
  2. Floor and ceiling functions. Wikipedia. Rounding up to a whole number.
  3. Professional learning community. Wikipedia. Teachers supporting each other through change.

docs.title: Contract Clause Review
docs.text:
Run the Contract Clause Review MicroSim Fullscreen Chapter 21: Implementing the AI-Native Model Responsibly

To edit the sketch, paste the contents of contract-clause-review.js into the p5.js editor and set the editor's p5.js version to 2.x. The learning content is in the CONFIG block at the top of the file.

You can add this MicroSim to any web page with this iframe:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/ai-native-schools/sims/contract-clause-review/main.html"
        height="380px"
        width="100%"
        scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Before a district signs a contract for an AI product, someone has to read the clauses that protect students. The MicroSim shows eight clauses from a fictional contract, one at a time. You give each one a verdict:

Verdict Meaning Acceptable Protects the district and families as written Needs change Not harmful in intent, but too vague or one-sided; negotiate a fix Red flag Allows a use or risk the district should not accept; remove before signing

Check each clause for a deadline, a cap, an exit, and any use of data beyond providing the service. Two clauses cover breach notice: one sets a firm 72-hour deadline and one promises notice "in a timely manner." They get different verdicts. The clauses are fictional, and this MicroSim is not legal advice.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the clause in the white box.
  2. Click the verdict you think fits. The button turns blue.
  3. Press Submit. The box below the clause says whether you are right and why.
  4. If you are wrong, the button you chose turns orange. Choose again and press Submit. The second try does not change the score. After a second miss, the right answer turns green.
  5. Press Next to go on. After the last clause, press Finish to see your score, with the clauses grouped by verdict.
  6. Press Start over at any time to reshuffle and begin again.
  7. Check Show definitions to read what each verdict means. Uncheck it to go back.

Only your first try on each clause counts toward the score. The clauses are shuffled each run. Nothing moves until you act, and the MicroSim does not store your answers.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner can judge eight contract clauses from an AI product contract as acceptable, needing change, or a red flag, correctly judging at least seven of eight on the first attempt. (Bloom level: Evaluate.)

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Teachers, school administrators, school board members, education policymakers, and parents.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Contract due diligence, vendor lock-in, data ownership, breach notice, deletion, and the contract checklist, from the section "Buying Responsibly" in Chapter 21 and from Chapter 10.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Review the checklist (2 min). Check Show definitions and read the three verdicts.
  2. Judge (7 min). Give all eight clauses a verdict. Aim for 7 of 8 on the first try.
  3. Rewrite (5 min). Rewrite one "Needs change" clause so it becomes acceptable.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim, then check each answer by using it.

  1. "Vendor will notify the district of a breach in a timely manner." What is the verdict? (Needs change. There is no deadline that can be enforced.)
  2. Is every clause that favors the vendor a red flag? (No. A one-sided clause can often be fixed by negotiation. A red flag allows a use or risk the district should not accept.)
  3. A vendor says the student data it trains on is anonymous. Is that enough? (No. Using student data to train the vendor's own models is a use beyond providing the service.)

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Vendor lock-in. Wikipedia. How long terms and closed formats make it hard to leave a vendor.
  2. Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act. Wikipedia. The main U.S. law on student education records.
  3. Common Sense Privacy Program. Common Sense Media. Privacy evaluations of education products.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
The price of software is only one line in the cost of a digital textbook. This MicroSim itemizes the yearly cost per student at Levels 2, 3, and 4: content and hosting, a records platform, privacy governance, guardrail log review, teacher training, and, at Level 4, AI inference.

Three challenges come first: the Level 3 cost per student, the Level 4 cost per student at $2.00 per million tokens, and the Level 4 district cost for 12,000 students at $0.20. Then the controls unlock and the three totals, the district totals, and each level's share of $15,600 per-pupil spending update at once. Check Device purchased to add a $75.00 device share ($300 over four years).

All cost items are illustrative; replace them with your own quotes. The $20.00 and $0.07 prices are the Stanford AI Index 2025 values from Chapter 4; $2.00 and $0.20 are illustrative.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
Nothing moves until you act, and the MicroSim does not store your answers.

  • Your answer box and Check: type a dollar amount and press Check (or Enter). Two attempts per challenge; only the first counts.
  • Next: moves on; after challenge 3 it unlocks the controls.
  • Tokens per session, Sessions per day, School days: sliders for AI usage at Level 4.
  • Price per million tokens: menu of $0.07, $0.20, $2.00, and $20.00.
  • Students: slider from 100 to 20,000.
  • Device purchased: checkbox that adds $75.00 per student per year at every level.
  • Redo challenges and Defaults: start the challenges again, or reset the controls.

District costs are shown to the dollar; per-student costs to the cent.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner will calculate the yearly cost per student and the district cost for Level 2, Level 3, and Level 4 textbooks from itemized costs, to within one cent per student, in three of three challenges. (Bloom level: Apply.)

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Teachers, administrators, school board members, education policymakers, and parents.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 15 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Cost per student, cost modeling, total cost of ownership, and the cost items for each level, from the section "Putting a Cost on Each Level" in Chapter 7.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Calculate (6 min). Add the Level 3 column, then the Level 4 column with inference, then multiply by 12,000.
  2. Compare (4 min). Check Device purchased. Which is larger at Level 3: the device share or all the software items together?
  3. Explore (4 min). Set the price to $20.00 and raise usage. At what point does Level 4 cost more than the device?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim, then check each answer by using it.

  1. What does Level 3 cost per student per year without a device? ($12.80.)
  2. Level 4 at 3.6 million tokens and $2.00 per million? ($23.00, including $7.20 of inference.)
  3. Is a free textbook free to run? (No. Hosting, training, and governance still cost money.)
  4. Is software the main cost of a digital textbook? (Not when devices are bought: the $75.00 device share is larger than every software item combined at Levels 2 and 3.)

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Total cost of ownership. Wikipedia. Counting every cost over the life of a purchase.
  2. Open educational resources. Wikipedia. Free-to-use content that still has running costs.
  3. The 2025 AI Index Report. Stanford HAI. Reports the fall in the price of GPT-3.5-level performance from about $20 to about $0.07 per million tokens.

docs.title: Crossing the Chasm
docs.text:
Run the Crossing the Chasm MicroSim Fullscreen Chapter 15: Technology Adoption and the Diffusion of Innovation

You can add this MicroSim to any web page with this iframe:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/ai-native-schools/sims/crossing-the-chasm-overlay/main.html"
        height="720px"
        width="100%"
        scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
This infographic draws Rogers' adoption curve as a landscape. The ground rises and falls in the shape of the bell curve, so each adopter group stands on its share of the curve. Geoffrey Moore's chasm is a deep canyon between the early adopters (visionaries) and the early majority (pragmatists). The far rim is higher than the near cliff, because pragmatists hold an innovation to a higher standard than visionaries do.

The scene also shows Moore's two main ideas for getting across: a half-built bridge stands for the whole product, and a landing boat stands for the beachhead. A figure leaping off the end of the unfinished bridge shows the risk the chapter calls crossing by hope: spreading a pilot, unchanged, to everyone.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
• Explore: hover over a numbered marker or a label to read about that part of the scene. Many callouts include a tip at the bottom.
  • Quiz: click Quiz. The sim names a part of the scene, and you click the marker where it lives. Your score shows next to the buttons.
  • Calibrate (authors): open main.html?edit=true to drag markers, then copy the JSON into data.json.

docs.title: The 13 Callouts
docs.text:
1. Innovators (about 2.5%): technology enthusiasts, carrying lanterns
  2. Crack 1: the small gap between innovators and early adopters
  3. Early adopters: visionaries (about 13.5%): figures with telescopes on the ridge
  4. The chasm: the canyon between early adopters and the early majority
  5. Whole product: the half-built bridge, one plank per needed piece
  6. Crossing by hope: the risk of spreading an unchanged pilot to everyone
  7. Beachhead: the landing boat on one small beach
  8. Bowling pins: each group won helps win the next, similar group
  9. References: pragmatists listening to other pragmatists
  10. Early majority: pragmatists (about 34%): the broad slope up from the far rim
  11. Crack 2: the gap between the early and the late majority
  12. Late majority: conservatives (about 34%): the slope down from the summit
  13. Laggards: skeptics (about 16%): a few figures standing apart

The landscape image is a text-free SVG made by make-chasm-svg.py in this folder, so the ground line follows the bell curve exactly. If you prefer a painted look, image-prompt.md describes the same scene for a text-to-image tool.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will identify the five adopter groups, the chasm, the whole product and the beachhead on a picture of the adoption curve, and explain why an innovation can stall between early adopters and the early majority.

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: School and district leaders, teachers and instructional coaches.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10 minutes.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (5 minutes): hover over all 13 callouts. Note the two tips about visionaries and references.
  2. Quiz (3 minutes): run Quiz mode until you can find every callout without hovering first.
  3. Apply (2 minutes): name one innovation in your own school. Which group has it reached? What planks of its bridge are still missing?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: The learner finds at least 11 of 13 callouts in Quiz mode and can name two pieces of the whole product their own innovation still lacks.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Moore, G. A. (2014). Crossing the Chasm (3rd ed.). HarperBusiness.
  • Rogers, E. M. (2003). Diffusion of Innovations (5th ed.). Free Press.
  • Crossing the Chasm - Wikipedia

docs.title: Doubling Time Projection Calculator
docs.text:
Run the Doubling Time Projection Calculator MicroSim Fullscreen Chapter 5: Projecting AI Growth: Doubling Curves, Limits, and Uncertainty

To edit the sketch, paste the contents of doubling-time-projection-calculator.js into the p5.js editor and set the editor's p5.js version to 2.x. The learning content is in the CONFIG block near the top of the file.

You can add this MicroSim to any web page with this iframe:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/ai-native-schools/sims/doubling-time-projection-calculator/main.html"
        height="689px"
        width="100%"
        scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
If a quantity doubles at a steady rate, the time to reach a target is:

months to target = number of doublings × doubling time, where the number of doublings = log2(target ÷ start).

Starting from a 50-minute task horizon, 40 hours (2,400 minutes) is 48 times the start, which needs about 5.6 doublings. Three questions ask for the months to reach 40 hours at doubling times of 5, 4, and 6 months. Then the doubling-time slider and the target menu unlock, and a timeline and a bar chart show how the date moves.

This is an illustrative projection, not a forecast. The 50-minute start comes from Chapter 4; the 5-, 40-, and 160-hour targets are illustrative. The book uses a doubling time of about every five months.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
Nothing moves until you act, and the MicroSim does not store your answers.

  • Your answer box and Check: type a whole number of months and press Check (or Enter). Two attempts per question; only the first counts.
  • Next: moves on; after question 3 it unlocks the controls.
  • Doubling time: slider from 3 to 12 months.
  • Target: menu of 5, 40, or 160 hours.
  • Redo challenges and Defaults: start the questions again, or reset to 5 months and 40 hours.

The red marker on the timeline is your current setting; the blue markers are the 4-, 5-, and 6-month answers.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner will calculate how many months a 50-minute task horizon takes to reach 40 hours for doubling times of 4, 5, and 6 months, to within one month, and describe how the answer changes with the doubling time. (Bloom level: Apply.)

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Teachers, administrators, school board members, education policymakers, and parents.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Exponential growth, doubling time, number of doublings, trend extrapolation, and forecast uncertainty, from Chapter 5.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Calculate (5 min). Multiply 5.6 doublings by 5, 4, and 6 months on paper, then check each answer.
  2. Explore (5 min). Move the doubling time one month at a time. How far does the 40-hour date move each step?
  3. Discuss (4 min). A colleague says "40 hours will arrive in exactly 28 months." What would you add about uncertainty?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim, then check each answer by using it.

  1. Start 50 minutes, target 40 hours, doubling every 5 months. How many months? (About 28 (5.6 × 5).)
  2. The same at a 4-month and a 6-month doubling time? (About 22 and about 34 months.)
  3. Does 160 hours take four times as long as 40 hours? (No. It is only 2 more doublings: about 38 months at a 5-month doubling time.)
  4. Does a forecast have one answer? (No. A one-month change in doubling time moves the 40-hour date by about 5.6 months.)

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Doubling time. Wikipedia. The time for a growing quantity to double.
  2. Exponential growth. Wikipedia. Growth at a constant rate per period.
  3. Binary logarithm. Wikipedia. log2 counts how many doublings separate two values.
  4. Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Tasks. METR (2025), arXiv preprint. The source of the task-horizon method and the roughly 170-task suite.

docs.title: The EdTech Hype Cycle
docs.text:
Run the EdTech Hype Cycle MicroSim Fullscreen Chapter 15: Technology Adoption and the Diffusion of Innovation

You can add this MicroSim to any web page with this iframe:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/ai-native-schools/sims/edtech-hype-cycle-overlay/main.html"
        height="720px"
        width="100%"
        scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
This infographic draws the hype cycle as a landscape. The skyline is the curve itself: a steep climb from a rocket launch to a crowded summit, a long fall into a foggy valley, and a slow staircase up to a calm plateau. Six waves of educational technology sit on the curve where Chapter 15 places them: film, teaching machines, classroom computers, one-to-one tablets, MOOCs and generative AI.

Each wave went through its own cycle. The poster shows each one at the stage the chapter uses it to illustrate, so you can see the same shape repeat across a century. The placements are a reading of the evidence, not a measurement, and the hype cycle itself is a useful description, not a scientific law.

The poster also carries the book's story balance. The benefit: some technologies do reach the plateau. The risks: buying at the peak, and abandoning a useful tool at the trough. The response: realistic expectations, and staying on the slope of enlightenment, where a small group keeps learning what works.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
• Explore: hover over a numbered marker or a label to read about that stage or wave. Every callout has a tip at the bottom.
  • Quiz: click Quiz. The sim names a stage or a wave, and you click the marker where it lives. Your score shows next to the buttons.
  • Calibrate (authors): open main.html?edit=true to drag markers, then copy the JSON into data.json.

docs.title: The 11 Callouts
docs.text:
1. Innovation trigger: the rocket lifting off
  2. Peak of inflated expectations: fireworks over a cheering crowd
  3. Film, 1913: Edison's prediction that books would be obsolete in schools
  4. Generative AI, 2022: the glowing chat bubble sliding toward the trough
  5. Teaching machines, 1950s: a wooden machine left in the fog
  6. Trough of disillusionment: the fog in the valley
  7. One-to-one tablets, 2013: the tipped-over tablet cart
  8. Classroom computers, 1980s: teachers who kept experimenting after the boom
  9. Slope of enlightenment: the staircase out of the valley
  10. MOOCs, 2012: the certificate on the plateau
  11. Plateau of productivity: the calm, working classroom

The landscape is a text-free SVG made by make-hype-cycle-svg.py in this folder, so the skyline follows the curve exactly. The SVG is the working image. image-prompt.md describes the same scene, with the same object positions, for an optional painted upgrade; the markers in data.json will still fit after the swap. The sources for every date and claim are listed in claims.md.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will explain the five stages of the hype cycle and, given a wave of educational technology, explain which stage its story illustrates and what a school should do at that stage. (Bloom level: Understand. Bloom verb: explain.)

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Teachers, school administrators, school board members, education policymakers and parents.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10 to 15 minutes.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (5 minutes): hover over all 11 callouts in order along the curve. Notice that the waves come from different decades but show the same shape.
  2. Quiz (3 minutes): run Quiz mode until you can find every stage and wave without hovering first.
  3. Apply (5 minutes): pick one technology your school is considering. Where is it on the curve today? Write one thing your school should do at that stage, and one mistake to avoid.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
The learner finds at least 9 of 11 callouts in Quiz mode and can answer, without the sim:

  1. Why is the peak a risky time to buy? (Expectations are highest when evidence is thinnest.)
  2. Does the trough mean a technology has failed? (No. MOOCs and classroom computers both found real uses after it.)
  3. What should a school do during the trough? (Keep small, cheap pilots running and learn what works.)

After the poster, the practice sim Where Is It on the Hype Cycle? checks the same idea with eight events.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Gartner hype cycle. Wikipedia. The five stages, Jackie Fenn's 1995 origin, and criticism of the model.
  2. Quote Origin: Books Will Soon Be Obsolete in the Schools. Quote Investigator. Edison's 1913 prediction traced to its source.
  3. Massive open online course. Wikipedia. The MOOC wave of 2012 and its aftermath.
  4. Watters, A. (2021). Teaching Machines: The History of Personalized Learning. MIT Press.
  5. Bastani, H., et al. (2025). Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning: Evidence from high school mathematics. PNAS, 122(26).

docs.title: The EdTech Hype Cycle: Claim Audit
docs.text: Audit trail for The EdTech Hype Cycle, from Phases 1 to 4 of the verified-infographic guide. Each callout tip in data.json cites the source_ids below. Wave placements on the curve follow Chapter 15's own text and worked-example table; they are a reading of the evidence, not a measurement. Notes are paraphrases, not quotations.

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
# Claim (as used in the poster) Status Source IDs Note 1 The hype cycle was introduced by Gartner analyst Jackie Fenn in 1995 (chapter: "mid-1990s") verified S1, S2 Wikipedia and secondary methodology summaries agree on Fenn and 1995. 2 Five stages: trigger, peak of inflated expectations, trough of disillusionment, slope of enlightenment, plateau of productivity verified S1, S2 Gartner's current pages use "Innovation Trigger"; the original name was "Technology Trigger". The poster uses the chapter's "innovation trigger" and notes the older name in a tip. 3 The model is not a scientific law; many technologies do not follow it verified S1 Wikipedia summarizes analyses finding few technologies pass through an identifiable cycle. 4 Edison predicted in a July 1913 interview that books would soon be obsolete in the public schools verified S3, S4 Quote Investigator traces it to the New York Dramatic Mirror, July 9, 1913; the issue is digitized at the Internet Archive. 5 Film became a supplement, not a replacement for books downgraded S3 Kept as a qualitative statement; a 1913 trade editorial quoted by Quote Investigator already called film a supplement. 6 Skinner proposed teaching machines in 1954 verified S5, S6 His 1954 paper "The Science of Learning and the Art of Teaching" launched the movement. Chapter 3 gives the same date. 7 Interest in teaching machines faded by the late 1960s (costs, boredom, thin evidence) verified S5, S6 Both describe the late-1960s backlash and decline. This trough placement is an inference from the chapter's statement that each wave had a peak and a trough; the chapter does not name a stage for teaching machines. 8 Ideas from teaching machines returned in computer-based learning verified S5, S25 Qualitative only. 9 Apple II reached schools in 1977 verified (chapter) chapter 3, S7 Apple II released 1977; Minnesota's MECC chose it for state schools in 1978. 10 MECC packaged software with guides for teachers new to computers verified S7, S8 11 After the 1980s boom, a smaller group of teachers kept experimenting and developed effective practices downgraded chapter 15 The chapter's own event (practice sim, event 8). Kept qualitative; no numbers. 12 "By the early 1980s many districts were buying microcomputers" removed — Not checked against two sources; replaced with the chapter's wording, "computers spread into classrooms in the 1980s". 13 The New York Times called 2012 "the year of the MOOC" (November 2012) verified S9, S10 Laura Pappano's article, dated November 2 to 4, 2012 depending on edition. 14 In 2013 Sebastian Thrun said Udacity had a "lousy product" verified S11, S12 Fast Company profile, November 2013, widely quoted. 15 MOOC completion rates were often under ten percent verified S13, S14 Jordan (2014) found an average of 6.5%. Her 2015 follow-up found a median of 12.6% across 221 courses, so "often", not "always", is the right word. 16 MOOCs settled into a niche in professional and continuing education downgraded chapter 15 Qualitative, from the chapter; Udacity's 2013 pivot to vocational training (S11) supports it. 17 LAUSD began a plan in 2013 to give every student an iPad verified S15, S16 Cost figures differ across sources ($1 billion to $1.3 billion), so the poster gives no dollar amount. 18 Within days, students at one high school bypassed the security settings verified S16 About 300 Roosevelt High students, within hours, September 2013. Poster says "within days" (conservative). 19 After the FBI seized contract documents in December 2014, the district cancelled the contract verified S15, S16 20 A federal inquiry later ended with no charges verified S17 Added for fairness, since the chapter calls it a contract scandal. 21 ChatGPT released November 30, 2022 verified S18, S19 22 NYC schools blocked ChatGPT in January 2023 and lifted the block in May 2023 verified S20 Several outlets (NBC, Bloomberg, Chalkbeat op-ed by Banks) agree. Supports the chapter's "schools ban, then rush to adopt". 23 The company behind the Los Angeles district's chatbot collapsed in 2024 verified S23, S24 AllHere furloughed most staff in June 2024 and LAUSD took its "Ed" chatbot offline. Contract value differs across sources, so no dollar amount is given. 24 A randomized study found open chatbot access lowered later exam scores, and a tutor with guardrails largely avoided that harm verified S21, S22 Bastani et al., PNAS 2025: about 1,000 Turkish high school math students. The chapter's "guided tutors help" is softened to "largely avoided that harm", since the guided group scored about the same as the control on the exam. 25 Generative AI is "toward the trough"; the plateau is not yet reached downgraded chapter 15 The chapter's own reading, labelled as one on which reasonable people disagree.

Summary: 19 verified, 5 downgraded to qualitative or chapter-sourced language, 1 removed. No numeric claim in the poster lacks a source.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A teacher says, "I'm afraid this means my job won't exist in five years." The MicroSim shows eight replies to that one statement, one at a time. You sort each reply into one of four kinds:

Kind What it does Dismissive Tells the person the worry is unfounded or silly Defensive Argues with the worry or restates the plan without acknowledging the feeling Reassurance without substance Offers comfort with no facts, options, or commitments Empathic and substantive Acknowledges the concern and then offers facts, options, or a commitment

Each kind has two replies. Some kind-sounding replies turn out to be empty, and some factual replies turn out to be defensive. Only the empathic and substantive replies both acknowledge the worry and offer something concrete.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the reply in the white box.
  2. Click the kind of reply you think fits. The button turns blue.
  3. Press Submit. The box below the reply says whether you are right and why.
  4. If you are wrong, the button you chose turns orange. Choose again and press Submit. The second try does not change the score. After a second miss, the right answer turns green.
  5. Press Next to go on. After the last reply, press Finish to see your score, with the replies grouped by kind.
  6. Press Start over at any time to reshuffle and begin again.
  7. Check Show definitions to read what each kind of reply means. Uncheck it to go back.

Only your first try on each reply counts toward the score. The replys are shuffled each run. Nothing moves until you act, and the MicroSim does not store your answers.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner can classify eight replies to a worried teacher as dismissive, defensive, reassurance without substance, or empathic and substantive, correctly placing at least seven of eight on the first attempt. (Bloom level: Understand.)

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Teachers, school administrators, school board members, education policymakers, and parents.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Responding with empathy, legitimate concern, and fear of job loss, from the section "Resistance, Concerns, and Job Fears" in Chapter 19.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Predict (2 min). Before you start, say what makes "Don't worry, it'll all work out" different from an empathic reply.
  2. Classify (6 min). Sort all eight replies. Aim for 7 of 8 on the first try.
  3. Rewrite (5 min). Pick one dismissive or defensive reply and rewrite it so it acknowledges the worry and offers a fact, an option, or a commitment.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim, then check each answer by using it.

  1. "I understand, I'm sure you'll be fine." What kind of reply is this? (Reassurance without substance. It sounds kind but offers nothing concrete.)
  2. Is every reply that disagrees with the teacher defensive? (No. A reply can disagree with the facts and still acknowledge the feeling and offer support.)
  3. What two things does an empathic and substantive reply do? (It acknowledges the concern, and then it offers facts, options, or a commitment.)

docs.text:
1. Empathy. Wikipedia. What empathy is and how it differs from sympathy.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Three students need to reach a score of 80. The school has 45 tutoring hours, and each hour adds one point to the student who receives it.

Student Starting score Equal split (15 hours each) A 80 95 B 65 80 C 50 65

The equal split gives everyone the same 15 hours. Two students reach 80, and the gap between the highest and lowest score is 30 points. Student A gets 15 hours they did not need.

An equitable allocation matches hours to need. Only one allocation in steps of 5 hours brings all three to 80: A 0, B 15, C 30. It uses exactly 45 hours, and the gap closes to 0.

Equity here does not take anything away from Student A, who already met the target. It spends the same 45 hours where they close the gap. The numbers are an illustrative model, not measured data.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
• Answer Q1 (how many students reach 80 with 15 hours each) and Q2 (the gap between the highest and lowest score), then press Check Q1 and Q2. Each has one attempt.
  • The equal-split result appears and the three hour sliders unlock. Each moves in steps of 5 hours. The total cannot go above 45.
  • The bars update as you move the sliders. When you are ready, press Submit allocation. You have three submissions.
  • If a student is still short, the feedback names the student and the number of points. After three unsuccessful submissions, the working allocation is shown.
  • Reset returns to the opening state.

Nothing moves until you act. Mastery is Q1 and Q2 right and the allocation found within three submissions.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner can distinguish an equal allocation of tutoring hours from an equitable one by finding the split of 45 hours that brings all three students to a score of 80, and by stating the score gap that results from each. (Bloom level: Analyze.)

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Teachers, administrators, school board members, policymakers, and parents.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Achievement gap, educational equity, equality, and learning gains, from Chapter 3.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Calculate (3 min). Answer Q1 and Q2 on paper first, then check them.
  2. Search (5 min). Find the allocation that brings all three students to 80. Before each submission, predict each student's final score.
  3. Discuss (5 min). Did the equitable allocation take anything away from Student A? Where does your school give every student the same support even though needs differ?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim.

  1. With 15 hours each, what is the score gap? (30 points: 95 minus 65.)
  2. What allocation brings all three students to 80, and why? (A 0, B 15, C 30. Each student gets exactly the hours they need to reach 80.)
  3. Is treating everyone the same always fair? (No. The equal split left Student C 15 points short while Student A got hours they did not need.)

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Vendors describe their products with claims that sound like evidence. Some are. Many are not. The question to ask is how the comparison was built.

This MicroSim uses five levels. The first four follow the Every Student Succeeds Act (ESSA) evidence tiers. The fifth holds everything that is not evidence of effect.

Level What it needs Strong Random assignment, well designed and well carried out Moderate A comparison group, but no random assignment Promising A correlational study that adjusts for who chose the program Demonstrates a rationale A research-based reason to expect it to work; results not yet in No evidence of effect Testimonials, surveys, usage counts, uncontrolled before-and-after or self-selected comparisons

You judge ten claims about a fictional program called MathPath. Two claims test a common trap: a study of 12,000 students that sits in the lowest level, and a study of 1,200 students that sits in the highest. Sample size does not fix how the groups were formed.

The claims are fictional and written for this chapter.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
• Read the claim on the card, then press the evidence level you think fits.
  • Show definitions opens the one-line definition of each level.
  • If your first answer is wrong, you get a hint and a second try. Only the first try counts toward your score.
  • After the second try, the correct level and the reason appear. Press Next for the next claim.
  • After all ten claims, the results screen shows your first-try score and lets you step through the claims you missed. Play again reshuffles the claims for practice.

Mastery is 8 of 10 on the first try. Nothing moves until you choose, and the MicroSim does not store your answers.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner can judge the strength of the evidence behind ten vendor claims by placing each in one of five evidence levels, with at least 8 of 10 correct on the first try. (Bloom level: Evaluate.)

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Teachers, administrators, school board members, policymakers, and parents.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Evidence-based practice, randomized controlled trial, selection bias, and the five evidence levels, from Chapter 2.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Predict (2 min). Before you start, decide: is a study of 12,000 students always stronger than a study of 1,200? Write down why.
  2. Judge (8 min). Work through all ten claims. For each one, ask first how the groups were formed.
  3. Apply (5 min). Find a real vendor web page for an education product. Sort its claims into the five levels. How many are evidence of effect at all?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim.

  1. A program reports that 94% of teachers love it. Which level is that? (No evidence of effect. Satisfaction is not learning.)
  2. Students who chose an optional program scored higher than those who did not. Does a large sample make this Strong? (No. The groups chose themselves, so they differ in ways a large sample does not fix.)
  3. What is the one feature that separates Strong from Moderate? (Random assignment to the program or a control group.)

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Every Student Succeeds Act. Wikipedia. The 2015 federal law that defines the evidence tiers.
  2. Randomized controlled trial. Wikipedia. Why random assignment supports a causal claim.
  3. Selection bias. Wikipedia. How self-selected groups distort a comparison.
  4. What Works Clearinghouse. Institute of Education Sciences. Reviews of education research by study design.

docs.title: The Factory Day vs. the AI-Native Day

Run The Factory Day vs. the AI-Native Day MicroSim Fullscreen Chapter 3: School Structures, Equity, and the Industrial-Era Legacy Chapter 20: Designing the AI-Native School Day

You can add this MicroSim to any web page with this iframe:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/ai-native-schools/sims/factory-vs-ai-native-day/main.html"

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
The whole argument of this book is a comparison between two school days. This poster puts them side by side as two buildings cut open so you can see every floor.

The factory school on the left has a sawtooth roof and a smokestack. In its morning and afternoon classrooms, students of one age sit in identical rows facing one board, under a large clock and a bell. Upstairs, the teacher sits late at night behind stacks of ungraded paper.

The AI-native school on the right has the same three floors used differently. In the morning, students work at their own pace along a winding learning path while a coach moves between them, and one student takes a stretch break away from the screen. In the afternoon, the rooms open into a project table with a robot, a stage, a workshop and a garden. Upstairs, the teacher meets one student as a mentor.

The poster also shows the risks. One student in the AI-native morning works alone, hunched over a laptop, which is the isolation risk that screen-time limits and small-group coaching answer. The facts for each floor name the risk and the school's response.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
• Explore: hover over a floor to see its name, then click it to read a summary and facts from the chapters.
  • Quiz Me: the sim describes part of a school day, and you click the floor where it happens. Your score shows next to the buttons.
  • Calibrate (authors): open main.html?edit=true to drag zone corners, then copy the JSON into data.json.

docs.title: The Six Zones
docs.text:
1. Factory teacher: lecturer and grader: one adult lectures and grades for every student, working long weeks
  2. Factory morning: one lesson, one pace: the bell schedule, age-based grade levels, seat time and the Carnegie unit
  3. Factory afternoon: more of the same: the same rows and the same bell, one subject at a time
  4. AI-native teacher: coach and mentor: the changing teacher role, with about the same number of adults doing different work
  5. AI-native morning: compressed and self-paced: about two to three hours of mastery learning at each student's own pace, with screen-time limits
  6. AI-native afternoon: pro-social: projects, arts, making and service, structured so the time does not drift

Every number in the zones comes from the book's chapters, and each fact names its chapter. The length of the compressed morning, "about two to three hours", is the book's own phrase from Chapter 11.

The background is a text-free painted image made from image-prompt.md in this folder. The prompt leaves an empty band of sky at the top, where the overlay places the two column headers, Factory School Model and AI-Native School Model. An earlier hand-built SVG version, made by make-factory-day-svg.py, is kept in the folder for reference.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will compare the industrial-era school day with the AI-native school day, explaining for the morning, the afternoon and the teacher's role what changes, why it changes, and which risk each change brings and how a school responds. (Bloom level: Analyze; verb: compare.)

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: School and district leaders, teachers, school board members and parents.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 15 minutes.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (6 minutes): click all six floors. For each AI-native floor, find the factory floor directly across from it and note one difference.
  2. Quiz (4 minutes): run Quiz Me until you can place every description on the right floor.
  3. Apply (5 minutes): sketch your own school's day as a building with three floors. Which floor looks most like the factory school? Name one risk of changing it and how you would respond to that risk.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: The learner scores at least 8 of 9 in Quiz Me and can name, for each of the three floors, one change from the factory day to the AI-native day together with its risk and the school's response.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A detector that wrongly flags "only 1 percent" of human essays sounds safe. But most essays are written by humans, so 1 percent of many can outnumber the AI essays it catches. And if the detector flags English-language learners (ELL) more often, the false accusations pile up on them.

The MicroSim starts with three questions, using 10,000 essays, 5 percent written by AI, and 80 percent caught. With a 1 percent rate for all writers, 95 of 495 flags are false, about 19 percent. With a 20 percent rate for ELL writers, who write 950 of the essays, 190 wrong flags fall on them, 69 percent of all wrong flags, and about 41 percent of all flags are false. After the questions, six sliders unlock and the counts, the two shares, and a bar of every flagged essay update at once. The numbers are illustrative, not the performance of any real detector.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read Question 1. Type your answer and press Check. Type only the number.
  2. If you are wrong, you get a hint and one more try. After a second miss, the sim shows the answer and the working. Only a first-try answer counts toward the score.
  3. Press Next question. After Question 3, press See the results.
  4. The six sliders unlock. Change them and watch the results update at once.
  5. Defaults puts the inputs back to their starting values. Start over returns to Question 1.

The results stay hidden until you answer the three questions. Nothing moves until you act, and the MicroSim does not store your answers.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner can calculate how many human-written essays an AI detector wrongly flags, the share of flagged essays that are false accusations, and the share of false flags that fall on English-language learners, correctly answering three of three questions. (Bloom level: Apply.)

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Teachers, school administrators, school board members, education policymakers, and parents.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 15-20 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • AI cheating detector, detector false positives, and bias against ELL writers, from the section "Academic Integrity and the Detector Problem" in Chapter 20.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Calculate (7 min). Answer the three questions with paper and a calculator. Work from counts.
  2. Explore (5 min). Lower Share written by AI from 5 to 1 percent. What happens to the share of flags that are false?
  3. Discuss (5 min). Set the ELL rate equal to the most-writers rate. Why does the ELL share of wrong flags fall to 10 percent?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim, then check each answer by using it.

  1. With a 1 percent false-positive rate, are 1 percent of accusations wrong? (No. At the defaults about 19 percent are wrong, because human essays far outnumber AI essays.)
  2. Do a detector's errors fall evenly on all students? (Not when one group has a higher false-positive rate. Here ELL writers get 69 percent of the wrong flags.)
  3. What should a school do instead of relying on a detector? (Redesign assessment so it shows process, such as drafts and conversations.)

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. GPT detectors are biased against non-native English writers. Liang and others, 2023. The Stanford study of detector bias.
  2. Base rate fallacy. Wikipedia. Why a small error rate can produce many false positives.
  3. Artificial intelligence content detection. Wikipedia. How AI-writing detectors work and fail.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
This poster puts the two ladders from Chapter 6 side by side. The top row shows the six levels of driving automation from the SAE J3016 standard, from a driver with both hands on the wheel to a pod with no steering wheel at all. The bottom row shows the five levels of intelligent textbooks, from a closed print book to a laptop that writes pages on the fly. Both rows rise like a staircase from left to right, because higher levels shift more of the work from the human to the system.

The two ladders do not match one to one, and the poster does not pretend they do. SAE J3016 has six levels, numbered 0 to 5. The textbook model has five, numbered 1 to 5, and starts at static content instead of a human doing everything. So the textbook levels sit under car levels 1 to 5 by number only, and car Level 0 has no textbook partner. The chapter's own claim about the two ladders is narrower: in both, the rules change at Level 3. For cars, that is where the system takes primary control and liability questions arise. For textbooks, it is where the system starts keeping a record about each student and privacy questions arise. The dashed amber line marks that threshold in both rows.

The empty cell under car Level 0 holds the story-balance zone. Each level adds power, and each also adds cost, data and things that can go wrong. Vendors often claim a higher level than they deliver: the glossy brochure shows five bars, and the magnifying glass finds two. The chapter's response is the rule that a product's level is the highest defining capability it actually delivers to students in use.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
• Explore: hover over a column to see its label, then click it to read the summary and facts below the poster.
  • Quiz Me: click Quiz Me. The sim describes a car or a textbook, and you click the cell where it belongs. Your score shows next to the buttons.
  • Calibrate (authors): open main.html?edit=true to drag zone corners, then copy the JSON into data.json.

docs.title: The 12 Zones
docs.text:
Top row, the SAE J3016 levels of driving automation:

  1. SAE 0: No driving automation: a driver with both hands on the wheel; the car only beeps a warning
  2. SAE 1: Driver assistance: radar waves keep a set distance from the car ahead
  3. SAE 2: Partial automation: the car keeps its lane, but an eye shows the human must watch
  4. SAE 3: Conditional automation: the driver reads in a traffic jam until the bell asks for a takeover
  5. SAE 4: High automation: a driverless taxi inside the posts of a mapped city
  6. SAE 5: Full automation: a pod with no steering wheel on a mountain road

Bottom row, the five-level textbook model:

  1. Claimed vs. delivered level: a glossy brochure claims five bars; the magnifying glass finds two
  2. Level 1: Static: a closed print book and a PDF page
  3. Level 2: Interactive: a laptop with a slider, a graph and a checked quiz card
  4. Level 3: Adaptive: a branching path and a locked student record
  5. Level 4: Chatbot: a tutoring conversation in chat bubbles
  6. Level 5: Autonomous: pages generated on the fly, with a teacher checking one through a magnifying glass

The image is a text-free SVG made by make-five-levels-svg.py in this folder. The script also prints the zone positions used in data.json.

For practice placing real products on the ladder, try the Product Level Classifier MicroSim.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will compare the six SAE J3016 levels of driving automation with the five levels of intelligent textbooks, and explain why both frameworks put their key threshold at Level 3.

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: School and district leaders, teachers, curriculum coordinators and anyone who buys or reviews instructional products.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10 minutes.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (5 minutes): click the top row from left to right, then the bottom row. For each textbook level, note what it needs to know about the student.
  2. Find the threshold (2 minutes): look at the dashed line. Say in one sentence what new question each row raises on the right side of it.
  3. Quiz (3 minutes): run Quiz Me until you can place every description without hovering first.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: The learner places at least 9 of 10 quiz descriptions correctly and can explain, using Ms. Okafor's three vendor emails, why a product's level is set by what it delivers rather than what its brochure claims.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Chapter 6, The Five-Level Model of Intelligent Textbooks: the SAE level table, "The Five Levels at a Glance", the five-level summary table and the level-specific safeguards. Every label and fact in this poster comes from that chapter.
  • SAE International. SAE J3016, the standard that defines the levels of driving automation (first published 2014), as cited in Chapter 6.
  • McCreary, D. (2025, December). A Five-Level Classification Framework for Intelligent Textbooks: Lessons from Autonomous Vehicle Standards. Preprint, as cited in Chapter 6.

docs.title: Force Field Balance
docs.text:
Run the Force Field Balance MicroSim Fullscreen Chapter 17: Leading Change: Vision, Culture, and Early-Stage Concerns

To edit the sketch, paste the contents of force-field-balance.js into the p5.js editor. The forces and questions are in the content block at the top of the file.

You can add this MicroSim to any web page with this iframe:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/ai-native-schools/sims/force-field-balance/main.html"
        height="808px"
        width="100%"
        scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Kurt Lewin's force field analysis pictures a situation as a balance between driving forces, which push toward change, and restraining forces, which push against it. This MicroSim shows the chapter's force field for the compressed morning: four driving forces and four restraining forces, each scored from 1 (weak) to 5 (strong). At the start the two sides balance at 14 and 14.

You first answer three questions: the total driving force, the total restraining force after two restraining forces are reduced, and the net force after those reductions. Then eight sliders unlock so you can explore. The arithmetic shows Lewin's advice: lowering a restraining force by 3 moves the net exactly as much as raising a driving force by 3, without adding pressure. The strengths are illustrative judgments.

Force Kind Starting strength Evidence of learning gaps in the data Driving 4 Potential relief from teacher workload Driving 3 Free open textbooks Driving 3 Leadership support Driving 4 Culture of closed doors Restraining 4 Fear of job loss Restraining 3 Privacy concerns Restraining 3 Students without home devices Restraining 4

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
• Read the force field. Each arrow's length and number show its strength.
  • Type your answers to Q1, Q2, and Q3 in the boxes and press Check answers. A wrong answer gets a hint and one more try. Only your first try counts toward the score.
  • When all three are settled, press Unlock the sliders. The totals, the net force, and the balance bar appear.
  • Move the eight sliders to change the strengths. Reset strengths returns them to the starting values.

docs.title: Good to Know
docs.text:
• Net force = total driving minus total restraining. A net of 0 is balanced, a positive net favors change, and a negative net favors the status quo.
  • Mastery is 3 of 3 correct on the first try. Moving the sliders afterward is exploration. Nothing moves until you act.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will calculate the total driving force, the total restraining force, and the net force for a change situation, before and after reducing two restraining forces, correctly answering three of three questions. (Bloom level: Apply.)

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Teachers, school administrators, school board members, education policymakers, and parents.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Force field analysis, driving forces, restraining forces, and the unfreeze stage, from the section "Lewin: Unfreeze, Change, Refreeze" in Chapter 17.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Calculate (5 min). Answer Q1 to Q3 on paper first, then type them in.
  2. Explore (5 min). Raise one driving force by 3 and note the net. Reset, then lower one restraining force by 3. Compare.
  3. Discuss (5 min). Why might pushing harder on a driving force raise a restraining force in a real school?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim, then check each answer by using it.

  1. Driving forces are 4, 3, 3, and 4. What is the total? (14.)
  2. Restraining forces are 4, 3, 1, and 1. What is the net if driving is 14? (+5, which favors change.)
  3. Is a balanced field stable and safe? (No. It is stuck: nothing moves until a force changes.)
  4. Why reduce a restraining force rather than push harder? (It improves the net just as much without adding pressure that can raise resistance.)

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Force-field analysis. Wikipedia. Lewin's method of listing and weighing driving and restraining forces.
  2. Kurt Lewin. Wikipedia. The psychologist behind force field analysis and the unfreeze-change-refreeze model.

docs.title: Four-Fifths Bias Audit Calculator
docs.text:
Run the Four-Fifths Bias Audit Calculator MicroSim Fullscreen Chapter 10: Student Privacy and Data Governance

To edit the sketch, paste the contents of four-fifths-bias-audit-calculator.js into the p5.js editor and set the editor's p5.js version to 2.x. The learning content is in the CONFIG block near the top of the file.

You can add this MicroSim to any web page with this iframe:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/ai-native-schools/sims/four-fifths-bias-audit-calculator/main.html"
        height="659px"
        width="100%"
        scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
An AI system that recommends students for an advanced class should recommend students from every group at similar rates. A four-fifths screen checks this:

selection rate = recommended ÷ eligible. The highest group's rate is the reference. Ratio = a group's rate ÷ the reference rate. A group is flagged when its ratio is below 0.80.

Three questions come first: group B's selection rate, group B's ratio, and which groups the audit flags. Then three sliders for the recommended counts unlock, and the rates, ratios, flags, and a bar chart update at once. A flag is a prompt to investigate why, not proof that the system is unfair.

The counts are illustrative audit data. The four-fifths threshold is a screening convention from U.S. employment-selection guidance, applied here as an illustration.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
Nothing moves until you act, and the MicroSim does not store your answers.

  • Your answer box and Check: type a number and press Check (or Enter); for question 3 choose from the menu. Two attempts per question; only the first counts.
  • Next: moves on; after question 3 it unlocks the sliders.
  • Recommended, group A, B, C: sliders for the number recommended in each group.
  • Redo challenges and Defaults: start the questions again, or reset the counts to 200, 72, and 70.

If every recommended count is zero, the sim says "No recommendations to audit."

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner will calculate selection rates and four-fifths ratios for three student groups and identify which groups the audit flags, correctly answering three of three questions. (Bloom level: Apply.)

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Teachers, administrators, school board members, education policymakers, and parents.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Algorithmic bias, algorithmic bias auditing, selection rate, and the four-fifths rule, from the section "Algorithmic Bias, Auditing, and Transparency" in Chapter 10.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Calculate (5 min). Work the three rates and the ratios on paper first.
  2. Explore (4 min). Raise group B's recommended count until it is no longer flagged. What count does it take?
  3. Discuss (4 min). Group B is flagged. List two reasons that could explain the gap, and one that would show the system is unfair.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim, then check each answer by using it.

  1. Group B: 72 recommended of 300 eligible. Selection rate? (24.0%.)
  2. Group A's rate is 40.0%. Group B's ratio? (0.60 (24.0 ÷ 40.0).)
  3. Group C's rate is 35.0%. Is it flagged? (No. Its ratio is 0.875, about 0.88, which is above 0.80.)
  4. Does a flag prove the system is unfair? (No. It starts an investigation.)

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Disparate impact. Wikipedia. Includes the four-fifths rule of thumb.
  2. 29 CFR Part 1607: Uniform Guidelines on Employee Selection Procedures. Electronic Code of Federal Regulations. The source of the four-fifths convention.
  3. Algorithmic bias. Wikipedia. How automated systems can treat groups differently.

docs.title: Four Thinking Skills Sorter
docs.text:
Run the Four Thinking Skills Sorter MicroSim Fullscreen Chapter 12: AI Guardrails: Teaching Thinking Without Over-Reliance

To edit the sketch, paste the contents of four-thinking-skills-sorter.js into the p5.js editor and set the editor's p5.js version to 2.x. The learning content is in the CONFIG block at the top of the file.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Four thinking skills show up far beyond programming. Each has one defining move:

Skill Defining move Decomposition Breaking a big problem into smaller parts Pattern recognition Noticing what repeats or what examples share Abstraction Ignoring detail that does not matter, to focus on what does Algorithmic thinking Writing precise steps that solve the problem every time

The eight activities come from ordinary school life: a science fair, an essay, a subway map, a recipe. Look for the defining move. Breaking a task into steps is decomposition; writing steps so exact that anyone can follow them is algorithmic thinking. The activities are illustrative examples written for this chapter.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text: Read the activity, then choose one of the four skills. Press Show definitions to see the defining move of each skill. A wrong first answer gives a hint and lets you choose again, but only the first answer counts toward First-try correct. After eight activities, the results screen shows your score and the activities you misplaced.

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:
• Choice buttons: commit an answer. A wrong first answer gives a hint and lets you choose again; only the first answer counts.
  • Show definitions: opens or closes the reference table. Reading it is exploration, not evidence.
  • Next: moves to the next item after feedback. On the results screen, Previous missed and Next missed step through what you missed.
  • Play again: starts a practice run with the items reshuffled. Practice runs do not change the first-run score.

Nothing moves until you act, and the MicroSim does not store your answers.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner can classify eight student activities as decomposition, pattern recognition, abstraction, or algorithmic thinking, correctly placing at least seven of eight on the first attempt. (Bloom level: Understand.)

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Teachers, administrators, school board members, policymakers, and parents.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Decomposition, pattern recognition, abstraction, and algorithmic thinking, from the section "Teaching Thinking with AI" in Chapter 12

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Classify (5 min). Place the eight activities. Name the defining move before you choose.
  2. Notice (2 min). Count the chips in each bin on the right. What do you notice?
  3. Create (5 min). Write one activity from your own subject for each of the four skills.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Mastery is 7 of 8 correct on the first try. Only the first answer to each activity on the first run counts. Then ask learners to answer these without the MicroSim:

  1. A student lists the steps to make a sandwich so a robot could follow them. Which skill? (Algorithmic thinking.)
  2. Is every step-by-step activity an algorithm? (No. Splitting a task into parts is decomposition; an algorithm needs steps exact enough to follow without guessing.)
  3. Does abstraction make a problem harder to understand? (No. It drops detail that does not matter, which makes the structure easier to see.)

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Computational thinking. Wikipedia. The four skills and where they come from.
  2. Decomposition (computer science). Wikipedia. Breaking a system into parts.
  3. Abstraction (computer science). Wikipedia. Hiding detail to focus on structure.
  4. Algorithm. Wikipedia. A finite, precise sequence of steps.

docs.title: Generate Once Versus Generate for Each Student
docs.text:
Run the Generate Once Versus Generate for Each Student MicroSim Fullscreen Chapter 9: Learning Graphs, Interoperability Standards, and Access at Scale

You can add this MicroSim to any web page with this iframe:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/ai-native-schools/sims/generate-once-vs-live-cost/main.html"
        height="654px"
        width="100%"
        scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
There are two ways to use AI for textbook content. Generate once, serve many: pay a one-time production cost, then serve the same pages to every student at almost no cost. Generate live: pay for AI inference for each student, every year.

The chart plots the yearly total for both on log scales against the number of students. The generate-once line is flat; the live line rises with every student. Three questions come first: the generate-once cost per student for 12,000 students, the live total for 12,000 students, and the number of students where the totals are equal. Then the controls unlock and both lines and the break-even point update at once.

All values are illustrative: the $22,400 production cost is the Chapter 7 example for a 20-chapter AI-assisted book, and 3.6 million tokens at $2.00 per million are the Chapter 4 and Chapter 7 example values.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
Nothing moves until you act, and the MicroSim does not store your answers.

  • Your answer box and Check: type a number and press Check (or Enter). Two attempts per question; only the first counts.
  • Next: moves on; after question 3 it unlocks the controls.
  • Production cost: slider from $5,000 to $100,000.
  • Tokens per student per year: slider from 1 million to 10 million.
  • Price per million tokens: menu of $0.07, $0.20, $2.00, and $20.00.
  • Students: slider from 100 to 1,000,000 on a log scale, rounded to the nearest 100.
  • Redo questions and Defaults: start the questions again, or reset the controls.

Hover over a point on the chart, after the controls unlock, to read its value.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner will compare the total yearly cost of generating content once and serving it to all students with the cost of generating it live for each student, and determine the number of students at which the two are equal, to within 100 students. (Bloom level: Analyze.)

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Teachers, administrators, school board members, education policymakers, and parents.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Generate once serve many and web page hosting (Chapter 9), and AI inference cost (Chapter 4).

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Calculate (5 min). Answer the three questions on paper first.
  2. Explore (5 min). Lower the price to $0.20, then $0.07. Which way does the break-even point move, and why?
  3. Discuss (3 min). When might live generation still be worth its cost?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim, then check each answer by using it.

  1. Generate-once cost per student for 12,000 students? ($1.87 ($22,400 ÷ 12,000).)
  2. Live total for 12,000 students at $7.20 each? ($86,400.)
  3. Break-even number of students? (About 3,100 ($22,400 ÷ $7.20).)
  4. Does the generate-once total grow with students? (No. In this model serving costs nothing, so the line is flat.)

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Break-even (economics). Wikipedia. Where two cost curves meet.
  2. Fixed cost. Wikipedia. Costs that do not change with the number served.
  3. Variable cost. Wikipedia. Costs that grow with each unit.
  4. Static web page. Wikipedia. Pages served unchanged to every reader.

docs.title: Governance Readiness Judge
docs.text:
Run the Governance Readiness Judge MicroSim Fullscreen Chapter 10: Student Privacy and Data Governance

To edit the sketch, paste the contents of governance-readiness-judge.js into the p5.js editor and set the editor's p5.js version to 2.x. The learning content is in the CONFIG block at the top of the file.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A district is ready to adopt a Level 3 intelligent textbook only when its data governance is in place. This chapter names six must-have practices (M1 to M6) and four should-have practices (S1 to S4). The rule has two parts, and the order matters:

  1. If any must-have is missing, the district is Not ready.
  2. If all six must-haves are present and fewer than 3 should-haves, it is Ready for Level 3.
  3. If all six must-haves are present and 3 or more should-haves, it is Ready for Level 3 and well placed for Level 4.

Each card lists the practices a district has in place. You have to notice which must-have is missing. Should-haves cannot make up for one.

The practices and the rule are this chapter's recommended practice, not a legal standard. The six districts are fictional.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text: Read the district card, then choose one of the three verdicts below it. A correct first answer turns its segment green in the progress strip. A wrong first answer gives a hint and lets you choose again, but only the first answer counts toward the score shown as First-try correct. Press Show all practices to see the ten practices with their codes. Press Next to move on. After six districts, the results screen shows your score and lets you review each district you missed.

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:
• Choice buttons: commit an answer. A wrong first answer gives a hint and lets you choose again; only the first answer counts.
  • Show definitions: opens or closes the reference table. Reading it is exploration, not evidence.
  • Next: moves to the next item after feedback. On the results screen, Previous missed and Next missed step through what you missed.
  • Play again: starts a practice run with the items reshuffled. Practice runs do not change the first-run score.

Nothing moves until you act, and the MicroSim does not store your answers.

You can add this MicroSim to any web page by adding this to your HTML:

        height="785px"
