docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner can judge whether each of six districts is not ready, ready for Level 3, or ready for Level 3 and well placed for Level 4, by applying the must-have and should-have rule, correctly judging at least five of six on the first attempt. (Bloom level: Evaluate.)

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Teachers, administrators, school board members, policymakers, and parents.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Governance readiness, the six must-have and four should-have practices, and the readiness rule, from the section "Governance Readiness" in Chapter 10

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Predict (2 min). Before you start, decide: can a district with nine practices in place be not ready? Write down why.
  2. Judge (6 min). Work through the six districts. For each one, check the six must-haves before you count the should-haves.
  3. Discuss (4 min). Oakdale has the most practices of any district and is still not ready. Explain why to a colleague or board member.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Mastery is 5 of 6 correct on the first try. Only the first answer to each district on the first run counts. Then ask learners to answer these without the MicroSim:

  1. A district has every practice except M6, a breach response plan. What is the verdict? (Not ready. Any missing must-have means not ready.)
  2. A district has all six must-haves and two should-haves. What is the verdict? (Ready for Level 3. Two is fewer than 3.)
  3. Is readiness a score out of ten? (No. It is a two-step rule: must-haves first, then a count of should-haves.)

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act. Wikipedia. The main US federal law on student education records.
  2. Data governance. Wikipedia. The roles, policies, and processes an organization uses to manage data.
  3. Student Privacy Policy Office. US Department of Education. Guidance and training on student privacy for schools and districts.

docs.title: Is the Gap Closing?
docs.text:
Run the Is the Gap Closing? MicroSim Fullscreen Chapter 21: Implementing the AI-Native Model Responsibly

To edit the sketch, paste the contents of is-the-gap-closing.js into the p5.js editor and set the editor's p5.js version to 2.x. The learning content is in the CONFIG block at the top of the file.

You can add this MicroSim to any web page with this iframe:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/ai-native-schools/sims/is-the-gap-closing/main.html"
        height="474px"
        width="100%"
        scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
When both groups of students improve, it is tempting to say a program closed the gap. The only way to know is to compute the gap:

Gap = higher-income mean − lower-income mean. If the gap after is at least 1 point smaller than before, it is Closing. If it is at least 1 point larger, it is Widening. Otherwise it is Unchanged.

The MicroSim shows five schools, one at a time, each with four mean mastery scores. In two of the schools both groups improve, and the gap still widens. In another, both groups gain the same 6 points, and the gap stays the same. The data are illustrative.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the school in the white box.
  2. Click the result you think fits. The button turns blue.
  3. Press Submit. The box below the school says whether you are right and why.
  4. If you are wrong, the button you chose turns orange. Choose again and press Submit. The second try does not change the score. After a second miss, the right answer turns green.
  5. Press Next to go on. After the last school, press Finish to see your score, with each school's gap before and after.
  6. Press Start over at any time to reshuffle and begin again.

Only your first try on each school counts toward the score. The schools are shuffled each run. Nothing moves until you act, and the MicroSim does not store your answers.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner can differentiate five schools' results as closing, widening, or unchanged gaps by computing the gap before and after, correctly classifying at least four of five on the first attempt. (Bloom level: Analyze.)

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Teachers, school administrators, school board members, education policymakers, and parents.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Closing or widening gaps, the Matthew effect, and the achievement gap, from the section "Equity in Implementation" in Chapter 21 and from Chapter 3.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Compute (3 min). For School 1 (62 to 70 and 74 to 79), compute both gaps on paper before you start.
  2. Differentiate (6 min). Classify all five schools. Aim for 4 of 5 on the first try.
  3. Discuss (5 min). Why might an AI tutor widen a gap even when every group gains? Connect your answer to the Matthew effect.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim, then check each answer by using it.

  1. Lower-income 58 to 63; higher-income 72 to 80. Closing, widening, or unchanged? (Widening. The gap rose from 14 to 17, even though both groups improved.)
  2. If both groups improve, must the gap be closing? (No. It closes only if the lower group gains more.)
  3. Does an unchanged gap mean scores did not change? (No. In School 3 both groups gained 6 points and the gap stayed at 10.)

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Achievement gaps in the United States. Wikipedia. How gaps between student groups are measured and reported.
  2. Matthew effect. Wikipedia. Why advantages tend to grow when everyone gets the same help.
  3. Digital divide. Wikipedia. Unequal access to devices and connections.

docs.title: Is This a Normal Dip?
docs.text:
Run the Is This a Normal Dip? MicroSim Fullscreen Chapter 16: Organizational Change Models

You can add this MicroSim to any web page with this iframe:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/ai-native-schools/sims/is-this-a-normal-dip/main.html"
        height="732px"
        width="100%"
        scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Michael Fullan observed that performance often falls before it rises when a school adopts a new practice: the implementation dip. A dip is expected, but not every dip is normal, and no dip at all can be a warning that practice did not really change. This MicroSim shows three pilot series, each starting at a baseline of 70 percent correct, and a rule for judging them.

For each series you commit the month of the lowest point and a judgment, then submit. The sim then marks the low point in red and the recovery month in green, and shows the depth. Series C looks the safest, yet the rule flags it for a different reason. The data and the rule are illustrative, not research findings.

Judgment When it applies Normal dip The lowest point is in months 2 to 4, it is no deeper than 15 percent of the baseline, and it is back at or above the baseline by month 8. Deep or late: investigate The dip is deeper than 15 percent, bottoms after month 4, or has not recovered by month 8. No dip: check whether practice really changed The series never falls below 97 percent of the baseline.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
• Read the rule at the top. Hover over any point to read its value.
  • For each series, choose the lowest month and a judgment, then press Submit. You get one attempt per series.
  • The sim reveals the low point, the depth, and the recovery month, and explains the correct judgment.
  • On a narrow screen, use the Show menu to switch between the series. Start over clears every answer.

docs.title: Good to Know
docs.text:
• Depth = (baseline minus lowest value) divided by baseline. The recovery month is the first month at or above the baseline after the low point.
  • Mastery is 3 of 3 judgments correct. Looking at a chart after you submit is exploration. Nothing moves until you act.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will judge whether each of three pilot performance series shows a normal implementation dip, an unusually deep or late dip, or no dip, applying the stated rule, and correctly judging all three. (Bloom level: Evaluate.)

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Teachers, school administrators, school board members, education policymakers, and parents.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • The implementation dip, managing expectations, and the rule for a normal dip, from the section "Fullan, the Implementation Dip, and CBAM" in Chapter 16.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Predict (2 min). Before reading the charts, which is worse: a deep dip or no dip at all? Write your answer.
  2. Judge (8 min). For each series, read the low month, compute the depth, and find the recovery month before you submit.
  3. Discuss (5 min). What would you tell a school board that sees Series C and calls the pilot a success?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim, then check each answer by using it.

  1. Series A falls from 70 to 63 at month 3. What is the depth? (10 percent, which is within the 15 percent limit.)
  2. Series B bottoms at 54 in month 5. Why is it deep or late? (The low comes after month 4 and the depth, 22.9 percent, is over 15 percent.)
  3. Does any drop below baseline mean a pilot is failing? (No. A shallow, early dip with recovery by month 8 is normal.)
  4. Does no drop mean the pilot is going well? (Not necessarily. It can mean practice did not really change.)

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Michael Fullan. Wikipedia. Fullan's work on educational change and the implementation dip.
  2. Concerns-Based Adoption Model (CBAM). SEDL. Archive of the CBAM tools: stages of concern, levels of use, and innovation configurations.

docs.title: Is This Data Identifying?
docs.text:
Run the Is This Data Identifying? MicroSim Fullscreen Chapter 10: Student Privacy and Data Governance

To edit the sketch, paste the contents of is-this-data-identifying.js into the p5.js editor and set the editor's p5.js version to 2.x. The learning content is in the CONFIG block at the top of the file.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Removing a student's name does not make data anonymous. Some fields name a student on their own. Others are ordinary facts that point to one student once they are combined, or once the group is small enough. This MicroSim asks you to sort eight fields into three categories:

  • Direct identifier: identifies a specific student on its own.
  • Identifies in combination: not identifying alone, but identifies a student when combined with other facts or because the group is very small.
  • Not identifying: describes a large group or carries no link to any individual.

The birth date, ZIP code, and gender example comes from Latanya Sweeney's research, which found that about 87 percent of Americans can be singled out by those three facts. The other fields are illustrative examples written for this chapter.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text: Read the data field on the card, then choose one of the three categories below it. The category definitions are always shown on the right. A wrong first answer gives a hint and lets you choose again, but only the first answer counts toward First-try correct. Each answered field drops a numbered chip into its correct category. After eight fields, the results screen shows your score and the fields you misplaced.

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:
• Choice buttons: commit an answer. A wrong first answer gives a hint and lets you choose again; only the first answer counts.
  • Show definitions: opens or closes the reference table. Reading it is exploration, not evidence.
  • Next: moves to the next item after feedback. On the results screen, Previous missed and Next missed step through what you missed.
  • Play again: starts a practice run with the items reshuffled. Practice runs do not change the first-run score.

Nothing moves until you act, and the MicroSim does not store your answers.

docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner can classify eight data fields as direct identifiers, identifiers in combination, or not identifying, correctly placing at least seven of eight on the first attempt. (Bloom level: Understand.)

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Teachers, administrators, school board members, policymakers, and parents.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Student data, personally identifiable data, direct identifier, indirect identifier, and small-group identification, from the section "What Counts as Student Data" in Chapter 10

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Classify (6 min). Sort the eight fields. Before you choose, ask: could this field, alone or with one other fact, point to one student?
  2. Notice (2 min). Look at the chips in the middle category. Neither field contains a name. What makes each one identifying?
  3. Apply (4 min). List three fields your own school shares with a vendor. Classify each one.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Mastery is 7 of 8 correct on the first try. Only the first answer to each field on the first run counts. Then ask learners to answer these without the MicroSim:

  1. A report shows the average reading score for one class of 28 students. Which category? (Not identifying, as long as no subgroup in it is very small.)
  2. A spreadsheet has no names but lists birth date, ZIP code, and gender. Is it anonymous? (No. Together these three facts identify most people.)
  3. Can group data ever identify a person? (Yes. When the group has one member, the group's facts describe that student.)

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Personal data. Wikipedia. What counts as personally identifiable information.
  2. Quasi-identifier. Wikipedia. Fields that identify a person only in combination.
  3. Latanya Sweeney. Wikipedia. The researcher behind the birth date, ZIP code, and gender finding.
  4. De-identification. Wikipedia. Methods for removing identifying information, and their limits.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
The case for a shorter academic morning rests on claims of very uneven strength. This MicroSim gives you eight of them and asks you to place each at one of the five evidence levels from Chapter 2:

Level What it requires Strong Random assignment, well designed and carried out Moderate A comparison group, no random assignment Promising A correlational study with statistical controls Demonstrates a rationale A research-based reason; results not yet in No evidence of effect Testimonials, surveys, self-reported or uncontrolled results

Some claims support this book's own proposal and still sit at the bottom level. Judge the design of the study, not whether you agree with the result. The claims are summaries of the studies and reports described in Chapter 11 and the AI-First Stories appendix; check the sources before citing them.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text: Read the claim, then choose one of the five levels below it. Press Show definitions to see what each level requires. A wrong first answer gives a hint and lets you choose again, but only the first answer counts toward First-try correct. After eight claims, the results screen shows your score and the claims you misplaced, with the correct level and the reason.

docs.text:
• Choice buttons: commit an answer. A wrong first answer gives a hint and lets you choose again; only the first answer counts.
  • Show definitions: opens or closes the reference table. Reading it is exploration, not evidence.
  • Next: moves to the next item after feedback. On the results screen, Previous missed and Next missed step through what you missed.
  • Play again: starts a practice run with the items reshuffled. Practice runs do not change the first-run score.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner can judge the strength of the evidence behind eight claims about AI tutoring and the compressed morning by assigning each to one of the five evidence levels from Chapter 2, correctly placing at least seven of eight on the first attempt. (Bloom level: Evaluate.)

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Teachers, administrators, school board members, policymakers, and parents.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• The five evidence levels, randomized controlled trial, and self-reported results, from Chapters 2 and 3
  • The studies described in the section "AI Tutors" in Chapter 11

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Judge (8 min). Place the eight claims. For each one, ask first: was there random assignment? Then: was there any comparison group?
  2. Notice (3 min). Which claims reached Strong? What do they have in common? Is any claim about whole-school results Strong?
  3. Discuss (4 min). A board member quotes a school's reported gains as proof. Using this MicroSim, explain what kind of evidence would change your mind.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Mastery is 7 of 8 correct on the first try. Only the first answer to each claim on the first run counts. Then ask learners to answer these without the MicroSim:

  1. A school reports its own test gains with no comparison group. Which level? (No evidence of effect.)
  2. Is a published meta-analysis the same as a randomized trial? (No. It pools studies, and if most were not randomized, it is Moderate at best.)
  3. A tutor is built on solid research but has not been evaluated yet. Which level? (Demonstrates a rationale.)

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Randomized controlled trial. Wikipedia. Why random assignment supports causal claims.
  2. Every Student Succeeds Act. Wikipedia. The US law that defines the four tiers of evidence behind Chapter 2's levels.
  3. What Works Clearinghouse. Institute of Education Sciences. Reviews education studies against evidence standards.
  4. Meta-analysis. Wikipedia. How studies are pooled, and why pooled quality depends on the studies.

docs.title: Kotter's Eight Steps as a Mountain Trail
docs.text:
Run the Kotter's Eight Steps as a Mountain Trail MicroSim Fullscreen Chapter 17: Leading Change: Vision, Culture, and Early-Stage Concerns

You can add this MicroSim to any web page with this iframe:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/ai-native-schools/sims/kotter-mountain-trail/main.html"
        height="720px"
        width="100%"
        scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
This infographic draws John Kotter's eight steps for leading change as a trail up a mountain. Each step is a camp on a switchback, so the climb has a clear order of work: a team cannot reach the higher camps without passing through the lower ones. The base camp burns a red flare for urgency, and a finished stone cairn on the summit stands for anchoring the change in the school's culture.

Two hazards show what goes wrong. A climber who takes the shortcut gully slides back to the bottom, which is what happens when a school skips early steps. On a lower false summit, a climber celebrates beside a cairn that is only half built, which is what happens when a school declares victory after its first win. The response to both is the one the chapter gives: Lewin's refreeze and Kotter's anchoring, which say that a change is not done until it is the normal way of working.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
• Explore: hover over a numbered marker or a label to read about that camp or hazard. Most callouts include a tip from the chapter's Lincoln example.
  • Quiz: click Quiz. The sim names a step or a risk, and you click the marker where it lives. Your score shows next to the buttons.
  • Calibrate (authors): open main.html?edit=true to drag markers, then copy the JSON into data.json.

docs.title: The 10 Callouts
docs.text:
1. Sense of urgency: the red flare at the base camp
  2. Guiding coalition: a rope team of four climbers
  3. Change vision: a telescope aimed at the summit
  4. Communicating the vision: a signal-flag station
  5. Removing obstacles: fallen logs being cleared from the trail
  6. Short-term wins: a small flag planted on a ledge
  7. Building on change: a wider camp with more tents
  8. Anchoring in culture: the finished cairn on the summit
  9. Risk: skipping steps: a climber sliding down the shortcut gully
  10. Risk: declaring victory too soon: a half-built cairn on a false summit

The mountain image is a text-free SVG made by make-kotter-trail-svg.py in this folder. The script also prints the marker positions used in data.json.

For practice placing real school actions into the eight steps, try the Which Kotter Step Is This? MicroSim.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will identify Kotter's eight steps in order on a picture of a mountain trail, and explain why skipping a step or declaring victory too soon leaves a change effort stranded.

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: School and district leaders, teachers and instructional coaches.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10 minutes.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (5 minutes): hover over all 10 callouts in trail order, from the flare at the base to the cairn at the summit. Then read the two risks.
  2. Quiz (3 minutes): run Quiz mode until you can find every callout without hovering first.
  3. Apply (2 minutes): think of one change in your own school. Which camp has it reached? Is it on the trail, in the gully, or on a false summit?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: The learner finds at least 9 of 10 callouts in Quiz mode and can name the step their own school's change effort needs next.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Kotter, J. P. (2012). Leading Change. Harvard Business Review Press.
  • Lewin, K. (1947). Frontiers in group dynamics. Human Relations, 1(1), 5–41.
  • John Kotter - Wikipedia

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A level-specific policy matches each safeguard to the textbook capability that first creates the risk. A safeguard first required at one level keeps applying at every higher level.

For each of eight safeguards you choose the lowest level, from 1 to 5, at which it should first be required, and press Submit. The results screen stacks the safeguards required at each level, so you can see how the list grows.

The safeguards and levels follow the Chapter 6 section "Graduated Regulation and Level-Specific Policy." They are recommended practice written for this book, not legal requirements.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
Nothing moves until you act, and the MicroSim does not store your answers.

  • Level 1 to Level 5: choose the lowest level at which the safeguard should first apply.
  • Submit: commits your choice. Two attempts per safeguard; only the first counts.
  • Next: moves on; after the eighth it shows your score and the stacked view.
  • Show level definitions: checkbox that shows what each level adds.
  • Try again: reshuffles the safeguards and starts over.

Ask which capability creates the risk, then find the first level that has it.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner will apply the level-specific policy by choosing the lowest level at which each of eight safeguards should first be required, correctly matching at least seven of eight on the first attempt. (Bloom level: Apply.)

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Teachers, administrators, school board members, education policymakers, and parents.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • The five levels, level-specific policy, and graduated regulation, from Chapter 6.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Review (2 min). Check "Show level definitions" and say what each level adds.
  2. Match (6 min). For each safeguard, name the risk first, then the level where it appears, then submit.
  3. Discuss (4 min). Three safeguards first apply at Level 3. Why, and why does none of them depend on whether the product contains an AI model?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim, then check each answer by using it.

  1. At what level should an accessibility check first be required? (Level 1. Every student must be able to use any textbook.)
  2. At what level does a privacy review of student records begin? (Level 3, the first level that keeps records about individual students.)
  3. An adaptive product uses fixed rules and no AI model. Does it need data governance? (Yes. It stores student records, which is the Level 3 risk.)
  4. Is human review of AI-generated lessons needed at Level 4? (Not as a first requirement; it first applies at Level 5, where content is generated for each student.)

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG). W3C. The standard behind an accessibility check.
  2. Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act. Wikipedia. The U.S. law on student education records.
  3. Algorithmic bias. Wikipedia. Why systems that choose next steps need a bias audit.

docs.title: Listening Responses
docs.text:
Run the Listening Responses MicroSim Fullscreen Chapter 13: Social Learning and Human Skills

To edit the sketch, paste the contents of listening-responses.js into the p5.js editor and set the editor's p5.js version to 2.x. The learning content is in the CONFIG block at the top of the file.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A teammate says, "I'm not going to present. I always mess it up in front of people." There are many ways to reply. Three of them are active listening:

  • Paraphrase: restates what the speaker said in your own words.
  • Clarifying question: asks the speaker to say more about what they mean.
  • Reflecting feeling: names the feeling the speaker seems to have.

Two common replies are not listening, however kind they sound:

  • Advice: tells the speaker what to do.
  • Judgment: evaluates or argues with what the speaker said.

Classify each reply by what it does, not by its tone. The statement and replies are illustrative examples written for this chapter.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text: Read the reply, then choose one of the five kinds. Press Show definitions to see what each kind does. A wrong first answer gives a hint and lets you choose again, but only the first answer counts toward First-try correct. The feedback also says whether the reply is active listening. After eight replies, the results screen shows your score and how many replies were active listening.

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:
• Choice buttons: commit an answer. A wrong first answer gives a hint and lets you choose again; only the first answer counts.
  • Show definitions: opens or closes the reference table. Reading it is exploration, not evidence.
  • Next: moves to the next item after feedback. On the results screen, Previous missed and Next missed step through what you missed.
  • Play again: starts a practice run with the items reshuffled. Practice runs do not change the first-run score.

Nothing moves until you act, and the MicroSim does not store your answers.

docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner can classify eight replies to a teammate's statement as paraphrase, clarifying question, reflecting feeling, advice, or judgment, correctly placing at least seven of eight on the first attempt. (Bloom level: Understand.)

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Teachers, administrators, school board members, policymakers, and parents.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Active listening and its parts (paraphrase, clarifying question, reflecting feeling), advice, and judgment, from the section "Communication, Listening, and Conflict" in Chapter 13

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Classify (5 min). Place the eight replies. Ask: does this reply help the teammate say more, or does it steer them?
  2. Notice (2 min). "Just practice more and you'll be fine" is kind. Why is it still advice?
  3. Practice (5 min). In pairs, one person states a worry. The other answers with a paraphrase, then a clarifying question, then a reflected feeling.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Mastery is 7 of 8 correct on the first try. Only the first answer to each reply on the first run counts. Then ask learners to answer these without the MicroSim:

  1. "Have you tried writing notes on cards?" Which kind? (Advice. It is a question, but it tells the speaker what to do.)
  2. Is agreeing with someone the same as understanding them? (No. A paraphrase checks understanding; agreeing does not.)
  3. Name the three kinds of reply that are active listening. (Paraphrase, clarifying question, and reflecting feeling.)

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Active listening. Wikipedia. The practice and its parts.
  2. Reflective listening. Wikipedia. Paraphrasing and reflecting feelings back to the speaker.
  3. Conflict resolution. Wikipedia. Where listening skills matter most in teams.

docs.title: Mastery Threshold Chooser
docs.text:
Run the Mastery Threshold Chooser MicroSim Fullscreen Chapter 12: AI Guardrails: Teaching Thinking Without Over-Reliance

To edit the sketch, paste the contents of mastery-threshold-chooser.js into the p5.js editor and set the editor's p5.js version to 2.x. The learning content is in the CONFIG block at the top of the file.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A mastery rule such as "4 of 5 right" decides when a student moves on. Every rule makes two kinds of mistake. A false pass moves on a student who has not mastered the skill. A false fail holds back a student who has. The table shows how often a student whose true accuracy is 50, 70, or 90 percent passes each rule on a fresh set of questions:

Rule Student at 50% Student at 70% Student at 90% 4 of 5 18.8% 52.8% 91.9% 5 of 5 3.1% 16.8% 59.0% 8 of 10 5.5% 38.3% 93.0% 9 of 10 1.1% 14.9% 73.6% 10 of 10 0.1% 2.8% 34.9%

These are computed values from the binomial distribution. The sim computes them from the formula, so you can check them. The accuracy levels are illustrative. Each of the four requirements asks you to read across the table for more than one student, and no rule is best for every requirement.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text: Read the requirement, then mark every rule that meets it. Marked rules are shaded in the table. Press Check. A set is correct only when it has no missing and no extra rules. You get two checks per requirement, and only the first check counts toward First-try correct. After four requirements, the results screen shows your score and lets you review the requirements you missed.

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:
• Five rule buttons: mark or unmark a rule. Marked rules are shaded in the table.
  • Check: commits the marked set. Two checks per requirement; only the first counts.
  • Next: moves to the next requirement after feedback. On the results screen, Previous missed and Next missed step through what you missed.
  • Play again: starts a practice run. Practice runs do not change the first-run score.

Nothing moves until you act, and the MicroSim does not store your answers.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner can examine a table of pass probabilities for five mastery rules and select the rule or rules that meet each of four stated requirements, correctly answering at least three of four. (Bloom level: Analyze.)

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Teachers, administrators, school board members, policymakers, and parents.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Mastery threshold, false pass, false fail, and pass probability, from the section "The Mastery Threshold" in Chapter 12

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Read (3 min). Find how often a student at 70 percent passes "4 of 5." Is that a high standard?
  2. Select (8 min). Work through the four requirements. Check every condition for every rule.
  3. Decide (4 min). Your school values never moving on a weak student more than speed. Which rule would you choose, and what does it cost the strong student?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Mastery is 3 of 4 correct on the first try. Only the first answer to each requirement on the first run counts. Then ask learners to answer these without the MicroSim:

  1. Which rule passes a 70 percent student about half the time? (4 of 5, at 52.8%.)
  2. Is a stricter rule always better? (No. 10 of 10 fails the 90 percent student about 65 percent of the time.)
  3. Which rule meets: 70% student under 50% and 90% student at least 90%? (8 of 10.)

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Binomial distribution. Wikipedia. The formula behind the pass probabilities.
  2. Type I and type II errors. Wikipedia. False passes and false fails in general terms.
  3. Mastery learning. Wikipedia. Where mastery thresholds come from.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A pro-social afternoon is designed around the human skills that AI does not replace. This MicroSim uses five of them:

Most activities build more than one skill. The question is which skill the activity asks for most directly. The feedback names a second skill each activity builds, so the single answer is a primary emphasis, not the only one. The activities are illustrative examples written for this chapter.

A wrong first answer gives a hint and lets you choose again, but only the first answer counts toward First-try correct. docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Teachers, administrators, school board members, policymakers, and parents.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Collaboration, communication skills, empathy, creativity, computational thinking, and the activity-skill matrix, from Chapters 12, 13, and 14

  2. Notice (2 min). Count the chips in each bin. Read the feedback again: what second skill did each activity build?
  3. Design (5 min). List your school's current afternoon activities. Which of the five skills is missing?

  1. A robotics team designs, builds, and debugs a robot together. Primary skill? (Computational thinking, with collaboration as a strong second skill.)

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
How do you turn a pile of AI test results into one number? METR's method has six steps: assemble a task suite of roughly 170 tasks, time skilled humans on each one, run the AI model several times on every task, record each task's success rate, fit a success curve against human working time, and read off the task length where the curve crosses 50 percent.

The flowchart shows the six steps, and each arrow names what one step hands to the next. Click a step to read what it does. Then press Start the questions for five multiple-choice questions, one attempt each.

The steps and the figure of roughly 170 tasks are as described in a 2025 preprint, METR's Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Tasks.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
Nothing moves until you act, and the MicroSim does not store your answers.

  • Steps in the flowchart: click (or tab to and press Enter) to read a step's description. The step turns gold; steps you have read turn green.
  • Start the questions: shows question 1 of 5.
  • Answer options and Submit: choose one option and press Submit. One attempt per question; the correct option is then shown.
  • Next and Try again: move through the questions, and restart them after the score.

Notice that human working time, the unit of the horizon, appears in step 2 and again in step 6.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner will explain the six steps that turn AI task results into a 50 percent time horizon, correctly answering at least four of five questions about the steps. (Bloom level: Understand.)

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Teachers, administrators, school board members, education policymakers, and parents.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Benchmark task suite, human working time, task success rate, task horizon, and 50 percent time horizon, from the section "METR and the Task-Horizon Idea" in Chapter 4.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Read the steps (3 min). Click each step in order. For each, say what it produces and what the next step needs.
  2. Answer (5 min). Work the five questions. Before you submit, say which step the question is about.
  3. Explain (3 min). In two sentences, explain to a parent why a 2-hour horizon does not mean the AI is reliable on 2-hour tasks.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim, then check each answer by using it.

  1. What unit measures how long a task is? (The human working time the task needs.)
  2. A model has a 50 percent horizon of 2 hours. What does that mean? (It succeeds about half the time on tasks that take a skilled human about 2 hours.)
  3. A model succeeds on 9 of 10 attempts. What is the task success rate? (90 percent.)
  4. Why is human time used instead of AI running time? (Human time is a common yardstick for difficulty; AI run time depends on hardware.)

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Tasks. METR (2025), arXiv preprint. The source of the task-horizon method and the roughly 170-task suite.
  2. METR. The research organization that publishes the task-horizon measurements.
  3. Logistic regression. Wikipedia. The kind of curve fit used to relate success to task length.

docs.text:
Each of six project descriptions is strong on every essential element but one. You read the description and name the element that is missing. Because every description sounds good, you cannot judge by overall impression: you have to check each element in turn and look for what is absent.

The elements follow the PBLWorks model described in the chapter. The sim merges the seven elements to six by combining the challenging question with sustained inquiry. The projects are fictional, written for this chapter.

Element Definition Challenging question An open-ended driving question that cannot be answered by looking it up Authenticity The work connects to real people, data, or problems Student voice and choice Students make real decisions about the topic, method, or product Reflection Students think and talk about what they learned and how Critique and revision Students get feedback and improve their work Public product Students present their work to an audience beyond the class

  • The projects are shuffled once per run. Nothing moves until you act, and the MicroSim does not store your answers.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will attribute the weakness of each of six project descriptions to the one essential element it lacks, correctly attributing at least five of six on the first attempt. (Bloom level: Analyze.)

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Teachers, school administrators, school board members, education policymakers, and parents.

docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.text:

  2. Attribute (8 min). Work through the six projects. For each one, check the elements one at a time before you choose.
  3. Discuss (5 min). Pick a project you have seen in a real school. Which element was weakest, and what one change would add it?

docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim, then check each answer by using it.

  1. Students build a model to a teacher's exact plans and show it at a fair. Which element is missing? (Student voice and choice. Every decision was made by the teacher.)
  2. A project uses invented numbers from a worksheet but is otherwise strong. Which element is missing? (Authenticity. The data and the problem are not real.)
  3. Does producing a product make a project a good project? (No. A project can produce something and still lack a driving question, feedback, or reflection.)

docs.title: Morning Time Budget
docs.text:
Run the Morning Time Budget MicroSim Fullscreen Chapter 11: Mastery Learning and the Case for a Compressed Morning

To edit the sketch, paste the contents of morning-time-budget.js into the p5.js editor and set the editor's p5.js version to 2.x. The questions and slider ranges are in the QUESTIONS and INPUTS blocks at the top of the file.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Today's five academic periods take about 250 minutes a day: 50 minutes of settling and wrap-up, 100 of explanation, and 100 of practice (the illustrative Chapter 2 schedule). A compressed morning keeps some of each and frees the rest for the afternoon. The arithmetic is simple:

  • Compressed morning = settling + explanation + practice
  • Freed per day = 250 − compressed morning
  • Hours freed per year = freed per day × school days ÷ 60
  • School days freed = freed minutes per year ÷ (length of school day in hours × 60)
  • Required speedup = 250 ÷ compressed morning

The last line is the hidden cost. If students are to learn the same amount in less time, each minute has to be more productive. A 150-minute morning needs students to learn about 1.67 times as fast. The settings are an illustrative scenario, not evidence that any school achieves this.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text: Answer the three questions first. Type a number in Your answer and press Check. You get two tries per question, and the score counts only first tries. The bar chart shows each scenario, but the freed time stays hidden until you finish. After the third question press Unlock the sliders. The five sliders then set settling, explanation, practice, school days per year, and the length of the school day, and every result updates at once. Reset sliders returns them to 10, 50, 90 minutes, 180 days, and 6.5 hours.

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:
• Your answer and Check: type a number and press Check. Two tries per question; only the first counts.
  • Next question: moves to the next question after feedback. On the last question it reads Unlock the sliders.
  • Five sliders: settling and wrap-up (0 to 50 min), explanation (0 to 100 min), practice (0 to 150 min), school days per year (150 to 200), and length of school day (6 to 7 hours). They unlock after the three questions.
  • Reset sliders: returns the sliders to 10, 50, and 90 minutes, 180 days, and 6.5 hours.

Nothing moves until you act, and the MicroSim does not store your answers.

docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner can calculate the minutes freed per day, the hours freed per year, and the equivalent school days freed by a compressed academic morning, and the speedup it requires, correctly answering three of three questions. (Bloom level: Apply.)

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Teachers, administrators, school board members, policymakers, and parents.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Academic morning, compressed academic morning, reduced direct instruction, and freed-up school time, from the section "The Compressed Academic Morning" in Chapter 11

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Calculate (6 min). Answer the three questions on paper first, then enter them. Show the working for each step.
  2. Explore (5 min). After the sliders unlock, lower explanation to 30 minutes. What happens to the freed time, and to the required speedup?
  3. Discuss (4 min). Find settings that free about 30 school days a year with a speedup below 1.4. Is that speedup realistic for your students?

docs.text:
Mastery is 3 of 3 correct on the first try. Only the first answer to each question on the first run counts. Then ask learners to answer these without the MicroSim:

  1. Settling 10, explanation 50, practice 90. How many minutes are freed per day? (100 minutes.)
  2. For the same settings and 180 days, how many hours are freed per year? (300 hours.)
  3. Settling 10, explanation 70, practice 110, 180 days, 6.5-hour day. How many school days are freed? (About 27.7 days.)
  4. What speedup does a 190-minute morning require? (250 ÷ 190, about 1.32.)

  2. Bloom's 2 sigma problem. Wikipedia. Tutoring's large effect, and the search for a way to scale it.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Chapter 16 introduces eight models of change. Each one answers a different question, from "What should leaders do, and in what order?" (Kotter) to "Where is each teacher, in concerns and in use?" (CBAM). You read eight situations, one per model, and choose the model that best addresses each one.

The trick is to find the question the situation is really asking: sequence, phase, an individual's gap, feelings, culture, learning capacity, the school-specific dip, or teacher concerns. The models do not compete; each is best for a different question. The situations are illustrative, written for this chapter.

Model Question it answers Kotter's eight steps What should leaders do, and in what order? Lewin's change model What are the basic phases of a change? ADKAR Where is this individual stuck? Bridges' transition model How are people feeling, and what do they need now? Schein's culture model Why does the organization resist what it says it wants? Senge's learning organization How do we become a place that keeps learning? Fullan's educational change What is distinctive about changing a school, and why does it dip first? CBAM Where is each teacher, in concerns and in use?

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
• Read the situation on the card. The progress strip shows which situation you are on and your running score, "First-try correct".
  • Choose one of the eight models with the buttons. If your first answer is wrong, a hint appears and you choose again. Only your first answer counts toward the score.
  • Show questions opens a table of the models. Reading it is exploration, not evidence of mastery.
  • Next moves on after you read the feedback. On the results screen, Previous missed and Next missed page through the ones you missed, and Play again reshuffles the situations for a practice run.

docs.title: Good to Know
docs.text:
• Mastery is 7 of 8 correct on the first try, on the first run. Practice runs give the same feedback but do not change the first-run score.
  • The situations are shuffled once per run. Nothing moves until you act, and the MicroSim does not store your answers.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will classify eight school change situations by the model that best addresses them, correctly placing at least seven of eight on the first attempt. (Bloom level: Understand.)

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Teachers, school administrators, school board members, education policymakers, and parents.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • The eight models (Kotter, Lewin, ADKAR, Bridges, Schein, Senge, Fullan, and CBAM), from the section "The Models at a Glance" in Chapter 16.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Recall (3 min). Without the sim, write the question each of the eight models answers.
  2. Classify (8 min). Work through the eight situations. Press Show questions only after you have tried to recall them.
  3. Discuss (4 min). Pick a change your school is making now. Which two models would you use first, and why?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim, then check each answer by using it.

  1. Teachers are grieving the loss of a familiar role. Which model? (Bridges' transition model.)
  2. Scores fell before they rose and leaders are worried. Which model expects this? (Fullan's educational change, which names the implementation dip.)
  3. Can a model for individuals, such as ADKAR, diagnose a whole culture? (No. Schein's culture model is built for that.)
  4. Is one model right for every change problem? (No. Each model answers a different question.)

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Change management. Wikipedia. Overview of organizational change models, including Lewin and Kotter.
  2. Learning organization. Wikipedia. Senge's idea of an organization that keeps learning.
  3. Concerns-Based Adoption Model (CBAM). SEDL. Archive of the CBAM tools: stages of concern, levels of use, and innovation configurations.

docs.title: One Lesson, Many Readiness Levels
docs.text:
Run the One Lesson, Many Readiness Levels MicroSim Fullscreen Chapter 1: The Building Blocks of Schools, Students, and Learning

To edit the sketch, paste the contents of one-lesson-many-readiness-levels.js into the p5.js editor and set the editor to p5.js 2.x. The learning content is in the CONFIG block at the top of the file.

You can add this MicroSim to any web page with this iframe:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/ai-native-schools/sims/one-lesson-many-readiness-levels/main.html"
        height="812px"
        width="100%"
        scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A real classroom holds students at many readiness levels. This illustrative class of 28 students spans grade levels 3 to 10:

Readiness (grade level) 3 4 5 6 7 8 9 10 Students 1 2 4 6 7 5 2 1

A whole-class lesson has one pitch, the grade level it is taught at. For each student:

  • In reach: the lesson is at the student's level or one level above.
  • Too hard: the lesson is more than one level above the student.
  • Already known: the lesson is below the student's level. In this model the student waits.

You predict the best pitch before you can move it. Then the slider unlocks and every student marker shows its state. The best single pitch reaches 13 students, fewer than half the class. Every pitch leaves at least 15 students either lost or waiting.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
• Type your prediction for Q1 (the pitch that reaches the most students) and Q2 (how many it reaches), then press Check Q1 and Q2.
  • A wrong answer gets a hint and one more try. After the second try the answer is shown. Only first tries count toward your score.
  • When both are checked, the Pitch slider unlocks. Move it from 3 to 10 and watch the markers and the three counts change.
  • Set the pitch to 7, type your answer to Q3, and press Check Q3.
  • The score appears when all three questions are checked. Reset returns to the opening state with the pitch locked at 7.

Nothing moves until you act. Mastery is 3 of 3 on the first try.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner can examine how the pitch of one whole-class lesson splits a mixed-readiness class into students in reach, students for whom it is too hard, and students who already know it, and identify the pitch that reaches the most students. (Bloom level: Analyze.)

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Teachers, administrators, school board members, policymakers, and parents.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Learning gap, direct instruction, classroom, readiness as a grade level, and the "in reach" rule, from Chapter 1.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Predict (3 min). Many teachers teach "to the middle." Before you touch the sim, write down how many of the 28 students you think a middle pitch reaches.
  2. Check and explore (6 min). Answer Q1 and Q2, then move the pitch through every value. Record the in-reach count at each pitch in a table.
  3. Answer Q3 (2 min). Set the pitch to 7 and count the students for whom the lesson is too hard.
  4. Discuss (4 min). No pitch reaches more than 13 students. What could a school change so that more students are in reach at the same time?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim.

  1. Which pitch reaches the most students, and how many? (Pitch 7 reaches 13 of 28.)
  2. At pitch 7, how many students find the lesson too hard, and how many already know it? (7 too hard and 8 already known.)
  3. Can a more skilled teacher find one pitch that reaches the whole class? (No. Readiness spans eight levels, and a single pitch reaches only two of them.)

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Differentiated instruction. Wikipedia. Teaching approaches that adjust to students' different readiness levels.
  2. Zone of proximal development. Wikipedia. The range of tasks a learner can reach with the right level of challenge.
  3. Direct instruction. Wikipedia. Teacher-led whole-class instruction and its assumptions.

docs.title: Prerequisite Chain Diagnosis
docs.text:
Run the Prerequisite Chain Diagnosis MicroSim Fullscreen Chapter 2: Evidence, Motivation, and the Stakeholders of Schooling

You can add this MicroSim to any web page with this iframe:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/ai-native-schools/sims/prerequisite-chain-diagnosis/main.html"
        height="724px"
        width="100%"
        scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
When a student fails a concept, the place to reteach is not always the concept they failed. It may be a prerequisite further down the chain.

This map shows eight concepts on the path from whole-number arithmetic to proportional equations. Each arrow points from a concept to a prerequisite it depends on. Concepts 1 and 2 have no prerequisites.

The root gap is the failed concept whose direct prerequisites all passed, or a failed concept with no prerequisites. Everything that failed above it failed because of it.

You work through five cases. Each shows one student's pass or fail result on every concept and the target concept the student failed in class. You select the root gap. In only one of the five cases is the target itself the root gap.

The pass and fail results are illustrative, written for this chapter.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
• Explore. Click any concept to read its description and its direct prerequisites.
  • Press Start the cases. Green concepts passed, red ones failed, and the target has a purple border.
  • Click the concept you judge to be the root gap. It turns orange. Click it again or press Clear to unselect.
  • Press Submit. A wrong answer gets a hint and a second try. Only the first try counts toward your score.
  • After the answer, the root gap gets a green border and the failed concepts above it are joined by red arrows. Press Next case.
  • After five cases you see your first-try score.
  • Zoom in, Zoom out, and Reset change the view. The mouse wheel does not zoom.

Mastery is 4 of 5 on the first try. The MicroSim does not store your answers.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner can attribute a student's failure on a target concept to its root gap by examining a prerequisite map and pass/fail results, correctly identifying the root gap in at least 4 of 5 cases. (Bloom level: Analyze.)

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Teachers, administrators, school board members, policymakers, and parents.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Prior knowledge, prerequisite concept, root gap, and the meaning of a dependency arrow, from Chapter 2.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (3 min). Click each concept and read what it depends on. Which two concepts have no prerequisites?
  2. Diagnose (8 min). Work through the five cases. For each failed concept, check its prerequisites before you decide.
  3. Discuss (4 min). In case 2 the student failed five concepts. How many need reteaching first? What would happen if the teacher retaught the target, Proportional equations, instead?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim.

  1. Define the root gap. (The failed concept whose direct prerequisites all passed, or a failed concept with no prerequisites.)
  2. A student fails Unit rates and Proportional equations, but passes Multiplying and dividing fractions and Ratios. Where is the root gap? (Unit rates.)
  3. Is the concept a student failed in class always the place to reteach? (No. In four of the five cases the root gap was below the target.)

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Mastery learning. Wikipedia. Why students should master prerequisites before moving on.
  2. Knowledge space. Wikipedia. A model of which concepts a learner must know before others.
  3. Directed acyclic graph. Wikipedia. The structure of a prerequisite map.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A product's level is the highest defining capability it actually delivers to students, not the words in its marketing. "AI-powered" does not make a product Level 3, and a product with no AI model can still be Level 3 if it adapts from a stored record.

For each of eight fictional products you read the description and the vendor's claimed level, assign the actual level, and press Submit. After each product the claim is labeled Overclaim, Accurate, or Underclaim. The results screen counts the three kinds of claim.

The level definitions follow the Chapter 6 section "The Five Levels at a Glance." The products are fictional, written for that chapter.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
Nothing moves until you act, and the MicroSim does not store your answers.

  • Level 1 to Level 5: assign the level of the highest capability the product delivers.
  • Submit: commits it. Two attempts per product; only the first counts.
  • Next: moves on; after the eighth it shows your score and the claim summary.
  • Show level definitions: checkbox that shows the defining capability of each level.
  • Try again: reshuffles the products and starts over.

Judge the features, not the marketing words. Ask: does it respond, does it store a record, does it converse, does it generate the textbook itself?

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner will judge the level of eight fictional learning products by assigning each the highest defining capability it delivers, and will identify whether the vendor's claimed level is an overclaim, accurate, or an underclaim, correctly assigning at least seven of eight levels on the first attempt. (Bloom level: Evaluate.)

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Teachers, administrators, school board members, education policymakers, and parents.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 15 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • The five levels and their defining capabilities, vendor level claims, and AI-powered marketing claims, from Chapter 6.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Review (2 min). Read the five definitions. Write the one question that separates each level from the one below it.
  2. Judge (8 min). Work the eight products. Underline the feature that decides the level before you submit.
  3. Discuss (4 min). Which three claims overclaim, and which marketing word did each lean on?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim, then check each answer by using it.

  1. A PDF with search and a hyperlinked glossary is sold as an "AI-powered interactive textbook." Its level? (Level 1. The content is fixed and does not respond to the learner. The claim is an overclaim.)
  2. A flashcard app stores each user's answers and schedules the next card. Its level? (Level 3. It adapts from a stored record. Sold as Level 2, it is an underclaim.)
  3. A tutor chat that can also write extra practice problems. Is it Level 5? (No. The lessons are still the authors' chapters; it is Level 4.)
  4. Does an adaptive textbook need a large language model? (No. Fixed rules on a stored record are enough for Level 3.)

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Adaptive learning. Wikipedia. Systems that adjust to each learner.
  2. Intelligent tutoring system. Wikipedia. Tutoring software, with and without language models.
  3. Self-driving car: classification. Wikipedia. The SAE levels that inspired level models for textbooks.

docs.title: Promise and Peril: Five AI-First Cases
docs.text:
Run the Promise and Peril: Five AI-First Cases MicroSim Fullscreen Chapter 22: AI-First Case Studies I: Promise and Peril

You can add this MicroSim to any web page with this iframe:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/ai-native-schools/sims/promise-and-peril-cases/main.html"
        height="720px"

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
This poster fills in Chapter 22's risk-and-response framework for all five cases at once. Each column is one case, with a school scene at the top: a small private school, a student at home in a virtual class, a math classroom split into two groups, a university lecture hall, and a large public-school classroom. Under each scene, a green band shows the case's benefit, a red band its risk, and a blue band the response to that risk.

Two of the blue bands are empty. For Alpha School and Unbound Academy, the sources checked for this poster show no response from the school to the risk, so the bands are left blank with a dashed border instead of being filled with a guess. Their zone notes give the book's proposed response and say plainly that it is the book's, not the school's. The Summit response is real, but it came from protest, not design. Only the two research studies show a response that was designed in from the start, and in both it was the design of the tutor.

Every number on the poster was checked against at least one outside source, usually two, and each fact names its source, such as "(source: S13)". The full list of sources and the claims they support is in claims.md in this folder. Several of these stories are still unfolding, so check figures against the sources before you quote them.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
• Explore: click any band to read its benefit, risk or response in the panel below the poster. Each note starts with what the picture shows.
  • Quiz Me: the sim asks about a benefit, risk or response, and you click the band where it lives. Your score shows next to the buttons.
  • Calibrate (authors): open main.html?edit=true to drag zone corners, then copy the JSON into data.json.

docs.title: The 15 Zones
docs.text:
Case Benefit (green) Risk (red) Response (blue) 1. Alpha School A short academic morning frees the day for people and projects Cost and equity; self-reported results Empty: none found 2. Unbound Academy Free to families Early results far below the school's own targets Empty: none found 3. Turkish high school study Practice scores rose with AI help Exam scores fell after open-chatbot use A hint-first tutor with guardrails 4. The poster image is a text-free SVG made by make-promise-peril-svg.py in this folder. The script also prints the zone rectangles used in data.json. The SVG is the working image. image-prompt.md holds a prompt for an optional painted version of the same five panels, laid out so the same zone coordinates still fit.

For practice, try Which Benefit or Risk? to sort statements from AI-first stories, and Alpha or Unbound? to compare the first two cases fact by fact.

docs.title: Ready Concepts Finder
docs.text:
Run the Ready Concepts Finder MicroSim Fullscreen Chapter 9: Learning Graphs, Interoperability Standards, and Access at Scale

You can add this MicroSim to any web page with this iframe:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/ai-native-schools/sims/ready-concepts-finder/main.html"
        height="724px"
        width="100%"
        scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A learning graph links each concept to the concepts it depends on. A concept is ready when it is not mastered and every one of its direct prerequisites is mastered. Adaptive textbooks use this rule to decide what a student can start next.

The graph shows sixteen concepts from this book's learning graph: Five-Month Doubling and everything it depends on. An arrow points from a concept to a prerequisite. For each of six problems, some concepts are mastered (green). Click every concept you judge to be ready, then press Submit. After you answer, the ready concepts get a blue border and the prerequisite arrows that make them ready turn blue.

The concepts and dependencies are copied from docs/learning-graph/learning-graph.json in this repository.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
Nothing moves until you act, and the MicroSim does not store your answers.

  • Concepts in the graph: click to pick or unpick a concept and see its prerequisites. Mastered concepts cannot be picked.
  • Submit: commits your set. Two attempts per problem; only the first counts.
  • Clear picks: removes all your picks.
  • Next: moves on; after problem 6 it shows your score.
  • Try again: starts over at problem 1.

A set is correct only when it has every ready concept and nothing else.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner will solve six problems by selecting exactly the set of ready concepts in a 16-concept learning graph for a given set of mastered concepts, correctly answering at least five of six on the first attempt. (Bloom level: Apply.)

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Teachers, administrators, school board members, education policymakers, and parents.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Learning dependency, foundational concept, directed acyclic graph, learning path, and the ready rule, from the section "Learning Graphs: Maps of Concepts" in Chapter 9.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Practice the rule (2 min). Click three concepts and read their prerequisites.
  2. Solve (8 min). For each problem, check every unmastered concept in turn: are all its prerequisites green?
  3. Discuss (3 min). The number of ready concepts went 2, 3, 2, 2, 4, then 1. Why does it rise and then fall?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim, then check each answer by using it.

  1. Nothing is mastered. Which concepts are ready? (Artificial Intelligence and Exponential Growth, the two with no prerequisites.)
  2. Can a mastered concept be ready? (No. Ready concepts are not yet mastered.)
  3. Long-Running Task needs Task Horizon and AI Agent. Only AI Agent is mastered. Is it ready? (No. Every direct prerequisite must be mastered.)
  4. Can more than one concept be ready at once? (Yes. In problem 5, four are ready.)

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Directed acyclic graph. Wikipedia. The kind of graph a learning graph is.
  2. Topological sorting. Wikipedia. Ordering concepts so prerequisites come first.
  3. Knowledge space. Wikipedia. The theory behind "ready to learn" in adaptive systems.
  4. vis-network documentation. The library used to draw the graph.

docs.title: Reinforcing or Balancing?
docs.text:
Run the Reinforcing or Balancing? MicroSim Fullscreen Chapter 18: Sustaining Change: Systems Thinking and National Adoption

You can add this MicroSim to any web page with this iframe:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/ai-native-schools/sims/reinforcing-or-balancing/main.html"
        height="648px"
        width="100%"
        scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A causal loop diagram shows how variables push on each other in a circle. Each arrow has a sign: + when the next variable moves the same way, − when it moves the opposite way. The rule is simple: count the minus signs around the loop. An even number, including zero, makes the loop reinforcing; an odd number makes it balancing.

You see six loops from school change, one at a time, and decide the type of each. The center marker shows ? until you answer, then R or B. The type is about structure, not about whether the loop is good: the workload, burnout, and absences loop is reinforcing even though it is harmful. The loops are illustrative.

Try the sim before you read this table: it gives the answers.

Loop Minus signs Type Student results → Teacher confidence → Quality of use 0 Reinforcing Rollout speed → Teacher overload → Resistance 1 Balancing Family trust → Willingness to share data → Quality of personalization 0 Reinforcing Data collected → Breach risk → Family trust → Data allowed 1 Balancing Teacher workload → Burnout → Absences 0 Reinforcing Screen time → Family complaints → Pressure to cut screen time 1 Balancing

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
• Follow the arrows around the loop and count the red minus signs.
  • Press Reinforcing or Balancing. If your first answer is wrong, a hint appears and you choose again. Only your first answer counts toward the score.
  • Use +, −, and Reset view to zoom. The mouse wheel does not zoom, so the page scrolls normally.
  • Press Next after the feedback. The results screen lists the minus-sign count for every loop. Play again reshuffles the loops.

docs.title: Good to Know
docs.text:
• Mastery is 5 of 6 correct on the first try, on the first run. Nothing moves until you act, and the MicroSim does not store your answers.
  • Authors: add ?edit=true to the URL to drag the nodes of the current loop and copy the updated JSON into reinforcing-or-balancing-cld.json.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will distinguish six causal loops from school change as reinforcing or balancing by counting the minus signs around each, correctly classifying at least five of six on the first attempt. (Bloom level: Analyze.)

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Teachers, school administrators, school board members, education policymakers, and parents.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Feedback loops, reinforcing and balancing loops, causal loop diagrams, and the counting rule, from the section "Seeing the System" in Chapter 18.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Predict (2 min). Is a reinforcing loop always good? Write your answer.
  2. Distinguish (5 min). Work through the six loops. Count the minus signs aloud before you choose.
  3. Discuss (3 min). Pick one balancing loop. What does it protect, and what does it slow down?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim, then check each answer by using it.

  1. A loop has two minus signs. Which type is it? (Reinforcing, because two is even.)
  2. Can a loop with a minus sign be reinforcing? (Yes, if the number of minus signs is even.)
  3. Does the number of variables decide the type? (No. Only the number of minus signs does.)
  4. Is a reinforcing loop always good? (No. Workload, burnout, and absences form a harmful reinforcing loop.)

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Causal loop diagram. Wikipedia. How to read signed links and identify reinforcing and balancing loops.
  2. Systems thinking. Wikipedia. The broader approach that causal loop diagrams support.
  3. The Fifth Discipline. Wikipedia. Senge's book on systems thinking in learning organizations.

docs.title: Rider, Elephant, or Path?
docs.text:
Run the Rider, Elephant, or Path? MicroSim Fullscreen Chapter 19: Microstrategies for Leading Change

To edit the sketch, paste the contents of rider-elephant-path.js into the p5.js editor and set the editor's p5.js version to 2.x. The learning content is in the CONFIG block at the top of the file.

You can add this MicroSim to any web page with this iframe:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/ai-native-schools/sims/rider-elephant-path/main.html"
        height="386px"
        width="100%"
        scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
The Switch framework from Chip and Dan Heath says a change needs three things. The rider is the thinking mind, which needs clear direction. The elephant is the feeling mind, which needs a reason to want the change. The path is the situation, which can make the right behavior easier or harder.

The MicroSim shows nine tactics for a school adopting an AI tutor, one at a time. You decide which part each tactic serves. There are three tactics for each part. The key question is whom the tactic is aimed at: the thinking mind, the feeling mind, or the situation. Three of the tactics change nothing about people and everything about the situation.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the tactic in the white box.
  2. Click the part you think fits. The button turns blue.
  3. Press Submit. The box below the tactic says whether you are right and why.
  4. If you are wrong, the button you chose turns orange. Choose again and press Submit. The second try does not change the score. After a second miss, the right answer turns green.
  5. Press Next to go on. After the last tactic, press Finish to see your score, with the tactics grouped by part.
  6. Press Start over at any time to reshuffle and begin again.
  7. Check Show definitions to read what each part means. Uncheck it to go back.

Only your first try on each tactic counts toward the score. The tactics are shuffled each run. Nothing moves until you act, and the MicroSim does not store your answers.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner can classify nine change tactics as directing the rider, motivating the elephant, or shaping the path, correctly placing at least eight of nine on the first attempt. (Bloom level: Understand.)

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Teachers, school administrators, school board members, education policymakers, and parents.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • The Switch framework, direct the rider, motivate the elephant, shape the path, and the nine tactics, from the section "The Switch Framework" in Chapter 19.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Recall (2 min). Name the three parts of the Switch framework and say whom each part is aimed at.
  2. Classify (6 min). Sort all nine tactics. Aim for 8 of 9 on the first try.
  3. Apply (5 min). For a change in your own school, write one tactic for each part.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim, then check each answer by using it.

  1. "Fix the single sign-on so the login works on the first try." Which part does it serve? (Shape the path. It changes the situation so the behavior is easier.)
  2. Is a vivid picture of the destination aimed at feelings? (In this framework it directs the rider: it shows the thinking mind where the change leads.)
  3. Why is shaping the path still leadership? (Because removing friction often changes behavior more than persuasion does.)

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Switch: How to Change Things When Change Is Hard. Heath Brothers. The book that introduced the rider, the elephant, and the path.
  2. Positive deviance. Wikipedia. Finding and copying the bright spots that already work.
  3. Change management. Wikipedia. Approaches to helping people through organizational change.

docs.title: The Rider, the Elephant and the Path
docs.text:
Run the Rider, the Elephant and the Path MicroSim Fullscreen Chapter 19: Microstrategies for Leading Change

You can add this MicroSim to any web page with this iframe:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/ai-native-schools/sims/rider-elephant-path-overlay/main.html"
        height="720px"
        width="100%"
        scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Chip and Dan Heath's Switch (2010) describes a change as a rider sitting on an elephant, on a path. The rider is the thinking, planning side of a person. The elephant is the feeling side: much stronger, and the part that tires of effort and balks. The path is the situation around them. This infographic draws that image and places each of the framework's nine moves in the scene as an object you can find.

The rider holds a map and a scroll and points toward a school on the far hilltop. The elephant looks tired, with a heart floating near it, a medal on its harness and one small stone in front of its foot. The path is fenced and worn smooth, with a blank signpost beside it and a herd already walking ahead. The overall callout names the risk the chapter warns about: a clear plan for the rider, with an unmotivated elephant, stalls. The response is to address all three parts.

The companion MicroSim Rider, Elephant, or Path? asks you to sort the same nine moves, written as school tactics, into the three parts.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
• Explore: hover over a numbered marker or a label to read about that part of the scene. Each move includes a school example as a tip.
  • Quiz: click Quiz. The sim names a move, and you click the marker where it lives. Your score shows next to the buttons.
  • Calibrate (authors): open main.html?edit=true to drag markers, then copy the JSON into data.json.

docs.title: The 10 Callouts
docs.text:
1. Rider, elephant and path: all three: the overall idea, its risk and the response
  2. Follow the bright spots (direct the rider): the glowing patch on the far hillside
  3. Script the critical moves (direct the rider): the scroll in the rider's back hand
  4. Point to the destination (direct the rider): the school on the hilltop
  5. Find the feeling (motivate the elephant): the heart floating near the elephant
  6. Shrink the change (motivate the elephant): the small stone in front of its foot
  7. Grow your people (motivate the elephant): the medal on the harness
  8. Tweak the environment (shape the path): the signpost beside the road
  9. Build habits (shape the path): the worn groove in the road
  10. Rally the herd (shape the path): the elephants walking ahead

The scene is a text-free SVG made by make-rider-elephant-svg.py in this folder. The script also prints the marker coordinates used in data.json.

docs.title: Learning Objective
