docs.title: Scale, Extend, or Stop?
docs.text:
Run the Scale, Extend, or Stop? MicroSim Fullscreen Chapter 20: Designing the AI-Native School Day

To edit the sketch, paste the contents of scale-extend-or-stop.js into the p5.js editor and set the editor's p5.js version to 2.x. The learning content is in the CONFIG block at the top of the file.

You can add this MicroSim to any web page with this iframe:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/ai-native-schools/sims/scale-extend-or-stop/main.html"
        height="452px"
        width="100%"
        scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A pilot needs a decision rule written before it starts, so that the results decide what happens next and not the mood of the room. The rule in this MicroSim is:

  • Stop if there is a serious privacy incident, or if any subgroup is more than 0.1 standard deviations (SD) below the comparison.
  • Otherwise, Scale if the gain is 0.15 SD or more, the teacher workload increase is 2 hours a week or less, and family satisfaction is 70 percent or more.
  • Otherwise, Extend the pilot and fix what fell short.

The MicroSim shows six pilot results, one at a time. You check the stop conditions first, then the scale conditions. The two largest gains, 0.30 SD and 0.18 SD, both lead to a stop. The rule and results are illustrative; each district should set its own thresholds.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the pilot result in the white box.
  2. Click the decision you think fits. The button turns blue.
  3. Press Submit. The box below the pilot result says whether you are right and why.
  4. If you are wrong, the button you chose turns orange. Choose again and press Submit. The second try does not change the score. After a second miss, the right answer turns green.
  5. Press Next to go on. After the last pilot result, press Finish to see your score, with each result and its decision.
  6. Press Start over at any time to reshuffle and begin again.

Only your first try on each pilot result counts toward the score. The pilot results are shuffled each run. Nothing moves until you act, and the MicroSim does not store your answers.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner can judge whether each of six pilot results leads to scaling, extending, or stopping by applying the stated decision rule, correctly judging at least five of six on the first attempt. (Bloom level: Evaluate.)

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Teachers, school administrators, school board members, education policymakers, and parents.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Pilot program, pilot goals, and decision rule, from the section "Readiness and Pilots" in Chapter 20.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Read the rule (2 min). Say in your own words why the stop conditions are checked first.
  2. Judge (6 min). Decide all six results. Aim for 5 of 6 on the first try.
  3. Discuss (5 min). A board member says, "A 0.30 SD gain is too good to stop." How would you answer?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim, then check each answer by using it.

  1. Gain 0.30 SD with a serious privacy incident. What does the rule say? (Stop. A serious privacy incident is a stop condition, whatever the gains.)
  2. Gain 0.16 SD, workload +2 hours, satisfaction 65 percent. What does the rule say? (Extend. Satisfaction is below 70 percent, and no stop condition applies.)
  3. Does a pilot that misses one goal fail? (No. It is extended so the district can fix what fell short.)

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Pilot experiment. Wikipedia. Small trials run before a full rollout.
  2. Effect size. Wikipedia. Measuring gains in standard deviations.
  3. Program evaluation. Wikipedia. Judging whether a program meets its goals.

docs.title: Schein's Culture Iceberg
docs.text:
Run the Schein's Culture Iceberg MicroSim Fullscreen Chapter 17: Leading Change: Vision, Culture, and Early-Stage Concerns Chapter 18: Sustaining Change: Systems Thinking and National Adoption

You can add this MicroSim to any web page with this iframe:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/ai-native-schools/sims/schein-culture-iceberg/main.html"
        height="720px"
        width="100%"
        scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Edgar Schein describes an organization's culture in three layers, and an iceberg shows the most important thing about them: how much you cannot see. Above the water are a school's artifacts, such as its building, schedule, trophy case and pep rallies. At the waterline are its espoused values, the framed mission statement and the banner. Below the water is the huge, heavy mass of basic assumptions, with beliefs like "a good teacher works alone" and "learning takes a fixed time" frozen into the ice.

The scene shows both sides of culture. The hidden mass is what holds a school steady through hard years. It is also what sinks a reform that steers only at the visible tip, which is the pattern Chapter 18 calls reform without real change. The diver with a lamp is the school's response: assess the culture before announcing the change.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
• Explore: hover over a numbered marker or a label to read about that part of the iceberg. Several callouts include a tip at the bottom.
  • Quiz: click Quiz. The sim names a part of the scene, and you click the marker where it lives. Your score shows next to the buttons.
  • Calibrate (authors): open main.html?edit=true to drag markers, then copy the JSON into data.json.

docs.title: The 10 Callouts
docs.text:
1. Cultural artifacts: the school building with its bell tower, the schedule and the trophy case
  2. School rituals: the crowd at a pep rally
  3. Espoused values: the framed mission statement and banner at the waterline
  4. Shared beliefs and norms: closed doors just below the surface
  5. Basic assumptions (the hidden mass): the wide shelf of ice under the water
  6. Assumption: a good teacher works alone: a single desk in a small, closed room
  7. Assumption: learning takes a fixed time: a clock fused into the ice
  8. The grammar of schooling: rows of desks all facing the front
  9. Reform without real change: the small boat steering at the tip
  10. Culture assessment (the diver): a diver shining a lamp on the hidden ice

The iceberg image is a text-free SVG made by make-iceberg-svg.py in this folder. The script prints the marker positions it uses, so the callouts stay on their objects if the drawing changes.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will locate Schein's three levels of culture on a picture of a school, give an example of each, and explain why a reform aimed only at artifacts and espoused values can leave practice unchanged.

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: School and district leaders, teachers and instructional coaches.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10 minutes.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (4 minutes): hover over all 10 callouts, starting at the top of the iceberg and working down. Note where the stated value and the hidden assumption disagree.
  2. Quiz (3 minutes): run Quiz mode until you can find every callout without hovering first.
  3. Apply (3 minutes): list one artifact, one espoused value and one basic assumption at your own school. Which assumption would your next reform run into, and what small, low-risk step could test it?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: The learner finds at least 9 of 10 callouts in Quiz mode and can name one assumption in their own school that disagrees with its stated values.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Schein, E. H., & Schein, P. A. (2017). Organizational Culture and Leadership (5th ed.). Wiley.
  • Tyack, D., & Tobin, W. (1994). The "grammar" of schooling: Why has it been so hard to change? American Educational Research Journal, 31(3), 453–479.
  • Edgar Schein - Wikipedia

docs.title: Where the Minutes Go in a Traditional School Day
docs.text:
Run the Where the Minutes Go in a Traditional School Day MicroSim Fullscreen Chapter 1: The Building Blocks of Schools, Students, and Learning

You can add this MicroSim to any web page with this iframe:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/ai-native-schools/sims/school-day-minute-map/main.html"
        height="704px"
        width="100%"
        scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A school day feels like seven hours of teaching. This MicroSim asks you to take one illustrative middle-school day apart and see where the 425 minutes actually go.

The schedule has seven 50-minute periods, homeroom, lunch, and passing time. Periods 1 to 5 are academic. Each runs 5 minutes of settling and attendance, 20 minutes of whole-class direct instruction, 20 minutes of guided and independent practice, and 5 minutes of wrap-up. Periods 6 and 7 are art and physical education.

Category Minutes Share of 425 Whole-class direct instruction 100 23.5% Guided and independent practice 100 23.5% Arts and physical education 100 23.5% Settling, attendance, and wrap-up 50 11.8% Passing time 35 8.2% Lunch 30 7.1% Homeroom 10 2.4%

You make two estimates before you see the chart. The chart then shows the true totals beside your estimate. Whole-class direct instruction is less than a quarter of the day. The non-instructional minutes add up to 125, more than direct instruction.

The schedule is an illustrative composite, not a real school's timetable. Three categories tie at 100 minutes, so any of the three counts as a correct answer to estimate (b).

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
• Read the schedule on the left.
  • Type estimate (a), the minutes of whole-class direct instruction, and choose estimate (b), the largest single use of time.
  • Press Reveal the chart. Your estimates are scored once and cannot be changed.
  • Click any bar to highlight the schedule rows that add up to it.
  • Try again clears your estimates and hides the chart.

Nothing moves until you act, and the MicroSim does not store your answers.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner can differentiate the minutes of an illustrative middle-school day into whole-class direct instruction, practice, and non-instructional time, and estimate the direct-instruction total to within 10 minutes. (Bloom level: Analyze.)

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Teachers, administrators, school board members, policymakers, and parents.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • School day, direct instruction, the I-do, we-do, you-do pattern, and classroom, from Chapter 1.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Estimate (3 min). Read the schedule and make both estimates before you reveal anything.
  2. Analyze (5 min). Reveal the chart. Click each bar. Add up the four non-instructional categories yourself and compare the total with direct instruction.
  3. Discuss (5 min). If an AI tutor took over some practice time, which category would change? Which minutes in this day could a school get back without cutting any teaching?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim.

  1. How many minutes of whole-class direct instruction are in the 425-minute day? (100 minutes, about 23.5%.)
  2. How many minutes are non-instructional (settling and wrap-up, passing, lunch, homeroom)? (125 minutes.)
  3. Why is the direct-instruction total not 7 times 50 minutes? (Only five of the seven periods are academic, and only 20 minutes of each academic period is whole-class explanation.)

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. School day. Wikipedia. How long school days run and how they are divided.
  2. Block scheduling. Wikipedia. An alternative to the seven-period day.
  3. Direct instruction. Wikipedia. Teacher-led explanation and its place in a lesson.

docs.text:
Run the School Decision Stakeholder Match MicroSim Fullscreen Chapter 2: Evidence, Motivation, and the Stakeholders of Schooling

        height="748px"

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Anyone who wants to change how a school uses AI needs to know who can say yes. In a typical U.S. public school district, five groups hold different decisions:

Stakeholder Role Teacher Plans and delivers daily instruction in one classroom Principal Leads a single school District administrator Manages district-wide operations, such as the superintendent and department directors School board The elected body that governs the district Parent and family The adults responsible for the child at home

This MicroSim shows ten decisions, one at a time, in a shuffled order. You choose who typically holds each one. The decisions mix the classroom, the school, the district, and the home, so you have to think about authority, not topic.

The pattern is typical, not universal. Rules vary by state and district. The decisions are illustrative, written for this chapter.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
• Read the decision on the card, then press the stakeholder you think holds it.
  • Show definitions opens the one-line description of each role.
  • If your first answer is wrong, you get a hint and a second try. Only the first try counts toward your score.
  • After the second try, the correct stakeholder and the reason appear. Press Next for the next decision.
  • After all ten decisions, the results screen shows your first-try score and lets you step through the decisions you missed. Play again reshuffles the decisions for practice.

Mastery is 8 of 10 on the first try. Nothing moves until you choose, and the MicroSim does not store your answers.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner can classify ten school decisions by the stakeholder who typically holds each one, with at least 8 of 10 correct on the first try. (Bloom level: Understand.)

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Teachers, administrators, school board members, policymakers, and parents.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • The roles of parent and family, teacher, principal, school administrator, and school board, from Chapter 2.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Predict (2 min). Before you start, guess how many of the ten decisions belong to the school board.
  2. Match (6 min). Work through all ten decisions.
  3. Map your own district (7 min). Pick one AI tool your school might adopt. List the decisions it needs (a pilot, a contract, data terms, a family opt-in) and name who holds each one where you work.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim.

  1. Who approves a $900,000 district-wide contract? (The school board, in a public vote.)
  2. Does the school board set one school's bell schedule? (No. The principal sets it. The board governs the district; it does not run daily operations.)
  3. Name one decision that belongs to families. (Whether their child joins an optional program, or what the child reads at home.)

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Board of education. Wikipedia. How elected school boards govern districts.
  2. Superintendent (education). Wikipedia. The district's chief executive and the board's one employee.
  3. Head teacher. Wikipedia. The role of a school principal.
  4. School district. Wikipedia. How U.S. public schools are organized into local districts.

docs.title: Schooling and EdTech Timeline
docs.text:
Run the Schooling and EdTech Timeline MicroSim Fullscreen Chapter 3: School Structures, Equity, and the Industrial-Era Legacy

You can add this MicroSim to any web page with this iframe:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/ai-native-schools/sims/schooling-edtech-timeline/main.html"
        height="644px"
        width="100%"
        scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Schools have been promised a technology revolution for more than a century. This timeline places twenty events from 1848 to 2022 in three groups:

  • Structure: how schools are organized, such as age grading, the Carnegie unit, and virtual schools.
  • Policy: laws and court rulings, such as Brown v. Board of Education and the Every Student Succeeds Act.
  • Technology: tools promised to change teaching, from Edison's films and Pressey's testing machine to ChatGPT.

Shaded bands mark five eras: 1840 to 1909, 1910 to 1959, 1960 to 1989, 1990 to 2009, and 2010 to the present.

Look at where each group falls. The structures that still shape the school day, such as age-graded classrooms and the Carnegie unit, were set in the first era. The technology waves came later, and each one met those same structures.

Dates come from the chapter. They should be checked against primary sources before the book is published.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
• Explore. Click any event to read its description, its date, and its era.
  • Use the Structure, Policy, and Technology checkboxes to show or hide a group.
  • Zoom in, Zoom out, the arrow buttons, and Fit all change the view. You can also drag the timeline. The mouse wheel does not zoom, so the page scrolls normally.
  • Press Start the era quiz. The timeline is hidden, and eight events appear one at a time without dates, in a shuffled order. Choose an era for each. You have one attempt per event.
  • After eight events you see your score and any misplaced events with their dates. Explore the timeline brings the timeline back. Retry the quiz reshuffles the events.

Mastery is 7 of 8 on the first try. The MicroSim does not store your answers.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner can classify eight events from the history of schooling and educational technology into one of five eras, with at least 7 of 8 correct on the first try. (Bloom level: Understand.)

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Teachers, administrators, school board members, policymakers, and parents.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • The industrial-era school model, Carnegie unit, education policy, charter school, virtual school, and the history of EdTech, from Chapter 3.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Predict (2 min). Before you open the timeline, guess the decade of the first teaching machine.
  2. Explore (6 min). Show only the Technology group, then only the Structure group. In which eras does each group cluster?
  3. Quiz (5 min). Place the eight events in their eras.
  4. Discuss (4 min). Edison predicted in 1913 that film would replace textbooks. Which later technologies made similar promises? What school structures did they meet?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim.

  1. In which era was the Carnegie unit defined? (Era 1, 1840 to 1909. It was defined in 1906.)
  2. Is technology in schools a recent idea? (No. Pressey's testing machine dates from 1924 and Skinner's teaching machine from 1954.)
  3. Did age grading and the Carnegie unit come from the computer age? (No. Both come from the first era, decades before computers.)

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. History of education in the United States. Wikipedia. The growth of public schooling and its structures.
  2. Educational technology. Wikipedia. The history of tools used in teaching, from film to computers.
  3. Teaching machine. Wikipedia. The machines of Sidney Pressey and B. F. Skinner.
  4. PLATO (computer system). Wikipedia. The University of Illinois computer-based instruction system begun in 1960.

docs.title: Seat Time vs. Mastery
docs.text:
Run the Seat Time vs. Mastery MicroSim Fullscreen Chapter 3: School Structures, Equity, and the Industrial-Era Legacy

To edit the sketch, paste the contents of seat-time-vs-mastery.js into the p5.js editor and set the editor to p5.js 2.x. The learning content is in the CONFIG block at the top of the file.

You can add this MicroSim to any web page with this iframe:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/ai-native-schools/sims/seat-time-vs-mastery/main.html"
        height="836px"
        width="100%"
        scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
The Carnegie unit measures a course in hours of seat time. Every student sits for the same number of hours, but students do not need the same number of hours to master the material.

This illustrative class has 20 students. The hours each one needs range from 70 to 260:

Students 1 to 10 70 80 90 95 100 105 110 115 120 125 Students 11 to 20 130 135 140 150 160 170 185 200 230 260

With a fixed course length L, a student masters the course when the hours they need are L or fewer. Students who finish early sit idle for the rest of the course. Students who need more than L leave with hours still needed.

L (hours) Master Do not Idle hours Hours still needed 100 5 15 65 835 150 14 6 535 305 200 18 2 1,320 90

The mastery-based view lets every student take exactly the hours they need. Every student finishes, and the total is 2,770 hours, less than the 3,000 hours of a fixed 150-hour course for 20 students. No single fixed length gives both zero idle hours and zero students who fall short.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
• With the length locked at 150 hours, type your answers to Q1, Q2, and Q3, then press Check answers.
  • A wrong answer gets a hint and one more try. After the second try the answer and its working are shown. Only first tries count toward your score.
  • When all three are checked, the Length slider (60 to 300 hours) and the Mastery-based view checkbox unlock. Each bar shows whether that student mastered the course, the idle hours above it, or the hours still needed.
  • Reset returns to the opening state with the length locked at 150.

Nothing moves until you act. Mastery is 3 of 3 on the first try.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner can calculate, for a fixed course length, how many of twenty students master the course and how many hours the early finishers sit idle, answering all three questions correctly on the first try. (Bloom level: Apply.)

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Teachers, administrators, school board members, policymakers, and parents.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Seat time, the Carnegie unit, mastery, and hours needed to master, from Chapter 3.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Calculate (5 min). Answer Q1 to Q3 on paper first. For Q2, list each early finisher's idle hours before you add them.
  2. Explore (5 min). Move the length from 60 to 300. Record the length where idle hours first pass 1,000 and the length where every student masters the course.
  3. Compare (3 min). Tick the mastery-based view. Compare its total with 20 × 150 = 3,000 hours.
  4. Discuss (4 min). Does letting students take different amounts of time mean the course takes more total time? What would a school need to change to run on the mastery-based schedule?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim.

  1. With a 150-hour course, how many of the 20 students master it, and how many idle hours do they have? (14 students and 535 idle hours.)
  2. How many master a 200-hour course, and what does the longer course cost? (18 master, but idle hours rise to 1,320.)
  3. Does a mastery-based schedule take more total time than a fixed 150-hour course? (No. It takes 2,770 hours, compared with 3,000.)

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Carnegie Unit and Student Hour. Wikipedia. The seat-time credit defined in 1906.
  2. Mastery learning. Wikipedia. Letting time vary so that learning can stay constant.
  3. Competency-based learning. Wikipedia. Advancing students when they show mastery rather than after a fixed time.

docs.title: Seat Time vs. Mastery
docs.text:
Run the Seat Time vs. Mastery Poster Fullscreen Chapter 3: School Structures, Equity, and the Industrial-Era Legacy Chapter 11: Mastery Learning and the Case for a Compressed Morning

You can add this MicroSim to any web page with this iframe:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/ai-native-schools/sims/seat-time-vs-mastery-poster/main.html"
        height="720px"
        width="100%"
        scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
This poster draws the same five concepts as two staircases. Each concept is a colored block, and each block rests on the ones below it, so the first block is the foundation for everything above.

On the left, seat time holds time fixed. A calendar sheds its pages, a clock and a bell keep the schedule, and a conveyor belt carries the class along together. The class moved on before the first two blocks were solid, so the foundation is cracked and has a hole in it. The top blocks sag into the hole, and the student who reached the top on schedule is wobbling.

On the right, mastery learning holds learning fixed. The same five blocks are all whole, and each carries a check shape for the mastery threshold. That is the benefit: no hidden gaps. The risk is that students now stand at different heights, and the slowest fall behind in time. The school's response is in the far right corner: a coach hands a stuck student the missing block, and students from every step build one project together at an afternoon workbench.

The numbers in the panels come from the illustrative class of 20 students in Chapter 3, who need between 70 and 260 hours to master a 150-hour course, and from the worked examples in Chapter 11.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
• Explore: hover over a part of the poster to see its name, and click it to read about it in the panel below the image.
  • Quiz Me: click Quiz Me. The poster asks a question, and you click the part of the picture that answers it. Your score shows next to the buttons.
  • Calibrate (authors): open main.html?edit=true to drag the zone corners, then copy the JSON into data.json.

docs.title: The 6 Zones
docs.text:
1. Seat time: the calendar: a wall calendar shedding pages, a clock, a ringing bell, and a conveyor belt of students
  2. Seat time: the cracked blocks: the bottom two blocks, one cracked and one with a hole
  3. Seat time: the wobbling top: the upper blocks sagging into the hole, with a student struggling to balance
  4. Mastery: the solid blocks: the bottom two blocks, whole and marked with check shapes
  5. Mastery: spread of students: students standing at different heights on the solid stairs
  6. Mastery: help and shared work: a coach handing a stuck student the missing block, and an afternoon workbench where students of every pace build together

The poster image is a text-free SVG made by make-seat-time-svg.py in this folder. The script also prints the zone rectangles used in data.json.

To practice the arithmetic behind the poster, try the Seat Time vs. Mastery MicroSim, which asks how many of the 20 students master a fixed-length course and how many hours the early finishers sit idle.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will compare seat time with mastery learning by explaining, for each model, what is held fixed, what varies, and what goes wrong, and will describe how a school responds to the students who fall behind in time under mastery learning. (Bloom level: Analyze.)

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Teachers, administrators, school board members, policymakers, and parents.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10 minutes.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (5 minutes): read the three left zones from the calendar up to the wobbling top, then the three right zones. For each side, write one sentence: "In this model, ___ is fixed and ___ varies."
  2. Quiz (2 minutes): run Quiz Me until you can answer all six questions on the first try.
  3. Discuss (3 minutes): look at the two students at the bottom right. What would your school need to change to give the slowest students more time and coaching without separating them from their class?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: The learner answers all 6 quiz questions correctly and, without the poster, can name the hidden cost of seat time (gaps that build up silently), the risk of mastery learning (students spread apart in time), and one response to that risk (gap filling and tutoring, or shared afternoon work).

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Carnegie Unit and Student Hour. Wikipedia. The seat-time credit defined in 1906.
  2. Mastery learning. Wikipedia. Letting time vary so that learning can stay constant.
  3. Chapter 3: School Structures, Equity, and the Industrial-Era Legacy. Seat time, the Carnegie unit, and the 20-student worked example.
  4. Chapter 11: Mastery Learning and the Case for a Compressed Morning. Mastery learning, personalized pacing, and gap filling.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Not every report about an education product deserves the same weight. This MicroSim gives you one rule and eight sources to apply it to.

The rule. First, if there is no comparison group of other students studied at the same time, the rating is Lead only. A comparison with national norms does not count as a comparison group. Otherwise, add one point if the evaluator is independent (did not build, sell, or buy the product, and the results are published whatever they show) and one point if the work has been peer reviewed.

Points Rating No comparison group, or 0 Lead only 1 Use with caution 2 Reasonable weight

Three sources test the edges of the rule. A vendor-paid study can still be independent when the contract guarantees publication. A preprint has not been peer reviewed. A school's comparison with national norms is not a comparison group.

The sources are fictional and written for this chapter.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
• Read the source on the card, then press the rating you think it deserves.
  • The rule is shown beside the card on wide screens. On narrow screens, Show definitions opens it.
  • If your first answer is wrong, you get a hint and a second try. Only the first try counts toward your score.
  • After the second try, the correct rating and the reason appear. Press Next for the next source.
  • After all eight sources, the results screen shows your first-try score and lets you step through the sources you missed. Play again reshuffles the sources for practice.

Mastery is 7 of 8 on the first try. Nothing moves until you choose, and the MicroSim does not store your answers.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner can judge how much weight each of eight sources of evidence deserves by applying the comparison-group, independence, and peer-review rules, with at least 7 of 8 correct on the first try. (Bloom level: Evaluate.)

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Teachers, administrators, school board members, policymakers, and parents.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Independent evaluation, self-reported results, preprint, peer review, and comparison group, from Chapter 3.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Predict (2 min). Before you start, decide whether a study paid for by a vendor can ever count as independent. Write down your reason.
  2. Rate (8 min). Work through all eight sources. Apply the rule in order: comparison group, then independence, then peer review.
  3. Compare (5 min). Find the two sources that describe the same randomized trial. What single change moves the rating up?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim.

  1. A school compares its growth with national norms. Is that a comparison group? (No. National norms are not other students studied at the same time, so the rating is Lead only.)
  2. Can a vendor-paid study be independent? (Yes, when the contract guarantees publication whatever the results show.)
  3. An independent team posts a randomized trial as a preprint. What rating does it get, and what would raise it? (Use with caution. Peer review would raise it to Reasonable weight.)

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Peer review. Wikipedia. How experts check work before a journal publishes it.
  2. Preprint. Wikipedia. Papers shared publicly before peer review.
  3. Treatment and control groups. Wikipedia. Why a comparison group studied at the same time matters.
  4. Conflict of interest. Wikipedia. Why the people who build or sell a product are not independent judges of it.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Maya has three short reviews before a test on day 30. When should she do them, and how?

Schedule Reviews (days after the lesson) No review none Massed 1, 2 and 3 hours after the lesson Evenly spaced days 1, 3 and 7 Expanding days 1, 4 and 12

Each review can be done by rereading or by retrieval (recalling from memory). In this model, memory fades along a forgetting curve. Each review makes the memory more stable. A review helps more when some forgetting has already happened, and retrieval helps more than rereading.

You commit two predictions before any curve is drawn. Then the curves appear and you can switch the method and the exam day. On a day-1 exam the massed schedule wins, which is why cramming feels effective. On a day-30 exam it falls to 0%, while expanding retrieval holds 65%.

This is an illustrative model, not experimental data. It shows the direction of effects reported by Ebbinghaus (1885), Cepeda and colleagues (2006), and Roediger and Karpicke (2006).

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
• Choose your answer to P1 (the best schedule for a day-30 exam) and P2 (the better method), then press Submit predictions. Each gets one attempt.
  • The curves appear for the Reread method and a day-30 exam. Dots mark retention on the exam day, and the legend lists each value. Dashed lines show the other method for comparison.
  • Switch the Review method and the Exam day. After you have tried exam days 1 and 7, P3 unlocks.
  • Choose an answer to P3 and press Check P3. P3 has two attempts; only the first counts toward the score.
  • Reset returns to the opening state with no curves.

Nothing moves until you act. Mastery is 3 of 3.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner can compare predicted retention under massed, evenly spaced, and expanding review schedules, each done by rereading or by retrieval, and predict which schedule and method retain the most on a day-30 exam. (Bloom level: Understand.)

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Teachers, administrators, school board members, policymakers, and parents.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Learning versus performance, forgetting curve, spaced practice, massed practice, retrieval practice, and desirable difficulty, from Chapter 1.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Predict (2 min). Before you submit, write down which schedule you used the last time you studied for a test.
  2. Compare (6 min). Look at the day-30 curves for Reread, then for Retrieval. Write down how much each schedule gains from switching methods.
  3. Explain (4 min). Switch to a day-1 exam. Explain to a partner why a student who crams might honestly believe cramming works.
  4. Apply (3 min). Plan three reviews for a unit test 30 days away. Which days, and what will students do in each review?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim.

  1. Which schedule gives the highest day-30 retention, and with which method? (Expanding reviews done by retrieval: 65% in this model.)
  2. Why does the massed schedule win on a day-1 exam but fall to 0% by day 30? (Its reviews come before any forgetting, so they add little lasting strength. They help only a test that comes soon.)
  3. Two students spend the same total time reviewing. Why can their day-30 results differ? (When the reviews happen and how they are done matter, not only total time.)

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Forgetting curve. Wikipedia. Ebbinghaus's finding that memory fades quickly without review.
  2. Spaced repetition. Wikipedia. Reviewing at increasing intervals.
  3. Testing effect. Wikipedia. Why recalling from memory strengthens learning more than rereading.
  4. Roediger and Karpicke (2006), Test-Enhanced Learning. Psychological Science. The study that compared rereading and retrieval after five minutes and after one week.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A Level 3 textbook keeps a detailed record about each student. That record is the benefit, because it lets the textbook adapt, and it is also the risk. This infographic draws the record as a glowing folder at the center of a round vault. Four walls, each with a gate, decide who may come close:

  • the innermost ring holds the student and the family, who hold the key
  • the second ring holds the teacher and the school, behind the FERPA gate
  • the third ring holds the district, where governance lives
  • the outer ring holds the vendors and researchers

Around the walls are the protections and the failures. A funnel at the main gate stands for data minimization, a shredder for the retention policy, a balance scale for bias auditing, a crack with papers blowing out for a data breach, and a boarded-up warehouse for inBloom, the central store that families did not trust.

The poster explains who may see a record. Two practice sims then check it: Who May See This Record? (Chapter 8) and Is This Data Identifying? (Chapter 10).

The facts about the laws and the two cases were checked against primary and news sources. The audit trail is in claims.md in this folder, and each checked fact carries a source id such as "(source: S3)". The descriptions are general information, not legal advice.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
• Explore: hover over a numbered marker or a label to read about that part of the vault. Most callouts include a tip using the chapter's examples.
  • Quiz: click Quiz. The sim names a part of the vault, and you click the marker where it lives. Your score shows next to the buttons.
  • Calibrate (authors): open main.html?edit=true to drag markers, then copy the JSON into data.json.

docs.title: The 14 Callouts
docs.text:
1. The student's record: student data and identifying data, the glowing folder
  2. Behavioral data: the click trail from the student's laptop
  3. Informed consent: the family's key in the innermost ring
  4. FERPA: the school's gate, with a bell
  5. COPPA: the low gate for children under 13
  6. GDPR: the gate flying the ring-of-stars flag, for students in the EU
  7. The district ring: data governance and governance readiness
  8. Data minimization: the funnel at the main gate
  9. Retention policy: the shredder
  10. Vendors and researchers: vendor risk in the outer ring
  11. The breach crack: the PowerSchool breach
  12. inBloom: the boarded-up central warehouse
  13. Algorithmic bias auditing: the tilted scale on a desk
  14. The trust paradox: a parent holding papers back, a school leader with an open hand

The vault image is a text-free SVG made by make-vault-svg.py in this folder; it is the working image. If you prefer a painted look, image-prompt.md describes the same scene with the same object positions, so the markers in data.json still line up after you swap the image in.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will explain who may see a student's record and why, by locating the four rings of access, the three laws (FERPA, COPPA and GDPR) and the governance practices that protect a record, and by connecting the inBloom and PowerSchool cases to the practices that would have helped.

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: School and district leaders, teachers, technology directors and parents.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 15 minutes.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (6 minutes): hover over all 14 callouts, starting at the folder in the center and working outward ring by ring. Then read the three outside the walls: inBloom, the breach and the scale.
  2. Quiz (4 minutes): run Quiz mode until you can find every callout without hovering first.
  3. Apply (5 minutes): pick one tool your school uses with students. Which ring does each party that sees its data stand in? Which law's gate does it pass through? If the vault were breached tonight, what would an attacker walk away with?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: The learner finds at least 12 of 14 callouts in Quiz mode and, for one real tool, names the laws that apply and one governance practice the school still lacks.

docs.title: Notes for the chapter
docs.text:
• Chapter 10 says "The PowerSchool data breach came in December 2024. PowerSchool ... disclosed that attackers had gained access". The intrusion was in late December 2024, but the disclosure came in early January 2025 (S13, S14). Consider "came to light in January 2025".
  • The chapter hedges that the missing multi-factor authentication "should be checked against the latest reports". PowerSchool itself told TechCrunch the portal did not support MFA at the time (S13), so the hedge can be dropped.

You can add this MicroSim to any web page with this iframe:

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A model's 50 percent time horizon H is the task length, in human working time, at which it succeeds about half the time. This MicroSim uses a simplified rule:

P = 1 / (1 + t/H), where t is the task's human working time in minutes.

Three questions come first, with the horizon locked: the chance on a 15-minute task when H = 60 minutes, the task length where that chance reaches 80 percent, and the chance on a 60-minute task for a later model with H = 240 minutes. Then the horizon slider unlocks, and the curve on a logarithmic time axis and the six task success rates update at once.

The rule is a simplified illustrative model written for Chapter 4, in the spirit of the curves METR fits. It is not METR data.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
Nothing moves until you act, and the MicroSim does not store your answers.

  • Your answer box and Check: type a percent or a number of minutes and press Check (or Enter). Two attempts per question; only the first counts.
  • Next: moves on; after question 3 it unlocks the slider.
  • Horizon H: slider from 15 to 960 minutes in steps of 15.
  • Redo challenges and Defaults: start the questions again, or return H to 60 minutes.

The dashed lines mark the 50 percent point, at H, and the 80 percent point, at a quarter of H.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner will calculate a model's chance of completing tasks of different human working times from its 50 percent time horizon, to within 2 percentage points, and identify the task length at which the chance reaches 80 percent. (Bloom level: Apply.)

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Teachers, administrators, school board members, education policymakers, and parents.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Human working time, task success rate, task horizon, 50 percent time horizon, and the rule P = 1/(1 + t/H), from the section "METR and the Task-Horizon Idea" in Chapter 4.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Calculate (5 min). Answer the three questions on paper first.
  2. Explore (5 min). Move H from 15 to 960 minutes. Where do the 50 percent and 80 percent points sit each time?
  3. Discuss (3 min). A vendor says its model "handles hour-long tasks." Using the curve, what would you ask?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim, then check each answer by using it.

  1. H = 60 minutes. What is the chance on a 15-minute task? (80%. 1/(1 + 15/60) = 0.80.)
  2. Where is the 80 percent point for any H? (At H/4.)
  3. Does the chance drop to zero just past the horizon? (No. At t = H it is 50 percent, and it falls gradually after that.)
  4. Is a model with a 1-hour horizon reliable on all tasks up to an hour? (No. At one hour it succeeds only about half the time.)

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Tasks. METR (2025), arXiv preprint. The source of the task-horizon method and the roughly 170-task suite.
  2. Logarithmic scale. Wikipedia. Why task lengths from 1 minute to 16 hours are drawn on a log axis.
  3. Logistic function. Wikipedia. The S-shaped curve family that success curves come from.

You can add this MicroSim to any web page with this iframe:

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
At the district budget meeting in Chapter 7, the finance director, Mr. Patel, asks what a textbook will cost per student, per year, all in. This poster answers with a picture. Four stacks stand on a table: a pile of print textbooks and the Level 2, Level 3 and Level 4 digital textbooks. Each block is one cost item, and each item has the same color in every stack.

The heights are to scale. One dollar is the same height everywhere, so the print pile (about $53.33) stands more than nine times taller than the Level 2 stack ($5.80). The Level 3 stack is $12.80 and the Level 4 stack is $23.00, with the glowing chat-bubble block for AI inference on top.

Behind the stacks stands a faded laptop. It is not part of any stack, because the chapter's totals assume the school already owns its devices. Its height above the table is drawn on the same scale: $75 a year for a $300 laptop over four years. That one picture carries the poster's three-part story. The benefit is that content costs collapse. The risk is the hidden costs, the device, training and governance, that a software price leaves out. The response is a total-cost-of-ownership model with stated assumptions.

All figures are illustrative. They come from the comparison table in the Chapter 7 section "Putting a Cost on Each Level", and a district should replace them with its own quotes.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
• Explore: click a stack or the faded laptop. The panel shows its cost per student per year and how the blocks add up.
  • Quiz Me: the poster names a cost or a total, and you click the stack or the laptop it belongs to. Your score shows next to the buttons.
  • Calibrate (authors): open main.html?edit=true to drag zone corners, then copy the JSON into data.json.

docs.title: The 5 Zones
docs.text:
1. Print baseline: one tall pile of closed books, about $53.33 (an $80 book, six years, four core subjects)
  2. Level 2: content and hosting $1.80 (blue) plus training $4.00 (gold), $5.80
  3. Level 3: adds a records platform $3.00 (purple) and privacy governance $2.00 (green); training $6.00; $12.80
  4. Level 4: adds guardrail log review $1.00 (thin red), training $8.00 and AI inference $7.20 (glowing orange with a chat bubble); $23.00
  5. The device (faded): a laptop behind the stacks, $75 a year, not included in any stack

Block colors, bottom to top: blue content and hosting, purple records platform, green privacy governance, red guardrail log review, gold teacher training, orange AI inference.

The image is a text-free SVG made by make-cost-stacks-svg.py in this folder. The script computes every block height from the chapter's figures at about 7.87 pixels per dollar and prints the stack heights and zone positions used in data.json.

To practice the arithmetic behind these stacks, try the Cost per Student by Level MicroSim, which follows this poster in the chapter.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text:
The learner will compare the yearly cost per student of print and of Level 2, 3 and 4 digital textbooks, name the cost items that each level adds, and explain why the cost of a device can outweigh every software item.

Bloom level: Analyze (verb: compare).

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: School board members, district finance and technology staff, school leaders and teachers.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10 minutes.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (4 minutes): click the four stacks from left to right. For each digital level, name the blocks it adds to the level before it.
  2. Compare (3 minutes): click the faded laptop. Why is it drawn behind the stacks and not on top of them? What happens to the gap between print and Level 4 when a district has to buy devices?
  3. Quiz (3 minutes): run Quiz Me until you can place all five costs without exploring first.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: The learner places at least 4 of 5 costs in Quiz Me mode and can explain, in one or two sentences, why Mr. Patel's question cannot be answered by comparing software prices alone.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Chapter 7, "Putting a Cost on Each Level": the source of every figure on this poster. All values are illustrative.
  2. Total cost of ownership. Wikipedia. Counting every cost over the life of a purchase.
  3. Open educational resources. Wikipedia. Free-to-use content that still has running costs.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A good tutor keeps the thinking with the student. The four-level hint ladder from Chapter 2 measures how much of the solution a reply gives away:

Level What the reply does 1 Asks what the problem is asking, without giving any part of the method 2 Narrows the plan, such as naming which quantities to use or which operation type 3 Gives the specific step to carry out, leaving the final computation 4 States the final answer or does the whole solution

Every reply in this MicroSim answers the same question: "A 6-pack of juice costs $4.50. What is the price per bottle?" Look at what each reply reveals, not at how friendly it sounds. After each answer the feedback says whether the reply suits a first response: Levels 1 and 2 do, Levels 3 and 4 do not. The replies are illustrative examples written for this chapter.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text: Read the tutor's reply, then choose Level 1, 2, 3, or 4. Press Show the four levels to see the ladder. A wrong first answer gives a hint and lets you choose again, but only the first answer counts toward First-try correct. After eight replies, the results screen shows your score and lets you review the replies you missed.

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:
• Choice buttons: commit an answer. A wrong first answer gives a hint and lets you choose again; only the first answer counts.
  • Show definitions: opens or closes the reference table. Reading it is exploration, not evidence.
  • Next: moves to the next item after feedback. On the results screen, Previous missed and Next missed step through what you missed.
  • Play again: starts a practice run with the items reshuffled. Practice runs do not change the first-run score.

Nothing moves until you act, and the MicroSim does not store your answers.

docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner can classify eight AI tutor replies to the same question by hint level (1 to 4), correctly placing at least seven of eight on the first attempt. (Bloom level: Understand.)

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Teachers, administrators, school board members, policymakers, and parents.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Productive struggle, the four-level hint ladder, cognitive offloading, and AI tutor, from Chapter 2 and Chapter 11

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Classify (5 min). Place the eight replies. For each one, ask: what is left for the student to do?
  2. Compare (3 min). Two replies sound very different and are both Level 4. Which are they, and what do they share?
  3. Rewrite (4 min). Take a Level 4 reply and rewrite it as a Level 1 or Level 2 reply.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Mastery is 7 of 8 correct on the first try. Only the first answer to each reply on the first run counts. Then ask learners to answer these without the MicroSim:

  1. "Divide the total by the number of bottles." Which level? (Level 3. It gives the step and leaves only the computation.)
  2. Is a worked example of a similar problem a Level 1 hint? (No. It shows the step, so it is Level 3.)
  3. Why does a polite reply that states the answer still count as Level 4? (The level measures what the reply reveals, not its tone.)

docs.text:
1. Instructional scaffolding. Wikipedia. Support that is faded as the learner gains skill.
  2. Intelligent tutoring system. Wikipedia. Computer tutors and how they give hints.
  3. Generative AI Can Harm Learning. Bastani and colleagues. The Turkish high-school study that compared open GPT-4 with a hint-first tutor.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A district compares two AI tutor vendors on seven criteria. Each criterion has a weight, and the weights add to 100. Each vendor gets a score from 1 to 5 on each criterion. The weighted score is the sum of weight × score ÷ 5. The knockout rule says a vendor that scores 2 or below on privacy and data governance, or on vendor viability, may not proceed until the problem is resolved.

The MicroSim starts with three questions. Vendor A scores 75 and Vendor B scores 74, but Vendor A's viability score of 2 knocks it out, so only Vendor B may proceed. After the questions, the score menus unlock. The weighted points, the bars, and the knockout status update at once. Raise Vendor A's viability from 2 to 3 and it may proceed, as the higher-scoring choice. The scorecard is illustrative.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read Question 1. Type your answer and press Check. Type only the number.
  2. If you are wrong, you get a hint and one more try. After a second miss, the sim shows the answer and the working. Only a first-try answer counts toward the score.
  3. Press Next question. After Question 3, press See the results.
  4. The score menus unlock. Change them and watch the results update at once.
  5. Defaults puts the inputs back to their starting values. Start over returns to Question 1.

The results stay hidden until you answer the three questions. Nothing moves until you act, and the MicroSim does not store your answers.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner can calculate the weighted scores of two vendors from criterion scores and weights, and apply the knockout rule to decide which vendor may proceed, correctly answering three of three questions. (Bloom level: Apply.)

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Teachers, school administrators, school board members, education policymakers, and parents.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Procurement criteria, vendor evaluation, weighted scoring, and the knockout rule, from the section "Procurement and Vendor Evaluation" in Chapter 20.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Calculate (6 min). Compute both weighted scores on paper, then answer the three questions.
  2. Explore (4 min). Raise Vendor A's viability from 2 to 3. What changes?
  3. Discuss (5 min). Why should some criteria be knockouts instead of just heavier weights?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim, then check each answer by using it.

  1. Vendor A totals 75 and Vendor B 74. Does Vendor A win? (No. Vendor A's viability score of 2 knocks it out.)
  2. Can a weak privacy score be offset by strong scores elsewhere? (No. A privacy score of 2 or below is a knockout whatever the total.)
  3. What is the weighted value of a score of 4 on a criterion with weight 15? (15 × 4 ÷ 5 = 12 points.)

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Weighted sum model. Wikipedia. Scoring options by weighted criteria.
  2. Multiple-criteria decision analysis. Wikipedia. Methods for decisions with several criteria, including thresholds.
  3. Vendor lock-in. Wikipedia. Why vendor viability matters.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
An AI-written summary can be fluent and still be wrong. Some statements match the source, some are subtly changed, and some are invented. The habit that protects against this is simple: check each statement against the source.

The source passage describes a six-week math pilot at Lincoln Middle School. For each of six statements from an AI-written summary, you choose Supported or Not supported and press Submit. After each answer the matching sentence of the passage is highlighted, if there is one. Missing information counts as Not supported.

The passage and the summary are fictional, written for practice. The figures are the Chapter 2 pilot: 280 students, 140 per group, 30 minutes a day, six weeks, and averages of 34 and 30.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
Nothing moves until you act, and the MicroSim does not store your answers.

  • Supported, Not supported: choose your judgment for the statement.
  • Submit: commits it. Two attempts per statement; only the first counts.
  • Next: moves to the next statement; after the sixth it shows your score.
  • Show the rule: checkbox that shows how to judge a statement.
  • Try again: starts over from statement 1.

Read the passage first. Statements are in a fixed order.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner will judge whether each of six statements in an AI-written summary is supported by a source passage, correctly judging at least five of six on the first attempt. (Bloom level: Evaluate.)

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Teachers, administrators, school board members, education policymakers, and parents.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • AI hallucination, grounding in a source, and AI literacy, from the section "AI Hallucination and AI Literacy" in Chapter 5.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Read (2 min). Read the passage once without looking at the statements.
  2. Judge (5 min). For each statement, find the sentence that supports it before you submit. If you cannot find one, it is Not supported.
  3. Discuss (3 min). Statement 6 sounds reasonable. What would a busy reader have to do to catch it?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim, then check each answer by using it.

  1. The summary says the pilot lasted a full semester. Supported? (Not supported. The passage says six weeks.)
  2. The summary says students were assigned at random. Supported? (Supported. A computer randomly assigned them.)
  3. The summary says a university team ran the evaluation, and the passage does not say who did. Supported? (Not supported. Missing information counts as not supported.)
  4. Five of six statements check out. Can you trust the summary whole? (No. Each statement must be checked; one invented claim can mislead.)

docs.text:
1. Hallucination (artificial intelligence). Wikipedia. Why language models produce fluent but false statements.
  2. Fact-checking. Wikipedia. Checking claims against sources.
  3. Randomized controlled trial. Wikipedia. The design of the pilot in the passage.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
The Concerns-Based Adoption Model describes eight levels of use, from 0 Nonuse to VI Renewal. A level describes what a teacher does with an innovation and how fluently, not how often. You read eight behaviors with a new textbook and place each at a level. Each level has exactly one behavior.

Two behaviors both describe daily use, yet sit at different levels: one is mechanical and step by step, the other is smooth and routine. On a wide screen, the results screen lists the levels in order. The behaviors are illustrative, written for this chapter.

Level Description 0 Nonuse No involvement and no plan to be involved I Orientation Learning about the innovation and deciding whether to use it II Preparation Getting ready to use it for the first time III Mechanical use Using it in a short-term, disjointed way, focused on each step IVA Routine Using it in a stable way with few changes IVB Refinement Varying the use to increase its impact on students V Integration Combining efforts with colleagues for collective impact VI Renewal Re-evaluating the innovation and seeking major modifications or alternatives

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
• Read the behavior on the card. The progress strip shows which behavior you are on and your running score, "First-try correct".
  • Choose one of the eight levels with the buttons. If your first answer is wrong, a hint appears and you choose again. Only your first answer counts toward the score.
  • Show descriptions opens a table of the levels. Reading it is exploration, not evidence of mastery.
  • Next moves on after you read the feedback. On the results screen, Previous missed and Next missed page through the ones you missed, and Play again reshuffles the behaviors for a practice run.

docs.title: Good to Know
docs.text:
• Mastery is 7 of 8 correct on the first try, on the first run. Practice runs give the same feedback but do not change the first-run score.
  • The behaviors are shuffled once per run. Nothing moves until you act, and the MicroSim does not store your answers.

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Teachers, school administrators, school board members, education policymakers, and parents.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • The eight levels of use, from the section "CBAM, Completed" in Chapter 18.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Predict (2 min). A teacher uses the tool every day. Is she at a high level? Write your answer.
  2. Classify (8 min). Work through the eight behaviors. Ask what the teacher is doing and how fluently.
  3. Discuss (5 min). Which support would move a teacher from mechanical use to routine use?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim, then check each answer by using it.

  1. A teacher uses it daily but follows each step with the guide and often loses track. Which level? (III Mechanical use.)
  2. Three teachers compare dashboards weekly and redesign the morning together. Which level? (V Integration.)
  3. Are level of use and stage of concern the same? (No. Level of use describes behavior; stage of concern describes feelings and thoughts.)
  4. Is a higher level always better? (No. Routine use can be appropriate, and renewal may mean replacing the innovation.)

docs.text:

  2. Michael Fullan. Wikipedia. Fullan's work on educational change and implementation.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
The hype cycle describes how expectations for a new technology rise to a peak, fall into a trough, and then recover as people learn what the technology is good for. You place eight events, one at a time, on one of the five stages. The events come from three stories: the MOOC wave of 2012 to 2013, a large district's 2013 tablet rollout, and the 2022 release of a general-purpose AI chatbot.

Classify by the pattern of expectations an event shows, not by how good the technology is. On a wide screen, the results screen draws every event along the cycle, so you can see the MOOC and tablet stories follow the same shape. The stage assignments are a reading of the evidence, not a measurement.

Stage Definition Innovation trigger A breakthrough or launch sparks interest Peak of inflated expectations Publicity and expectations exceed what the technology can do Trough of disillusionment Failures meet the inflated expectations and interest falls Slope of enlightenment Experiments clarify what the technology is good for Plateau of productivity The technology is understood and used for what it does well

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
• Read the event on the card. The progress strip shows which event you are on and your running score, "First-try correct".
  • Choose one of the five stages with the buttons. If your first answer is wrong, a hint appears and you choose again. Only your first answer counts toward the score.
  • Show definitions opens a table of the stages. Reading it is exploration, not evidence of mastery.
  • Next moves on after you read the feedback. On the results screen, Previous missed and Next missed page through the ones you missed, and Play again reshuffles the events for a practice run.

docs.title: Good to Know
docs.text:
• Mastery is 7 of 8 correct on the first try, on the first run. Practice runs give the same feedback but do not change the first-run score.
  • The events are shuffled once per run. Nothing moves until you act, and the MicroSim does not store your answers.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will classify eight events in the history of educational technology by the stage of the hype cycle they illustrate, correctly placing at least seven of eight on the first attempt. (Bloom level: Understand.)

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Teachers, school administrators, school board members, education policymakers, and parents.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • The five stages of the hype cycle and EdTech hype waves, from the section "The Hype Cycle and Educational Technology" in Chapter 15.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Predict (2 min). Where do you think AI tutoring is on the cycle today? Write down your guess and one reason.
  2. Classify (8 min). Place the eight events. Before each choice, ask: are expectations rising, peaking, falling, or settling?
  3. Discuss (5 min). On the results screen, compare the MOOC and tablet stories. What came after the trough in each case?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim, then check each answer by using it.

  1. A district announces a plan to give every student a tablet. Which stage? (Peak of inflated expectations.)
  2. Does the trough mean a technology has failed? (No. The trough is often followed by the slope of enlightenment, where people learn what works.)
  3. Randomized studies show which uses of an AI tutor help and which harm. Which stage? (Slope of enlightenment.)
  4. Is the peak the moment a technology is most useful? (No. It is the moment expectations most exceed what the technology can do.)

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Gartner hype cycle. Wikipedia. The five stages and criticism of the model.
  2. Massive open online course. Wikipedia. History of the MOOC wave, including 2012 and completion rates.
  3. ChatGPT. Wikipedia. The November 2022 chatbot release used as an innovation trigger.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Everett Rogers found that five perceived attributes of an innovation shape how fast it spreads: relative advantage, compatibility, complexity, trialability, and observability. You read eight teacher comments about a new tool and name the attribute that is the barrier behind each one.

Some comments sound alike but differ in cause. "It doesn't fit my pacing guide" is a fit problem (compatibility); "I couldn't get the students logged in" is a difficulty problem (complexity). None of the comments is a matter of willingness. The comments are illustrative, written for this chapter.

Attribute Definition Relative advantage Perceived as better than what it replaces Compatibility Consistent with existing values, practices, and needs Complexity Perceived as difficult to understand and use Trialability Can be tried on a limited basis Observability Results are visible to others

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
• Read the comment on the card. The progress strip shows which comment you are on and your running score, "First-try correct".
  • Choose one of the five attributes with the buttons. If your first answer is wrong, a hint appears and you choose again. Only your first answer counts toward the score.
  • Show definitions opens a table of the attributes. Reading it is exploration, not evidence of mastery.
  • Next moves on after you read the feedback. On the results screen, Previous missed and Next missed page through the ones you missed, and Play again reshuffles the comments for a practice run.

docs.title: Good to Know
docs.text:
• Mastery is 7 of 8 correct on the first try, on the first run. Practice runs give the same feedback but do not change the first-run score.
  • The comments are shuffled once per run. Nothing moves until you act, and the MicroSim does not store your answers.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will attribute each of eight teacher comments to the innovation attribute that is the barrier, correctly attributing at least seven of eight on the first attempt. (Bloom level: Analyze.)

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Teachers, school administrators, school board members, education policymakers, and parents.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Relative advantage, compatibility, complexity, trialability, and observability, from the section "The Five Innovation Attributes" in Chapter 15.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Predict (2 min). When teachers do not adopt a tool, what reason do leaders usually give? Write it down.
  2. Attribute (8 min). Work through the eight comments. Ask what the reason behind each comment is before you choose.
  3. Discuss (5 min). For two comments, name a response that removes the barrier without more training.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim, then check each answer by using it.

  1. "It would mean giving up the group discussions I believe in." Which attribute? (Compatibility: it conflicts with a valued practice.)
  2. "The contract is for three years with no exit." Which attribute? (Trialability: it cannot be tried on a limited basis.)
  3. Are complexity and compatibility the same? (No. Complexity is about difficulty; compatibility is about fit with values, practices, and needs.)
  4. Is every adoption problem a training problem? (No. Only some barriers, such as complexity, respond to training.)

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Diffusion of innovations. Wikipedia. Rogers' theory, including the five attributes of innovations.
  2. Everett Rogers. Wikipedia. The sociologist who developed diffusion of innovations theory.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Stories about AI-first schools mix promise and peril. This MicroSim uses the book's framework of two benefits (own pace, time for people) and the risks (screen time, handing thinking over, wrong answers, privacy, cost and equity, and an unstructured afternoon). Fear of job loss, the seventh risk, is left out because none of the statements concerns it.

You see eight statements, one at a time, and place each in one bin. Ask what the statement says about the effect on students. A single story often supplies one benefit and one risk: freed afternoons can mean projects with adult guides, or phones and games with no plan. Check figures against the sources.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the statement in the white box.
  2. Click the benefit or risk you think fits. The button turns blue.
  3. Press Submit. The box below the statement says whether you are right and why.
  4. If you are wrong, the button you chose turns orange. Choose again and press Submit. The second try does not change the score. After a second miss, the right answer turns green.
  5. Press Next to go on. After the last statement, press Finish to see your score, with each statement and its bin.
  6. Press Start over at any time to reshuffle and begin again.
  7. Check Show definitions to read what each benefit or risk means. Uncheck it to go back.

Only your first try on each statement counts toward the score. The statements are shuffled each run. Nothing moves until you act, and the MicroSim does not store your answers.

  1. "Tuition of $40,000 to $65,000 a year limits who can attend." Which bin? (Risk: cost and equity. Price is an equity issue when it leaves students out.)
  2. Is every complaint about AI a privacy risk? (No. A walkout over screen hours is a screen-time risk.)
  3. Can one story show both a benefit and a risk? (Yes. The freed afternoon is a benefit when planned and a risk when it is not.)

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
John Kotter's eight steps describe what leaders do, in order, to lead a large change: from creating a sense of urgency to anchoring the change in culture. You read eight actions from one school's change effort and choose the step each one carries out. Each step has exactly one action.

Some actions sound alike but serve different purposes. Sharing a pilot's results is a short-term win; using those results to add two more grades is building on change. On a wide screen, the results screen lists the steps in order, so the eight actions read as the story of one change. The actions are illustrative, written for this chapter.

Step Definition 1. Sense of urgency Enough people believe change is needed now 2. Guiding coalition A group with the power and trust to lead the change 3. Change vision A clear picture of the future the change creates 4. Communicating the vision Repeating the vision in many ways and actions 5. Removing obstacles Clearing barriers in structures, systems, and skills 6. Short-term wins Early, visible successes 7. Building on change Using early success to take on bigger problems 8. Anchoring in culture Making the new way part of the normal way

docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Kotter's eight steps, from the section "Kotter: From Urgency to Anchoring" in Chapter 17.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Recall (2 min). List the eight steps in order from memory.
  2. Classify (8 min). Work through the eight actions. Ask what purpose each action serves before you choose.
  3. Discuss (5 min). Read the results screen in step order. Which step does your own school most often skip?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Ask learners to answer without the MicroSim, then check each answer by using it.

  1. The vision is repeated at every staff meeting, in newsletters, and at family nights. Which step? (Communicating the vision.)
  2. The district fixes the login problem that blocked teachers. Which step? (Removing obstacles.)
  3. Does a short-term win mean the change is finished? (No. Step 7 uses early wins to take on bigger problems.)
  4. Is communicating the vision a single announcement? (No. It is repetition through many channels and actions.)

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. John Kotter. Wikipedia. Kotter's work on leading change and the eight-step process.
  2. The 8-Step Process for Leading Change. Kotter Inc.. The steps as described by Kotter's firm.

docs.title: Which Learning Theory?
docs.text:
Run the Which Learning Theory? MicroSim Fullscreen Chapter 13: Social Learning and Human Skills

To edit the sketch, paste the contents of which-learning-theory.js into the p5.js editor and set the editor's p5.js version to 2.x. The learning content is in the CONFIG block at the top of the file.

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Four learning theories have similar names and different defining features:

Theory Defining feature Constructivism A learner builds new understanding from what they already know and revises their own ideas Social constructivism A learner builds understanding with help from others, within reach of what they can do alone Constructionism A learner learns especially well by making a tangible, shareable artifact Social constructionism A group learns by building a shared artifact together

Two questions sort them. Is something being made? Is a helper or a group involved? The scenarios come in near pairs, such as a catapult built alone and a dashboard built by a team, so you have to find the defining feature. The scenarios are illustrative examples written for this chapter.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text: Read the scenario, then choose one of the four theories. Press Show definitions to see each theory's defining feature. A wrong first answer gives a hint and lets you choose again, but only the first answer counts toward First-try correct. After eight scenarios, the results screen shows your score and the scenarios you misplaced.

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:
• Choice buttons: commit an answer. A wrong first answer gives a hint and lets you choose again; only the first answer counts.
  • Show definitions: opens or closes the reference table. Reading it is exploration, not evidence.
  • Next: moves to the next item after feedback. On the results screen, Previous missed and Next missed step through what you missed.
  • Play again: starts a practice run with the items reshuffled. Practice runs do not change the first-run score.

Nothing moves until you act, and the MicroSim does not store your answers.

        height="622px"

        scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: After using this MicroSim, the learner can classify eight classroom scenarios as constructivism, social constructivism, constructionism, or social constructionism, correctly placing at least seven of eight on the first attempt. (Bloom level: Understand.)

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Teachers, administrators, school board members, policymakers, and parents.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Constructivism, social constructivism, zone of proximal development, constructionism, and social constructionism, from the section "How Students Learn: Four Theories" in Chapter 13

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Classify (5 min). Place the eight scenarios. For each one, answer the two sorting questions before you choose.
  2. Compare (3 min). The catapult and the food-waste dashboard both involve building. What single detail separates them?
  3. Apply (4 min). Describe one afternoon project at your school. Which theory does it draw on most?

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Mastery is 7 of 8 correct on the first try. Only the first answer to each scenario on the first run counts. Then ask learners to answer these without the MicroSim:

  1. Are constructivism and constructionism the same? (No. Constructionism adds making a tangible artifact.)
  2. Is every group activity social constructivism? (No. If the group builds a shared artifact, it is social constructionism.)
  3. A student builds a model bridge alone and improves it after a test. Which theory? (Constructionism.)

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Constructivism (philosophy of education). Wikipedia. Piaget and learning as building on prior knowledge.
  2. Social constructivism. Wikipedia. Vygotsky and learning through interaction.
  3. Zone of proximal development. Wikipedia. What a learner can do with help but not yet alone.
  4. Constructionism (learning theory). Wikipedia. Papert and learning by making.

docs.text:
Run the Which Lesson Does the Failure Teach? MicroSim Fullscreen Chapter 23: AI-First Case Studies II: Lessons for Practice

To edit the sketch, paste the contents of which-lesson-does-failure-teach.js into the p5.js editor and set the editor's p5.js version to 2.x. The learning content is in the CONFIG block at the top of the file.

You can add this MicroSim to any web page with this iframe:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/ai-native-schools/sims/which-lesson-does-failure-teach/main.html"
        height="534px"
        width="100%"
